arXiv Papers with Code in Computer Science (October 2026)

PaperId: 1, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32978.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuhan Liu, Lianhui Qin, Shenji Wan
Title: SceneBloom: Agentic Indoor Environment Generation with Realistic and Diverse Layouts for Embodied Learning
Abstract:
Training generalizable embodied agents requires realistic, varied, and simulation‑ready indoor environments. Language‑guided methods support semantic planning and object‑level reasoning, but precise spatial grounding remains difficult. Visual generative models offer rich priors over plausible arrangements, yet their outputs require geometric reasoning to become physically valid 3D scenes. We introduce SceneBloom, an agentic framework that combines visual layout sampling with contract‑guided 3D compilation. A hierarchical sampler uses diffusion priors to generate furniture arrangements within functional zones. A compiler then uses relations extracted from each proposal to guide geometric fitting and local pose correction. Across five room types, SceneBloom attains the highest visual quality and physical stability among the compared methods and is the only method with no detected mesh collisions and out‑of‑bounds objects. Its layouts are also closer to the distribution of real rooms than those of all compared baselines. Object navigation policies trained in these realistic scenes achieve a higher success rate in held‑out real scans than those trained on an equal number of real training scans. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/scenebloom.

PaperId: 2, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32976.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Philipp Lindenberger, Paul-Edouard Sarlin, Ondrej Miksik, Marc Pollefeys
Title: FlexGlue: Sparse-to-Dense Feature Matching and Visual Disambiguation
Abstract:
To estimate correspondences across images, existing approaches match either sparse interest points, which is highly efficient but limited by repeatability, or dense pixel grids, which is robust but expensive. Furthermore, these approaches are trained with only matching pairs and thus often fail to reject unrelated pairs that exhibit visual symmetries, which is equally important in applications like Structure‑from‑Motion (SfM). We bridge these gaps by introducing FlexGlue, a neural network for asymmetric sparse‑to‑dense matching and disambiguation. Given two images and coordinates of points in the first image, FlexGlue estimates the coordinates of the corresponding points in the second image while simultaneously rejecting the pair if non‑matching. By searching for a limited set of correspondences among dense pixels, our approach is both fast and effective at both matching and disambiguation: it combines the sub‑pixel accuracy of dense matching with the speed of sparse matching, while rejecting incorrect pairs with high precision. Experiments on multiple datasets show that FlexGlue pushes the Pareto frontier in relative pose estimation and significantly outperforms existing approaches for SfM and visual localization. FlexGlue is publicly available at https://github.com/cvg/flexglue .

PaperId: 3, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32969.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Amber Xie, Jiawei Fu, Xiaofeng Guo, Carmelo Sferrazza, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
Title: DexPort: A Hand-Held Skill Interface for Dexterous Hand Data Collection
Abstract:
Collecting high‑quality demonstrations remains a central bottleneck for learning dexterous manipulation. Teleoperation records executable robot actions, but it requires a complete robot setup and places the burden of coordinating many finger joints on the operator. Human demonstrations are easier to collect, but their motions must be estimated and retargeted to the robot, and they do not directly provide robot actions. In this paper, we introduce DexPort, a portable data‑collection interface for high‑DoF robot hands. It uses the same hand hardware for collection and deployment, avoiding a hand embodiment gap, and records both commanded joint targets and measured joint states. Our key observation is that a small set of skills can support a wide range of dexterous tasks. During collection, the operator moves the hand‑held interface to specify the robot wrist motion and selects or adjusts skills that coordinate the finger motion. This removes the need to control each joint independently while retaining behaviors such as precise grasping and in‑hand manipulation. We collect demonstrations across several real‑world tasks and in unstructured environments without a robot arm. We then use behavior cloning to train visuomotor policies directly on the recorded wrist motions and hand commands, without skill labels. We evaluate across 4 tasks: pick‑and‑place with diverse objects, screwing with in‑hand tool use, drawer stowage which requires simultaneous grasp and pulling, and a bimanual scanning task. We collect over 2,500 demonstrations with our portable device, in both laboratory and in‑the‑wild settings. Across our tasks, we see an improvement from 11% to 64% when using recorded robot commands instead of states, and an improvement from 36% to 78% for task success when using in‑the‑wild data.

PaperId: 4, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32966.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zimo He, Tianyi Bian, Zizhong Yang, Hongjie Li, Nan Jiang, Jieming Cui, Baoxiong Jia, Yizhou Wang, Siyuan Huang, Yixin Zhu
Title: ViT-H: Generative Video-To-Humanoid Control with Motion Tracking Feedback
Abstract:
Learning humanoid control from monocular human videos offers a scalable way to acquire diverse whole‑body behaviors. Yet, existing reconstruction‑retargeting‑tracking pipelines are limited in system‑level scalability by separately optimized intermediate stages and cannot directly optimize reference motion executability using downstream tracking feedback. We present ViT‑H, a video‑to‑humanoid control framework following a generation‑and‑tracking paradigm. ViT‑H directly generates humanoid reference motions from videos with a diffusion model, bypassing human motion reconstruction and retargeting, and uses motion‑tracking outcomes to post‑train the generator with direct preference optimization. We further introduce an autoregressive variant that enables real‑time humanoid video teleoperation with sub‑400 ms latency. Extensive experiments on the Unitree G1 demonstrate that ViT‑H outperforms state‑of‑the‑art reconstruction‑retargeting‑tracking pipelines in both motion quality and executability. We further show that ViT‑H scales favorably with model size and with both pre‑training and post‑training data scale, while motion‑tracking feedback consistently improves executability across different motion trackers.

PaperId: 5, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32964.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Bernardo Perrone Ribeiro, Erkut Akdag, Egor Bondarev
Title: Flownomaly: Single-Step Conditional-Mean Recovery for Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
Abstract:
Few‑shot industrial anomaly detection requires modeling category‑specific normality from only a handful of defect‑free images. Common approaches tie inference to stored exemplars, impose rigid linear structure, or risk reproducing anomalous content. Flownomaly instead casts the problem as normal‑counterpart recovery in frozen DINOv2 feature space. Given normal supports, a velocity field is learned through conditional flow matching over frozen patch tokens to transport Gaussian noise toward normal features. Along straight paths, a single recovery step using one evaluation of the optimal field yields the posterior mean of the clean normal token without trajectory integration. The operating time governs how strongly recovery modifies a query token. With no anomalous validation samples available for tuning, a normal‑only Jacobian gain‑to‑noise criterion selects this time from the supports alone. Squared residuals between query tokens and their recovered counterparts yield anomaly signals for both dense localization and image‑level detection. Across 1‑, 2‑, and 4‑shot benchmarks on MVTec‑AD and VisA, together with sample‑shot evaluations on Real‑IAD, Flownomaly achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance against recent category‑specific methods. In the 1‑shot setting, image‑ and pixel‑level AUROC reach 97.8% and 98.0% on MVTec‑AD and 95.3% and 98.7% on VisA, with a 2.1‑point image‑level AUROC improvement over the strongest baseline on VisA. Code is available at https://github.com/b‑rbmp/Flownomaly.

PaperId: 6, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32919.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xinrui Li, Pawan Sasanka Ammanamanchi, Siddharth Bhat, Rianna Jamdar, Yongxi Lin, Stella Biderman
Title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements
Abstract:
Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. P \leftrightarrow Q holds trivially for any two statements P and Q that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through P \leftrightarrow \mathrmTrue \leftrightarrow Q. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq‑Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9‑fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non‑equivalent pairs. SemantEq‑ProofAudit audits each model‑written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non‑equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq

PaperId: 7, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32914.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rahul Golder, Bimol Nath Roy, MM Faruque Hasan
Title: A Tutorial on Physics Constrained Machine Learning for Hybrid Modeling, Optimization, and Control
Abstract:
Physics‑constrained machine learning (PCML) integrates domain knowledge, first‑principles, and physical constraints into AI/ML models. In this work, we present a step‑by‑step tutorial of a modular PCML framework, KKT‑HardNet, and illustrate how it could be used for hybrid modeling, process simulation, optimization and model predictive control in a single platform. KKT‑HardNet combines fast inference capabilities of neural networks with guaranteed satisfaction of algebraic constraints through differential projection. It can handle heterogeneous data and enforce both linear and nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. The modular design supports custom neural‑network backbones and user‑defined projection mechanisms for PCML. To enable efficient end‑to‑end training, KKT‑HardNet exploits implicit function theorem to backpropagate through the projection layer. This avoids computationally expensive automatic differentiation. This work also introduces an exact reduced‑order Fischer‑Burmeister reformulation and a primal‑dual interior‑point method as an alternative projection solve strategy. We also provide a diverse set of benchmarking problems for PCML in engineering applications. KKT‑HardNet achieves orders of magnitude better performance in terms of both constraint satisfaction and inference time. The KKT‑HardNet code and the benchmark datasets are available at https://github.com/souls‑tamu/kkt‑hardnet .

PaperId: 8, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32876.pdf   GitHub
Authors:ZhiHong Liu, Shuyao Gao
Title: Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence
Abstract:
Pipelines that combine large language models (LLMs) with static analysis let the model consume the analyser's output as evidence, but whether the model distinguishes true from false evidence, and whether its scrutiny depends on what the evidence claims, has not been measured. We built an intraprocedural analyser for C/C++ that produces proof obligations and audited vulnerable and patched functions from PrimeVul under six evidence conditions that differ only in the notes, including fabricated assurances that a missing check exists and fabricated alarms that an added check is missing. The study covers 916 pairs in four disjoint sets, eleven model configurations from four vendors and 16,572 audits; no model is trained or fine‑tuned. True evidence barely improved accuracy (+0.02). False evidence acted asymmetrically: relative to true notes about the same operations, false assurances lowered the detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points, whereas false alarms never significantly lowered accuracy and were disputed far more often. An internally registered replication on seven new models confirmed that false assurances move verdicts towards their claim more than false alarms do (mean asymmetry +0.16, 95% CI +0.10 to +0.24). Instructions in the audit prompt did not reliably reduce deference; the best one failed to replicate. Verifying each claim in a separate call and showing the refuted claims raised accuracy under false assurances by 12 points in a pre‑specified test (p=0.002) without loss under true evidence; for a second model the gain was smaller and not significant. Pipelines should therefore verify a tool's guarantees before the model relies on them, and studies should measure deference in a direction‑aware way.

PaperId: 9, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32866.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Marek Masiak, Andrzej Szablewski, Nicola Cancedda, Constantin Venhoff
Title: Interpretable sparse fine-tuning with TopKLoRA enables faithful circuit discovery
Abstract:
Fine‑tuning on datasets of unknown origin can create a backdoor in the trained model when the data includes poisoned examples. Difficult to localise and remove, backdoors can persist through safety training. While parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning methods capture the full parameter changes introduced during training, they are not easily interpretable. We present the full method of TopKLoRA, extending the preliminary proposal of Masiak et al. (2025), an interpretable‑by‑design LoRA variant in which only the k largest adapter latents are active at each token. Unlike SAEs, TopKLoRA is trained purely on downstream loss, where optimisation pressure incentivises learning functionally causal latents. We demonstrate this sparse LoRA adapter in a sleeper‑agent backdoor case study where we create model organisms by fine‑tuning gemma‑2‑2b, Qwen2.5‑1.5B, and Qwen2.5‑7B on a poisoned instruction‑following dataset. For each organism, we identify and ablate a circuit that is both necessary and sufficient to implement the backdoor. Furthermore, our new fine‑tuning method produces sparse circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than a dense LoRA baseline, allowing surgical ablation of the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction‑following performance. Finally, we propose a technique to construct model organisms with localised circuits using TopKLoRA latents and gradient‑routing, which we use to validate the findings of our circuit search algorithm. We consider these findings as a step toward interpretable‑by‑design architectures that provide faithful units of analysis without compromising model performance. We share our code: https://github.com/interpretable‑finetuning/TopKLoRA.

PaperId: 10, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32864.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Joao P. A. Dantas, Andre N. Costa, Diego Geraldo, Marcos R. O. A. Maximo, Takashi Yoneyama
Title: PoKER: A Probability of Kill Estimation Rate Model for Air-to-Air Missiles Using Machine Learning on Stochastic Targets
Abstract:
This work introduces PoKER, a novel probabilistic model engineered to optimize missile launch effectiveness in air‑to‑air scenarios, specifically within Beyond Visual Range (BVR) air combat. Unlike conventional Weapon Engagement Zone (WEZ) models that delineate zones based on static distances such as maximum, minimum, and no‑escape ranges, PoKER applies machine learning to predict kill probabilities more accurately by integrating the stochastic behaviors of targets and missile miss distances. This model dynamically evaluates target behavior, greatly expanding the predictive capabilities of engagement analysis. By factoring in elements such as warhead lethality, target and shooter orientations, and the specific conditions of engagement, PoKER provides important insights into engagement dynamics and quantifies success probabilities. Consequently, it can potentially be an important tool for BVR air combat pilots, improving operational decision‑making within this specialized combat domain.

PaperId: 11, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32848.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yichun Peng, Yansong Li, Jin Hou, Qi Song, Xi Guo, Ning Zhang, Degang Wei, Huang Yang, Yu Guan, Jianping Ge, Lei Bao, Tianming Wang
Title: OpenStripe supports open-set identification and spatial stripe profiling in wild Amur tigers
Abstract:
Non‑invasive camera‑trap monitoring of endangered wildlife requires open‑set individual identification‑‑‑grouping field images into identities without predefined classes or a known population size‑‑‑yet pose deformation and cluttered backgrounds complicate image comparison. Here, we present OpenStripe, a multi‑agent framework that reconstructs canonical two‑dimensional (2D) tiger torso patterns and encodes four interpretable local stripe structures: breakpoints, bifurcations, irregular structures, and round structures. We evaluated OpenStripe on 100 camera‑trap records from 28 wild Amur tigers (Panthera tigris altaica), representing nearly one‑third of the documented population in the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park. Combining all four complementary structures enabled automatic identity grouping with 0.90 matched accuracy and a 0.85 adjusted Rand index (ARI), outperforming 49 baseline configurations under the same backend (up to 0.43 accuracy and 0.14 ARI). In addition, results from OpenStripe indicate that stripe similarity in Amur tigers declines with geographic distance and suggest that traits such as fractal dimension and inter‑stripe spacing are associated with geographic proximity. OpenStripe thus provides an interpretable representation that connects automated individual grouping with spatial phenotypic profiling in wild populations.

PaperId: 12, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32800.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dong-hwi Kim, Chaewon Moon, Hojun Song, Dongbeom Kim, Junyeong Jang, Aro Kim, Gahyeon Kim, Heejung Choi, Jehee Kim, Gianella Cravioto, Sohyun Lee, Gyeongjin Choi, EunHye Jeong, Soo Ye Kim, Jaehyup Lee, Sang-hyo Park
Title: CompMVR: Compression-Aware Multi-View Restoration Using Diffusion Models for Geometrically Consistent 3D Reconstruction
Abstract:
Real‑world 3D reconstruction pipelines often rely on multi‑view images degraded by lossy compression. While compression artifacts have been extensively studied in single‑image or video restoration, their impact on multi‑view geometry remains largely overlooked. In this work, we identify compression‑induced cross‑view geometric inconsistency as a critical failure mode, where view‑dependent artifacts disrupt feature matching, dense correspondence, camera parameter estimation, and downstream 3D reconstruction tasks such as novel view synthesis. To address this problem, we propose CompMVR, a compression‑aware multi‑view diffusion restoration framework that jointly refines compressed views while preserving cross‑view consistency, and construct compressed datasets for systematic evaluation. Unlike conventional restoration methods that optimize each image independently for 2D perceptual quality, CompMVR leverages learned compression priors and cross‑view correspondence to recover visual details while improving geometric reliability across views. Experiments across diverse datasets, codecs, and compression levels demonstrate gains in restoration quality and downstream 3D tasks, including novel‑view synthesis, camera pose estimation, and view matching. These results establish compressed multi‑view restoration as a distinct problem and highlight its importance for 3D reconstruction under lossy compression. Code and data for this paper are available at https://mchaewon.github.io/CompMVR‑project‑page/.

PaperId: 13, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32784.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yonghui Niu, Yuhao Ji, Chang Nie, Jiao Zhang, Yilong Li, Junlan Feng, Ran He, Caifeng Shan, Chaoyou Fu
Title: Video-MemComp: Taylor-Guided Sensitivity-Aware Memory Management for Streaming Video Understanding
Abstract:
The rapid growth of video data has created an urgent need for efficient video understanding systems that can handle long and continuous visual inputs, posing significant challenges for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) due to severe memory bottlenecks. Moreover, existing compression methods often overlook the explosive accumulation of approximation errors. To address this issue, we propose Video‑MemComp, a training‑free and sensitivity‑aware context management framework for memory‑constrained streaming video understanding. Our method theoretically decomposes compression error into orthogonal local approximation error and layer‑wise structural sensitivity via a first‑order Taylor expansion. To minimize local approximation error, we perform token aggregation in a pre‑RoPE safe zone with an attention‑conserving logit bias, mitigating geometric distortions caused by RoPE rotations. To manage layer‑wise structural sensitivity, we dynamically allocate the KV cache budget based on offline gradient priors and online context entropy, prioritizing high‑sensitivity layers. Video‑MemComp outperforms or achieves performance comparable to full‑cache and state‑of‑the‑art compression methods on benchmarks including MLVU, VideoMME, and EgoSchema. Notably, it improves the overall accuracy of Qwen2.5‑VL‑3B from 62.3% to 64.1% while reducing the KV cache to an equivalent of 6,000 tokens per layer, saving over 90% of KV memory.

PaperId: 14, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32781.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Juan Felipe Duran, Arthur Tobler, Martin Vallières
Title: Every Edge Needs a Quote: Building a Quote-Grounded Knowledge Graph of Healthcare Software Adoption with Language-Model Agents
Abstract:
Hospitals regularly buy software that clinicians and patients depend on. Because these purchases are costly, hard to reverse and can affect patient care, buyers look for evidence of which peer institutions already use a product and which systems it connects to. This evidence is public but scattered across vendor websites, press releases and third‑party pages. Language‑model agents can now collect it at low cost, but the correctness of the extracted claims is difficult to establish, and a wrongly listed customer can mislead buyers and misrepresent an organisation. We present a pipeline that builds a knowledge graph of customer and integration relations from the open web under one rule: every edge must be supported by a verbatim quote from its source page. Pages come from a deterministic crawl of each vendor's site and a budgeted ReAct agent that searches the rest of the web. A permissive extractor proposes relations with quotes, and a layered grounding stage decides which to keep, using a referent step that reads the whole page when a quote names only one side, deterministic checks, and a panel of five model calls voting on nine criteria. On 61 vendors, the pipeline reaches 0.94 precision and 0.71 recall against a page‑level key covering the 6,428 candidate relations proposed by its extractor, whose verdicts were drafted by one model and re‑checked with a second. Against the golden reference, the marketplace's own curated list, it scores lower, but 89% of the relations it keeps that the reference lacks are stated on a page. A confidence score built from the panel's votes keeps more correct relations than the fixed rule at the same precision, and reaches 0.90 precision at 0.90 recall. We also discuss how narrow, bounded model calls, string‑matched evidence and voting address long‑context degradation and run‑to‑run variance.

PaperId: 15, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32758.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Luis Bauer, Annalena Kofler, Andrés Asensio Ramos, Aparna Venkataramanasastry, Valentín Martínez Pillet, Bernhard Schölkopf
Title: ARENA: Active Region attENtion Aggregation for interpretable solar flare prediction
Abstract:
Predicting solar flares is a challenging space‑weather forecasting problem with potentially significant impacts on Earth's upper atmosphere, including disruptions to radio communications. We propose Active Region attENtion Aggregation (ARENA), a neural network architecture that predicts solar flares from a variable number of active‑region cutouts while learning to identify the region most relevant to the prediction. ARENA is trained using multiple‑instance learning under weak supervision, requiring only a flare/no‑flare label for the observation and no labels specifying the flare origin. The learned attention mechanism therefore provides a means of localizing the active region driving the prediction without explicit origin annotations. ARENA achieves a heidke skill score of 0.45 which is comparable to other flare prediction approaches. These results demonstrate that active‑region‑based aggregation can provide an efficient and interpretable approach to solar flare prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/LuisBauer22/ARENA.

PaperId: 16, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32748.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yubo Ye, Maryam Toloubidokhti, Sumeet Vadhavkar, Xiajun Jiang, Huafeng Liu, Linwei Wang
Title: On the Identifiability of Hybrid Deep Generative Models: Meta-Learning as a Solution
Abstract:
The interest in leveraging physics‑based inductive bias in deep learning has resulted in recent development of hybrid deep generative models (hybrid‑DGMs) that integrate known physics‑based mathematical expressions in neural generative models. To identify these hybrid‑DGMs requires inferring parameters of the physics‑based component along with their neural component. The identifiability of these hybrid‑DGMs, however, has not yet been theoretically probed or established. How does the existing theory of the un‑identifiability of general DGMs apply to hybrid‑DGMs? What may be an effective approach to construct a hybrid‑DGM with theoretically‑proven identifiability? This paper provides the first theoretical probe into the identifiability of hybrid‑DGMs, and presents meta‑learning as a novel solution to construct identifiable hybrid‑DGMs. On synthetic and real‑data benchmarks, we provide strong empirical evidence for the un‑identifiability of existing hybrid‑DGMs using unconditional priors, and strong identifiability results of the presented meta‑formulations of hybrid‑DGMs. Code is available at https://github.com/GoForIt‑YYB/Meta‑Hybrid‑VAE.

PaperId: 17, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32728.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haoran Gong, Jie Feng, Chenxu Wang
Title: CityLift: Compositional 3D Urban Generation from a Single Image
Abstract:
Generating editable 3D urban scenes from a single image requires detailed building assets with a coherent spatial arrangement. Occlusion and perspective ambiguity make it difficult to infer complete building geometry together with consistent relative scales and positions. We present CityLift, a framework that generates individual textured building meshes from an urban image by coupling scene‑level spatial modeling with building‑level synthesis. CityLift first learns building shape and placement jointly through coupled scene and instance streams, producing coarse sparse structures in a common coordinate system. We then introduce generative spatial inheritance, which maps each building's coarse occupancy and scene‑conditioned 3D feature field into a local volume to guide a flow model that generates finer structure. The same coordinate mapping places the generated meshes back into the scene, preserving their spatial relationship to the scaffold. To address the scarcity of urban data pairing scene images with individual 3D buildings, we construct CityLift‑5K, comprising 4,997 synthetic scenes with instance masks, building meshes, and placement annotations. Experiments on CityLift‑5K and scene blocks from UrbanScene3D and InstanceBuilding demonstrate improved building geometry and scene composition. The project page is available at https://ranhaogong.github.io/CityLift/.

PaperId: 18, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32725.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Aayush Acharya, Qi Zhang, Eduard Dragut, Longin Jan Latecki
Title: Ontology-Guided Knowledge Graph Construction from Structured Metadata and Climate Science Publications
Abstract:
The rapid expansion of scientific literature far outpaces the speed of manual curation, creating a fundamental bottleneck in extracting structured knowledge from scientific texts. To address this, we introduce an agentic, ontology‑guided framework for knowledge graph (KG) construction. Our framework utilizes specialized agents for document understanding, information extraction, ontology conformance, and entity linking. First, an LLM extracts factual knowledge in the form of triples with explicit textual evidence from research papers. Then the triplets undergo a multistage verification process to ground the triplets in the ontology. By enforcing schema constraints and requiring evidence in the form of text fragments, we ensure the data is both semantically consistent and traceable. In an agreement study over 1,000 extracted triplets, Gemini‑2.5‑flash achieves Cohen's κ scores of 0.640‑‑0.700 against three human annotators, matching the human‑‑human agreement range of 0.616‑‑0.689. We applied this framework to 2,000 scientific publications and construct a novel, ontology‑grounded KG for climate science with 133,990 nodes and 755,308 relations; of the 23,327 triplets that the publications contribute after validation, 98.96% are judged correct. The pipeline code and KG is publicly available https://github.com/aayushacharya/climatekg.

PaperId: 19, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32663.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Roy Amoyal, Shira Ifergane, Oren Freifeld
Title: SemGeo-Gen: Unsupervised Generation of Approximate Cross-Instance Semantic-Geometric Correspondences
Abstract:
We introduce SemGeo‑Gen, an unsupervised method for generating approximate cross‑instance semantic‑geometric supervision from weakly aligned 3D object collections. Our goal is not to recover exact point‑level correspondences, which are often ambiguous across different instances and would require expensive, impractical manual supervision at scale. Instead, we automatically produce approximate correspondences that are semantically meaningful, geometrically consistent, and diverse enough to train modern correspondence models. Given only coarse category‑level rotation alignment, SemGeo‑Gen lifts multi‑view DINOv2 features to 3D, aligns object instances using continuous piecewise‑affine registration, and prunes candidate matches using semantic consistency. The resulting 3D correspondences can be projected into rendered views, yielding scalable 3D‑3D, 3D‑2D, and 2D‑2D supervision without manual annotation. We validate the generated correspondences against sparse human annotations from KeypointNet, obtaining 93% PCK@0.10 and 97% PCK@0.15. More importantly, we show that using the generated correspondences for synthetic pretraining improves recent state‑of‑the‑art semantic correspondence models on SPair‑71k after fine‑tuning on real data, with gains of up to 5 PCK@0.10 points. Together, these results indicate that approximate semantic‑geometric supervision generated from 3D assets can improve real‑image correspondence learning and serve as a scalable alternative to costly manual annotation. Project page: https://bgu‑cs‑vil.github.io/SemGeo‑Gen/.

PaperId: 20, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32660.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chunchun Yang, Yang Cao, Zhitang Chen
Title: WiMoT: Replay-Free Continual Wi-Fi Sensing via Moment Transport
Abstract:
Continual Wi‑Fi sensing must balance plasticity, learning new rooms or users, against stability, keeping earlier ones, yet nodes often cannot retain channel state information (CSI) for privacy and storage reasons. We propose WiMoT (Wi‑Fi Moment Transport), which stores the per‑class feature mean and covariance of every earlier domain instead of samples. When the representation changes, stored statistics become stale. WiMoT restricts the change to an affine map on a frozen feature basis and applies the same map to the statistics, so they stay valid without old samples. Supervised contrastive learning learns the new domain, a closed‑form loss on the stored statistics keeps earlier classes separable, and a Gaussian discriminant classifier, refitted from the transported statistics with equal weight per domain, predicts without domain identity. On 3DO, WiMANS, and Widar3.0, WiMoT's average final accuracies are 94.02%, 89.61%, and 95.16% with at most 0.58 percentage points (pp) of forgetting. On 3DO and Widar3.0, it also has the highest balance of new‑ and earlier‑domain accuracy and is 3.77 and 13.11 pp ahead of the strongest of 21 baselines, which uses replay, staying ahead across domain orders and label budgets. On WiMANS, it matches the strongest replay baseline in accuracy (+0.41 pp) while reducing forgetting from 2.78 to 0.00 pp, and has the highest six‑order average accuracy. Because full covariances dominate the memory, storing them as rank‑32 factors shrinks the moment memory to 6.4%, losing at most 0.49 pp of accuracy, within edge‑node storage budgets.

PaperId: 21, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32650.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Iakovos Evdaimon, Giannis Nikolentzos, Achilleas Tsimichodimos, Christos Xypolopoulos, Michalis Vazirgiannis
Title: WL-SeqVAE: Sequence-Based Graph Generation Using Variational Autoencoders and Weisfeiler-Leman Colors
Abstract:
In this paper, we introduce WL‑SeqVAE, a sequence‑based variational autoencoder for generating graphs. The key observation behind WL‑SeqVAE is that node colors induced by the Weisfeiler‑Leman (WL) algorithm provide compact discrete summaries of local graph structure and can therefore serve as structural tokens for generation. Rather than learning a distribution over adjacency matrices directly, our method maps each graph to a sequence of WL colors and employs a variational autoencoder that encodes this sequence into a Gaussian latent distribution, from which an autoregressive decoder reconstructs the graph. During generation, compatibility constraints derived from the WL colors guide node and edge predictions, combining global information from the latent representation with local structural consistency. This formulation turns graph generation into a sequence generation problem and avoids directly parameterizing a quadratic adjacency matrix. We evaluate WL‑SeqVAE on molecular and general graph generation tasks. Across the evaluated datasets, WL‑SeqVAE is competitive with established baselines on several local structural and molecular quality metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/iakovosevdaimon/WL‑SeqVAE

PaperId: 22, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32633.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiyeong Chae, Hyunkyo Seo, Heonjae Lee, Kyung-Joon Park
Title: Natural-Language to Nav2: Operational Policies for Costmap-Based Navigation
Abstract:
Autonomous mobile robots support material transport in warehouses and industrial facilities, where navigation must adapt to changing operating conditions. Sensor observations reveal physical obstacles, but do not by themselves specify temporary access rules, route preferences, or exceptions known to operators. This paper presents a natural‑language policy interface that brings this knowledge into ROS 2 Nav2. A local large language model converts instructions into JSON policies specifying destinations, spatial constraints, and temporal or event conditions. Deterministic checks govern mission acceptance, and three costmap adapters project accepted policies into the existing navigation stack without changing its planner or controller. On 150 researcher‑authored English commands, four local models produce 107‑142 correct accepted policies, compared with 44 for a rule‑based parser, with 3‑20 incorrect acceptances per model. Fault injection records rejection of eight endpoint/JSON faults and 29 validator‑stage faults. Navigation experiments use correct task policies to evaluate keepouts, zone costs, person‑dependent regions, and event‑conditioned passage in simulation and on a TurtleBot3. For Tasks 1‑3, mean travel times are 18.4‑24.5% lower in simulation and 23.1‑35.0% lower on the physical testbed than with the baseline lacking those policies. A native KeepoutFilter comparison and two‑robot demonstrations examine basic keepout behavior and shared policy projection. The interface connects operator instructions to explicit navigation policies while retaining Nav2's planning and control components.

PaperId: 23, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32630.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hawar Dizayee
Title: The Standard Deviation in VICReg Buys a Safety Margin
Abstract:
VICReg prevents collapse with a hinge on the standard deviation of each embedding dimension, and its authors argue from the gradient that a hinge on the variance would fail. To our knowledge, this claim has not been tested experimentally. We test it in a controlled setting (ResNet‑18, CIFAR‑10 and CIFAR‑100), changing only the hinge and sweeping its weight μ over five orders of magnitude. At the default weight (μ= 1), the two hinges reach the same linear‑probe accuracy on CIFAR‑10 (about 89.5%). Both collapse below a threshold weight, but the standard‑deviation hinge's threshold is 35‑130× lower. CIFAR‑100 shows a consistent gap. In training, the variance hinge's gradient fades as the feature variance shrinks, while the standard‑deviation hinge's does not until that variance is very small. The standard‑deviation hinge therefore buys a safety margin: it keeps training at weights far below the point where the variance hinge collapses.

PaperId: 24, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32627.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zenghui Zhou, Xiaoke Fang, Zheng Zheng
Title: LGMT: A Tool for Testing the Logical Reasoning Reliability of LLMs
Abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly serve as reasoning components in modern software systems, yet a model that answers a logical query correctly can contradict itself when the same problem is restated in an equivalent form. Static benchmarks evaluate queries in isolation and therefore fail to expose such inconsistencies. To address this limitation, we present LGMT, an open‑source tool that detects reasoning inconsistencies through metamorphic relations grounded in first‑order logic. Given a source test case in premise‑conclusion form, LGMT generates logically equivalent follow‑up cases and checks whether the model's entailment predictions agree across the pair, without ground‑truth labels. The tool provides 20 built‑in metamorphic relations, supports custom ones verified by the Z3 theorem prover, and runs from a CLI or a web studio, including an offline mock mode requiring no API key. Across six widely used LLMs on a bundled benchmark of 3,091 metamorphic groups, LGMT reveals inconsistency rates ranging from 20.84% to 29.44%. LGMT is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/MaxwelsDonc/lgmt‑tool, with a demonstration video at https://youtu.be/gou4opptu1U.

PaperId: 25, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32612.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhiran Yan, Savankumar Bhanderi, Sourabh Lolge, Rui Song, Girdharbhai Paneliya, Shiva Agrawal, Gordon Elger
Title: DriveOSS: Dataset and Benchmark for 3D Anomaly Segmentation and Open-set Semantic Segmentation in Autonomous Driving
Abstract:
Recent advances in 3D semantic segmentation have significantly improved scene understanding in autonomous driving. However, existing methods are typically developed under a closed‑set assumption and evaluated under standard driving conditions, where all categories are known in advance. In real‑world driving, autonomous vehicles inevitably encounter previously unseen objects, making closed‑set perception insufficient for safe deployment. To address this challenge, we introduce DriveOSS, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first real‑world multimodal dataset and benchmark specifically designed for 3D anomaly segmentation and open‑set semantic segmentation. It contains 12,661 synchronized and annotated frames captured using six surround‑view RGB cameras, a 128‑beam LiDAR, and a GPS/IMU unit. The dataset comprises 52 real‑world driving scenes collected under clear, nighttime, cloudy, rainy, and snowy conditions and is organized into ID (in‑distribution) and OOD (out‑of‑distribution) subsets. The ID scenes contain only known classes and are used for training, whereas the OOD scenes additionally contain unknown objects annotated as the outlier class and are used for validation and testing. Extensive experiments show that unseen objects remain a major challenge for current 3D perception systems. The dataset, benchmark protocols, and code are available at https://github.com/chrisyan/DriveOSS.

PaperId: 26, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32517.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Gibran Benitez-Garcia, Hiroki Takahashi
Title: VERA-Hand: A Verified Multidimensional Benchmark for 2D Hand Pose Estimation in Third-Person Dynamic Gesture Videos
Abstract:
Hand landmarks serve as input for gesture recognition, sign language understanding, and touchless human‑computer interaction. Yet hand pose estimators are typically evaluated with frame‑wise localization metrics such as PCK or MPJPE, which are computed over matched predictions and overlook missed or spurious hands, handedness errors, and temporal instability. To address these limitations, we present VERA‑Hand, a benchmark that evaluates estimators using manually verified, frame‑level 2D annotations for 10,690 hands across four complementary dimensions (detection, localization, identification, and temporal stability), as well as a joint Pose‑F1 metric that requires both correct detection and accurate localization. Evaluating six estimators spanning hand‑specific, whole‑body, reconstruction‑based, and foundation‑model paradigms, we find that no estimator dominates: rankings reorder sharply across dimensions. VERA‑Hand also exposes failures that localization‑only and downstream evaluations may not reveal, including cross‑hand overlap in over 85% of frames for a recent foundation model. A post‑hoc cleanup case study demonstrates how the benchmark can validate corrective interventions, while stratified analyses show that robustness varies across motion‑blur classes and hand regions. We release the verified annotations, protocol, and code at https://gibranbenitez.github.io/VERA_Hand/

PaperId: 27, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32511.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ashish Kumar Meena, Chandra Sekhar Seelamantula
Title: Augmentation Strategy for DINO in Glaucoma Classification
Abstract:
Self‑supervised learning (SSL) offers a promising approach to medical image representation learning, yet augmentation strategies of SSL frameworks validated on natural images do not reliably transfer to specialized medical imaging domains. We analyze DINO, a knowledge‑distillation based SSL framework, and empirically demonstrate that its default augmentation strategy produces unreliable representations for retinal fundus images, degrading downstream glaucoma classification performance. Guided by the principle that effective cropped views should share minimal redundant information while retaining clinically relevant signal, we redesign DINO's augmentation strategy. Our approach biases the learned representations toward diagnostically critical features rather than low‑level image statistics. We evaluate our method for glaucoma classification by training a linear classifier on the frozen representations, achieving strong generalization across seven benchmark datasets. URL for code and weights: https://github.com/ashish‑256/task_dino

PaperId: 28, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32501.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qing Liu, Xinrui Chen, Yi Du, Ou Wu, Weiyao Zhu
Title: DRIVE: Fine-tuning via Data Contribution- and Diversity-aware Weighting with Prior Regularization
Abstract:
Single‑stage fine‑tuning is pervasive, yet catastrophic forgetting persists when the source pre‑training data is inaccessible. Data weighting affords a natural lever to modulate sample influence. Yet existing weighting methods lack a principled mechanism to explicitly arbitrate knowledge retention against new‑task adaptation, and provide no unified differentiable objective to accommodate auxiliary signals such as sample diversity and sample characteristics. This is because current schemes privilege one goal over the other, and no explicit gradient‑compatible encoding exists for such signals. To address this, we propose DRIVE, a principled and efficient weight assignment framework. It derives per‑sample weights via a unified differentiable objective where three coupled signals co‑evolve: Shapley additivity splits contribution into anti‑forgetting and adaptation components, which are reshaped by a covariance‑based diversity term and stabilized by a sample‑characteristic prior. Far from a mere combination, this yields an end‑to‑end gradient‑based scheme balancing stability against plasticity. Theoretically, we prove that DRIVE enjoys superior stability‑plasticity guarantees over existing weighting schemes and enhances parameter estimation robustness. Empirically, it attains superior overall performance, faster convergence, and stronger robustness. Code at https://github.com/luciabcd/DRIVE.

PaperId: 29, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32486.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Khaled Waleed Dawoud, Muhammad Haris Khan
Title: Efficient Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection via Signal-Aware Adaptive Fusion (SAAF)
Abstract:
Deploying Vision‑Language Models for video anomaly detection confronts a fundamental constraint. Their semantic reasoning demands computational budgets incompatible with the scale of real‑world video streams. We present Signal‑Aware Adaptive Fusion (SAAF), a framework that achieves efficient zero‑shot anomaly detection through three key innovations. First, we introduce a dual‑signal adaptive sampler operating in semantic embedding space: a delta signal captures sudden events via frame‑to‑frame cosine distance, while a drift signal detects static and gradual anomalies through deviation from rolling temporal context. Their OR‑gated combination with adaptive EMA‑based thresholding provides comprehensive anomaly coverage without training data. Second, we propose a threshold‑gated cascaded architecture where lightweight frame‑level scoring precedes expensive video‑level temporal analysis, invoking it only when confidence warrants additional context. Third, we design a signal‑aware weighted fusion mechanism that dynamically adapts score combination based on which signal triggered frame selection. Across four benchmarks, SAAF delivers competitive accuracy at substantially lower cost. Among training‑free zero‑shot methods, SAAF sets a new state of the art on XD‑Violence (92.07%), MSAD (86.70%), and ShanghaiTech (80.54%) AUC‑ROC, with XD‑Violence and MSAD also surpassing supervised baselines. SAAF sustains 44.95, 48.61, and 41.06 FPS on XD‑Violence, UCF‑Crime, and MSAD, a 2.43×, 2.63×, and 2.22× throughput improvement over the prior best zero‑shot method. Code: https://github.com/kdawoud91/SAAF

PaperId: 30, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32485.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shengchao Chen, Ting Shu, Sufen Ren
Title: PCFBench: How Far Can Large Vision-Language Models Go in Physics-aware Photonic Inverse Design?
Abstract:
Photonic crystal fibers (PCFs) underpin critical applications in telecommunications, sensing, and high‑power laser delivery, yet their design remains a manual, expert‑intensive process that couples geometric intuition with deep waveguide physics. Vision‑language models (VLMs) offer a promising path toward automating PCF design, but can they truly reason about photonic physics from microscopy images, or do they merely recognize visual patterns? We introduce PCFBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs on the perception, reasoning, and decision steps of the photonic inverse‑design loop. PCFBench spans 26 tasks organized into six categories of increasing cognitive demand (Geometry Perception, Physics Understanding, Text Generation, Multi‑modal Reasoning, Inverse‑Design Decision, and Code Generation), built from over 220K FDTD simulation samples across 18 structurally diverse fiber families. We evaluate both individual VLMs on isolated tasks and multi‑agent systems (MAS) on the full sequential pipeline from perception to design. Our results reveal a striking perception‑design gap: current models can identify fiber geometry with moderate success, yet consistently fail to translate that visual understanding into physics‑aware design actions. Moreover, cascading agents through the pipeline exposes significant error propagation, where upstream perception mistakes compound into downstream design failures. These findings suggest that neither model scaling nor naive agent chaining suffices, and that closing the loop demands explicit physical grounding. PCFBench provides the community with a rigorous, multi‑dimensional testbed to measure progress toward AI‑assisted photonic engineering. The project is available at https://pcfbench.github.io/.

PaperId: 31, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32478.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Cristian Tommasino, Antonio M. Rinaldi
Title: PathJev: Decision-Native Vision-Language Modelling for Histopathology
Abstract:
Vision‑language models used for decisions in histopathology rarely return calibrated probabilities over the candidates a user cares about. Decision‑native models write a question and a candidate set chosen at run time into the input and return a normalised distribution from a small decision head in one forward pass. We build PathJev‑P, a decision‑native model for histopathology: MedGemma‑1.5‑4B with LoRA adapters and a decision head, trained on 40,000 patch states from three public collections whose expert labels are turned into typed questions with organ‑specific candidate sets and a "none of these" option. In a comparison over 3 seeds with an analysis plan fixed before testing, on test sets without documented overlap with the training data of the backbone, PathJev‑P is more accurate than a generative model trained with the same backbone, data and selection rule, the zero‑shot pathology model CONCH and a general medical decision model (balanced accuracy 0.541 against 0.492, 0.345 and 0.213); its advantage over the generative model comes from two organs absent from training. The calibration advantage depends on how the generative model's probabilities are read out. With the summed candidate log‑likelihood used in previous work, PathJev‑P has the lower calibration error (ECE 0.204 against 0.279); with a length‑normalised read‑out of the same generative model, examined post hoc, the two have similar mean calibration error (0.201) and the generative model is better calibrated on the unseen organs, where PathJev‑P remains over‑confident. A supervised linear probe on a pathology foundation model is better calibrated in every setting. In a qualitative whole‑slide demonstration, PathJev‑P labels unsupervised tissue clusters with abstention and separates carcinoma from other tissue while running the model on a fraction of the tiles.

PaperId: 32, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32468.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Moritz Schillinger, Maximilian Bader, Adrian Buehler, Felix Wachter, Ferdinand Knieling, Vasilis Ntziachristos, Katharina Breininger
Title: OPTARI: An open-source software framework for clinical translation of optoacoustic imaging
Abstract:
Combined optoacoustic (OptA) and ultrasound imaging is a promising modality across a wide range of pathologies. Its use in clinical research, however, is limited by a lack of analysis software accessible to users without programming expertise. Existing tools are either script‑based engineering frameworks or proprietary vendor applications. We present OPTARI, an open‑source graphical software application to facilitate large‑scale clinical optoacoustic‑ultrasound (OPUS) studies. OPTARI builds on the napari image viewer and the PATATO toolkit for OptA data processing. It supports native vendor and open HDF5 data formats, aligns with the IPASC standard, and is distributed as a standalone executable. Features include region‑of‑interest annotation, reconstruction, chromophore unmixing, deep‑learning‑based tissue segmentation, and temporal and spectral analysis modules. OPTARI offers a combination of features for clinical study analysis that none of the compared tools provide. The automated tissue segmentation produced results comparable to expert labeling for muscle tissue, and batch processing reduced analysis time from minutes to under one second per scan. The tool is used in ongoing clinical OPUS studies. OPTARI connects engineering frameworks with medical research and provides an open‑source basis for reproducible and standardized analysis in clinical OptA imaging studies.

PaperId: 33, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32441.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianyun Zhong, Wei Wang, Jialin Li, Jianhong Tu, Liyao Li, Chuqiao Kuang, Tianshi Zheng, Songchi Zhou, Weiqi Zhai, Qile Jin, Jiajia Li, Jiasheng Zheng, Boxi Cao, Yaojie Lu, Hongyu Lin, Shiwei Ye, Bing Zhao, Hu Wei, Lin Qu, Xianpei Han
Title: SCI-AGENT-EXAM: Benchmarking Agents on Scientific Research Tasks
Abstract:
Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of supporting scientific workflows, but their capabilities across diverse research activities remain difficult to assess systematically. Existing benchmarks often focus on selected scientific capabilities or task types, limiting a comprehensive characterization of scientific agents' strengths and weaknesses in realistic research workflows. We introduce SCI‑AGENT‑EXAM, a workflow‑oriented benchmark comprising 120 expert‑curated tasks across 11 scientific fields and 7 research task types defined by the Scientific Workflow Task Taxonomy (SWTT). Each task requires both executable artifacts (e.g., code and scripts) and textual artifacts (e.g., reports and explanations). To evaluate the heterogeneous task outputs, we develop a hybrid evaluation protocol combining deterministic programmatic verification for executable artifacts with a calibrated, expert‑validated LLM‑based judge for textual artifacts. Beyond outcome assessment, we analyze progress and solution stability along execution trajectories to characterize how agents reach their final results. Experiments with 10 frontier LLM agents reveal substantial performance gaps: GPT‑6 Astra achieves the highest overall score of 80.9, yet only 26.0% of its runs exceed the 0.95 success threshold. Further analyses uncover distinct capability profiles across scientific task types and substantial variation in execution efficiency and stability. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/SKYLENAGE‑AI/Sci‑Agent‑Exam.

PaperId: 34, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32433.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jingmin Zhu, Yanyan Zou, Xiuyu Li, James Bailey, Dinh Phung, Tao Yu, Yunyun Hou, Jun Liu, Jun Zhou, Sirui Wang, Nan Duan, Jiachen Liu, Qiuhong Ke
Title: Tempo-Zero: Recursive Self-Play in Executable Worlds for Video Reasoning
Abstract:
Video reasoning requires understanding how events unfold over time, yet videos with accurate temporal annotations are expensive to collect. Self‑play offers an alternative by letting a model generate and solve its own tasks without manual annotation. However, existing video self‑play methods train on fixed sets of recorded videos, so they cannot alter the underlying event dynamics and rely on noisy pseudo‑labels derived from the model's own outputs, such as majority voting, that risk reinforcing shared model errors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Tempo‑Zero, a self‑improvement framework that closes a loop of executable environments, execution‑verified self‑play, and environment evolution, where executing a program renders a video with the ground‑truth option and interval of every question. A single policy plays both Questioner and Solver, proposing questions and answering them with timestamped evidence lines, and is trained on execution‑grounded rewards instead of model consensus. The Solver's performance steers a curriculum over tasks and difficulty levels, and the policy selects rule changes that enrich the event dynamics of later rounds. Despite being trained solely on simple programs, without supervised fine‑tuning or external video data which prior methods typically require, Tempo‑Zero outperforms the base models and recent self‑play baselines on average across twelve real‑world video benchmarks at different model scales, with particularly strong gains on temporal grounding tasks. Project page: https://alchemist‑jo.github.io/tempo‑zero/

PaperId: 35, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32429.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Detao Zeng, Guilin Ou, Nuo Chen, Yunhao Feng, Hongliang Wang, Qinli Yang, Junming Shao, Zhong Zhang
Title: Async-RBench: Benchmarking Asynchronous Task Execution in LLM Agents
Abstract:
Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly execute tasks asynchronously: a main agent continues working while its subagents run, and the task state may change before their results arrive. The main agent must decide which work to update or preserve and which checks to repeat, while avoiding prohibited changes. Final task success alone does not reveal whether these results were handled correctly, and natural asynchronous arrivals are hard to reproduce. We introduce Async‑RBench, a benchmark for asynchronous task execution in LLM agents, with 200 executable tasks covering eight scenarios. A scenario controller regulates result delivery using predefined task‑state conditions, while an Event Response Contract (ERC) specifies what each response must change, preserve, avoid, and re‑verify. The Dynamic Replanning Score (DRS) weights the response process and outcome equally and is reported separately from task success. We evaluate nine agents and find DRS scores of 19.2 to 45.1, with the lowest scores on duplicate reports and subagent failures. Under our execution protocol, all nine agents obtain lower task success with asynchronous than with batched delivery (26.0% vs. 29.7% on average). For three agents, prompting the main agent to rebuild its plan after every result improves DRS by only 2.6 to 3.5 points. Together, these findings highlight the challenges of reliable asynchronous task execution and the need to evaluate how agents handle incoming results alongside end‑to‑end task success.

PaperId: 36, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32415.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaopeng Ke, Zhixin Wang, Xuebo Liu, Xinyu Ma, Xing Zheng, Bowen Song, Weiqiang Wang, Min Zhang
Title: Can LLM Annotators Match Human Consistency? Benchmarking Human Agreement and Optimizing Multi-Agent with Contrastive Knowledge
Abstract:
LLM‑based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real‑world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task‑specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single‑labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single‑agent and workflow‑based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce ANT‑A Benchmark, a real‑world multi‑annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task‑specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT‑A enables a distribution‑aware evaluation, using Fleiss kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose ANT‑OR, a multi‑agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT‑OR improves agreement@>=2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT‑OR.

PaperId: 37, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32407.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sujung Hong, Tae Eun Choi, Youngjun Jun, Chanyong Yoon, Seong Jae Hwang
Title: TIE: Training-free CLIP Embedding Guidance for Compositional Text-to-Image Alignment
Abstract:
Text‑to‑image (T2I) diffusion models have advanced notably, but still fail to satisfy prompt conditions, resulting in attribute mismatches and missing objects. These errors normally fall into two categories: concept loss, when an object or attribute (i.e., concept) goes missing, and concept confusion, when an attribute is assigned to the wrong object or multiple objects blend together. Recent studies suggest that these challenges are caused by the limited capacity of CLIP text encoder to capture fine‑grained semantic details. Although several methods have been proposed, concept loss and concept confusion persist in recent T2I models when handling multi‑object, multi‑attribute prompts. In this paper, we conduct an embedding‑level analysis to develop a training‑free, inference‑time solution for concept loss and concept confusion across CLIP‑based T2I models. We find that (1) concepts mentioned later exhibit higher embedding entropy, reflecting less concentrated representations that are more often associated with concept loss, and (2) the first CLIP attention layer captures the strength of binding between each object and its attribute. Guided by our findings, we introduce TIE, a method that improves semantic alignment through a single text‑embedding update. TIE addresses concept loss via entropy‑aware singular value amplification and resolves concept confusion through interpolation‑extrapolation binding based on CLIP attention scores, all in a training‑free manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TIE enhances semantic fidelity in multi‑concept scenarios with minimal sampling overhead. The project page is available at https://hong‑sujung.github.io/TIE/.

PaperId: 38, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32398.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Soheil Kooklan
Title: An Error Budget for Shuffled Multimodal Windows in the 3rd WEAR Challenge: Stacking, Count Constraints and Seam Matching
Abstract:
The 3rd WEAR Dataset Challenge asks for an activity label for every one‑second window of four unseen participants. Each window has 15 VideoMAEv2 frame embeddings, the accelerometer signal of one random limb, and the windows are shuffled. This report is an empirical analysis of one system built after the challenge deadline. Window classifiers are stacked with features averaged over per‑participant graphs of video neighbours and scored successor candidates, and a mean‑field style decoder with a soft count constraint per activity labels all windows of a participant together. The setting is offline and transductive, and the count constraint relies on each activity being performed once. In a participant‑wise simulation with participant‑level bootstrap intervals, stacking added 0.051 macro F1 over stage‑1 fusion and the count constraint 0.011 (95% interval 0.006 to 0.017). A quadratic seam distance ranks the true same‑limb successor first among about 720 candidates in 83.9% of cases, but adding it to the link model changed macro F1 by ‑0.0001 (‑0.0006 to 0.0005). With the decoder settings and the mixing weight chosen inside the folds and the mislabelled spans left out of training, the system scores 0.936 in simulation (0.940 for participants who performed each activity once); the submitted configuration scores 0.938 (0.943). Per‑participant scores range from 0.80 to 0.97. These results come from a non‑nested stacking protocol that uses unlabelled features transductively, so they are not a fully inductive estimate. An oracle that averages the final unary scores over the true segments reaches 0.973, and 79% of the remaining errors involve the null class. On the private leaderboard, which no choice used, the selected Kaggle submission scored 0.9231 (public 0.9254, with bounds partly tuned there), and a later one with bounds chosen in simulation scored 0.9247 (public 0.9253).

PaperId: 39, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32379.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fanxing Ning, Jianguo Zhu
Title: Do LLM-derived text features improve electricity price forecasts beyond document activity? Evidence from Australia's National Electricity Market
Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) can turn market notices and news into features for electricity price forecasting. Such features also record when documents arrive and whether their extraction failed, so a gain measured against a model without text can reflect document activity as well as content. We add the counts of the same documents and of their failed extractions to a no‑text LightGBM model and measure each LLM representation against this activity reference, which needs no additional LLM requests. With gpt‑6‑luna as the extractor, we forecast Australian electricity prices from operator notices (5‑30 minutes ahead) and WattClarity news (day‑ahead) after the extractor's documented knowledge cutoff, averaging forecasts over three training seeds. For news, the counts alone lower mean absolute error (MAE) by 3.0%, most of the 3.6% reduction that the better LLM representation achieves relative to the no‑text model; its increment beyond the counts is not significant. For notices, two of the three LLM representations lower MAE beyond the counts, by 0.14‑0.21% and 0.45‑0.52%, whether the counts are cumulative or cover recent windows, whereas the third shows no significant reduction. Time‑shifted placebos give mixed evidence on whether these gains require text aligned with the target. Benchmarks using the operator's pre‑dispatch forecasts (notices) or price history alone (news) are more accurate than all these text models. Gains against the no‑text model and the activity reference differ in sign at individual seeds and, for notices with cumulative counts, in seed‑averaged forecasts. Text gains should be reported against both references.

PaperId: 40, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32367.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Karyamsetty Martin
Title: Tightening the Online Bin Packing Gap from Both Sides, and the Limits of the Current Methods
Abstract:
The asymptotic competitive ratio of online bin packing has been bracketed since 2018 by the lower bound 1.54278 of Balogh, Bekesi, Dosa, Epstein and Levin and the upper bound 1.57829 of their Advanced Harmonic algorithm. We revisit both sides with exact rational computation and prove what the computations say. On the upper bound, we rebuild the certification of Advanced Harmonic as an exact optimization over its dual parameters; with the published parameters this already certifies a ratio strictly below the published one, and re‑tuning the algorithm's proportion parameters gives a certified ratio of 1.5782147437 (an exact rational), independently re‑verified on all 402 scenarios. To our knowledge this is the first movement of the upper bound since 2018. On the lower bound, we prove that the 2018 adversary construction is rigid: extending it by any finite number of new batches of ordinary size (outside the window of sizes s with 2s > 1 and rational part at most 0.64819), placed anywhere, with counts depending on the observed statistics, adaptive or not, never improves the bound at any truncation level. The load‑bearing fact is that the construction is volume‑tight at every stop. A single window‑sized batch added to the truncation‑3 tree is shown by machine‑verified certificates to leave its value below the published limit. A computational map covers the remaining natural extensions: unions of structural variants, two‑statistic multi‑batch adversaries, and three families of adaptive conditions that the paper's separation theorem allows but never uses; none improves the bound. On the algorithm side we show that the marking, bonus‑item and red‑sand mechanisms of Extreme Harmonic bind nowhere in Advanced Harmonic, whose bottleneck is a two‑medium‑item bin that no known mechanism targets. We record two corrections to commonly cited numbers.

PaperId: 41, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32336.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianyi Sun, Pengfei Yao, Yanze Wang, Hongda Chen, Yunyun Han, Jun Sun, Chuanrui Hu, Yafeng Deng
Title: SkillRep: Characterizing and Understanding the Representation Design Space of Agent Skill Retrieval
Abstract:
Retrieving the right skill from a large library is essential for LLM agents, yet requests and skills are written for different purposes and in different words. Existing retrievers narrow this request‑skill gap with one or two representation choices each, so it is unknown whether their gains hold in combination. No prior work measures the gap itself, so it is also unclear which part of it each choice narrows. We define a representation design space by five choices ‑‑ encoder fine‑tuning, query‑side and document‑side expansion, background projection and a lexical channel ‑‑ and evaluate them together for the first time, as modules of one retriever, SkillRep. With a 0.6B encoder and LLM expansion, SkillRep improves MRR@10 on SRA‑Bench over the strongest same‑size retriever by 7.02 points with the official skill pool and 8.79 with UniPool, a 111,247‑skill pool we build from public registries, and is best on SkillsBench. The value of each choice depends on the others. Fine‑tuning, for instance, reverses the ranking of the four training‑free modules and turns them from complementary into overlapping. To understand why, we measure the gap with three quantities: background, the embedding component that does not separate skills; unsaid vocabulary, the gold skill's content a request leaves unsaid; and dilution, the information lost when a skill is encoded into a single vector. They show which part each module narrows and by what mechanism. This reveals that modules narrowing the same part compete for it, while those narrowing different parts complement each other.

PaperId: 42, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32333.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haocheng Jiang, Herun Wan, Yongyuan Peng, Minnan Luo
Title: Beyond Final Outcomes: Quantifying Claim-Level Information Dynamics in Multi-Agent LLM Interaction
Abstract:
When LLM‑powered agents interact, information is repeatedly shared, expanded, and forgotten, yet multi‑agent evaluation typically focuses on final task outcomes. We study such interaction as claim‑level information dynamics and propose RIVER, which decomposes agent outputs into atomic claims and evaluates three complementary dimensions: convergence, exploration, and retention. Convergence captures cross‑agent claim correspondence and stance alignment; exploration captures semantic breadth and extension beyond the source; and retention tracks source preservation and the persistence of new claims across stages and lineages. We evaluate five interaction strategies on 40 controlled news‑generation cases. Repeatedly pooled interaction promotes convergence but narrows the information space, whereas distributed relay yields broader, less shared information. Further comparisons show that method‑specific constraints increase exploration while weakening convergence and retention. Our findings suggest that collective information dynamics are better explained by underlying information‑flow mechanisms than by simple downstream performance.

PaperId: 43, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32330.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Meng Li, Lijiang Chen, Qi Zhao, Jun Jiang, Longhao Zou, Shuchang Lyu, Guangliang Cheng
Title: DynaSlots: Slot-Centric 3D Dynamics Pretraining for Robot Manipulation
Abstract:
Robot manipulation involves localized changes: picking up a cup moves the cup while leaving the surrounding scene largely unchanged. Yet existing 3D visual pretraining methods, including recent dynamics‑aware variants, model state transitions at the scene level, compressing the motion of everything in a scene into a single global latent action. This conflates semantically distinct transitions in scenes with multiple moving parts, obscures dependencies between changing regions, and leaves the learned representation vulnerable to task‑irrelevant scene content. We introduce DynaSlots, an action‑free, label‑free pretraining framework that decomposes each point cloud frame into a small set of temporally consistent slots and models dynamics at this per‑slot level rather than the scene level. A temporal slot propagation module promotes consistent slot assignments across frames; an inverse dynamics model then extracts one latent action per slot from feature differences, and a diffusion‑based forward dynamics model, paired with a self‑supervised interaction head, predicts each slot's future state while learning pairwise proximity‑and‑motion relations. Experiments on Meta‑World, Adroit, and a RealMan RM65‑B robot demonstrate that DynaSlots outperforms prior scene‑level baselines. It achieves superior success rates in simulation and exhibits strong robustness to scene clutter and unseen objects in real‑world manipulation. Code is available at \hrefhttps://zhucezhanghao12345‑source.github.io/DynaSlots‑Anonymous/https://zhucezhanghao12345‑source.github.io/DynaSlots‑Anonymous/.

PaperId: 44, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32322.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yanze Wang, Pengfei Yao, Tianyi Sun, Hongda Chen, Yunyun Han, Jun Sun, Chuanrui Hu, Yafeng Deng
Title: Beyond Gain: Measuring Skill Internalization for Agent Skill Retirement
Abstract:
LLM agents retrieve skills from public hubs that hold up to about 100,000 entries and serve many models. As models improve, a hub must find the skills a given model has internalized, meaning it can do without them, and retire them for that model, yet internalization has not been measured with known reliability. Published rules that compare runs with and without a skill retire on the gain alone. The gain is near zero both for an internalized skill and when neither the model nor the skill delivers the capability, a state we call uncovered. We instead withhold the skill, score the model on a task synthesized from it, and trust a high unaided score only when another model gains from the skill, since nearly half of high scores come from tasks no model benefits from. Under four models, a published gain rule applied with one task per skill removes over half of the uncovered skills. On SkillsBench, 28 of its 31 retirements rest on probes no run passed in full, while retiring on the unaided score costs no detectable reward. Unaided verdicts reproduce across tasks more often than the gain rule's (Cohen's kappa 0.42 against 0.23) but differ across models, so a hub must read them per model. We release 1,251 skills with tasks and item scores under four models.

PaperId: 45, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32308.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yifei Wang, Botian Wang, YiFei Wang, Jiangtao Feng, Xinbo Zhang, Yawen Ouyang, Yixin Wu, Lihao Wang, Xiaoqing Zheng, Xuanjing Huang, Hao Zhou
Title: Solvent: Long-Horizon Reasoning for Multi-Step Retrosynthesis
Abstract:
Multi‑step retrosynthesis requires recursively transforming a target molecule through successive reaction steps into purchasable building blocks, and recent work has begun to draw on large language model (LLM) reasoning to tackle the task. In its latest evolution, LLM reasoning has entered the long‑horizon regime: models pursue objectives across interdependent steps, interact with environments, and adapt to feedback. This shift has markedly advanced LLM capabilities, as illustrated by breakthroughs in AI‑driven mathematical research. At this frontier, we introduce Solvent, an 8B LLM that successfully extends long‑horizon reasoning to multi‑step retrosynthesis. Through a two‑round post‑training curriculum, Solvent learns to interleave iterative synthesis planning, external availability verification, and adaptive route revision. Experiments show that, following a 2.1× performance boost from RL, Solvent scores 61.86% across four benchmarks, surpassing mid‑scale language models and prior search‑based retrosynthesis systems, and rivaling frontier trillion‑parameter LLMs.

PaperId: 46, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32305.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Shan Peng, Shuaiqi Cheng, Miao Peng, Chenyi Zi, Jia Li
Title: DMAIC-Bench: From Self-Reflection to Self-Restraint for Agents in Multi-Stage Analytical Tasks
Abstract:
Multi‑stage analytical tasks require LLM agents to use intermediate evidence to decide whether to continue, redirect or stop. Self‑reflection, in which an agent critiques its output, is widely studied, yet a critique does not show whether evidence changed the next action. We call that capability self‑restraint. Existing agent benchmarks largely measure task completion or output quality and leave it untested. DMAIC‑Bench evaluates it with 97 seeded tasks across 15 industrial cases in four sectors, built around Lean Six Sigma's explicit statistical prerequisites. Paired counterfactual variants require opposite actions at the same workflow position, distinguishing warranted restraint from indiscriminate stopping. We assess execution traces with a private scorer and final claims through independent expert review. Across 13 models from six providers, execution‑level routing accuracy averages 92% on matched GO decisions and 19% on NO‑GO decisions, counting any forbidden downstream computation as a route error. Execution traces show agents reporting correct diagnostics before performing analyses that those results disallow. Separately, blinded expert review of the 11 audited agents estimates that reports act on invalid evidence at 47% of reached NO‑GO decisions, with an interval from 31% to 61%. Explicit stopping permission helps some models without consistently restoring correct decisions at both GO and NO‑GO forks. Sixteen life‑sciences tasks in bulk ribonucleic acid sequencing (RNA‑seq) and case‑control genome‑wide association studies (GWAS) show that the same framework can evaluate evidence‑dependent decisions beyond industrial workflows. Project code and data are available at: https://github.com/psptpx/DMAIC‑Bench‑public.

PaperId: 47, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32295.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianyi Xu, Huazheng Wang
Title: Lifelong Context Adaptation through Bidirectional Memory-Skill Learning
Abstract:
Lifelong LLM agents must learn from an expanding history of interactions while making each decision within a bounded context window. Memory makes past experience available, but the agent may still need to infer how to solve each new task from the retrieved records. Skills provide reusable procedures, yet may omit the task‑specific facts needed to apply them. Because retrieved memory and skills shape the agent's behavior, they also influence the experience available for future learning.
