We introduce MemCryst, a framework for lifelong context adaptation through bidirectional learning of memory and skills with a frozen language model. Recurring episodes stored in memory support skill creation and revision, and the interactions guided by those skills supply new memory for subsequent learning. Facts retrieved from memory and learned skills jointly form the agent's context, while task outcomes adjust the future retrieval influence of the records actually served without rewriting their content. Across ten settings spanning embodied control, long‑document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code, MemCryst leads seven reported comparisons. On ALFWorld, joint serving achieves 63.17% success, compared with 59.83% for memory‑only and 50.50% for skill‑only serving. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi0216/Memcryst.git

PaperId: 48, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32289.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Julia Simon, Daniel Steininger, Andreas Trondl
Title: ReLEAP: Upcycling Vision Datasets through Cross-Task Unification and Semi-Supervised Annotation
Abstract:
Developing robust vision models requires large amounts of annotated data, especially for tasks involving fine‑grained class distinctions under variable environmental conditions. Even in domains with numerous existing datasets, differences in annotation formats, label definitions and targeted learning tasks hinder data reuse and integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ReLEAP, a scalable Python framework for unifying heterogeneous image datasets through data‑source abstraction, systematic reuse of annotations across learning tasks, and mapping of labels to a shared hierarchical taxonomy. We demonstrate its applicability in precision agriculture by integrating fifteen diverse datasets covering a broad range of plant species and annotation types. Beyond unification, ReLEAP enables systematic recycling of existing data and provides a robust foundation for learning‑based annotation upcycling. Leveraging this foundation, we conduct extensive cross‑dataset and fine‑tuning experiments to investigate how domain‑specific models trained on unified data and foundation models can be used to automatically generate higher‑level annotations under unsupervised, weakly supervised and semi‑supervised settings, and how dataset characteristics influence their effectiveness. Our results show that unified data access and annotation upcycling substantially expand the pool of reusable training data and annotations while improving data transparency, enabling more sustainable and resource‑efficient use of existing datasets. We release the framework and trained models for academic use to support accessible and collaborative research, particularly in data‑scarce and heterogeneous domains.

PaperId: 49, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32279.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chi Zhang, Yi Sun, Weichuang Zhang, Quan Chen, Jieru Zhao
Title: TranSAGE: Automating Spatial Accelerator Generation for Large-Scale Transformer Models
Abstract:
Large‑scale Transformers have achieved remarkable success across NLP, computer vision, and robotics, but their growing computational and memory demands challenge efficient inference. Spatial accelerators offer advantages in on‑chip bandwidth and energy efficiency, yet designing them for large models remains costly and time‑consuming. Existing accelerator generators typically focus on single‑operation support, overlooking the benefits of multi‑operation pipelining, which limits throughput and energy efficiency. We propose TranSAGE, a compiler‑based framework that jointly optimizes scheduling for large‑scale Transformers under multi‑operation pipelining and generates corresponding accelerator implementations. Our approach integrates a design space exploration (DSE) engine with multi‑operation dataflow optimization and a dynamic programming‑based graph partitioning algorithm to efficiently identify pipeline‑friendly operation clusters and their optimal dataflow parameters. We further design spatial architecture primitives and lowering passes to automatically generate efficient RTL implementations. Evaluations on four representative LLMs demonstrate that TranSAGE achieves up to 2.41x higher throughput and 13.04x higher energy efficiency than commercial GPU/NPU baselines. Compared with state‑of‑the‑art accelerator generators, TranSAGE achieves up to 11.33x higher throughput and 6.07x higher energy efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjtu‑zhao‑lab/TranSAGE.

PaperId: 50, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32275.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Gerardus Croonen, Andreas Trondl, Julia Simon, Daniel Steininger
Title: RootDown: Deploying and Benchmarking Models for Beet-Root Detection on Edge Devices
Abstract:
Quality inspection of sugar beets after harvest and storage is critical to preserve sugar content and ensure optimal processing efficiency. The transfer of harvested beets to field clamps or trucks provides an opportunity to visually inspect individual beets automatically on loader conveyors. However, this is a challenging task as the large number of beets causes partial overlap and occlusion, complicating both annotation and detection. In this work, we propose an end‑to‑end image‑based pipeline for detecting partially occluded sugar beets in loading scenarios as a first step toward automated quality inspection. We introduce a dedicated benchmark and present an automatic annotation strategy that leverages the SAM 3 foundation model to generate bounding boxes. We compare models trained on manually annotated and automatically generated labels. Additionally, we investigate deployment considerations by benchmarking multiple inference configurations, including execution on an edge device, under realistic operational constraints regarding precision, inference time and power consumption. Our results show that, despite substantial occlusion and inherent annotation ambiguity, foundation‑model‑based labels can substitute for a substantial share of manual annotation, trading labeling effort for data volume at a modest accuracy cost. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a Raspberry Pi 5 equipped with a Hailo accelerator enables high‑performance, low‑power inference, making it a practical solution for mobile outdoor deployment.

PaperId: 51, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32268.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yue Feng, Boshen Xu, Zihao Yue, Xiaokun Liu, Miao Yang, Xin Tao, Pengfei Wan, Qin Jin
Title: RVG-Bench: A Benchmark for Reasoning-Driven Audio-Visual Temporal Grounding
Abstract:
Existing temporal video grounding (TVG) benchmarks primarily focus on localizing target video segments according to descriptive text queries of the visual content. However, real‑world queries are more diverse and often require the model to first understand the user's intent before localization, such as finding visual evidence, identifying the cause of an event, or recalling a remembered moment, yet such queries remain largely overlooked. To mitigate this gap, we introduce RVG‑Bench, a benchmark for reasoning‑driven audio‑visual temporal grounding, where every query is constructed such that the target segment can only be identified through reasoning about the query's underlying intent. We carefully construct the benchmark and rigorously verify its data quality to ensure models truly comprehend the audio‑visual content. RVG‑Bench comprises 1,255 videos and 1,890 query‑interval pairs across eight reasoning types. We evaluate 22 models and find that the strongest, Qwen3.8‑Omni‑Flash, achieves only 49.6 mIoU. Through a series of controlled analyses, including oracle‑grounding probes and test‑time scaling experiments, we systematically examine where and why current models struggle, providing insights for future model development.

PaperId: 52, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32262.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Weihong Li, Hao Jiang, Yaohua Zha, Tao Dai, Shu-Tao Xia
Title: Beyond Pattern Matching in 3D MLLMs: Part-Level Functional Reasoning for Generalizable Recognition
Abstract:
3D MLLMs recognize objects via pattern matching, which fails when geometrically similar objects require functional reasoning to disambiguate (e.g., dresser vs. wardrobe). Our per‑sample Geometric Confusion Score (GCS) exposes this failure: baseline accuracy is 33.7% on ModelNet40's most ambiguous 20% versus 84.0% on its least ambiguous 20%. We identify a function‑as‑annotation pattern, in which functional language decorates a known identity instead of supporting inference, and hypothesize that reversing this information flow should concentrate improvements on the most ambiguous samples. PFIR (Part‑level Functional Inference for Recognition) reverses that flow. Built on PartNeXt part segmentation, its data pipeline produces 507K QA pairs with functional CoTs (geometry \to function \to identity), and its progressive curriculum culminates in dual‑objective GRPO: strict functional reasoning and descriptive grounding for Objaverse's diverse distribution. The two RL objectives yield nearly orthogonal task vectors (\cos = 0.056), enabling composition via Task Arithmetic. Under a strict dual OOD protocol (Objaverse \to ModelNet40; XYZRGB \to XYZ‑only), PFIR raises zero‑shot accuracy from 60.5% to 66.7%, with gains concentrated 2.6× more on geometrically ambiguous samples‑‑‑supporting part‑level functional reasoning as an effective route to more generalizable 3D recognition. Code: https://github.com/this233/pfir‑3d.

PaperId: 53, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32230.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Linye Lyu, Jiawei Zhou, Daojing He, Yu Li
Title: Towards Effective and Transferable Physical Camouflage against Multi-View BEV-based 3D Perception in Autonomous Driving
Abstract:
Modern autonomous driving systems widely adopt multi‑view Bird's‑Eye‑View (BEV) based 3D perception models due to their superior performance. Despite their success, the robustness of these models against adversarial camouflage attacks remains largely unexplored. Existing camouflage attacks primarily target single‑view 2D detectors, limiting their effectiveness in multi‑view 3D perception settings. To address this gap, we propose BEVCA, a novel adversarial camouflage generation framework tailored for multi‑view BEV‑based 3D perception. Our framework integrates a BEV‑feature‑based adversarial loss with a multi‑view neural rendering module, enabling effective and transferable camouflage attacks across different models and tasks. Extensive experiments in both digital and physical settings demonstrate that BEVCA outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines and exhibits strong robustness under real‑world conditions. Our code is available at https://github.com/WAVE‑AT‑IDEA/BEVCA.

PaperId: 54, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32221.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiaxing Sun, Junyuan Gao, Ruikang Zhang, Hao Zheng, Lingli Ge, Xiao An, Jiang Wu, Huazheng Zeng, Jiahe Song, Chen Zhu, Haote Yang, Jingchao Wang, Lu Chen, Yuanyuan Cao, Ruijie Zhang, Shengxin Lu, Weijia Li, Lijun Wu, Conghui He
Title: RxnExBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Structured Chemical Reaction Extraction from Scientific Literature
Abstract:
Screen Tables and Substrate Scopes are information‑dense figures widely used in synthetic chemistry literature, yet automated extraction of structured reaction data from them remains challenging. We introduce RxnExBench, a multimodal benchmark for fine‑grained reaction‑level evaluation. Built from high‑impact chemistry journals, it contains 3,565 expert‑annotated reactions and 2,361 molecular structures. The dataset adopts a unified schema with 15 reaction roles and 26 core fields, supporting downstream AI‑for‑Chemistry tasks such as retrosynthetic planning, yield prediction, and reaction condition recommendation. RxnExBench further provides a reasoning‑driven difficulty taxonomy, a modular annotation pipeline, and the Oracle‑MolRec protocol, which disentangles molecular recognition from higher‑level reasoning. Evaluation of 9 state‑of‑the‑art VLMs shows that performance degrades substantially as schema complexity and reasoning demands increase. Under the Oracle‑MolRec setting, results further reveal that accurate molecular recognition alone is insufficient, with multimodal integration and chemistry‑aware reasoning remaining the primary bottlenecks. We release all data and code to facilitate future research in chemistry‑aware multimodal understanding and AI‑for‑Chemistry dataset construction. The dataset and code will be released at https://github.com/opendatalab/RxnExBench.

PaperId: 55, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32212.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiawei Dong, Zilong Bai, Pengtian zhu, Peng Zhou
Title: SOPO: Socratic Guided Policy Optimization for Span-Level Hallucination Detection
Abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span‑level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi‑turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher‑guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn‑based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT‑5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out‑of‑domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.

PaperId: 56, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32205.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hyojun Kim, Hyeseon An, Yo-Sub Han
Title: Watermarking Diffusion Language Models with Learned Foresight and Balanced Bands
Abstract:
Green‑red watermarks favor tokens from a green list that a secret key derives from the preceding tokens. Diffusion language models, however, often choose a token before its preceding tokens, and the token later shapes its neighbors' green lists. Prior work therefore tilts each choice to raise the expected number of green tokens at its own and its neighbors' positions. Building on this objective, we first learn two components that prior work keeps fixed: vocabulary bands that serve as green lists, separate competing candidates and keep the null distribution exact, and a foresight predictor that estimates how each candidate shifts its neighbors' predictions. Second, we count green tokens as the detector does, once per distinct context‑token pair, so repetition earns nothing. On WaterBench with LLaDA‑8B‑Instruct, each learned component raises the z‑score at equal distortion, and their gains are nearly additive. With a strong watermark, ours detects at least 96% of responses at a 1% false‑positive rate while matching the LLM‑judge score of unwatermarked text. Ours also detects more responses on Dream and as many or more on code and question answering without a significant loss in task accuracy.

PaperId: 57, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32196.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Victor Shea-Jay Huang, Rongqing Li, Zhangyue Yin, Kelong Mao, Yaqi Zhao, Xinyuan Wang, Yao Yin, Lirui Luo, Renrui Zhang, Hongsheng Li
Title: SWE-Shift: Evaluating Coding Agents in Evolving Workspaces
Abstract:
Repository‑level coding benchmarks largely assume that tasks and environments remain unchanged throughout execution. In software development, code, dependencies, runtime state, and requirements can change while an agent is still working. We introduce SWE‑Shift, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under such mid‑execution changes. From the same saved history and workspace, a Clean continuation proceeds without intervention, while a matched Shifted continuation receives a task‑relevant update. Success requires completing the current task, preserving still‑valid work, and satisfying the applicable state and evidence checks. The benchmark contains 120 scenarios across 12 change families, each evaluated at nine scheduled intervention positions. We evaluate 17 coding‑agent systems, all of which have lower Shifted than Clean success. GPT‑6 Astra drops from 67.35% to 24.79%, with 20.34% paired success. Tool/session changes and stale evidence yield zero paired success across all systems. Late‑position paired success is lower for some systems and higher for others. These results show that success on the unchanged task can coexist with failures to preserve work, recover state, or refresh evidence after an update.

PaperId: 58, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32195.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dongki Kim, Sangwoo Park, Jinheon Baek, Soyeong Jeong, Sung Ju Hwang
Title: Principia: Test-Time Hypotheses to Principle Construction for Scientific Discovery
Abstract:
Scientific discovery requires identifying the scientific principles underlying observed phenomena to guide further investigation. As these empirical principles are often unknown in complex discovery processes, they are constructed via a hypotheses‑to‑principle pipeline to obtain recurring causalities from progressively accumulated observations during test‑time discovery. However, constructing this knowledge requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, making this translation stage a bottleneck for scientific discovery. To address this limitation, we propose Principia, an LLM‑based framework that constructs and continually refines scientific principles at test time. Drawing on how human researchers develop principles, Principia forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and their observed outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships across these hypotheses into inductive principles. By applying the constructed hypotheses and inductive principles to the task, it obtains new observations, revises the hypotheses used based on these new observations, and reconstructs principles from the updated hypotheses, allowing scientific knowledge to continuously evolve throughout test‑time discovery. Across benchmarks spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction, Principia outperforms baselines relying on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, while generating principles that are plausible and consistent with the scientific literature, demonstrating its effectiveness in constructing and refining task‑specific hypotheses and principles at test time for scientific discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongkiKim95/Principia.

PaperId: 59, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32164.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wenyu Liang, Hongzhi Yin, Tongtong Wu, Fan Liu, Kexin Dai, Weiqing Wang
Title: PersonalQuery-Benchmark:Evaluating Retrieval Robustness to Personalized User Expression Differences
Abstract:
Existing personalized information retrieval methods mainly model differences in user needs through user preferences and query intent, while paying little attention to the personalized expression differences that arise when different users express the same retrieval need. Existing real query data typically lack stable user identities, long‑term expression histories, and intent‑matched counterparts, making it difficult to systematically evaluate the impact of personalized expression differences on retrieval outcomes. To this end, we propose PersonalQuery‑Benchmark (PQB). PQB models personalized syntactic expression and personalized writing errors from users' historical texts, constructs personalized syntactic expression queries and personalized writing‑error queries, and validates benchmark quality through LLM assessment and independent human evaluation. PQB covers three Amazon product domains with 6,516 query instances in total, and is evaluated on five retrieval models representing lexical, learned sparse, dense bi‑encoder, late‑interaction, and hybrid architectures, together with two LLM‑based ranking models. Results show that even when the information need is held fixed, personalized expression differences still induce measurable ranking variation; different retrieval models exhibit clearly different sensitivities to syntactic variation and writing‑error variation, while higher overall retrieval effectiveness does not necessarily correspond to stronger robustness against expression variation. PQB provides a new benchmark and evaluation framework for systematically studying personalized expression robustness. The associated code and dataset are available at the following address: https://github.com/cpxjazz123/PersonalQuery‑Benchmark.

PaperId: 60, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32127.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yanshuo Chen, Chenxi Liu, Reza Shirkavand, Heng Huang
Title: MPQ: A Message-Passing View of Post-Training Quantization
Abstract:
Post‑training quantization (PTQ) is a key technique for efficiently deploying large language models, as it compresses weights into low‑bit representations without retraining. Existing PTQ solvers, including GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent, commit each weight block to a single codeword before its neighbors are considered, leaving near‑optimal alternatives unexplored. In this work, we cast row‑wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks, in which existing solvers correspond to a zero‑temperature, hard‑decision limit retaining only the top codeword per block. We propose Message‑Passing Quantization (MPQ), which preserves soft posterior information across blocks during inference and commits to hard codewords only at the output stage. MPQ first uses vector approximate message passing to compute approximate blockwise posteriors, then refines a hard‑decision initialization by exact block coordinate descent. Across 2‑bit lattice and 3‑ and 4‑bit scalar quantization on dense language models from Llama, Qwen, and Mistral families, MPQ improves perplexity and zero‑shot accuracy over strong hard‑decision baselines, and composes favorably with preprocessing techniques such as activation‑aware scaling and incoherence processing. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/MPQ.

PaperId: 61, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32122.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mahdi Naser Moghadasi
Title: Semantically Rich, Metrically Affect-Blind: A Geometric Blind Spot in Modern Text Embedders
Abstract:
We report a systematic dissociation in modern text embedders: sentiment is almost perfectly decodable from their embeddings, yet almost entirely absent from their metric. Across eleven frozen encoders spanning 2021 to 2026, including 2026‑generation models and the 4B‑parameter LLM embedder Qwen3‑Embedding‑4B, a linear probe recovers sentence polarity at up to 91.3% accuracy while cosine similarity separates polarity by a margin of only 0.003‑0.064. Qwen3‑Embedding‑4B, the strongest probe in the panel, reaches 91.3% probe accuracy but only 64.3 retrieval MAP. Because retrieval, clustering, deduplication, and retrieval‑augmented generation operate on the metric rather than on a trained probe, these systems are effectively blind to information their encoder demonstrably contains. A task‑conditioning control suggests this reflects the pretraining objective rather than a prompting artifact: conditioning Jina‑v5 on its classification task rather than its retrieval task recovers only about half of the MAP gain that injection achieves on the same weights (63.2 to 73.8, versus 85.1), and leaves the alignment gap essentially unchanged. Sentiment‑Injected Sentence Embeddings (SISE) train a small (0.13M‑0.69M‑parameter) supervised‑contrastive head on a frozen encoder in seconds on a CPU, using the labelled training set. The head improves every encoder released since 2022 on full‑data probe accuracy (up to +5.8 points), retrieval MAP (up to +26.0) and polarity margin (7‑61x). This is a specialization, not a free gain: the compact 128‑d head loses 38‑41 Spearman points on STS‑B, while a fused variant that concatenates it with the base embedding loses 2.4‑12.0. With the head, a 0.6B encoder at 128 dimensions matches a 4B encoder given the same head (91.8 vs. 90.3 MAP). We release a CPU‑reproducible pipeline and a reusable diagnostic, the Attribute Alignment Gap.

PaperId: 62, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32110.pdf   GitHub
Authors:William Jeffries
Title: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
Abstract:
Agents and verifiers often rely on the text a tool prints, and that text can misrepresent what the tool actually did, even when the tool's computation is correct. We saw this happen in a production RAG research system used by the Pilsudski Institute in New York, where tool output formatters misled an agent into giving wrong or incomplete information to users. Each tool did its job correctly, but its output omitted search limits, result caps, or identifier namespaces. We also recreated an unlabeled estimate caught in code review before release. We studied whether these formatters misled agents and verifiers and how much the repaired wording helps. We fed tool results to agents using two formatter versions: one with the key omissions and one with all missing details clearly stated. That difference alone changed what the agents claimed and what the verifiers accepted. Unsupported agent claims dropped substantially for three of the four failure types. In one test, verifiers went from accepting incorrect answers 90 out of 90 times to rejecting them 90 out of 90 times. A control showed the verifiers could catch the errors once they were given the missing facts and asked to judge correctness. We include the audit prompt we used with Codex and Claude Code in an exploratory demonstration, written with prior knowledge of our own system's defects. When pointed at an old version of our own system, it rediscovered the defects that were still live and surfaced twelve more we had not catalogued. When pointed at OpenClaw and Hermes, two of the best‑known open‑source agentic systems, it found warped formatters in both. We opened PRs to fix both, and the OpenClaw fix has already been merged. Practitioners can run the same prompt on their own systems today.

PaperId: 63, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32102.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiabing Yang, Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Chenhang Cui, Tao Yu, Zichen Wen, Wen Ye, Bowen Fang, Ziheng He, Xiangnan Wu, Yingda Li, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
Title: Coupling Execution Horizon and Sampling Depth in Flow-Matching VLA Policies
Abstract:
Flow‑matching Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real‑time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. Standard deployment workflows typically treat numerical solver depth and execution horizon as decoupled choices. The horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver depth is kept high to preserve integration fidelity. In this paper, we reveal a fundamental compute‑execution coupling in flow‑matching VLAs governed by a systematic sign reversal. While coarse numerical integration degrades precision under rapid replanning, it markedly improves task performance under extended open‑loop commitment. Geometrically, numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer that suppresses compounding open‑loop drift. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real‑world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones including π_0, π_0.5, and GR00T, exploiting this joint coupling consistently achieves superior task success while drastically lowering inference latency, entirely training‑free and without architectural modifications. These findings establish numerical sampling depth as an operational variance regulator, shifting its role from a static precision budget to an active deployment knob in robot learning. Project page: https://jiabingyang01.github.io/Horizon‑Depth‑VLA/

PaperId: 64, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32093.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Minho Park, Kinam Kim, Donghu Kim, Byungkun Lee, Dongyoon Hwang, Yongjae Shin, Junha Hyung, Hojoon Lee, Jaegul Choo
Title: DiscoDemo: Discovering Efficient and Diverse Robot Demonstrations for Imitation Learning
Abstract:
Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning. Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution. We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent‑conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success‑gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success. The trained generator produces multiple successful closed‑loop behaviors, which are safety‑filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning. Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful‑state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world. Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62% from 40% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78% from 39% on the real robot, respectively. These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow‑matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection. Project page: https://davian‑robotics.github.io/DiscoDemo

PaperId: 65, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32073.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mulugeta Weldezgina Asres, Lei Jiao, Christian Walter Omlin
Title: Guided Zero-Shot Anomaly Explanation for Anonymized Crowd Video Monitoring: Context, Categorization, and Spatial Localization
Abstract:
Despite the promising development of deep learning for video anomaly detection (VAD), explainability (XAI) of these models remains a challenge. Explainable and privacy‑protecting VAD builds transparency and trust that facilitates adoption of computer vision systems, including safety and security monitoring. However, anomaly explainability in privacy‑preserving VAD systems is underexplored. In this study, we present the XAVAD approach, a unified descriptive anomaly XAI for an anonymized VAD, that integrates flexible zero‑shot anonymization, anomaly type categorization, visual localization, and scene context description. We provide empirical and qualitative assessments of multifaceted explanations integrated with full‑body visual anonymization for privacy protection. We adopt a multimodal CLIP embedding for videos, using improved LLM‑assisted prompting and pool‑scoring mechanisms for anomaly‑type identification. We enhance Grad‑ECLIP for spatial anomaly heatmap localization, leveraging computation and accuracy through our novel prompt‑guided patching autofocus mechanism. We employ VLMs to generate context and reasoning descriptions of detected anomalies through curated prompt engineering. We have evaluated the accuracy and computational cost of XAVAD on several publicly available CCTV and video datasets. Our experiments demonstrate substantial gains of our XAVAD over state‑of‑the‑art benchmark approaches and provide insights into privacy protection trade‑offs in XAI for VAD. We further present ablation studies and assessments across diverse configurations and modeling alternatives to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods. Code: https://github.com/muleina/XAVADhttps://github.com/muleina/XAVAD .

PaperId: 66, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32059.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yiran Xiahou, Siliang Qin, Kai Chen, Shengzhi Zhang, Renyang Liu
Title: Concept Acupuncturist: An Efficient and Precise Concept Erasure Method for Diffusion Models via Sparse Autoencoders
Abstract:
Diffusion‑based image generation models produce high‑quality images but may generate harmful or policy‑violating content, motivating machine unlearning (MU) to selectively remove target concepts while preserving general capabilities. However, existing MU approaches often struggle with the distributed and entangled nature of concept representations, leading to inefficient optimization and imprecise edits when applied through large‑scale fine‑tuning over full diffusion trajectories. To bridge this gap, we propose Concept Acupuncturist (ConceptACP), a novel MU framework that integrates interpretability‑guided analysis with inference‑free fine‑tuning for efficient and precise concept removal. By establishing mappings between semantic concepts and cross‑attention blocks in the U‑Net denoiser and localizing the most concept‑relevant block for targeted optimization, ConceptACP avoids full diffusion trajectory optimization, thereby improving fine‑tuning efficiency. To mitigate concept entanglement, we propose a feature‑level correction mechanism based on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), where SAE‑derived sparse, semantically meaningful feature activations are manipulated to construct targeted correction signals, which are then projected back to the output space of the corresponding block and used as supervision for precise concept removal. Consequently, ConceptACP eliminates the need for external inference‑time modules while achieving efficient and fine‑grained unlearning. Instantiated on SDXL‑Turbo, ConceptACP improves the forgetting success rate by 36.34 percentage points in the standard one‑step generation setting on average over the best‑performing baseline, while preserving image quality and prompt fidelity, and generalizes effectively across other Stable Diffusion backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/Eran‑Xia/ConceptACP.

PaperId: 67, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32009.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Carson Cary, Yukai Jin, Yihao Huang, Zhankai Ye, Fangyi Li, Ting Hua, Xin Liu, Shangqian Gao
Title: GS-MoE: Training-Free MoE Compression via Groupwise Subspace Sharing and Pruning
Abstract:
Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) models reduce computation through sparse activation, but storing their expert parameters remains a major memory bottleneck. We introduce GS‑MoE, a training‑free compression framework that addresses redundancy across and within experts through two compression axes: shared‑subspace rank and expert intermediate width. Groupwise low‑rank representations capture shared structure across experts while retaining expert‑specific projections, and Nyström‑based neuron compression reduces intermediate width within each expert. For fixed shared subspaces, we derive per‑expert reconstruction‑error reductions from the reconstruction objective and use them to guide expert grouping. Budgets are allocated hierarchically using a gradient‑free layer‑importance score to guide the allocation of rank and width budgets across layers, which eigenvalues and leverage then distribute as non‑uniform ranks across groups and intermediate widths across experts. Experiments demonstrate the complementary benefits of compression along both axes, particularly at high compression rates on fine‑grained MoE models. On DeepSeek‑MoE‑16B‑Base, at a 60% reduction in total model parameters, GS‑MoE retains approximately 90% of the uncompressed model's average reasoning performance, compared with 73% for D^2‑MoE, while achieving 20% lower out‑of‑domain perplexity. We provide a code implementation at: https://github.com/cbacary/GS‑MoE

PaperId: 68, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32007.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jakub Poćwiardowski, Mateusz Modrzejewski
Title: MI-MIDI 2: From Observation to Control with Sparse Autoencoders in Text-to-MIDI Generation
Abstract:
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can expose features of a generative model without predefined labels, but in language models the evidence used to interpret these features has proven an unreliable guide to which of them steer the output. Whether interpretations of SAE features predict control in music generators has not, to our knowledge, been tested. We develop an end‑to‑end protocol for discovering and evaluating SAE features in text‑to‑MIDI generation and apply it to text2midi and MIDI‑LLM. The protocol characterizes features through correlations with musical metrics, shared instrument programs, and automated descriptions, each with its own control: note‑density adjustment, matched inactive excerpts, and permutation calibration. It then tests candidates by intervention, measured directly in the generated MIDI against unmodified generation and a matched random direction, ranks them in screens, and confirms selected features on new prompts. Evidence that survives these controls points to features that steer the output. Descriptions exceed permutation controls for instrumentation, and a feature whose description names a synth‑lead program introduces that program in a prespecified confirmation and in a replication on disjoint prompts and reappears in independently trained dictionaries. Features selected by density‑adjusted correlations show a small positive shift of their target metric as a family, whereas features selected by raw correlations show none. An atlas provides MIDI, piano‑roll, and audio examples for every feature of the targeted screen.

PaperId: 69, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32004.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Monojit Banerjee, Zhujun Lan, Defu Cao
Title: CRM-Agent-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using Agents in Stateful Enterprise Environments
Abstract:
Deploying language agents in real applications demands more than the right answer: an agent must execute a multi‑step business process correctly, follow domain‑specific rules, and interact with a user across a dialogue, where the gap between saying and doing is the gap between a satisfied customer and a real loss. We argue that a deployable‑agent benchmark should jointly assess four facets: the outcome an agent reaches, the trajectory it takes, its operational viability, and its policy compliance. Customer relationship management (CRM), where mutable records meet operational rules and consequential effects, exercises all four. We introduce CRM‑Agent‑Bench, an execution‑grounded benchmark of 555 stateful, multi‑turn tasks across nine business domains and 36 capability tags. Each task supplies a task‑specific executable contract drawn from checks over actions, arguments, order, response, target state, and protected state; success is the strict conjunction of the checks declared for that task. We evaluate the complete agent system through these contracts and report scored coverage, latency, and cost. Across sixteen systems evaluated on the audited final release, strict success spans 64.32% to 83.60%; the closely grouped leading systems nonetheless diverge sharply in cost and per‑domain reliability. CRM‑Agent‑Bench offers an auditable framework for measuring contract‑grounded business‑transaction integrity and adherence to task‑declared benchmark policies, with a portable structure designed for extension as models improve. Github repository: https://github.com/salesforce‑misc/crm‑agent‑bench

PaperId: 70, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31974.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Eric Yocam, Varghese Vaidyan, Paris Kalathas, Patrick Tague, Bruce DeBruhl, Yong Wang
Title: Agentic AI Defense: Decode-Time Provenance Binding for MCP
Abstract:
Agentic AI systems using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection through untrusted tool outputs. We demonstrate cross‑modal trust laundering, in which instructions concealed in an email‑signature image using least‑significant‑bit (LSB), discrete cosine transform (DCT), or metadata steganography bypass text scanners and enter a multi‑agent workflow when decoded by a tool. To counter this threat, we propose decode‑time provenance binding, which combines HMAC‑authenticated trust labels with an MCP‑maintained provenance ledger and context‑taint tracking. The mechanism labels decoded content as untrusted and blocks critical tool calls influenced by that content, even when a compromised agent substitutes a valid trusted label. We evaluate the approach using a real MCP testbed with three steganographic carriers and 24 adaptive payloads. The undefended pipeline exhibits 100% attack success, while keyword and regex defenses each permit 62.5% of attacks. Our mechanism blocks all attacks (0% success), including adversarial label substitution across mediated agent boundaries. A four‑component ablation validates the roles of decode marking, cryptographic authentication, lineage tracking, and sink enforcement. An audited trusted‑promotion mechanism increases legitimate‑task completion from 67% to 100% without compromising protection. The approach provides carrier‑independent containment within fully mediated MCP execution environments. Code and data are publicly available.

PaperId: 71, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31966.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Muhammad Azam Afridi, Rajab Ali, Marco Passarotti
Title: POS-Signature Demonstration Retrieval for In-Context Dependency Parsing
Abstract:
Demonstrations for in‑context learning are often retrieved by semantic similarity, which may be a poor proxy for relevance in structured prediction. We study demonstration selection for Universal Dependencies parsing with a POS‑signature policy that represents sentences with weighted part‑of‑speech statistics and retrieves three length‑compatible, gold‑parsed examples from the labeled training split. We evaluate two open‑weight language models without fine‑tuning on all 2,077 sentences of the UD English Web Treebank test set, comparing the policy with shot‑ and format‑matched fixed and semantic three‑shot baselines, as well as zero‑shot, chain‑of‑thought, and critique‑refinement systems. POS‑signature retrieval yields the highest labeled attachment score among the tested prompting systems for both models (72.4 and 73.2), outperforming semantic retrieval by 1.9 and 2.7 points; paired‑bootstrap 95% confidence intervals exclude zero for both contrasts. Chain‑of‑thought and refinement comparisons vary across models. These exploratory results favor the tested POS‑signature retrieval approach on English‑EWT. We release the prompts, archived outputs, and evaluation code.

PaperId: 72, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31946.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Brianne Lee
Title: Which Answer Did the Seventeen-Year-Old Write? A Behavioral Case Study of Author-Age Misattribution, Miscalibrated Confidence, and Non-Corrective Self-Explanation in Six Frontier Language Models
Abstract:
Three students answered the same exam prompt by hand: "What is happiness? Are you happy?" Their ages, recorded at collection, are 17, 28, and 45. The 17‑year‑old's answer is hedged and formally phrased. Asked to match each answer to an age and gender label, most frontier language models confidently assign it to an adult. This paper reports a structured case study of that failure across six models: Claude Fable 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT‑5.6 Sol, Grok 4.5, GPT‑4o (2024), and DeepSeek V4. We ran 1,081 API sessions and scored 3,225 responses across six experimental conditions that manipulate framing, disclosure format, and audience‑awareness instruction. Three of six models perform at or near chance (1/3) on the matching task while reporting 73‑88% mean confidence. The youngest writer's answer is misattributed to an adult in up to 90% of trials. Removing the multiple‑choice scaffold collapses accuracy further: three models never place within three years of the true age once open‑ended estimation is required. Institutional framing ("a community‑college biology final") significantly degrades the best‑performing model's accuracy; a neutral label does not. A single audience‑awareness instruction significantly improves one model (+21 points) and moves another to ceiling, with no detectable effect on the three weakest models. Stated confidence is uncorrelated or inversely correlated with correctness for five of six models. After ground truth is revealed, one model names its own stereotyping in 68 of 114 explanations, yet shows the lowest accuracy and highest confidence of any model under blind presentation: articulate retrospective diagnosis that does not track the quality of its judgments. This is a three‑item, single‑topic, single‑language case study meant to isolate a mechanism, not to estimate a population bias rate. Data, code, and raw model outputs are publicly released.

PaperId: 73, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31932.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Victor Morand, Yuxuan Zong, Mathias Vast, Josiane Mothe, Benjamin Piwowarski
Title: MICE to Meet You: From Re-ranking Only to End-to-End Retrieval
Abstract:
Late‑interaction models offer state‑of‑the‑art efficiency‑effectiveness trade‑offs for neural retrieval by enabling document representations to be pre‑computed and efficiently indexed. Yet, their relatively simple interaction mechanisms, typically MaxSim, can limit their effectiveness compared to cross‑encoders. MICE, a recently introduced re‑ranking architecture, aims to combine cross‑encoder‑like effectiveness through expressive transformer‑based scoring with reduced inference‑time computation through document‑side pre‑computation. However, no practical way to store these document representations was explored. We address this limitation here and introduce MICE‑P, the first end‑to‑end retrieval pipeline with MICE, based on PLAID to index the contextualized document token representations. We conduct a controlled comparison of MICE, ColBERT and cross‑encoders by training comparable models using the Ettin Family under matched experimental conditions. Our results show that MICE‑P defines a new class of retrieval architecture with an efficiency‑effectiveness trade‑off of its own: it matches late‑interaction retrieval throughput while retaining the effectiveness of cross‑encoders.

PaperId: 74, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31908.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Ranran Huang, Wenjing Bian, Weixun Luo, Ye Mao, Krystian Mikolajczyk
Title: PixGR: Pixel-Space Generative Decoding for Fast Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
Abstract:
We present PixGR, an efficient framework that integrates lightweight pixel‑space generative modeling into feed‑forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction to model scene uncertainty. Context observations are encoded once into a scene latent representation, which conditions generative decoding from noisy target views to produce a shared 3D Gaussian representation. We formulate this process using pixel‑space flow matching, enabling end‑to‑end optimization of 3D reconstruction with direct pixel‑space generative supervision through differentiable rendering. This avoids VAE‑based latent compression and error propagation inherent in previous two‑stage pipelines. To preserve feed‑forward efficiency, PixGR caches the scene representation and performs iterative inference using a lightweight DiT decoder. Experiments demonstrate that PixGR outperforms regression‑based approaches in challenging sparse‑view settings, particularly with widely spaced observations and view extrapolation. Meanwhile, it maintains sub‑second inference and remains competitive with substantially heavier pretrained generative models. Our project page is available at https://ranrhuang.github.io/pixgr/.

PaperId: 75, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31897.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianxiang Xia, Kai Lion, Niao He, Michael Muehlebach, Melanie Zeilinger, Hao Ma
Title: Learning Structured Sparsity for Large Models: Bridging Model Compressibility and Efficient Inference
Abstract:
Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse‑plus‑low‑rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S‑SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low‑rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware‑compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget‑aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S‑SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

PaperId: 76, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31855.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Damian Hattler, Qiang Liu, Nils Thuerey
Title: Cautious Conflict-Free Inverse Gradient Methods
Abstract:
Partial differential equations (PDEs) are indispensable tools for modeling complex phenomena in physics and engineering. Physics‑Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful alternative to traditional numerical solvers by directly incorporating physical constraints into neural network loss functions. Despite their advantages, PINN training requires multi‑objective optimization, which often leads to significant gradient conflicts among boundary, initial, and residual loss terms. The Conflict‑Free Inverse Gradient (ConFIG) method addresses these conflicts; however, integrating ConFIG with adaptive optimizers such as Adam introduces a critical vulnerability: the conflict‑free direction generated by ConFIG is further processed by the optimizer, and the resulting weight update may no longer be conflict‑free with respect to the task gradients. To address this issue, Cautious ConFIG is proposed as a concise three‑line extension to the ConFIG algorithm that empirically restores the conflict‑freeness guarantee prior to the weight update. The method is evaluated on three PINN benchmarks: the 1D Viscous Burgers' equation, the 1D Nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and the 2D Kovasznay flow. Experimental results demonstrate consistent performance improvements over the standard ConFIG baseline. Additionally, the stabilizing effect of cautious masking and its reaction to conflict severity, task number, and optimizer lag are investigated using a simple toy system.

PaperId: 77, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31854.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Jialei Li, Dingxian Wang, Xiaoyan Zhao, Yimeng Bai, Xuanyi Zhu, Yang Zhang, Chao Yin, Wentao Shi, Ganesh Prabhu, Karthik Gomadam Rajagopal, Brett Levert, Darvin Yi, Andrew Rabinovich, Zhao Chen
Title: SWE-Clar: Can Coding Agents Clarify Incomplete Client Requirements and Deliver Greenfield Software?
Abstract:
Greenfield software development in freelance settings requires coding agents to turn incomplete client requests into working software. This makes requirement clarification essential, yet clients may be unable to provide continuous feedback over long development cycles, and receiving their answers does not guarantee correct understanding of complex requirements. These challenges motivate two benchmark design choices: clarification precedes code implementation, and its effectiveness is assessed through explicit tests of requirement understanding. Guided by these choices, we introduce SWE‑Clar, a benchmark grounded in real, high‑value client commissions to evaluate requirement clarification and code implementation in this setting. It comprises 100 tasks based on real software development jobs on Upwork, each with at least US\4,000 in total payments. Each task begins with multi‑round interaction between a coding agent and a client agent, followed by separate runs for code implementation with acceptance testing and clarification assessment. For the latter, we construct 512 questions paired with reference answers from real client‑freelancer interactions, covering both explicitly stated requirements and those inferred from the conversational context. Both runs begin from the same clarification context but remain isolated, preventing assessment questions from guiding code implementation. Experiments with nine frontier models show that even GPT‑6 Astra, which has the highest observed implementation score, achieves a task pass rate of only 67%, underscoring the challenge of independent software delivery in this setting. The dataset and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/upwork/SWE‑Clar.

PaperId: 78, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31852.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Youyuan Long, Gokhan Solak, Arash Ajoudani
Title: Multimodal MPC via Bayesian Set Optimization for Dynamic Manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects
Abstract:
Dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects (DLOs) remains challenging due to underactuated, high‑dimensional dynamics, delayed deformation responses, and the presence of multiple feasible motions under obstacle constraints. This paper presents BM2PC, a Bayesian Multimodal MPC framework for agile manipulation of DLOs. Building on the control‑as‑inference posterior, BM2PC formulates multimodal planning as a set optimization problem that balances control quality and behavioral diversity. An efficient incremental update maintains multiple promising control modes with low additional computational overhead. For real‑world deployment, BM2PC incorporates an execution dynamics model that predicts actual end‑effector motion and compensates for execution mismatch during fast manipulation. We evaluate BM2PC on rope tracking and obstacle avoidance in simulation and hardware, and on simulated disturbance rejection. In trajectory tracking, BM2PC generalizes better to unseen trajectories than a learning‑based baseline without task‑specific policy training or fine‑tuning. Real‑world experiments demonstrate accurate long‑horizon tracking, reducing RMSE by 44.0% on the longest task. In obstacle avoidance, BM2PC achieves comparable performance to existing multimodal MPC methods while reducing planning time by 29% to 66%. These results demonstrate accurate dynamic control and efficient multimodal planning within a unified MPC framework. The core implementation of BM2PC and supplementary videos are available at https://github.com/Longyouyuan/BM2PC.

PaperId: 79, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31841.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiao Tan, Yixuan Wang, Zhexi Wang, Wenzhen Yuan
Title: FORCA: A Force-Aware Coding Agent for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
Abstract:
Coding agents can translate language instructions into robot programs. For contact‑rich manipulation, a key challenge is to generate and refine control logic that responds to physical interaction. We present FORCA, a coding agent that takes visual observations and wrist force/torque (F/T) measurements as input to write Python programs for contact probing and force‑responsive motion. Between executions, the agent inspects force records alongside visual outcomes to diagnose failures and revise both motion and force‑feedback control logic. FORCA requires no demonstrations, task‑specific training, or simulation. Across five real‑robot tasks, we demonstrate its effectiveness in three forms of contact‑rich manipulation: improving manipulation accuracy, adapting to changes in object or surface properties, and regulating contact under surface variation and object motion. Compared with a vision‑only variant of the same agent, FORCA improves grasp accuracy and task success and reduces contact loss in wiping and peeling.

PaperId: 80, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31835.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Jiaxi Liu, Keshu Wu, Weizhe Tang, Bofeng Cao, Sikai Chen, Xiaopeng Li, Steven T. Parker, Bin Ran
Title: SAGE: A hybrid vision-language and geometry framework for work-zone pathway prediction under temporary traffic control
Abstract:
Temporary traffic control redirects vehicles through work zones, requiring automated vehicles to connect an interpretation of the visible devices to a continuous passing path. Geometric predictors can provide several plausible paths, yet selecting the one consistent with the temporary control remains difficult. We propose SAGE (Semantic‑to‑Action Grounded Execution), a read‑decide‑execute‑check framework that separates path construction, path preference, and control compliance within a shared candidate space. The central idea is to use a vision‑language model's (VLM's) trajectory as a preference over intact geometric candidates. A role‑decoupled generator constructs the candidates, and rank fusion combines each candidate's geometric score with its agreement with the VLM trajectory. Supervision structured around the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) trains SAGE‑VLM to state the lane status and hazard side before its passage decision and trajectory. The predicted hazard side enters image‑space predicates derived from MUTCD provisions, which support a final intervention bounded in score and displacement. On 2,306 real‑world ROADWork validation episodes, the candidates include a path within 10 px of the human demonstration in 87% of episodes, yet selection regret accounts for 53% of the geometric ranker's error. SAGE reduces average and final displacement errors by 8.3% and 12.0% relative to the ranker, mostly in the far field, and hard‑constraint violations by 37%. The trajectory opinion improves all four tested generator‑selector combinations. SAGE is comparable to state‑of‑the‑art VLM modules in accuracy, with a faster‑responding VLM, and outperforms four other adapted driving VLMs in displacement error and safety measures. Project page: https://hhjj233.github.io/SAGE‑page/.

PaperId: 81, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31833.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Peter Potash
Title: Latent Coherence: Do Frontier Language Models' Probability Judgments Obey the Law of Total Probability?
Abstract:
LawZero's Scientist AI trains a Predictor toward the Bayesian posterior, with an objective that penalizes inconsistent probabilities among latent explanations. We ask whether current frontier language models, with no such training, are already consistent in this sense zero‑shot: do their probability judgments satisfy the law of total probability, P(X)=\sum_z P(z)P(X|z), when the latent z must be inferred from records in the context? In separate single‑turn calls, models are asked for P(X), for P(z) over the latent's states, and for P(X|z); a causal family applies the same test to P(y|do(x)) and the back‑door adjustment. Every query has an exact ground‑truth probability, and a subset of items is asked in three wordings to separate persistent incoherence from rewording noise. Across seven models, GPT‑6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 are the most coherent (mean absolute residual 0.08 and 0.12 log‑odds, about 2 percentage points). Claude Haiku 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash and DeepSeek V4‑Pro show persistent incoherence (0.27‑0.35 log‑odds) that is mostly item‑specific rather than a shared offset. Within every model, larger residuals go with larger errors against the truth (Spearman 0.40‑0.62), so the residual, which needs no ground truth, flags unreliable answers. Reasoning length does not predict coherence, across models or within a model across rewordings of the same question. Simple consistency checks pass almost everywhere; the failures are specific to reasoning through a latent variable. Code and data: https://github.com/ppotash/latent‑coherence

PaperId: 82, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31821.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Omar Farouk Zouak, Selma Mani, Larbi Said Chikh, Raid Abderrezak Ouahioune
Title: What the Query Remembers: Query Abstraction Governs Lexical and Dense Retrieval of Classical Arabic Poetry
Abstract:
How well a poetry archive can be searched depends on what the user still remembers, not only on what the model understands. We show this for Classical Arabic poetry, benchmarking nine dense encoders and BM25 over two corpora, three indexing modes and two evaluation protocols. Which retriever wins is governed by how much of a poem's wording the query still carries. On tip‑of‑the‑tongue queries BM25 leads every dense encoder, including an 8B state‑of‑the‑art model (0.746 vs. 0.717 Recall@5); on abstract queries it falls to eighth out of ten (0.392 vs. 0.748). Editing the wording of the same queries shows that this ranking largely reflects query composition: adding one remembered half‑verse raises BM25 by 38 points, rewriting the quoted words by hand leaves BM25 level with the 8B encoder, and BM25's sensitivity to remembered wording is significantly steeper than that of the strongest dense encoder. The same axis controls explanation augmentation, whose effect swings from +37 to ‑39 points. The mechanism splits by system type: lexical containment predicts BM25's behaviour, while embedding proximity predicts dense encoders. Finally, the field's two standard protocols, known‑item retrieval and thematic relevance, dissociate on the same systems, a result reproduced by two blind human annotators and by two open‑weights judges, one of them under a rubric with no literal‑match criterion. A benchmark that reports one protocol, or one query register, can give a materially wrong picture. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ellzo/what‑the‑query‑remembers.

PaperId: 83, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31818.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianzhe Chu, Druv Pai, Yi Ma
Title: Nested Sparsity for Scalable Pretraining and Continual Learning
Abstract:
Mixture‑of‑experts (MoE) transformers, the standard backbone for modern large‑scale deep learning, employ conditional computation: only a sparse subset of model weights is used in each forward pass. In MoE transformers, this sparsity arises in the MoE operator, which generalizes the multi‑layer perceptron in the classical transformer. In this work, we explore an alternative mechanism for conditional computation that analogously generalizes the attention operator. The sparsity induced by this mechanism naturally nests (i.e., hierarchically composes) with the sparsity induced by the MoE operator. We show that a transformer employing this nested sparsity mechanism, which we call Nestor, performs better than a conventional MoE transformer at equal compute and equal sparsity in language model pretraining. We also show that Nestor is well‑suited for continual pretraining: it can be adapted to longer contexts more effectively than conventional MoEs, as well as adapt more efficiently to new domains while forgetting less on old domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length grow. Our results demonstrate the potential of alternative conditional computation mechanisms for deep neural network architectures. Code and checkpoints are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Ma‑Lab‑Berkeley/Nestor .

PaperId: 84, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31810.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiyuan Tan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Jose Blanchet
Title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
Abstract:
Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean‑based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean‑verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan‑Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.

PaperId: 85, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31803.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaopeng Zhang, Luzhe Sun, Yiqing Xu, Matthew R. Walter
Title: StackGen3D: Stable 3D Block Stack Generation from Multiview Silhouettes
Abstract:
Generating physically stable 3D structures from visual specifications requires resolving geometric ambiguity while accounting for physical interactions among objects. We present StackGen3D, a framework for generating stable block assemblies conditioned on a given block inventory and three orthographic silhouettes. Our approach consists of two stages. First, we develop a physics‑informed graph neural network (PI‑GNN) that models support relations between blocks and serves as a fast stability predictor for curating a diverse dataset of stable structures. Second, we train a conditional flow‑matching model on this dataset to capture the multimodal distribution of block configurations consistent with the target silhouettes. At inference time, lightweight geometric selection and refinement reduce inter‑block penetration without physics simulation. Preliminary experiments show that the PI‑GNN generalizes from simple stacks to complex structures substantially better than a parameter‑matched multilayer perceptron. For structure generation, Best‑of‑10 selection improves physical stability from 45.3% to 72.4% while achieving a silhouette IoU of 0.970. These results highlight the potential of combining relational physical reasoning, scalable data curation, and conditional generative modeling for creative 3D assembly. Project website: [https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D‑web/](https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D‑web/)

PaperId: 86, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31801.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shuangyu Xie, Kaiyuan Chen, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Richard Cheng, Sergey Zakharov, Ken Goldberg
Title: KiRoSe: Using Kinematic Data for Efficient Segmentation of Robot Demonstrations
Abstract:
Segmenting robot demonstration data into disjoint temporal and semantic subsegments is valuable for learning, cleaning, retrieval, and analysis. Segmentation is often performed manually in a tedious and error prone process. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have the potential for automating this process, but directly ingesting raw multi camera video streams into MLLMs can be costly and can quickly exhaust context windows. In this paper, we introduce KiRoSe (Kinematics for Robot Segmentation), a novel framework that focuses on the companion stream of robot kinematic data. Inspired by the principle of classical entropy coding, such as Huffman coding, where frequently occurring symbols are represented more compactly, we propose Sparse Motion Tokens (SMTs), a discrete kinematic vocabulary designed to compactly represent recurring, temporally localized motion patterns, which we refer to as kinematic events. SMTs are learned by encoding kinematic trajectories with temporal segment supervision and quantizing the resulting features. We use increasingly available robot demonstration subtask annotations to supervise an open language model to interpret the resulting token sequences. Evaluation against human labeled segmentation shows that KiRoSe can substantially outperform baseline segmentation methods in F1 quality and transfers zero shot to unseen robot embodiments and egocentric human motion, while preserving the language models open vocabulary knowledge. Beyond segmentation, KiRoSe tracks task progress on an unseen robot and detects when an action is being reversed.(website: https://berkeleyautomation.github.io/kirose/)

PaperId: 87, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31765.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Farhad G. Zanjani, Animesh Karnewar, Fatih Porikli, Amirhossein Habibian
Title: SyncVid: World-Equivariant Diffusion for Synchronized Video Generation
Abstract:
Generating multiple videos of a dynamic scene from a single reference video requires synthesizing both observed and unobserved content consistently across viewpoints. Existing camera‑control methods for video diffusion typically rely on architectural mechanisms, including camera embeddings, cross‑view attention, and geometric conditioning. Although effective for static scene content, these approaches often struggle with the fine‑grained, dynamic geometry that must remain coherent across views and over time. We synchronize the diffusion process itself by sampling the Gaussian noise prior in a canonical 3D space derived from the source video and rasterizing it into target cameras, rather than sampling independently in each 2D image plane. Our method, SyncVid, lifts a monocular video into a canonical 4D representation, associates noise with scene geometry and unseen space, and rasterizes the resulting structured noise into arbitrary views. Because rendering can introduce local correlations, we further propose a cross‑view‑consistent whitening procedure that decorrelates neighboring pixels while preserving correspondence across views. The structured noise serves as the diffusion prior for a LoRA‑adapted pretrained video diffusion model, requiring no architectural modifications. By enforcing spatiotemporal and cross‑view coherence at the source of stochasticity, SyncVid generates synchronized videos and improves both perceptual quality and cross‑view consistency in our experiments. Project page: https://qualcomm‑ai‑research.github.io/SyncVid‑Webpage.

PaperId: 88, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31762.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiawei Chen, Yinxi Wang, Zihan Yang, Meijun Gao, Yaowei Liu, Shuming Zhang, Zecheng Li, Xiangju Mi, Yuxuan Liu, Runzhong Huang, Tianlin Li, Xun Zhang, Zhengyang Wang, Xu Miao, Tong Yang
Title: See What I Need, Dream What I Want: A Navigation Foundation Model on a Self-Constructed Representation Space
Abstract:
What visual representation should a navigation policy act on? Navigation policies built on vision foundation models largely leave representation design to the encoders' pretraining objectives. We present RepresentNav, a navigation foundation model built on a self‑constructed representation space: a visual representation constructed by the policy's own objectives from vision foundation models. RepresentNav builds this space with Representation Residuals, a compact three‑layer transformer that attends over features spanning the full depth of multiple complementary vision foundation models, so that the policy learns to see what it needs for navigation. In the same space it dreams what it wants: before every action a latent chain‑of‑thought predicts the representation of the scene a moment ahead. The dream is trained end‑to‑end with the policy as a joint‑embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), with a next‑representation prediction loss and a regularizer on its targets. RepresentNav sets a new state of the art on VLNVerse, VLN‑CE R2R, EVT‑Bench, and two point‑goal benchmarks, and its gains carry over to a physical robot amid clutter and moving people. On VLNVerse fine‑grained, RepresentNav achieves 83.80% success, outperforming the previous state of the art by 20.05 percentage points, and on EVT‑Bench distracted tracking it reaches 85.5% with a single camera (+10.1). With the same encoders, the self‑constructed space clearly outperforms concatenating their outputs and learns to weight their layers unevenly, and a dream in it cuts collisions by a quarter. A single dreamed latent decodes into the depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy of the scene a moment ahead, more accurately than pretrained encoders applied to the real future frame, although occupancy is never supervised, and the rollout tracks the robot's own motion over the next second: the dream emerges as a compact latent world model.

PaperId: 89, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31747.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhuoyuan Jiang, Weijie Lyu, Xiaoyuan Wang, Tiancheng Shen, Ming-Hsuan Yang
Title: AudioLift: Audio-Driven Single Image to Full-Head Gaussian Avatar via Multi-view Video Generation
Abstract:
Existing 3D talking avatar methods mainly rely on parametric face models including 3DMM or FLAME, whose compact motion representations limit their ability to synthesize extreme expressions and to model accessories such as headwear. We introduce AudioLift, a two‑stage framework that uses generated multi‑view videos as the intermediate representation for audio‑driven avatar generation without parametric face models or per‑instance optimization. Our framework combines a synchronized multi‑view video generation stage with an inconsistency‑robust Gaussian reconstruction stage to recover coherent full‑head geometry from a single portrait image. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AudioLift produces 3D talking avatars capable of capturing more extreme facial expressions than existing methods, with improved geometric completeness and strong multi‑view consistency across the full 360^\circ viewing range.

PaperId: 90, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31743.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mingxiu Cai, Haoyang Xian, Xinyu Ma, Yutong Wang, Zhenxi Song, Jing Li, Xuebo Liu
Title: Not Every Agent Needs the Strongest Model: Unified Prompt-Model Optimization for Heterogeneous LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
Abstract:
Large language model (LLM)‑based multi‑agent systems (MAS) rely on role‑specific prompts and execution models to solve complex tasks collaboratively. However, prompt optimization typically keeps model assignments fixed, leaving differences in role requirements and their associated inference costs outside the search. We present UniMASO, a Unified framework for heterogeneous Multi‑Agent System Optimization through the joint adaptation of prompts and model assignments. UniMASO evaluates candidate updates through local, downstream, and global feedback, using cost‑aware Pareto search to retain useful quality‑cost trade‑offs. Topology‑aware co‑evolution then coordinates these updates according to agent roles and dependencies. Cross‑level trajectory memory further supplies historical successes and failures to guide subsequent optimization. Experiments on five benchmarks and five execution topologies show that UniMASO achieves competitive task performance at substantially lower deployment cost than the strongest homogeneous configurations. Under centralized execution, it improves the average score from 69.79 to 70.40 while reducing token‑weighted deployment cost by 85.2% relative to DeepSeek‑V4‑Pro with MASPO. These results support joint prompt‑model adaptation as an effective approach to efficient multi‑agent collaboration. The code is available at https://github.com/Achilles008/UniMASO_main.

PaperId: 91, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31733.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qiang Fu, Xinyue Li, Andre Wibisono, Arman Cohan
Title: Learning to Be Monitored: Causal Bounds and Intervention-Aware Post-Training Recipes for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
Abstract:
Chain‑of‑thought (CoT) monitoring aims to detect potentially harmful behaviors in large language models (LLMs) from their CoTs. Intervention‑based evaluations measure this property by asking whether a monitor can detect the role of an intervention from the CoT when the targeted behavior occurs, typically using minimal‑criterion sensitivity (\mathsfTPR_mc) proposed by~\citepguan2025monitoring. However, a target behavior observed under intervention is not necessarily caused by it, and we show that this metric can overestimate how often a monitor detects target behaviors actually caused by the intervention. Specifically, we establish \mathsfTPR_mc as an upper bound on this causal detection rate and derive a complementary lower bound, which provides a tighter evaluation framework for CoT monitorability. With this framework, we study whether LLMs can be trained to make their CoTs easier to monitor. We first construct a training dataset of paired control‑‑intervention tasks spanning multiple intervention types. Using the dataset, we design and apply three intervention‑specific training methods based on off‑policy self‑distillation, reinforcement learning, and on‑policy self‑distillation to train separate variants of each base model. Across various model‑monitor configurations, all three methods generally improve CoT monitorability over the corresponding base models under our extended evaluation framework. Our code is available at https://github.com/xinyue‑lxy/learning‑to‑be‑monitored.

PaperId: 92, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31719.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhe Zhang
Title: Two-colour crossing minimization in complete geometric graphs is NP-hard
Abstract:
Given a fixed straight‑line drawing of a complete graph, we seek a two‑colouring of its edges that minimizes the number of monochromatic crossing pairs. We prove that the threshold decision problem is NP‑complete, even when the vertices are in general position and have integer coordinates of polynomial binary length. Thus exact minimization is NP‑hard, answering the complexity question posed at the Crossing Number Workshop in 2019. The reduction is from MaxCut on permutation graphs. Its main difficulty is to control the edges required by completeness, whose colours must remain free. We construct a large comparison grid with two stable colour phases and use additional points to assign costs to the edges that encode the source graph. A geometric separation eliminates one large class of unwanted crossings. The costs of all remaining edges are included in a computable baseline and bounded errors, with each unit of the source objective amplified beyond the total error. The construction is deterministic and has polynomial size and coordinate bit length.

PaperId: 93, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31718.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Dennis Heijmans, H. Çağrı Bilgi, Rui Wang, Kubilay Atasu
Title: Towards Adversarially Robust Multigraph Neural Networks for Financial Crime Analysis
Abstract:
Financial transaction networks are naturally represented as multigraphs, where repeated transactions between the same pair of accounts are modeled as distinct edges.
