Recently proposed multigraph neural network architectures leverage this structure explicitly to achieve a strong performance on anti‑money laundering (AML) tasks. However, their robustness to adversaries that manipulate transaction structures to evade detection remains largely unexplored. We present the first scalable framework for structural attacks and adversarial training of multigraph neural networks using node‑edge incidence matrices, adapting projected gradient descent and projected randomized block coordinate descent methods to optimize structural perturbations over such matrices. We further introduce a cycle‑based regularizer that penalizes changes in the global counts of directed 2‑ and 3‑cycles, providing a structural measure of attack plausibility. Experiments on synthetic pattern‑detection and realistic AML datasets show that our learned attacks substantially outperform non‑learnable perturbation baselines in reducing detection performance (PR‑AUC), while adversarial training consistently improves robustness against these attacks. These results demonstrate that multigraph neural networks are vulnerable to learned structural attacks and that adversarial training provides an effective defense. Our code is available at https://github.com/denheijmans/robust_multignn.

PaperId: 94, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31710.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ruopei Sun, Jianfeng Cai, Kangwen Zhao, Wengang Zhou, Houqiang Li
Title: Compact-Bench: Measuring What Context Compaction Costs Long-Horizon Coding Agents
Abstract:
Context compaction lets long‑horizon coding agents continue beyond their context windows, but can erase the state needed to finish a task. Prior evaluations measure efficiency, retained information, or end‑to‑end success, leaving the effect of a specific history replacement difficult to isolate. Compact‑Bench pairs full‑history and summary‑only continuations from a shared repository state, and evaluates recurring details and successive production compactions. It covers 35 SWE‑bench repairs, 146 agentic sessions, and 106 production chains. Across 14 summarizer backbones, stable damage ranges from 5‑64% of 22 full‑history successes: Claude Opus 4.8 preserves the most repairs, while DeepSeek‑Flash damages the most. With Kimi‑K3 as summarizer, the Kimi Code prompt preserves the most task continuations (19/22), whereas Claude Code retains the most recurring details (15.0%). LLM summaries retain at most 16.0% of recurring details, compared with 79.1% for mechanical extraction; production summaries retain 15.7% at the first boundary. Failures recur across methods: one repair is damaged by 13/14 backbones, and another by all 5 prompts. These results show that reliable compaction requires preserving the progress needed to complete a task, and that retaining relevant information alone does not ensure successful continuation. Code is available at https://github.com/cai‑jianfeng/compact‑bench and data is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/caijanfeng/compact‑bench.

PaperId: 95, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31695.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Utkarsh Kanwat
Title: Fooling LLM Safety Guards into Judging the Wrong Text
Abstract:
Safety guards check content before an LLM application acts on it, and most paste that content into a plain‑text prompt. Content that imitates the prompt can append a second task, and the guard answers that one instead. We call this target rebinding. Our explanation is that the guard grades the last complete task in its input, here a harmless decoy, so the harmful request goes through unchanged. In a pre‑registered test, an appended forged query and decoy clear all 75 held‑out AdvBench requests that Shieldstral‑1.0‑3B flags. The guard is not persuaded: a directive to ignore the text above clears none of them, and in a follow‑up run a harmful decoy stops the attack. On our GuardRebind benchmark, each of five guards has an attack family, chosen per guard, that clears at least 93% of its flagged items. Rebinding explains this best on Shieldstral and gpt‑oss‑safeguard; on ShieldGemma and Llama Guard 3, generic evasion and trailing text respectively do part of the work, and Qwen3Guard falls mainly to a forgery of its whole task. Training the guard to score content no lower than its most harmful part cuts attack success from 75% to 0.8‑1.6% on attack families, decoys and forged queries held out of training. All of these attacks append the forged structure after the request, and we added the held‑out‑decoy evaluation after a first round of test runs. Clean AUROC falls by at most 0.01, but our test of non‑inferiority is inconclusive. A score‑guided search still beats this trained guard on 47 of 50 items, usually by placing forged structure before the request. On about half of the items where the search wins, the same search also finds benign text, with no forged structure, that clears the guard.

PaperId: 96, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31686.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianda Sun, Dimitar Kazakov
Title: From Target Selection to Condition Reuse: Auditing Residual Interventions in Tool-Use Models
Abstract:
Activation interventions can make a language model produce a target answer, but can the model use the intended condition in other computations? We study this question in Qwen3.5‑27B on tool‑use tasks where time or permissions determine eligibility and selection. Across 32 fresh worlds, two case‑specific residual‑writing variants raise familiar target‑selection correctness from 35/128 to 119/128 and from 33/128 to 114/128. Yet these gains disappear when familiar facts and identifiers are recombined within the same selection task, while selection of previously rewarded identifiers increases. The gains persist across output formats but yield little improvement in independent judgments about whether a candidate is eligible or should be selected. Internal edits can nevertheless change how a source fact affects a judgment: in a prespecified secondary comparison, an early‑layer source patch changes 50/64 judgments when that source is used, with one adverse change among 64 cases where it is not. This selective effect does not ensure correct complete actions. Together, these results separate target‑selection control, condition‑sensitive judgments, and complete‑action correctness. Evaluating how an edited state is used, rather than only its trained answer, exposes these differences.

PaperId: 97, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31671.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qiwen Gu, Xin Zhou, Xiwu Chen, Zhongyang Zhu, Zhuo Zhang, Junqiao Zhao
Title: A Unified Framework for Image-to-3D Part Generation via Variable Granularity
Abstract:
Controllable 3D part generation is pivotal for digital asset creation, yet existing methods lack the flexibility to accommodate diverse user workflows requiring varying levels of control. In this paper, we introduce FlexPart, a unified image‑to‑3D part generation framework that supports variable‑granularity geometric conditions within a single model. By seamlessly integrating heterogeneous inputs, ranging from sparse points to dense bounding boxes and masks, via gated adaptive modulation, FlexPart unlocks a powerful cross‑modal synergy. We also propose an asymmetric geometric guidance mechanism that leverages strong spatial priors to align representations across granularities, improving geometric consistency and facilitating inter‑task synergy. Under mask conditioning on PartVerseXL, FlexPart reduces Part CD by 16.6% relative to TripoSG + SAM3D and by 10.5% relative to OmniPart, while maintaining competitive whole‑mesh quality. The code can be found at https://github.com/Gucci233/FlexPart

PaperId: 98, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31670.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yunfei Xie, Howard H. Qian, Shiyi Lan, Kaiyu Hang, Chen Wei
Title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
Abstract:
Robot foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed‑loop rollouts, motivating low‑cost offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To test this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment (S^2), a training‑free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that S^2 correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families, making it a low‑cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed‑loop evaluation. S^2 can also identify promising vision‑language model (VLM) backbones before costly fine‑tuning into vision‑language‑action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, S^2 offers representation‑level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With S^2, we extend PRH to robotics and make sensorimotor alignment measurable, offering a low‑cost, representation‑level view of robot foundation models that closed‑loop success rates alone cannot reveal.

PaperId: 99, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31668.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shengqiong Wu, Meng Luo, Bobo Li, Ziwei Liu, Shuicheng Yan, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Philip Torr, Hao Fei
Title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
Abstract:
Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip‑level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.

PaperId: 100, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31651.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ava Pun, Kevin Dai, Sally Chen, Maxwell Jones, Ruixuan Liu, Kangle Deng, Changliu Liu, Maneesh Agrawala, Deva Ramanan, Jun-Yan Zhu
Title: BrickWright: Agentic Creation of Physically Feasible Brick Builds
Abstract:
Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre‑trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT‑6 Luna) to 69% (GPT‑6 Astra), BrickWright‑guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text‑to‑brick task. Code is available on our project page: https://avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright/

PaperId: 101, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31649.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Xiaolin Li, Zihao Huang, Fanpeng Meng, Chen Yang, Guanjun Wu, Kai Zhang, Jiemin Fang, Qi Tian
Title: Gate3DGen: A Pre-processing Model that Selectively Purifies Real-World Images for 3D Generation
Abstract:
Single‑image 3D generation has achieved high fidelity on curated benchmarks, yet degrades sharply on real‑world images with uneven illumination, blur, and occlusions. Purifying such inputs requires deciding when to intervene and preserving the visual cues needed for 3D generation, while leaving clean inputs unchanged. We introduce Gate3DGen, a selective pre‑processing model that gates image inputs to existing 3D generators without retraining them. A degradation‑aware router bypasses inputs classified as clean and extracts features to guide purification of the remaining inputs. Conditioned on these features, a 3D‑oriented one‑step purifier purifies degraded inputs with spatial losses that encourage preservation of object identity, contours, and textural cues. To provide paired supervision, we construct a synthetic data engine that renders clean views of 3D assets and synthesises composite degradations. On the synthetic benchmark, the purifier improves image fidelity and downstream 3D geometry in only 2.3s on average, reducing TRELLIS.2 mesh distance by 61.5% relative to degraded inputs. VLM evaluation and human preferences on real photographs further support identity preservation and degradation correction. More demos and code are available at https://supra‑3d.github.io/gate3dgen.

PaperId: 102, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31645.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Namitha Guruprasad, Abhay Yadav, Cheng Peng, Rama Chellappa, Anand Bhattad
Title: OmniRay: Camera-Agnostic Monocular 3D Reconstruction with Composite Ray Fields
Abstract:
Monocular models recover 3D geometry from a single image in one pass, but most assume a pinhole camera and produce distorted geometry on the wide‑angle imagery produced by fisheye and panoramic lenses. Camera‑aware models remove this assumption by predicting a per‑pixel ray field. However, they represent different camera geometries using a single fixed basis to capture both the overall camera projection and its finer variations. We argue that camera geometry can be viewed as having a hierarchy of complexity for representing rays. We present OmniRay, a feed‑forward model whose Ray Module is composed of three components: a monotone radial base that captures radially symmetric structure, a spherical‑harmonic residual for smooth deviations from it, and a free‑form residual for remaining local variation. These components are composed as successive rotations on the sphere, allowing the representation to accommodate diverse camera geometries. Given a single image, OmniRay predicts a ray direction and an up‑to‑scale radial distance for every pixel, from which a 3D point cloud is recovered without needing camera information at inference time. Extensive experiments across different camera configurations demonstrate that OmniRay establishes a new state‑of‑the‑art in camera‑agnostic monocular 3D reconstruction.

PaperId: 103, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31644.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Matteo Fusconi, Alex Costanzino, Pierluigi Zama Ramirez, Luigi Di Stefano
Title: GigaBench: Benchmarking Learnable Representations for Gigapixel Image Compression and Super-Resolution
Abstract:
Learnable Representations (LRs) can fit parametric families of functions to diverse kinds of signals. These emergent neural‑native data formats are gathering interest in the scientific community due to their compactness, resolution‑agnosticism and amenability to direct neural processing. On the other hand, gigapixel images are becoming increasingly widespread across a variety of scientific, cultural, and industrial domains. In this paper, we present GigaBench, the first benchmark and experimental evaluation focused on deploying LRs with gigapixel imagery. GigaBench includes images collected, acquired, and synthetically rendered across diverse domains, and addresses image compression and super‑resolution. We adapt a representative set of LRs, spanning Implicit, Hybrid, and Explicit methods, so as to operate reliably at the gigapixel scale on consumer hardware. Through systematic evaluation across reconstruction quality, model size, compression and inference times, we identify consistent trends across methods and suggest actionable guidance for future investigation.

PaperId: 104, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31635.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zunnan Xu, Shangchen Zhou, Yihang Luo, Chen Change Loy
Title: HiP3R: Hierarchical Pose Graphs for Long-Horizon 3D Reconstruction
Abstract:
Feed‑forward models accurately estimate camera motion and 3D geometry from short video windows. However, computational and memory costs prevent direct inference on sequences containing thousands of frames. Long videos must therefore be processed as overlapping chunks. This division produces independent local reconstructions with inconsistent coordinate frames and duplicate estimates of shared cameras. Achieving global consistency requires propagating constraints from adjacent overlaps and distant revisits across the sequence. This requirement naturally motivates pose graph optimization. However, the choice of graph level creates a trade‑off. Chunk‑level graphs efficiently resolve scale drift and close large loops. Yet, their rigid transformations cannot correct internal errors or conflicting frame predictions. Conversely, frame‑level optimization offers local flexibility, but scaling it globally is computationally expensive and can break metric scale. HiP3R resolves this trade‑off using a hierarchical pose graph. HiP3R first optimizes a robust chunk‑level \mathrmSim(3) graph to establish the global layout and scale. It then holds this layout fixed and estimates one shared \mathrmSE(3) camera per frame, turning overlapping window predictions into a single trajectory. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of HiP3R in improving camera trajectories and 3D reconstruction. Our method applies to both chunk‑based and streaming backends without additional training or fine‑tuning. The codes are available at https://kkakkkka.github.io/HiP3R.

PaperId: 105, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31625.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Matteo Frascarelli, Lucia Pallottino, Alberto Landi
Title: Extending Harmonic Function Methods via Root Locus for Coordinated Path Generation
Abstract:
We consider the offline generation of coordinated paths for N interchangeable robots and N goals in planar environments with polygonal obstacles. After a conformal map to a circular domain, starts and goals become the poles and zeros of a rational function R, and the paths are the branches of its Generalized Root Locus (GRL), i.e. the streamlines of the logarithmic potential log R. We show that, for every phase outside a finite set of critical phases and a set of boundary phases, the induced gradient motion drives each robot to a distinct goal along pairwise disjoint paths that never reach the obstacles; the robot‑goal assignment is produced by the construction, and with the gain used as a clock all robots move as the closed‑loop roots of the GRL and arrive together at a prescribed time. Obstacles become streamlines through successive Milne‑Thomson reflections, and for a finite number of reflections a finite test certifies safety for the potential that is actually computed. Reciprocal root‑locus planning is recovered as a special case. The method is illustrated on two polygonal workspaces, 100 random instances compared with independent harmonic planning and artificial potentials, and a scene with ten robots and ten obstacles.

PaperId: 106, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31623.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jinyu Zhang, Haitao Lin, Jiashu Hou, Xiangyang Xue, Yanwei Fu
Title: F2G-Pose: Geometry-Aware Foundation Feature Lifting for Direct RGB-D Category-Level Object Pose Estimation
Abstract:
This paper studies category‑level RGB‑D object pose estimation, which recovers an object's 3D rotation and translation without instance‑specific CAD models or reference views. This task is highly ambiguous due to intra‑class variations, symmetries, and partial observations. Current solutions struggle to balance reliability and efficiency: methods based on intermediate structures are prone to error propagation, while diffusion models suffer from high inference latency and complex post‑hoc candidate extraction. To address this, we present F2G‑Pose, a real‑time direct, single‑pass framework that predicts category‑level pose, metric size, and camera‑frame completed shape from a single RGB‑D observation in one feed‑forward pass. F2G‑Pose lifts dense visual foundation features to partial point clouds, encodes local geometry with DGCNN tokenization, and integrates object‑level structure with a Mixture‑of‑Experts Transformer. Joint size prediction and camera‑frame shape completion encourage metric consistency through dense geometric supervision. With its task‑specific network trained only on pose‑annotated synthetic SOPE data and its frozen RADIO backbone externally pretrained, F2G‑Pose achieves state‑of‑the‑art accuracy on SOPE and ROPE while running at 28 FPS for pose‑only inference, and further demonstrates strong camera‑frame geometry on HouseCat6D and real‑object transfer on HANDAL. Analyses of latency, robustness, shape completion, and GenPose++ candidate behavior further demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of F2G‑Pose, with real‑world manipulation experiments demonstrating deployment potential under segmented RGB‑D inputs. The project page, code, and pretrained models are made available at https://jrryzh.github.io/F2G‑Pose/.

PaperId: 107, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31572.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Andrea Giuseppe Di Francesco, Rishabh Jain, Franco Maria Nardini, Nicola Tonellotto, Pietro Liò, Fabrizio Silvestri
Title: On the Token Collapse Phenomenon in Textual Graph Soft Prompting
Abstract:
Recent methods for injecting graph structure into LLM prompts include graph soft prompting, in which a graph neural network (GNN) learns graph‑specific tokens that capture relational information among entities in textual prompts. G‑Retriever combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal. We conduct an in‑depth analysis of G‑Retriever and uncover a pathological behavior we term token collapse. Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and both frozen and LoRA‑adapted models, G‑Retriever's graph tokens become almost indistinguishable across inputs. We provide evidence that the same failure is inherited by subsequent methods, even with multi‑token pooling. Under the standard setup, swapping a token with the dataset mean, a token from another example, or one derived from a corrupted graph produces no resolved answer‑level effect in accuracy. Moreover, a learned constant prompt that never accesses the graph matches or surpasses G‑Retriever on all three benchmarks. These findings indicate that, rather than conveying graph content as intended, the collapsed token functions primarily as a generic soft prompt. We also examine conditions linked to this collapse and propose a two‑stage procedure that yields non‑collapsed tokens while maintaining competitive performance in most cases. However, token variability alone does not prove that the model uses graph information: via interventions and decoding probes, we show that depending on the configuration, a token can reflect the question, an answer prior, or graph‑derived content that the LLM may or may not use. Overall, our results offer a practical approach to evaluating graph‑token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy alone. Code to reproduce our experiments is available at https://github.com/difra100/Token_Collapse_KGQA.

PaperId: 108, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31569.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yufeng Liu, Bohao Fan, Juntu Zhao, Xinyi Wang, Hang Yu, Wenzhuan Luo, Yingzhi Wang, Qinghai Li, Yingdong Hu, Junliang Guo, Richard Wang, Dequan Wang, Yang Gao, Cheng Ma
Title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models
Abstract:
Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions. However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine‑grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored. We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame‑level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions. Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine‑grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties. To enable status signal‑guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction. Extensive real‑world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.

PaperId: 109, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31566.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ilan Theodoro, Jordão Bragantini, Loïc A. Royer
Title: CellTrack-Bench: Microscopic Cell Tracking Benchmark for Vision-Language Models
Abstract:
Large language models have shown outstanding performance on text‑first tasks such as coding, math, and writing. Recent efforts are shifting models' training to include scientific problems that often live in highly specialized domains beyond text, such as protein structure and biological images. However, in these scenarios, their general‑purpose accuracy compared with specialized algorithms remains in question. One such domain is cell tracking, which requires spatiotemporal awareness of cell dynamics. To evaluate this, we created a new benchmark, CellTrack‑Bench, which assesses Vision‑Language Models' (VLMs) cell‑tracking‑related performance against specialized trackers. The full benchmark draws from 15 standard cell‑tracking datasets across four imaging modalities and comprises 1,537 problems corresponding to 9,041 cell‑linking decisions. We selected a hard subset requiring greater reasoning effort by identifying failures shared across distinct algorithmic trackers. With this proposed dataset, we: (i) evaluated different environment harnesses for VLMs; (ii) benchmarked 9 frontier closed‑source models and 13 open‑weight models; and (iii) provided a detailed analysis of their failure modes. Code, the stored model outputs, and a pipeline that regenerates the benchmark from the source datasets are available at https://github.com/royerlab/celltrack‑bench.

PaperId: 110, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31554.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhengyi Liu, Li Liu, Songtao Liu, Xianglong Liu, Xiangzhen Zhou, Mingyu Huang, Dingchao Gao, Shenggang Ying, Bolong Chen, Ji Guan
Title: ArcTN: Efficient Tensor-Network Contraction Planning for Quantum Circuit Simulation
Abstract:
Tensor‑network simulation of quantum circuits depends on contraction orders with low computational cost and small intermediate tensors, found without excessive planning time. We present ArcTN, a contraction‑order optimization framework with two search presets. Light keeps planning overhead low, and Heavy spends more effort on refinement. Both combine randomized‑greedy construction, subtree reconfiguration, and parallel tempering with stage‑specific stopping rules. ArcTN also provides Fixed and Dynamic slicing to meet tensor‑size limits and executes the returned orders. On the 30 QC32 quantum‑circuit networks completed by all eight compared configurations, Light reduces FLOPs by 61.32% and plans 1.62× faster than Cotengra Auto/CMA‑ES, and Heavy reduces FLOPs by 43.83% and plans 7.21× faster than Cotengra AutoHQ/Optuna. Heavy also needs 11.85% fewer FLOPs than OMECO TreeSA‑8 and plans 1.33× faster. Dynamic slicing meets the size limits in all 90 runs on 18 scalar‑output networks and reduces total sliced FLOPs by 31.99% relative to Fixed slicing, at the cost of longer planning. With a common NumPy executor, Heavy has the lowest combined planning and execution time among five configurations on the runs that all of them completed. On 672 networks built from 320 MQT Bench circuits, Heavy obtains the lowest geometric‑mean FLOPs on the 142 large networks while planning 3.1× and 31× faster than Cotengra AutoHQ and Hyper128.

PaperId: 111, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31538.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jihoon Hong, Alireza Kheirandish, Rohan Sanda, Sara Fridovich-Keil
Title: LACToS: Local Anomaly Detection via Conditional Typicality of Superpixels
Abstract:
Local anomaly detection is the task of identifying spatially confined anomalous or out‑of‑distribution (OOD) regions within an otherwise in‑distribution (ID) image. Most existing methods are designed for a specific context, with a strong focus on industrial defect detection, where they achieve excellent performance on well‑established benchmarks. However, we observe that these methods can exhibit significant performance drops in other contexts, especially when the inlier distribution is multimodal. To account for this inlier complexity, we propose LACToS, a principled local OOD detection method based on statistical typicality and made tractable through two innovations: (i) grouping pixels into superpixels and (ii) using a computationally efficient proxy to estimate typicality. We evaluate LACToS across three diverse applications spanning medical imaging, human faces, and X‑ray security screening. LACToS performs more robustly than prior methods across these benchmarks. The code is released here: https://github.com/voilalab/LACToS.

PaperId: 112, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31494.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Advait Gupta, Sachin Konan, Tom Yin, Gabriel Sarch, Zhuang Liu
Title: AgentVQA: A Unified Benchmark for Agentic Visual Understanding
Abstract:
Vision‑language models (VLMs) can perform a broad range of tasks across diverse settings, yet their performance in agentic contexts remains poorly understood. Although online evaluations in simulators and real‑world environments are essential for measuring interactive agent performance, they are costly and challenging to scale. Complementary offline VQA benchmarks can enable faster and more reliable comparisons across agentic domains, yet existing benchmarks remain limited and fragmented. To address this gap, we introduce AgentVQA, an offline benchmark for evaluating VLMs on realistic agentic scenarios across five agent domains: Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning. We build AgentVQA by manually selecting 1000 challenging, real‑world agent examples from 23 source datasets and adapting them for reliable offline evaluation. The resulting benchmark preserves realistic scenarios from interactive environments across diverse domains, and its model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations. Across the 22 evaluated models, the best achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Our cross‑domain analysis shows that errors are driven primarily by failures to ground and maintain accurate representations of the current and evolving visual state, including localizing relevant UI elements, interpreting motion, tracking state changes over time, and inferring 3D spatial relationships, rather than by task misinterpretation or downstream logical reasoning.

PaperId: 113, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31478.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Khaled Waleed Dawoud, Muhammad Zaigham Zaheer, Khan Muhammad, Muhammad Haris Khan
Title: MoG-VLM: Efficient Video Anomaly Detection through Motion-Guided Vision-Language Models
Abstract:
Vision‑Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong potential for video anomaly detection, but dense frame‑level inference makes them impractical for real‑time deployment. Existing acceleration commonly relies on uniform sampling, which ignores content dynamics and can either waste computation on static segments or miss localized anomalies. We propose MoG‑VLM a motion‑adaptive anomaly detection framework that leverages motion purely as a lightweight control signal to decide when VLM inference is necessary. To this end, we introduce Temporal Gradient Magnitude (TGM) which performs content‑aware sampling to concentrate computation on informative regions while avoiding redundant processing. We further introduce a hierarchical dual‑stream design in which dense multi‑frame VLM reasoning is activated only around frames with elevated anomaly likelihood, via anchor‑triggered context‑window expansion with early termination. A fusion module then reconciles these instantaneous semantic cues with temporal action dynamics. Across four benchmarks, our method achieves 91.91%, 84.30%, 87.88%, and 78.96% AUC‑ROC on XD‑Violence, UCF‑Crime, MSAD, and ShanghaiTech, respectively, establishing new state of the art on three benchmarks under the zero‑shot, training‑free setting. On XD‑Violence, we improve over the previous best result by +0.57% while delivering a 1.31x inference speedup. These results demonstrate that content‑aware allocation of VLM capacity, processing fewer frames more intelligently rather than all frames uniformly, is a more effective axis of progress than uniformly densifying VLM inference across frames. Code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/kdawoud91/MoG‑VLM.

PaperId: 114, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31474.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qi Lv, Jiayi Lin, Yuxin Jiang, Jianzong Wang, Xiang Deng, Mike Shou Zheng
Title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models
Abstract:
Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions. Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions. However, reconstruction‑driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton‑guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics. Cross‑modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB‑derived and skeleton‑derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction. The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future‑derived residual information. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world‑model fine‑tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions. On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end‑effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo. Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero‑shot human‑to‑robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.

PaperId: 115, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31472.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jian Hou, Xin Zhou, Adam J. Spiers
Title: VecTile: A Low-Cost Flexible Tactile Array for 3-DoF Force Sensing
Abstract:
Tactile sensing provides robots with contact information difficult to obtain from vision alone. Shear force is particularly important for understanding tangential contact, guiding corrective motions, and maintaining grasp stability, yet flexible and low‑cost tactile arrays often measure only normal force. We introduce VecTile, a low‑cost, 6 mm thin, flexible tactile array capable of three‑axis force sensing. VecTile combines a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs that convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns. The sensor can be fabricated in‑house without specialized equipment. The complete system costs less than 35 USD for a 4x4 array. We validate the sensing mechanism through finite element analysis and hardware experiments. In controlled single‑taxel tests over 1‑5 N normal force and up to 1.5 N shear force, VecTile achieves root‑mean‑square errors of 0.39 N and 0.16 N for normal and shear forces. A VecTile calibrated while flat retains accuracy when curved, while a five‑minute manual calibration is sufficient for practical use. Two applications demonstrate its utility. First, shear readings are sensitive enough to stop a sharp scalpel from puncturing a balloon after contact. Second, the sensor substantially improves Diffusion Policy‑guided power‑plug insertion. All designs and code will be released upon paper acceptance. Project website: https://jiannnh.github.io/VecTile/.

PaperId: 116, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31455.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Minkyun Seo, Hyungtae Lim, Jaesik Park
Title: MixPT: Point Transformer with Interleaved Window and Global Attention
Abstract:
Point cloud transformers aim to capture detailed local geometry and relationships across a scene at a manageable computational cost. Two common approaches are window attention and global attention. They differ in how they enable scene‑wide interaction, which refers to information exchange among tokens across a scene. Window attention reduces computational cost by restricting self‑attention to groups of tokens called windows; in serialized designs, each window contains a fixed number of consecutive tokens from a spatially ordered sequence. Because each block only directly connects tokens within the same window, information exchange across windows relies on changes in window membership across blocks and hierarchical pooling. Global attention, in contrast, directly connects all tokens within a scene, but computing attention over all token pairs can be costly when the number of tokens is large. To balance computational cost and scene‑wide interaction, we introduce MixPT, a point transformer that uses a mix of window and global attention blocks in an interleaved schedule, while retaining a single fixed serialization pattern for its window blocks. For scenes with a large number of tokens, MixPT applies global attention to spatially pooled tokens and returns residual updates to the original‑resolution stream. Across indoor and outdoor benchmarks, MixPT achieves competitive accuracy with lower latency than representative window and global attention baselines. We further demonstrate the feasibility of scaling the attention stage in depth by repeating the interleaved pattern of window and global attention blocks.

PaperId: 117, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31429.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Taekoan Yoo, Wonkyung Jung, Kyunghun Kim, Kyeongbo Kong
Title: PhysTrace: Interpretable Temporal Evaluation of Physical Consistency in Video Generative Models
Abstract:
World action models increasingly rely on pretrained video models assumed to capture physical dynamics for prediction, planning, and action generation. Existing evaluations assess plausibility, probe representations, or measure predictive surprise, but rarely identify which history‑conditioned physical expectations conflict with observations. We introduce PhysTrace, a training‑free framework aligning MLLM‑generated, history‑conditioned expectations with observed video windows to temporally localize physical violations and provide interpretable descriptions without task‑specific probes or classifiers. We also introduce IntPhys2‑Timing, adding violation intervals to IntPhys2. PhysTrace achieves a Hit Rate of up to 70.7% across physical principles on IntPhys2‑Timing and outperforms the compared methods in overall possible‑impossible discrimination accuracy on IntPhys2. Applied to reconstructed videos along the trajectories of pretrained diffusion/flow‑based video models, PhysTrace reveals attribute‑ and noise‑dependent patterns in physical violation localization, enabling interpretable physical consistency analysis across timesteps.

PaperId: 118, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31427.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tao Lin, Yuxin Du, Haoxiao Wang, Zile Zhong, Bo Zhao
Title: FastHarness: Experience-Driven Review Scheduling for Vision-Language-Action Policies
Abstract:
Agentic robot systems combine language‑model reasoning with robot policies to monitor execution and recover from failures. However, reviewing every action chunk incurs substantial overhead, even in familiar situations. We introduce FastHarness, an experience‑driven execution harness that adaptively schedules GPT‑6 Astra supervision of a π0.5 policy. A fast path uses stage memory and reviewed outcomes to reduce review frequency as experience accumulates, while a complementary recovery path focuses supervision on correcting errors. Once recovery is verified, routine execution resumes, with failure experience retained to guide future interventions. The policy remains frozen and generates fresh actions from current observations. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, reviewer token use decreases by an average of 57.2% per task from the first evaluated episode to the mean of the final five episodes. Mean episode time decreases from 85.5 to 52.0 minutes over the same interval. On the same tasks, mean success increases from 80% for GPT‑as‑Policy (π0.5 + GPT‑6 Astra) to 97.19% with FastHarness. These results highlight adaptive supervision as a practical route to more efficient agentic robotics without additional model training.

PaperId: 119, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31326.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ze-Yu Peng, Qing-Yu Lan, Zhan-He Wang, Jun Zhang, Yun-Song Piao
Title: AgenticEvolve: Evolutionary Program Search with Persistent Language Model Agents that Design and Run Experiments
Abstract:
Evolutionary program search with large language models keeps the structure of an evolutionary algorithm and uses the model as its variation operator. Typically, the model generates each candidate program in a single request from parent programs and their scores. We present AgenticEvolve, an evolutionary program search framework in which each island is run by a persistent large language model agent. Between evaluations, the agent designs and runs experiments on the candidate program. To measure the contribution of experimentation, we compare AgenticEvolve with No‑analysis, an otherwise identical configuration with experiments disabled. On two heuristic design tasks with three large language models, AgenticEvolve produces better programs than No‑analysis and OpenEvolve on both hidden and unseen instances. It reaches the baselines' final quality with far fewer evaluations and comparable cost. On twelve equation discovery problems, it recovers the ground‑truth structure of more equations than No‑analysis and existing language‑model and genetic programming baselines.

PaperId: 120, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31321.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xinyang Lu, Shengzhe Wei, Sheng Tang, Weiqi Zhang, Juntong Fang, Zesong Li
Title: MVLoMa: Multi-View Local Feature Matching with Any Geometry Foundation Model
Abstract:
Local feature matching is typically formulated for image pairs, although structure‑from‑motion and visual localization commonly match one reference image against many retrieved or covisible neighbours. Applying a pairwise matcher independently to these centre‑neighbour edges duplicates reference‑side computation and prevents the matcher from exploiting complementary multi‑view geometric evidence from the remaining observations. To address these limitations, we introduce MVLoMa, a sparse star‑graph matcher that extends LoMa from image pairs to multiple views. MVLoMa first uses a frozen multi‑view geometry model to jointly describe all images in a star, then injects the resulting cross‑view geometric context into local descriptors. It then matches the centre image to all neighbours in a single forward pass through per‑view self‑attention and bidirectional centre‑neighbour cross‑attention. For supervision, we derive positive correspondences only from depth‑valid, mutually visible dense warps and explicitly penalize high‑confidence matches that violate epipolar geometry. On 25‑view star graphs from HyperSim, ScanNet++, Mip‑NeRF 360, and Tanks and Temples, MVLoMa obtains the best macro‑average relative‑pose AUC among the compared methods at all three thresholds (58.65/85.41/90.99). Its matcher is 2.20 times faster than sequential evaluation of the 24 centre‑neighbour edges. The same design supports four tested frozen geometry encoders ‑‑ DA3, π^3, VGGT, and VGGT‑Ω ‑‑ with DA3‑Giant performing best on all reported encoder‑ablation metrics. Controlled ablations further isolate the effects of geometry‑aware descriptors, visibility filtering, geometric negative supervision, and joint multi‑view inference.

PaperId: 121, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31317.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yifan Yuan, Yancheng Zhu, Zuoyu Zhang, Xiaogang Peng
Title: SurveyGraph: Generating Academic Surveys via Methods-Entity Knowledge Graphs
Abstract:
Most automated survey generation systems retrieve papers as flat documents, limiting their ability to capture research structure. We present SurveyGraph, a framework built around a Methods‑Entity Knowledge Graph (MEKG) encoding method‑level follow‑on, competition, and shared‑resource relations. The graph supports core‑paper discovery, retrieval, hybrid outlining, and evidence‑gated narrative synthesis. We evaluate retrieval, semantic edges, citation grounding, collection coverage, and generation‑stage components. In a controlled seven‑method equal‑budget benchmark, MEKG‑anchored fusion balances recall and structural density, with an independent co‑citation check. In a separate archived graph‑native diagnostic, graph‑aware retrieval nearly doubles recall over flat lexical baselines across eight runs (p = 0.004). A semantic evidence gate achieves AUC = 0.75. Audits of 160 generated sentences find 80.6% anchored‑or‑partial citation support. Human adjudication of 108 stratified semantic edges finds 68.5% supported‑or‑partial relations (binary‑support Cohen's kappa = 0.64), with improves strongest (80.6%) and extends weakest (52.8%). A SurveyBench‑facing collection probe reaches mean reference coverage of 0.521 across four topics with an eight‑paper budget. Same‑backend Qwen diagnostics on a 30‑paper/74‑relation graph show reduced organization signals when hybrid outlining is removed. Concurrent‑system comparisons provide bounded context rather than matched‑backend end‑to‑end evidence. The results position MEKG as an auditable structural layer for typed diagnostics, relation‑specific filtering, and controlled survey generation. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/SurveyGraph.

PaperId: 122, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31314.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yancheng Zhu, Yifan Yuan
Title: When LLMs Forget What They Believe: Characterizing State Integrity Collapse in Long-Horizon Dialogues
Abstract:
Large language models can repeat an instruction while failing to keep obeying it. We study this recall‑compliance dissociation in long‑horizon dialogue and define State Integrity Collapse: a model preserves a stated constraint in memory but stops applying it to later turns. We introduce StateTrack‑Bench, a controlled suite of conversations covering numerical, format, role/persona, factual‑memory, and logical‑rule constraints. Across seven provider‑pinned model snapshots and five dialogue‑depth probes, strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with degradation concentrated in symbolic constraints and in one especially brittle model. A forked recall audit shows that 88.6% of observed failures are behavioral‑drift failures rather than ordinary forgetting; excluding the brittle outlier preserves this diagnosis (84.4% of failures). Extended evaluations at depths up to 50 turns confirm that the dissociation persists beyond the core benchmark, while Structured State Anchoring recovers up to 24.4 points on immutable constraints. The results show that reliability cannot be inferred from single‑turn instruction following alone; evaluation must track whether remembered constraints remain operational as dialogue state grows. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/StateTrack.

PaperId: 123, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31309.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiacheng Liu, Yaxin Luo, Xiaohan Zhao, Peng Sun, Xinyi Shang, Jiacheng Cui, Yonina C. Eldar, Zhiqiang Shen
Title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
Abstract:
Scaling embedding capacity alongside Transformer computation is an emerging trend in language models. This trend makes high compression rates increasingly useful. Hence, we study extreme compression of Per‑Layer Embeddings (PLE), which follow this trend and account for 35.2% of the parameters of Gemma 4 E4B. At such rates, conventional quantizers give each token‑layer vector its own code of only a few bytes. We instead develop OPTIC (Output‑Path‑fitted, Token‑shared Indexed Codes), which stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at every layer with a layer‑specific affine decoder. Codes and decoders are fitted to the PLE output path rather than to the stored vectors. At about 100× PLE compression of bfloat16 (BF16) E4B, OPTIC retains an aggregate 97.8% of the uncompressed model's performance across seven benchmarks, whereas product quantization, the strongest of six conventional baselines, retains 66.3%. At 594× and 1,002× PLE compression of BF16 E4B, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. On the official E4B release with 4‑bit linear weights and 16‑bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about 100× PLE compression. During inference at about 100× PLE compression, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory than with uncompressed PLE at the same key‑value cache size, while running at most 0.40% slower.

PaperId: 124, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31282.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Changseon Yu, Hyeokjun Kweon
Title: ReCoG: Relational Concept Graph for Training-Free Personalization
Abstract:
Training‑free personalization adapts a frozen vision‑language model (VLM) to recognize user‑defined concepts from only a few exemplars by retrieving concept entries at inference time. While recent retriever‑based methods enrich each concept with descriptive evidence, they largely treat concepts in isolation, so the retrieved information can be plausible yet non‑discriminative, especially when the personalized concept set contains highly confusable, fine‑grained categories. We argue that personalization is inherently relational: correct recognition depends on the specific distinctions between a concept and its nearest alternatives. To this end, we propose ReCoG, a Relational Concept Graph for retrieval‑augmented personalization. ReCoG represents concepts as nodes and augments them with directed edges that explicitly capture discriminative cues between concept pairs, elicited by a frozen VLM during database construction. At inference, ReCoG retrieves a shortlist and resolves ambiguity via explicit pairwise comparisons conditioned on the corresponding relational edges, selecting the concept that consistently wins against competing candidates. We also introduce FINGER benchmark to test personalized recognition on confusable concept sets. Across FINGER, ReCoG substantially outperforms prior methods, with the largest gains in the most confusable regimes. ReCoG also achieves consistently best performance on established personalization benchmarks including captioning and VQA, confirming that relational evidence is broadly beneficial beyond fine‑grained settings. Project Page: https://csy‑98.github.io/ReCoG/

PaperId: 125, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31274.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Valentino Sacco, Saurabh Pandey, Alexander Florian Jercher, Maximilian Schilling
Title: PointerBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Fine-Grained GUI Grounding
Abstract:
Multimodal Large Language Models have shown promising performance in computer‑use tasks, from planning user workflows to grounding natural‑language actions to precise UI targets. Existing end‑to‑end benchmarks primarily emphasize long‑horizon task completion, while GUI grounding benchmarks remain focused on conventional controls and a limited set of professional interfaces. We introduce POINTERBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 1,500 screenshot‑instruction pairs probing three complementary capabilities: thin sub‑element identification and geometric grounding in spreadsheets (POINTERBENCH‑Sheets), character‑level grounding in long‑text documents (POINTERBENCH‑Text), and mixed GUI grounding across 100 professional applications (POINTERBENCH‑Pro). We carefully curate each task with pixel‑exact target geometry and evaluate both general‑purpose multimodal models and 39 specialist GUI grounding configurations. We find text grounding to be the most challenging setting, with Claude Fable 5, GPT‑5.6 Sol, and the leading native specialist UI‑Venus‑2‑9B achieving 69.6%, 53.4%, and 25.8% success on POINTERBENCH‑Text despite respective 83.2%, 77.7%, and 54.5% average success across POINTERBENCH. These results reveal substantial headroom in fine‑grained GUI grounding across frontier and specialist models. We publicly release the benchmark and evaluation code at https://github.com/warmwindOS/pointerbench.

PaperId: 126, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31256.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tirana Noor Fatyanosa, Ummu Ditya Erliana, Mahendra Data, Muhammad Nurwegiono, Eleazar Tadeo Eman, Alham Fikri Aji
Title: IndoNutriQA: An Indonesian Clinical Nutrition Question Answering Benchmark
Abstract:
Clinical Question Answering (QA) underpins Clinical Intelligent Decision Support Systems, but progress is severely limited for low‑resource languages such as Indonesian by the absence of public domain‑specific data. We introduce IndoNutriQA, an expert‑curated Indonesian clinical QA benchmark of 911 question‑answer pairs built from real clinical‑nutrition reports. Rather than a large‑scale training corpus, it is positioned as a high‑quality evaluation resource: every pair is grounded in a clinically relevant context, enriched with structured metadata (anthropometric assessment, medical diagnosis, document provenance, chunk segmentation). Eight standardised question types following the Nutrition Care Process (NCP), including the Problem, Etiology, Sign and Symptom (PES) diagnosis statement, are answered for every report, which was written by a graduate‑level dietetic intern, by one of three nutritionists. Answers are free‑form clinical prose rather than extractive spans, and an expert validation study finds 6‑10% of reference answers contestable. The dataset supports generative, extractive and retrieval‑augmented QA as well as zero‑ and few‑shot LLM evaluation. We report fine‑tuned baselines (IndoBERT variants, mT5, RAG) with 5‑fold cross‑validation, learning curves and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and benchmark eight contemporary LLMs zero‑ and five‑shot. We further calibrate our LLM‑as‑judge rubric against three expert raters (one RD, two nutritionists), finding it human‑comparable on factuality and completeness but unreliable on clinical safety, and a human error analysis shows it misses unsupported content that the raters identify. IndoNutriQA is released to foster research in Indonesian clinical NLP and nutritional decision support.

PaperId: 127, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31246.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yulong Tian, Lei Wang, Jincan Yang, Hao Wu, Hao Han, Fengyuan Xu, Sheng Zhong
Title: Weaponizing the Exit: Input Privacy Leakage via Exit Routing Manipulation in Multi-Exit Networks
Abstract:
Multi‑exit networks improve inference efficiency by allowing inputs to terminate early at intermediate exits. We identify a privacy vulnerability in cloud deployments of these networks: a malicious Cloud Service Provider (CSP) can infer sensitive properties of individual user inputs solely from inference latency, without accessing inputs, intermediate states, or model outputs. The attack exploits the CSP's control over the model supply chain. Prior to deployment, the CSP supplies a specially crafted multi‑exit network manipulated so that inputs carrying a target sensitive property are routed to a designated exit with high probability, while other inputs exit elsewhere. At serving time, the CSP infers the exit index from per‑query latency, thereby determining whether each input possesses the target property without accessing inputs, outputs, or internal model states. We propose a training framework combining selective label smoothing and entropy‑covariance optimization to control confidence distributions across exits and reduce premature termination. We conduct experiments on four datasets across ten target properties. The results demonstrate strong attack effectiveness and stealthiness. The attack achieves an average F1 score of 0.73, compared to 0.25 for the strongest baseline, while main task accuracy drops by less than 1.3% and inference speedup degradation remains below 0.1 in most settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/kazefjj/Weaponizing_the_Exit.

PaperId: 128, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31211.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Miha Ožbot, Seiichi Ozawa, Igor Škrjanc
Title: Evolving Federated Density Peak Clustering with Shuffler-Based Anonymization
Abstract:
In this paper, we present a novel one‑shot federated clustering approach based on evolving fuzzy clustering and shuffler‑based anonymization. In federated clustering, each round reveals additional model information to the server and can increase the opportunity to infer properties of local datasets, even when raw samples are never shared. Consequently, fewer client‑server exchanges and unlinkability are important, so transmitted information cannot be attributed to any single client. Data‑stream clustering algorithms, which learn in a single pass over the data, align well with the one‑shot federated learning paradigm, where a single communication round can be sufficient. The proposed Evolving Federated Density Peak Clustering (eFDPC) method combines evolving fuzzy data‑stream clustering and density peak clustering in a federated setting. Each client independently evolves micro‑clusters from private data mini‑batches through cluster addition and merging. To limit communication, density peak clustering is applied to the learned micro‑clusters and only the selected peaks are transmitted, rather than the full local models. A shuffler‑based layer is introduced between the clients and the server to anonymize contributions prior to reconstruction and global peak selection. We consider a peak‑only variant, eFDPC‑P, as well as eFDPC‑G with server‑side label propagation. Experiments on synthetic and real‑world benchmark datasets show that eFDPC outperforms recent federated clustering baselines in one‑shot settings and scales to higher‑dimensional, non‑IID data.

PaperId: 129, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31209.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wenhua Jin, Tiancheng Chen, Sheng Tang, Jiahao Li, Yupeng Liu, Weiqi Zhang, Juntong Fang, Zesong Li
Title: Moving Regions, Not Moving Objects: Segmenting What Actually Moves under Camera Motion
Abstract:
Moving object segmentation is conventionally formulated at the sequence and object level, marking an entire instance as moving once it moves anywhere in a video. Recent instantaneous formulations distinguish moving from stationary intervals, but still generate masks at the object level through frozen segmentation foundation models. Because the mask is derived from an instance‑level proposal, motion is typically attributed to the entire instance rather than localized to the regions that actually move. Moreover, such instance‑level predictions can produce masks even when no part of the instance is actually moving, revealing a more fundamental issue: motion is not an intrinsic property of an instance; it can only be determined by comparing at least two frames. Building on this premise, we introduce MoRSe, which jointly interprets two frames to predict a moving‑region mask, distinguishing actual scene motion from apparent motion induced by the camera. A single RGB encoder replaces multi‑stage foundation stacks, so no optical flow, point tracks, or separate mask generator is needed at inference. We release MoRSe‑5K, a benchmark of 42 sequences with Static, Dynamic‑Static, and Dynamic settings designed to evaluate the model's ability to distinguish and localize moving and stationary regions under different camera and scene motion conditions. MoRSe outperforms both specialized moving object segmentation methods and dense 4D reconstruction methods with motion‑thresholded predictions, while producing the fewest false positives on sequences where nothing moves.

PaperId: 130, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31158.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiahao Meng, Qize Yang, Yuxuan Wang, Yunfei Chu, Wensi Dai, Jin Xu, Yunhai Tong
Title: Beyond Watching and Searching: Benchmarking Agents for Video-centered Deep Research Reports
Abstract:
Deep research agents synthesize open‑web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video‑Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill‑based workflow and OmniDR‑Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni‑ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task‑specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR‑Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3 out of 100. Current agents still need broader content coverage, stronger causal and logical analysis across modalities, and more accurate citation support. We further analyze models, harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and research trajectories. The code and data are released at https://github.com/marinero4972/OmniDR‑Bench.

PaperId: 131, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31140.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yudhistira Arditya Pratama, Yi-Zeng Hsieh
Title: GM-GReFEL: Geometry-Guided Spatiotemporal State-Space Learning for Robust Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition
Abstract:
Recognizing facial expressions in unconstrained video suffers from two coupled problems: self‑attention grows quadratically in cost with clip length, and crowdsourced labels are noisy. We present GM‑GReFEL, a spatiotemporal state‑space network with a geometry‑aware decision stage. Its Modulated GroupMamba backbone replaces a spatiotemporal Vision Transformer. Six channel groups are scanned separately, four over the frame plane and two over time, so the cost grows linearly with sequence length (\mathcalO(N)); after each layer, a Channel Affinity Modulation gate mixes the groups again. On top of the backbone, a GReFEL reliability module turns the normalized entropy of each prediction into a mixing weight between the classifier output and a vote from trainable geometric anchors, so that facial geometry counts for more when the network is unsure. The model is initialized by static‑to‑dynamic weight transfer and trained with a Triple Loss. In five‑fold cross‑validation, the best fold scores 66.57%/76.46% UAR/WAR on DFEW, 0.3 points or less below the strongest compared method, and 45.66%/62.27% on MAFW, ahead of all compared methods; on FERV39k the mean over five splits, 42.30%/52.66%, is competitive. The five‑fold means are 64.07%/74.54% on DFEW, on par with recent large pre‑trained models, and 38.90%/54.37% on MAFW, below the best of them. A paired t‑test on DFEW indicates a modest benefit of temporal modeling (+1.61 UAR points, one‑sided p=0.031). Attention stays on plausible facial regions, and latency is close to a ViT‑B/16 baseline (47.4 vs.\ 46.8 ms per clip). Code: https://github.com/ardiytama/GroupMamba‑DFER.

PaperId: 132, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31139.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Wenjie Xuan, Yapeng Li, Hang Su, Chen Cheng, Juhua Liu, Sheng Zhao, Ziming Huang, Bo Du
Title: Pos4CHD: A Positive-Free Mask-Guided Counterfactual Synthesis Framework for Fetal Congenital Heart Defect Analysis
Abstract:
The scarcity of positive cases remains a major bottleneck in developing automated diagnostic systems for fetal Congenital Heart Defects~(CHDs), particularly for rare subtypes. Although normal cases are accessible with effort, positive cases are hard to collect due to low incidence rates and privacy concerns, causing severe class imbalance or absence of positive training samples. Existing works resort to synthesizing positives with conditional generative models, but they are task‑specific and require positive training samples, hindering application for fetal CHDs. To this end, we propose a positive‑free mask‑guided counterfactual generation framework for fetal echocardiography, namely Pos4CHD, which enables realistic, high‑quality synthesis of pseudo‑positive samples from semantic masks, with only normal samples at hand. Technically, we first develop FE‑Gen, a mask‑guided generative model tailored for fetal heart ultrasound synthesis that mitigates histogram drift and enhances image‑mask spatial alignment. Building on FE‑Gen, Pos4CHD employs a mask‑to‑image generation paradigm for CHD synthesis. It first manipulates semantic masks to simulate fetal‑heart structural anomalies and then renders anatomically consistent images. Extensive experiments on in‑house datasets, together with expert evaluations, demonstrate the visual fidelity~(‑12.97 FID) and anatomical consistency~(+3.96% DSC) of synthesized images. Further validations across diverse real‑world CHD diagnosis tasks exhibit promising results and consistent increments, including zero‑shot classification~(achieving 93.25% ACC on EbA and 72.92% ACC on TAPVC), lesion detection~(+6.95% mAP50 on VSD), and anatomy segmentation~(+10.49% DSC on fetal heart) compared with baselines. Codes and models are publicly available on \hrefhttps://github.com/DREAMXFAR/Pos4CHDGitHub.

PaperId: 133, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31135.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Aman Behera, Namit Solanki, Mehul Anand
Title: Mixing Matters: Evidence Position Bias Across Sequence Mixers in Long-Context Question Answering
Abstract:
Long‑context models often use answer‑bearing evidence less effectively when it appears away from a prompt boundary. We compare this position bias across Transformer, state‑space, and hybrid Mamba architectures by moving one gold document through a fixed set of nine distractors. The evaluated Transformers show a beginning advantage that the evaluated state‑space models lack, while both families favor evidence near the end. A matched pure‑versus‑hybrid Mamba comparison points in the same direction but remains statistically uncertain. The family difference appears among models that can answer the task. Transformer primacy reappears on synthetic retrieval, where state‑space ceiling prevents a family comparison. A corpus swap within one state‑space architecture changes overall accuracy without a detectable change in curve shape. Prompt changes can create or nearly remove a beginning advantage. Position remains decodable across architectures even when response curves differ, and attention concentration near initial tokens covaries with beginning sensitivity in the tested Transformer family. These exploratory results show that effective context use depends on the evaluated architecture family, capability, task, and prompt, without isolating the sequence mixer as the sole cause.

PaperId: 134, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31133.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Junyu Lin, Bosong Qi, Pengcheng Shi, Jiayuan Li
Title: Is High Local Accuracy Enough? Geometric Consensus with Support-Adaptive Statistical Personalization for Federated Learning
Abstract:
Real‑world deployment of personalized federated learning (PFL) requires adapting to heterogeneous clients while preserving recognition performance beyond local distributions. However, high local accuracy can conceal failures on locally rare or absent classes. Effective personalization should therefore strengthen global recognition while raising the personalization floor. We propose an evaluation protocol that complements local accuracy with global, rare‑class, and unseen‑class evaluations to reveal generalization obscured by local scores, and assesses personalization floors among the worst‑performing clients to expose weaknesses hidden by aggregate performance. To meet these deployment challenges, we propose FedGRC, a unified PFL framework integrating generalization and personalization through (i) Consensus‑Guided Representation Learning (CGRL), which learns discriminative representations through shared directional and magnitude guidance; (ii) Multilayer Metric Synthesis (MMS), which constructs a shared covariance metric from these multilayer representations for statistical classification; and (iii) Support‑Adaptive Shrinkage Personalization (SASP), which adapts class means within this metric by shrinking local estimates toward shared means according to local sample support, enabling adaptation while retaining shared knowledge. Extensive experiments, including benchmarking against 21 methods across 5 heterogeneity settings on 3 datasets and comprehensive ablation studies, validate the effectiveness of FedGRC. On CIFAR‑10 and CIFAR‑100, FedGRC surpasses state‑of‑the‑art (SOTA) baselines in global recognition and personalization floors by at least 2.17% and 2.13%, respectively. On the real‑world heterogeneous FedRS dataset, it outperforms the respective best baselines by 2.15%, 3.30%, and 4.61% in local adaptation, global recognition, and the personalization floor.

PaperId: 135, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31130.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Aman Behera, Payal Payal
Title: Post-Audit Mirage: Identifiability Limits of Offline Agent Verification
Abstract:
Offline tests can fail to reveal whether an agent update will remain safe after deployment. We operationalize this post‑audit mirage using matched safe and harmful lifecycles that expose identical verifier‑visible evidence while an isolated scorer records opposite deployment truth. Our theorem applies standard observational‑equivalence and indistinguishability ideas to this executable audit boundary and states the resulting error‑abstention tradeoff. The Post‑Audit Mirage benchmark makes that boundary executable across authorization, scheduling, and shared‑capacity environments. IdentifiedRangeMonitor uses fresh group‑labelled harm outcomes to return deploy, hold, cannot determine, or unsupported. Experiments show that monitoring can recover the missing distinction in favorable settings but may remain undecided for rare groups, small effects, or missing observations. Verifier‑agent evaluation must therefore test both calculation validity and whether the available evidence supports the deployment decision.

PaperId: 136, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31125.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hao Wu
Title: Delta N-gram: Forward-Only Continual Writing into a Language Model's Native N-gram Memory
Abstract:
Our previous analysis found that a model's native hashed N‑gram table is where continual updates disturb the base least, but its writes needed backpropagation and changed the pretrained table. We present Delta N‑gram, a forward‑only write path into that table. The pretrained table T^0 is never modified. Evidence is written into a sparse patch Δon the rows it addresses: a 4.1M‑parameter writer emits a target and a gate per (position, hash head) event, and a block‑averaged delta rule keeps each row a convex combination of its old value and the gated targets. The writer is trained offline on raw text with the pretraining objective; at use time writing takes forward passes only, and clearing Δrestores the original model. A 0.6B prototype trained to answer questions keeps 16/16 facts after a second write; online gradient writes keep 2‑‑4/16. We study two writers: a plain writer that encodes evidence with the T^0‑only model, and a delta writer that reads its current memory while encoding. On Qwen3.8‑Flash‑Next, the plain writer's memory is document‑specific: on 64 held‑out news events it lowers continuation NLL by 0.068 nats/token against empty memory and by 0.024 against another document's memory, and 0.063 and 0.013 after 16 intervening articles. The delta writer's memory is more document‑specific and keeps more of it under distraction (70% vs 54%). Over 35,000 writes on our previous seven‑task chain both writers stay stable and the delta writer drifts less (layer‑2 math drift 176% vs 188%); later accuracy changes by ‑0.26/‑0.52pp (‑7.29pp for gradient updates) and small‑k_i drift is 17.9/17.5% (39.2%). Acquisition is negative, and general‑input drift reaches 32.8% (20.75%): format rows read by every example grow to 4‑‑12 times their pretrained norm. Zeroing eight such rows removes over 98% of layer‑2 drift on math inputs, together with their NLL gain.

PaperId: 137, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31121.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Aleksandr Lazarev, Sofia Zimina, Roman Kuznetsov, Tatiana Zemskova, Iaroslav Koshelev, Dmitry Yudin
Title: RGraph-Eval: Task-Grounded Scene Graphs for Evaluating Robot Video Generation
Abstract:
Generated robot videos can look convincing while depicting the wrong interaction: a different object is moved, a grasp disappears, or a placement ends outside its destination. We introduce RGraph‑Eval, a reference‑based framework that makes these discrepancies explicit through task‑grounded temporal scene graphs. Unlike approaches that construct separate evidence representations for different evaluation dimensions, we organize task entities, interactions, and motion within a unified, interpretable scene graph representation. A foundation‑model pipeline identifies manipulation roles, grounds persistent object masks, infers and verifies state transitions and action intervals, and reconstructs manipulated‑object motion in three dimensions. Applying this representation to a generated video and a reference demonstration supports an interpretable RGraph‑Eval score with visible‑object, relation‑change, and 3D path‑shape components. We also introduce ShareRobot‑SG, a collection of 1,000 manipulation scenes from ten ShareRobot sources annotated with the multimodal representation. Our evaluation separates graph‑generation quality from agreement with human video judgments and includes comparisons with adapted SVG2 and SG‑Ego, as well as a benchmark of three video generators. The framework connects robot‑video assessment to the observable entities and interactions underlying a task while making the graph annotations reusable beyond evaluation. Code will be publicly available at https://github.com/SashaDance/rgraph‑eval.

PaperId: 138, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31120.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuannuo Feng, Yubing Ye, Wenshuai Yao, Yizhe Chen, Ngai Wong, Wenyong Zhou, Wang Kang
Title: SetCommit: Coordinated Token Commitments for Few-Step Diffusion Language Model Decoding
Abstract:
Diffusion language models generate multiple token positions in parallel, but few‑step decoding makes parallel commitment difficult: tokens that appear reliable individually may be jointly inconsistent, while premature commitments can prevent later context‑dependent refinement. In this paper, we introduce SetCommit, a training‑free method for coordinated parallel token commitment. Instead of selecting tokens independently by confidence, SetCommit selects a commitment set that balances token reliability against local joint commitment risk, preserving conditioning opportunities for subsequent denoising steps. It further performs budget‑neutral local exchanges, replacing vulnerable earlier commitments when newly revealed context supports more reliable alternatives. SetCommit requires no retraining or architectural modification and is compatible with existing diffusion decoding strategies. Experiments with LLaDA‑8B and Dream‑7B on GSM8K, MATH‑500, MBPP, and HumanEval show accuracy/pass@1 gains of up to 7.4 percentage points over native decoding at 32 model evaluations. At common quality targets, geometric‑mean incremental speedups range from 1.44 to 1.74×. Code is available at https://github.com/Kissmetothemoon/SetCommit.

PaperId: 139, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31095.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yun Li, Ehsan Javanmardi, Simon Thompson, Jiachen Gong, Qunli Zhang, Zifan Zeng, Shiming Liu, Peng Wang, Yidu Zhang, Manabu Tsukada
Title: To Route or to Adapt? Multi-Expert Diffusion Planners in Unseen Regions
Abstract:
Diffusion trajectory planners with domain‑specific experts face a practical question in unseen regions: can they rely on selecting among existing experts, or must the planner itself adapt? We study this question using a planner with a shared adapter and per‑domain expert adapters. Across three real‑world held‑out maps, none of eight test‑time routing schemes improves the fleet‑mean lateral offset over the static default, which uses the same expert for every scene. Even an oracle that selects the best expert for each scene reduces the mean offset by only 0.9 m. In contrast, reward‑based fine‑tuning on just 20 target‑region scenes yields substantially larger gains. On matched evaluation slices, joint replay achieves a fleet‑mean offset of 6.9 m, compared with 12.4 m for the static default. Comparisons under the same target‑region training budget show that target‑region training drives the improvement, while replaying training scenes limits forgetting on the original ODDs. On nuPlan, fine‑tuning across training cities also improves open‑loop offsets, although closed‑loop performance deteriorates. Further diagnostics reveal that two test‑time adaptation baselines achieve low offsets by producing degenerate trajectories. These results show the limited headroom for selecting among existing experts and the greater open‑loop gains available from adapting the planner.

PaperId: 140, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31093.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuhang Zhang, Yang Li, Qiang Wu, Mingyuan Li
