Title: HARMONY: Hierarchical Anchor Retrieval on Manifold for Oblivious-source Machinery Acoustic Anomaly Detection
Abstract:
In standard acoustic anomaly detection (ASD), models are usually trained separately for each machine or domain using explicit metadata. However, in realistic deployments, machine identifiers are incomplete, unreliable, or simply unavailable. Thus, metadata‑free machinery ASD asks a single model to monitor mixed machine populations without machine IDs. In this paper, we argue that the main failure mode is not a weak detector family, but representation entanglement. The heterogeneous normal modes overlap in frozen pre‑trained feature spaces, making anomaly scoring and approximate retrieval unreliable. We study this problem directly and propose HARMONY (Hierarchical Anchor Retrieval on Manifold for Oblivious‑source acoustic aNomalY detection), an anchor‑guided geometric repartitioning framework that reorganizes mixed‑source features into compact Voronoi regions and reuses this structure for hierarchical retrieval. On DCASE 2020, HARMONY improves mean AUC from 75.40% to 90.00% (14.60 percentage points) over the strongest unified baseline and from 83.90% to 90.00% over a strong foundation‑feature baseline. On a single CPU, its hierarchical retrieval achieves a 7.8x speedup over exhaustive search with only a 0.20 percentage‑point AUC drop. These results suggest that incorporating explicit geometric partitioning can improve both detection accuracy and retrieval efficiency for ASD. Code is available at https://github.com/Zzyh0208/HARMONY.

PaperId: 141, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31080.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fabian Isensee, Constantin Ulrich Harsy, Maximilian Rokuss, Benjamin Hamm, Philipp Vollmuth, Klaus H. Maier-Hein
Title: nnInteractive Agent: General-Purpose AI Agents as 3D Image Annotators
Abstract:
Interactive 3D segmentation models such as nnInteractive turn a few spatial prompts (points, scribbles, boxes) into accurate volumetric masks, but a human still does the annotation work: finding each structure, placing prompts, checking the result and correcting it. General‑purpose AI agents can now interpret images, call tools and write code. We show that such agents can take over this work without additional training: the user makes a request in plain language, and the agent works out what has to be segmented, locates the targets, prompts nnInteractive, inspects the 3D result, corrects it and responds to feedback. Asked for 'the muscles used for chewing', an agent identifies and segments the masseters and pterygoids; asked to count liver lesions, it writes its own code to find candidates and splits a merged lesion on request. Our open‑source nninteractive‑agent provides nnInteractive as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), together with a skill that encodes how experienced users prompt it. On a benchmark spanning CT, MRI, PET and micro‑CT of humans, a mouse and an ant (14 images; 51 targets from organs and tumours to muscles, foot bones, vessel trees and an insect brain), Claude Code and Codex reach a mean Dice of 0.81 and 0.84 from the request alone; when told where each target is, both reach 0.85 and prompt nearly as effectively as an oracle that places prompts using the reference segmentation. A text‑prompted 3D model (VoxTell) is more accurate on most standard radiological targets but less robust: it returns an empty mask for one of them and fails on the leg muscles, the foot bones, the mouse and the ant, where the agents remain accurate. Code: https://github.com/MIC‑DKFZ/nninteractive‑agent

PaperId: 142, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31064.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Zizhe Wang, Jia Deng, Xin Lu, Zehao Jia, Yi Huang, Yao Zhu
Title: AstroBench: Benchmarking Free-Floating Capture and Space Robotic Manipulation
Abstract:
Capturing a loose object inside a spacecraft requires a robot to approach a target that can translate and rotate, and whose motion changes when contact is made. These conditions motivate evaluation beyond manipulation of supported objects. We introduce AstroBench, an open benchmark for free‑floating capture and space robotic manipulation with a fixed‑base arm. The task suite combines four initial‑motion tracks with sample‑storage operations based on MELFI hardware and cap and captive‑screw servicing based on the Robotic Refueling Mission. The two workcells provide nine task definitions and 29 task‑target combinations. A metadata‑filtered Objaverse inventory supplies 8,414 object instances for asset expansion, alongside five cabin visual contexts and versioned task instructions. We report two acquisition‑focused experiments using existing checkpoints. A frozen π_0.5 DROID joint‑position policy captures 2 of 200 static targets and 4 of 200 moving targets across twenty object identities. A cube‑specific ACT policy captures 8 of 10 static targets and 6 of 10 moving targets in a separate experiment. Each experiment retains its recorded observation, action and capture configuration. The results document difficult direct transfer for the tested generalist checkpoint and successful task‑specific capture behavior, while identifying concrete settings for studying motion‑aware perception and contact‑sensitive control. Code, task definitions and editable workcell assets are available at https://github.com/AstroUpLab/AstroBench.

PaperId: 143, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31011.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Noah Gießing, Ankit Satpute, Hamid Rahkooy, André Greiner-Petter, Moritz Schubotz
Title: Formal-Informal Mathematical Alignment through and beyond Human Annotations
Abstract:
Formalized mathematics libraries such as Lean's \textttmathlib provide machine‑verifiable representations of mathematical knowledge, including definitions, theorems, and their relationships. If effectively connected to informal mathematical resources, formal mathematics could help uncover previously implicit links between mathematical concepts and improve access to existing formalizations. However, connections between informal and formal mathematics libraries are currently sparse and unsystematic. In this paper, we make first strides towards better formal integration. We construct a dataset linking informal statements from the Stacks Project to their formalizations in \textttmathlib by exploiting expert annotations. We evaluate retrieval, LLM‑based reranking, and LLM‑assisted verification to discover new unannotated informal‑to‑formal links. To facilitate exploration and reuse of formalized knowledge, we integrated the newly discovered alignments into the MaRDI knowledge graph, enabling mathematicians to find formal counterparts to informal mathematical content. We discuss the difficulties and challenges in using LLMs for linking formal and informal mathematical content. All code and data necessary for reproducing this paper can be found at: https://github.com/AnkitSatpute/Formal‑Informal‑Mathematical‑Alignment

PaperId: 144, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31005.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qiuyu Kong, Zanxi Ruan, Marco Cristani, Yiming Wang
Title: Mitigating Saliency Collapse: Robust Saliency-Aware Long-Text Image-Text Alignment
Abstract:
Long‑text image‑text alignment is essential for fine‑grained scene understanding, yet existing methods mainly focus on extending context length or improving local alignment. We identify an overlooked failure mode, saliency collapse, where models over‑rely on text that features visual prominence while underutilizing non‑salient context. Consequently, retrieval performance degrades sharply when salient content is reduced, despite that the non‑salient context remains informative. To address this, we propose RoSA, a saliency‑aware finetuning framework that decomposes image‑text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views, enabling joint learning of prominent and contextual semantics. We propose a modality‑independent decomposition strategy to combine object‑level visual saliency estimation with LLM‑based text decomposition to bridge vision and language. We employ auxiliary objectives to explicitly align these views, ensuring robust representation with both salient and contextual features. RoSA greatly improves long‑text retrieval and demonstrates strong robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks. Moreover, our auxiliary objectives are plug‑and‑play, bringing consistent gains to existing tuning methods. Code and checkpoints are available at: https://github.com/intelligolabs/RoSA.

PaperId: 145, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31000.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yifan Wang, Dongliang Xu, Xiaoyong Li, Jing Li, Peter S. Pan, Yue Yao
Title: SecLog-Bench: A Scalable Benchmark for Cybersecurity Log Reasoning with Scaffolded Evidence
Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for cybersecurity, leading to growing interest in LLM‑based automated cybersecurity log analysis. However, current datasets (1) are limited in scale; (2) rely mainly on single‑source evidence; and (3) have only binary or multi‑class attack labels, without dense annotations of the reasoning process. To address these limitations, SecLog‑Bench has three key features. First, we build an extensible simulation platform that covers 29 attack scenarios, supports repeated execution and the integration of new scenarios, and enables scalable generation of cybersecurity logs with attack‑stage labels. Second, we use multi‑source logs, including audit logs, application logs, and network traffic, to jointly analyze cyber attacks. Third, we annotate each sample with the essential context for cybersecurity log reasoning and a structured step‑by‑step evidence chain. We evaluate eight mainstream LLMs on this benchmark for post‑detection attack‑progress reasoning. Results show that, when provided with scaffolded evidence, current LLMs exhibit modest capability in attack‑progress reasoning, with the best model achieving only 44.44% accuracy and 45.07% Macro‑F1. Their reasoning remains unreliable; i.e., the highest Stage Reasoning F1 (SRF1) score is only 54.87%. Moreover, even correct predictions may be accompanied by flawed reasoning, and reasoning quality is often misaligned with prediction accuracy.

PaperId: 146, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30997.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Abhishek Barali, Aayush Paudel
Title: Padding to k: A Minimum Count in the Schema Makes Open-Weight Models Pad Their Extraction Lists
Abstract:
Extraction pipelines ask language models for JSON that follows a schema, and the schema can set a minimum number of list entries. We ask what models do when the document holds fewer items than that minimum. Under a preregistered plan, we test eight open‑weight models on 558 real documents from nine annotated datasets, with six more models on hosted services as a reference. Three findings stand out. First, models treat the count as a target: a minimum shown in the schema, but not enforced, raises the share of lists longer than the true count from 34.5% to 55.4%. Second, the padding is hard to catch, because most added entries are real text taken from the document; about half of them pass a check that each entry occurs in the source. Third, common fixes help only partly: a line saying fewer items are fine removes the effect on average but misses more true items, a count in prose ("up to k") also raises over‑counting, an "N/A" option under an enforced minimum still leaves half the lists padded, and re‑asking with the validation error makes padding far more common. We release the code, answer lists and run records at https://github.com/AbhishekBarali/padding‑to‑k

PaperId: 147, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30996.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Gregor Cerar, Denis Sodin, Matjaž Škrlec, Urban Rudež, Mihael Mohorčič, Miha Smolnikar
Title: Archive coverage constrains abstaining retrieval for transient stability screening more than conditional accuracy
Abstract:
Power‑grid transient stability is assessed by simulating credible faults, but repeating simulations as operating conditions change is costly, motivating faster critical clearing time estimators. Within the AI‑ASSIST project, we developed a retrieval‑based estimator around three adopted requirements: estimates retain their supporting states, retrieval abstains without compatible support, and support statistics are tested against observed error. Abstention turns estimator uncertainty into a demand on the archive. Exact switching‑configuration equality is used. The dense synthetic BUS39 archive covers 99.9996% of 1,044,797 records; the operational ELES archive covers 73.47% of 322,823 records. At query time, 59.37% of ELES states have an earlier same‑topology candidate. Under causal availability, retrieval covers 56.34% of records; on records covered under both protocols, mean absolute error increases by 10.0%. No tested support diagnostic ranks first on both grids. Most tested supervised regressors have lower error than retrieval on BUS39, all higher on the matched retrieval‑covered ELES population. On ELES, gradient boosting becomes more accurate than retrieval when temporally adjacent states are excluded, so the accuracy trade depends on the archive. Under the adopted compatibility key, archive availability constrains deployment more than conditional accuracy on ELES. Compatible coverage and chronological availability are auditable before an estimator is fitted.

PaperId: 148, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30991.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jialin Tian, Zhuofan Li, Xinkai Wang, Bokai Lin, Chenyi Wang, Xinyu Zhan, Cewu Lu, Lixin Yang
Title: UniFlowWAM: A Unified World-Action Model with Visual Semantics and 4D Geometry
Abstract:
Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did. They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between. Scene‑level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry. Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output learned together with the action. In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module or as an extra prediction head. We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World‑Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a third modality on par with vision and action. Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own supervision. UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three experts exchange information through joint attention. We train UniFlowWAM under a ten‑objective role grid, where each objective assigns every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent. The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future visual features or 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa‑GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO‑Plus in simulation, and on four real‑world bimanual manipulation tasks. On RoboCasa‑GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow from 52.1% to 56.4%. It preserves in‑distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7% zero‑shot on LIBERO‑Plus. On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.

PaperId: 149, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30980.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Ignacy Kolton, Wenxuan Li, Zongwei Zhou, Jarosław B. Ćwikła, Arkadiusz Sitek, Pedro R. A. S. Bassi, Szymon Płotka
Title: Diagnostic Loss: Asymmetric Supervision for Radiology Report Generation
Abstract:
Automated radiology report generation requires models to do more than produce fluent clinical narratives: they must explicitly state supported diagnoses while avoiding unsupported ones. However, existing medical vision‑language models (MedVLMs) are typically trained with token‑level maximum likelihood objectives, which prioritize text agreement over diagnostically critical terms. As a result, models can miss key diagnoses and introduce wrong ones. We identify this as an objective misalignment between conventional language modeling and the asymmetric diagnostic requirements of radiology reporting. To encode these requirements, we introduce Diagnostic Loss (DLoss), a differentiable, architecture‑agnostic objective that operates directly on decoder token probabilities. DLoss separately aggregates probability mass over vocabularies associated with diagnoses supported by the reference report and with unsupported alternatives. Using asymmetric pooling across token positions in the report, it encourages supported diagnoses to receive sufficient probability in at least one position while suppressing spurious probability spikes for unsupported diagnoses across all positions during training. The loss can be applied to existing 3D MedVLMs without modifying their vision backbones, language decoders, or inference procedures, and introduces no additional inference‑time computation. We train and evaluate DLoss on 50,000 abdominal CT scans across several 3D MedVLM architectures on both in‑distribution and out‑of‑distribution report‑generation benchmarks. Across these settings, DLoss improves diagnostic faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance on conventional language‑generation metrics, showing the value of asymmetric sequence‑level supervision for radiology report generation. The code for DLoss is available at https://github.com/gmum/DLoss.

PaperId: 150, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30970.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tardelli Ronan Coelho Stekel
Title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters
Abstract:
Many language‑model pipelines end in a closed‑set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order‑sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately. In a three‑seed study at 32 million parameters, per‑option scoring beats joint scoring on a held‑out sample of a 37‑benchmark decision suite by 5.8 points of chance‑corrected skill at matched optimizer steps and by 2.8 at approximately matched training compute; two external benchmarks agree, though not significantly on their unseen tasks. Crossing reader with initialisation shows that the advantage requires a reranker initialisation, whose query‑candidate pair input matches per‑option reading; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Per‑option scoring needs 5 to 13 times more encoder passes: at most twice the median latency, but more than four times the mean. Of six released joint encoders (17 million to 1 billion parameters), the 68‑ and 150‑million‑parameter models exceed a 435‑million‑parameter DeBERTa‑v3 zero‑shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap‑audited System1‑Arena tasks and are at least on par with it on the 145 tasks unseen in training. The smallest answers a median request in 14 milliseconds on 16 processor threads, against 728 for the classifier. Reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the joint models' answers (per‑option scoring: none). Up to 68 million parameters, they lead their size range on a public leaderboard's private, mainly in‑distribution tests.

PaperId: 151, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30951.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Hyunwoo Yu, Jongbeom Lee, Hyunbin Kim, Sungjun Park, Jaemin Choi, Jincheol Yang, Seunghun Moon, Bongjoon Hyun, Kyomin Sohn, Kyeongbo Kong, Suk-Ju Kang
Title: OpenAttention: One Percent Is Enough with Tail Proxies
Abstract:
Sparse attention reads only a small subset of the key‑value cache, and how to treat the unread tail remains a key challenge. Discarding the tail biases the output, and sampling it as previous approaches do fails at reads of 5% and below, where the tail likely holds heavy hitters the selector missed. Our key observation is that the simplest possible proxy, one token that folds the entire tail into its count‑aware mean, already yields lower output error than a sample at every read behind a practical selector. We further show in closed form that at low reads sampling nearly doubles the weight error of discarding while a single proxy stays below it. Building on these findings, we explore approximating the dense attention distribution with a few proxies that target the tail. We propose OpenAttention, a pipeline of clustering, ErrorGate and top‑k selection followed by a count‑aware mean proxy. To implement clustering and selection both efficiently and effectively, we design training‑free Query‑Geometry Clustering (QGC) and a Query‑Geometry Selector (QGS), which compress the keys while respecting the query directions. Additionally, unlike prior methods that rank clusters by centroid alone, ErrorGate allocates the exact read by the estimated weight error of each cluster. On RULER‑32K HARD with Llama‑3.1‑8B, OpenAttention retains 99% of dense accuracy at a 1% read. It also achieves state‑of‑the‑art accuracy across models, context lengths and datasets. Our customized attention kernel for OpenAttention runs the decode attention stage 10× faster than dense attention at a 1% read.

PaperId: 152, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30947.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Bo Liu, Lianyu Wang, Meng Wang, Ching-Yu Cheng, Huazhu Fu
Title: RetiJev: Fast and Source-Grounded Ophthalmic Decision Models
Abstract:
Ophthalmic clinical decision support requires fast, accurate, and privacy‑preserving inference, yet autoregressive large language models (LLMs) incur substantial latency and computational overhead for decisions among predefined actions. We therefore investigate a decision‑oriented alternative to generative reasoning. Specifically, we first introduce RetiJev‑Data, a source‑grounded ophthalmology corpus comprising 78,158 clinical‑decision and diagnosis questions derived from articles in PubMed Central and a MeSH vocabulary covering 531 eye diseases, and 50,074 guideline‑grading questions spanning 11 grading systems, along with a 24,662‑question evaluation benchmark. Based on this, we develop RetiJev, a family of 0.8B‑9B decision models that directly score candidate answers without autoregressive decoding. Across all model sizes, RetiJev outperforms both a 27B LLM and the commercial Jev 1.13 decision model on guideline grading by 10.4‑23.0 points. RetiJev‑9B further achieves the highest accuracy on clinical decisions, improving over both baselines by 5.4‑6.5 points while matching them on diagnosis. It answers a case in 158 ms on one GPU, 3.5x faster than LLM generation and 470x faster than reasoning. Models are released at https://github.com/Awenbocc/RetiJev.

PaperId: 153, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30912.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Pengfeng Song, Shaozhong Zhang, Pengfei Shao
Title: Hierarchical Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Alignment via Dynamic Granularity Discovery and Optimal Transport
Abstract:
Fine‑grained image‑text retrieval requires a model not only to assess global semantic consistency between an image and a text, but also to model visual evidence for local textual semantics, including objects, attributes, quantities, actions, and relations, so as to distinguish semantically similar candidates. Existing methods commonly use fixed image patches, detected regions, or text tokens as the basic matching units and then aggregate local interactions through max pooling, cross attention, or similarity accumulation. Such strategies remain limited in semantic unit construction and global matching consistency. This paper proposes a hierarchical fine‑grained cross‑modal alignment framework, termed HFCMA. The framework progressively transforms low‑level patch and token representations into adaptive visual regions and textual phrases, and then performs structured region‑phrase matching within a global retrieval scoring process. Specifically, HFCMA first adopts dynamic granularity discovery (DGD) to aggregate raw patches and tokens into semantically compact visual regions and textual phrases. It then formulates region‑phrase matching as an entropy‑regularized optimal transport problem, thereby estimating a structured alignment matrix under global marginal constraints. To reduce background noise and local semantic drift, HFCMA further introduces background debiasing, textual importance weighting, and prototype consistency regularization. Experiments on Flickr30K and MS‑COCO show that HFCMA effectively combines dynamic semantic unit construction with OT‑based structured matching under a dual‑encoder retrieval framework. The resulting fine‑grained score provides structured local alignment information for candidate ranking and improves the discrimination of subtle semantic differences.

PaperId: 154, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30873.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xuyang Zhong, Jiuding Yang, Yiwen Guo, Chen Liu
Title: MOER: Mix-Policy Optimization under Expert Prefix Guidance with Selective Rollback
Abstract:
Mix‑policy optimization incorporates off‑policy expert data into the reinforcement learning (RL) loop to transcend the capability boundary of on‑policy RL. However, existing methods either provide static full‑trace guidance that suppresses self‑exploration, or adopt expert prefix guidance without correctness guarantees, leading to suboptimal performance or even training collapse. In this paper, we propose MOER, a mix‑policy optimization framework that harmonizes expert guidance with self‑exploration. MOER injects a decaying expert chain‑of‑thought prefix into the prompt and lets the model complete the remaining reasoning, with the prefix length progressively annealed to encourage self‑exploration. A selective rollback mechanism replaces failed completions with the original full expert trace, guaranteeing the correctness of every off‑policy trajectory. Furthermore, a harmonized mix‑policy objective optimizes on‑policy tokens with a GRPO loss while supervising both expert prefix and completion tokens with a trust‑region SFT loss, substantially stabilizing training. Extensive experiments show that MOER achieves the highest average scores in mathematical and general domain reasoning tasks, outperforming all basic and mix‑policy baselines, and generalizes consistently across diverse tasks, model scales, and base model categories. Codes are available at https://github.com/CityU‑MLO/MOER.

PaperId: 155, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30868.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Jing Wei, Guanyi Chen, Qi Chen, Chuyu Zhang, Zheng Zhou, Chutian Wang, Jian Zhang
Title: uGDS: A User-Space Development Kit for High-Performance GPU Direct Storage
Abstract:
Data‑intensive GPU applications increasingly rely on NVMe SSDs to extend GPU memory. NVIDIA GPU Direct Storage (GDS) enables direct SSD‑GPU transfers via PCIe peer‑to‑peer DMA, eliminating host staging. However, GDS retains three key limitations: (1) its control path traverses the kernel for every I/O request, introducing software overhead; (2) its stream‑ordered path imposes strict total ordering even when workloads only require batch‑level ordering; and (3) its closed‑source user‑space engine hinders diagnosis and custom scheduling. We present uGDS, https://github.com/ScaleX‑IO/uGDS, an open‑source user‑space GPU Direct Storage library built on four principles: user‑space control, unified cross‑vendor abstraction, workload‑aware scheduling, and end‑to‑end transparency. The host CPU manages the entire NVMe command lifecycle in user space, while payloads move via PCIe P2P DMA without consuming GPU compute. A minimal kernel module is used only for one‑time privileged setup. uGDS partitions hardware queues between synchronous and batch traffic, enforces DMA‑safe buffer lifetimes, and provides cuFile‑compatible synchronous, batched, and stream‑ordered APIs with polling or interrupt completion on both NVIDIA CUDA and AMD HIP. Evaluated on an A100 with a Samsung 990 PRO, uGDS achieves up to 12.12x GDS's batch‑read bandwidth and 30.69x its batch‑write bandwidth (8‑ and 4‑KiB requests, batch size 128), and reduces 4‑KiB synchronous write latency by 84.1% with two threads. Its stream‑ordered path sustains 5.49 GiB/s on a single stream, where GDS retains only 40.8% of its synchronous bandwidth. In LMCache, uGDS reduces median time‑to‑first‑token (TTFT) by up to 62.7% and raises serving goodput by 2.63x. On AMD, uGDS achieves up to 1.19x hipFile's synchronous‑write bandwidth.

PaperId: 156, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30860.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Firoj Paudel
Title: Synthetic-to-Real Code-Switched ASR: A Spontaneous Nepali-English Podcast Benchmark
Abstract:
Nepali‑English code‑switched conversational speech presents severe challenges for automatic speech recognition (ASR), chiefly through script confusion (inappropriate mixing of Devanagari and Latin orthography) and elevated error rates at language switch points. Supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) can adapt multilingual foundation models, but human code‑switched audio is expensive to collect and annotate. We curate a new benchmark of 13,044 spontaneous podcast utterances (15.45 h total; 10,214 test, 2,830 dev), audited and verified to eliminate machine translation leakages and acoustic loops. We investigate a two‑stage synthetic‑to‑real adaptation framework: Stage 1 applies SFT on 0.95 h of speech synthesized via a multi‑speaker, dual‑engine TTS pipeline; Stage 2 explores Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with transcription and script rewards. We find that synthetic SFT provides the primary cross‑domain transfer to spontaneous human speech, reducing Mixed Error Rate (MER) from 23.40% to 21.52% (‑1.88 pp) and switch‑point error rate (SPER) from 35.89% to 28.77% (‑7.12 pp). Subsequent GRPO yields small, statistically significant adjustments on 173 test utterances (1.69%), driving English script confusion (SCR_en) from 6.45% to 6.36% (p <= 0.001) and SPER to 28.70% (p = 0.022 clustered). Crucially, ablation reveals that in this SFT‑converged encoder‑decoder setting, an auxiliary script reward term yields performance identical to MER‑only optimization because rollout candidate groups exhibit near‑zero script variance on synthetic data. On monolingual benchmarks, SFT improves Nepali MER by 2.71 pp (stabilizing at 18.42% after GRPO, a 2.38 pp gain over baseline) while preserving English lexical WER (3.38% vs. 3.33%). Verified transcripts, timestamps, episode metadata, and reconstruction scripts are publicly released.

PaperId: 157, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30828.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yeon Su Park, Chanyoung Park, Tae Soo Kim, Seungju Kim, Hyunwoo Kim, Daho Jung, Jinsung Yoon, Juho Kim
Title: TutorCaseBench: A Case-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Tutors in Supporting Students with Challenging Behaviors
Abstract:
LLMs are increasingly used as AI tutors, yet existing benchmarks overlook the challenging behaviors common among students with learning and behavioral difficulties. We introduce TutorCaseBench, a benchmark that grounds AI‑tutor evaluation in qualitative case studies from pedagogy, educational psychology, and special education. Our pipeline converts documented student categories into case‑specific scenarios, tutor‑student dialogues, and rubrics grounded in source evidence. The benchmark contains 923 dialogues across five challenge types, evaluated through open‑ended response generation (1,560 items) and multiple‑choice selection (2,537 items). Across 11 state‑of‑the‑art LLMs, even the strongest model satisfies a rubric criterion in only 55.8% of open‑ended cases, while models are better at selecting appropriate strategies than generating situated responses. These results reveal a gap between intervention recognition and context‑specific adaptation, especially for open‑weight models. All data are publicly available at https://github.com/kixlab/TutorCaseBench.

PaperId: 158, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30823.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chenyu Zhu, Ruoyu Zhao, Zhichao Lu
Title: Neural Spectral Capacity with Residual Context for Heterogeneous Resource Allocation within Transformers
Abstract:
Predicting relative trained performance from architectural specifications can guide design when training costs limit experimentation. Neural Spectral Capacity (NSC) provides such a heuristic, but scores projections independently and assigns identical scores to compatible reorderings of the same layer configurations. We introduce Residual‑Aware Neural Spectral Capacity (ResNSC) for Transformers, using a specification‑derived statistical reference for accumulated residual updates to determine the input and residual‑state statistics in each projection's capacity calculation, while retaining additive evaluation without data or instantiated weights. When residual widths vary, earlier choices affect later scores, so we augment NSC's allocator (NSC‑DP) with residual history beyond its layer‑and‑budget state. ResNSC‑DP jointly allocates residual and feed‑forward widths under a resource budget, with certified bounds on the best numerically evaluated ResNSC score within a specified finite candidate set. At the 121M and 374M pretraining scales, selected architectures achieve lower mean perplexity than uniform, variable‑width, and tapered allocations on FineWeb‑Edu, WikiText‑2, and LAMBADA at comparable parameter budgets. In inherited‑weight LLaMA‑7B pruning using the LoNAS supernet, ResNSC‑DP improves eight‑task average accuracy over NSC by 3.28‑‑5.46 percentage points across eight matched parameter budgets. Paired reversals preserve the projection shapes and NSC scores yet worsen performance in both settings, exposing performance differences hidden by position‑independent scoring. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/Optima‑CityU/neural‑spectral‑capacity.

PaperId: 159, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30817.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Taehyun Byun, Taemoon Jeong, Yoonbyung Chai, Woojin Wie, Insu Park, Kyungjae Lee, Sungjoon Choi
Title: Robot Motion Transition with a Human Motion Prior
Abstract:
Humanoid motion‑tracking policies can reproduce diverse behaviors, yet connecting independently acquired motions into a continuous sequence remains challenging. Interpolation connects boundary poses without considering whether their relative position, heading, and timing provide suitable conditions for a transition. A generative motion prior can produce richer motion, but poorly arranged boundaries may cause it to generate excessive locomotion, turning, or another unintended action. We present Spatio‑Temporal Alignment with a Motion Prior (STAMP), a framework for connecting independently acquired humanoid motions through a Robot‑to‑Human‑to‑Robot process. STAMP uses human motion space to draw on rich motion priors and reuse transition knowledge across robot embodiments. Its key component is a learned alignment model that determines the boundary conditions for motion inbetweening. Given the two motions retargeted to a human rig, the alignment model ranks candidate positions, headings, and transition durations for the following motion. A human motion prior generates the transition under the selected alignment. The completed sequence is retargeted to the robot and used as a reference to train a motion‑tracking policy. We evaluate the tracking success of the generated transitions on Unitree~G1 and~ROBOTIS K1. Physical robot demonstrations further show that STAMP connects independently acquired motions into long‑horizon sequences. Project page: https://childtoy.github.io/STAMP‑project

PaperId: 160, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30808.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haoran Lv, Chengjin Ni, Manqin Wang, Shenli He
Title: Global Convergence of Detailed Balanced Mass Action Systems
Abstract:
We give a self‑contained proof that, for a finite detailed balanced mass‑action system with positive rate constants, each positive stoichiometric compatibility class contains exactly one positive equilibrium and every positive trajectory converges to it, together with a Lean 4 formalization of the complete argument from persistence to convergence. Boundedness and persistence come from the barrier argument of OpenAI (2026) for weakly reversible systems: an arbitrary‑tolerance affine approximation yields a finite‑minimum barrier whose superlevel sets confine trajectories and give one logarithmic bound for all solutions from a given initial state. The Horn‑Jackson dissipation identity identifies the positive equilibria as an exponential family with parameters in the orthogonal complement of the stoichiometric subspace, which gives uniqueness in each class. A bounded‑speed descent argument replaces LaSalle's invariance principle; it uses neither uniqueness of solutions nor continuous dependence on initial data, and it places every cluster point in that family. The route given here is direct and elementary, and its main theorem is checked by the Lean kernel against explicit definitions. The proofs, the Lean development, and the manuscript were produced in ClawsGO Science, an agent harness that packages a complete research environment: Claude Opus 5.5 made the research decisions, GPT 6 Astra carried them out, and the Lean kernel checked every formal step.

PaperId: 161, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30799.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhiyang Li, Ruijiang Jin, Thibaut Klenke, Yusuke Sekikawa, Nakamasa Inoue
Title: WovenAnchor Matcher: Specialized Intra- and Inter-Image Context Modeling for Feature Matching
Abstract:
Semi‑dense local feature matching commonly aggregates contextual information before coarse‑to‑fine correspondence estimation. However, intra‑image and inter‑image aggregation serve different roles: the former should propagate spatial evidence within each image while retaining structured two‑dimensional dependencies, whereas the latter should gather information from plausible corresponding regions while limiting noise from unrelated locations. We propose WovenAnchor Matcher (WAM), a semi‑dense matching framework based on role‑specialized context aggregation. WAM introduces two complementary operators. WovenMamba performs intra‑image aggregation through horizontal‑then‑vertical state‑space propagation, allowing vertical updates to operate on horizontally contextualized features and thereby encouraging a structured two‑dimensional receptive‑field bias. AnchorCrossAttention performs inter‑image aggregation by using cross‑attention to gather context from plausible corresponding regions across the image pair. It performs this exchange over local representative anchors that aggregate feature evidence within each window. On MegaDepth, WAM achieves 66.1 pose AUC@5^\circ, improving on the JamMa baseline by 2.0 AUC points under the same evaluation setup. Ablations show that removing or replacing either specialized component reduces accuracy, providing evidence that intra‑image propagation and inter‑image retrieval benefit from role‑specific aggregation designs. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/mmaiLab/WovenAnchorMatcher.

PaperId: 162, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30796.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shijie Li, Yilin Gao, Tieyuan Chen, Yun Luo, Weiyao Lin, Hang Yu
Title: GIFT: Gradient Informed Filtering for Distillation Augmented Reasoning RL
Abstract:
Training large language models for complex reasoning tasks relies on two complementary signals: sparse, outcome‑grounded reinforcement learning (RL) for correctness, and dense, token‑level distillation for guidance. However, complementarity in supervision does not guarantee compatibility in optimization; imitation‑focused distillation can conflict with the outcome‑driven RL objective, and existing hybrids lack a principled resolution. We propose GIFT (Gradient‑Informed FilTering for Distillation‑Augmented Reasoning RL), a novel method that directly addresses the allocation problem of which teacher updates to apply. GIFT performs a token‑level geometric analysis, decomposing the distillation gradient into a component parallel to the RL gradient, which measures first‑order conflict and provides a safety filter, and a component orthogonal to it, which quantifies novel directional guidance and provides a measure of value. This decomposition yields a principled scoring rule to rank token‑level guidance. We combine this with a progressive coverage annealing schedule that shrinks the budget of tokens receiving distillation, ensuring that the most conflicting updates are discarded first while the most complementary ones are retained at full strength. This facilitates a smooth transition from dense, geometrically‑filtered guidance to a pure, outcome‑grounded objective at convergence. Extensive experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks show that GIFT consistently outperforms strong baselines across multiple model scales, achieving relative gains of up to 9.5% on difficult mathematical reasoning tasks. Code: https://github.com/lilifree/GIFT

PaperId: 163, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30780.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Seon Gyeom Kim, Hannah Kim
Title: ABRA: Agent-Bound UI for Human-Agent Communication beyond Chat with Reusable Views
Abstract:
Agents can create rich representations, yet these representations are rarely used as a medium for expressing user intent. We present Agent‑Bound UI, an interaction model that separates reusable interaction structures from task‑specific meanings. Agents bind task‑specific meanings to interactions in reusable views and publish the resulting bindings as shared state, enabling humans and agents to understand and act on shared surfaces whose meanings vary across tasks. We implement ABRA, a framework‑agnostic prototype of Agent‑Bound UI, in which users and agents collaborate through chat and shared interactive canvases. We demonstrate ABRA through a representative use case and evaluate four LLM‑backed agents on canvas authoring, owner‑side consequence resolution, and cross‑agent invocation. The code and demo video are available at https://github.com/megagonlabs/abra.

PaperId: 164, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30779.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiaqi Chen, Xianglong Yan, Chengzhu Bao, Xie Chen, Yulun Zhang
Title: ProQuant: Preserving Expert Quality over Quantity in Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization of Mixture-of-Experts Models
Abstract:
Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) large language models reduce computation through sparse activation but still incur substantial storage costs. Mixed‑precision post‑training quantization (PTQ) reduces these costs by quantizing different model components at different bit widths, but existing methods often struggle to preserve generation quality under tight bit budgets. We identify two key challenges: (1) nonlinear quantization errors at extremely low precision are underestimated when cross‑layer propagation is ignored; (2) direct router fine‑tuning may cause routing drift, and calibration gains may not generalize to downstream tasks. To address these issues, we propose ProQuant, a weight‑only PTQ framework for MoE models. Prune‑or‑Prioritize Mixed‑Precision Allocation (PoP) jointly optimizes expert pruning and bit‑width assignment. It allows higher‑precision experts to substitute for severely degraded ones while improving bit‑budget utilization. Routing‑Consistent RMSNorm Finetune (RoCo) adapts expert input representations through mathematically equivalent transformations. It compensates for quantization errors to reduce routing drift. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ProQuant outperforms existing methods across diverse generative tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ThrowBug/ProQuant.git.

PaperId: 165, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30765.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Angel Raychev, Nathan Lile, Rafael Rafailov
Title: Scaling Laws for Generative Reward Models
Abstract:
We study generative reward models (GenRMs) as online preference providers for policy optimization in creative writing. Across Qwen3 reward‑model sizes from 0.6B to 14B, Thinking judges trained with GRPO have higher static Gold‑label accuracy than Answer‑Only judges trained with SFT. This ranking often reverses when the judges train policies through online DPO: Answer‑Only rewarders yield higher peak and top‑five‑average policy Elo in seven of eight matched settings under a fixed, learned 32B Gold evaluator. Intermediate Thinking‑judge checkpoints can also outperform later, more statically accurate checkpoints as rewarders. Sweeps over rewarder size, policy size, training duration and DPO regularization show substantial benefits from reward‑model capacity, including judges larger than the policy. We analyze trajectories with evaluator‑specific Elo arenas, conditional match‑resampling intervals and descriptive scaling fits. These results demonstrate an evaluator‑rewarder gap in the studied pipelines: fixed‑distribution judging accuracy does not determine downstream optimization quality. The comparison changes judge‑training objective as well as response format, and the main ranking is conditional on its learned reference rather than a universal human‑quality result. A limited follow‑up using a different learned judge is inconclusive overall.

PaperId: 166, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30752.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Cristian Espinal Maya, Santiago Jiménez Londoño
Title: The Delegation Divide: An Open Index of AI-Agent Delegability across Occupations and Countries
Abstract:
35.2% of task time in world employment is at least partly delegable to AI agents in 2026, and only 2.5% can be handed over in full. Existing measures score exposure to generative AI, mostly for the United States. We build the Agent Delegability Index (ADI): two language models rate all 18,796 ONET 30.2 task statements on a frozen, preregistered rubric of delegation levels and barriers; tasks are mapped to 433 ISCO‑08 unit groups and weighted by ILOSTAT employment in 146 countries. Four findings. First, delegable employment rises with income, from 22.5% in low‑income to 48.7% in high‑income countries, a slope of 7.23 percentage points per log point of GDP per capita. This delegation divide is compositional: the physical barrier dominates the jobs poorer countries employ most. Second, at the occupation level ADI tracks exposure closely (r = 0.93 with Eloundou et al. and 0.89 with Felten et al.), above the preregistered bound of 0.80; ADI adds delegation levels and barriers on top of exposure, for the world, not a new ranking of occupations. Third, full delegation is rare and peaks for tasks that take a human about twelve minutes (11.8 minutes). Fourth, the preregistered adoption gap is not supported: across 101 countries, delegability and observed AI usage correlate at r = 0.86, and the gap between them is not wider in middle‑income countries (p = 0.27). Model agreement is kappa = 0.77; a blind human rating of 300 tasks agrees with the model consensus at kappa = 0.85, and an agentic panel with web search at kappa = 0.87. We release the index, the atlas, the prompts and an MCP server at https://github.com/Cespial/delegation‑divide.

PaperId: 167, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30738.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jie Ying, Xutao Zhang, Ningyuan Chen, Mengce Zheng, Jun Li, Zhongjie Zhu, Tiantian Zhu
Title: AgentTriage: Replayable Security Diagnosis Across Heterogeneous Agent Runtimes
Abstract:
When tool‑use agents write files, execute code, or send data, their final responses do not explain the resulting security events, and heterogeneous runtimes expose the relevant evidence through incompatible interfaces. We present AgentTriage, an executable contract for replayable security diagnosis across heterogeneous runtimes. The contract admits conclusions whose claims cite canonical runtime events and requires abstention when mandatory evidence is missing. Runtime overlays normalize native observations, while a deterministic pipeline joins invocation and result lifecycles, constructs a typed provenance graph, selects a policy‑decisive slice, and binds claims to recorded evidence. Given the same normalized trace, overlay version, and pre‑run policy oracle, the diagnosis can be recomputed and its claims re‑checked without language‑model judgment. Across five runtimes, one contract captures all 159 applicable executions, with an audit of native and synthesized identifiers. On 120 adjudicated cases, AgentTriage achieves 0.858 grounded joint diagnosis, 0.966 required‑evidence coverage, and a 0.036 unsupported‑claim rate, improving joint diagnosis by 0.175 (95% CI [0.092, 0.258]) over the strongest same‑schema baseline. These results quantify the precision of replayable diagnosis and the observation boundaries that require abstention. We release an open‑source implementation and selected sanitized evidence at https://github.com/AsnGs/agenttriage‑open‑source.

PaperId: 168, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30732.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shiyang Zhang, Miao Yang, Zhengda Li, Yang Shao, Ruifang Zhai, Hui Peng, Peng Song
Title: SmolVLA-MoE: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts for Efficient Multi-Task Robotic Manipulation
Abstract:
Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in multi‑task robotic manipulation by leveraging visual and language understanding for action generation. However, existing lightweight VLA models employ a single dense action expert to handle all tasks, which limits their multi‑task capability under constrained computational budgets. To address this issue, we propose SmolVLA‑MoE, a novel framework that introduces sparse Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) into the FFN layers of the action expert in VLA models. SmolVLA‑MoE replaces dense FFN layers with multiple parallel expert FFNs and a token‑level router, enabling each token to adaptively select the most suitable expert for action generation. We further introduce a shared expert with a tunable weight parameter to balance the inheritance of pre‑trained capabilities and task‑specific expert specialization. Through sparse activation, SmolVLA‑MoE activates only a single expert FFN during inference, with a total activated parameter count of approximately 500M including the frozen VLM backbone, while benefiting from approximately 800M total stored parameters. We evaluate our method on four task suites of the LIBERO benchmark. SmolVLA‑MoE achieves an average success rate of 84.25%, outperforming SmolVLA (82.75%) and OpenVLA‑7B (76.5%), while maintaining comparable inference efficiency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/dudu435/smolvla‑moe.

PaperId: 169, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30715.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Andrés Daniel Godoy Ortiz
Title: Meaning Contracts: Local Semantic Geometry in Large Language Models
Abstract:
This paper studies the local geometry of semantic meaning in large language models. Current representation analyses ask whether meanings are close in embedding space, or whether linear probes separate semantic classes, but they do not characterize the within‑concept local geometry: what is invariant across realizations of a single semantic factor, what varies, and what changes when meaning is refined. This paper characterizes that geometry through two controlled probes evaluated on four architecturally diverse decoder‑only LLMs (Gemma 4, Llama 3.2, Qwen 2.5, Pythia). A cross‑lingual probe uses language as a perturbation to separate exact meaning matches, same‑factor realizations, nearby concepts, and out‑of‑domain contrasts. A refinement probe separates specificity‑bearing semantic narrowing from high‑probability attributive elaboration and adversarial controls; both probes are validated by blind human judgments. Four findings recur across all models: under mean pooling, once dominant variance directions are removed, sentence pairs order by semantic relatedness (same factor, then same domain, then different domain) without overlap over a band of layers; semantic factors organize around an invariant core surrounded by structured realization‑specific variation; refinement produces directed displacement into tighter neighborhoods, including against controls built on the same base noun; and sentence‑level and token‑local readouts expose complementary geometry (volume contraction at the sentence level, sharper anisotropic endpoints at token‑local readout). We interpret these results as evidence that LLM semantics are organized as local anisotropic neighborhoods in which meaning contracts under refinement.

PaperId: 170, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30704.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jianrong Lu, Zhiyu Zhu, Hui Liu, Junhui Hou
Title: ParaLin++: Accelerating Parallel Diffusion Integrator via Intrinsic Partially Linear Structure
Abstract:
Training‑free few‑step samplers are often described as nearly quality‑lossless under conventional FID/CLIP‑style evaluation. It remains unclear whether that conclusion transfers to more realistic and complex generation‑quality benchmarks. We first systematize the quality metrics used to evaluate training‑free sampling acceleration for diffusion and flow‑matching models. We find that representative training‑free step‑shortening methods often remain nearly lossless under FID/CLIP‑class metrics, yet can suffer substantial quality degradation when evaluated with semantic‑composition, dense‑instruction, and long‑text‑rendering benchmarks such as GenEval, DPG‑Bench, and LongTextBench. Parallel sampling is a notable exception: by retaining the full‑step discretization and removing only the solver's temporal dependency, it can preserve near‑lossless quality while accelerating sampling. Building on this observation, we propose ParaLin++, a step‑parity parallel sampler that preserves the full‑step discretization while accelerating the solver iterations. Experiments across Stable Diffusion‑v2, LSUN Church, FLUX.1‑dev, and Ming‑Flash‑Omni 2.0 show that ParaLin++ preserves the full‑step Euler quality profile at 2.6×‑‑4.8×, 1.68× on FLUX, and 1.21× on Ming. Project page: https://paralinplus.github.io/.

PaperId: 171, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30680.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shiming Chen, Shuhuang Chen, Salman Khan, Fahad Shahbaz Khan
Title: Zero-Shot Domain Generalization via Domain Prompt Learning
Abstract:
Domain generalization (DG) aims to improve the generalization of the model to any unseen domains. Targeting this goal, existing DG methods mainly focus on learning domain‑invariant features or prompts from the given source domains. However, these methods rely on source‑domain data, and collecting and annotating large‑scale single‑ or multi‑source datasets is often infeasible, limiting the practical applicability of DG. To tackle this challenge, we propose \underlineDomain \underlinePrompt Learning (DoP), a method built on a large vision‑language model (e.g., CLIP) for zero‑shot domain generalization, which recognizes unseen classes in unseen target domains without access to source‑domain data. DoP essentially learns the target domain knowledge via prompt both in text and visual modalities to overcome the domain shift in text‑visual modalities under the test‑time adaptation formulation. Specifically, DoP first takes text domain learning (TDL) to simulate various distribution shifts by learning diverse style tokens implicitly in the text space with inter‑style diversity loss and intra‑style consistency loss. Subsequently, DoP employs visual domain learning (VDL) to further refine the target‑domain‑relevant style token generated by TDL by making use of the test visual data with self‑supervised learning. Extensive experiments on popular DG benchmark datasets (e.g., PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, and DomainNet) and ImageNet show that our DoP consistently outperforms the state‑of‑the‑art DG approaches. Codes are available at: https://github.com/shiming‑chen/DoP.

PaperId: 172, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30646.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Ali Abedi, Q. M. Jonathan Wu, Ning Zhang, Farhad Pourpanah
Title: One-shot federated unsupervised domain adaptation with Smoothed Knowledge Distillation and teacher refinement
Abstract:
Federated unsupervised domain adaptation (FUDA) addresses the challenge of adapting models to an unlabeled target domain using decentralized source domains while preserving data privacy. However, existing FUDA methods typically require multiple communication rounds, rely on complex aggregation strategies, and often struggle with noisy pseudo labels and inconsistent source knowledge. To address these challenges, we propose SKD‑ETR, a novel one‑shot FUDA framework that combines Smoothed Knowledge Distillation (SKD) and Exponential moving average‑based Teacher Refinement (ETR). SKD trains a student model on the target domain using smoothed soft pseudo labels generated by the ensemble of source models. This reduces overconfidence, mitigates noise, and improves robustness. ETR further refines each source model by interpolating its parameters toward the student via exponential moving average (EMA), thereby transferring target‑domain knowledge back to the teachers. This bidirectional refinement enhances pseudo‑label quality and student generalization without additional communication overhead. SKD‑ETR eliminates complex aggregation by initializing the student model randomly and performing a single‑round distillation process. Extensive experiments on OfficeHome, Office‑Caltech, and DomainNet demonstrate that SKD‑ETR achieves competitive performance while being communication‑ and computation‑efficient, and robust under noisy supervision. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/A‑Abedi/SKD_ETR.

PaperId: 173, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30645.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ruixuan Deng, Zhengfeng Ji, Jiayu Zhang, Li Zhou
Title: FVQKD: A Formal Verification of Quantum Key Distribution Security in Rocq
Abstract:
Quantum key distribution (QKD), whose security is derived from quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions, is moving into standardization and commercial deployment. Yet its security guarantees rest on technically delicate proofs checked by hand. Formal verification closes this gap, establishing a two‑factor assurance: unconditional security from physical principles, and machine‑checked proofs against reasoning errors. We present FVQKD, a Rocq library for machine‑checking QKD security proofs. Its first result is a complete, end‑to‑end machine‑checked proof of composable, finite‑key security for BB84. The mechanization reconstructs the complete proof infrastructure from first principles, including the smooth entropy framework, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. It uncovers necessary side conditions that the published argument leaves unstated, one of which reveals a missing proof branch, and it grounds the information‑theoretic bound in a formal semantics of protocol execution, which the pen‑and‑paper analysis lacks. The proof is entirely admit‑free, relying only on the Rocq kernel and standard foundational axioms. To our knowledge, this is the first end‑to‑end formal verification of a QKD security proof. Built on MathComp, MathComp‑Analysis, and CoqQ, the development provides quantum‑information infrastructure designed for reuse across broader QKD variants and quantum cryptography applications.

PaperId: 174, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30639.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Siran Dai, Qianqian Xu, Peisong Wen, Yang Liu, Xiaochun Cao, Qingming Huang
Title: CODI: Improving Self-Supervised Vision Transformers with Cross Distillation
Abstract:
Self‑supervised Vision Transformers learn strong image‑level representations, but their patch‑level representations can be unreliable for dense prediction. We study this mismatch and find that the class token concentrates global semantics on a small number of representative patches, while dense prediction errors often occur on low‑attention regions. We provide a local gradient analysis showing that, along the [CLS] attention readout, image‑level self‑distillation gradients are weighted by [CLS]‑to‑patch attention mass. To provide masked patches with global semantics without changing the architecture, we propose Cross Distillation (CODI), which mixes a small amount of the teacher class‑token distribution into each teacher patch‑token target. CODI gives every masked patch an attention‑independent semantic correction while preserving the standard self‑distillation architecture. Experiments on dense and image‑level benchmarks show that CODI improves both dense and image‑level performance under aligned pretraining settings. Code is available at https://github.com/EldercatSAM/CODI.

PaperId: 175, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30593.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhao Tan, Xianglong Bao, Zhipeng Xi, Ming Jin
Title: TT-SAX: A Two-Track Time Series Symbolization for Natural Language Shape Querying
Abstract:
Natural language querying for time series databases aims to let users find what they need in long histories of data by asking in plain language. Shape queries ask how a series moves. They are the main challenge of this task. Recent work makes them feasible by using symbolization as a bridge between the query and the long history. However, existing symbolizations were designed for compression, similarity indexing, or classification. What a symbolization should provide for natural language querying has not been systematically studied. We therefore examine the definitions of six classical symbolizations against this task and identify three limitations. (1) Direction is missing from the string, (2) direction is measured at too small a scale, and (3) the letters are arbitrary. Three design principles follow. We follow these principles and make a minimal redesign of SAX called TT‑SAX (two‑track SAX). The level letters stay. Each segment gains a trend letter. It is measured across neighboring segments rather than inside one, and graded to match the adjectives that queries use. We conduct extensive experiments on the public NLQTSBench benchmark, comparing TT‑SAX with the six classical symbolizations across six LLMs. TT‑SAX outperforms all six on shape queries, and ablations trace its gains back to the three limitations one by one. This paper is the first systematic study of time series symbolization with natural language querying as the design goal. It provides a foundation for future research on this task. Our code is available at https://github.com/Atlamtiz/tt‑sax.

PaperId: 176, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30577.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Victor Li, Owen Tucker, Michael S. Hughes, Temiloluwa Prioleau, Shengpu Tang
Title: Evaluating Type-1 Diabetes Digital Twins by Decision Quality
Abstract:
A digital twin (DT) for type 1 diabetes (T1D) can predict how an individual's blood glucose will respond to different insulin treatments without actually trying them. For each treatment, downstream statistics of predicted glucose trajectories, such as glycemic risk, can be computed to guide clinical decisions. However, the quality of DTs is usually measured by the accuracy of their predicted glucose trajectories, which may not reflect the quality of the downstream treatment decisions they inform. In this work, we directly evaluate DTs by this decision quality on downstream treatment ranking, i.e., whether a DT predicts glucose trajectories that can be used to rank candidate treatments as the real patient would. We present an evaluation protocol over 30 virtual patients from the FDA‑accepted UVA/Padova model, each simulated under 21 different basal‑bolus treatments. For each patient, a DT is fitted under one treatment and then produces glucose trajectories for the remaining 20 treatments. Our results show that prediction accuracy and decision quality disagree. A baseline that models the average patient, never seeing the individual's glucose data, has the lowest prediction accuracy of all six methods (RMSE: 63.6 mg/dL) but ranks treatments with the second‑highest mean Spearman (0.766), while a black‑box neural network that predicts glucose nearly twice as accurately (RMSE: 32.9 mg/dL) ranks them no better than a random ordering of the 20 treatments (0.049 Spearman). Therefore, selecting a DT based on prediction accuracy alone can prefer one that recommends treatments at chance, and decision quality must be evaluated directly rather than assumed to follow from prediction accuracy.

PaperId: 177, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30573.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhixin Lin, Dongliang Xu, Jungang Li, Shidong Pan, Jun Feng, Yanbin Sun, Jing Li, Liang Liu, Yue Yao
Title: Diagnosing Personalization Failures in Mobile GUI Agents
Abstract:
Unlike conventional GUI agents, personalized GUI agents require user preferences to guide sequential execution over changing GUI states. This raises two challenges: determining HOW each preference should alter execution strategy and WHEN it should take effect along the interaction trajectory. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate overall task success, offering limited insight into these questions. We introduce PrefDiag‑Bench with two components: (1) a categorization of preferences into five types, characterizing HOW they affect execution; and (2) a stage‑wise diagnostic framework with 1,664 probes, tracing WHEN preferences should take effect and where failures occur. We evaluate eleven GUI agent systems, including end‑to‑end agents and agentic workflows, under two forms of user context: explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs. Although existing agents achieve relatively high completion rates on non‑personalized tasks, performance is substantially lower on preference‑personalized tasks. Even the best‑performing model, Seed‑2.0‑Pro, achieves only 47.17% on Process preferences under explicit user profiles. Agents struggle particularly with Ranking and Process preferences. Further analysis reveals two key capability bottlenecks: selecting relevant evidence from user history and recognizing when preferences should take effect during execution. Controlled interventions that explicitly provide relevant evidence improve end‑to‑end task success by up to 7.06%. PrefDiag‑Bench offers a more systematic evaluation of GUI agents' personalization capabilities beyond overall task success. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Zhixin‑L/PrefDiag‑Bench.

PaperId: 178, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30571.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaonan Xu, Wenjing Wu
Title: Stale Instruction Files Override the Code in Coding Agents: A One-Sentence Fix
Abstract:
Purpose: Coding agents follow a project's instruction file, such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, even when it disagrees with the existing code and even when they notice the disagreement. We measure this behaviour and test whether one sentence in the user's own instruction file makes agents follow the code instead. Methods: We built 40 Python projects in which the instruction file asks for one convention while the existing code uses another, for example print instead of logging. Claude Code and Codex CLI added a feature to each project, with and without a sentence in the user‑level instruction file that gives the existing code precedence, in 320 runs. Results: Without the sentence, 90.1% of the agents' choices followed the stale file. Claude Code pointed out the conflict in 79 of 80 runs and still followed the file. Codex CLI rewrote the existing code to match the file in 20 of 80 runs, and the project's own tests then failed in 17 of them. The sentence raised the share of choices that follow the code from 4.2% to 91.4%, stopped the rewrites and raised the test pass rate from 89.4% to 100%. Conclusion: We attribute the behaviour to how agents receive the two sources: the instruction file reaches the model as an instruction and the code as tool output, which models are trained to rank lower. Users can add the sentence today, and makers of agents and models can build the same rule into their products.

PaperId: 179, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30557.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yebo Feng, Jingyang Dai, Liangrui Pan, Nelson Lau, Jiahua Xu, Yang Liu
Title: Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core
Abstract:
LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web content. We present Steward, a multi‑agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self‑evolution in its type system. First, nine role‑specialised agents decide jointly: four analysts read news feeds, SEC filings, macroeconomic series and market data and emit typed reports, from which a Portfolio Manager sets target positions that a protected Risk Manager audits. Second, a seven‑layer shared memory, assembled by code from the system's own record, gives each decision its position context, the market narrative, calibration and the agent's past decisions. Third, the system improves itself by review: code grades every trade and forecast nightly and writes the grades into memory, and each quarter a reflector proposes prompt learnings that a deterministic gate applies reversibly and replay of recorded inputs verifies. All three operate around an invariant core of order arithmetic, risk rules and discipline‑agent prompts that no self‑edit can reach. In a five‑month live deployment (102 trading days, 1,632 LLM calls), the system contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; in replay of its recorded inputs, a single model given the same raw data traded more and lost 1.35 points against the market over five days where the joint design showed no significant loss, and no injected instruction was followed; and a 2015‑2026 backtest shows the core alone lowering the maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry policies. The reflector traced the dominant failure to its root cause, and the gate applied a learning that the agent adopted on trigger evenings and on no control evening. Code: https://github.com/yebof/quant‑agent

PaperId: 180, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30530.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Isaia Nisoli
Title: The reverse Ritz inclusion: computable bounds on the pseudospectra of an operator by those of a finite-rank compression
Abstract:
We consider a bounded operator on a separable complex Hilbert space, reached only through its action on vectors and that of its adjoint, and split it along a subspace of finite dimension into a compression, a far block acting on the complement, and the two couplings between them. Given upper bounds on the norms of the couplings and of the far block, we show that outside a disc a pseudospectrum of the operator lies in a pseudospectrum of the compression, with an explicit loss in the level; this reverses the classical inclusion of the Ritz values in a pseudospectrum of the operator. The same bounds, with the smallest singular value of the shifted compression, bound the resolvent of the operator, count its eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity inside every contour outside the disc on which a computed inequality holds, and enclose its spectral projector; no normality, self‑adjointness or positivity is used.

PaperId: 181, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30524.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhipeng Cao, Peiyang Song, Nikolaus Vertovec, Weiru Cui, Zhihao Yang, Mingkang Liu, Luxia Lin, Bai Xue, Alessandro Abate
Title: LLM2Cert: LLM Synthesis of Certificates with SMT/Lean Verification
Abstract:
Lyapunov functions and barrier certificates give state‑space guarantees of stability and safety, but synthesizing and verifying them‑‑‑especially for nonlinear, high‑dimensional systems‑‑‑remains an open challenge. Existing pipelines verify candidates with numerical solvers (sum‑of‑squares programs), interval methods, or satisfiability‑modulo‑theories (SMT) solvers, which often require relaxations, are conservative, or scale poorly with model dimension and nonlinearity. These limitations have also shaped benchmark design: standard test suites are dominated by low‑dimensional polynomial systems chosen to suit what solvers can handle rather than what engineering applications require. We address both sides of this challenge. First, we introduce DynaCertBench, a benchmark of 105 instances: 80 non‑redundant systems curated from the literature, extended with high‑dimensional and control‑constrained variants and new nonlinearly coupled systems, comprehensively spanning stability, region‑of‑attraction, forward‑invariance, and safety tasks. Second, we present LLM2Cert, an LLM‑driven framework that synthesizes candidate certificates and verifies them against their proof obligations: each obligation is routed to an SMT solver or directly to the Lean Proof‑Repair agent. On DynaCertBench, LLM2Cert verifies 81 of 105 instances (77.1%), a 17.1 percentage point improvement over one‑shot proposal without feedback. On the 81 fixed certificates, LLM2Cert verifies 22 that All‑SMT leaves unresolved. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert‑AI/llm2cert.

PaperId: 182, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30512.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Louise Yorke
Title: Behind Aggregate Scores: What Systematically Varying Arena-Hard's LLM Judge Reveals
Abstract:
LLM judges are used to determine which of two answers is better. Trusting these verdicts requires knowing how repeatable they are and how much they depend on the judge's instructions. We show that similar aggregate scores can conceal substantial changes in individual verdicts, both when the same setup is repeated and when the instructions change. Using 500 Arena‑Hard v2.0 prompts with two models' answers held fixed, we run GPT‑4.1 as the judge under all eight combinations of criteria, output format and task framing, and repeat every setup unchanged at temperature zero on a pinned model version. Rerunning the default setup moves the aggregate score by about one point but changes the win/tie/loss outcome on 21.2% of prompts. Instruction changes introduce further sensitivity: in one setup, which asks for the verdict without reasoning and also drops several other instructions, outcomes change on 28.2 percentage points more prompts than the two setups' unchanged reruns do on average, and the aggregate score falls by 4.09 points. In another, where the criteria prioritise accuracy, outcomes change on 6.7 percentage points more prompts by the same comparison, while the aggregate score barely moves. A stable aggregate score therefore does not establish that individual verdicts are repeatable. This distinction matters when those verdicts are used as preference labels or to assess individual responses. Evaluations that rely on individual verdicts should repeat each setup they use and report both aggregate scores and prompt‑level agreement.

PaperId: 183, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30505.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hiroyasu Usami
Title: The Cost of Missed States: Online Tracking with Current-Observation Resets
Abstract:
An online tracker retains one state and may reset only to the current observation, although its complete observed history is available. Offline knows the future and obeys the same reset rule. Under a hard discrepancy radius, for every horizon T\ge5 and every feasible randomized causal policy, a fixed path on a known five‑point metric requires at least (T+1)/2 expected refreshes, against exactly two offline refreshes with a strict radius margin. Missing the useful prefix center forces a refresh at every suffix observation. The path visits four values, with resolution fixed as T grows. Write J_λ for cumulative discrepancy plus a charge λ>0 per refresh, and V_T for the sum of successive observation distances. A candidate prefix adapts Bienkowski and Schmid's randomized lower bound to this objective under current resets, even with a known horizon and V_T<3λ. This construction needs finer grids; a fixed finite metric with positive minimum separation instead admits a competitive policy for penalized tracking. An anytime policy satisfies J_λ\leλ+4\sqrtλTV_T without knowing the horizon or final variation. Clipping for a known horizon gives J_λ\leλT and a factor‑three comparison with the minimum of three analytical bounds, without knowing final variation. Current‑value diameter and readout sensitivity give same‑input output bounds for mixtures, including squared‑distance softmax.

PaperId: 184, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30495.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yifeng He, Jiachen Liu, Hao Chen
Title: From Prose to Properties: Testing Research Claims with ARATest for Agent-Native Science
Abstract:
AI agents now run experiments and report findings, so research produces claims faster than researchers can check them. Each empirical claim implies a property that must hold over its cases, but it states that property only in prose. Without an explicit property, no test can decide which evidence would falsify a claim, so validation cannot keep pace with the claims agents produce. To make claims testable, we approximate a claim's semantics by abstracting its property skeleton, a parameterized relation that recurs across claims. We present ARATest, a property‑based testing library that checks these skeletons as executable tests. A typed declaration binds a claim to a skeleton and fixes the claim's compared quantities, cases, scope, and numerical policy. A shared case type makes every generator supply cases in the claim's statistical unit. A three‑valued semantics assigns each property one of three verdicts: holds, violated, or inconclusive. Every violation carries a replayable witness. A default generator reads the evidence that agent‑native research artifacts (ARA) link to each claim, and auto‑research generators dispatch an agent to run released code for fresh cases. Our DissClaimer plugin supplies that agent and runs these generators as continuous testing. Of 243 claims in 33 ARA artifacts, 54 received faithful declarations bound to evidence: 32 held, eight were violated, and 14 remained inconclusive. Two violations exposed errors in published papers that their authors confirmed. ARATest detected all 553 seeded faults without a false alarm on 19 valid controls, outperforming two LLM judges. Fresh runs exposed behaviors that reported evidence could not show. These results suggest that one fixed test can check explicit claim properties against both reported and fresh evidence.

PaperId: 185, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30478.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Cheng-Yin Tu
Title: Externalise the Memory: A Pre-Registered Study of Where an Embodied Agent's Experience Should Live
Abstract:
Should an embodied agent's experience be baked into its policy weights, or kept external and retrieved at inference? A memory‑augmented teacher (a VLM that retrieves lessons, with their episode images, from its own past attempts) produces trajectories on a vision‑conditioned reach task; from the same trajectories we distil LoRA student policies and evaluate them under matched protocols, including one that re‑attaches the teacher's frozen retrieval buffer to a fixed set of student weights. We pre‑registered the hypotheses, arms, tests, and analysis rules before training and before any p‑value. Distilling the memory‑augmented behaviour into weights beat an action‑only control by +1 pp (n.s.); the registered test proves underpowered for its own minimum effect, so we withdraw ‑ rather than refute ‑ the memory‑in‑weights claim. Attaching retrieval to a fixed set of student weights added +34 pp (z=5.15), reaching the pooled memory‑augmented teacher reference (49.3%); the pre‑registered protocol contrast agrees (+23 pp, z=3.36); under a pre‑registered auto‑reset sensitivity count the two are +36 and +29 pp. An exploratory behavioural probe with pre‑registered per‑arm predictions is consistent with behavioural distillation transferring the marginal correction but not the conditional, situation‑specific correction that retrieval supplies.
