The recipe that follows is to externalise the memory: in follow‑up controls registered before they ran, the same frozen buffer lifts the base model with no adapter to 48% (sensitivity 48%) and the other three adapters from 19‑26% to 53‑55% (sensitivity 17‑21% to 50‑55%), and the adapter adds nothing detectable once the buffer is attached. On a second, harder task, the retrieval advantage points the same direction but falls short of significance (+6 pp, 95% CI [‑4.5, +16.4]); exploratory diagnostics tie the attenuation to memory coverage.

PaperId: 186, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30474.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Riteng Zhang, Xiaoqian Wang
Title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy
Abstract:
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were originally motivated by discovering monosemantic features, a property that characterizes individual features but does not specify what the learned feature set should look like as a whole. As SAEs have increasingly been adopted for attribution, circuit discovery, and intervention, researchers have begun evaluating metrics that describe global properties of the feature set, such as sparsity, dead feature rates, reconstruction fidelity, and disentanglement, a diverse set that extends far beyond monosemanticity. However, this implicit shift beyond monosemanticity has not been formalized as a clear, well‑defined objective that comes before these evaluation metrics. Without such an objective, existing metrics remain ad hoc, with their necessity unjustified. In this work, we formalize this ultimate objective by introducing a new paradigm for SAE evaluation: requiring that SAE features, and more generally dictionary‑based decompositions of model representations, form an atomic interpretable unit basis, a coordinate system for semantically meaningful explanation. Under this paradigm, we organize existing and new measurements such as DAME (Dominance‑Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) as proxy metrics and introduce a comprehensive benchmarking framework. Evaluating hundreds of SAEs across multiple architectures and model families, we uncover failure modes in which some SAEs appear monosemantic under existing evaluation metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic: the most dominant features, those contributing most to model computation, are systematically less interpretable and more redundant. These failure modes warrant attention from SAE researchers as targets for improved training and architectures, and motivate dominance‑aware evaluation as a standard check for practitioners before SAE features are deployed for attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention.

PaperId: 187, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30472.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Alankrita Bhatt, Mukur Gupta, Andrea Montanari, Pulkit Tandon
Title: DiffLTM: Continuous Diffusions Large Tabular Models for Conditional Generation
Abstract:
Conditional generation is a key capability to be supported by Large Tabular Models, enabling a number of applications. Accurate conditional generation has to contend with two key challenges: (i) Data comprise a mixture of numerical and categorical entries, the latter often with high cardinality and heavily unbalanced proportions; (ii) Conditional generation becomes increasingly difficult for rare sub‑populations. The best models in this class use a hybrid of continuous and discrete diffusions. In this paper, we design a continuous diffusion model with strong generation quality. An important element is the use of cross‑entropy loss for categoricals, for which we provide a first theoretical justification. We introduce metrics that focus on rare subpopulations. Further, we generalize conditional generation techniques to enable new types of conditioning. Finally, we show that our model (trained on labor data) can capture classical insights from econometrics. Code is available at https://github.com/granica‑ai/DiffLTM

PaperId: 188, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30468.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Seemandhar Jain, Manmohan Chandraker
Title: SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research
Abstract:
Reproducing a published 3DGS paper takes weeks of expert engineering before any extension can be proposed. Prior autonomous‑research systems read papers, draft hypotheses, and write code, but are limited by short fixed templates, low executability, and weak traceability, and none has been demonstrated end‑to‑end in a live computer‑vision subfield with intense activity. SplatLab is an autonomous research system for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses these limitations. Given a research prompt, a target‑paper URL, or no input at all, it reproduces a published baseline, proposes an extension, trains and ablates across Mip‑NeRF 360 and LLFF, writes the manuscript, and binds every reported number to a logged training run. Five design choices distinguish it: (i) candidates mutate plugins from a verified‑reproduction backbone matched to published baselines; (ii) a cascade‑weighted Elo tournament across eight islands scores candidates on measured GPU PSNR with verbal‑gradient feedback; (iii) a standing falsifier subtracts Elo on failure, integrating stress‑test survival into selection; (iv) every reported number is bound to a logged training run, and the run cannot terminate while any claim is unbacked; (v) a seven‑category 3DGS taxonomy wraps EVOLVE‑BLOCK markers in domain‑aligned scaffolds transferable across 3DGS repositories. On PSNR‑targeted runs, SplatLab's manuscripts beat their reproduced targets by +0.18 to +3.78 dB, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, for which no prior 3DGS method exists. The research cycle compresses from months of graduate‑student time to days of mostly autonomous compute. Code, all manuscripts, experiment ledgers, and the cross‑run paper store are available on the project page.

PaperId: 189, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30465.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zi Yang, Ying Li, Alejandro Lancho, Darío C. Larese, Pablo M. Olmos, Michael Minyi Zhang
Title: Flow-based Spectral Kernel Learning for Nonstationary Attention
Abstract:
Kernelized attention provides a useful perspective for understanding self‑attention as a similarity‑based aggregation mechanism, but existing approaches often rely on fixed or stationary kernels, limiting their ability to adapt the similarity structure to complex token interactions. In this paper, we propose flow‑based spectral kernel attention (FSKA), a framework for learning expressive nonstationary attention kernels. FSKA formulates kernelized attention through spectral density learning and parameterizes the resulting bivariate spectral density with normalizing flows. This design enables flexible and regularizable kernel learning while remaining compatible with scalable linear‑attention computation. We further show that expressive kernel learning enables a simplified attention design with removed query‑‑key projections and fixed orthogonal value projections, resulting in a more parameter‑efficient architecture. Controlled experiments on classification, ablation, and scalability profiling show that FSKA achieves competitive or improved performance over existing attention mechanisms, while reducing projection‑related trainable parameters by approximately 40%‑‑47% compared with most baselines and maintaining favorable linear‑attention memory scaling. Code Available: https://github.com/ziyang18/FSKA.

PaperId: 190, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30456.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Ronaldo Cristiano Prati
Title: aggmetrics: Aggregating Classification Performance Measures for Machine Learning
Abstract:
aggmetrics is a Python package that extends any binary performance measure expressed in the four confusion‑matrix counts to multiclass, multilabel, ordinal, cost‑sensitive, soft‑label and cross‑validation settings, by substituting one of four aggregation operators for what libraries usually expose as an average switch. The package also stores, for every measure, the structural properties that decide which identities apply to it, can infer those properties from a user‑supplied formula, and uses them to warn when a measure is used where it does not behave as commonly assumed. Its test suite encodes the results of the companion theory as executable tests. The package is BSD‑3 licensed, depends only on NumPy, and is available at https://github.com/rcprati/aggmetrics; documentation at https://aggmetrics.readthedocs.io.

PaperId: 191, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30442.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ahmed Mehdi Inane, Mahdi Haghifam, Gintare Karolina Dziugaite, Ioannis Mitliagkas
Title: Towards Faithful Data Selection: Statistical Limits and Scalable Algorithms
Abstract:
What does it mean to have an optimal data selection algorithm? Optimality is conventionally framed as finding a subset that minimizes the population error of the classifier trained only on that subset. Our starting point in this work is first to show that this goal is information‑theoretically impossible unless the data selection algorithm has access to a validation set order‑wise larger than the training set. This impossibility result motivates shifting from unverifiable population risk minimization to a one‑sided guarantee that we refer to as faithfulness: for any candidate subset, we provide an estimable proxy that upper‑bounds the difference between training on the full training data and on only the subset. We model training with the Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm and bound the Kullback‑‑Leibler divergence between subset‑trained and full‑data‑trained parameter distributions by the trajectory‑accumulated gradient discrepancy. Minimizing this discrepancy gives a principled way to select a subset. Even though the resulting problem is NP‑hard, we propose a swap‑based local search that decreases the bound at every accepted step. It can therefore refine the output of any selector without worsening its bound. Finally, we provide experimental results on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 showing that it matches existing data selection baselines. Implementation of our algorithm and the code for reproducing the results are available at: https://github.com/Mehdi‑Inane/data_selection_swap.

PaperId: 192, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30432.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Muhammad Danial, Muhammad Taimoor Khan
Title: TrustedCode: Evaluating Large Language Models for Developing Trusted Code through Automated Program Verification
Abstract:
Recent reports, such as "Who is using AI to code?", indicate that approximately 30% of Python code contributions to GitHub are AI‑generated. Given the inherent unreliability of this code, formal verification emerges as a promising approach to establish trust in software correctness. Although leveraging large language models (LLMs) for formal verification has garnered increasing attention, practical adoption remains limited due to the challenges in writing formal specifications and verifying program correctness against them. Existing tools predominantly support verification for languages such as Java and C, with minimal support for Python. We present TrustedCode, an automated framework for verifying AI‑generated Python code. TrustedCode uses LLMs to (i) type‑check Python code, (ii) translate it into WhyML via the Why3 framework, and (iii) verify it against formal specifications using Why3 back‑end automated theorem provers. Our method integrates chain‑of‑thought prompting through LangGraph to identify and address LLM limitations in specification generation and proving the specified programs. To evaluate TrustedCode, we conducted experiments on ten Python programs of varying complexity. Our analysis reveals that 50% of the observed errors stem from domain knowledge gaps, 30% from syntactic inaccuracies, and the remaining 20% from semantic and type‑related issues. These findings underscore the importance of targeted improvements in LLM‑guided formal verification workflows for Python. TrustedCode is an open source tool available at: \hrefgithub.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCodegithub.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode. The video demonstration is available at: \hrefyoutu.be/Nr5I2g8ec‑syoutu.be/Nr5I2g8ec‑s

PaperId: 193, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30379.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tengwei Song, Robert Hoehndorf
Title: MemPlan: Memory-Conditioned PDDL Planning for Partially Observable Text Environments
Abstract:
LLM agents are flexible in language interaction, but using them as long‑horizon planners is costly and prone to hallucinated or invalid actions. This paper targets a different role for LLMs: constrained bridges between language and symbolic planning. We propose MemPlan, a memory‑conditioned PDDL planning framework for partially observable interactive text environments. MemPlan keeps the PDDL domain fixed and reconstructs the PDDL problem at each step from parsed observations, candidate hypotheses, and interaction memory. Positive graph memory assigns relevance‑based action costs to candidate hypotheses for missing objects, locations, or conditions, guiding the planner toward more plausible checks. Negative memory records execution‑refuted assumptions and compiles them into exclusion constraints, preventing repeated attempts at candidates already contradicted by feedback. A unified schema‑conditioned language‑‑symbol interface, trained offline with supervised fine‑tuning, connects text environments to the planning loop through observation‑to‑fact parsing and symbolic‑action‑to‑command grounding. Experiments on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille show that MemPlan improves task completion and step efficiency over language‑only and PDDL‑aware baselines, while substantially reducing online token cost compared with LLM‑planning baselines such as ReAct. The same fine‑tuned interface is also reused across TextWorld task types without task‑specific fine‑tuning. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/tewiSong/MemPlan.

PaperId: 194, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30363.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Nimun Bajwa, Massimo Poesio
Title: Probing and Steering for Safety-Relevant Behaviours in Large Language Models
Abstract:
Activation probes are computed directions in a language model's residual stream, used both to detect safety‑relevant behaviours and, by adding their direction back into the stream, to steer them. We explore how the main design choices behind such probes interact, within one pipeline, on one model (Llama‑3.1‑8B‑Instruct), and across three behaviours: deception, high‑stakes awareness and sycophancy. The pipeline crosses two estimators (difference‑of‑means and logistic regression) with three token‑pooling schemes (last, mean and learned attention), selects appropriate layers to detect or steer a behaviour, and evaluates every direction twice: as a detector of the behaviour, and as a steering vector to push outputs towards the behaviour. Prior work read together suggests a read/write dissociation, in which logistic regression reads (detects) best but difference‑of‑means directions write (steer) best. We find that it holds for deception and high‑stakes but not for sycophancy, where the pattern reverses. The reversal appears to follow partially from the data rather than from the estimators. The best pooling technique and the layer choice depend on the behaviour and data, and the layer that steers best can sit well before the layer that detects best. The right steering metric to use between changing a model's perception and eliciting behaviour depends on the task ‑ and the two can disagree outright. The exported probes and directions power an interactive interface through which a user can score and steer text directly.

PaperId: 195, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30355.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chenyi Tong, Ping Nie, Yu Zhang
Title: CiteAnchor: Source-Aware Grounding for Hallucinated Citation Detection and Resolution
Abstract:
Hallucinated citations make it harder to trace sources and verify the evidence behind scientific claims. Detecting them is difficult because bibliographic records can be incomplete or differ across source types and publication versions. A plausible match alone neither validates the citation nor establishes its underlying source. We introduce CiteResolve, a benchmark of 423 real‑world hallucinated citations annotated for source recoverability. We further propose CiteAnchor, a source‑aware grounding framework that adapts retrieval and field‑level verification to each source type and separately determines citation validity and whether a unique source can be recovered. On an existing detection benchmark, CiteAnchor achieves 0.841 F1 with GPT‑5.6 Luna and 0.784 with an open‑weight backbone, outperforming the baseline with the same backbones by 7.9 and 36.8 points. On CiteResolve, it achieves 74.7% and 70.7% end‑to‑end task success, outperforming the corresponding web search baselines by 16.3 and 65.3 percentage points. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/oldwizard7/CiteANCHOR_code.

PaperId: 196, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30350.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Saurabh Kumar
Title: Who Patches the Lightning Network? Evidence from Release Lines in Gossip, 2023-2026
Abstract:
Every implementation of Bitcoin's Lightning payment network disclosed security vulnerabilities in 2026, and every advisory told operators to upgrade. Whether they do has never been measured, because Lightning gossip carries no software version. Matching the feature bits a node announces against the source of every LND, Core Lightning, Eclair and LDK release, we show that gossip reveals a node's release line after all. Where Core Lightning nodes state their version, the inferred line is exact for 132 of 136 node‑line pairs. Across 814 daily snapshots of the public graph from 2023 to 2026, the network patches on release and platform schedules, not on disclosures. Half of LND nodes upgrade within 88 days of a release; small nodes and those that skipped releases lag far behind. The three largest upgrade waves came about a day after the Umbrel app store shipped a new LND version. Since June 2025, 17% of LND upgrades came in the 48 hours after a platform release, windows that cover 4.4% of the time. Disclosures, a median 256 days after the fix, moved few operators: of 12 we can test, only Core Lightning's of July 2026 sped up upgrades, and only among nodes one release line behind. Its later call to restart offline was followed mostly by nodes already patched. Two months after Lightning Labs' August 2026 batch, 71% of the LND nodes exposed at disclosure still ran an affected release. For maintainers, the lever on the nodes that lag is the platforms that package their releases.

PaperId: 197, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30326.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Bangpu Chen, Yaxuan Li, Shirui Peng, Xiangtian Si, Liuxin Chu, Xitong Cao, Hongbo Jin, Jiayu Ding
Title: R4DGS: Referring Segmentation in 4D Gaussian Splatting
Abstract:
Dynamic representations based on 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) have shown strong capabilities in reconstruction and rendering, yet current methods remain limited in supporting complex natural‑language referring in dynamic scenes. Existing 4D Gaussian methods are primarily designed for rendering‑oriented dynamic modeling, while current semantic extensions often rely on scene‑specific semantic optimization or are evaluated on relatively simple query settings. In this paper, we study Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a task for grounding temporally varying, multi‑target or reasoning‑intensive, and zero‑target or distractor expressions in dynamic 4D scenes. To support this task, we introduce R4D‑Bench‑QA, a benchmark with structured query annotations. We further present ReferGaussian, a unified framework built upon 4DGS that converts low‑level dynamic Gaussians into persistent, language‑addressable entities for training‑free referring inference. ReferGaussian organizes mask‑supported Gaussian entities in an EntityBank, uses Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to decompose complex queries into trackable object phrases and structured referring constraints, and performs constraint‑aware grounding without scene‑specific semantic optimization. Experiments on R4D‑Bench‑QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol demonstrate improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding without scene‑specific semantic training. Project resources are available at https://chenbangpu.github.io/R4DGS/.

PaperId: 198, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30320.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Huiwon Jang, Suhyeok Jang, Hyeonmo Kang, Seungku Kim, Jinwoo Shin, Sihyun Yu
Title: Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models
Abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre‑trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self‑Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self‑distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground‑truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real‑world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long‑horizon and out‑of‑domain tasks under zero‑shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human‑to‑robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.

PaperId: 199, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30307.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ripon Chandra Malo, Zimeng Yu, Tong Qiu
Title: The Customer Is the Builder: How AI Coding Agents Are Rewriting the Economics of Software
Abstract:
AI coding agents could change whether organizations buy software or build the functionality they need. We focus on organizations and professional buyers whose domain knowledge can help them specify and evaluate tools for their work. We define the software substitution frontier as the functions customers could build and maintain at an acceptable standard for less than buying them. Using public data, we compare growing capacity to build with indicators of market change. Since 2023, the length of benchmark tasks that leading agents can complete at 50 percent success, measured in human working time, has doubled about every 129 days. A broad search identified 575 potential open‑source alternatives to selected commercial products, although some functional matches still require independent validation. The Craft suite produced 12 application repositories over 12.0 days of public development, but these remain early versions with unverified completeness and reliability. Market evidence is mixed: purchased software gained US investment share and tracked commercial installations grew. Yet 32 percent of respondents to an organizational survey reported forgoing at least one software purchase because their organization could build the functionality with coding agents. These self‑reports do not establish the spending displaced or the reliability of the resulting tools. The gap motivates a warning: customers' capacity to build could affect individual buying decisions before a broad purchasing shift becomes visible. We examine this possibility using benchmark projections and observable market tests. The projections are an extrapolation, not a forecast of customer switching.

PaperId: 200, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30292.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Muheng Li, Wenlong Mou
Title: GAV: A scientific experimentation environment for PDE agents
Abstract:
Reliable feedback is essential for coding agents to develop programs for partial differential equations (PDEs). Yet evaluating these programs on new PDE problems often requires expensive reference computations, while fixed datasets restrict the range of experiments. We introduce Generator‑Agent‑Verifier (GAV), a scientific experimentation environment that makes new PDE problems verifiable by construction. The Generator learns a distribution of continuous reference solutions using data from numerical simulations or experimental measurements to represent a target physical regime. Using the method of manufactured solutions, it works backward from the generated reference solutions to construct matching PDE problems without a separate numerical solve. The Agent designs experiments, investigates failures, and iteratively improves its program. The Verifier evaluates candidate programs against the reference solutions and provides numerical feedback on accuracy and computational cost. This feedback can also guide the generation of new problems that probe the current program's weaknesses. We provide a theoretical analysis of evaluation reliability and guided development. Experiments on Navier‑Stokes and Vlasov‑Poisson‑type equations across different data sources and regimes demonstrate the effectiveness of GAV. In particular, on the numerical Navier‑Stokes task, GAV reduces the mean test error of three existing PDE agents by more than an order of magnitude relative to their original setups. Code is available at https://github.com/PotatoJnny/PDE‑GAV.

PaperId: 201, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30284.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kaijian Zou, Vaibhav Chennareddy, Yunxiang Zhang, Naihao Deng, Longju Bai, Jiaxin Pei, Rada Mihalcea, Lu Wang
Title: SWE-VERIFIER: Selective Verification for Cost-Efficient Coding Agents
Abstract:
Coding agents spend substantial computation generating actions and processing long interaction histories. Poor action choices can steer agents into low‑value states, wasting computation and increasing API costs. Sampling and verifying alternative actions can improve the agent's decisions, but applying this procedure at every step adds substantial overhead. We introduce SWE‑Verifier, a lightweight generative model that selectively triggers candidate sampling and verification. It scores the coding agent's proposed action to determine when additional candidate sampling is needed, then ranks the resulting actions before execution. We train SWE‑Verifier from Qwen3.5‑4B using preference data that groups contrasting actions with their resulting environment observations and rubric‑guided teacher scores. Using the mini‑swe‑agent harness, SWE‑Verifier improves resolution from 75.47% to 77.20% on MiniMax‑M2.7 at 1.09 times cost and generalizes to DeepSeek‑V4‑Flash without training on its actions, improving resolution from 72.60% to 74.27% at 1.13 times cost. Across both models, SWE‑Verifier verifies fewer than 4% of steps and achieves comparable or higher resolution than the trajectory and all‑step baselines at substantially lower cost. These results demonstrate that selective candidate sampling and lightweight verification provide complementary gains in coding‑agent performance and inference efficiency. Our model, code, and data are available at https://github.com/zkjzou/SWE‑Verifier.

PaperId: 202, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30272.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Henry M. Haase, Andrew R. Winters, Jan Glaubitz
Title: Summation-by-parts operators for general function spaces: Flux differencing, entropy stability, and accuracy
Abstract:
Summation‑by‑parts (SBP) operators are a cornerstone of provably stable high‑order methods for hyperbolic conservation laws. For nonlinear problems, the flux‑differencing framework of Fisher and Carpenter combines such SBP operators with entropy‑conservative two‑point fluxes to obtain semi‑discretizations that are conservative in the sense of Lax‑‑Wendroff and discretely entropy‑conservative or stable. So far, this framework has been developed exclusively for operators that are exact for polynomials. Function‑space SBP (FSBP) operators lift this restriction by being exact on a general finite‑dimensional function space that can be tailored to the problem at hand. In this work, we extend flux differencing to FSBP operators for general (potentially non‑polynomial) function spaces. We prove that, whenever the operator has a diagonal norm and its function space contains the constants, the resulting semi‑discretization is conservative in the sense of Lax‑‑Wendroff, semi‑discretely entropy‑conservative within a single element, and entropy‑stable across element interfaces. We also provide the first theoretical accuracy analysis of FSBP operators: We characterize their design order through an algebraic criterion on the underlying function space, prove that suitable non‑polynomial spaces achieve the same design order as polynomial spaces of equal dimension, and show that the flux‑differencing semi‑discretization retains this order. Notably, the entropy‑conservative two‑point flux is reused unchanged; only the underlying function space differs from the polynomial case. Numerical experiments for the Burgers' equation and the compressible Euler equations in one and two dimensions confirm these properties.

PaperId: 203, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30223.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Saad B. Alarifi, Mohammed A. Alam
Title: How Prompt Style Affects AI Accuracy and Speed in Competitive Programming
Abstract:
Large language models are increasingly used in competitive programming, and their outputs are sensitive to how a prompt is phrased. Prior work has compared prompt strategies for accuracy on competitive programming, but not for runtime speed, and has not situated the results against human performance. In an exploratory study of one prompt in each of nine styles on GPT‑5.5 across three accuracy tasks from the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) and two NP‑hard speed tasks, we found that no single prompt was best: the strongest prompt depended on the task type and on whether results were summarized by the mean or the median, suggesting that, at least for these tasks, prompt style should be matched to the objective rather than treated as universal. Many differences in mean scores came from a few outlier runs, showing that evaluating prompting by a single metric can obscure how much its effectiveness varies. Compared descriptively with human IOI contestants, who worked under different conditions, the AI was neither strictly better nor strictly worse, exceeding the average contestant on one task but falling short on the other two. By extending prompt comparison from accuracy to runtime speed and grounding it against human performance, this study gives a broader picture of how prompt style affects competitive programming performance.

PaperId: 204, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30215.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Siavash Golkar, Jake Kovalic, Shirley Ho
Title: AI Mindmeld: A Latent Interconnect Protocol
Abstract:
LLMs can act as scientific agents using tools to consult specialists and run experiments. Yet specialist information must enter their context, generally as text, images, audio or video: a bottleneck between models with rich, high‑dimensional representations. We advocate direct representation exchange: a mindmeld conveying many properties, including information an LLM would not think to request. It should be extensible to new specialists, flexible across questions and tasks, and compositional across independently connected specialists without joint training. The Latent Interconnect Protocol (LIP) learns connectors mapping specialist representations into LLM internal states. Training only connectors keeps this practical as LLMs grow and evolve. We connect three protein and three small molecule specialists to Gemma 3 (4B and 12B parameters) and Kimi K2.6 (1T total, 32B active), freezing all pretrained models. Independently trained connectors provide useful information without changing the LLM or existing connectors, supporting familiar and new question types about unseen objects. We demonstrate zero‑shot transfer to cross‑domain tasks without joint training. Task performance and compositionality generally improve with LLM capability, with especially strong gains in zero‑shot task transfer. Limitations remain: current LLMs were not trained for specialist representations as native inputs; access does not ensure reliable interpretation, integration or use in reasoning. We call on specialist developers to provide consistent representation interfaces and, especially, on LLM developers to train models to receive, combine and reason with these inputs. These efforts could expand scientific agents' information while preserving conventional tools' flexibility. Data, pretrained connectors, and code for training, evaluation and interactive inference: https://github.com/PolymathicAI/AI‑Mindmeld

PaperId: 205, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30205.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Esmail Gumaan
Title: Feedback That Backfires in Games: Do LLM Players Repeat the Move They Just Watched Fail?
Abstract:
When an LLM agent's move fails, the harness writes the move and the failure message into the transcript and asks again. In tool calling, this record makes small models more likely to repeat the failed action. We test whether the same holds in games (Sokoban, Connect Four, Othello), where a move can fail by being illegal or by being legal but losing, both verified exactly. On fixed probe items built by perturbing a correct move, the record backfires: pooled over 8 instruction‑tuned models (135M‑1.7B) it makes the failed move more likely (corrective gain G = ‑1.38 nats per token), through the move's surface form, for illegal moves but not for losing ones, and not for every model. An exploratory analysis shows what sets the sign: after the record, the failed move's log‑probability barely depends on how likely it was before (slope 0.18). Moves the model would not have played become more likely, and greedy decoding starts to produce them; moves it was about to play become less likely, but greedy decoding still repeats 38% of them. A description of the failure that omits the move string keeps the model's preference instead. Along the OLMo 2 1B post‑training ladder the inversion is present in the base model and largely removed at the DPO stage. RAGEN's default models invert in RAGEN's own Sokoban format before any RL. A "do not repeat" instruction does nothing, a clean retry is the worst harness, and a decoder ban stops exact repeats but not illegal play. All measurements ran in float32 on a free Colab GPU, which first reproduced the original paper's number.

PaperId: 206, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30200.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Vaidehi Hegde
Title: Detection Is Not Enough: Reasoning Traces as Testable Program Hypotheses
Abstract:
When a language model is deployed, no reference solution exists, so the reasoning trace it writes is the only evidence for judging its answer. The reference‑free substitutes each fail differently: self‑assessment degrades the answer it was meant to protect, sampling agreement measures stability rather than correctness, and perturbation studies read the expected answer off a human‑written template, grading a model rather than a trace. We ask how far a single trace can be verified with no reference solution, no judge model and no weight update, and find, for a frozen LLaMA‑2‑7B‑chat on GSM8K, that detection is not what limits such a pipeline. Checking a trace against itself reaches an AUROC of 0.741 and stops there for a structural reason: two thirds of wrong traces state no false equation, having executed a mistaken plan correctly, and on wrong‑plan failures the detector flags a wrong trace less often than a right one. A candidate‑derived metamorphic probe exposes many of these failures: we abstract the trace into a program over the question's quantities, perturb one quantity, execute the program, and ask the model the rewritten question once, so every trace supplies its own test. Valid perturbations exist for 937 of 1,319 test questions (71.0%); among the 847 that also have a parseable first trace, supported traces are correct 60.6% of the time against a 31.6% base rate, although the probe also refutes 45.5% of correct traces. No tested policy yields a statistically significant improvement in accuracy. A flag earns its retry only when detector precision exceeds D/(R+D), where R and D are the rates at which a retry repairs a wrong trace and damages a correct one; our repair rate is so low that, at the same retry budget, even a perfect detector would recover an estimated 66 of 1,319 questions. Repair, not detection, is the open problem.

PaperId: 207, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30197.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jona Joy
Title: Alpha: Systematic Fault Injection and Robustness Evaluation for LLM-Driven Embodied Manipulation
Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into embodied robotic planning, yet standard benchmarks primarily evaluate end‑to‑end task completion in nominal environments, obscuring failure origins across the execution stack. We present Alpha, a systematic fault‑injection and robustness‑evaluation framework for LLM‑driven manipulation in simulation. Alpha injects calibrated faults across perception (sensor lag), actuation (grip slip), kinematics (unreachable targets), and planning (planner‑output corruption), alongside concurrent conditions. To separate physical vulnerabilities from planner sensitivities, we introduce a matched methodology pairing an LLM agent (Llama‑3 via Ollama) against a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner across a balanced 150‑episode matrix under identical seeds, geometries, and safety criteria. Across the matrix, the Oracle achieves 64.0% (48/75) success while the LLM achieves 44.0% (33/75) (paired McNemar p = 3.01 x 10^‑4). Crucially, excluding planner‑output corruption, performance across all physical and kinematic conditions is identical: 55.0% (33/60) for both planners with zero discordant pairs (McNemar p = 1.00). This demonstrates that physical actuator slip, kinematic reach boundaries, and perceptual staleness affect deterministic controllers and LLM planners equivalently. The performance gap is driven entirely by planner‑output corruption (100% Oracle vs. 0% LLM), isolating the prompt‑to‑JSON serialization and validation interface rather than a cognitive reasoning deficit. We also audit 169 historical pilot attempts for transparency.

PaperId: 208, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30186.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jeongbin Sohn, Jina Lee, Max Yen, Dowan Gwon, Jeahn Han, Floyd Hepburn-Dickins, Brian Coltin, Ryan Soussan, Pyojin Kim
Title: SIGNN++: Robust Graph Neural Star Identification on Earth
Abstract:
We present SIGNN++, a learning‑based star identification (SID) framework for celestial navigation in GNSS‑denied nighttime environments. Although researchers have developed learning‑based SID methods to improve robustness to observation noise, prior evaluations have focused mainly on synthetic or non‑terrestrial environments, leaving their reliability under real terrestrial conditions unclear. To address these limitations, SIGNN++ extends SIGNN, a graph neural network‑based SID method, with three components: a more realistic noise model for training data, Fourier Transform (FT) of angular‑distance edge features, and RANSAC‑based Perspective Star Alignment for identification and attitude refinement. The results show that SIGNN++ is more robust to terrestrial observation disturbances and achieves higher star identification accuracy and solved rates than the original SIGNN and publicly available SID baselines, while maintaining comparable attitude accuracy and practical computation time for continuous operation. The implementation code of SIGNN++ and datasets will be available at https://signnpp.github.io/signnpp/.

PaperId: 209, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30179.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yatin Kumar, Shivani Saini, Ramesh Kumar Vats
Title: GeoDiv KAN Solver for Time Fractional Navier Stokes Equations on Complex Domains to Realistic CFD Reconstruction
Abstract:
Scientific machine learning provides a promising framework for solving complex problems in science and engineering. Notably, physics informed neural networks (PINNs) have shown considerable potential for solving differential equations and modelling engineering systems. Solving time fractional Navier Stokes equations (TFNSEs) on complex domains is challenging due to temporal nonlocality, nonlinear flow dynamics, geometric complexity, and incompressibility constraints. To address these challenges, we propose a geometry gated, divergence‑free Gaussian radial basis function Kolmogorov Arnold network (GeoDiv KAN). The proposed architecture uses geometry dependent feature gating and a streamfunction formulation to preserve incompressibility by construction. GeoDiv KAN is evaluated for the time fractional incompressible Navier‑Stokes equations on square, circular, and star‑shaped domains. Numerical experiments show that GeoDiv KAN achieves higher predictive accuracy than PINN, PIKAN, RBF KAN, and DF RBFKAN across the considered benchmark problems. To establish practical relevance, GeoDiv KAN is applied to two data driven CFD cases: unsteady flow past a circular cylinder using the \hrefhttps://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5039610Zenodo dataset and turbulent RANS flow through a complex U bend using the \hrefhttps://huggingface.co/datasets/JDecke/ubend‑cfdU‑bend dataset.

PaperId: 210, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30175.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Vineeth Venugopal, Elsa Olivetti, Jonathan Welch
Title: FormBench: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Retrieval in Formulation Patents
Abstract:
We introduce FormBench, a platform for testing the ability of models to retrieve precise chemical information from technical documents. FormBench contains 55,352 queries and two retrieval corpus variants each with ~1M passages: FormBench‑Random (C0), with randomly sampled distractors, and FormBench‑Structured (C1), with structurally proximate distractors. Each query is paired with an anchor passage, a hard negative, and a soft negative ‑ derived from a materials ontology through entity overlap scoring, providing a deeper graded signal on a model's discriminatory power. We evaluate 10 model configurations spanning commercial API encoders (OpenAI, Voyage), open‑source encoders (Nomic, GTE‑large, Qwen3‑Embed), and their task‑adaptive fine‑tuned (TAPT) variants. We find: (1) commercial APIs score very poorly across all configurations (OpenAI‑3‑large: 0.009 on C1, 0.213 on C0); (2) TAPT on FormBench triplets lifts Qwen3‑Embed to 0.4085 on C1, 0.4835 on C0; (3) BM25 remains competitive (0.375 on C1, 0.467 on C0), exceeded only by TAPT‑Qwen3; (4) corpus size has a significant impact on retrieval behavior, as demonstrated through a corpus‑size ablation; (5) the API failure traces to within‑domain geometric collapse; (6) APIs outperform even the TAPT variants on classification and clustering tasks. FormBench is released in BEIR‑compatible format at huggingface.co/datasets/vinven7/FormBench under CC‑BY‑4.0.

PaperId: 211, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30162.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shuo Cai, Yanggan Gu, Yuhang Liu, Su Lu, Yuanyi Wang, Yang Yu, Zhen Li, Zhitian Hou, Guanghao Zhu, Ming Li, Hongxia Yang
Title: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models
Abstract:
Model fusion aims to integrate the capabilities of multi‑expert models into a single model. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage of reasoning with long chains of thought and tool use, while strong average performance can mask substantial losses in individual expert capabilities. We introduce FusionEval, a benchmark that provides controlled expert pools, integrates fusion methods with and without additional training, and offers a unified evaluation suite. The pools contain domain experts independently trained from Qwen3 and Llama base models across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use. The suite evaluates capability retention and computational cost on eight public benchmarks under comparable data access rules, reporting normalized average and worst performance, runtime, and peak GPU memory usage. Extensive experiments show that training‑free methods preserve reasoning performance but substantially degrade tool use at both model scales. In contrast, MOPD preserves tool use and achieves a more balanced capability profile, but requires additional data preparation, inference, and training. Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low computational cost remains a challenge. We hope FusionEval supports future research on efficient model fusion that jointly preserves expert capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/Baicaihaochi/FusionEval_Benchmark.

PaperId: 212, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30161.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Krishanu Adhikary, Prashant Devadiga
Title: TauIndianBankBench: Procedure-Aware, Action-Oriented Evaluation of Tool-Using Conversational Agents
Abstract:
Many Indian banks serve customers through FAQ pages and scripted chatbots. Assistants based on language models could respond faster and carry out requests such as blocking a card, but only if they give correct information and follow the bank's rules. These rules prescribe a procedure, a set of required steps, such as obtaining a closure quote before closing a deposit. Adapting models to this domain requires measuring how well they follow the procedure, before and after training. Benchmarks usually judge only the records left at the end of a conversation. Many required steps, however, leave the records unchanged, so an assistant that skips them can still be judged successful. We present TauIndianBankBench, an action‑oriented benchmark of 1,000 Indian retail‑banking tasks where an assistant helps a simulated customer. Besides the final records, it checks that the assistant took every required step and made no unrequested change. For every model, 6.5‑12.0% of sessions are judged successful when only the final records are checked, although the assistant skipped a required step or made an unrequested change. Scoring both procedure and outcome shows more accurately how well language models perform in Indian retail banking.

PaperId: 213, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30151.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Pranav Varshney
Title: The Cost of Saying Hello: An Empirical Study of Handshake Overhead in AI Agent Communication Protocols
Abstract:
Every interaction between AI agents begins with a handshake: the initiating agent must locate its counterpart, learn what it can do, and establish a session before the first useful message can be sent. Surveys of agent communication protocols name handshake overhead as an efficiency criterion, yet none report measurements. This paper presents the first empirical, phase‑decomposed benchmark of the handshake in three major agent protocols: MCP (in both its 2025 initialize and 2026 discover eras), A2A, and ACP. Using each protocol's official SDK, we instrument every request for round trips, per‑phase latency, wire bytes, and token cost across cold‑start, warm‑repeat, capability‑mismatch, and degraded‑metadata scenarios (N=50 per cell, on loopback and under an emulated 50 ms RTT). Round‑trip count dominates handshake cost. A legacy MCP handshake takes three round trips and 230 ms at 50 ms RTT; A2A needs one round trip and 61.0 ms. Round trips are not the whole bill: when an LLM reads the counterpart's metadata, handshake cost scales with the counterpart's capability inventory at 24‑107 tokens per capability, so a 200‑capability counterpart spends 11% of a 200k‑token context window before the agent reads its own task. MCP's own 2026 revision cuts its handshake from three round trips to two and, with era pinning, to zero on warm reconnects, protocol evolution that corroborates the cost we measure. We release the full harness, raw data, and analysis at https://github.com/pvarshh/handshake‑benchmark.

PaperId: 214, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30132.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhennan Wan, Jianfei Chen
Title: LongZero: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs from Zero Data
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective way to strengthen the long‑context reasoning of large language models (LLMs), but it needs training data that are long, diverse, challenging, and verifiable. Human annotation of such data is expensive, naturally occurring data are too scarce to sustain RL, and existing synthesis methods depend on external corpora or stronger teacher models, which become harder to obtain as the trained models get stronger. Recently, RL from zero data, in which a model learns from tasks it proposes itself, has achieved excellent performance, but existing methods target short‑context tasks. Therefore, we propose LongZero, a method that lets an LLM improve its own long‑context reasoning without any external data. Instead of writing questions and answers over existing documents, LongZero first has the model synthesize the question and answer with its supporting evidence in a compact structured form, and only then separately expands the evidence into a long multi‑document context. LongZero combines these self‑written multi‑hop reasoning tasks with self‑written multi‑round retrieval tasks and trains the model with GRPO. We evaluate LongZero on two LLMs across five long‑context reasoning benchmarks and compare it with RL on data synthesized from external corpora. Experimental results show that LongZero can generalize to real tasks, and outperforms both baselines, suggesting a viable and promising path to improving long‑context reasoning of LLMs.

PaperId: 215, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30128.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhanshuo Cao, Jiakai Tang, Yuqi Zhou, Sunhao Dai, Jun Xu
Title: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
Abstract:
Existing sequential recommenders usually allocate a fixed computational budget to every item in a user's interaction history, regardless of the item's contribution to the final prediction. We challenge this de facto design with two diagnostic findings. (1) Non‑uniform computational need: items within the same sequence vary drastically in how much computation they require. Most converge after shallow processing while a critical minority only stabilizes at full depth. (2) Suboptimality of fixed allocation: given oracle access to the target item, a non‑uniform depth assignment consistently outranks the fixed one, indicating that existing uniform computation both wastes capacity on already‑converged items and sacrifices overall recommendation quality. These observations motivate a shift from fixed‑depth computation to item‑level adaptive reasoning. To this end, we propose LoopRec. LoopRec recursively applies a single weight‑shared block and introduces a lightweight gate at each recursion boundary that makes a binary exit‑or‑continue decision for every item independently. Items whose representations have sufficiently matured exit early, while those requiring deeper reasoning continue to subsequent recursions. This design converts the fixed global depth into a learned, per‑item property without auxiliary depth labels, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks with four backbone families demonstrate that LoopRec consistently outperforms matched fixed‑depth counterparts. Further analysis reveals that LoopRec's learned allocation exhibits interpretable patterns aligned with our post‑hoc oracle analysis: lower‑frequency items and more recent interactions naturally receive deeper computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Elpmis117/LoopRec.

PaperId: 216, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30120.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yanqing Liu, Letian Zhang, Chengzhi Liu, Zijun Wang, Jieru Mei, Hongliang Fei, Yuyin Zhou, Cihang Xie
Title: ALPS: Visual State Encoders for World Models
Abstract:
World models turn visual representations into predictions and actions. We argue that their visual foundation should combine physical‑state information, native language alignment, and pixel reconstruction, so that a single representation can support prediction, instruction, and inspection. However, existing encoders typically specialize in only one or two of these capabilities; we therefore introduce ALPS, a pretrained visual state encoder that unifies all three in a single set of patch tokens. Using only still images and text, we pretrain a ViT‑B/16 from scratch with language, reconstruction, and spatial correspondence objectives, and then refine it via cross‑view self‑distillation. In a unified evaluation across fifteen public encoders, ALPS achieves the lowest aggregate LIBERO state‑probe error among ViT‑B models (matching the 3.5x larger V‑JEPA 2‑L) while maintaining strong language alignment and accurate pixel reconstruction. Downstream, frozen ALPS tokens reach the highest mean policy success on LIBERO (85.5%) when paired with our native text tower, match or exceed leading encoders on world‑model planning across PushT, Wall, and Granular, and allow predicted future tokens to be decoded directly into pixels for visual inspection. We hope this work helps establish visual pretraining as a shared foundation for understanding, prediction, and action in world models.

PaperId: 217, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30116.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shibo Jin, Zhiqiu Xu, Yiling Zou, Shangyu Gong, Mayur Naik
Title: Environment Duels: A Microcosm of LLM Co-Evolution
Abstract:
Through a tangle of real‑world interactions, from synthetic training pipelines to data shared on the open web, frontier LLMs absorb what their predecessors and competitors create. How well does each model play its role in this ecosystem, as a creator and as a solver? We introduce Environment Duels, a dynamic agentic benchmark that evaluates both capabilities on interactive environments. Each model writes environments, each with a privileged hint, aiming for tasks that capable solvers fail without the hint and pass with it. Across nine frontier LLMs, solving and authoring prove to be distinct skills: the strongest solvers are not the strongest authors, while smaller models learn more from how others played and write the hardest environments and the most useful hints. Beyond the scores, the pairwise interactions form a microcosm of how models affect one another. Head‑to‑head outcomes are transitive and so yield a stable ranking; independent authors converge on the same designs; and in a reinforcement‑learning study with Qwen3.8‑27B, the learner's hint lift on an author's environments tracks how much training on those environments improves it on held‑out reasoning and agentic benchmarks, whether the environments are its own or another model's. Each of these patterns has a counterpart in how models shape one another outside the duel. By staging these interactions under controlled conditions, Environment Duels offers a window onto how LLMs teach, challenge and learn from one another. Code is available at https://github.com/LLM‑Duels/EnvDuels.

PaperId: 218, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30108.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yanzhe Chen, Ziyi Yang, Jifeng Zhu, Qiming Huang, Ruihe An, Peiyao Xu, Hesen Yang, Runda Liu, Chang Gong, Zhijun Cao, Zechen Bai, Wenzheng Zeng, Yiqi Lin, Guoqiang Liang, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Mike Zheng Shou
Title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use
Abstract:
Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer‑use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal‑directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer‑use to robot‑use? We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability‑centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome. Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors. Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.

PaperId: 219, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30103.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Nurul Labib Sayeedi, Md. Faiyaz Abdullah Sayeedi, Zabir Al Nazi, Mahbub E Sobhani, Shubhashis Roy Dipta
Title: Did the Problem Actually Get Harder? Testing LLMs on Paired P and NP-Complete Problems Hardened by Adversarial Multi-Agent Rewriting
Abstract:
Many NP‑complete (NPC) problems have a polynomial‑time (P) twin that differs in a single structural detail, such as 3‑ versus 2‑colouring a graph. A model that reasons rather than recalls should notice which side of this boundary a problem falls on, yet existing benchmarks either fix the wording of each task or ignore its complexity class, so they cannot separate the two. We introduce P2NPCBench, a benchmark of 12 problem families in which every NPC problem is paired with a P twin posed over the same surface. To remove the textbook cues that enable recall, we build it with AgentGAN, an adversarial multi‑agent framework in which a generator rewrites each statement until a panel of frozen code models fails, while an executable validity gate keeps every rewrite answer‑ and class‑preserving. The result is 2,114 hardened statements with hand‑verified reference human solvers. Evaluating 12 proprietary and open‑source models, we find that every model scores lower on NPC statements than on their P twins (35.4% vs. 63.8% pass@1), and that 95.1% of model‑family pairs fail more often on the NPC side. A tenfold time limit raises NPC accuracy only from 28.5% to 31.9%, so failures stem from wrong or crashing programs rather than slow ones. Hardening also narrows the class gap from 24.8 to 14.6 points, showing that part of the apparent gap reflects familiarity with textbook phrasing rather than complexity class.

PaperId: 220, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30068.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Adrien Deschenaux, Nadezhda Ilieva, Justin Deschenaux, Manuel Madeira, Dorina Thanou, Aurélien Lucchi, Antonio Orvieto, Caglar Gulcehre, Pascal Frossard
Title: Loopholing All the Way: Language Modeling with pure Self-Conditioning
Abstract:
Recent Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) use Self‑Conditioning (SC), or Loopholing, to improve their performance. While SC is traditionally seen as an auxiliary heuristic, its empirical success raises the question: can a continuous generative model be based purely on Self‑Conditioning? We answer affirmatively with LAW (``Loopholing All the Way''), which propagates the Expected Embedding under the denoiser's prediction across steps, decoding the tokens once, at the end. On Sudoku, LAW outperforms previous Discrete and Continuous Diffusion Models, including Loopholing Discrete Diffusion. On Maze, LAW is the most accurate from 2 to 64 NFE. After training on TinyGSM and sampling at temperature 1 with 1024 NFE, LAW solves 42.2% of GSM8K problems against 34.5% for uniform Loopholing Discrete Diffusion. Additionally, fine‑tuning a pre‑trained Uniform Diffusion Model (Duo) with LAW increases its accuracy from 17.2% to 48.1%. Finally, on OpenWebText, LAW pushes the Pareto frontier and approaches Autoregressive Models (ARMs) with 64 NFE. Find our code at https://github.com/ilievanadezhda/law.

PaperId: 221, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30067.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Quang Anh Kiet Tran, Nam Anh Tran, Manh Hung Trinh, Thanh Danh Le, Khang Nhat Hoang Vo, Huynh Dai Nhan Tran
Title: GoiBERT: Compact Vietnamese Language Models via Two-Stage Knowledge Distillation
Abstract:
Vietnamese pre‑trained encoders have improved rapidly, but the strongest ones are large, multilingual‑vocabulary models or depend on external word segmentation, which makes them costly to deploy. We present GoiBERT, a family of two compact Vietnamese encoders with 26M and 49M parameters that operate directly on raw text. GoiBERT learns from two complementary teachers. A same‑tokenizer Vietnamese encoder first teaches general‑purpose representations. A much larger teacher then provides task‑level guidance through soft labels that are generated without ever labeling its own training data. Across eight benchmarks covering text classification, aspect‑based sentiment analysis, natural language inference, and named entity recognition, GoiBERT‑large achieves the highest average score among non‑teacher models. It does so with fewer than half the parameters of the strongest compact baseline and twice its throughput. GoiBERT‑base retains 99% of that baseline's performance at a quarter of its size. Our analysis shows that compression is nearly lossless for sentiment and classification tasks but remains costly for inference and entity recognition, which points to clear directions for future work. Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/Nhantran65/GoiBERT.git

PaperId: 222, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30061.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Osher Azulay, Cheng-Lin Hsieh, Stella X. Yu
Title: Test-Time Motion Steering for Perceptive Humanoid Fall Recovery
Abstract:
Humanoid fall recovery requires selecting a motion that suits both the surrounding scene and the task. The same fallen pose can admit several ways to stand, with different routes, support transitions, and final headings. Yet reliable recovery alone does not provide control over which of these alternatives the robot executes. Steering this choice requires anticipating the physical consequences of a requested movement. We present RISE, an approach to perceptive humanoid recovery that lets task objectives steer how the robot returns to standing at inference time. It builds on two insights: diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movements, and anticipating how these movements unfold allows recovery to be steered toward a task objective. We learn a recovery vocabulary that connects intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback. A visual diffusion planner learns from executions of this vocabulary to predict motion intent as future body states. Task costs guide this prediction toward a desired heading, rise speed, or path. The planner then generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent, allowing the requested movement to shape its execution. Simulation experiments demonstrate diverse recoveries, terrain adaptation, and test‑time steering without retraining, complemented by real‑world demonstrations on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://osheraz.github.io/RISE/

PaperId: 223, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30051.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:May Espinola, Qifan Zhang, Yu Xiang
Title: From Reasoning to Action: Benchmarking Frontier AI Models on LIBERO-10 Robot Manipulation Tasks
Abstract:
Recent advances in frontier AI models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use, raising the possibility of using general‑purpose AI models for robot manipulation without task‑specific training. However, their manipulation capabilities have not been systematically evaluated on standardized robotics benchmarks. In this report, we present a unified closed‑loop manipulation framework for evaluating frontier AI models on the LIBERO‑10 benchmark. Our framework enables models to control a robot directly through visual observations, robot proprioception, and structured tool calls, primarily by specifying target end‑effector poses and gripper commands, without task‑specific fine‑tuning or pretrained manipulation skills. We evaluate six frontier AI models, including GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Luna, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini‑4 Argon, across three reasoning effort levels, resulting in 18 configurations and 1,800 evaluation episodes. Our results show that GPT‑6 Astra achieves the highest success rate of 44%, followed by Gemini‑4 Argon at 43%. Increasing reasoning effort generally improves manipulation performance, but the benefits vary across models and come at additional inference cost. We also observe substantial differences across tasks, with models performing relatively well on object placement tasks but struggling with precise spatial arrangements and complex multi‑step interactions. These findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of frontier AI models for robot manipulation, highlighting the challenges of translating reasoning capabilities into reliable physical actions. We release our evaluation framework and experimental results to support reproducible benchmarking and future research on reasoning‑based robot manipulation.

PaperId: 224, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30047.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Lorenz Brehme, Benjamin Steenhoek, Ruth Breu
Title: SWE-DIVE: Multi-Turn Coding Agent Evaluation with Dynamic User Simulation
Abstract:
Coding agents are typically evaluated using one‑shot, well‑formulated prompts. Benchmarks such as SWE‑bench use existing GitHub issues as input for a coding agent and evaluate whether the agent successfully solves the task. However, in real‑world use cases, prompts are often not as well‑formulated or structured as existing GitHub issues. Additionally, a coding agent session is not limited to a single prompt; it typically involves a multi‑turn interaction in which the user iteratively adds new tasks and requirements that the agent must fulfill. To benchmark these abilities, we developed SWE‑DIVE, a dynamic, interactive validation and evaluation framework for benchmarking coding agents in a multi‑turn environment. To achieve this, we introduce a user simulator that can simulate different behavioral patterns and communicate with the coding agent. We also introduce a conversation validator that evaluates the user simulator's outputs to determine whether they fulfill the initial requirements and guide the agent toward successfully solving the task. The entire framework is embedded in a Harbor environment, which orchestrates the coding agent, user simulator, and conversation validator, and executes the test environment to determine whether the agent successfully solves the task. Our results and source code are available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/lorenzbrehme/swe‑dive_usersim).

PaperId: 225, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30044.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Zhaohui Yang, Quanbao Lin, Chengqi Shi, Zhenglang Weng, Jicheng Lin, Boyu Chen, Tengjie Zhu, Guanzhu Ren, Jiahao Xu, Yang Feng, Xiaokang Yang, Yao Mu
Title: SP-HLM: Sparse-Pose-Driven Motion Generation and Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Abstract:
Humanoid loco‑manipulation requires an effective interface between high‑level task policies and whole‑body control. Existing interfaces typically rely on a single action representation for both task intent and whole‑body coordination. This may burden the high‑level policy or leave one aspect underspecified. We present SP‑HLM, a framework built on a sparse‑pose‑driven interface. The interface combines five task‑critical body poses with a learned latent motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole‑body coordination in complementary forms. SP‑VLA, a vision‑language‑action model, first predicts task‑relevant sparse poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions using asynchronous action‑chunk inference. Given these sparse targets, SP‑MGM, a motion generation model trained through two‑stage distillation, reconstructs coordinated full‑body motion in real time. A pretrained motion encoder maps this motion to a compact latent representation. SP‑GMT, a general motion tracker, then integrates the explicit sparse targets with this implicit motion prior for whole‑body control. Experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid robot demonstrate improved motion tracking, whole‑body coordination, and loco‑manipulation success over existing approaches. Additional results and videos are available on our \hrefhttps://sp‑hlm.github.io/\textcolorblueproject page.

PaperId: 226, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30043.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yicheng Xu, Zhikai Xu, Ziyuan Chen, Yuhang Dong, Tao Zhang, Zhucun Xue, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
Title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments
Abstract:
Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied‑agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot‑oriented full‑stack framework for physically and socially grounded long‑horizon embodied agents. TARSphere‑Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event‑driven finite‑state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere‑Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi‑level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent‑in‑the‑loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere‑Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate‑and‑report and fetch‑and‑deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general‑purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.

PaperId: 227, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30033.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Chunlei Li, Siyuan Yu, Yang Gao, Shuai Li, Peng Yu, Aimin Hao, He Wang
Title: RLMuscle: Muscle-Driven Character Animation via Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
Body deformation caused by muscle contraction plays a vital role in the visual realism of character animation, yet in most 3D animation pipelines artists have to manually specify muscle activations, which is time‑consuming and gives no guarantee of physical realism. To address this, we propose a new method in which a reinforcement learning (RL) controller discovers per‑muscle activations that track reference motions without manual tuning. Existing RL muscle controllers stop at 1D muscles; we go one step further, keeping the 1D model inside the RL control loop as a fast surrogate, and using a 3D volumetric simulation to produce the final deformation. Because both stages share the very same constitutive law, the muscle deformation is produced by the same activations that generated the motion. We further add a measured electromyography (EMG) prior that steers the redundant activation solution toward real human muscle recruitment. To achieve stable, efficient, and realistic simulation, we propose a novel geometric multigrid for Extended Position‑Based Dynamics (XPBD) that is built on a coarse tetrahedral cage with barycentric‑coordinate prolongation and closes a V‑cycle on tetrahedral meshes. Within this GPU‑parallelized solver, we inject the same Hill‑type force‑length law as an energy‑based fiber constraint that turns per‑fiber activation into realistic muscle contraction and bulging. We demonstrate volumetric muscle simulation on a 194‑muscle human body with a diverse set of motions (walk, kick, swim, overhead‑squat, etc.), simulating the full‑body model at 18 ms per frame on a single RTX 4090. Our work takes a step toward character animation that is not only visually convincing but also biomechanically grounded. The website with code and videos is at https://chunleili.github.io/project‑page‑rlmuscle/.

PaperId: 228, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30023.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chenxu Zhou, Zhiyuan Yu, Yudong Jin, Yinji Shentu, Yu Zhang, Jiaming Sun, Xiaowei Zhou
Title: RealMe: Immersive Volumetric Video from Minimal Captures
Abstract:
This paper addresses the problem of creating immersive volumetric videos from sparse and low‑resolution capture resources. Conventional dense multi‑view reconstruction methods can produce high‑quality volumetric videos, but their reliance on costly capture setups makes them impractical in real‑world scenarios. Recent approaches use generative models to relax capture requirements, but still suffer from limited resolution and 4D inconsistency. To overcome these constraints, we propose RealMe, a unified framework built around a high‑resolution video diffusion model that enhances limited captures into high‑resolution (2K), 4D‑consistent videos for volumetric video reconstruction. Specifically, RealMe constructs auxiliary data from capture videos and encodes them into latents along with layout‑aware positional embeddings. The video diffusion model adapts factorized spatio‑temporal attention to the multi‑view capture layout, denoises these latents across viewpoints and time, and decodes them into enhanced videos to refine the 4D representation. This adaptation helps the model capture temporal dynamics and multi‑view relationships, leading to more 4D‑consistent generation. To reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures, we apply a latent frequency loss that provides frequency‑domain supervision in latent space. Extensive experiments on the public DNA‑Rendering benchmark and our self‑captured RealVV dataset demonstrate that RealMe is able to create immersive volumetric videos and outperforms state‑of‑the‑art methods in visual fidelity and 4D consistency.

PaperId: 229, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.30004.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Madhulatha Mandarapu, Sandeep Kunkunuru
Title: Every Alarm Has a Cause: An Open Generator of Telecom Alarm Storms with Exact Root Causes, Bound to NORIA-O, RFC 8632 and TMF642
Abstract:
Alarm root‑cause analysis is studied on data that cannot be shared. Operator logs are confidential, so what the field publishes is a causal graph between alarm types rather than per‑incident causes, a fixed scenario set, gated, or never released. Two recent benchmarks carry per‑incident root causes at scale; neither states a download location or a licence. We give a generator rather than a dataset. It runs on real backbone topologies from the Internet Topology Zoo and records the exact root cause and the propagation path of every alarm ‑‑ a by‑product of generation, not a labelling pass. Every emitted field binds to a term in NORIA‑O, RFC 8632, RFC 8345 or TMF642, and an unknown term fails the run. We ship fixed configurations, splits, a scorer and nine baselines. A one‑line rule ‑‑ rank the device that raised the earliest critical alarm ‑‑ takes top‑1 at 0.650 against 0.575 for our own temporal method, and wins 13 of 15 runs over three backbones and five seeds. An LLM given the same view reaches 0.600, the same model allowed to query the graph 0.625, and the rule wins on real operator alarms too, at 0.773: a property of alarm streams, not of our generator. One fault class separates the table: when a site loses power its PoP reports nothing, so every method that ranks alarmed devices scores 0.000 or near it, while the two that walk the topology to a silent candidate take 1.000 and 0.833.

PaperId: 230, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29999.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Chengxi Li, Hanlin Wu, Zhicheng Cai, Huan-ang Gao, Wei-Ying Ma, Jingjing Liu, Hao Zhou
Title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO‑style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token‑level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long‑response and off‑policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite‑horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance‑difference identity under behavior‑policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy‑improvement term. Starting from the monotonic‑improvement principle of trust‑region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix‑level trust region using the exact reverse‑KL coordinate r‑1‑\log r, whose behavior‑policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix‑distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO‑style sequence‑clipping method that directly regulates prefix‑level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert‑routing replay. Experiments on off‑policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture‑of‑experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence‑level clipping baselines across mathematical‑reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing‑replay‑based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC.

PaperId: 231, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29989.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ruopeng Gao, Yukun Huang, Jiarui Hu, Shuai Wang, Wenbo Hu, Ying Shan, Limin Wang
Title: Looking Ahead: Modeling Future Evolution in Autoregressive Video Generation
Abstract:
Autoregressive video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk, yet producing plausible continuations does not guarantee that they capture how scenes evolve. Under teacher forcing, strong temporal redundancy may allow local visual continuity to serve as a shortcut for current‑chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to model visual evolution. We introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective jointly optimized with teacher‑forced denoising that predicts temporally separated chunks without access to the intervening visual context. Drawing supervision directly from training videos, FCP requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and leaves autoregressive inference unchanged. Our method achieves superior physical plausibility over standard teacher‑forced autoregressive training with a lower overall training compute budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future‑chunk supervision for modeling visual evolution. Intriguingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP fosters a more structured representation space, which may be valuable for building autoregressive world models.

PaperId: 232, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29987.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Davide Carnemolla, Dario Catalano, Mario Di Raimondo
Title: GhostFaceMPC: Privacy-Preserving Face Recognition with Multi-Party Computation
Abstract:
Facial recognition has become central to modern authentication systems, security frameworks, and personalized services.
