However, its widespread adoption is hindered by severe privacy risks, particularly surrounding unauthorized access to sensitive biometric data. To address these challenges, this paper presents GhostFaceMPC, the first end‑to‑end, privacy‑preserving face recognition system to evaluate a deep convolutional neural network extractor and matching under secure multi‑party computation. GhostFaceMPC enables secure processing of facial data across all stages of a face recognition process, from feature extraction and storage to matching, without exposing raw images or biometric embeddings at any stage. We introduce a multi‑party computation‑friendly quantization of the GhostFaceNet model and circuit optimizations that make face recognition under multi‑party computation practical. The code is available at https://github.com/crypto‑unict/GhostFaceMPC.

PaperId: 233, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29968.pdf   GitHub
Authors:My Chiffon Nguyen, Tianyi Hu, Vinod Anbalagan, Henry Gagnier, Pouya Sadeghi, Farah Abdou, Tidor-Vlad Pricope, Diego MMS Oliveira, Jocelyn K D'Arcy, Madeline Smith, Oluwaseun A Ajayi, Yusser Al Ghussin, Zena Al-Khalili, Micol Altomare, Shayan Amir, Ahanaf Aziz, Bryan Chen, Ruchira Dhar, Abdellah El Mekki, Rawan Mohammed Elframawy, Akhil Eppa, Silvia Fernandez, Alex Gimei, Arya Hariharan, Christian Hoang, RamMohanRao Kadiyala, Diana Kozachek, Peerat Limkonchotiwat, Ankita Maity, Di Mo, Ayush Munot, Aylin Naebzadeh, Anastasiia Nikitina, Dina Pisarevskaya, Divas Poudel, Jebish Purbey, Md Rabius Sany Apu, Ahmad Mufli Ramadhan, Ralitza Nikolova Rizova, Diogo M. Serrano-Miranda, Vivek Gopalkrishna Silimkhan, Luis Fernando Solis Navarro, Kaiser Sun, Arya Suneesh, Manaswitha Sunkara, Tejaswi Sunkara, Jonathan E Swindell, Hanna Yukhymenko, Jingyi Zheng, Esther Adenuga, Ilia Afanasev, Wafa Aissa, Lisa Alazraki, Lauren C Altomare, Priscilla Amondi Amuok, Emile Anand, Gabriel Assis, José Matías Avalos, Silvia Lorena Avila, Zakaria Baannou, Niyati Bafna, Yash Bagla, Sarah Bahrami, Bontu F Balcha, Vanya Bannihatti Kumar, Irene Baucells, Abdumutalib Begmuratov, Naman Bhatia, Souvik Bhattacharyya, Isabel Blanco Ferreiro, Felipe Bochini, Sayuru Bopitiya, Angana Borah, Tulika Bose, Olena Bugaiova, Juliana Carvalho, Nancy F Chen, Stephy Chen, Rochelle Choenni, Jayanth Krishna Chundru, Leandro A Cossio, Nebojša Damnjanović, Ona de Gibert, Marco De Santis, Pedro Delgado, Kaustubh Dholé, Adnan El Assadi, Wesam El-Sayed, Nadine M Elframawy, Oumayma Essarhi, Naome A Etori, Reuben Chagas Fernandes, Saanidhi Pravin Gade, Javier García Gilabert, Álvaro González-Escapa, Bin Hu, Kaiyu Huang, Abderrahmane Issam, Danka Jokić, Ulugbek Khalilov, Dominik Krzemiński, Roy Ka-Wei Lee, Haichang Li, Chen Cecilia Liu, Zhengyuan Liu, Cedric Lothritz, Houman Mehrafarin, Antonio Miranda-Escalada, Fengran Mo, Mehrnaz Mofakhami, Wafaa Mohammed, Felipe Moreno-Vera, Prahitha Movva, Jannatul Nayem, Van Ngo, Joy Olusanya, Marc Pàmies, Avinash Kuney Pandey, Yurii Paniv, Fred Philippy, Vladislav Poritski, Dikshya Poudel, Joanna Radoła, Sara Rajaee, Swati Rajwal, Prerana Rane, Muhammad Ravi Shulthan Habibi, Lucas Resck, Shubhashis Roy Dipta, Ananya Sahu, Eduardo Sánchez, Borja Sánchez Clemente, Aleix Sant, Nobin Sarwar, Istiak Shihab, Santhoshini Pranathi Singaraju, Jane Smith, David Stap, Emily Z Su, Ananth K Suresh, Sajag Swami, Ruiyang Tan, Nazia Tasnim, Khalid Tounoussi, Patteera Triamamornwooth, Muhammad Saad Umar, Shankar Venkitachalam, Oksana Volchek, Lingbo Wang, Debela Desalegn Yadeta, Rushikesh Zawar, Jinghan Zhang, Mike Zhang, Weihua Zheng, Marzieh Fadaee, Akhil Arora, Károly Boczka, Julia Kreutzer
Title: CulturalRiddles: A Multicultural Benchmark of Riddles
Abstract:
As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English‑centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real‑world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large‑scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.

PaperId: 234, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29961.pdf   GitHub
Authors:M. Mikail Demir
Title: Commit or Abstain? System One Decision Models, LLMs, and Missing Legal Authority
Abstract:
Given the enormous number of claims to be checked, verifiable legal AI requires scalable, cost‑effective models that answer the practical needs of law. System One decision models are built on large language models but, instead of generating text, return a calibrated probability for each option. This suits the verification of legal authority, where the question is closed: a given holding, or none of them. We test whether such models abstain when the correct authority is missing. We extend CaseHOLD with an abstention condition in which the correct holding is replaced in 1,670 of 5,314 items, and compare four decision models with six generative LLMs. When no option is correct, generative LLMs still pick one in 38‑86% of items; the most cautious decision model does so in 30%. On standard CaseHOLD, a decision model matches the best generative LLM (88.1% vs. 88.2%) at 1/55 of the cost. Accepting that LLM's answer only when a decision model agrees halves its wrong citations, and distilling a decision model's probabilities into Qwen3‑8B, without labels, yields a well‑calibrated local model. Legal AI should be judged by its wrong citations, not by accuracy alone.

PaperId: 235, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29936.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Naru Suzuki, Satoshi Ikehata, Takehiko Ohkawa, Yoichi Sato, Shuhei Kurita
Title: DewHand: Direct Metric World-Space Hand Motion Reconstruction from Egocentric Videos
Abstract:
Recovering metric world‑space hand motion from egocentric video supports understanding human interactions and transferring them to embodied agents. Three challenges complicate this task: multi‑stage pipelines propagate errors from independently estimated hand and camera motion; monocular observations leave physical scale ambiguous; and occlusion and out‑of‑view hands admit multiple plausible motion trajectories. We present DewHand, a unified model for direct joint reconstruction of world‑space hand and camera motion. To avoid compounding errors from multi‑stage estimation, DewHand jointly predicts hand and camera motion in a shared world coordinate system within a single‑stage pipeline. To resolve metric‑scale ambiguity, it combines scene‑level geometric features from VGGT‑Ω with metric‑space supervision, while hand‑specific features preserve fine‑grained articulation. To handle occlusion and out‑of‑view hands, we formulate reconstruction as conditional motion generation with flow matching. Under the same architecture, this generative formulation outperforms direct regression in both accuracy and temporal smoothness with only two sampling steps. Experiments on HOT3D and ARCTIC demonstrate improved world‑space accuracy and temporal consistency over state‑of‑the‑art methods. DewHand reduces rigid‑aligned world‑space error relative to StableHand from 32.9 to 28.4 mm on HOT3D and from 76.2 to 36.2 mm on ARCTIC. It also recovers camera scale within 10% on two thirds of HOT3D clips, versus about a quarter for SLAM. Moreover, in zero‑shot evaluations on HoloAssist, H2O, and TACO, captured with different devices, DewHand achieves the lowest rigid‑aligned world‑space error (WA‑MPJPE) on each dataset.

PaperId: 236, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29934.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Nithin Sivakumaran, Ali Payani, Hyunji Lee, Mohit Bansal, Elias Stengel-Eskin
Title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination
Abstract:
Forming an accurate theory‑of‑mind (ToM) is key to successful multi‑agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories‑of‑mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test‑time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed‑motive settings (Overcooked‑AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi‑agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train‑time, including a proprietary model (GPT‑5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task‑specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.

PaperId: 237, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29932.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qiuyang Mang, Wenhao Chai, Runyuan He, Dongruixuan Li, Zihan Zheng, Yujun He, Xuanyi Zhou, Hao Wang, Siddhant Ray, Bo Peng, Ruyi Ji, Shuo Yang, Haocheng Xi, Boru Chen, Xinyang David Han, Melissa Pan, Mayank Mishra, Boxi Yu, Sijia Liu, Kerem Akillioglu, Yi Pan, Zirui Wang, Mert Cemri, Diogo Antunes, Yichuan Wang, Aiwei Ivy Zhang, Zhenyang Chen, Qizheng Zhang, Kaiyuan Liu, Wenyuan Huang, Sherry Ruan, Shu Liu, Dacheng Li, Zerui Cheng, Zeyu Shen, Shang Zhou, Hanfei Chen, Yuzhong Zhang, Bohan Lyu, Qu Ao, Han Zheng, Chonghe Jiang, Jingzhuo Hu, Xiaokun Chen, Kunjun Li, Zhiqing Zhong, Haoye Tian, Tong Zhao, Yunzhong He, Hanchen Li, Ofir Press, Jiantao Jiao, Kunle Olukotun, Karthik R. Narasimhan, Jingbo Shang, Koushik Sen, Matei Zaharia, Alex Dimakis, Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Alvin Cheung
Title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
Abstract:
Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open‑ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open‑ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development‑suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held‑out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference. The tasks span 13 domains, from machine‑learning systems and high‑performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future. We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.

PaperId: 238, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29903.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Liu Cao, Botian Xu, Ruoqu Chen, Jiajun Liu, Mingzhi Pei, Zihao Wang, Zhongyu Li, Mengdi Xu
Title: HuMiT: Low-Latency Whole-Body Humanoid Teleoperation via Compact Reference Tracking
Abstract:
Real‑time whole‑body humanoid teleoperation remains challenging due to the computational latency introduced by optimization‑based retargeting pipelines and future‑frame conditioning. Existing motion tracking policies typically require dense reference targets including full joint positions, body‑part transformations, and even future frames, which tightly couples the controller to expensive upstream modules. In this work, we present HuMiT, a whole‑body teleoperation system built on a unified tracking policy that requires only a compact reference target, consisting of root height, root velocity, and the SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints at the current frame, yet achieves competitive tracking fidelity compared to methods relying on more diverse reference states including complete joint positions, dense body‑part transformations, and even future frames. Experiments show that our policy achieves a communication‑to‑inference latency of ～20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video‑based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) across different motion types. We validate the system on a Unitree G1 humanoid, showcasing split‑second reactive responses such as catching a tossed ball, as well as coordinated loco‑manipulation capabilities. Project page: https://xiaohu‑art.github.io/Track/.

PaperId: 239, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29869.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Arshan Dabirsiaghi
Title: Compaction Laundering: Provenance Destruction in Context-Compacting Coding Agents
Abstract:
Coding agents that run long enough must compact their context, summarizing the conversation, discarding the original, and carrying the summary forward as memory. We show that in popular open‑source coding agents this step is an exploitable trust boundary. Harnesses that flatten the typed conversation into a single plain string, marking each message with a text label such as [User]:, destroy message provenance in code, before the summarizer runs. An attacker who controls anything the agent reads can forge a user turn that survives compaction as a genuine instruction. Across five flattening harnesses (pi, opencode, Cline, Aider, OpenHands) the forged approval launders into the agent's memory 87‑100% of the time, up to a ~908,000‑token context window; across four role‑typed harnesses (Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Continue) the identical attack succeeds 0% of the time. We follow the attack to executed consequences. A laundered standing approval drives real tool‑running agents to execute attacker‑controlled curl | sh in a sandbox, and end to end in the live pi TUI at ~50% against a 0% paired clean arm. The same channel reliably steers an agent's plan away from a file an attacker designates off‑limits, which can blind a code review to a planted backdoor. Because the provenance is destroyed deterministically in harness code, no prompt‑level defense can restore it; we measure a code‑level provenance check that catches 77% of laundering while demoting 2% of legitimate summary content. The defect also has a straightforward fix at the serializer, escaping the role labels before flattening; the role‑typed harnesses avoid it entirely by keeping messages role‑typed.

PaperId: 240, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29845.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Samuel Foo Enze, Manthan Patel, Fan Yang, Linus Kramer, Pascal Roth, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
Title: RangeNav: Task-Aligned LiDAR Range-Image Pretraining for Robot Navigation
Abstract:
Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require 360^\circ perception to react to surrounding hazards. While panoramic LiDAR offers full‑surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample‑inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point‑cloud encoders are too memory‑heavy for massively parallel RL simulation. We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range‑image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images. We pretrain the network using a navigation‑aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's‑eye‑view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction‑only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out‑of‑distribution realistic test environments, respectively. Zero‑shot real‑world deployments on a Unitree B2‑W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low‑light settings, and construction zones where limited‑field‑of‑view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open‑sourced. Project website: https://rangenav.github.io/.

PaperId: 241, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29832.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yawei Li, Jiazheng Li, David Rügamer, Bernd Bischl, Yulan He, Mina Rezaei
Title: S-EDL: Eliciting Self-Evidence from Sequence Likelihoods for Semantic Calibration of LLMs
Abstract:
Calibrating large language models (LLMs) in open‑ended generation is uniquely challenging because many distinct token sequences can express the same underlying meaning. Prior calibration techniques target either fixed‑set classification confidence or the binary correctness of individual strings, making them inherently ill‑suited for the dynamic, multi‑string nature of open‑ended semantic outcomes. To bridge this gap, we introduce S‑EDL, a novel evidential method that natively optimizes LLMs for semantic calibration. By eliciting evidence from the sequence likelihoods of the model itself, S‑EDL constructs a differentiable Dirichlet prior over prompt‑specific semantic classes. Optimizing the evidential loss under this prior yields a calibration‑aware training signal over variable semantic classes, completely bypassing the need for fixed multiple‑choice options. Evaluations across four open‑ended benchmarks and three models demonstrate that S‑EDL substantially reduces semantic calibration error while improving accuracy. By aligning generative likelihoods with semantic correctness, this work establishes a framework for deploying trustworthy LLMs in complex, open‑ended applications. Code is available at: https://github.com/sandylaker/s‑edl.

PaperId: 242, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29825.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Taddeo D'Adamo, Simon Thivet, Catherine Pothier, Riccardo Simionato, Allan Fries, Jonathan Lemus, Costanza Bonadonna, Laure Tougne Rodet, Bertrand Kerautret
Title: GuidedSAM-Plume: An Expert-Guided Segmentation Framework for Volcanic Plumes
Abstract:
Quantitative analysis of environmental phenomena increasingly relies on image‑based measurements. In volcanology, the geometric characterization of volcanic plumes and clouds from RGB images remains hindered by the scarcity of dedicated segmentation solutions and partially handcrafted annotations remain widely prevalent. We present GuidedSAM‑Plume, an open‑source expert‑guided framework tailored for the interactive segmentation of volcanic plumes and clouds. It leverages the zero‑shot, spatial prompt‑based capabilities of SAM2. The framework was thoroughly validated on a challenging dataset through dedicated segmentation metrics and field‑relevant volcanological descriptors. From minimal user inputs, it is able to significantly increase performance compared to fully automatic dedicated solutions while preserving the reliability of derived volcanological parameters. The absence of retraining requirements lowers adoption barriers within the volcanological community, and the framework's demonstrated suitability for complex, diffuse plume‑shaped phenomena extends its applicability to broader environmental science domains. The re‑annotated dataset, produced under the guidance of expert volcanologists within the proposed framework, ultimately yields a more standardized release. The framework and accompanying dataset are made available at https://github.com/tad‑damo/GuidedSAM‑Plume.

PaperId: 243, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29816.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Niclas Flehmig, Mary Ann Lundteigen, Shen Yin
Title: COMET: A coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework for human-supervised AI-enabled safety systems
Abstract:
Incorporating AI systems into safety systems requires monitoring to avoid silent faults and ensure safe and reliable operation. Single monitors often do not provide actionable information for human supervisors, who act as the system's adaptive controller. We present COMET, a coordinated multi‑layer runtime monitoring framework for human‑supervised AI‑enabled safety systems in which each monitor is anchored in a different fault mode. Monitor outputs are combined in a coordination layer and mapped by a communication layer to a traffic‑light display. In this work, COMET consists of three monitoring layers: signal integrity, physics consistency, and the AI system's competence envelope. The framework is evaluated on an open dataset of compressed‑air leaks, where an AI system detects leaks from acoustic emissions, with held‑out conditions simulating covariate shift, semantic shift, and sensor faults, events expected during runtime but unknown in their exact appearance. All monitors are frozen after development and tested zero‑shot, and the framework is compared against no‑monitoring and single‑monitor setups. The bare AI system fails silently and confidently under all three shift types, whereas COMET reduces the trusted‑wrong‑answer rate to zero on covariate‑shifted no‑leak data and on three of four sensor faults, at a nominal false‑alarm rate of \approx 1%. Single monitors come close in detection but cannot attribute the fault mode. COMET converts their anonymous detection flags into diagnoses. Residual silent misses under semantic shift define the boundary of passive monitoring. Runtime monitoring frameworks for AI‑enabled safety systems must therefore combine quantitative fault detection and isolation with qualitative, human‑oriented feedback.

PaperId: 244, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29815.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Julian Silva, Jaliya Kodithuwakku, Navindu Sirimanna, Shaveen Herath, Wageesha N. Manamperi, Joshua P. Kulasingham
Title: NeuroCodec: EEG-Guided Latent-Domain Generative Model for High-Fidelity Target Speaker Extraction
Abstract:
Driven by recent advancements in hearing assistive devices, target speaker extraction (TSE) in multi‑talker environments has drawn significant attention. To address this, hearing technologies identify attention using neural signals recorded via electroencephalography (EEG) to guide TSE, enabling neuro‑steered auditory attention decoding. However, most existing techniques rely on time‑frequency masking, which suffers from low fidelity in spectro‑temporally overlapping regions and is often restricted to narrowband audio. In contrast, we introduce NeuroCodec, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first generative EEG‑guided TSE framework operating in the latent space of a neural audio codec. Specifically, NeuroCodec models spatial EEG dependencies via graph convolutions and fuses cross‑modal EEG and speech representations through attention mechanisms and Mamba‑based temporal modeling. We further introduce a six‑phase training curriculum that progressively incorporates latent reconstruction, multi‑scale spectral, and adversarial objectives to ensure stable, high‑fidelity speech generation. Experiments on the public Cocktail Party and KUL datasets show NeuroCodec outperforms baselines, across several perceptual metrics. A listening experiment with 20 participants validated that NeuroCodec offers greater perceptual accuracy, achieving a mean score of 82.24 compared with 49.63 for M3ANet. Additionally, the proposed method is seen to enable 44.1 kHz reconstruction with spectral content extending up to 20 kHz, further supporting the perceptual results. Finally, we extend NeuroCodec with a causal streaming formulation suited for real‑time processing, providing a basis for hearing assistive devices.

PaperId: 245, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29812.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mohammed Saqlain
Title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
Abstract:
Literature‑searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed‑book answering, single‑shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct‑style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single‑shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49‑59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79‑86% accuracy, a significant 17‑24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed‑book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross‑family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real‑pmids‑wrong‑papers.

PaperId: 246, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29811.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Puru Vaish, Meelad Dashti, Christoph Brune, Pascal Mettes, Tatiana Tommasi, Nicola Strisciuglio
Title: Compositionality with Primitives: A Unified View from Euclidean to Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models
Abstract:
Compositional zero‑shot learning (CZSL) aims to recognize novel combinations of previously observed objects and attributes. Prior work showed that large‑scale vision‑language models encode decomposable semantic structures that can be recomposed to enable generalization. The Geodesically Decomposable Embeddings (GDE) framework formalizes this by identifying directions in the tangent space at the Frechet mean of the embedding distribution, which encode primitive visual concepts. Unseen attribute‑object compositions can be synthesized through vector addition of these primitives. We revisit the assumption that compositional generalization requires explicit attribute‑object pair re‑composition. By means of new compositional scoring functions and extensive evaluations, we show that directly using the decomposed primitives suffices for recognizing unseen compositions. In that, we gain insights on how the geometry of the embedding manifold (Euclidean, spherical, or hyperbolic) and dataset structure affect compositional reasoning. Across models (CLIP, DINOv2, MERU, HyCoCLIP), we show that compositional structure consistently emerges as primitive representations, enabling inference on CZSL benchmarks (MIT‑States, VAW‑CZSL, UT‑Zappos50K, Clothing16K) and group robustness on Waterbirds and CelebA. Code: https://github.com/nis‑research/Compositionality‑with‑Primitives.

PaperId: 247, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29792.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xinze Li, Dingwen Zhang, Zhenghao Liu, Yukun Yan, Shuo Wang, Yu Gu, Ge Yu, Maosong Sun
Title: MAPS: Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning for Regulating Search Momentum in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Abstract:
Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by retrieving external knowledge. Recently, some RAG methods interleave reasoning and retrieval, enabling LLMs to progressively generate sub‑queries and retrieve external knowledge. However, these methods may suffer from redundant or ineffective sub‑queries and insufficiently diverse query exploration. Moreover, due to the tightly interleaved nature of reasoning and retrieval, it remains unclear how the evolving reasoning process influences query intent. To characterize the evolution of query intent during reasoning, we introduce search momentum, which captures the accumulated retrieval tendency induced by historical changes in generated sub‑queries along the reasoning trajectory. Through momentum‑based analysis, we find that the query generation process tends to continuously evolve along existing retrieval trajectories. Based on this observation, we propose MAPS, a Macro‑Adaptive Parallel Reasoning framework for regulating search momentum and mitigating query‑intent drift. MAPS first retains the retrieved knowledge and a refined reasoning state, thereby reducing the influence of historical reasoning trajectories on subsequent sub‑query generation. Subsequently, MAPS extends the conventional sequential reasoning process into a parallel reasoning paradigm. At each iteration, MAPS identifies complementary retrieval directions, generates corresponding sub‑queries for parallel retrieval, and consolidates the retrieved evidence to update the knowledge and reasoning states. Experiments on six question‑answering benchmarks demonstrate that MAPS consistently outperforms representative RAG methods across different backbone models. All code and resources are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/MAPS.

PaperId: 248, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29768.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Linfei Li, Ruining Hu, Lin Zhang, Zhong Wang, Fengyi Zhang, Ying Shen, Binqiang Wang, Xin Zhang
Title: UniRAP: Towards Unified Part-level Physical Affordance Reasoning and Actionable Perception
Abstract:
Vision‑language perception has achieved impressive progress in aligning natural language with visual observations, yet grounding high‑level semantics into part‑level physical interaction remains challenging. To address this gap, we propose UniRAP, a unified model for inferring part‑level physical affordances and mapping language instructions to actionable geometric representations. UniRAP formulates this problem as a conditional multimodal generation task, integrating visual inputs, textual instructions, and optional prompts into a shared spatiotemporal representation space through a unified interface token mechanism. To predict executable contact geometry, we introduce a Unified Affordance Decoder (UAD), which jointly performs object detection, part‑level affordance segmentation, and 4‑DoF interaction pose estimation by leveraging intermediate segmentation features. In addition, we propose a curriculum‑based transfer training strategy that progressively adapts the model from general visual parsing to interaction‑aware perception, improving data efficiency under limited textual annotations. Experiments show that UniRAP achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance on referring expression segmentation, affordance grounding, and interaction pose estimation, while maintaining strong spatiotemporal consistency in dynamic video scenarios. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of UniRAP as a unified perception framework for language‑guided physical manipulation.

PaperId: 249, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29767.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Arslan Bisharat, Mujtaba Nazari, Khushboo Bhadauria, Brian Ortiz, Eric Spencer, Beatriz Santos, TaiNing Wang, George K. Thiruvathukal, Konstantin Laufer, Mohammed Abuhamad
Title: ALIAS: Evaluating Performance and Memorization in LLM-Written TLA+ Specifications
Abstract:
Memorization inflates the benchmark scores of large language models (LLMs), since a model can reproduce answers it saw in training. Researchers test for it with consistent identifier renaming (CIR), which gives every identifier in a task a new name, and treat a lower score on the renamed task as evidence of recall. We test this method on the Temporal Logic of Actions Plus (TLA+) language, whose model checker acts as an oracle by confirming whether a renamed task preserves the exact behaviors of the original. Across 111 TLA+‑Bench tasks, renaming lowers the correctness of Claude Opus 4.8 from 28% to 18% and of GPT‑5 from 9% to 7%. Most of this decrease comes from how the test grades, which requires exact names that most descriptions never state. Grading by behavior shrinks the decrease to about 3 percentage points for Opus 4.8 and to 0 for GPT‑5. In two model families fine‑tuned on disjoint halves of the tasks, renaming removes about half of the training gain in likelihood and costs 4.9 percentage points (Qwen) and 1.3 percentage points (Gemma) on unseen tasks. A lower score after renaming therefore mixes memorization, name‑based grading, and the cost of new names.

PaperId: 250, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29730.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Johannes Keller, Albrecht M. Bloße, Adrian Lindenmeyer, Thomas Neumuth, Daniel Schneider
Title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies
Abstract:
Vision‑language‑action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies. We propose post‑hoc kernel‑variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO‑10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two‑policy ensemble scores in task‑level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance. For SmolVLA, the head on the vision‑language backbone reduces uncertainty‑scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs. We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO‑10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within‑task rankings. Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality‑specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs. With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within‑task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.

PaperId: 251, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29727.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Jungseob Lee, Seungyoon Lee, Hyeonseok Moon, Seongtae Hong, Suhyune Son, Sugyeong Eo, Minhyuk Kim, Chanjun Park, Jaehyung Seo
Title: Accept or Repair: Preserving Passage-Supported Answers in Contrastive Decoding
Abstract:
Large language models often answer from knowledge learned during training, even when a provided passage contradicts that knowledge. To address this problem, contrastive decoding contrasts the predictions under the full and a modified prompt at every token, but it also alters correct answers that the passage supports. We show that checking answers against the passage removes this trade‑off. Based on this observation, we propose Accept‑or‑Repair (AoR), a training‑free procedure. AoR keeps a sampled answer if the passage supports it. Otherwise, it tries up to two replacements with contrastive decoding, returning one as soon as it passes this check. It rejects replacements that repeat the answer generated without the passage when the passage favors another answer. Our experiments show that AoR raises the score over sampling by 12.5 points on counterfactual passages and 2.3 on ordinary ones, surpassing eight contrastive and prompting baselines on both, including when each receives the same rejection rule. Replacing only initial answers that the passage does not support improves the average score of every decoder. These results suggest that models can follow passages that contradict their knowledge while preserving accuracy on passages that agree with it. Code will be released at https://github.com/js‑lee‑AI/AoR.

PaperId: 252, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29722.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Ido Levy, Segev Shlomov, Leshem Choshen
Title: Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality
Abstract:
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre‑declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open‑source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.

PaperId: 253, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29695.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yanze Zhang, Maggie Yongqi Guan, Shudong Liu, Qi Hao, Kanye Ye Wang, Meng Qu, Xiaobo Zhou
Title: Benchmarking Coding Agents for System-Level Performance Optimization
Abstract:
Coding agents are becoming an increasingly important paradigm for automating software engineering tasks. However, existing coding benchmarks primarily evaluate agents at the function or repository level, leaving their capabilities in more complex distributed software systems largely unexplored. In practice, many modern applications adopt microservice architectures, where end‑to‑end performance emerges from interactions among multiple independently running services, requiring agents to reason beyond local code changes. To study this capability, we introduce MicroPerf‑Bench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on end‑to‑end performance optimization in microservice systems. Constructing such a benchmark is challenging because reproducible system‑level performance fixes are sparse and difficult to attribute. We address this challenge by injecting empirically grounded performance anti‑patterns into real‑world open‑source systems while preserving functionality and ensuring measurable performance degradation. The resulting benchmark contains 65 optimization instances across seven systems and nine anti‑patterns, each with an executable environment, functional tests, and mixed‑workload evaluation. Across 1,755 runs covering nine agent‑model configurations, the best configuration recovers only 42.0% of the injected performance degradation. The dominant failure is not invalid code, but functionally correct and constraint‑compliant changes that fail to improve end‑to‑end performance, highlighting system‑level bottleneck localization as a key challenge for current coding agents. The source code and data are available at https://github.com/zyzcjnb/microperf.

PaperId: 254, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29676.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Alessandro Canevaro, Julian Schmidt, Hang Yu, Ye Jin, Sajad Marvi, Georg Martius, Julian Jordan
Title: DriveMLP: When Training Strategy Outperforms Model Complexity in Autonomous Driving
Abstract:
Learning motion planning policies that remain reliable under closed‑loop execution is a central challenge in Autonomous Driving (AD). Imitation Learning (IL) scales well to large AD datasets but suffers from distribution shift, causal confusion, and compounding errors under closed‑loop execution. In contrast, Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically requires handcrafted rule‑based rewards and massive simulation. We study a simple closed‑loop IL framework that uses RL purely as an optimization tool, guided by a trajectory‑distance reward derived from logged expert data. We refer to this training strategy as Expert‑Guided RL (EGRL). Through a controlled empirical study we find evidence that the training procedure, rather than model size and complexity, accounts for a substantial part of the performance gains. We then introduce DriveMLP, a lightweight MLP policy trained with EGRL, as a simple instantiation of these findings. It achieves a score of 86.51 on the nuPlan Val14 Reactive benchmark, a +3.2 point improvement over the previous best IL planner (Flow Planner), with >15x faster inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/alessandro‑canevaro/DriveMLP .

PaperId: 255, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29651.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Venkatesh Thirugnana Sambandham, Torsten Schon
Title: Spatially Gated Demographic Steering for Debiasing Multi-Person Text-to-Image Generation
Abstract:
Text‑to‑Image models reproduce societal stereotypes, and existing mitigation applies one demographic correction to the whole scene. In multi‑person scene generation this creates a trade‑off: global steering improves aggregate balance only by homogenizing the people within an image. Steering‑based methods like Embedding Arithmetic drive the intra‑image diversity below the unsteered baseline. Text‑ and latent‑projection approaches shift the aggregate skew with only marginal gains in intra‑image diversity. We present Spatially Gated Steering (SGS), which steers the demographics of each person independently by extracting per‑person masks from the Diffusion Transformer's (DiT) internal attention maps at a critical denoising timestep and applying a distinct demographic vector within each mask for the remaining steps. SGS needs no fine‑tuning, inversion or layout specifications, and uses a lightweight segmentor over frozen DiT attention features to localize subjects at early timesteps. On skewed occupational prompts, SGS reaches high intra‑image racial and gender diversity while keeping aggregate balance competitive and image quality near baseline, a result we validate on two architecturally distinct diffusion transformers, FLUX.1‑Dev and SD3.5‑Large. Codebase and model weights are available at https://github.com/cvims/spatially‑gated‑steering

PaperId: 256, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29617.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhuoyu Wu, Wenhui Ou, Qiawei Zheng, Xuhong Qiu, Wenqi Fang, Raphaël C. -W. Phan
Title: TernScope: Model-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient Ternary Endoscopic Segmentation
Abstract:
Edge medical segmentation must reconcile small model size, high accuracy, and fast inference. TernScope addresses this tradeoff through model‑‑hardware co‑design, learning a compact segmentation network whose low‑bit operators also simplify hardware execution. Split‑channel large‑kernel blocks preserve spatial context with limited computation, while branch fusion removes redundant inference paths. Ternary Progressive Quantization‑aware Training (TPQ) then adapts the fused network from deep to shallow layers, through the decoder, and finally to the input and prediction layers. All 25 convolutions use ternary weights and 8‑bit activations, enabling packed storage and multiplier‑free computation. The resulting model uses 0.2483 M parameters and 0.0949 GMACs while retaining competitive segmentation accuracy on in‑domain and external datasets. Under the same 45 nm technology, TernScope reduces compute‑array area by 88.46% compared with the original Gemmini, a systolic‑array accelerator with 8‑bit × 8‑bit multipliers. These results demonstrate a path from accurate lightweight medical segmentation to compact low‑bit hardware.

PaperId: 257, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29612.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Matthias Heyrman, Chenhao Li, Ioannis Dadiotis, Marco Hutter
Title: Watch Your Step: Anticipated Perception for Humanoid Locomotion
Abstract:
Perceptive locomotion policies typically observe a dense robot‑centric elevation map, although only the terrain beneath and around the next footsteps informs the control decision. Learned encoders compress the whole visual input, leaving the policy to work out which inputs matter while learning the baseline locomotion task. Learning both at once slows training and, without computationally expensive attention mechanisms, makes generalization to new terrain harder. We instead remove redundant inputs from the elevation map before the policy sees it. A lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts future footholds from proprioception and the velocity command alone, and we sample the elevation map only in small patches around these predicted footholds. We train the prediction model alongside the locomotion policy, periodically retraining it on new policy rollouts as the robot's gait matures. This allows the perception to anticipate where the policy will step, while the policy learns to leverage terrain information around those steps. With the proposed lightweight preprocessing, the policy reaches a given terrain difficulty in roughly a third of the training iterations required with the complete map. It outperforms policies that observe the complete map where footholds are sparse, including in narrow walled corridors, and on unseen terrain, and it matches an attention‑based encoder trained at several times the cost. The policy transfers zero‑shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid traversing various obstacles, stairs, gaps, and step‑downs beyond the training distribution in both indoor and outdoor environments.

PaperId: 258, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29604.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Takumi Fujimoto, Hiroaki Nishi
Title: Local and Global Recursive Ridge Regression for Online Residual Correction of Frozen Multivariate Forecasters under Label Delay
Abstract:
A frozen multi‑horizon forecaster can be corrected online from its own residuals. However, under label delay the target of a block arrives only after the whole horizon has passed, and the corrector's retained state grows with the number of channels. Aiming to combine a small retained state with a large error reduction, we propose DRiC (DCT Ridge Corrector), which fits a ridge regression of the leading discrete cosine transform (DCT) coefficients of the next residual block on those of the frozen forecast and of the latest input block, with sufficient statistics updated recursively. Its local variant, DRiC‑L, keeps one such regression per channel; its global variant, DRiC‑G, pools all channels into one regression, whose statistics do not depend on the channel count. A guard tracks a running scale of the frozen forecast's residual for each channel; it skips updates on blocks far outside that scale and clips the issued correction. We evaluate on seven datasets (four ETT series, Weather with its missing‑value codes filled, Electricity, and Traffic) with DLinear, PatchTST, and iTransformer backbones, against 10 naive, gradient‑trained, and closed‑form methods. DRiC‑L with eight DCT coefficients (DRiC‑L8) reduces the mean squared error (MSE) by 14.55% on average over 126 conditions, against 12.98% for ELF, the most accurate comparator, while retaining 15‑17 times less state, although ELF is more accurate on Traffic. DRiC‑G retains 14.6 kB on the 321‑channel Electricity data and 18.9 kB on the 862‑channel Traffic data and is the most accurate method at or below its state on both. However, 5 to 7 of the 10 comparators, all with at least 10 times its state, are more accurate there. On the unfilled Weather file, DRiC‑L8 without the guard has on average 8.0 times the frozen forecast's MSE, whereas with the guard it reduces the MSE by 7.94%. Code: https://github.com/keiotakmin/dric.

PaperId: 259, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29590.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jingzhe Zhang, Peixuan Zhang, Genying Li, Bing Ma, Shuchen Weng, Si Li, Boxin Shi
Title: CineEvolve: An Agentic Self-Evolution Framework for Cinematic Multi-Shot Video Generation
Abstract:
Cinematic multi‑shot video generation requires both narrative planning and iterative refinement. Existing methods either lack narrative reasoning or rely on feed‑forward workflows without policy updates. In this paper, we propose CineEvolve, an agentic self‑evolution framework for cinematic multi‑shot video generation that unifies a Director and a Critic within a single vision‑language policy. Emulating real‑world filmmaking that couples iterative direction with critical feedback, we train CineEvolve via alternating reinforcement learning, where the Director surfaces flaws to sharpen the Critic, and the updated Critic guides the Director's targeted revisions. To stabilize co‑evolution, we introduce Evolutionary GRPO (E‑GRPO), leveraging historical anchoring and revision safeguarding to mitigate advantage inflation. Additionally, we contribute CineTraj, a 40K cinematic trajectory dataset spanning creation, critique, and revision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CineEvolve outperforms existing approaches. Our code will be available at https://github.com/JingZhe‑8/CineEvolve.

PaperId: 260, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29589.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rafael Lopes Almeida, Ina Pöhner
Title: Fragment-Level Graph Encoding for Interpretable Molecular Property Prediction
Abstract:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) are among the standard tools for molecular property prediction, but the atom‑level explanations of their predictions are hard for medicinal chemists to act on. We propose a change of input representation rather than a new model: molecules are encoded as fragment‑level graphs from BRICS decomposition, where each node is a synthetically meaningful fragment whose features are the element‑wise sum of its atoms' features. Because only the representation changes, any message‑passing GNN and any post‑hoc attribution method produces explanations at the resolution of functional groups instead of single atoms. Across four architectures, four prediction tasks, and two explainers under scaffold splits, fragment‑level encoding matches atom‑level test accuracy on roughly five‑fold smaller graphs. Integrated‑Gradients attributions recover known pharmacophores above chance on two enzyme targets, namely BACE at 1.5 times the chance rate, and PTR1 at 3.2 times. A like‑for‑like comparison against an aggregated atom‑level baseline shows that post‑hoc aggregation is not a stable substitute: its BACE hit rate range both exceeds and falls below the fragment model's hit rate depending on two arbitrary aggregation choices, whereas fragment‑level training yields a single convention‑free attribution at no predictive cost. The code is available at: https://github.com/4D‑Lab/frame

PaperId: 261, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29585.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Thorsten Altenkirch
Title: Any colour you like, as long as it's UIP: Semi-simplicial types from weakenings and thinnings
Abstract:
We explain an attempt to define semi‑simplicial types (SST) in homotopy type theory by first defining a small type theory whose contexts are exactly the data of semi‑simplicial types, constructing \mathrmSST\,n uniformly in that syntax, and then interpreting the syntax in the universe. The syntax can be defined without any truncation and without K, and the construction of \mathrmSST\,n goes through. The naive interpretation does not: it transports along the semantic images of equations that hold only propositionally, and making these transports agree needs uniqueness of identity proofs (UIP) for the semantic types. Moving the problem into the syntax, by making composition a constructor of a higher inductive‑inductive type (HIIT), does not remove it either: it reappears as a coherence problem in the syntax. Fording the HIIT (storing equations instead of computed indices), with conditional rules, makes the syntax provably a set. This is UIP for the syntax, obtained by encode‑decode, and it does not by itself restrict the semantics; but the naive interpretation of the conditional rules again needs UIP for the semantic types. A semantics into groupoids that avoids UIP will be discussed in a separate note. The Agda development accompanying this note is in the repository https://github.com/txa/sst‑new.

PaperId: 262, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29580.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Colin Doumont, Henry Moss, Philipp Hennig
Title: Fast Bayesian Optimization Through Linear Models
Abstract:
Bayesian optimization (BO) is typically used only for problems where the underlying function is deemed "expensive" (e.g. in time or money), with the speed of the BO algorithm being of little importance. In the real world, however, problems span a continuous range of values, going from cheap to expensive. In this paper, we present BO algorithms through the lens of a speed‑performance Pareto frontier: we compare BO against faster algorithms like CMA‑ES, and highlight how certain regions of the Pareto frontier are currently empty. As a solution, we propose a new set of fast BO methods that exploit the linear structure in existing BO algorithms, for both continuous and combinatorial inputs (from ~10 to 6000+ dimensions). Our methods achieve performance similar to state‑of‑the‑art BO, while being more than 10^2× to 10^3× faster, opening the field of BO to an entirely new class of problems.

PaperId: 263, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29577.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ahmed Mahrous, Roberto Di Pietro
Title: The Reflexivity Threshold: A Phase Transition for Multi-Agent Performative Prediction
Abstract:
Many learning systems are performative: once deployed, their predictions change the data distribution on which future models are trained. In multi‑agent settings, this feedback is routed through a network of interacting learners, so stability depends not only on the strength of performativity but also on who affects whom. We study repeated retraining in multi‑agent performative prediction and identify a spectral threshold that separates stable learning from worst‑case learning obstruction. Prior work often collapses cross‑agent feedback into a scalar contraction constant, missing this network structure. We instead introduce the reflexivity matrix Γ, which records how strongly one agent's deployment can move another agent's best response, defined from per‑agent gradient sensitivities and curvature parameters. The threshold occurs when the spectral radius of this matrix crosses one. Below the threshold, repeated retraining converges geometrically to a unique performatively stable equilibrium, with cumulative excess loss bounded uniformly in the time horizon. Above the threshold, we construct noisy supercritical instances in which every local‑information learner incurs expected cumulative excess loss growing linearly for horizons up to order 1/(ρ(Γ)‑1). Together, these results characterize the threshold behavior through upper and lower bounds and recover the single‑agent scalar threshold from prior work as a special case.

PaperId: 264, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29552.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xin Zhang, Haochen Wang, Beibei Lin, Zhaoxiang Zhang, Robby T. Tan, Jason Li, Dacheng Tao
Title: Generalized CycleGRPO for Fine-Grained Multimodal Understanding and Grounding
Abstract:
Fine‑grained multimodal intelligence requires models to both understand a designated region and localize it from language. Existing methods learn these directions with separate objectives and task‑specific annotations. We present Generalized CycleGRPO, the first unified reinforcement learning framework coupling region understanding and localization across spatial, temporal, and spatio‑temporal domains. Given a region, a multimodal large language model generates candidate descriptions and then localizes each description to reconstruct the input region. Reconstruction overlap provides a verifiable reward for captioning, while individual localization rewards improve the inverse mapping. A common region‑space formulation extends this cycle from image masks and boxes to video intervals and timestamped spatial evidence, without reference captions or an external language‑model judge during reinforcement learning. In videos, the cycle encourages descriptions that distinguish a target event from similar recurrences. We introduce DOVE (Distinctive Occurrence‑level Video‑caption Evaluation), a human‑verified contrastive benchmark for this temporal distinctiveness. CycleGRPO improves SAMTok's overall gIoU from 57.5% to 68.2% on GroundingSuite and average gIoU from 71.2% to 78.7% on GRES. For temporal tasks, it achieves 51.9% tIoU on Charades and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE, compared with 45.6% and 14.8% for the Qwen3‑VL initialization. These results establish region‑text cycle consistency as a general self‑evaluation principle for multimodal understanding and localization. Models, code, and DOVE are available at https://devinxzhang.github.io/Generalized‑CycleGRPO‑Page/.

PaperId: 265, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29517.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Bei Huang, Yixin Chen, Hongbin Zha, Yuru Pei, Siyuan Huang
Title: AutoPhyX: Automatic Text-Condition Physics Property Generation
Abstract:
High‑fidelity 4D physical simulation requires accurate physical parameter assignments that align with diverse material properties. Previous methods struggle with critical bottlenecks: they either rely on computationally intensive per‑scene optimization or predict parameters from purely visual inputs. The latter suffers from inherent ambiguity, e.g., the inability to distinguish the stiffness of rubber from its appearance alone. To bridge this gap, we propose AutoPhyX, a text‑conditioned framework for predicting spatially‑varying physical properties. Since training robust feed‑forward models requires fine‑grained supervision, we first introduce a novel part‑controllable data generation pipeline that decomposes complex 3D assets into semantically distinct components and pairs them with physically plausible, diverse parameters and corresponding text descriptions. Leveraging this dataset, AutoPhyX employs a cross‑modal modulation mechanism where text features dynamically modulate visual features for precise physical grounding. By formulating property prediction within a voxel field, AutoPhyX ensures compatibility with diverse 3D representations, including meshes, point clouds, Gaussian Splatting, and NeRF. Experiments demonstrate that our method enables physically plausible, text‑driven parameter assignment in a single forward pass. It achieves high accuracy and robust generalization to in‑the‑wild objects, paving the way for future physics‑intensive embodied and robotic applications.

PaperId: 266, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29508.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wenhai Wan, Teng Zhang, Shao-Yuan Li, Xinrui Wang, Qiang-Sheng Hua, Songcan Chen
Title: Shortcut-Resistant CAM Distillation for Long-Tailed Recognition
Abstract:
Real‑world datasets often follow a long‑tailed distribution, making generalization to tail classes difficult. We revisit this problem through the lens of shortcut learning, where models prefer the easiest predictive cues (e.g., background or textures) over object‑centric semantics, especially under scarce and biased supervision. We find that this tendency is amplified for tail classes: limited examples often share similar contexts, making non‑semantic signals highly correlated and thus tempting shortcuts, whereas head classes with diverse appearances and environments encourage more stable object‑focused representations. Motivated by this observation, we propose Shortcut‑Resistant CAM Distillation (SRCD), a plug‑and‑play framework that transfers object‑focused explanations from head to tail classes. SRCD operates in the Class Activation Map (CAM) space, where a CAM provides a class‑specific spatial evidence map for a prediction. SRCD aggregates CAMs from a small set of head‑class candidates into a shortcut‑resistant teacher using an energy‑model weighting based on coherence and concentration, and distills it to the tail‑class CAM. We provide a theoretical analysis that quantifies shortcut reliance as shortcut‑region evidence mass in CAM space and shows that SRCD suppresses tail shortcuts. Extensive experiments on long‑tailed benchmarks consistently improve strong baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/Haifeng3/SRCD.

PaperId: 267, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29506.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Julian Herold, Markus Götz, Alexander Schug
Title: Asynchronous, Generation-Free ABC: Streaming AMIS Reweighting for Heterogeneous Simulator Workloads on HPC
Abstract:
Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) enables Bayesian inference for models with intractable likelihoods by estimating parameter posterior distributions from simulated data. Sequential ABC methods improve sampling efficiency by iteratively adapting the proposal distribution toward regions of high posterior probability. However, these methods typically operate in generations, where each generation must wait for its slowest simulation before the next can begin. On a parallel machine, this synchronization barrier leaves workers idle and reduces throughput, particularly when simulation runtimes vary substantially. We introduce a generation‑free ABC sampler that updates its proposal when simulation results arrive and sends a new candidate to each available worker. The proposal is based on the best particles evaluated so far. To estimate the posterior, we reuse the full history and reweight particles against a reconstructed mixture of sampling proposals. We show how errors in approximating the mixture of sampling proposals affect the estimated posterior and establish consistency for the smooth‑ABC posterior when the approximation becomes asymptotically exact. In our experiments, the method achieves well‑calibrated posterior estimates where a pyABC baseline with the same kernel and bandwidth schedule under‑covers. From the asynchronous run's timing alone, we predict how much a synchronization barrier would slow the sampler. These predictions agree with measured synchronization penalties ranging from 1.2x to 400x. On a Cellular Potts tissue simulator, the asynchronous sampler completes 2.1‑2.4x as many evaluations as pyABC in the same hour, and the discrepancy threshold for its best 100 evaluations is 4.1x smaller. With the starting bandwidth set from prior‑predictive discrepancies, it also produces a more concentrated two‑parameter posterior with a larger effective sample size than pyABC.

PaperId: 268, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29501.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiaru Qian, Yihong Dong, Xue Jiang, Chun-Wah Hsu, Zhi Jin, Ge Li
Title: Parallel Thinking for Large Language Model with Path Diversity
Abstract:
Parallel thinking has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by exploring multiple reasoning paths simultaneously. However, we identify that parallel thinking via Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically suffers from the mode collapse of reasoning paths, where parallel thinking trajectories degenerate into similar ones. This homogeneity undermines the fundamental motivation of parallel thinking, that is, maintaining multiple hypotheses concurrently to prevent premature loss into a suboptimal solution. In this paper, we propose Diverse Parallel Thinking (DPT), a simple yet effective RL approach for parallel thinking designed to encourage path diversity. DPT rewards the model to develop distinct reasoning strategies by penalizing the prefix similarity of parallel thinking paths, thereby enhancing a more comprehensive exploration of the reasoning space. We conduct various experiments and analyses across multiple reasoning benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of DPT. Results show that DPT successfully outperforms previous parallel thinking methods, achieving state‑of‑the‑art performance over baselines. We validate path diversity as a key element to improve parallel thinking. Our code is available at https://github.com/JiaruQian/DPT.

PaperId: 269, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29467.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jian Zhong, Zeyu Liu, Pingchuan Cao, Rongduo Han, Shunye Tang, Guohuan Xie, Mingyuan Qin, Ran Ji, Xiao Liang, Wei Wang, Haining Zhang
Title: PreCoMem: Predictive Cognitive Memory for Self-Evolving Long-Term Dialogue Agents
Abstract:
Long‑horizon dialogue agents need to keep user memories stable enough for personalization while adapting when the user genuinely changes. Existing memory systems often append every observation or overwrite old entries by heuristic rules, which makes transient noise hard to distinguish from real belief drift. We introduce PreCoMem, a memory consolidation framework inspired by predictive coding that represents memory as confidence‑weighted beliefs about the user's state. Its core signal, Effective Surprisal, combines semantic deviation and contradiction evidence, then downweights this signal when retrieval is diffuse and unreliable. According to effective surprisal, a two‑threshold gate maps each turn to one of three deterministic updates: MAINTAIN reinforces supported beliefs, PROFILE stores ambiguous cues as low‑confidence hypotheses, and CORRECT softly decays reliably contradicted facts. The PROFILE stage acts as an explicit waiting room, preventing premature commitment to noisy evidence. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval‑S, and PersonaMem‑v2 show consistent state‑of‑the‑art accuracy; our new DiMoBench confirms that PreCoMem adapts to non‑stationary belief drift without over‑reacting to noise. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhongWishing/PreCoMem.

PaperId: 270, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29455.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuan Ge, Pei Zhang, Xize Cheng, Lingzhou Mu, Mingyang Wang, Jin Xu, Baosong Yang, Shengxiang Gao, Jingbo Zhu, Zhengtao Yu, Tong Xiao
Title: Omnilingual-MsASR: Benchmarking Multimodal, Multilingual, Long-Form Multi-Speaker ASR of Omni Large Language Models
Abstract:
Omni‑modal large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio and video understanding. However, existing models struggle with long‑form, multi‑speaker videos, especially in understanding the entire video and recognizing who says what and when. To characterize the capability limit of current omni LLMs and guide future model development, we introduce Omnilingual‑MsASR, a multilingual, multimodal benchmark for long‑form Multi‑speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (MsASR) covering six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers. Omnilingual‑MsASR provides parallel audio and video inputs to evaluate models' cross‑modal consistency and their ability to exploit complementary cues across modalities. Extensive evaluations of leading omni‑modal LLMs reveal substantial performance bottlenecks, while their tcpWERs frequently exceed 100%. These findings highlight fine‑grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross‑modal synergy as key challenges for future omni‑modal foundation models. Our work is available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua‑Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua‑MSpeaker.

PaperId: 271, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29454.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shujun Yao, Junhui Lin, Congying Han, Tiande Guo, Ziwen Liu, Bonan Li
Title: BlazeVGGT: 13x Faster VGGT at 2,000 Frames via Camera Token without Training
Abstract:
Feed‑forward visual geometry models, exemplified by VGGT, have demonstrated strong multi‑view reconstruction capabilities through dense global attention. However, the resulting all‑to‑all cross‑view computation scales quadratically with the number of input views, making long‑sequence inference particularly expensive due to substantial frame‑level redundancy among highly overlapping observations. We uncover a topology‑first, geometry‑later evolution in VGGT camera tokens: shallow‑layer tokens reliably capture local view neighborhoods, whereas deeper‑layer tokens progressively encode globally organized inter‑view geometry. Motivated by this observation, we introduce BlazeVGGT, a training‑free framework for structure‑aware frame‑level key‑‑value sparsification. At each global‑attention block, BlazeVGGT constructs a view‑level similarity kernel from camera‑token relations and employs greedy determinantal point process inference to select a compact set of mutually complementary views. The selected views constitute the key‑‑value context, while all input frames are retained as queries. This asymmetric attention design preserves dense per‑frame predictions while eliminating redundant cross‑view computation, allowing our method to be directly integrated into pretrained VGGT as a plug‑and‑play module without parameter updates. Its advantages become increasingly pronounced with sequence length: at 2,000 frames, BlazeVGGT achieves approximately 13× faster inference than VGGT while reducing the Chamfer Distance from 0.41 to 0.32. Extensive experiments demonstrate a favorable accuracy‑‑efficiency trade‑off in point‑cloud reconstruction and camera‑pose estimation, compatibility with existing VGGT accelerators such as FastVGGT and LiteVGGT, and transferability to VGGT‑based models including StreamVGGT and PAGE‑4D. Codes are publicly available at https://github.com/MagiciannnY/BlazeVGGT.git.

PaperId: 272, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29443.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xuan Yang, Chunxiao Liu, Hongsheng Xin, Hao Xu, Ning Miao
Title: DynaWeave: Learning to Adapt through Dynamic Scenario Synthesis
Abstract:
Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use tools to complete tasks in stateful environments. However, many training environments remain largely static apart from changes caused by the agent's own actions, whereas external events introduced by other users, services, or sudden contingencies in real environments can invalidate ongoing plans. To address this gap, we introduce DynaWeave, an automated synthesis framework that transforms existing static tasks into verifiable dynamic scenarios. The framework generates exogenous events relevant to each task, covering changes in task requirements, environment state, and external information. It uses directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to represent dependencies between events and an execution engine to activate them during agent interaction. A dynamic verifier revises only the evaluation checks affected by events that actually occur and retains all other checks. Using DynaWeave, we collect 2,095 verified interaction trajectories across 36 environments and use them for supervised fine‑tuning of Qwen3.5 models. Experiments on Gaia2, CostBench, and ToolMaze show that DynaWeave achieves consistent improvements in overall performance across all three evaluated model sizes, increasing the task completion rate on CostBench by 67.34 percentage points and even exceeding the performance of Gemini‑3.1‑Pro‑Preview on ToolMaze. These results support dynamic scenario synthesis as a practical approach to training agents to adapt to changing environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow‑Lab/DynaWeave.

PaperId: 273, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29439.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jay Agarwal, Siddharth Khare, Dhruv Kumar
Title: How Far Can Foundation Models Be Distilled for Efficient Jet Tagging?
Abstract:
Jet tagging is one of the most important applications of machine learning at the Large Hadron Collider. Recent models build in more physics knowledge or rely on large‑scale pretraining, but the experiments place strict limits on their inference cost. Knowledge distillation can transfer their performance to small students that are cheap to run. We ask which properties of a teacher help the student, how small a student can get and how close it can come to the state of the art. On a jet tagging benchmark, we distil six teachers that differ in architecture, symmetry and pretraining, including two foundation models, into five small students. Every teacher improves every student, and the gain depends mainly on the strength of the teacher. We then shrink our two strongest distilled students, Transformer and L‑GATr‑slim, in width and in depth. With 20 thousand parameters, a distilled L‑GATr‑slim outperforms every published jet tagger trained from scratch at a fraction of the inference cost of every teacher. Even with two thousand parameters, it matches ParT, a model with a thousand times as many parameters. We also study what the students learn from their teachers. Our benchmark of inference cost shows that students of the same size can differ by almost an order of magnitude in speed. We release the code and the weights of all trained models.

PaperId: 274, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29434.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chihiro Arata, Shohei Taniguchi, Gouki Minegishi, Kan Hatakeyama-Sato
Title: RubatoCodec: Budgeted Adaptive Speech Tokenization with Streaming Decoding
Abstract:
Neural speech codecs provide discrete tokens for speech generation. Lower frame rates shorten token sequences, but each token must then carry more linguistic and acoustic information. Variable‑frame‑rate codecs address this trade‑off by adapting token allocation to speech content, but threshold‑based allocation lets content determine the token count, so the sequence length a speech generator must produce varies across utterances and datasets at a fixed setting. We present RubatoCodec, a variable‑frame‑rate speech codec built on X‑Codec‑2 with an exact utterance‑level event budget and streaming decoding. Its Adaptive Firing mechanism uses changes in codec features and waveform spectra to divide speech into variable‑duration events without a learned boundary predictor. Discrete codes and an explicit duration represent each event, allowing a speech generator to predict and decode one event at a time. Controlled experiments show that adaptive allocation outperforms fixed‑rate coding in reconstruction fidelity and intelligibility at low event rates. A model trained on large‑scale multilingual speech achieves competitive reconstruction quality across English, Japanese, and Mandarin, with the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the evaluated English and Japanese benchmarks at comparable bitrates. In a matched text‑to‑speech comparison, the adaptive representation yields lower WER and higher UTMOS and UTMOSv2 with comparable speaker similarity. The speech generator also learns the codec's utterance‑level event budget without an explicit generation‑time rate constraint. These results demonstrate that budgeted adaptive speech representations support both high‑quality reconstruction and streaming text‑to‑speech generation. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/third‑intelligence/RubatoCodec and https://huggingface.co/third‑intelligence/RubatoCodec.

PaperId: 275, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29432.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Xiujian Liang, Jiacheng Liu, Mingyang Sun, Qichen He, Anda Cheng, Cewu Lu, Jianhua Sun
Title: PRISM: Learning Realistic Depth via Physics-Grounded Noise Disentanglement with Semantic-Geometric Collaboration
Abstract:
Real‑world physical sensing exhibits complex, heterogeneous noise patterns that deviate significantly from idealized simulation, posing a fundamental bottleneck for sim‑to‑real transfer. Existing sensor modelings typically treat depth noise as a monolithic black‑box process, overlooking the distinct physical mechanisms that govern different error modalities. In this work, we introduce a physics‑grounded paradigm that disentangles monolithic noise into two complementary modalities: sensing invalidation and measurement inaccuracy, enabling a tailored treatment of noise sources based on their physical origins. Building on this insight, we propose PRISM, a tripartite framework that distills 3D Visual Foundation Model features as rich spatial‑semantic priors for physics‑based reasoning. To address the inherent sparsity and class imbalance of invalidation regions, we develop Hierarchical Positive‑Prioritized Supervision, integrating multi‑scale positive‑weighted objectives with a positive‑preserving dynamic hard mining strategy to enforce precise artifact delineation. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate that PRISM achieves state‑of‑the‑art fidelity in noisy depth synthesis. Furthermore, downstream robotic experiments show that PRISM facilitates a 92.1% average success rate in the real world, marking a significant improvement over monolithic baselines. Our project page is available at: \resizebox\linewidth!\hrefhttps://shawnleung‑sii.github.io/prism‑icml2026/https://shawnleung‑sii.github.io/prism‑icml2026/.

PaperId: 276, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29430.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chuangxin Zhao, Meimei Zhang, Canran Xiao, Jiachen Luo, Jiajun He, Kaijie Chen, Huy Phan, Tomoki Toda, Biörn W. Schuller
Title: MERP: A Latent-Bottleneck Framework for Robust Multi-Modal Multi-Label Emotion Recognition
Abstract:
Multimodal multi‑label emotion recognition is important for affect‑aware systems, but models trained with complete text, visual, and acoustic streams often degrade sharply when some streams are unavailable at deployment. We address this train‑test gap by learning a compact representation that preserves emotion‑specific evidence from any available subset of modalities. We propose the Multi‑modal Emotion Recognition Perceiver (MERP), which maps the joint sequence into a fixed‑size latent bank, thereby keeping repeated reasoning independent of raw input length; it extracts label‑specific evidence before and after latent reasoning and aligns the two levels through reconstruction. MERP further uses positive and negative class prototypes, a noise‑gated feature enhancer with frequency‑shaped perturbations during training, and confidence‑aware class‑wise fusion to strengthen separability, reduce sensitivity to missing inputs, and combine complementary predictors. Under 20 percent test‑time random modality drop, MERP achieves micro‑F1 scores of 0.563 on CMU‑MOSEI and 0.780 on M3ED, exceeding the strongest evaluated baselines by 0.004 and 0.005, respectively; in the severe CMU‑MOSEI audio‑only setting, it retains 0.473 micro‑F1 versus 0.022 for LDDU. These results show that fixed latent reasoning provides a practical, testable route to robust multimodal emotion recognition without requiring missing‑modality examples during training. Code is available at https://github.com/Creative‑zcx/MERP.

PaperId: 277, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29413.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Keith Kwok, Wanting Ning, Tej Deep Pala, Desmond C. Ong, S. Supraja, Renwen Zhang, Soujanya Poria
Title: Beyond Small Talk: Modeling Disclosure Trajectories in Human-AI Conversation
Abstract:
