Recently, we see a rise in conversational agents as a form of social and emotional support, where disclosure will unfold over time. Yet, current evaluations of these agents typically examine isolated conversational states. In analyses of naturally occurring conversations, disclosure history and current disclosure are confounded which tends to make their effects difficult to isolate. We thus introduce Trajectory‑based Disclosure Evaluation (TraDE), an evaluation framework grounded in Social Penetration Theory that utilizes predefined disclosure trajectories and evaluates how preceding disclosure history shapes model behavior under matched current disclosure. Through the use of TraDE, we demonstrate across multiple models and relational behavior benchmarks that responses to disclosures matched on depth can differ depending on the preceding trajectory, particularly in whether models accept or challenge the user's framing. We also observed that these differences track accumulated exposure to deeper disclosure rather than any single moment of vulnerability or the order of disclosures. It also tends to persists for several turns after disclosure returns to shallow levels. For several behaviors, we also demonstrate that models diverge most consistently from human supporters in the Emotional Support Conversation corpus (ESConv) not when users open up but rather when they step back in their disclosure. TraDE thus provides a systematic way to expose history‑dependent relational behavior that evaluations of isolated conversational states would otherwise miss.

PaperId: 278, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29396.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuta Horioka, Naoya Chiba, Yuki Uranishi
Title: Progressive Permutation Alignment with Temperature-Controlled Spectral Sharpening
Abstract:
In implicit neural representations (INRs), 3D signals are encoded directly in network weights, making stable weight‑space operations essential. However, permutation symmetry causes independently trained yet functionally equivalent models to appear distant in weight space, often inducing large loss barriers under linear interpolation. Existing neuron alignment methods either commit early to discrete matches and become trapped in inconsistent local optima or rely on computationally expensive gradient optimization over continuous relaxations, both of which are unreliable in challenging cases such as NeRF. We adopt progressive alignment, a layer‑wise strategy that follows inter‑layer dependencies from input to output. At each layer, a correlation matrix is estimated and aligned with a discrete anchor obtained by the Hungarian algorithm, after which temperature‑controlled spectral annealing gradually sharpens the correlation structure toward a permutation matrix. This update is deterministic and lightweight, avoiding the inner‑loop gradient optimization required by continuous relaxation methods. A final refinement stage further optimizes the network layer‑by‑layer via weight matching, starting from the aligned solution. Experiments on MLPs, CNNs, and Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) show that the proposed method reliably recovers neuron correspondences and achieves stable alignment across architectures. In practical experiments aligning independently trained NeRF models, our method reduces the loss barriers under weight interpolation compared with existing approaches.

PaperId: 279, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29374.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rodion Shkokov, Tatiana Zemskova, Dmitry Yudin
Title: AOV-GS: Active Open-Vocabulary Semantic Mapping with 3D Gaussian Splatting
Abstract:
Robots deployed in human‑centered environments need maps that support both geometric navigation and open‑vocabulary semantic queries beyond a fixed label set. A key challenge is enriching such maps with semantic information without relying on manually annotated segmentation masks or closed‑set semantic categories. Existing geometry‑driven active mapping maximizes coverage but treats semantics as a passive by‑product of the collected trajectory, whereas active semantic mapping typically depends on supervised semantic segmentation. We present AOV‑GS, an active 3D Gaussian mapping system that guides exploration using frozen foundation models. During coarse exploration, AOV‑GS re‑ranks geometrically promising candidate views according to CLIP mask‑embedding novelty computed from SAM instance segmentation, biasing exploration toward semantically informative regions. Frozen SAM and CLIP provide instance masks and language‑aligned embeddings throughout mapping, while a lightweight scene‑specific language field is fitted offline directly to the collected CLIP embeddings rather than manually annotated masks, enabling open‑vocabulary text‑query segmentation on novel views. In a controlled comparison using the same SAM‑CLIP perception stack, AOV‑GS improves average language‑field mIoU over geometry‑only active planning by 1.3 percentage points on Replica (34.6% on eight scenes) and by 1.8 points on Matterport3D (23.1% on five scenes). With CorrCLIP, AOV‑GS reaches 35.6% on Replica, 2.0 points above the matched Geometry‑based + CorrCLIP baseline. Novel‑view PSNR remains comparable to the geometry‑only baseline on both datasets while depth L1 improves on Replica. Code is available at https://github.com/OptimusFaber/AOV‑GS.

PaperId: 280, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29342.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ju-Chun Ko
Title: Uncensored Is Not Unbiased: Abliteration Removes Refusals but Not Script-Dependent Bias About Taiwan
Abstract:
"Abliterated" ("uncensored") builds of open‑weight language models remove the activation direction that mediates refusal, and are popular partly on the assumption that a model that no longer refuses is free of political censorship. We test this on two matched pairs of 2‑bit models: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B‑A9B and Qwen3.8‑Flash‑Next, each against a community abliteration. Each model judged 22 statement pairs (on the Republic of China (Taiwan), 1989 Tiananmen, control countries) in Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese (a character‑level conversion) and English, and answered 27 open questions per script. Script mattered far more than abliteration: the original Bolt scored +0.58 on Index S (‑1: People's Republic of China (PRC) position; +1: ROC position) in Traditional Chinese, +0.57 in English and +0.05 in Simplified Chinese, and affirmed "Taiwan is part of the PRC" with probability 0.91 in Simplified but 0.06 in Traditional characters; abliteration changed its scores by at most 0.06, mostly by raising "yes" on both sides. In Qwen, abliteration removed every refusal on 1989 and raised scores by 0.21 to 0.34, yet the abliterated Qwen still affirmed that Taiwan is part of the PRC in all three scripts. Naming the state the Republic of China (Taiwan) raised every model's score by 0.10 to 0.33 but left the script gap. Control pairs showed no script gap; both edits changed only their declared tensors. In 740,000 web documents, Simplified text on Taiwan used PRC‑framing terms 3.7 times as often as Traditional text. Steering the script gap away failed; a stance direction from the ROC wording raised scores on new statements by 0.04 to 0.06; negated, it lowered them more. A four‑sentence system prompt raised the abliterated Qwen to +0.93 to +0.97. Keyword scoring rules failed the models closest to the ROC position mostly for attributing or denying the PRC claim. Uncensored is not unbiased.

PaperId: 281, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29330.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Changshun Wu, Mengyu Li, Mathis Marsault, Xiaowei Huang, Chih-Hong Cheng
Title: AgentMonopoly: Behavioral Patterns and Persona Control in LLM Agents
Abstract:
How do LLM agents' strategies differ, and how much can instructions to adopt a persona change their behavior over a game? We study these questions with AgentMonopoly, an environment where agents communicate, buy and trade properties, and make decisions that affect later turns. We compare models from four families, each at two sizes, in games with identical models, different sizes of the same family, or different families. We also assign one agent a persona, a description of how it should behave, intended to change a tendency observed in games without that persona. The tested models differ in how often they trade, waive rent, and manage cash and properties. Larger models do not consistently win more games. Persona instructions change the words agents use and some of their actions, but the changes do not always match the role across all decisions. These results show why persona following should be assessed through actions and outcomes as well as language. As our findings are conditional on the tested checkpoints, prompts, and five seeds per configuration, the open‑source nature of AgentMonopoly provides the experimental infrastructure for further extending these comparisons. Our code is available at https://github.com/SuELS‑Group/Agent_Monopoly.

PaperId: 282, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29329.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qinghang Liu, Conglin Wang, Zongsheng Li, Boyong He, Han Gao, Pengcheng Wang, Tao Sun, Lige Liu, Chang Liu
Title: Plan First, Act Later: Streaming Reasoning for Executable Memory in Robot Control
Abstract:
Long‑horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to remember task‑relevant information beyond its short observation window. Existing memory‑augmented policies typically retrieve relevant information from history and reason over it at execution time, placing a heavy reasoning burden on the high‑level model. To address this challenge, we propose PAL (Plan first, Act Later), a hierarchical memory framework for vision‑language robot manipulation. It maintains a short‑term visual buffer, a semantic‑event memory, and an executable \textttsubtask\_list. A high‑level vision‑language model (VLM) converts streaming visual observations into the \textttsubtask\_list. At execution time, the VLM selects the currently relevant subtask from the \textttsubtask\_list and passes it to a low‑level vision‑language‑action (VLA) policy. To teach the model what to write to memory and when to update it, we introduce a two‑stage data generation procedure that first expands sparse update supervision and then uses self‑labeling with task‑grounded verification to generate training data that better match the state distribution encountered during execution. We evaluate our approach on memory‑dependent benchmarks and real‑world manipulation tasks. On RoboMME, PAL achieves a 56.05% success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline, FrameSamp‑Modul, at 44.51%. In real‑world experiments across four manipulation tasks, \pal reaches 60.83% overall success, surpassing MemER (45.00%) and FrameSamp‑Modul (28.33%). These results show that proactively writing future‑relevant subtasks into hierarchical memory improves long‑horizon visual reasoning and robot control. Code and videos can be found on our website: https://qinghangliu.github.io/pal‑webpage/

PaperId: 283, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29328.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Adi Simhi, Yaniv Nikankin, Jonathan Herzig, Idan Szpektor, Yonatan Belinkov, Shay B. Cohen
Title: Seeing the Forest for the Trees: Emergent Agreement from Individual Conversations
Abstract:
As LLM agents interact in the wild and shape each other's decisions, understanding how they converge toward agreement becomes important. We study this in multi‑turn conversations where two LLMs discuss subjective matters, can agree or disagree, and may change their stances. Using a linear classifier on individual conversation activations, we identify an internal representation of agreement. We find that it varies substantially across turns and conversations and does not reliably track external agreement at the individual conversation level. We therefore move beyond the representation of agreement in individual conversations, by aggregating the agreement representation across conversations. Externally, this aggregate view reveals a simple structure: when pooled across conversations, agreement can be predicted well with a Markov process, with agreement at each turn being a direct function of agreement at the previous turn. Similarly, when internal agreement is aggregated, it couples with the external Markov agreement through a power‑law mapping, exposing Markovian dynamics in internal representations. Additionally, we find that after a change of stance, models express agreement externally before their internal representations reflect the same shift. These results reveal a joint structure between internal and external agreement that emerges only when internal features are aggregated across conversations. Code available at https://github.com/technion‑cs‑nlp/SeeingTheForestForTheTrees.

PaperId: 284, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29312.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yongjin Yi, Jinyong Park, Sejoong Kim
Title: A Stratified Multi-Rater Evaluation of LLM-Based Virtual Standardized Patients with a Deployed Data-Generation Platform
Abstract:
The Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) is widely used to assess clinical communication skills in medical education, requiring trainees to take histories and reason clinically with standardized patients (SPs). Large language model (LLM)‑based virtual standardized patients (VSPs), typically built by persona‑injected prompting, offer a practical alternative. However, existing evaluations rely on a single backbone LLM, small human rater panels, or LLM‑as‑a‑judge scoring without an utterance‑aligned human‑expert reference, and so cannot identify the specific shortcomings of individual models. We evaluated four LLMs (GPT‑4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama‑3.1 70B, and HyperCLOVA X), spanning commercial, open‑source and Korean‑developed models, against a human‑expert reference across three Korean OSCE cases (hematuria, fever in pregnancy, and chronic cough). In a double‑blind, fully crossed design, 17 senior medical‑student raters scored every model utterance on three sentence‑level and six encounter‑level Likert metrics, yielding 7,480 data points. We analyzed the scores using a stratified linear mixed‑effects model based on an 11‑category history‑taking and 3‑level linguistic‑form taxonomy. At the encounter level, three of the four LLMs fell 0.08 to 0.47 Likert points below the human‑expert reference on Comprehensibility, Consistency and Hallucination‑freeness. The difference was not statistically significant for Hallucination‑freeness in Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT‑4o, Consistency in GPT‑4o, and Engagement in HyperCLOVA X. Llama‑3.1 70B fell significantly below the reference on all six metrics. We also introduce a web‑based OSCE platform that supports virtual practice across diverse clinical cases and continuously collects student‑VSP dialogues under research and privacy consent.

PaperId: 285, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29300.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Boning Li, Longbo Huang
Title: When Are We Near Nash? Certifying Solutions in General-Sum Games
Abstract:
Heuristic solvers for general‑sum extensive‑form games produce a stream of iterates, and practice reports the NashGap of the returned profile. We ask what a solver can know about its own iterates from the regret accumulators and the terminal‑distribution accumulators its updates already maintain. In two‑player games the NashGap of a weighted average strategy equals, at the maximizing player, the weighted external regret plus a signed value correction. Bounding the regret by the running counterfactual‑regret accumulator gives an online certificate whose cost per checkpoint is linear in the number of terminal histories. The certificate stays sound under alternating updates and in games with three or more players. The mismatch between what alternation evaluates and what the averages record enters as one signed comparator term, maximized in a single backward pass per player whose comparator weight is nonzero. The bound is read off the regret state, with no best response against the average. Run a portfolio of training‑free regret‑matching solvers, output the iterate with the smallest certificate, and verify that iterate once. On the benchmark's biased Leduc family a pool of sixteen training‑free solvers, seven original and nine recent variants, solves 89% of the 64 instances at threshold 10^‑5 this way, matching the trajectory‑minimum union of the solvers. The same protocol solves 92% of the 64 pre‑registered held‑out instances and 89% again on a third set of 64 instances that no earlier stage used. The zero‑best‑response certificate certifies all 57 in‑sample solves and all 57 fresh ones, and 58 of the 59 held‑out ones. Its exact‑comparator refinement certifies every solve in the three sets. The certificate states both and attributes its bound. Code is available at https://github.com/lbn187/CertNE.

PaperId: 286, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29271.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ruqi Chen, Zilei Wang, Wei Wang
Title: ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning
Abstract:
Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning ‑ reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real‑world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid‑based transformations, different from the well‑known ARC‑AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors. We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs. All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.com/density‑11/arcana‑test. All ARCANA data and task instances can be accessed and explored at https://arcanacogtest.org/.

PaperId: 287, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29264.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chun Gu, Xiaofei Wei, Yiming Chen, Bozhou Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
Title: Training in Deployment: Human-in-the-loop Online Post-Training for Robot Manipulation
Abstract:
Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact‑rich, recovery, and precision‑critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human‑in‑the‑loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post‑training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor‑critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human‑in‑the‑loop online post‑training system. TIDE introduces a provenance‑conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy‑generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real‑world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone‑normalized task progress and binary full‑task completion over the warm‑start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed‑policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task‑specific online post‑training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.

PaperId: 288, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29248.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Peize Li, Hanzhen Zhao, Xingguo Xu, Yilong Fan, Zhen Tao, Bo Yin, Zhifei Liu, Qingdong He, Xiaobin Hu
Title: ER-Chord: Spatially Consistent One-Step Image Editing via Equal-Energy Reliability Redistribution
Abstract:
One‑step generative models enable fast text‑guided image editing, yet they often introduce unintended changes to regions that should remain unchanged. Temporal aggregation stabilizes editing fields across noise levels, but leaves their spatial allocation insensitive to local variations in reliability. Consequently, temporal stability alone does not ensure spatially consistent editing. To address this lim‑ itation, we propose ER‑Chord, a training‑free and inversion‑free framework for reliability‑guided spatial redistribution. Our key insight is that agreement between editing fields at neighboring noise levels provides a local reliability signal for allocating editing strength. We formulate this allocation as an equal‑energy op‑ timization that redistributes control energy according to local reliability while preserving the original editing directions and total control energy. This formu‑ lation admits a unique global solution that can be efficiently computed using existing field evaluations, requiring no additional denoiser calls. Experiments on two benchmarks, PIE‑Bench and TEdBench, demonstrate improvements over state‑of‑the‑art one‑step editing baselines, achieving superior source preservation alongside consistent gains across multiple generative backbones.The project page is at https://github.com/Peizeli1/ER‑Chord.

PaperId: 289, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29246.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiujian Liang, Liuyuan Na, Zehao Du, Jiacheng Xu, Weixi Song, Mingyang Sun, Xingjun Ma, Cewu Lu, Jianhua Sun
Title: DepState-JEPA: Learning Depth-Grounded State Representation for Visual Perception and Manipulation
Abstract:
Predictive representations for robot manipulation should connect scene geometry with the state changes induced by actions. Our intuition is that understanding what an action will change starts with understanding where things are: complementary RGB and depth observations ground a common scene representation from which to infer those changes. Guided by this intuition, we introduce DepState‑JEPA, a dual‑stream RGB‑‑Depth joint‑embedding predictive architecture that connects spatial understanding with action‑conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, DepState. Built on V‑JEPA~2.1, the framework uses depth both as a complementary observation stream and to ground both modalities in metric 3D space, aggregating shared information into DepState while retaining modality‑private features for decoding. Ray‑conditioned readouts predict local features without target depth; after an action‑conditioned transition, the same decoders predict future RGB and depth features using the predicted state and fixed initial private features. Robot‑state readouts provide recursive proprioceptive inputs; object‑trajectory supervision and calibrated forward kinematics shape state learning through motion targets and joint‑‑TCP consistency. Comparisons show stronger RGB‑encoder transfer after RGB‑D adaptation, feature completion, conditioned visual forecasting, and manipulation success. Within‑model ablations identify contributions from depth content, metric coordinates, and future‑state matching, with additional control gains from FK regularization. The project page is available at https://shawnleung‑sii.github.io/depstate‑jepa/.

PaperId: 290, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29232.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Junjie Wang, Zhihao Yuan, Yunhan Tang, Sheng Xu, Jiaqi Mao, Xiaoyu Ye, Yueru Luo, Xu Yan, Chun-Mei Feng, Zhen Li
Title: Think-Capture: Active 3D Geometry Acquisition for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
Abstract:
Vision‑Language Models (VLMs) excel at 2D recognition but often fail to maintain consistent 3D relations across sparse viewpoints, leading to spatial hallucinations under occlusion and perspective changes. Existing methods commonly fuse all frames with dense geometry, incurring substantial computation and context overhead while encouraging blind reliance on imperfect estimators. We present Think‑Capture, a query‑conditioned framework that first identifies task‑critical objects and then acquires their geometry on demand. A 3D toolkit lifts zero‑shot masks into a common coordinate frame, and a Symbolic 3D State Abstraction compresses object and camera states into structured text. Hierarchical Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trains the VLM on cases in which geometry either helps or misleads, teaching it when to use tool evidence and when to fall back on visual cues. Think‑Capture‑4B reaches 54.4% on MindCube‑Tiny (+21.5 points over its backbone), 39.1% on the MMSI‑Bench positional subset (+7.9), and 42.8% on ViewSpatial (+5.2). It also remains robust under coordinate and mask perturbations. The full stack fits one 24 GB GPU and serves as an asynchronous high‑level reasoner on an Agibot G1. Our code is available at https://github.com/819346675/Think‑Capture.

PaperId: 291, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29225.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hongyu Li, Xinlong Huang, Zhan Yu, Jing Zhao, Zhe Zhao, Juntao Zhong, Xiong Kuang, Rui Yuan, ZhenXiang Yan, Huilin Xu, Haitao Yu, Lilin Wang, Rui Chen, Blaze Chen, Fengzong Lian, Renfen Hu
Title: Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics
Abstract:
Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt‑level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment. To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a bilingual (English‑Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive 84‑label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets: DiagBase, which covers single‑ and multi‑turn prompts with direct harmful queries and template‑based jailbreaks, and DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex instruction‑following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM‑as‑a‑judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations ‑‑ substantially higher than the 69%‑87% achieved by the baselines ‑‑ and high inter‑judge consistency (Cohen's κ = 0.864). Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi‑turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.

PaperId: 292, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29217.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rushab Munot
Title: When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models
Abstract:
Decision models return normalized probability distributions over candidate choices, which downstream applications can use to select among choices. Although their providers emphasize the reliability of these probabilities, calibration on tasks with a single correct choice does not establish their reliability when multiple choices are correct. We evaluate three decision models (Jev, Liquid d1, and GPT‑6 Luna Decisions) on three diverse datasets (MetaTool, HotpotQA, and ECtHR) to study probability allocation and thresholding. Even when models rank every correct choice above every distractor, in 28% to 50% of those lists, at least one correct choice receives a probability below the uniform probability of 1/n, where n is the number of choices. We also present each model with five identical copies of a correct choice and observe probability disparities, with mean gaps ranging from 17 to 79 percentage points. We further show how these allocation disparities affect the recovery of multiple correct choices under probability thresholding. Decision‑model probabilities can rank correct choices, but a probability threshold does not identify the set of correct choices.

PaperId: 293, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29210.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Jungseob Lee, Giyoon Jang, Chailin Nam, Jiwoo Kum, Sihyeon Lee, Kyojun Choo, Jihun Song, Eunseo Song, Chanjun Park
Title: Understanding Target Probability Reuse in Speculative Decoding
Abstract:
Speculative decoding uses a target model to verify a tree of draft tokens in parallel. We study whether the resulting next‑token distributions can help select the next tree. For unrestricted target models, we show that guaranteed exact reuse requires a distribution computed at the next round's complete context. We characterize when retaining this distribution requires sacrificing accepted tokens and establish conditions under which this loss persists across decoding rounds. Across six targets, we find that reranking first‑token branches with a separately computed distribution at the current context improves expected acceptance over draft ranking, especially with small tree budgets. Drawing the first token from this distribution before allocating the tree further improves expected acceptance over pruning a preselected tree, even at equal mean tree size. In our experiments, both selection rules also decode faster than draft ranking when the separate target pass overlaps standalone drafting. Our findings show that making target probabilities available before tree allocation can improve the efficiency of speculative decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/js‑lee‑AI/TargetRows.

PaperId: 294, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29205.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Md Ali Ashraf Yad, Nazifa Tabassum Nabila
Title: Reconstruction differences rival individual differences in the fly compass connectome and break trained circuit models
Abstract:
Neural network models are increasingly constructed from synapse‑resolution connectomes, and the same circuit is now available in reconstructions from other animals and pipelines. We do not know whether such models are dependent on the reconstruction they are built from, and whether connectome differences are biological or measurement errors. We studied the Drosophila head‑direction circuit in nine versions: four flies (male CNS, hemibrain, Fly Wire, BANC) and five variants of the same fly varying only by thresholds, proofreading or synapse detection. Using wiring‑based correspondences validated by anatomical labels, we place all differences on one scale. A change of synapse detection within one fly changed the circuit more than halfway to the smallest inter‑fly difference on four distances; proofreading differences were smaller but depended on the metric, and left and right halves of one fly differed no more than a random half. Networks trained on each wiring to hold a cued heading developed near‑perfect ring attractors, but their error increased from below 1 degree to 10‑28 degrees when all weights changed by 1%. Training on each wiring did not transfer to any other connectome, including other versions of the same fly; refitting thirty cell‑type gains, we repaired filtering‑level differences but remaining error depended on wiring distance. Training with noise lowered precision and enhanced transfer. Imaging data indicate compasses drift smoothly and do not break; they function despite differences comparable to those of this study.Therefore, connectome‑constrained models need to reflect the reconstruction they stem from and the robustness normal circuits exhibit and models lack.

PaperId: 295, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29200.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yipeng Lu, Youqi Liao, Zhenyu Wang, Yuning Peng, Zhen Dong
Title: NeuralSRender: G-Buffer Guided Video Diffusion for Sim-to-Real Rendering
Abstract:
The scarcity of high‑quality annotated visual data remains a critical bottleneck for autonomous‑driving perception. Simulators provide training data at scale, but the limited realism of synthetic videos compromises perception performance in real‑world applications. To address this limitation, we propose NeuralSRender, a sim‑to‑real video translation framework that enhances the photorealism of synthetic videos while maintaining geometric consistency with the source scenes. Built on a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT), NeuralSRender uses a lightweight projector to inject geometric and material priors from G‑buffers, and LoRA enables parameter‑efficient adaptation. The model is trained in two stages: it first learns G‑buffer conditioning from synthetic videos with accurate G‑buffers, then adapts to real‑world appearance using real videos with estimated G‑buffers. During the second stage, an additional LoRA module is trained while the projector and first‑stage LoRA remain frozen to reduce interference from estimation noise. NeuralSRender introduces only 1.45% parameter overhead and can be trained on consumer‑grade GPUs with 24 GB of memory. To support training and evaluation, we introduce GenReal, a large‑scale driving video dataset comprising synthetic and real‑world videos with corresponding G‑buffers. Experiments demonstrate improved photorealism with competitive geometric consistency. Training perception models on our translated videos instead of raw simulator renders improves detection \mathrmAP_50 on nuImages from 35.1 to 40.6 and segmentation mIoU on Cityscapes from 32.4 to 40.8. Our code, data, and model weights are available at: https://github.com/WHU‑USI3DV/NeuralSRender.

PaperId: 296, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29196.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Eric Liang, Alan Luo, Kaiwen Yuan
Title: A Unified Evaluation Framework of Physical Adversarial Robustness in the Edge VLM Era
Abstract:
Recent advancements in Vision‑Language Models (VLMs) enable end‑to‑end visual grounding via language prompts and generative decoding, demonstrating largely improved zero‑shot and open‑vocabulary detection capabilities. As a result, VLMs are rapidly being deployed at the edge in safety‑critical real‑world systems. However, the physical adversarial robustness of edge VLMs has not been systematically studied, and the fundamental differences in output with modern object detectors create methodological challenges for fair evaluation. To compare the two families directly, we evaluate every selected representative model on one outcome: whether an adversarial patch worn on a person evades detection of the model. We report this by introducing a unified metric, conditional attack success rate (cASR), counted only on images the model still localizes under a matched gray occluder, and partition every failure into omission (no box), substitution (a box on the patch), and displacement (a box on neither). We benchmark the physical adversarial vulnerability of compact grounding VLMs against a range of object detectors, and find that the VLMs can be as vulnerable as the detectors. We disclose that failure mode is largely associated with the output format of a model rather than its architecture family. Of the three, only omission is visible to a downstream system; displacement and substitution return confident, well‑formed boxes, making them potentially more dangerous failures. Further, we find that, under distribution shift, VLMs that primarily failed by omission instead shift to failing more by displacement/substitution. Thus, a grounding VLM can inherit the detector's vulnerability while showing the possibility to adopt more dangerous failure modes. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ericliang1/physical‑adversarial‑robustness.

PaperId: 297, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29187.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Angela P. Schoellig, Matthias A. Müller, Sebastian Trimpe, Melanie N. Zeilinger, Mahathi Anand, Andrea Carron, Oliver Hausdörfer, Victor G. Lopez, Friedrich Solowjow, Haocheng Zhao, Siqi Zhou
Title: A Decade of Learning-Based Control: From Theoretic Foundations to Practical Deployment
Abstract:
Motivated by ten years of Learning‑Based Control Invited Sessions at the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC), this tutorial paper reviews key advances at the intersection of machine learning and control. We focus on methods that combine the flexibility of machine learning techniques with the structure and theoretical foundations of control to design autonomous systems that are capable, reliable, and safe. We first introduce core notions for establishing stability and safety guarantees, then review approaches that learn dynamics models to improve control under uncertainty, and finally discuss data‑driven methods that directly synthesize or learn policies, including reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and Bayesian optimization. We further discuss representative applications and open challenges. The goal is to provide an accessible entry point to the field and to support continued progress toward reliable learning‑based control in real‑world systems. To support learning and practical exploration, we share implementations and illustrative examples along with our discussion, together with additional resources on our website: https://learning‑based‑control.github.io/tutorial/.

PaperId: 298, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29185.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hoang Tran, Huong Ha, Tri Dang, Jeffrey Chan, Hongyu Zhang
Title: CloudIR-Bench: A Benchmark for Root Cause Analysis and Mitigation of Cloud Incidents
Abstract:
Root cause analysis (RCA) and mitigation prediction are essential for incident management, enabling the identification of underlying causes of failures and ensuring the reliability of complex cloud‑based systems. With rising incident volume and system complexity, incident reports have become a valuable resource for these tasks. Recent studies have shown promising results using Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict root causes and mitigation actions from textual descriptions in incident reports. Despite these advances, further progress is hindered by the lack of publicly available datasets; existing work relies on private data, which limits transparency, reproducibility, and generalization. To address this gap, we introduce CloudIR‑Bench, the first publicly available benchmark providing a dataset and evaluation framework for incident report‑based RCA and mitigation prediction. Curated from incident reports across five leading cloud‑based systems, CloudIR‑Bench captures a diverse range of real‑world production scenarios representing authentic failures and engineers' reasoning. We also release an open‑source evaluation framework that includes eight recent LLM‑based approaches. Our comprehensive evaluation includes zero‑shot and in‑context learning experiments, along with a qualitative analysis to identify where and why LLMs fail. Benchmarking results reveal the capabilities and limitations of existing LLMs in this domain. The benchmark, including the dataset, framework and supplementary materials, is available at https://github.com/hoangtnm/CloudIR‑Bench.

PaperId: 299, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29174.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiachen Guo, Xinshan Zhu, Boyun Wang, Yanyan Liang, Jun Wan, Feng Lin, Ajian Liu
Title: LocalAgent: Collaborative Agentic Verification for Fine-Grained Instance-Level Consistency
Abstract:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress in general visual understanding, yet they still struggle with fine‑grained instance‑level consistency verification, where the goal is to determine whether two images depict the exact same physical object under varying viewpoints, illumination, and backgrounds. This task requires both global semantic perception and precise examination of subtle local evidence, since semantically similar objects may differ only in small suspicious regions. To address this challenge, we propose LocalAgent, a collaborative agentic framework that integrates the complementary strengths of a generalist MLLM and lightweight specialist verifiers. The MLLM first reasons globally to identify suspicious local regions, which are then delegated to a Local Evidence Verifier (LEV) toolkit for fine‑grained appearance and geometric matching. LEV comprises Local Appearance Consistency (LAC), which estimates appearance similarity under illumination and color changes, and Local Geometric Correspondence (LGC), which estimates spatial correspondence under viewpoint changes. LEV returns structured scalar evidence that the MLLM integrates for the final decision. We further introduce an auxiliary‑capped reinforcement fine‑tuning (RFT) strategy, in which answer correctness dominates auxiliary tool‑use and format signals, enabling the policy to learn when verification is necessary. Experiments show that LocalAgent improves mean accuracy by 4.9% over the strongest CoT‑RFT baseline while invoking a verifier on only 12.13% of samples and preserving the general multimodal capabilities of the underlying MLLM. The open‑source repository is available at https://github.com/Firefly‑zoo/LocalAgent‑main.

PaperId: 300, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29169.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chun Gu, Juntong Zhang, Jingyu Li, Li Zhang
Title: SMR: Learning streaming motion retargeting for humanoids from human semantic
Abstract:
Retargeting human motion to humanoids requires preserving motion semantics while accounting for the robot's physical constraints. Kinematic pipelines prescribe a robot trajectory through geometric matching, without establishing whether it can be executed under the robot's dynamics. Prior physics‑supervised neural methods train bidirectional full‑sequence models on physics‑refined kinematic trajectories, remaining tied to prescribed kinematic solutions and requiring noncausal context. We propose SMR, a streaming neural motion retargeter learned from semantic‑conditioned physics experts. We convert human motion into robot‑aware task‑space targets for body landmark positions, orientations, and velocities. Physics experts track these targets directly in simulation under contact, dynamics, and actuator constraints. We train a single strictly causal Transformer on their executed state trajectories that complete the motion and pass semantic and physical validity checks. At each incoming frame, the student uses only current and past human observations to generate a robot motion reference for a downstream whole‑body controller. Experiments demonstrate that semantic‑conditioned physics experts generate motion with higher semantic fidelity and physical validity than direct optimization‑based retargeting, while the resulting streaming retargeter achieves improved closed‑loop performance over kinematic and physics‑refined baselines under a common whole‑body controller.

PaperId: 301, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29159.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhangchi Hu, Zilong He, Yifan Zhao, Xiangyu Yu, Jie Chen, Peixi Wu, Yansong Peng, Hebei Li, Xiaoyan Sun
Title: RiO-DETRv2: Geometry-Aware Uncertainty Modeling Meets Real-Time Oriented Object Detection Transformer
Abstract:
RiO‑DETR is the first real‑time end‑to‑end transformer for oriented object detection, yet further localization gains require a more expressive box representation. Although distributional regression has succeeded in horizontal DETRs, extending it to oriented detection introduces geometry‑misaligned boundary modeling and topology‑inconsistent orientation refinement. We present RiO‑DETRv2, a geometry‑aware uncertainty modeling framework for real‑time oriented object detection. To resolve the geometry mismatch, Object‑Aligned Boundary Distribution Refinement represents box boundaries as probability distributions in an object‑aligned coordinate system and progressively refines them across decoder layers. For better orientation topology consistency, we introduce Circular‑to‑Local Angular Residual Refinement that transitions from global periodic search to local fine‑grained estimation. Unified OBB Quality‑Aligned Learning further aligns classification, boundary and angular refinement with complete‑OBB localization quality. Together, these designs improve localization without compromising efficiency, achieving a better balance between speed and accuracy. Specifically, RiO‑DETRv2‑l/x achieves 53.7/54.1 mAP50‑95 on DOTA, outperforming RiO‑DETR‑l/x by 1.2/1.5 points with nearly unchanged computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/RicePasteM/RiO‑DETRv2.

PaperId: 302, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29129.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Austin Meek, Kyle Cox, Matthew Nguyen, Austin J. Brockmeier, Steven Basart
Title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Realistic Scenarios Through Representation Engineering
Abstract:
Reward hacking is a major problem in current production machine learning systems, resulting in costly and dangerous failures. Here we study how to monitor for and mitigate reward hacking in realistic settings, including tool calls and long contexts. We apply a dynamic intervention to steering directions obtained by three different methods: difference‑in‑means vectors from labeled rollouts, gradient optimization‑based vectors, and vectors extracted when models reference an anti‑reward‑hacking model spec. This dynamic intervention perturbs model representations less than uniform steering vector addition to the residual stream, allowing for more precise edits. We find that we are able to cheaply and significantly reduce reward hacking without correspondingly significant costs to model coherence or capability, and that steering vectors originally extracted from coding environments also generalize to reducing reward hacking in other domains. Our results pave the way towards latent space monitoring and control over realistic production systems.

PaperId: 303, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29098.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Derong Yu, Qingsong Zhao, Yanbing Yue, Yikai Li, Zhi Zhang, Guoyan Zheng
Title: UNIVERS: Learning UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis for generalizable one-shot landmark localization
Abstract:
One‑shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying fields of view (FOVs) is challenging. While existing self‑supervised learning methods have shown promising performance, they rely on contrastive learning built upon augmented views of the same image, which inherently limits their generalization in cross‑modality scenarios. This motivates research on cross‑modality embedding learning using paired multi‑modality images. However, existing methods suffer from not only limited training data, but also the requirement of multi‑stage iterative training. To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end‑to‑end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel‑wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. Our framework leverages diverse pseudo‑data synthesized from organ shape templates, with randomization applied to semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. Coupled with cross‑domain discriminative voxel‑wise contrastive learning, this domain randomization strategy forces the network to disregard domain‑specific biases and learn features that are robust against variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Consequently, the trained model enables one‑shot landmark localization in multi‑modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. In this study, the efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated by applying it to the task of localizing the adrenal glands, which are paired, small, and irregular endocrine organs. In particular, comprehensive experiments are conducted on three challenging adrenal gland datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that UNIVERS consistently outperforms the state‑of‑the‑art (SOTA) one‑shot landmark localization approaches, with particularly prominent advantages in cross‑modality scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Kendra9999/UNIVERS.

PaperId: 304, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29096.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Truong-Son Hy
Title: AMP Atlas: A Browser-Only Workbench for Antimicrobial Peptide Exploration and Interactive Helical-Wheel Design
Abstract:
Accessible research software can connect published antimicrobial peptide (AMP) records to sequence analysis, molecular visualization, and interactive design without requiring a dedicated application server. We present AMP Atlas, an open‑source, browser‑only workbench that combines a DRAMP‑derived database with local physicochemical calculations, published‑neighbor retrieval, and sequence‑guided structural comparison. The reported snapshot contains 12,784 source records, 10,579 canonical records, 5,183 source SMILES annotations, and 433 PDB chain structures. An inverse helical‑wheel editor lets users specify peptide length, fill residues gradually, and immediately retrieve exact‑length database matches under positional and property constraints. Selected‑position residue frequencies support further editing while preserving the remaining constraints. A Web Worker performs searches and numerical calculations; a WebGL viewer provides interactive molecular representations. The static distribution occupies 138.8 MB and supports GitHub Pages hosting. Verification includes 23 Python tests, 30 browser‑core/worker checks, a designer DOM integration suite, and agreement against fixed numerical references. This report describes the implemented algorithms and assumptions; it does not establish predictive accuracy for antimicrobial activity or experimentally validate designed peptides. The website is available at https://hysonlab.github.io/amp‑atlas/ and the source code and database are available at https://github.com/HySonLab/amp‑atlas

PaperId: 305, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29061.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Genpei Zhang
Title: OccJEPA: Occlusion as Masking for Amodal Video Segmentation
Abstract:
Amodal video segmentation asks for the complete mask of an object in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The best current methods generate these masks with fine‑tuned video diffusion models, which need many denoising steps and an extra depth network, and give a different answer for every sample. Self‑supervised video world models of the JEPA family are trained on a closely related task: predicting the representation of masked space‑time regions from the visible ones. We therefore treat occlusion as masking. The tokens that the object's visible mask does not cover are dropped, the pre‑trained V‑JEPA 2.1 predictor fills them in, and a light head decodes the observed and predicted features into amodal masks. The resulting model, OccJEPA (Occlusion‑as‑masking JEPA), is deterministic and 33.5x faster than the diffusion‑based state of the art, and more accurate on SAIL‑VOS, on TAO‑Amodal, including a held‑out test split (+4.00 AP50) and visible masks tracked by SAM2, and on Kubric. Controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre‑trained weights rather than to its capacity, for world models from 87M to 1.85B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/zgp110/occjepa.

PaperId: 306, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29034.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Oleksandr Kholodniak, Oleksandr Prokhorov
Title: Gate Initialisation versus Recurrent Dropout and Zoneout in Learning Long Dependencies: A Controlled Study of LSTM and GRU Networks on Synthetic Tasks
Abstract:
Dropout and zoneout are routinely added to long short‑term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks, but, to our knowledge, their placements have not been crossed with gate initialisation in a factorial design, and it is not known whether early gradient propagation tells which runs will learn long dependencies. We trained one‑layer LSTMs and GRUs on the adding problem and on delayed recall in a factorial grid of 720 runs, crossing conventional and chrono gate initialisation with up to six recurrent regulariser placements at one rate each, with pre‑specified follow‑ups, and recorded how sensitive the final hidden state was to the input at every lag. Because both tasks supply fresh or exhaustive training data, the study measures the regularisers' effects on optimisation and does not assess generalisation from a finite training set. At lengths chosen to make conventional initialisation difficult, all 360 chrono‑initialised runs reached the validation criterion within 5000 updates, as did 119 of 120 unregularised runs with a horizon about four times too short or too long, whereas conventionally initialised networks learned slowly or did not reach the criterion within the budget at the longer lengths. Under conventional initialisation, dropout generally delayed learning and zoneout helped only in some conditions. The early input sensitivity added little to predicting which conditions learn once the early validation loss was modelled per task, architecture and initialisation. Within conditions, a flatter early decay went with the seeds that learned, but in a pre‑specified test the association was modest (concordance 0.61), condition‑dependent and not robust to resampling seeds. The results support chrono initialisation, even with a rough horizon, on such tasks.

PaperId: 307, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29025.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yongsheng Lian
Title: Single-Image Food Mass Estimators Do Not Transfer Their Gram Scale Across Datasets
Abstract:
Estimating food mass from a photograph is central to image‑based dietary assessment, but whether trained models transfer to new cameras and foods is unclear. We fine‑tuned DINOv2‑base on 2,253 weighed Nutrition5k dishes to predict mass from one RGB photograph and compared it with a zero‑shot vision‑language model, Qwen3‑VL‑32B, on Nutrition5k and three external datasets: ASA24 studio portions, ECUSTFD whole foods and Food Portion Benchmark meal trays. In domain, the fine‑tuned model's mean absolute error was 24.8 g, less than half of Qwen's. On external datasets it did not beat Qwen. For a food it had never seen, it ranked portions by size, but no better than a count of food pixels. Its gram scale was wrong in two ways: it changed with how much of the scene the photograph showed, and it was off by a different factor for each food. Training on other foods or trays from the tested dataset cut the external error by 38 to 65%. DINOv2‑large, a larger backbone trained on the same dishes, did not reduce the external error. One labeled photograph of the same food cut the model's ASA24 error to 28.3 g, better than that photograph achieved alone. Prediction intervals that held the true mass for 90% of Nutrition5k dishes held it for at most half of external photographs. Nutrition5k often photographed the same plate several times, so a random test split shared near‑identical photographs with training and overstated accuracy. Single‑image mass estimators therefore need labeled photographs from the setting where they are used.

PaperId: 308, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29014.pdf   GitHub
Authors:William Huang, David Li, Xiang 'Anthony' Chen, Xun Qian, Nels Numan, Zhongyi Zhou, Hyunsung Cho, Salman Muin Kayser Chishti, Ding Xia, Xincheng Huang, Jiahao Ren, Faraz Faruqi, Tianyu Xu, Yang Zhang, David Kim, Ruofei Du
Title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development
Abstract:
Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single‑file generation to long‑horizon repository‑scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR‑Bench, the first benchmark for the end‑to‑end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR‑Bench contains 112 expert‑authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held‑out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR‑Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR‑Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR‑Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.

PaperId: 309, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29013.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Jungseob Lee, Hogun Seong, Euijun Choi, Sugyeong Eo
Title: Target Regeneration Shrinks the Gains of Draft-Training Objectives in Speculative Decoding
Abstract:
Speculative decoding accelerates large language models by verifying drafted tokens in parallel. New draft‑training objectives are usually credited with the acceptance they add over cross‑entropy on externally written responses, yet many pipelines let the target rewrite them. We ask how much of that gain survives. With a vision‑language target and a block drafter, we train three objectives on four versions of one corpus: cross‑entropy on corpus tokens, token‑level distillation from the target, and distillation gated to positions that would survive verification. Distillation and the gate add large gains on external responses, but after greedy regeneration, distillation adds a smaller gain and the gate little or none. The shrinkage persists across data orders, position weights, verifiers, decoding temperatures and, for distillation, initializations and learning rates. Most of it remains at matched supervised length and at each objective's best measured training length. A second vision corpus shows the shrinkage, as does a text‑only replication, for distillation also with an autoregressive drafter. Objective gains should therefore be measured against a target‑regenerated baseline and across training lengths. Our code is available at https://github.com/js‑lee‑AI/TargetRegeneration.

PaperId: 310, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28968.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Md Khalid Syfullah, Alvi Ataur Khalil
Title: Unit-Aware Differentially Private Quantum Machine Learning for Clinical and Wearable Health Data
Abstract:
Clinical registries and wearable sensors support early health‑risk assessment, yet models trained on these records may leak sensitive information when released. Differential privacy (DP) bounds this leakage by injecting noise whose total magnitude grows with the number of trainable parameters, a cost especially severe for small health cohorts. This motivates parameter efficient models including quantum machine learning (QML), whose variational circuits can represent complex decision boundaries with few trainable parameters. It raises a question: at matched input dimensionality and privacy budget, does a quantum model retain more utility than a classical one? We investigate this question on three clinical cohorts and one wearable cohort, treating each clinical record or participant as a privacy unit. We compare capacity‑matched quantum, multilayer perceptron, and logistic regression models across five privacy budgets and five seeds. The quantum model leads on three clinical cohorts by up to 0.104 ROC AUC averaged across budgets; however, trails on the wearable cohort, where the small number of participants requires substantial noise. No difference survives Holm correction across 24 tests, so these results indicate a trend rather than a quantum advantage. An analytic gradient bound shows that lower clipping thresholds can improve utility by reducing noise despite clipping bias. Finally, an experiment on IBM quantum computer (ibm_fez, a 156‑qubit superconducting processor) using eight fixed test cases yields mean absolute probability errors of 0.046 (private) and 0.063 (non‑private) relative to simulation, supporting the feasibility of inference on noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/TITANS‑Lab‑Artifacts/DP‑QML‑Health.

PaperId: 311, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28964.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Md Khalid Syfullah, Alvi Ataur Khalil
Title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?
Abstract:
As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault‑tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum‑enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision‑language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA‑OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4‑ and 8‑qubit basic‑ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum‑classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage‑points above classical full fine‑tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed‑forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum‑classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS‑Lab‑Artifacts/QuantumVLM.

PaperId: 312, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28958.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sergey Salishev, Zeev Volkovich, Oleg Granichin
Title: Transformers as Generic Deep Neural Networks: Exact Compilation, the Cost of Removing Activation-Activation Products, and Multi-Agent Attention Clustering
Abstract:
Transformers are deployed as a special model class. Neural processing units (NPU) add dedicated operators for attention and normalization, and quantization relies on Transformer‑specific algorithms. We show the computation does not force this. Every Transformer block, with attention, LayerNorm and a GELU MLP, compiles exactly into a generic deep neural network built from fixed affine maps, routing and the square, sigmoid and inverse square root, plus GELU or its sigmoid approximation. Without activation‑activation products, every transform‑wise compilation adds at least N^2 scalar nonlinear evaluations per head for dense scores. Keeping that one operation type removes this cost; its elementwise form, present on every surveyed NPU, suffices with the sigmoid and inverse square root. For top‑k attention with exchangeable tail scores, we prove that exact or conditional‑mean tail mass gives an unbiased, minimum‑mean‑square‑error estimate of the attention distribution, while tail drop is conditionally biased. When queries or agents cluster, centroids choose the keys first, reducing the number of computed scores from N^2 to Nk per head. On DeiT‑Tiny, MambaIRv2‑Light and Pythia‑70M the compiled models match their references with all keys, standard post‑training quantization applies, and the exact tail‑mass estimate beats tail dropping with half as many keys on DeiT‑Tiny and, for k\le8, on Pythia‑70M.

PaperId: 313, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28954.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Gonzalo Gómez-Nogales, Daohan Lu, Peiye Zhuang, Tinghui Zhou, Yi Zhou
Title: Pair-Free Coarse-to-Real Video Generation via Real-to-Coarse Image Supervision
Abstract:
Coarse‑to‑real (C2R) video generation converts coarse animation, simulation, or game‑rendered videos into photorealistic videos while preserving scene layout, camera motion, and dynamics. Training such models requires aligned (coarse, realistic) video pairs, which are expensive to create and confine prior systems to narrow synthetic domains. We exploit a simple asymmetry: paired videos are hard to obtain, but paired real‑to‑coarse images are easy to construct with existing editing and 3D reconstruction tools. Using these image pairs, we train the DINO‑R2C model to transfer realistic images to coarse images in DINO feature space, and apply it frame‑wise to ordinary real videos to synthesize pseudo‑coarse videos. The C2R# model then learns to generate each real video from its pseudo‑coarse counterpart, free from needing (coarse, realistic) video pairs. At inference, the DINO‑R2C model is discarded and actual coarse videos drive the C2R# model directly. Thus, our pair‑free training scales with any real‑video corpora rather than with paired synthetic videos. We will release the model and project webpage at https://gonzalognogales.github.io/coarse2real‑sharp/.

PaperId: 314, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28893.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Audrey Lee, Nathaniel Dennler, Ilia Sucholutsky, Andreea Bobu
Title: Flexible Language-Guided Representation Editing for Adaptive Robot Behavior
Abstract:
Trajectory demonstrations show robots how to behave but not why, leaving them to guess which features of the task actually matter. Incorrect guesses produce misaligned internal representations and lead to incorrect robot behaviors. Because task features are often semantically defined, we argue that natural language is better suited for specifying features rather than relying on demonstrations. Although existing representation editing methods have proposed using language to specify new features, only allowing additive edits produces feature sets that are often over‑specified or too narrowly scoped, especially in sequential editing tasks. We propose the Flexible Feature Editing Pipeline (FLEX), which uses language models to iteratively refine a robot's internal representation of task features from natural language corrections via three complementary operations: Add missing features, Generalize existing specific features, and Mask irrelevant features. We evaluate FLEX on 2D navigation scenarios, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation tasks, and a real‑world study using naturalistic human language corrections and real‑robot demonstrations. Comparisons against single‑operation and unscaffolded baselines show that all three operations are necessary in interactive scenarios, and that FLEX achieves consistently higher normalized reward compared to other feature editing approaches while maintaining compact, transferable representations. Project available at https://mit‑clear‑lab.github.io/FLEX/

PaperId: 315, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28891.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Anrui Gu, Zhichao Wang, Nicolai Ouporov
Title: Fig: Automated Multiagent Behavior Elicitor
Abstract:
Many social evaluations for multiagent systems study behaviors as they emerge from environments instead of systematically intervening in the environment to elicit such behaviors. We introduce Fig (Finding Interactions in Games), an agentic system that performs targeted elicitation interventions on game environments. It takes a natural language behavior description, decomposes it into sub‑behaviors, generates new social games or selects existing ones, and executes single or combined interventions to the games' engine, opponents, instructions, and context. To evaluate model behavior, it combines built‑in mechanical checks and synthetic rubric judgments. We validate the interventions, generated games, and evaluation mechanisms via human review. Models attempt the target behavior in 45.2% of episodes on average for valid scenarios generated by Fig for six test behaviors ‑‑ cooperation, exploitation, deception, covert coordination, betrayal, and sabotage. For game‑behavior pairs with available controls, Fig's interventions increase attempt rates by 10.9% on average compared to matched control games. Fig shows that multiagent environments can serve as programmable test beds for intentional, controllable, and reproducible behavior evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/fleet‑ai/fig.

PaperId: 316, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28880.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Matthew Strong, Ankush K. Dhawan, Julien Poffet, Giuse Pham, Jinho So, Monroe Kennedy
Title: Real2Sem2Real: 3D Semantic Augmentations for Robot Learning from a Single Human RGB Demonstration
Abstract:
Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects. We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), a real‑to‑semantic‑to‑real pipeline that turns one monocular RGB video of a human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across the semantic object instances of a category. R2Sem2R tracks the SE(3) pose of each object with DINOv3‑distilled Gaussian splats, outperforming existing methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth. R2Sem2R then aligns digital cousins, each generated from one or a few photographs, to the demonstrated objects with a semantic alignment. This alignment matches whole objects and the functional regions of target objects, such as a coffee machine's tray. R2Sem2R maps the human hand to a feasible robot grasp that extends to the cousins. Robot demonstrations are generated either in IsaacSim, for photorealistic rendering, or MuJoCo, for contact physics, and R2Sem2R can generate over 2,000 episodes in about two hours. On two real robots and four tasks, we train a vision‑language‑action policy on data from one human video per task, and policies trained on our data match or exceed policies trained on teleoperation across diverse object instances. The project page is available at https://real2sem2real.github.io/.

PaperId: 317, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28871.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Aur Shalev Merin
Title: How Much Gradient Does Truncated Backprop Lose in Looped Transformers?
Abstract:
Looped transformers reuse one block of layers many times and are often trained by backpropagating through only the last k loops. We measure how much of the weight gradient this throws away, exactly and for every k from one backward pass, on nine looped language models, and report three findings. First, on a trained model this lost gradient is set near the output: once the loop count is well above k, it barely changes with the loop count (within about 0.03 from 32 to 64 loops on the three models we tested, as a pre‑registered test predicted for Parcae). Where the backward signal shrinks, ρ^k, with ρ the signal's fitted shrink per loop, approximates it at moderate loop counts but overstates it at long ones, because the fitted ρ drifts up as the fit takes in more loops. On Ouro the signal grows, and keeping two of four loops still loses 81% of the final output's gradient. Second, the lost gradient falls during fine‑tuning, by 0.07‑0.22 within 300 steps on three of four models, on held‑out problems too. The fall is not just the read‑out's share of the gradient; training only the layers outside the loop reproduced up to half of it, and it also falls under truncated training. So a trained model's value overstates what truncation removes later. Third, we could not show that it predicts the training cost of truncation better than rules that need no measurement: on two new models it tied Parcae's cost at the same k, in a test too small to separate them.

PaperId: 318, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28859.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Eric Yocam, Varghese Vaidyan, Paris Kalathas
Title: AI Security Literacy: Ecosystem-based Competency Framework and K-12 Learning Platform
Abstract:
Adoption of artificial intelligence in K‑12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators. Existing AI‑literacy frameworks emphasize understanding and use; cybersecurity frameworks predate AI‑specific threats, and neither defines AI security literacy as a competency domain in its own right. We propose an AI Security Literacy (AISL) framework of six dimensions spanning the school ecosystem, ground its technical dimensions in public AI‑safety benchmarks and a reproducible multi‑seed adversarial evaluation, and ground its attitudinal dimensions in nationally representative survey micro‑data from U.S. teachers and adults. Only 34.5% of teachers report a school AI policy, and teachers see their own AI use as easing their work but students' use as complicating it; on the technical side, a reported robustness figure depends as much on the attack and the particular trained model as on the system evaluated. NeuralFortify, a browser‑based K‑12 platform built on real AI models, is presented as an illustrative operationalization.

PaperId: 319, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28855.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Gabriel Wedson Mendonça de Souza Veloso, Luan Borges Teodoro Reis Sena, Denis Oliveira Correa, Francisco Galuppo Azevedo
Title: Speedrunning Relational Foundation Model Pretraining
Abstract:
Progress on foundation model pretraining is gated by who can afford a trial, and relational pretraining is no exception. Recipes are developed inside individual labs, reported under private protocols, and do not accumulate. Speedrun leaderboards remove that barrier by decentralizing the search rather than the training run. The problem is fixed, the stack is open, entries are ranked by wall‑clock time to a quality target, and one GPU is enough to hold the record. We introduce modded‑nanoRT, the first such leaderboard for Relational Transformers. Which database to hold out decides whether the benchmark can resolve improvements at all, so we fix it by calibration, ranking six candidates by how sharply a 45‑minute learning curve separates improvement from seed noise. We open the leaderboard with typed trilinear attention, a relational operator that conditions attention scores and values on the foreign key traversed, together with Muon and SIGReg. The recipe reaches the target in 305.63 seconds on one NVIDIA H200, 8.11x faster than the reference implementation, and wins 13 of 15 pairs outside the development database. We will release the benchmark, its frozen artifacts, and the record runs. Our code is available at https://github.com/kunumi/nanoRT.

PaperId: 320, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28821.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zheng Qin, Junhua Xi, Yan Huang, Jiahong Lai, Anwen Huang, Qiong Li, Guangda Zhang, Kai Xu
Title: Register Anything Model for Generalizable and Robust Point Cloud Registration
Abstract:
We present Register Anything Model (RAM), a unified model for generalizable 3D point cloud registration that robustly estimates 6‑DoF transformations across diverse domains spanning sensors and environments. Existing registration methods are typically tailored to a single domain, with carefully tuned architectures and hyperparameters, and thus degrade markedly when applied to novel domains. We bridge this gap by training a single model on diverse data from indoor, outdoor, and object domains. A central challenge is the severe geometric discrepancy across domains, i.e., differences in scene scale, sensor noise, point density, and structural patterns, which hinders processing with a unified point‑based model. To address this, we introduce a geometry‑aware normalization strategy that jointly voxelizes and normalizes point clouds into a standardized geometric space, adaptively based on their geometric properties to preserve salient local structures while standardizing resolution. Built on this normalization, RAM follows a hierarchical coarse‑to‑fine paradigm, and employs an efficient geometric transformer that models local geometric consistency instead of globally over all points. This design mitigates discretization noise introduced by voxelization, and improves computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on 12 benchmarks demonstrate state‑of‑the‑art performance in terms of inlier ratio and registration recall. Notably, our method outperforms the counterparts trained on each separate domain, showing superior generalization capability.

PaperId: 321, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28814.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kaichen Zhou, Yuzhen Chen, Hannah Yao, Chonghe Jiang, Rao Fu, Xihang Yu, Wei Dai, Bashar Kabbarah, Haoyu Chen, Ishita Goluguri, Zhiyang Dou, Haonan Chen, Fangneng Zhan, Mengyu Wang, Wojciech Matusik, Antonio Torralba, Paul Pu Liang
Title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch
Abstract:
In contact‑rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan. Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task. We introduce T‑WLA, a world‑language‑action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction. At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base‑action generation. The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch. Future‑image and future‑pressure prediction provide training‑only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction. We evaluate T‑WLA on tactile‑conditioned hand‑motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real‑world dexterous manipulation tasks. T‑WLA reduces finger‑joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest reported baseline and achieves an average success rate of approximately 50.0% across real‑robot manipulation tasks. Videos and code are available at https://anonymous‑submission‑20.github.io/T‑WLA.github.io/.

PaperId: 322, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28811.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wendy Zheng, Liang Wu, Yinhan He, Mayank Darbari, Jundong Li, Liangjie Hong
Title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems
Abstract:
Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)‑based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time‑ and labor‑intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA).
