These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow‑up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference‑time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emphknows‑but‑won't‑say gap: models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emphgrafting, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground‑truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct‑prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.

PaperId: 323, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28810.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Pedro H. Barcha Correia, Matheus Azevedo de Sá, Paulo H. Gomes de Senna, Giovanni Mandel Martignago, Victor Takashi Hayashi, Charles Christian Miers, Marcos A. Simplicio
Title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise
Abstract:
The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross‑session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM‑as‑a‑service platforms, highlighting its real‑world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)‑connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared‑memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory‑injection.

PaperId: 324, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28806.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Piotr Keller, Fayyaz Minhas
Title: SAIL: A Learnable Generalisation of Spatial Autocorrelation over Graph-Structured Data
Abstract:
In vision and scientific domains involving spatial data, a key question is whether node feature values vary independently across space or form coherent spatial structures. Classical spatial autocorrelation statistics such as Moran's I and Geary's C quantify this phenomenon but operate on a single scalar variable with fixed neighbourhood weights, limiting their use for high‑dimensional graph‑like data. We introduce SAIL (Spatial Autocorrelation Index Learner), a differentiable framework that generalises spatial autocorrelation into a learnable operator by jointly learning feature projections defining candidate scalar fields and inter‑node neighbourhood affinities. SAIL produces interpretable local and global spatial coherence descriptors, enabling supervised prediction and unsupervised discovery of spatial autocorrelation modes and hotspots. We show that SAIL exactly recovers classical spatial statistics under appropriate parametrisations and, for tasks driven by latent spatial autocorrelation, can approximate the Bayes‑optimal predictor with an inductive bias matched to such tasks. Experiments on synthetic data and large‑scale biomedical graphs demonstrate statistical correctness and discovery of spatial coherence with applications across vision, geospatial analysis, and biomedicine. The code repository is available at: https://github.com/pkeller00/SAIL.

PaperId: 325, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28801.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Jiahan Li, Huangyuan Su, Shengbang Tong, Shusheng Yang, Ruihan Guo, Suozhi Huang, Hexu Zhao, Pratyusha Sharma, Sherry Yang, Jiatao Gu, Rob Fergus, Kyunghyun Cho
Title: JUICE: Unified Multimodal Modeling in Pretrained Representation Spaces
Abstract:
Most unified multimodal models treat images and text asymmetrically: a pretrained language model generates text, an attached diffusion head generates images, and outputs that contain both are produced in a fixed order, so the first output cannot adapt to the second. We ask whether both modalities can instead be generated by one process that is trained on them jointly from scratch. Pretrained encoder spaces hold both modalities in one continuous form and carry knowledge learned at scale, and recent work finds them effective as generative targets for vision and language. We therefore model the joint distribution directly in these spaces. We introduce JUICE (Joint Unified multimodal modeling In Continuous Encoder spaces), a single flow matching Transformer over frozen image and text representations, in which each modality has its own noise level. Which modalities are clean and which are generated then decides the task: image generation, captioning, visual question answering, or joint generation. Controlled pretraining runs test each design choice. At equal guidance, generating text as continuous states leaves image generation intact (48.41 GenEval, against 47.86 for a model trained only for text‑to‑image generation), while captions lose some exact wording. Training on joint and conditional denoising together beats either alone, and semantic encoder spaces beat VAE latents and raw pixels as targets. At 2.1B parameters, with no language model initialization and at 224x224, JUICE reaches up to 0.88 on GenEval and 73.1 on VQAv2. By sampling both modalities from the joint distribution (coupled sampling), it can also draw a route on a map while writing out the matching moves. On mazes with several valid solutions, joint success rises from 54.6% with independent sampling to 93.7%, and no modality has to go first. On visual spatial planning, JUICE solves 99.8% of maps at its training sizes.

PaperId: 326, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28771.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Vahid Hosseinzadeh, T. Anderson Keller, Michael Puthawala
Title: Motion Equivariant Convolutional LSTM: When Motion Becomes a Gauge Symmetry
Abstract:
Objects move, cameras pan, and weather drifts with the wind: much of what changes in sequential data is motion. Motion changes where things are, not what they are, and is therefore a symmetry of the data. Yet standard recurrent networks are not equivariant to it: their memory stays put while the input moves on. Flow equivariant recurrent networks first brought this symmetry into sequence models, for motions of constant velocity, or flows, by enumerating a bank of velocities. We extend this idea in three directions: from simple recurrent networks to convolutional LSTMs, from flows to motions whose velocity changes in time, and from enumerating velocities to estimating them. Treating a sequence as a field over time, we show that motion becomes a gauge symmetry: a global symmetry made local in time. Built on this view, our motion equivariant convolutional LSTM (MELSTM) uses its velocity model as the gauge field and is provably equivariant to every motion. Across future‑frame prediction, classification of digits visible only through their motion, and action recognition under camera shake, MELSTM outperforms a convolutional LSTM and its flow equivariant counterpart with the same number of parameters: it is more accurate, generalizes to longer horizons and to unseen motions, and carries a fraction of the flow equivariant model's state.

PaperId: 327, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28767.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Berke Arda, Peng Cui, Qiaoyuan Zheng, Rudolf Debelak, Mubashara Akhtar, Mrinmaya Sachan
Title: SkillEval: Learning Interpretable Ability Profiles of LLMs via Cognitive Diagnosis Models
Abstract:
Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score. This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets. To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross‑model, skill‑level analysis. The framework integrates advances from two areas: (1) it leverages the meta‑cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and (2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per‑skill abilities of LLMs. We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval). Compared to the traditional average‑based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items. We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks: (1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and (2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM. Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction‑tuned models differ from their base models.

PaperId: 328, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28763.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ming Zhong, Stacy Li, Nicholas Carlini, Matthew Jagielski
Title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
Abstract:
Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end‑to‑end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long‑horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in‑the‑wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML‑engineering tricks rather than research‑level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under‑utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug‑in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain‑relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real‑world ML‑for‑science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

PaperId: 329, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28711.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chuanmeng Bian, Daren Chen, Peixin Chen, Zhigao Chen, Chong Deng, Zhiyun Fan, Zhifu Gao, Bo Gong, Qing Gu, Jiajun He, Yawei Hu, Yunjie Ji, Wei Ju, Jingbei Li, Xiangang Li, Xu Li, Zengxi Li, Zheng Li, Chengdong Liang, Baiji Liu, Yaming Liu, Ying Liu, Bin Ma, Yiping Peng, Yuezhang Peng, Zhendong Peng, Yu Pu, Yang Shi, Xin Shu, Jian Tang, Biao Tian, Peiyao Wang, Tianzi Wang, Wen Wang, Wupeng Wang, Cheng Wen, Yuzhong Wu, Zijian Xia, Yunchong Xiao, Nan Yang, Jianwei Yu, Jixing Yu, Binbin Zhang, Lei Zhang, Sitong Zhao, Guangdong Zhou, Yuan Zhou, Jianheng Zhuo
Title: Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR Technical Report
Abstract:
We present Qwen‑Audio‑3.1‑ASR, a family of audio‑language models that builds upon its predecesor Qwen‑Audio‑3.0‑ASR with improved speech recognition and expanded capabilities in speaker‑diarized transcription and general audio understanding. The family retains support for 30 languages and 16 Chinese dialects, together with instruction‑controlled capabilities including historical‑context conditioning, hierarchical hotword customization, and native transcription polishing. Speaker‑diarized ASR produces structured outputs containing speaker labels, timestamps, and recognized text, maintaining consistent speaker labels across turns and the representation of overlapping speech. The general audio understanding capabilities cover audio‑, speech‑, and music‑captioning, temporal grounding and sound event detection, as well as audio question answering and multiple‑choice reasoning. These tasks broaden the application scope from recognizing spoken words to interpreting speakers, acoustic events, and their temporal relations. To accommodate different deployment requirements, the family includes variants for asynchronous file transcription, low‑latency streaming, interactive voice input, and non‑streaming recognition, with speaker‑diarized transcription and general audio understanding available in certain variants. Evaluations span conventional ASR, multilingual and dialectal speech, speaker‑diarized transcription, and general audio understanding, demonstrating the capabilities of the Qwen‑Audio‑3.1‑ASR family across transcription and broader audio analysis tasks.

PaperId: 330, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28673.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Amr Abdelkhalik
Title: How Far Can the Gemma 4 Speech Encoder Go Without Changing Its Weights? Saudi and Gulf Arabic Speech Recognition with a Frozen and an Adapter-Augmented Encoder
Abstract:
We study the 305M‑parameter audio encoder shared by Gemma 4 and EmbeddingGemma 2 (bit‑identical to that of Gemma 4 E2B except for the final audio‑embedding projection) for Saudi and Gulf Arabic speech recognition, without changing any of its pretrained weights; the adapters of our adapted system are additive and kept separate. A frozen system trains only a 22.6M‑parameter CTC reader over a learned mix of four intermediate encoder layers and the encoder output; an adapted system adds 3.1M low‑rank adapter parameters, a 41.5M‑parameter hybrid CTC/attention reader and joint decoding with a sub‑word language model. Against Cohere Transcribe Arabic (2.07B parameters), re‑run on identical audio, the frozen system trails in word error rate (WER) but is not significantly different in character error rate (CER) on five of six human‑labelled conditions, while running 3.4 times faster on CPU with greedy decoding. The adapted system is not significantly different in WER on a public Saudi customer‑service call (19.20% against 19.27%) and on clean Emirati speech, is significantly better on telephone‑coded Emirati speech, has a significantly lower CER on all six conditions of these sets, and beats a 0.6B recogniser fine‑tuned on SADA in WER on all six; it still trails Cohere in WER on long‑form Saudi speech. On a blind, human‑corrected public call‑centre sample it ranks 4 of 15 systems, behind three commercial APIs (significantly only one) and ahead of the other self‑hostable systems by point estimate. An optimised joint decoder runs it at 139 times real time on one GPU. We also find, on our data, that references made by correcting machine drafts favour the drafting system. Code and public‑set results are released.

PaperId: 331, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28667.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sion Israel Sion, Alain April
Title: Who Verifies the Builder? Toward Independent Assurance for Agent-Produced Software
Abstract:
Coding agents can now implement a specification, write and run tests, repair failures, and declare the result ready for release. When the same agentic system produces both the software and the evidence of its correctness, a passing test suite is no longer independent evidence: visible tests become an optimization target, code and tests may share one misinterpretation of the specification, and the builder's own tests may simply be incomplete. This paper argues that agent‑produced software requires an assurance plane that is structurally independent of the build plane. We characterize four gaps between stakeholder intent and production (requirement, conformance, evaluation, and model gaps) and identify which of them verification can close. We propose a framework that separates building from verifying, introduces a Verification Contract stating what must be demonstrated before release, and organizes verification in a specification‑first phase without access to the implementation and an implementation‑aware phase based on mutation analysis, property‑based testing, and fuzzing, with an assurance report that leaves the release decision to a human. We evaluate the framework in a pre‑registered study on three stateful services, two of them written by third‑party models, and an EvalPlus pilot. The builder's programs were correct, but its own tests missed subtle interactions: a verifier in a fresh context detected more of the 46 seeded faults than the builder's tests (Holm‑corrected p = 0.006) and surfaced the ambiguities of the specification, at the price of rare false oracles. A verifier from another provider did not add detection.

PaperId: 332, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28642.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haichao Zhang, Zhixuan Liang, Chong Zhang, Zixi Chen, Wen Wang, Jia Wang
Title: Controllable Generative Recommendation via Guided Token Refinement
Abstract:
Generative recommendation over discrete Semantic IDs has become a powerful paradigm for item retrieval. Real‑world systems, however, frequently require real‑time controllability to balance accuracy against objectives such as diversity. Existing autoregressive methods generate tokens strictly from left to right. This fixed direction locks in early decisions, preventing holistic planning and making control difficult. Consequently, direct interventions often break the semantic structure, producing non‑existent items. To address this, we propose ReGen, a framework that shifts from sequential decoding to parallel iterative refinement. ReGen reformulates generation as a mask‑filling task, predicting all tokens simultaneously rather than one by one. This global view allows us to apply control signals directly to tokens with high‑level semantics without retraining the model. To ensure that decoded candidates map to real items, we introduce a topology‑constrained tree that iteratively corrects low‑confidence predictions while strictly enforcing valid codebook paths during beam‑based inference. Experiments show that ReGen provides a favorable accuracy‑diversity trade‑off under moderate guidance while maintaining high validity of generated Semantic IDs. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zhang‑haichao/ReGen.

PaperId: 333, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28637.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dong Liu, Yanxuan Yu, Eric Jiang, Shu Wang, Ying Nian Wu
Title: To Keep or Not to Keep: Learning KV Cache Retention in Disaggregated LLM Serving Systems
Abstract:
Disaggregated \textscLLM serving separates prefill and decode across node pools, placing a network fabric between \textscKV‑cache computation and consumption. This breaks a key assumption of classical cache policies: a miss no longer incurs only local recomputation, but also network transfer to the decode node. Likewise, admitting a block to the global cache requires an additional transfer, so poor retention decisions waste both memory and bandwidth. We present KVLearn, a learning‑based framework for cost‑aware \textscKV‑cache retention in disaggregated serving. KVLearn includes: (i) a lightweight Prefix Reuse Predictor (\textscPRP) that estimates reuse probability from structural and temporal prefix features without modifying model weights; (ii) a Cost‑Aware Retention Score (\textscCARS) that converts reuse probability into keep/admit decisions using recomputation, transfer, and storage costs; and (iii) an Adaptive Threshold Controller (\textscATC) that adjusts admission thresholds online from observed hit rates and memory pressure. We integrate KVLearn into a globally disaggregated serving topology and evaluate it on text and multimodal workloads, including large image/video‑derived \textscKV blocks with heterogeneous reuse patterns. KVLearn reduces end‑to‑end time‑to‑first‑token by up to 56% versus No‑Cache, 38% versus LRU‑Pool, and 33% versus Mooncake‑style baselines, while cutting inter‑node \textscKV transfer volume by up to 53% versus LRU‑Pool. On MM‑Session, throughput remains within ～5% of oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/FastLM/KVLearn.

PaperId: 334, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28498.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Aur Shalev Merin
Title: Present but Hard to Read: Probing Latent Reasoning with Minimal Pairs
Abstract:
Probing studies of latent reasoning often read a model's state where the answer begins and take a failed probe as evidence that a value is absent. We test this with a digit copied from the question, in the looped model Ouro‑1.4B and the standard transformer Qwen 2.5‑1.5B. Comparing prompts that differ only in that digit shows it is present at the last prompt token, in a code shared across questions (readout about 0.9). A probe that sees one prompt at a time, the usual setting, barely reads it: 0.36 in Ouro and 0.19 in Qwen even after 5,249 training questions. The digit's change is small rather than crowded: random noise lands on equally busy directions, while a random word in its place moves the state far more and is readable. Since every varied token leaves a trace, a successful probe is ambiguous too. We give a protocol, including a synthetic null for generic mixing, for testing computed values against copies and mixtures of the inputs. In pre‑registered studies of two‑step problems it finds a small signal for the unwritten intermediate a+b just before Ouro writes the answer's last digit, and its sign follows the operation, though mixing alone produces much of that sign‑following part. Holding that value at another problem's from the first loop on does not move the written digit toward the other problem's, while the same patch of the answer does: the value is readable but not used.

PaperId: 335, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28490.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Changrui Zhu, Simon Julier
Title: Learning from Automatic 3D Gaussian Splatting Edits for Online Bayesian Scene Change Detection
Abstract:
Online scene change detection requires integrating incoming observations to determine which regions have changed relative to a reference scene. We update change beliefs as new images arrive using generalised Bayesian evidence fusion. However, the prior probability of change and evidence models are unknown beforehand, and numerical Bayesian inference can be costly. We address these challenges by learning offline from automatic edits to a reference 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. These edits generate labelled training views without manual annotations. Together with unchanged reference observations, they provide supervision for learning scene‑specific evidence models and estimating the effective pixel prior and response statistics. Online prediction combines current evidence with historical support, while closed‑form local Bayes factors, parameterized by the learned response statistics, update an accumulated 3D Gaussian field. Object‑guided refinement produces the final change masks. Our method achieves state‑of‑the‑art accuracy on PASLCD and CCS3D, with 67.64% and 75.82% mIoU, respectively. On PASLCD, the complete pipeline runs at 17.2\,FPS over complete query sequences, the fastest among the evaluated online methods. Project page: https://changruizhu96.github.io/work/lego‑scd/

PaperId: 336, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28474.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhizhuo Kou, Heming Li, Jian Yang, Junyu Luo, Jingshu Peng, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
Title: Answering in the User's Variety: Calibrated Accommodation Pairs for Post-Training
Abstract:
People adapt how they talk to the person in front of them. However, chat models tend to respond in Standard English regardless of the dialect used by the user. A uniform answer can hide whether training treats these users alike, and output audits cannot tell as well. We trace how each post‑training stage, from supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) to preference optimization (DPO) and reinforcement learning, changes a model's tendency to match the user, and read what each update prefers from two content‑matched replies, one matching the user and one not. Across 10 open model lineages, post‑training standardizes replies to every informal cue, yet after adjusting for how likely each reply already was, the DPO update still favours matching British and Australian spelling over AAE and Singlish on 10 lineages, and models still produce AAE features when asked. We then introduce calibrated accommodation pairs (CAP), preference data that reward matching users' dialect density while preserving Standard English for Standard‑English users. On a fully open model, CAP raises convergence on features it was not trained on without a detectable increase in dialect for Standard‑English users or a cost in instruction following. In contrast, one‑sided pairs reach a similar gain only by overshooting the user and imposing dialect. Our findings show that uniform replies can hide selective updates and audits should read the update as well as the output. Code: https://github.com/kouzhizhuo/cap‑accommodation.

PaperId: 337, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28470.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Daniel Marew, Sangjun Park, Nisal Perera, Donghyun Kim
Title: Fast Motion Retargeting Pipeline for Scalable Humanoid Robot Learning
Abstract:
While large‑scale human motion capture datasets provide a rich source of demonstrations for humanoid robot learning, retargeting the diverse motions to different humanoid robots remains a nontrivial challenge. Existing kinodynamic trajectory optimization pipelines are computationally expensive and often require manual adjustments per motion. We present FRDV (Fast Retargeting with Dynamics Validation), a scalable framework consisting of rapid constrained kinematic retargeting and an additional dynamics validation pipeline. Its kinematic stage integrates a custom Sequential Quadratic Programming solver, Real‑Time Iteration, and parallel chunk‑based processing, achieving up to 9,156 frames per second, approximately up to 136 times faster than GMR and ProtoMotions, while robot‑specific constraints are incorporated into the optimization to reduce common retargeting artifacts, such as ground penetration and self‑collision. For motions requiring additional verification, a contact implicit iLQR controller is utilized to test the retargeted reference under full rigid body dynamics. This dynamics‑based validation identifies dynamically infeasible motions and refines contact‑related artifacts such as foot floating and foot skating. We evaluate retargeting quality by training motion tracking reinforcement learning policies using several state‑of‑the‑art pipelines and comparing their tracking fidelity and success rates. Furthermore, sim‑to‑real transfer is demonstrated on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Videos and code are available at: https://daroslab.github.io/frdv/.

PaperId: 338, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28465.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Raúl Castilla-Arquillo, Miguel Olivares-Mendez
Title: MARE: An Open-Source Lunar Rover Simulator with Shadow Ground Truth for Perception and Autonomy
Abstract:
Lunar surface exploration increasingly relies on autonomous rovers that must perceive and traverse unstructured terrain under extreme illumination conditions. Near the lunar poles, low sun elevations produce long, high‑contrast shadows that challenge stereo vision, terrain segmentation, and localization. Developing perception and navigation algorithms for these conditions requires large amounts of sensor data with accurate ground truth, which field campaigns and analog facilities can only provide at high cost and with limited variety. This paper presents MARE (Modular Autonomy and Rendering Environment), an open‑source simulation suite for lunar rover perception and autonomy built on Unreal Engine 5 and ROS 2. MARE consists of three integrated components. Terrain Studio generates cratered and rocky lunar Digital Elevation Maps (DEMs) to build simulation scenes. A dedicated Unreal Engine project hosts two physics‑based rovers with plugins for stereo, lidar, event, and Single‑Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) cameras, streaming time‑stamped sensor data and pixel‑accurate ground truth. Lastly, a Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) stack provides web‑based mission control. Validation shows a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.79 between predicted and rendered shadows at low sun elevations, and stereo depth analysis verifies decreased pixel coverage in shadowed regions relative to sunlit terrain.

PaperId: 339, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28458.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kartik Tandon, Alessio Borgi, Pavel Snopov, Inés García-Redondo, Davide D'Ascenzo, Sebastiano Cultrera di Montesano, Fabrizio Silvestri, Pietro Liò, Francesca Dominici, Randall Balestriero, Claudio Battiloro
Title: LocaLeJEPA: Maximum Entropy Representations under Geometric Priors
Abstract:
Joint‑Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) offer an appealing approach to self‑supervised learning, but are typically prone to representation collapse. LeJEPA resolves this by introducing a theoretically grounded distribution‑matching objective that drives the embedding towards an isotropic Gaussian. However, this approach is fundamentally tied to Euclidean assumptions, and its global target does not reflect domain‑specific geometric priors, such as the use of non‑Euclidean embedding geometries, e.g., equivariant CNNs or hyperbolic ViTs. We thus introduce LocaLeJEPA, a framework motivated by a manifold‑theoretic reformulation of LeJEPA's entropy‑maximization property. The accompanying LocaLeReg, a novel locally Euclidean distribution‑matching regularizer, enables a stable and scalable implementation of the LocaLeJEPA framework. We then perform extensive experiments in the vision setting on models trained on ImageNet‑1K. LocaLeJEPA significantly outperforms LeJEPA when paired with hyperbolic ViT‑S/8 and equivariant ResNet‑50 backbones, and also with ordinary Euclidean ViT‑S/8 and ViT‑L/14 backbones. This holds both in terms of linear and k‑NN classification performance on ImageNet and on a series of downstream tasks tested. We view the LocaLeJEPA formalism as a principled approach to the JEPA paradigm that better respects intrinsic data geometry while also accommodating generalizations to exotic embedding geometries. Code available at https://github.com/alessioborgi/LocaLeJEPA.

PaperId: 340, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28454.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhenwei Tang, Di Bai, Jintao Liu, Xidong Wu, Qianfeng Wen, Xinwu Cheng
Title: Toolflation: Seller Agents Distort Tool Markets Through Spontaneous Generative Engine Optimization
Abstract:
Agents are starting to sell to other agents. Seller agents write the listings of tools, services and products, and buyer agents read these listings when they choose what to use. We show that seller agents told only to be selected more often practice generative engine optimization on their own, and that this distorts the market for sellers and for buyers. We build tool markets from real data tools on Amazon and Instagram and run every tool on every question, so we know which tools can answer each question. Under all five production models we test, sellers rewrite their descriptions to claim more and more fields, including fields that their tools return for fewer than half of the targets. We call this process toolflation. Nothing in the market limits it, and how far it goes depends on the model, as the number of claims that contradict the sellers' own evidence differs by an order of magnitude between models. Toolflation shifts the buyers' choices between sellers, and the most capable tool loses share in seven of the ten combinations of seller model and platform. Under four models, the choices stay with capable tools and buyer agents keep their task success. Under the fifth, sellers copy one another until the descriptions no longer tell the tools apart. Buyer agents then pick tools by their position in the list, tools that answer almost nothing win a quarter to two fifths of the choices, and task success falls from 89% to about 30% on Amazon, close to random choice, and from 77% to 40% on Instagram. The sellers did only what their vendors asked, and the cost fell on buyers they never dealt with. We therefore argue that honesty toward third parties under competition is part of safety alignment, and that models should be tested as sellers before they are deployed as sellers.

PaperId: 341, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28452.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Nikita Ganziuk, Innokentiy S. Humonen, Ilya Makarov, Pavel Lebedev
Title: MythoSemantic: An Interactive System for Discovering Semantic Parallels Across Mythological and Religious Traditions
Abstract:
We present a tool for the comparative study of mythological and religious texts. Traditional manual analysis is highly labor‑intensive and difficult to scale. To address this, we use neural language models to embed texts into a shared semantic space, so that users can find semantic parallels across cultural traditions in an interactive interface. Embedded fragments form distinct semantic structures whose coarse geometry aligns with well‑documented historical relations between traditions. We quantify how much of that geometry is already explained by lexical overlap and by proper names. The current system is available at https://mythoscope.io, and the installable package is available at https://github.com/haafus/MythoSemantic/blob/main/RUN.md.

PaperId: 342, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28444.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaoxing Hu, Wenxi Yao, Chaoyuan Shi, Ziqi Ye, Xiaorong Guo, Peixuan Li, Zhuoran Sun, Ziyang Gong, Peiyuan Zhang, Mingxin Liu, Shuran Ma, Hongbo Liu, Xiaomin Yu, Yu Tian, Wentao Wang, Zhenjie Yang, Jian Hu, Yunhang Shen, Haoyu Cao, Xue Yang
Title: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning
Abstract:
Omni LLMs can naturally locate key audio and visual evidence and integrate information across modalities for audiovisual reasoning. Existing audio‑visual reasoning benchmarks that mainly rely on multiple‑choice questions usually score models solely based on answer correctness, making it difficult to assess whether a model truly forms a reasoning chain from evidence to the correct answer. In addition, textual or unimodal shortcuts may allow models to answer correctly without analyzing the necessary audio‑visual evidence, further weakening the reliability of evaluation benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce EvaOmni, an evidence‑grounded benchmark containing 392 videos and 1,027 purely human‑annotated question‑answer pairs, covering 15 capabilities and three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. We design a series of rigorous annotation procedures in which experts annotate audio and visual evidence and construct video‑based distractors; humans review whether questions meet strict inspection criteria, and finally models filter textual and unimodal shortcuts. Beyond high‑quality question‑answer pairs, we require models to simultaneously return the answer and supporting evidence intervals in order to evaluate the complete reasoning chain. We propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies, and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality; both are incorporated into answer correctness. Across 7 open‑weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs, Gemini3.7‑Flash achieved the highest overall accuracy (79.4%), C.G. (70.8%), and B.G. (35.1%). At Level 3, it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. These results show that even the most advanced models still have room for development in grounded audio‑visual reasoning.

PaperId: 343, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28441.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sahil Joshi, Prithvi Dixit, Aryan Katiyar, Agniva Chowdhury, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Anshumali Shrivastava, Aditya Desai, Kumar Krishna Agrawal
Title: Stratified Sparse Attention: Reducing the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity
Abstract:
Large Language Model inference over long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by the cost of attending to a growing Key‑Value (KV) cache. Sparse attention reduces this cost by accessing only a fraction of the cache, but existing methods face a trade‑off between deterministic retrieval, which captures high‑scoring tokens but discards residual attention mass, and sampling, which improves coverage at the cost of higher variance. Hybrid methods combine top‑k retrieval with uniform sampling, yet still exhibit a substantial gap from dense attention at aggressive sparsity. We introduce \emphStratified Sparse Attention (SSA), a unified framework combining deterministic retrieval with score‑guided sampling. SSA deterministically attends to high‑scoring tokens while sampling the residual using proxy attention scores and correcting for their inclusion probabilities, thereby recovering attention mass beyond the retrieval set. SSA encompasses top‑k, top‑p, and hybrid top‑k+sampling as special cases. Across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME, and five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters, SSA consistently improves over the baselines at matched sparsity. On RULER‑HARD with Ministral‑3‑8B, SSA improves accuracy over the strongest practical baseline from 81.8% to 84.2% at 32K and from 63.8% to 69.3% at 128K under 50× attention sparsity, recovering 94% and 85% of dense‑attention performance, respectively. With optimized CUDA kernels, SSA achieves up to 2.96× decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M context, demonstrating that its accuracy gains translate into practical long‑context inference acceleration. We open‑source our code at https://github.com/skylight‑org/SSA‑Paper‑Code.

PaperId: 344, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28435.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhuchenyang Liu, Yao Zhang, Yu Xiao
Title: Multimodal Reranking Is a System One Decision
Abstract:
Multimodal rerankers are usually dedicated models: a vision‑language model (VLM) is trained on retrieval data to score the candidates of a query. Scoring options is not specific to reranking. System One decision models such as Jev map a state and a typed question to one probability per option without generating text, and general models can make such decisions with little or no training. Reranking is one such decision, with the query and its candidates as the state and the candidates as the options. We therefore argue that a general VLM can serve as a multimodal reranker through System One decisions, and that decision tuning can improve its reranking. We ask a VLM one choice question over the top 16 candidates of a first‑stage retriever and rank the candidates by the probabilities of their labels, read from one forward pass. On MMEB‑V2 image retrieval, this choice scores 5.4 to 7.3 hit@1 above a yes/no question per candidate, and the yes/no question falls below the first stage. With the choice, zero‑shot Qwen3.8‑27B beats the supervised Qwen3‑VL‑Reranker‑2B on all three benchmarks and comes within 1.6 points of Reranker‑8B on each. It matches Reranker‑8B on MMEB‑V2 visual documents (84.79 vs. 84.78 nDCG@5), at 1.1 to 1.5 times its latency. JEV‑27B‑VL, the same backbone tuned on text decisions only, improves page reranking by 0.6 to 1.1 points, with gains on most tasks (sign test, p <= 0.017), and leaves natural images unchanged. The zero‑shot model is larger than the supervised rerankers and of a newer generation, so these comparisons are confounded; we discuss this and other alternative views, and the experiments that would test the position.

PaperId: 345, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28423.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Junyuan Deng, Xinyi Wu, Zhenyao Wu, Song Wang, Yu Wang, Congchao Zhu
Title: WorldSR: Harnessing World Knowledge Search for Grounded Image Super-Resolution
Abstract:
Generative‑prior‑based super‑resolution (SR) methods leverage implicit knowledge learned from large‑scale models to enhance low‑resolution inputs. However, such priors are inherently stochastic and optimized for diverse generation, conflicting with the deterministic, high‑fidelity reconstruction required for SR. It is also tied to the base model, costly to update, and prone to hallucinations as real‑world data evolves. To address these limitations, we introduce WorldSR, a novel framework that augments SR with explicit, entity‑aligned visual world knowledge. WorldSR automatically decomposes the input into semantic entities and performs entity‑wise retrieval of structurally and semantically aligned images from a large‑scale external corpus. For efficiency and reliability, we incorporate a memory mechanism to reuse previously retrieved results and a multi‑step filtering process to refine candidate references. The selected references as world knowledge are then integrated through a novel multi‑reference super‑resolution model, which provides fine‑grained constraints for detail synthesis and structural recovery. Experiments on real‑world SR benchmarks show that WorldSR consistently improves structural fidelity and visual quality, outperforming existing generative super‑resolution methods. Our results suggest that entity‑level grounding in external visual world knowledge provides a simple and effective complement to model‑bound generative priors.

PaperId: 346, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28411.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Spiros Maggioros, Guray Erus, Gareth Harman, George Aidinis, Alexander Getka, Aristeidis Sotiras, Christos Davatzikos
Title: Brain2Vec: A Self-Supervised 3D Foundation Model for Structural Brain MRI
Abstract:
Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end‑to‑end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre‑trained on 74,425 T1‑weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine‑tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine‑tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state‑of‑the‑art foundation model pre‑trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region‑specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open‑source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.

PaperId: 347, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28393.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jinghui Zhang, Lang Gao, Zongfang Liu, Ruihong Zeng, Zirui Song, Rui Yan, Kentaro Inui, Xiuying Chen
Title: When Copying Is Hard: Copy-Constrained Decoding for Exact Span Reproduction
Abstract:
Precisely reproducing a target span verbatim within a long context is a fundamental capability test for LLMs: even when the target string is present in context, models often still drift within the span or fail to stop correctly, revealing limitations in source grounding and boundary control. This capability has broad practical relevance. For instance, code generation often requires embedding sensitive strings such as API keys exactly as they appear in context. In this work, we construct a benchmark to test exact span reproduction ability across contracts, scientific literature, code, and random sequences, and find that current models still make surprisingly frequent errors. To address this, we propose CopyGen, a lightweight copy‑constrained plugin for frozen LLMs that turns copying from a byproduct of next‑token prediction into a controlled process. Our key idea is to decompose copying into three distinct decisions: when to copy, how far to copy, and when to stop. Concretely, CopyGen first determines whether to enter copy mode, then predicts a tentative copy length, and finally verifies the generated span token by token. During verification, we adaptively adjust the logits of copy continuation tokens to incentivize or suppress continuation, and emit only the longest valid prefix. Across three LLM backbones and four benchmark tasks, CopyGen improves average exact match by 35% relative without model finetuning, and integrates seamlessly with SFT to further improve it by 4%, while substantially accelerating generation. These results suggest that reliable exact copying is not something LLMs obtain for free, but a decoding‑time control problem that requires explicit modeling. Code is available at https://github.com/mbzuai‑nlp/CopyGen.

PaperId: 348, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28386.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiawei Wang, Yucun Li, Xueqi Li, Shenghao Wang, Xinquan Gong, Dan Zhang, Zheqi Lv, Yuquan Le, Shaozu Yuan, An Zhang, Da Cao, Tat-Seng Chua
Title: VisualEvolve: A Skill Self-Evolution Framework for Visual Reasoning
Abstract:
Visual tool use enables vision‑language models (VLMs) to acquire task‑relevant evidence, but its effectiveness can be limited by predefined visual operations and the tool‑use strategies learned during training. Representing these operations and strategies as reusable external skills allows them to be refined through self‑evolution without updating model parameters. However, skill refinement can introduce performance regressions. Meanwhile, inspecting accumulated task execution trajectories together with skill evolution history may lead to evolution evidence overload. To address these challenges, we propose VisualEvolve, a self‑evolving framework that evolves executable visual operations and tool‑use strategies for VLMs through a Select‑‑Execute‑‑Evolve‑‑Evaluate cycle. Skill‑Library Snapshot Selection uses performance on a fixed validation set disjoint from execution tasks to select an effective historical snapshot for subsequent evolution, limiting the propagation of performance regressions. Progressive Evidence Access (PEA) guides capability‑gap diagnosis through a coarse‑to‑fine hierarchy comprising the Skill‑Performance Report, Evolution Log, Trajectory Summaries, and relevant raw trajectory segments. Across four VLM backbones and six evaluation sets from three benchmarks, VisualEvolve improves over the Initial Skill Library in 23 of 24 settings, with a maximum gain of 15.1 percentage points on VisualProbe Hard using Qwen3.5‑Plus. Ablation studies support the contributions of Snapshot Selection and PEA, while further experiments show that skills can be improved using experience from different data settings and directly reused across backbones. Moreover, VisualEvolve enables effective skill self‑evolution with over an order of magnitude fewer task‑solving trajectories than estimated for representative RL‑based methods.

PaperId: 349, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28361.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zijun Dou, Kun Luo, Chaofan Li, Shuqi Lu, Zheng Liu
Title: FALCA: Falsification-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Deep Search Agents
Abstract:
Long‑horizon deep search requires LLM agents to iteratively decompose complex information needs, gather evidence from external sources, and maintain a reliable research state under multiple constraints. A central challenge is that early mistakes can be amplified over the search trajectory: agents may anchor on an incorrect candidate, collect partially supporting evidence, overlook contradictions, and accumulate errors that misguide subsequent reasoning. We propose FALCA, a falsification‑aware framework that formulates deep search as a propose‑falsify process. FALCA adopts a collaborative Searcher‑Falsifier architecture, where the Searcher proposes candidate answers or sub‑answers, while independent Falsifiers actively seek counterevidence, check unmet constraints, identify conflicts, and produce concise falsification reports for research‑state revision. To strengthen this loop, we introduce falsification‑aware training, combining SFT warmup on falsification trajectories with agentic RL based on parallel rollouts and hierarchical credit assignment over research stages, state transitions, and actions. Experiments on five search benchmarks show that FALCA improves long‑horizon deep search performance over backbone and harness ablations, while reducing confirmation bias and error accumulation through more effective falsification and research‑state revision.

PaperId: 350, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28355.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianyu Wu, Zhuohan Wang, Jonathan Geuter, Yu Yao, Weifan Jiang, Chengxi Zhang, Ju Li, Minlan Yu
Title: Beyond the Point Mass: Acceptance-Derived Weights and Distributional Losses for Speculative Decoding
Abstract:
In speculative decoding, a lightweight draft model proposes tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, speeding up generation without changing the target distribution. D‑PACE (Wu et al., 2026) trains such drafters with a loss that weights each position by its contribution to the expected accepted length. Both its weights and its cross‑entropy (CE) loss use only the draft's probability of the recorded target token, treating the target as a point mass. Under rejection sampling, however, a sampled draft token is accepted with probability equal to the overlap of the draft and target distributions, one minus their total variation (TV). We derive D‑PAL (Dynamic Position‑wise Acceptance Loss) from the exact expected accepted length, using this overlap as the acceptance signal. This yields overlap‑based position weights with log acceptance (LA) as the per‑position loss, and the objective reduces to D‑PACE for a point‑mass target. Since the weights are detached, any per‑position loss can replace LA in practice. We show that forward KL divergence and Rényi divergence of order 1/2 match or exceed LA, and that Rényi‑1/2 provably bounds the true acceptance rate from above and below. Replacing CE with Rényi‑1/2 improves acceptance length under both D‑PACE's weights and ours. On six benchmarks with a Qwen3‑4B target, D‑PAL raises mean acceptance length over D‑PACE from 4.50 to 4.57 at T=0 and from 4.20 to 4.28 at T=1, and consistently achieves higher throughput at both temperatures.

PaperId: 351, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28350.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sumaiya Fazal, Rizwan Qureshi, Laleh Behjat, Samira Ebrahimi Kahou
Title: Gated Prototype Transfer for Zero-Support Medical Vision Language Model
Abstract:
Realistic few‑shot adaptation of medical vision‑language models (VLMs) can leave low‑prevalence classes without any labeled support. The training‑free SS‑ Text+ solver remains operational in this setting, but its zero‑support prototypes receive no visual adaptation and fall back to a purely textual class prototype. We in‑ troduce Gated Knowledge‑Guided Prototype Transfer (GProtoT), a pre‑repulsion module that transfers supported‑class visual residuals to missing classes using VLM similarity and an ontology‑based clinical distance. A validation‑free evidence gate scales transfer based on semantic relevance and residual agreement, thereby limiting unsupported extrapolation. In 50 paired realistic one‑shot trials on MESSIDOR with FLAIR features, severe and proliferative diabetic retinopathy were absent from every support set. Relative to SS‑Text+, gated ProtoT improved missing‑class recall by 5.23 points, average class accuracy by 1.37 points, and the missing/supported recall harmonic mean by 1.83 points. It reduced negative‑ transfer frequency from 46‑48% for ungated transfer to 2%, while at the cost of reductions of 1.20 percentage points in supported‑class recall and 0.45 percentage points in top‑1 accuracy. These results indicate that evidence‑based gating provides a safety mechanism for the knowledge source. GProtoT is based on SS‑ Text+ and requires no gradients, validation data, or additional model inference, of‑ fering a low‑compute path toward accountable adaptation under incomplete clini‑ cal supervision. Code is available: https://github.com/sumaiyaafridi/GProtoT

PaperId: 352, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28340.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Atharva Thakur, Abulhair Saparov, Bruno Ribeiro
Title: DeclineCraft: A RAG Abstention Benchmark for Jointly Measuring Combined Retrieval and Parametric Knowledge
Abstract:
Reliable retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) requires recognizing when neither retrieved documents nor parametric knowledge supports an answer. We introduce DeclineCraft, a dynamic abstention benchmark whose unanswerable questions target Minecraft feature additions after a corpus cut‑off, with audits of possible parametric exposure. Later cut‑offs support evaluation of future models. Across 27 LLMs, we measure Correct Abstention Rate (CAR; how often models acknowledge insufficient knowledge on unanswerable questions), Answerable Attempt Rate and Answer Accuracy. We find that (1) single‑shot retrieval significantly raises CAR in 38 of 40 configurations (model and thinking setting) versus no retrieval. (2) Iterative RAG, in which the model self‑assesses its context and can request up to two further retrieval rounds, significantly lowers CAR versus single‑shot RAG in 30 of 40 configurations (mean 46.4%), with little change in Answer Accuracy (68.5% to 69.3%). Adding query rewriting and reranking to hybrid (dense & sparse) retrieval lowers CAR for all 12 models tested. (3) Larger models answer more accurately (Spearman ρ= +0.60 with total parameters), but neither model size nor release date shows a significant association with CAR. (4) Without retrieval, enabling thinking on the same weights lowers CAR significantly for 8 of 13 models (by 14% points on average), and the responses shift from acknowledged uncertainty to premise denial.

PaperId: 353, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28316.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Aymen Lassoued, Angelique Loesch, Romaric Audigier
Title: ABACUS: A Benchmark for Image Editing Models to Assess Object Category and Counting Under Scene Conservation
Abstract:
Instruction‑based image editing models can now add, remove a specified number of objects or change their category while preserving the scene. Yet these models often fail to produce the correct number, and these failures grow sharply as scenes become more complex and the requested count increases. Current benchmarks largely miss this problem: they score edits with holistic similarity metrics or with vision‑language model (VLM) judges that are themselves poor at counting, so numerical errors go unnoticed or are graded incorrectly. As a result, the true numerical ability of today's editing models has never been accurately measured. We address this issue with ABACUS, a new benchmark, evaluation protocol and dedicated scoring metric for numerical image editing. Our protocol is judge‑free: no VLM or MLLM scores an edit or counts objects (a VLM only confirms the category of rare ambiguous crops). Instead, it verifies each edit at the instance level against panoptic ground truth confirmed by detector consensus, checking both that the exact requested count was achieved and that the rest of the scene was preserved, across the add, remove and change operations. By evaluating leading image editors, our method reveals substantial numerical editing failures that worsen with increasing scene complexity and object count; failures that prior benchmarks often overlooked or misjudged.

PaperId: 354, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28303.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianyi Lorena Yan, John Hewitt
Title: Reward Misspecification Degrades Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
Abstract:
Monitoring the chain‑of‑thought (CoT) of language models (LMs) is a key strategy for detecting and preventing misbehaviors for AI safety. As such, it is critical to identify reinforcement learning (RL) practices that lead to unmonitorable chain‑of‑thought. One such practice may be unavoidable: reward misspecification. As RL environments become more complex, it is infeasible to have perfect verification, and models are rewarded for behaviors that are different from the true task intent. We show that reward misspecification alone already degrades monitorability. We create a testbed with pairs of true reward aligned with task intent and misspecified rewards that favor a different behavior, so that reward hacking can be induced by training and labeled verifiably. Across three models and three tasks, CoT monitorability remains low as models' hack rates increase: the CoTs keep reasoning about the task intent while the outputs violate the intent and get rewarded. To mitigate unmonitorability without prior knowledge of the true reward or the hack, we collect rollouts with diverse rewards across training steps and use a LM to infer a reward description. We then inject the description into the input, which teaches the model to verbalize the reward. This reward description training improves monitorability by an average of 24% or 42% absolute, depending on the metric, across all models and tasks, and yields CoTs that reason about the misspecified reward explicitly. Code is available at https://github.com/Lorenayannnnn/reward‑misspecification‑degrades‑cot‑monitorability.

PaperId: 355, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28294.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ahsan Bilal, Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin, Muhammad Umer, Ayesha Mohsin, Sarmad Bilal, Dean F. Hougen
Title: Adaptive Replay Refinement: Allocating Test-Time Compute Between Revision and Resampling
Abstract:
Test‑time scaling allocates additional inference compute to refining existing solutions or generating new ones. This raises a fundamental question: Should I keep improving this solution, or stop working on it and try a completely new solution? Existing methods make this decision using fixed refinement schedules, self‑verification judgments, or learned controllers, which can waste compute or rely on signals that may be incorrect or require additional training. We introduce Adaptive Replay Refinement (ARR), a training‑free method that detects when a stationary revision reaches a fixed point and reallocates the released compute to a new independent sample; replay decoding treats the current solution as a draft and verifies unchanged tokens in parallel, enabling efficient fixed‑point detection. Across seven models from five families and seven benchmarks, ARR matches majority voting on three of five mathematical reasoning benchmarks at equal compute, while reducing critical‑path serial passes by up to 2.4 times. On MATH500, ARR achieves 84.6% accuracy with only 41% of the serial passes required by majority voting. These results demonstrate that detecting refinement exhaustion enables adaptive reallocation from revision to independent sampling, improving inference efficiency while highlighting the limits of self‑revision. Code is available at https://github.com/AhsanBilal7/adaptive_refine.

PaperId: 356, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28286.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ivan Ilin, Peter Richtárik
Title: Local Work, Global Progress: A Convergence Theory of AI Agent Collaboration
Abstract:
Teams of large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to complex tasks, but their collaboration protocols are mostly designed empirically, without convergence guarantees. We formalize collaborative problem solving as block optimization: each agent improves one part of a shared solution, guided by its local objective plus a correction for how its changes affect the other parts. A coordinator checks every proposal against the global objective and merges proposals that do not interfere with each other. We prove linear convergence up to an error floor that vanishes when the corrections are exact. Interfering proposals can also be merged once their combination has been checked; the rate then depends on how well the proposals actually combine, not on worst‑case interactions. With GPT‑OSS‑120B agents on robot routing, a three‑agent team finds collision‑free plans in every run, better than those of a single agent that controls all robots. On a larger routing task, a six‑agent team completes its search about twice as fast as the single agent (in median). Merging the best checked combination of proposals, rather than only proposals that do not interfere, cuts the team's search time by about 30%. With constants measured on the runs, our convergence bound holds in every round and follows the observed progress. We also test the theory on query planning in SQLite and on a synthetic task.

PaperId: 357, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28284.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Huachen Gao, Yang Yang, Xiaoqian Liang, Xingyu Chen, Youjia Zhang, Qi Zhang, Baorui Ma, Anpei Chen, Wei Yang
Title: HRoPE: Homography Relative Positional Encoding
Abstract:
Geometric Relative Positional Encoding has become the primary mechanism for injecting spatial inductive biases into multi‑view transformers. Existing designs condition attention on camera‑level frustums or ray‑marched depth, associating cross‑view tokens through the sensor geometry. Such sensor‑centric formulations, however, describe only where a token is observed from, leaving the rich surface geometry of the scene region depicted by the token. In this paper, we advocate a shift toward surface‑aware positional encoding that explicitly grounds patch tokens in the geometry of physical surfaces. We introduce HRoPE, which represents the local geometry of each patch as a slanted 3D plane, following the slanted support‑window assumption of classical multi‑view stereo. We inject token‑level, plane‑induced homographies into attention as relative transformations. This equips the transformer with a geometric prior for rectifying perspective distortions and aligning patch features across viewpoints. Our encoding requires no ground‑truth geometry: the plane parameters can be predicted end‑to‑end under a view‑synthesis objective alone, or derived from foundation models. Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, and DL3DV show that our best variant of HRoPE consistently outperforms the evaluated geometric positional encodings for novel view synthesis. Extensive ablations and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed encoding. Please refer to our project page at: https://gaohchen.github.io/HRoPE

PaperId: 358, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28281.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tapan Parikh
Title: Forty Questions: Identifying a Language Model from One-Word Answers
Abstract:
A model behind an API can be identified from its one‑word answers to everyday questions such as "Name a sound" or "Name a poet". A model's profile records how often it gives each answer to each question. We attribute new answers to the model most likely to have given them. On a panel of 94 models, 40 answers identify the exact model 92.5% of the time, against 1.1% by chance. Profiles built through OpenRouter identified all ten models served by DeepInfra under blinded labels. A system prompt lowers accuracy by 6 to 16 points. We applied the method to 96 endpoints of 13 open models on OpenRouter, and 92 identify as the model they claim. Of the other four, one matches the claimed model with reasoning turned off. One serves Gemma 4 under the name Llama 4 Maverick: it names itself Gemma 4, and it is billed Gemma 4's token counts on every message. Two remain unresolved. Billing records also show context added to first‑party models. Grok 4.7 is billed 1,247 input tokens for a one‑line question that costs GPT‑4o only 12 tokens, and five models state the current date without being billed for it. The questions come from a public census of model defaults, and the method costs cents per endpoint.

PaperId: 359, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28280.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chucheng Xiang, Runze Wang, Zhi Deng, Ruchao Bao, Yuanwei Zhang, Yuxuan Xie, Hanliu Wang, Liangzhen Fei, Wenzheng Wu, Cheng Wan, Peifeng Li, Zhongyuan Liu, Ligang Liu
Title: GALA: Geometry-Aware Language Model for Controllable Object Arrangement
Abstract:
Reasoning about fine‑grained placement constraints, such as support and containment, is essential for realistic 3D scene creation. It remains a significant challenge for existing methods that rely on simplified object representations like oriented bounding box (OBB), which are blind to the detailed geometry. To address this limitation, we introduce GALA, a geometry‑aware language model with explicit point cloud perception for controllable object placement. Our model performs autoregressively by predicting the 6D pose of one target object at a time conditioned on the scene context and placement instruction. We utilize a two‑stage training strategy: the first stage aligns geometric and textual modalities through pretraining tasks, and the second stage fine‑tunes the model for placement. To facilitate this task, we also curate a multi‑source scene dataset covering diverse room types and fine‑grained furniture arrangements, which will be open‑sourced for community benefit. Experiments on our benchmark show our model significantly outperforms baselines without explicit geometric reasoning. We further develop a multi‑stage plan‑place‑verify agent pipeline that uses the model for text‑driven scene generation. Project Page: https://xccelephant.github.io/paper/gala/

PaperId: 360, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28171.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhiyuan Zhao, Hengrui Kang, Guang Liang, Bin Wang, Conghui He
Title: DocLayout-YOLO: Axis-Attentive Document Layout Detector with Mesh-Guided Synthetic Pretraining
Abstract:
Accurate and efficient document layout analysis is critical for modern document parsing systems. However, although the YOLO framework represents a leading paradigm for the real‑time detector, its adaptation to heterogeneous documents remains underexplored. To address this gap, we propose DocLayout‑YOLO, a document‑specialized real‑time detector that integrates diverse synthetic document pretraining and page‑axis context modeling. From the data perspective, we introduce MeshLayout‑1M, a synthetic pretraining corpus generated by the proposed Mesh‑candidate BestFit algorithm, which provides large‑scale and diverse document layouts for pretraining and improves adaptation to heterogeneous document scenarios. From the model perspective, we propose Page‑Axis Layout Attention (PALA), which captures long‑range dependencies along the horizontal and vertical page axes while remaining computationally efficient. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DocLayout‑YOLO achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance on four heterogeneous document benchmarks, obtaining 72.4%/75.5%/96.0%/73.1% mAP50:95 on D4LA, M6Doc, HJDataset, and PRIMA‑LAD, respectively. Compared with existing real‑time detectors, DocLayout‑YOLO establishes a superior accuracy‑efficiency trade‑off in document layout analysis. Code, model, and data are available at https://github.com/opendatalab/DocLayout‑YOLO/tree/release‑v2.

PaperId: 361, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28164.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaoxu Xu, Hao Li, Hongtao Zhang, Yili Tang, Jiafei Cao, Junhao Cai, Haoxiang Ma, Weixin Li, Weinan Zhang
Title: From Predictive Geometry to Action: Learning Complementary Predictive Representations for Embodied Manipulation
Abstract:
Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two‑stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi‑view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action‑relevant transitions. During downstream post‑training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action‑generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO‑Plus, SimplerEnv, and real‑world bimanual and single‑arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future‑world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.

PaperId: 362, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28118.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sivan Talaei, Fatemeh Daneshfar, Abdulhady Abas Abdullah, Mourad Oussalah
Title: Reliability-Guided Vision-Language Decoding with Text-Aware Skip Refinement for Medical Image Segmentation
Abstract:
Medical image segmentation remains challenging when targets exhibit limited visual distinction, irregular structure, or substantial variation across imaging modalities. Medical text can reduce this ambiguity, but indiscriminate fusion may introduce unreliable guidance. We present RELiF, a vision‑‑language framework that integrates text through reliability‑guided decoding. Its Reliability‑guided Fusion Gate (RFG) adaptively controls cross‑modal updates, while the Text‑guided Skip Refinement Adapter (TSRA) refines high‑resolution features using text guidance. RELiF is evaluated on radiographic, CT, and endoscopic segmentation tasks, where it shows competitive performance across diverse imaging characteristics and target appearances. Additional analyses examine efficiency and stability. The complementary uncertainty representation derived from the reliability response also shows an association with prediction difficulty, with higher uncertainty values occurring more frequently in pixels associated with segmentation errors. Code: https://github.com/SeivanTalaie/RELiF.

PaperId: 363, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28087.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zijian Yu, Hangwei Zhang, Jun Lan, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Jianfu Zhang
Title: WildAIGC-Bench: Can AI Image Detectors Handle the Wild? A Benchmark of Generated and Edited Images in Online Circulation
Abstract:
AI‑generated images linked to news events and online claims can mislead audiences, enable fraud, or cause public controversy. We introduce WildAIGC‑Bench, built through recurring collection across news websites, fact‑checking sources, and related social media content. The pipeline combines broad coverage, timely updates, and human‑verified labels through scheduled discovery, automatic screening and preliminary annotation, and human review of image‑specific evidence. The benchmark contains 407 verified AI‑generated or edited images, each accompanied by a source webpage link and an evidence summary. Images retain the conditions encountered online, including compression, screenshots, and recapture. Evaluation of dedicated visual detectors, multimodal large language models, and a simple Perception Encoder baseline reveals substantial recall gaps relative to existing benchmarks. WildAIGC‑Bench provides both a practical detection challenge and a basis for continued data expansion and source‑based verification. The dataset is released at https://github.com/YuZijian/WildAIGC‑Bench.

PaperId: 364, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28027.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Taiheng Pan
Title: From RL Papers to Framework Code: Inclusion and Review in Seven Open-Source Training Frameworks
Abstract:
Practitioners use reinforcement learning methods for language models through training frameworks, so a method that a framework includes is one configuration change away for its users. We measure how often this happens. We trace seven open‑source frameworks for RL post‑training through their commit histories and link them to 6,939 screened arXiv papers from January 2025 to June 2026. Of 1,598 papers that propose a general RL training method, 37 reached at least one framework. Across five quarterly cohorts of papers, the number included within 180 days stayed between 5 and 7 while the cohorts grew from 72 to 386 papers. Compared with papers from the same quarters, included papers more often trained policies of 30B parameters or more, at 41 against 10 percent, and more often changed a coefficient, clip, mask or weight in the existing loss, at 29 against 9 percent. Both gaps hold without papers from the companies that maintain the frameworks, while code release was equally common in both groups. The frameworks' issues and pull requests show that few methods are turned away in public. More than nine in ten of the general methods no framework included have no thread there that cites or names them, and many proposals that do appear stay open without a reply. Two further records, the frameworks' issues and the technical reports of 13 large open‑weight models, show that users rarely report training failures in public and that the reports state 8 of the 13 widely included methods. We release the data as a tracker that links training failures to framework implementations and lists each framework's contribution rules and earlier proposals.

PaperId: 365, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28003.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Cui Enhe, Jinyue Yang, Bojian Yin, Guoqi Li
Title: Dancing Diffusion: Learning Continuous Programs for Image Generation and Editing
Abstract:
Diffusion models generate samples through a multi‑step denoising trajectory, yet condition every step on the same instruction, so the trajectory cannot be addressed at the level of individual operations. We introduce Dancing Diffusion, which assigns each span of timesteps a dedicated continuous condition block and thereby turns conditioning into a latent program. A compiler maps text features into this program, and a fixed pretrained generator executes its blocks over successive sampling intervals. The trajectory can then dance, keeping its executed history while its continuation is redirected. A shared prefix is executed once and reused, and a later operation is rewritten while content fixed by earlier operations is preserved. The compiler is trained through the images it produces, with visual feedback on both the requested change and the retained content. On SANA, reusing an executed prefix preserves markedly more of the scene than regenerating from noise at a similar strength of edit, learned conditions preserve more background than native prompt switching from the same saved state, and the learned program improves generation quality over native SANA. Later branches weaken the edit, which leaves semantic control over individual operations limited. By converting a single‑instruction trajectory into a program of addressable operations, Dancing Diffusion lays a foundation for structured intermediate computation in diffusion models.

PaperId: 366, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27999.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jihai Zhang, Runjia Qian, Kaiqin Kong, Biao Jiang, Puyi Wang, Siru Chen, Tianle Li, Guanjie Chen, Junyi Wu, Chubin Chen, Yuanhang Li, Kaichen Huang, Haobo Zhang, Yangguang Li, Wei Yu, Guibin Chen, Yu Cheng, Yahui Zhou
Title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Harnessing Video Models for Real-Time Playable Game Worlds
Abstract:
Moving from controllable videos to genuinely playable worlds requires persistent world state, executable game rules, and low‑latency interaction. We outline a roadmap for the next generation of Matrix‑Game that separates game execution from visual generation through an executable game harness, and introduce Matrix‑Game 4.0 as the first system built on this design. A lightweight game engine maintains world state and executes interaction rules, a multimodal coding agent translates player ideas into game code and dynamic scene captions, and a renderer based on autoregressive video model transforms engine‑rendered low‑poly proxies into detailed visuals, conditioned on dynamic captions and memory references. This framework provides continuous guidance for visual generation and enables natural‑language creation and modification of scenes and gameplay. Our renderer is trained on aligned low‑poly and high‑fidelity video pairs and distilled into a causal generator that generates in four‑frame chunks with one or two denoising steps. Together with targeted inference optimizations, Matrix‑Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX5090 with a key‑press‑to‑display latency of 112ms. Single‑step generation achieves 83FPS steady‑state throughput with 18.2GiB of peak GPU memory usage. With fixed prompts, steady‑state throughput also reaches 67FPS on an RTX5080 and 58FPS on an RTX5070Ti. We demonstrate customizable shooter and driving games with engine‑enforced mechanics, and release code, model weights, and low‑poly game assets to support research and creation of playable game worlds.

PaperId: 367, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27998.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Antonio Langella, Giovanni Minelli, Giovanni B. Dessy, Lorenzo Amatucci, Giulio Turrisi, Victor Barasuol, Claudio Semini
Title: LocoPilot: Single-Operator Bilateral Teleoperation for Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning
Abstract:
Learning loco‑manipulation policies requires demonstrations that capture coordinated base and arm motion on the target embodiment.
