Robot‑free interfaces allow demonstrations to be collected independently of the target robot, increasing flexibility but without directly capturing platform‑specific commands, proprioception, and body‑mounted observations. On‑robot teleoperation allows to capture these signals directly, but requires an interface capable of commanding the complete system concurrently. This paper presents LocoPilot, a single‑operator bilateral teleoperation and data‑collection framework implemented on a 12‑DoF Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a 6‑DoF AgileX Piper L manipulator, an Intel RealSense D435 wrist camera, and an Intel RealSense D405 head camera. A second 6‑DoF Piper L arm, used as the leader and two handheld controllers provide simultaneous control of the base, body posture, manipulator, and gripper. The follower arm interaction forces are estimated without a dedicated force/torque sensor and rendered to the operator through a passivity‑constrained haptic channel. A ROS~2 pipeline records synchronized multimodal observations together with a unified 11D action shared by teleoperation and policy deployment. Compared to prior work, LocoPilot uniquely unifies robot‑in‑the‑loop legged data collection, force feedback without motion‑capture instrumentation, and the same action interface at deployment. We evaluate the interface across multiple loco‑manipulation tasks and validate the complete collection‑to‑deployment pipeline by fine‑tuning MolmoAct2 \citeMOLMO on pick‑and‑place demonstrations and deploying on the physical robot without action retargeting or additional inverse kinematics. Code available at: https://github.com/iit‑DLSLab/LocoPilot

PaperId: 368, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27986.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yukuo Ma, Cong Liu, Junke Wang, Junqi Liu, Haibin Huang, Zuxuan Wu, Xuelong Li
Title: Recast the Past: Stable Long Video Generation with Full Context Memory
Abstract:
Long‑horizon video generation requires retaining an ever‑expanding history, but conditioning on its growing token sequence is costly. Existing methods restrict or compress historical context, potentially losing information needed for future generation. This work proposes ReCam, which groups local spatiotemporal blocks of historical latents into vectors and projects them directly into the high‑dimensional hidden space of a Diffusion Transformer. The model learns to use the resulting memory tokens through native self‑attention, reducing token count while retaining block‑level access to the full history. To mitigate temporal drift during autoregressive rollout, we further introduce dual‑pointer denoising with separate noise schedules for recent context and target frames. Among the evaluated methods, ReCam achieves the highest VBench‑Long overall score of 80.1 and competitive static‑scene revisitation performance on R2M‑Bench. It also leads on all four consistency metrics for off‑screen subject reappearance, including clothing consistency of 4.09 versus 3.03 for the best baseline.

PaperId: 369, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27981.pdf   GitHub
Authors:JunHyeok Oh, Byung-Jun Lee
Title: Adaptive Stopping of Streamed Reasoning for Language Model Agents
Abstract:
Reasoning‑enabled language model agents can incur substantial computation before acting, although the reasoning needed varies across decisions. Existing stopping signals, such as confidence and intermediate‑answer stability, can vary in effectiveness across reasoning models; signals obtained from hidden states or token probabilities also require internal access that may be unavailable or impractical. We introduce StreamStop, which learns model‑specific stopping policies offline from prefix‑level action agreement. A frozen prefix reader encodes available reasoning text for a lightweight stop head, allowing stopping without access to the reasoning model's internal signals. We construct and publicly release a dataset of agent reasoning trajectories with prefix‑level action annotations. These annotations compare each prefix action with the full‑reasoning reference action, enabling offline comparison of stopping rules and exact expected‑return optimization of a discounted action‑agreement objective. Conditioning the head on the discount factor allows the agreement‑token trade‑off to be adjusted at inference without retraining. In closed‑loop evaluations on WebShop and ScienceWorld, StreamStop achieves higher observed success than most validation‑selected fixed‑budget settings while using fewer reasoning tokens than Full thinking. On WebShop with Qwen3.8‑27B, it uses 42% fewer reasoning tokens per episode with similar observed task success.

PaperId: 370, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27960.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wenbin Liao, Hao Zhu, Yike Ma, Hao Jiang, Feng Dai
Title: Efficient SAM3 Adaptation for Multi-Class Semantic Segmentation via Dense Competitive Representations
Abstract:
The Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) has achieved significant progress in Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS) by processing short noun phrases to generate segmentation masks with unique instance identifiers. While SAM3 excels at single‑concept segmentation, it falls short in complex, real‑world environments where multiple concepts must be segmented simultaneously. In particular, SAM3 typically fails to simultaneously process concepts with semantic overlap, leading to semantic misclassifications and redundant mask predictions. Moreover, as the number of concepts increases, the independent inference paradigm introduces prohibitive inference latency. To address these limitations, we propose the Dense Competitive Representations SAM (DCR‑SAM) framework. By decoupling cross‑modal interactions, the proposed method alleviates the inference latency. To resolve semantic misclassifications, DCR‑SAM dynamically aligns textual concepts with visual representations and incorporates a dense competition head to enforce explicit inter‑class competition. Furthermore, a learnable background token is applied to absorb non‑target objects dynamically. These mechanisms effectively suppress overlapping predictions and generate high‑fidelity masks. Extensive experimental evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework: (1) achieves a 2.3% ～ 10.7% performance improvement over state‑of‑the‑art methods, (2) delivers a 33× inference speedup compared to the native SAM3, and (3) exhibits strong robustness across diverse scenarios.

PaperId: 371, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27954.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Byeonghun Bang, Sangwoo Park, Jinheon Baek, Kangsan Kim, Youngwan Lee, Sung Ju Hwang
Title: Lost in Recovery: Demystifying Recovery Behavior of Computer-Use Agents via Goal-Oriented Action Replay
Abstract:
Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer‑use agents that automate digital workflows via fine‑grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long‑horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API‑based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model‑based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework for systematically studying recovery behavior in computer‑use agents. We formalize Transition‑Consistent Recovery: identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states must yield identical outcomes. We operationalize this criterion through goal‑oriented action replay following controlled error injection. Using ReTrace, we present the first systematic study of autonomous, model‑based recovery, revealing that (i) ideal recovery can unlock model's latent task completion capabilities, (ii) current computer‑use agents fail to exploit their latent recovery capabilities, and (iii) accurate model‑based recovery yields measurable end‑to‑end gains. Together, these findings establish recovery as a fundamental capability for building reliable computer‑use agents. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/BangProx/ReTRACE.

PaperId: 372, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27946.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yue Ma, Pengjie Song, Xinyu Wang, Yi He, Zeqian Long, Fangneng Zhan, Kaichen Zhou, Hongyu Liu, Hongfa Wang, Peihao Li, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Qifeng Chen
Title: Decoupling Action from Egocentric Observation for World Simulation
Abstract:
Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce them in new visual contexts, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. Existing approaches to transferring actions rely on condition‑guided video generation, which converts the observation video into explicit geometric controls (e.g., hand poses or meshes) to drive synthesis. However, these methods introduce geometric estimation errors, making it difficult to preserve physically plausible interactions when transferred to new scenes. Alternatively, motion transfer methods directly extract motion patterns from the observation video, yet motion‑level features alone cannot encode rich contact dynamics, frequently leading to severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout. To address both limitations, we present EgoACT, a test‑time framework for egocentric action transfer that operates directly on the denoising process of video diffusion models without requiring additional geometric estimators. EgoACT uses Velocity‑guided Structure Anchoring to stabilize reference‑consistent hand‑object structure in the early denoising stage, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration to refine reliable local correspondences in the mid‑to‑late denoising stages. Together, these two components preserve transferable action semantics while improving temporal coherence and interaction realism. We further establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating action preservation, visual quality, and hand‑object plausibility across diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios. Experiments show that EgoACT generates more coherent and physically plausible interaction videos than strong baselines.

PaperId: 373, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27930.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Benjamin Donnot, Sami Tazi, Eva Boguslawski, Nourredine Henka
Title: Benchmarking CPU, GPU, and ML Power-Flow Solvers from 14 to 70,000 Buses
Abstract:
Learned surrogates for power‑flow (PF) computation are usually motivated by speed, compared against a single CPU‑based baseline. We show this comparison is fragile: across 7 open‑source CPU‑based solvers evaluated on identical inputs, throughput varies by roughly 2.5‑3 orders of magnitude, so the choice of baseline alone can flip the conclusion. We build a benchmark spanning 9 physics‑based solvers: 7 CPU‑based and 2 GPU‑based, including a new batched GPU solver, gumsim2grid ‑ and 3 published ML surrogates, evaluated under a shared, independently implemented KCL‑mismatch check across 15 grids from 14 to 70,000 buses. On the PF task itself, a sufficiently parallelized CPU solver or gpusim2grid matches or exceeds the throughput of the ML surrogates we test while remaining orders of magnitude more accurate; we find no evidence that these GNN‑style surrogates are yet competitive for PF specifically, though prior work reports genuine gains on related but more combinatorial tasks such as optimal power flow or power grid control. Beyond this finding, we hope the benchmark suite, code and reference evaluator released at https://github.com/Grid2op/gpusim2grid helps close a broader reproducibility gap in this space, where batched GPU‑based PF solvers are rarely open‑sourced or evaluated against a common set of baselines.

PaperId: 374, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27913.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiahui Ning, Liang Chen, Yuchen Liang, Yi Zhang, Fenglei Fan
Title: ACE-Compression: An Ability-Centric Evaluation of Compressed Large Language Models
Abstract:
Model compression makes large language models deployable, but today's evaluation tells an incomplete story. Standard practice measures retained task performance and stops there. This misses a critical fact: compression perturbs the distributed knowledge embedded across billions of weights, and task scores alone cannot reveal which underlying abilities survive and which quietly collapse. To solve this question, we introduce ACE‑Compression, an ability‑centric evaluation framework. Instead of asking only "does the compressed model still answer correctly?", we ask "which of its core abilities remain intact?" Our framework probes four deployment‑facing dimensions: procedural reasoning and constraint execution, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition and affective understanding, and persona fidelity and stylistic consistency. Across more than 35 compressed checkpoints from six open‑weight LLMs‑covering quantization and pruning‑we find that compression redistributes ability profiles. Coarse, local, and surface‑level signals often persist, while fine‑grained, long‑tail, and context‑dependent abilities become fragile. Quantization consistently outperforms pruning in retention, but the practical meaning of that gap depends entirely on which ability an application requires. Based on our findings, deployers can choose compression methods by the ability profile their application needs, not just by a leaderboard average. And algorithm designers gain diagnostic signals to build compression methods that preserve what matters. We believe that ACE‑Compression turns compression from a black‑box accuracy drop into an interpretable intervention‑one we can measure, understand, and ultimately improve.

PaperId: 375, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27912.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Marcel Dreier, Dakota Pyles, Nora Gourmelon, Moritz Koch, Fei Wu, Thorsten Seehaus, Matthias Braun, Andreas Maier, Vincent Christlein
Title: ICIBS: Increasing the Context for Ice Boundary Segmentation
Abstract:
Mountain glaciers and ice sheets are undergoing rapid loss of ice mass. To assess their current volume and ice‑thickness distribution, and to accurately forecast their future, ground‑penetrating radar systems are employed to measure ice thickness. These instruments produce radio‑echo sounding data that reveal the internal structure of the ice and its boundaries at the surface and beneath the ice body. However, delineating these interfaces is time‑consuming as the surveyed area can span several hundred kilometers. To accelerate the labelling process, automated methods have emerged, but they often struggle to delineate the ice bottom, particularly in temperate glaciers. The high water content inherent in temperate ice increases both scattering and attenuation of the radar signal, resulting in weak and ambiguous reflections at the ice bottom and generally noisier data. As a result, the visual features corresponding to the ice bottom become ambiguous. To address this issue, we propose several extensions to deep learning models that incorporate additional contextual information into the prediction. Specifically, we integrate modifications that incorporate additional spatial and geo‑spatial contextual information into the network. With these enhancements, we achieve a new state‑of‑the‑art performance on the IceAnatomy benchmark dataset, with mean errors of 10.9 m for the FAU subset and 43.4 m for the CReSIS subset in a single combined system. We also demonstrate that our method generalises well to previously unseen data, outperforming the baseline by 49.6 % on new campaign data from Patagonia. The model code and the new dataset are available at https://github.com/ki7077/ICIBS/tree/main and https://zenodo.org/records/23392580.

PaperId: 376, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27911.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Seohyun Lee, Jongha Kim, Dohwan Ko, Ji Soo Lee, Seoung Choi, Jayun Ku, Hyunwoo J. Kim
Title: MMEnterprise-Bench: Evaluating Enterprise Agents over Evolving Multimodal Records
Abstract:
Enterprise agents answer questions over workplace records that evolve through team collaboration. As information is shared, corrected, and revised across documents, chats, and figures, multiple versions of the same information accumulate in the workspace. Reliable question answering therefore requires agents to reason over sufficient evidence, resolve cross‑source and temporal conflicts, and recognize when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce MMEnterprise‑Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, covering three categories: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open‑source multimodal LLMs and find that even the strongest models struggle when evidence contains cross‑source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple images. Moreover, increasing the retrieval budget or employing a larger retriever improves evidence recall but does not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy. These findings highlight the persistent challenges of reasoning over evolving workplace records and establish MMEnterprise‑Bench as a testbed for developing more reliable enterprise agents. Code and data are available at https://mlvlab.github.io/MMEnterprise‑Bench/.

PaperId: 377, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27908.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Diego Miguel Lozano, Erik Derner, Juan Antonio Pérez-Ortiz, Nuria Oliver
Title: Polarity Blindness in LLM Safety: A Systematic Study of Negation, Antonym Substitution, and Adversarial Framing
Abstract:
Negation remains a persistent challenge for language models across NLP tasks and modalities. We show that this weakness can undermine LLM safety guardrails through a structural vulnerability we term polarity blindness: the failure to recognize harmful intent after polarity‑altering linguistic transformations. We study two forms of polarity inversion: grammatical negation and antonym replacement, and use synonym replacement as a polarity‑preserving control. We further test whether an adversarial textual wrapper amplifies these failures. Using a 260‑prompt benchmark across 10 state‑of‑the‑art LLMs and 3 languages (English, Spanish, Czech), stratified by harmfulness potential and evaluated on a validated 0‑5 harm scale, we find that polarity blindness affects most evaluated models, with mean harm scores reaching 4.12 for the most vulnerable model. The effect persists across typologically differing negation systems, suggesting that polarity blindness reflects a broader limitation in semantic robustness rather than a language‑ or grammar‑specific failure.

PaperId: 378, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27907.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Amane Yamaguchi, Shohei Kamiguchi, Masashi Hamaya, Shigeo Yoshida, Takuji Narumi, Mai Nishimura
Title: What Novice Operators See Changes What the Policy Learns: A User Study of Keypoint Hand Visual Representation for Teleoperated Demonstration
Abstract:
Imitation learning increasingly relies on novice operators, whose demonstrations fall short of experts' in number and inter‑trial consistency. Operators act on what they are shown, yet how the rendering of the robot affects their demonstrations, and the policies trained on them, has not been examined. We study this question with PointHand, a teleoperation interface that renders a multi‑fingered robot hand as sparse keypoints at its fingertips and joints, the same keypoints a policy can observe. In a simulated mug‑in‑box task, 18 novices and 4 experts collected 2,200 trials under three renderings: the real shape of the hand, all keypoints emphasized, or the thumb and index finger alone emphasized. The novices shown the thumb and index finger emphasized collected 441 successful demonstrations from 600 trials, against 320 for those shown the real shape. We then trained diffusion policies on these demonstrations, replacing the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state they observe with the hand keypoints and two object keypoints. Within 400 steps these demonstrations went from the weakest of the three novice conditions under the point‑cloud policy (46.3%) to the strongest under the keypoint policy (57.3%), a gain of +11.0 percentage points in all five seeds. Those collected with all keypoints emphasized changed by at most +0.7 percentage points, and in no more than three seeds. The value of a demonstration therefore depends on the rendering shown during collection and on what the policy observes together. A shared representation can pay off on both sides, in the number of successful demonstrations and in the success rate of the policy trained on them. Project page: https://omron‑sinicx.github.io/point‑hand/

PaperId: 379, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27904.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Genshin Kakimoto, Atsushi Yanagisawa
Title: Staged Continual Adaptation of Multimodal Foundation Models for Japanese Financial Documents
Abstract:
Staged post‑training of multimodal foundation models chains vision‑language alignment, reasoning distillation, and domain tuning, yet how each phase trades capabilities against the others remains under‑characterised. Tracking an 8.4B‑parameter model from an un‑fine‑tuned baseline through three training phases on Japanese financial documents (evaluated on five text‑input benchmarks), we find the phases interact non‑additively: math‑only distillation overwrites the financial knowledge acquired earlier even as procedural math skill survives, and the domain phase repairs more than it installs. A skip‑phase ablation is best for domain knowledge but forfeits numerical‑reasoning gains, so per‑phase contributions are not decomposable and the best checkpoint is task‑dependent, with implications for checkpoint retention and scheduling rather than added stages.

PaperId: 380, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27889.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Younghyun Kim, Wooseok Seo, Minseo Kim, Seunghyuk Oh, Minjae Lee, Donghoon Kim, Hyung Il Koo, Jaehyung Kim, Wonjun Kang
Title: Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization
Abstract:
Recent studies in harness optimization have shown substantial performance gains in language model agents without updating model weights. A well‑designed harness more effectively leverages the underlying model's capabilities by shaping context, tool use, and execution workflows. However, naïve success rates alone do not fully characterize whether optimized harness yields more reliable success on tasks already within reach (elicitation) or a broader range of solvable tasks (expansion). This distinction is crucial for recursive self‑improvement and evolutionary search, as expansion may provide a broader range of successful experiences to push the capability boundaries. Despite the growing significance, this distinction remains underexplored in harness optimization. We conduct a systematic analysis to study the effect of gains from harness optimization. Building on pass@k analyses in the reinforcement learning (RL) literature that compare models before and after RL training, we compare optimized harnesses with their pre‑optimization counterparts. Specifically, we assess changes in reachable task coverage, compare harness optimization with model scaling and increased inference‑time compute, and examine how gains vary with task difficulty. Across static prediction and dynamic tasks, we find that pass@1 advantages of harness over stronger interventions can reverse at larger attempt budgets and aggregate gains conceal shortfalls on hard tasks, underscoring the need for a fine‑grained diagnosis.

PaperId: 381, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27883.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Peng Zhang, Shuaihao Han, Tingfa Xu, Jianan Li
Title: SGLDet: Spectral-aware Global-Local Dynamic Modeling for Multispectral Aerial Object Detection
Abstract:
Multispectral aerial object detection aims to exploit spectral‑spatial cues to address object detection challenges in complex aerial scenes. Existing methods mainly focus on spectral‑spatial decoupling and object‑aware spectral‑spatial fusion to improve spectral utilization. However, two critical issues remain underexplored: 1) severe foreground‑background imbalance caused by large scene coverage hinders reliable object recognition; 2) aerial objects exhibit substantial local variations in scale, orientation, and structure, which hinder accurate localization. To address these issues, we propose SGLDet, a spectral‑aware global‑local dynamic modeling framework for multispectral aerial object detection, which is motivated by the observation that object semantics are jointly determined by global spectral consistency and scene context, while precise localization requires dynamic feature modulation conditioned on the input spectral and spatial properties. To realize these properties, SGLDet consists of three coordinated components: a Spectral‑driven Global Dynamic Modeling module that aggregates spectrally related features across the scene via similarity‑guided sparse matching; a Multi‑scale Global Context Integration module that constructs a compact scene memory for scene‑guided contextual reasoning; and a Spectral‑aware Input‑dependent Calibration Aggregation module that performs expert‑kernel aggregation with scene‑guided spectral‑spatial calibration to enable adaptive local feature modulation. Extensive experiments on MODA, HOD3K, and DroneVehicle demonstrate that SGLDet achieves superior performance with competitive computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/Riiluo/SGLDet.

PaperId: 382, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27882.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Peng Zhang, Tingfa Xu, Jinrui Sui, Yuyang Tian, Jianan Li
Title: S$^3$E-Det: A Strict Spatial-Spectral Equivariant Detector for Multispectral Object Detection
Abstract:
Multispectral object detection requires detectors to exploit material‑dependent spectral responses while maintaining consistent localization under geometric variations. Existing MOD detectors learn discriminative spectral representations, yet lack a unified mechanism that preserves spectral order, adapts spectral‑context fusion across pyramid levels, and regulates geometric responses under rotation. To address these limitations, we propose S^3E‑Det, a strict spatial‑spectral equivariant detector that couples ordered spectral modeling with transformation‑consistent prediction. Spectral Order‑aware Sampling Calibration (SOSC) imposes local order constraints on input‑derived spectral features through first‑order variation, while Common‑Differential Equivariant Fusion (CDEF) adapts spectral‑context aggregation across pyramid levels. A compact Geometric Alignment Head (GAH) reconciles invariant and equivariant output properties within a unified prediction stage. Across MODA, HOD3K, and DroneVehicle, S^3E‑Det combines high detection accuracy with a compact parameter footprint and reduced rotation‑induced variation. Code is available at https://github.com/Riiluo/S3E‑Det.

PaperId: 383, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27877.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chuanyang Ma, Chenye Wang, Yixuan Wang, Huiling Zhou, Xingqun Qi, Muyi Sun, Man Zhang, Caifeng Shan, Zhenan Sun
Title: Gaze2HOI: Gaze-Aware Intention Disambiguation for Egocentric Hand-Object Interaction Forecasting
Abstract:
Anticipating how users will interact with their surroundings is essential for proactive systems that provide timely assistance in AR, VR, and embodied applications. Prior work typically forecasts hand‑object interactions directly from historical observations, leaving intention and contact geometry implicit. However, similar observation histories can precede semantically or geometrically distinct futures. Inspired by behavioral evidence that gaze can provide early cues for underlying intention, we propose Gaze2HOI, a gaze‑aware framework that formulates hand‑object interaction forecasting as a hierarchical problem comprising intention inference, contact grounding, and coupled hand‑object motion generation. Specifically, Gaze2HOI first weights gaze cues by fixation strength and recency, and uses them to modulate the visual representations of a vision‑language model (VLM) through Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation (TGSM), thereby reducing semantic ambiguity in intention inference. Subsequently, an Anticipatory Contact Grounding (ACG) module maps these structured intentions into explicit contact, support, and placement fields, effectively mitigating geometric ambiguity. Driven by these explicit conditions, a diffusion‑based model jointly generates the 6‑DoF object trajectories and future articulated motion of both hands. To evaluate Gaze2HOI, we further introduce EgoAIM, a phase‑aware benchmark that organizes egocentric hand‑object interactions into four phases defined by evolving hand‑object relations and provides fine‑grained intention annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Gaze2HOI achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance in both intention inference and motion forecasting, even approaching oracle‑level end‑to‑end performance in specific interaction phases. Project page: https://gaze2hoi.github.io/.

PaperId: 384, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27874.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shuqi Liu, Yingkai Zhang, Lin Gu, Tao Zhang, Ying Fu
Title: Manifold Prior Guided Deep Unfolding for Hyperspectral Image Reconstruction
Abstract:
Hyperspectral Image (HSI) reconstruction has made substantial progress with the deep unfolding framework by decomposing the problem into a projection module and a denoiser module. Nevertheless, existing methods still exhibit limitations of insufficient matching with HSI data. The issues lie in two aspects: 1) the data‑consistency projection module applies a fixed gradient descent step while ignoring the spectral content adaptivity of HSI; 2) the denoiser module either suffers from high computational complexity or is limited to the local receptive field, failing to efficiently capture the global spatial‑spectral dependencies. In this paper, we propose a deep unfolding framework centered on a two‑stage manifold learning strategy to obtain a degradation‑free structural prior, which is then strategically injected into both the projection and denoiser modules. In the data‑consistency projection, a prior‑guided spectral weight mechanism is introduced to adaptively modulate the weight of spectral band. In the denoiser module, a manifold‑guided Mamba is proposed to achieve the structure‑aware extraction of spatial‑spectral features through prior modulation. Quantitative and visual comparisons on synthetic and real‑world datasets show that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing state‑of‑the‑art approaches, while maintaining the structural interpretability of the unfolding framework. The code is available at https://github.com/SqLiu67/MPG‑DU.

PaperId: 385, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27864.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Imre Boros
Title: Front-pinned spectral collocation for the flame problem and related ignition problems
Abstract:
We consider global Chebyshev collocation for the ignition problems y'=y^q(1‑y), y(0)=δ, q\ge2; for q=2 this is the flame problem, a standard stiff test equation. After rescaling to [‑1,1] the solution has an interior layer of width O(μ), μ=(q‑1)δ^q‑1, at a δ‑dependent position. Two obstacles arise: plain Chebyshev collocation needs O(1/μ) nodes, and imposing the initial condition amplifies errors by a factor of order 1/μ, which makes the collocation equations severely ill‑conditioned. Our main contribution addresses the second one. Since all solutions are translates of one profile, the initial condition can be replaced by an equivalent interior condition. For an unknown u=φ(y), imposing it where the speed |φ'f_q| of u along the orbit is maximal bounds the propagator of the linearized equation by one; for u=\ln y this is y(x^\ast)=(q‑1)/q. For the first obstacle we use the sinh map of Tee and Trefethen: the time function is explicit, the complex singularities of the profile lie exactly at \pm(2k+1)πi, and the map parameters follow in closed form, so that O(\ln(1/μ)) nodes suffice. In double precision the pinned scheme reaches the interpolation error of the exact solution in five or six Newton iterations for μ down to 10^‑12, whereas the initial‑condition form fails or converges to wrong discrete solutions, also in an integral (Birkhoff) reformulation. Computations in 256‑bit arithmetic confirm the predicted rate down to errors of 10^‑70, AAA approximation locates the singularities to within 2%, and the method carries over to an Arrhenius reaction rate, with all parameters computed numerically.

PaperId: 386, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27861.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haocheng Wang, Youquan Liu, Weiyu Guo, Aokai Zhang, Donghang Wu, Hongyu Liu, Sha Zhang, Weidong Yang, Ben Fei
Title: RoboCasa-Shift: Stage-Aware Robustness Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Policies in Long-Horizon Household Manipulation
Abstract:
Vision‑language‑action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long‑horizon tasks. We introduce RoboCasa‑Shift, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single‑factor shifts, matched clean‑perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator‑grounded stage‑aware diagnostics. We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long‑horizon tasks that pass a predefined clean‑performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts. Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields Δ\mathrmSR=0 despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome. Stage‑aware analysis further shows that the same end‑to‑end degradation can correspond to different execution‑depth profiles. Camera L_2 and Gaussian blur L_1 both yield Δ\mathrmSR=0.188, yet their first‑stage failure rates are 19.0% and 36.4%, respectively. Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as a multi‑dimensional property of execution rather than a single end‑to‑end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaochengWang23/RoboCasa‑Shift.

PaperId: 387, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27851.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Junha Song, Geonmo Gu, Jeongeun Park, Heejeong Nam, Lucas Maes, Byeongho Heo, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
Title: LaLa-World: Scaling Latent World Models with Natural Language Actions
Abstract:
This paper shows that JEPA‑style latent world models (LWMs) can learn across diverse domains and data sources by adopting the language‑conditioned interface of video generation models. We establish this approach as an effective and efficient basis for planning with imagination and downstream policy fine‑tuning. To this end, we introduce LaLa‑World, a Language‑conditioned Latent World model that learns from simulation and robot trajectories together with broader image and video data. Two designs make this work. First, we describe both numerical actions and visual changes in language, enabling joint training of a single future predictor across heterogeneous datasets. Second, we build the predictor on a language model, allowing it to interpret language conditions while predicting future latent states. The resulting predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than existing LWMs trained separately for each domain or task. Adding image and video data further improves average planning performance and robustness to action phrasing. In a matched comparison with an RAEv2‑based video generation model baseline, LaLa‑World reaches comparable planning performance with 6× less training cost and 13.9× faster planning. Beyond planning, the pretrained LaLa‑World serves as an initialization for LaLa‑Policy, which jointly predicts actions and future visual representations. LaLa‑Policy performs competitively with Cosmos Policy on LIBERO and RoboCasa, with up to 5.5× faster inference.

PaperId: 388, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27850.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Theresia Veronika Rampisela, Maria Maistro, Tuukka Ruotsalo, Christina Lioma
Title: Robustness Analysis of Pareto-based Joint Evaluation of Fairness and Relevance in Recommender Systems
Abstract:
Recommender Systems (RSs) can be evaluated for many aspects, two of them being recommendation relevance and fairness. These two aspects can be evaluated either in isolation, using a measure for each aspect; or jointly with a single`relevance‑aware' fairness measure that quantifies fairness with respect to relevance. Yet, neither approach provides a simultaneous evaluation of both relevance and fairness: the first approach may result in two different rankings of models, each corresponding to an evaluation aspect; the second approach often provides an imbalanced evaluation of the two aspects. To address this gap, we propose Distance to Pareto Frontier (DPFR), a new approach to jointly evaluate RS fairness and relevance. DPFR is based on a Pareto frontier of relevance and fairness scores from existing measures. The frontier is generated from user‑item interaction data and represents various Pareto‑optimal trade‑offs between the two aspects. Thus, the distance from a point in the frontier provides a joint score of fairness and relevance. As DPFR can be used with existing measures, it is modular and intuitive. Our experiments with 4 recommenders and 3 fairness‑aware re‑rankers on 6 real‑world datasets reveal inconsistent associations between existing measures and DPFR, showing that they are not reliable proxies for evaluations based on Pareto optimality. We further examine the robustness of DPFR as a joint evaluation approach for fairness and relevance by conducting experiments with artificial recommendations and with various fairness‑relevance trade‑offs, as well as by analysing DPFR's agreement to simple measures of fairness and relevance. These analyses show that DPFR is more robust than existing joint evaluation approaches. Finally, we provide guidelines for evaluating fairness and relevance jointly with DPFR. Our code: https://github.com/theresiavr/robustness‑DPFR‑recsys‑evaluation.

PaperId: 389, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27812.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Guanchen Li, Yixing Xu, Xuanwu Yin, Dong Li, Emad Barsoum
Title: SliMOO: Interpretable Multi-Objective Evolutionary Search for LLM Depth Pruning
Abstract:
As large language models (LLMs) grow more powerful, their scale makes them costly to serve. Depth pruning offers a practical route to efficiency by directly reducing memory and latency without hardware‑specific support. However, we observe that transformer layers exhibit markedly different task‑dependent layer contributions, whereas existing depth‑pruning methods ignore this heterogeneity and thus tend to optimize for a narrow domain or benchmark rather than preserve broad capability. This suggests that LLM depth pruning should be formulated as a multi‑objective optimization problem rather than a single‑score ranking problem. We propose SliMOO, an interpretable multi‑objective evolutionary search framework for LLM depth pruning. SliMOO first uses single‑layer removal probing to construct a task‑layer importance map, which provides an interpretable view of task‑shared and task‑specific layers and serves as a search prior. It then performs a Pareto‑aware evolutionary search for pruning masks, where candidates are generated under the guidance of the task‑layer prior, scored by their deviation from the dense model on each task, and retained through NSGA‑II environmental selection. Across the Llama‑3.1 and Qwen3 model families, SliMOO consistently achieves stronger multi‑task trade‑offs than rule‑based, greedy, and scalarized baselines. For example, on Llama‑3.1‑70B at 25% sparsity, it improves the math‑domain average from 24.33% to 34.40% and the code‑domain average from 35.03% to 39.14%. Code will be made available at https://github.com/AMD‑AGI/SliMOO.

PaperId: 390, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27794.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Oliver Hausdörfer, Felix Minzenmay, Mani Majd, Maximilian P. Christof, Shiyuan Zhang, Angela P. Schoellig
Title: Multi-View Latent Action Pretraining for Cross-Embodiment Robot Learning from Videos
Abstract:
Action‑free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out‑of‑plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi‑camera views using cross‑attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone. We further evaluate in strict cross‑embodiment settings where task‑specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual‑view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground‑truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single‑view, while scaling single‑view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out‑of‑plane motions. The downstream policy improves success rate by +13.5% compared to +6.2% for single‑view LAM. A single cross‑embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments. The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by +20% over action‑only policies in 850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task‑dependent. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/

PaperId: 391, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27746.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yang Li, Yike Wang, Di Wan, Chujun He, Zongsi Xu, Yitao Yu, Quanfeng Lu, Xiyu Chen, Sheng Zhong, Deng Binjie, Yichen Guo, Zhenwei Guo, Hou Jun, Kunhan Guo, Weihao Lin, Tuo Zhou, Hai Liu, Chenwei Wu, Jianyuan Zhong, Xilin Dai, Ye Luo
Title: S$^2$-MAS: A Society-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation Framework with 500 Million Household Persona Agents
Abstract:
Simulating economic responses at society scale requires agents whose decisions reflect household circumstances. We introduce S^2‑MAS, a society‑scale multi‑agent simulation framework built on 500 million synthetic household personas grounded in real‑survey data. Its Genese engine separates decisions from state updates, while reusable financial scenarios and application ledgers track consumption, cash, debt and payments. Trained with SFT + RLCD on 2.93 million examples, sharp‑421m‑mlx achieves 74.55% accuracy and 38.37% question‑macro F1 on one‑shot consumer financial‑choice tasks derived from held‑out survey responses. Its accuracy exceeds GLM‑5.3‑Flash, Jev 1.13, DeepSeek‑V4.1‑Flash, GPT‑6‑Luna and GPT‑6‑Astra in the common benchmark (full test for the first four; matched 500‑group sample for Astra). We evaluate eight financial task families and simulate 12 million distinct household agents in paired purchase‑funding conditions. Jointly raising purchase goals and approved credit limits increases consumption, with responses differing across age and income groups. Education, employment and household‑size differences persist after age‑income standardization and mainly reflect transitions from deferral to purchase. Asset and debt groups differ in cash drawdown, repayment and closing debt. S^2‑MAS links heterogeneous household decisions to evolving consumption, cash and repayment paths, supporting economic experiments across household groups and population scales.

PaperId: 392, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27745.pdf   GitHub
Authors:An-Sheng Jhang
Title: Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judgment assistants and as stand‑in participants in psychology experiments, yet little is known about how much their probability estimates move in response to a single new piece of information. We pair premise‑hypothesis items from δ‑SNLI with one strengthener and one weakener each, elicit the prior and the posteriors in separate calls, and measure the directional movement s: the mean posterior change signed by the annotated direction, so that the prior cancels out. We vary whether the update is stated ("Here is something else you learned") or reported ("Someone said that"), and whether the model gives one probability or five weighted estimates. We test seven configurations: two local models (Qwen3‑8B, OLMo‑2‑7B; 240 pairs) and five configurations run through agent command‑line harnesses (120 pairs), with hypotheses and analysis rules fixed before the formal runs (not publicly registered). Under stated, direct elicitation all seven move in the annotated direction (s = 18‑28 percentage points). Reporting lowers s in all seven point estimates (significantly in six, by 2‑5 points) and raises the share of reverse movements in all seven: the effect is consistent but small. Five weighted estimates lower the share of responses at \leq5% or \geq95% in all seven, but in the two local models they also reduce s by 43% and 68%, whereas in the harnessed configurations the point estimates of the change lie between ‑3.7 and +0.5 points. An elicitation format that reduces extreme values thus need not preserve sensitivity to evidence; the two should be tested separately. Because δ‑NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about how large an update should be. Code, data and the frozen plan: https://github.com/asj252/llm‑judgment‑studies

PaperId: 393, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27728.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiyoung Lim, Jee-Hyong Lee
Title: CILA: Confusion-based Instance-wise Logit Adjustment for Long-Tailed Recognition
Abstract:
Real‑world datasets are inherently class‑imbalanced, leading models to favor majority classes and struggle with minority ones. Existing logit adjustment methods address this by modifying logits based on class frequencies, but their class‑wise adjustments ignore instance‑wise confusion and often suppress informative signals from confusing non‑target classes. This results in insufficient learning of such classes, increased prediction uncertainty, and limited generalization. To address this, we propose two complementary methods. First, Confusion‑based Instance‑wise Logit Adjustment (CILA) adaptively adjusts logits based on instance‑wise confusion between the target and non‑target classes, restoring informative gradients that class‑wise adjustment suppresses. Second, Batch‑adaptation Noise‑Injection (BNI) perturbs the target logit during training, extending the confusion‑aware update to correctly classified but near‑boundary samples that the penalty alone cannot reach. CILA is a loss‑agnostic plug‑in module that can be seamlessly integrated into existing long‑tailed learning methods, and consistently improves performance across multiple benchmarks. Our code will be available at https://github.com/maya0395/CILA.

PaperId: 394, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27726.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhipeng Cao, Taoran Wu, Weiru Cui, Luke Ong, Bai Xue
Title: Anytime-Valid Runtime Monitoring of Learned Barrier Certificates
Abstract:
Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime‑valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed‑loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier‑drift condition is formulated as an episode‑wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite‑sample false‑alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite‑horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime‑validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert‑AI/runtime‑barrier‑monitor.

PaperId: 395, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27725.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiushu Li, Haoran Wang, Yumeng Liu, Zhiyang Dou, Yuan Liu, Yuexin Ma, Cheng Lin
Title: World2HOSI: A Multi-Expert Harness for Long-Horizon Human-Object-Scene Interaction Generation
Abstract:
Long‑horizon human‑object‑scene interaction (HOSI) is central to embodied AI, animation, and game development. Existing human‑object interaction (HOI) and human‑scene interaction (HSI) models excel in their respective domains, but none alone covers tasks requiring multiple interaction skills. Training unified HOSI models is hindered by scarce and costly data. We introduce World2HOSI, a multi‑expert orchestration harness that generates continuous HOSI data from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes and natural language instructions. Our key insight is that long‑horizon HOSI hinges not on a stronger single model but on orchestration. Given a shared, structured scene state and an orchestration harness grounded in it, existing experts can jointly accomplish tasks beyond the reach of any of them alone. World2HOSI realizes this insight as a closed loop around a persistent scene state built from decoupled background and object assets. A harness plans action stages over this state, invokes experts via their native conditioning interfaces, and writes each action's effects back, so that every invocation is grounded in the evolving world. To reduce physical artifacts, bounded residual optimization and contact‑driven physics simulation further ensure the physical plausibility of human motion and object manipulation, respectively, while preserving interaction intent. Experiments and a perceptual user study show that World2HOSI achieves the best task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated HOSI tasks, while generating more diverse data.

PaperId: 396, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27720.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hayden Moore, Abhinav Verma, Anshuman Dutt
Title: Tracing Recurrent and Emergent Hallucination Patterns in Decomposed Text-to-SQL Generation
Abstract:
Large language models can achieve strong Text‑to‑SQL benchmark performance while still producing schema and query‑logic errors. Most evaluations characterize such failures only in the final generated query, making it difficult to determine whether a related error was also observed in an earlier, simpler step or appears only at the final stage. We present a drill‑down evaluation framework that decomposes Text‑to‑SQL queries into progressively more complex executable sub‑queries and corresponding natural‑language questions, allowing rule‑based hallucination categories to be examined across a generation path. We distinguish recurrent hallucinations, in which the same rule‑based category is observed in an earlier step and again in the final query, from emergent hallucinations, in which the category is observed at the final step without an earlier detection in the same path. Across five LLMs evaluated on an expanded BIRD‑mini benchmark, several categories show appreciable recurrence probabilities, while clause abuse shows comparatively higher conditional emergence. Under the conversational‑history condition, recurrence probabilities are generally higher and emergence probabilities are generally lower. These observations indicate that the two conditional measures do not move uniformly in the same direction under additional context and motivate trajectory‑level analysis in addition to final‑output evaluation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available in the project repository. https://github.com/HaydenMM/bird‑mini‑drilldown

PaperId: 397, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27712.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Injae Kim, Minseok Joo, Jihwan Park, Sehyung Kim, Minseong Bae, Hyunwoo J. Kim
Title: RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
Abstract:
Feed‑forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes from images in a single forward pass, making it well‑suited to applications that must operate within limited resource budgets. To further improve its practicality, recent budget‑controllable FF3DGS methods allow the number of Gaussians to be adjusted at inference, so that the output meets a given storage limit or rendering‑latency constraint. However, these methods overlook the cost of inference itself: to produce a representation with the target number of Gaussians, they first predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, requiring nearly constant latency and peak memory regardless of the budget. We therefore propose RLSplat, a resource‑linear budget‑controllable FF3DGS framework whose representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget is reduced. Instead of pruning or selection, RLSplat learns a Gaussian allocation policy that distributes the budget across local scene regions, so that exactly the requested number of Gaussians is generated. These Gaussians are then refined through resource‑linear Gaussian decoding, in which each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found via an efficient hierarchical neighbor search, so that the decoding cost decreases linearly with fewer Gaussians. In zero‑shot evaluation, RLSplat outperforms prior budget‑controllable methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4× fewer Gaussians, while running up to 4.1× faster with 9.6× less peak memory at low budgets.

PaperId: 398, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27704.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ruoyu Wang, Jiahan Li, Yong Liu, Kexin Zhang
Title: VEOcc++: Learning Persistent Voxel Feature Maps for Embodied Online Semantic Occupancy Mapping and Offline Refinement
Abstract:
Semantic occupancy mapping supports embodied perception during exploration and detailed scene understanding afterward, giving rise to two complementary requirements: online incremental mapping for maintaining an up‑to‑date global map under causal constraints, and offline global map refinement for improving the completed scene representation with additional computation. We present VEOcc++, a unified voxel‑centric framework that connects both stages through a persistent sparse voxel feature map. During exploration, the map expands with newly observed regions and integrates aligned local features through reliability‑guided updates, while context‑aware decoding produces the current semantic occupancy map. After exploration, cached local features are consolidated as complementary evidence and combined with the completed online representation for multi‑scale spatial refinement. On EmbodiedOcc‑ScanNet, VEOcc++ achieves 67.12% IoU and 58.40% mIoU, establishing new state‑of‑the‑art performance for online incremental mapping. With the local predictor fixed, our online mapping pipeline outperforms VEOcc fusion by 3.70 IoU and 3.74 mIoU points, demonstrating substantial gains from the proposed global mapping design. Offline global map refinement further improves the completed map to 67.79% IoU and 59.37% mIoU using only the observations acquired during exploration. Zero‑shot deployment on a mobile robot further demonstrates transferability to unseen environments, onboard feasibility, and scalability to large‑scale indoor mapping. Project page: https://wryzju.github.io/VEOccpp/.

PaperId: 399, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27696.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jinghan Gao, Siyu Wang, Dongyu Feng, Yiyuan Pan, Rong Xiong
Title: PanoGraphGS: Unifying Panoptic Segmentation and Hierarchical 3D Scene Graphs with Gaussian Splatting
Abstract:
3D scene graphs support language‑guided navigation by organizing physical entities and their containment and spatial relations into hierarchical maps. Building such structured maps requires a scene representation that consistently distinguishes semantic regions and object instances across viewpoints. To this end, we present PanoGraphGS, a unified framework that integrates panoptic 3D Gaussian representation learning with hierarchical 3D scene graph construction. The framework learns semantic and instance features on shared Gaussian geometry. Prototype‑based semantic learning and association‑based instance learning produce consistent panoptic predictions across viewpoints. The learned representation supports novel‑view panoptic segmentation and direct Gaussian‑level panoptic decoding. A semantic‑aware scene graph module further recovers a floor‑room‑stuff‑object hierarchy with containment and spatial relations. We further release NaviGS, a real‑world dataset for panoramic scene understanding. The dataset provides 3DGS, mesh, RGB, semantic, and depth data. For 3D scene graph identification, PanoGraphGS outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in object‑node accuracy by more than 50% points on average across Replica and NaviGS. PanoGraphGS also achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance among the evaluated methods in 2D panoptic segmentation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of PanoGraphGS in both hierarchical 3D scene understanding and 2D panoptic segmentation. The project website is available at: https://github.com/gaojh0333/PanoGraphGS.

PaperId: 400, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27692.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziwei Zhao, Yuhang Liu
Title: A Principled Optimal Transport Framework for Frame Selection in Long Video Understanding
Abstract:
Long‑video understanding with multimodal LLMs is fundamentally constrained by the mismatch between video length and the model's limited visual context budget, making frame selection essential for practical reasoning. Existing query‑aware methods typically rely on heuristic pipelines: they assign one‑dimensional query‑conditioned scores to frames and then apply sampling, ranking, or extraction rules to form the final subset. While effective in practice, such methods are generally not derived from an explicit optimization objective and struggle to capture the heterogeneous evidence required for complex reasoning. In this paper, we revisit long‑video frame selection from a principled optimization perspective. We formulate it as a structured evidence‑allocation problem and propose OTFS, an optimal transport framework that maps multiple evidence sources onto video frames. To reflect the asymmetry of this problem‑‑‑important evidence should be preserved, whereas redundant frames need not absorb mass‑‑‑we instantiate this view with a semi‑unbalanced entropic optimal transport objective and an efficient solver, OTFS‑Sinkhorn. Combined with an exact dynamic program for coverage‑aware subset extraction, OTFS yields a practical two‑stage training‑free pipeline. We further show that, in the single‑source case, our formulation induces a Gibbs‑type distribution over frames, making Q‑Frame's temperature‑scaled distribution a special case of our framework while also providing a broader perspective for understanding related prior methods. Experiments on three long‑video understanding benchmarks show that OTFS consistently outperforms strong training‑free baselines. Codes are available at https://github.com/barry664/OTFS.

PaperId: 401, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27670.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Thai Nguyen Van, Ibrahim Khan, Mury Fajar Dewantoro, Pratch Suntichaikul, Hai Van Pham, Ruck Thawonmas
Title: Reusing Multimodal Agents: Efficient Evaluation of Sound Designs in Games
Abstract:
This paper introduces a novel framework for efficiently evaluating in‑game sound designs using multimodal learning and reinforcement learning. Sound design significantly influences gameplay and accessibility; however, objective evaluation methods, defined here as automated assessments based on agent performance rather than human ratings, often require retraining agents from scratch for each sound design. Our approach first pre‑trains a multimodal encoder that encodes visual and auditory information into a shared latent space. A reinforcement learning agent is then trained using this latent representation. We fine‑tune the multimodal encoder for each sound design while keeping the trained policy fixed, allowing us to isolate the effects of sound changes on agent behavior. To evaluate the proposed method, we conducted experiments on games from multiple genres, comparing the performance of blind agents (agents using only sound input) under various sound designs. Experimental results suggest that this approach can detect differences in agent performance caused by degraded or altered sound design. Moreover, we significantly reduce the computational cost compared to retraining the agent from scratch. Experimental results suggest that this approach provides a practical and scalable solution for evaluating in‑game sound designs. The source code, data and supplementary document are available: https://github.com/thainv0212/tog‑reusing‑agents.

PaperId: 402, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27662.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Deyuan Liu, Zecheng Wang, Xuanyi Liu, Jungang Li, Yihao Hu, Mingjie Tang, Bryan Dai, Jie Fu
Title: When Can LLM Reasoning Reliably Reuse Intermediate Results?
Abstract:
Sampling complete solutions gives large language models more chances to solve a problem, but each attempt starts again. For tasks with several subproblems, all required answers must be correct in the same attempt. Retaining intermediate results can avoid repeating correct work, but errors in those results may affect later attempts. We study when this reuse is reliable and how much computation it requires. For local retries that stop when no candidate passes within the retry budget, we give conditions for correct completion and bound the average number of attempts. We also show how checking cost and the chance of passing a check affect total computation. Experiments across eight reasoning models examine composite mathematics and arithmetic. Across four DeepSeek models, average success on the second subproblem is 36.2 percent without first‑subproblem context, 57.2 percent with its answer, and 58.3 percent with its reasoning and answer. These scores measure second‑subproblem coverage and include continuations made when selection fails. Arithmetic experiments show that similar first‑attempt accuracies can lead to very different coverage after repeated attempts. Code is available at https://github.com/SempraETY/Intermediate‑State‑Reuse.

PaperId: 403, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27652.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wonsup Shin, Jingu Kim
Title: Corpus Quality Improves, Retrieval Utility Does Not: An Ablation of Preprocessing and Refinement in a Speech-to-QA Pipeline
Abstract:
Practitioners building training corpora with a pipeline of language models keep a preprocessing or refinement (post‑process) stage when switching it on raises the corpus quality. We ablate a production pipeline that turns conference speech into question‑answer pairs. The preprocessing stage rewrites the transcript, and the refinement stage filters the generated pairs. Switching each on and off gives four corpora from the same 40 Korean medical and finance sessions. On the corpus itself, quality rises as the stages switch on. Four LLM judges and six human domain experts rank the four corpora the same way, and the fully refined corpus leads by +0.18 and +0.22 on a 1‑5 scale. We then ask whether that gain carries downstream. We supply each corpus to six models at inference and measure retrieval accuracy. The ranking does not hold. Enabling the transcript rewrite lowers retrieval accuracy by 0.061, the only stage effect that survives correction for multiple comparisons. That stage also reads the whole session, so it almost doubles the cost of one. With both stages on, accuracy does not change. An equivalence test we declared in advance confirms this. The corpus itself is clearly valuable. It lifts retrieval accuracy from 0.231 to 0.748 in every model and domain we test. More than a third of its pairs carry knowledge that neither of two frontier models produces on its own. On our data, the null does not come from weak corpora. A rising score on a rubric of this kind did not predict what the corpus holds for a model.

PaperId: 404, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27645.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xu Hu, Haoming Li, Yuxiang Wang, Jinxin Yang, Kangshuo Li, Licheng Wang, Dingyi Kang, Jiayu Song, Tianhao Wang, Zhanhua Hu, Xu Yang, Qiannan Li, Bingzhe Li, Feng Chen
Title: CUA-Recovery: Benchmarking Error Recovery in Long-Horizon Computer-Use Agents
Abstract:
As computer‑use agents (CUAs) move to long‑horizon workflows spanning multiple applications, undetected errors can silently corrupt persistent state and cause cascading failures in subsequent actions. Reliable error detection and recovery have become critical bottlenecks for building robust CUAs. However, existing benchmarks focus primarily on end‑to‑end task performance, providing limited insight into whether agents can detect and recover from errors during execution. The few benchmarks that evaluate recovery rely largely on manually injected errors, which may not reflect the types or horizons of failures induced by real agent policies. We introduce CUA‑Recovery, a benchmark comprising test and training suites across multiple desktop applications. We construct it using ReRail, a framework for synthesizing long‑horizon tasks and trajectories in a persistent desktop environment. ReRail composes MyPCBench tasks into new long‑horizon workflows with executable ground truth, collects verifier‑confirmed failures from multiple policies, and turns them into verified recovery trajectories. CUA‑Recovery comprises a human‑verified test suite of 2,250 erroneous states over 100 tasks and a training suite of 8.6K trajectories over 377 tasks. Evaluation on the test suite shows that agents struggle both to recognize inherited errors and to complete the task. Across six agents and six takeover depths, Error Awareness Rate (EAR) reaches at most 44.0% and Pass@3 at most 25.5%. After fine‑tuning Qwen3.5‑35B‑A3B on the training suite, its average EAR rises from 19.9% to 35.2% on held‑out recovery states, and its Rubric Score goes from 5.0% to 16.1%. It also gains 15.3 points on MyPCBench and 10.8 points on Odysseys for Pass@3, showing that the training trajectories help both with recovery and with completing tasks from a clean start. Our code is available at https://github.com/xu‑hu‑2002/CUA‑Recovery.

PaperId: 405, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27641.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Daisuke Oba, Hiroki Furuta, Naoaki Okazaki
Title: BCT: Bayes-Consistent Tempering for Flow Language Models
Abstract:
Temperature scaling is typically applied as a post‑hoc transformation of model probabilities. In posterior‑induced flow language models, this creates two mismatches. First, posterior tempering implicitly changes both the endpoint distribution and the distribution of intermediate noisy states, while the denoiser remains trained on the original states. Second, the tempered posterior weights are combined with transport dynamics derived for the untempered flow. These mismatches are reflected empirically: lowering temperature improves GSM8K performance much less reliably in flow LMs than in discrete diffusion LMs. We introduce Bayes‑Consistent Tempering (BCT), which makes temperature explicit in both the distributions and dynamics of the generative flow. Its learned realization trains the denoiser on tempered intermediate states and tempers the endpoint distribution using the corresponding tempered dynamics. We also derive training‑free variants for conventionally trained checkpoints. Across hyperspherical flow LMs with two denoiser architectures and a von Mises‑‑Fisher flow LM, BCT improves GSM8K generation across broad temperature ranges and achieves the strongest tempering performance. The gains also extend to Sudoku, demonstrating benefits on tightly constrained generation. At very low temperatures, the learned realization is also markedly more robust than the training‑free variants, supporting temperature as a property of the generative flow across training and inference rather than a post‑hoc probability adjustment. Code and model weights are available at https://daioba.github.io/bct .

PaperId: 406, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27634.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tingxu Han, Wei Song, Ziming Li, Yuchen Chen, Weisong Sun, Zhenpeng Chen, Chunrong Fang, Zhenyu Chen, Yang Liu
Title: Standards-Guided and Dependency-Aware Code-Level Documentation Generation
Abstract:
Automatically generating high‑quality documentation for software repositories remains challenging: existing approaches largely treat documentation as unconstrained text generation, lacking explicit quality specifications, depending heavily on long‑context prompts over raw code, and offering limited support for reproducible evaluation. We argue that code‑level documentation generation should instead be a standards‑guided software engineering task, in which documentation is generated and assessed against explicit, reusable quality requirements derived from authoritative standards. We define code documentation as natural‑language descriptions of repository functions and classes, organized by source‑code path. We present CODEDOC, a standards‑guided and dependency‑aware framework that identifies dependencies between code entities via static call‑graph and AST analysis and constructs dependency‑aware structured prompts combining local code context, repository paths, and documentation criteria drawn from authoritative standards and style guides. We further introduce an interactive LLM‑as‑a‑judge protocol that supplies criterion‑aligned feedback to refine generated documentation along fine‑grained dimensions from formal and practice‑oriented standards. Experiments on ten open‑source Python repositories show that CODEDOC produces higher‑quality documentation than RepoAgent and a long‑context baseline under standards‑aligned evaluation, with relative improvements of 11.6%‑17.0% and 21.4%‑29.6%, respectively, while consuming roughly an order of magnitude fewer tokens per documentation entity than the long‑context baseline. A human study confirms substantial alignment between LLM‑based and human judgments (Spearman's rho = 0.72), and the relative findings hold across different judge LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/ControllableModel/CodeDoc.

PaperId: 407, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27620.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Anmol Pandey, Aditya Jain, Liang Chen, Carsten Maple
Title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents
Abstract:
Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per‑action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single‑trace safety versus relational k‑safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2‑safety hyperproperty with no per‑trace locus of blame, so a per‑action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross‑execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL‑SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per‑action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per‑action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single‑trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.

PaperId: 408, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27617.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tingxu Han, Zijie Shen, An Guo, Lyuke Wang, Chunrong Fang, Zhenyu Chen, Wei Song
Title: Provisioning Robust and Efficient LiDAR Perception for Autonomous Driving
Abstract:
LiDAR‑based 3D object detection is a core perception service for autonomous driving, but deployment requires robustness to point‑cloud corruption while meeting latency and memory requirements. Existing approaches address robustness and resource efficiency separately, resulting in compact detectors that are fragile under corruption or robust detectors that remain costly to deploy. We therefore formulate LiDAR perception provisioning as constructing a detector that remains accurate under point‑cloud corruptions while meeting constraints on inference latency and peak GPU memory. To achieve robustness, we first craft corrupted samples that mimic extreme weather conditions. Then we train candidate detectors offline by ordering clean and corrupted samples by perturbation sensitivity, through which detectors learn more from hard corrupted samples. We estimate perturbation sensitivity using an ensemble of seven heterogeneous 3D detectors by tracking changes in confidence, BEV overlap, and unmatched detections. To improve efficiency, we narrow the network and use offline neighborhood‑density measurements to determine how many points and neighbors each sampling stage processes. We evaluate our method using AP (Average Precision) under clean and corrupted conditions, inference latency, and peak allocated GPU memory. On KITTI for Car detection with PointRCNN, our method improves Moderate AP under corruption by 3.32 points over the original detector while reducing mean latency by 19.8% and peak allocated GPU memory by 53.9%. Across two datasets, two detector architectures, and three object classes, our method improves AP under corruption by 4.03 points on average over the corresponding original detectors, while reducing mean inference latency and peak allocated GPU memory by 14.4% and 38.0%, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/drunklibai/robust‑efficient‑lidar‑perception.

PaperId: 409, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27613.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yubang Wang, Zezheng Huai, Yifei Zhang, Jinhao Wu, Yitong Chen, Haozhe Zhang, Sixian Li, Jingjing Gong, Zhenyang Lin, Ziyang Chen, Xipeng Qiu
Title: Embodied Task Agents Can Perform Fine Manipulation through Tactile In-Context Learning
Abstract:
Can embodied task agents use tactile experience to perform fine manipulation without task‑specific model training? We investigate this capability through Tactile‑ETA, a system that incorporates tactile experience into an embodied task agent through in‑context learning. Successful expert demonstrations show how contact changes during manipulation. We pair each recorded robot movement with its camera views and bilateral tactile observations. We keep tactile observations at the start and end of each movement and add two neighboring time points when the tactile images change markedly in between. The agent combines these demonstrations with current vision, tactile observations, and proprioception to select actions through general‑purpose robot tools, without updating model parameters. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, adding tactile observations to the same two expert demonstrations increases average success from 15.75% to 24.00%, with current sensing and execution interfaces held fixed. Further experiments show that performance depends on the sensory content and representation of demonstrations, while comparing agent models on Lift Bottle reveals substantial differences under the same system configuration. On the real‑robot tasks, demonstrations with aligned visual and tactile observations increase the task success rate from 0% to 60%. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using tactile experience in context for fine manipulation and suggest a path toward extending embodied task agents to additional sensory inputs.

PaperId: 410, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27592.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xingsong Ye, Yongkun Du, Jiaxin Zhang, Chong Sun, Zhineng Chen
Title: Real In, Real Out: What If We Only Use Real Data for Scene Text Editing?
Abstract:
Aiming to modify textual content while preserving the original style, Scene Text Editing (STE) has significant practical value in many applications. STE typically requires paired images before and after editing for training. However, recent approaches rely heavily on synthetic paired data and complex disentanglement strategies. They struggle to faithfully capture the diversity and complexity of natural scenes, often producing artifacts or hallucinations. In this work, we challenge the common practice and investigate whether STE can be driven by turning each real sample into its own paired supervision. Concretely, we explore multiple ways to disrupt the original image (e.g., Crop, Shuffle, Mask) to construct self‑paired training data, and build a strong baseline (TextRIRO) upon a conditional diffusion architecture. Our experiments show that combining character‑column shuffling with image cropping (Shuffle&Crop) effectively destroys text semantics while preserving key style cues, enabling the model to learn editing behaviors directly from the real text image. With this concise yet real‑oriented design, TextRIRO achieves promising performance in both accuracy and visual realism across real‑world benchmarks, substantially mitigating the synthetic‑to‑real domain gap. Furthermore, we leverage TextRIRO to build TextRIRO‑3M, a large‑scale realistic dataset for long‑text recognition by concatenating edited and original images. Experimental results show that training recognition models with TextRIRO‑3M significantly improves recognition accuracy, demonstrating that TextRIRO provides highly useful training resources for downstream tasks. Overall, TextRIRO lifts STE to realistic, reliable, and widely applicable new levels. Code is available at https://github.com/YesianRohn/TextRIRO.

PaperId: 411, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27590.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wonsup Shin, Jingu Kim
Title: Benefit and Cost of Random-Token Replacement under Repeated Data: A Known-Entropy Decomposition and Evidence from Ten Real Corpora
Abstract:
When unique pretraining data is scarce, models see the same tokens many times and are thought to memorize. Random‑token replacement, an input‑corruption augmentation, is one remedy reported to lower validation loss, but a lower loss alone does not reveal which source of error it reduces.
