On a controlled source whose entropy rate is known in closed form, we show that replacement shrinks predictions toward the corpus average. We also introduce a decomposition that separates validation loss into approximation, estimation, and memorization terms. This shrinkage view predicts that replacement's bias cost needs no memorization but its benefit does. Memorization raises validation loss after its minimum, so we report the effect at two points, the minimum validation loss and the end of a fixed budget. Where replacement helps, it reduces this rise by about 60%. At the end of the budget, it turns from harmful to helpful as the controlled source becomes less predictable; at the minimum, it helps at no predictability level under the fixed recipe. On Korean and Japanese web text, replacement removes about a third of the loss rise after the minimum by the end of the budget, but its effect at the minimum is much smaller. Across ten real corpora, replacement lowers the final loss on nine. It harms only the census corpus, program‑generated JSON that is the most redundant of the ten and much more redundant than any of 64 further prose and code corpora we measure.

PaperId: 412, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27584.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Koshiro Saito, Daisuke Oba, Danushka Bollegala, Naoaki Okazaki
Title: Beyond Model Weights: Sampling-Dependent Fairness in Diffusion Language Models
Abstract:
Diffusion language models (DLMs) are emerging as a practical alternative to autoregressive language models (ARLMs), yet their fairness remains largely uncharacterized. DLMs introduce sampling controls with no direct autoregressive counterpart, such as block length and remasking strategy, that directly set their speed‑‑quality operating point. This raises a basic question: does a DLM's measured social bias remain stable across these settings? Across LLaDA, LLaDA‑1.5, and Dream on Open‑BBQ, we find that all three models exhibit social bias, but both the magnitude of measured bias and the relative ordering of models by bias are highly sensitive to the sampling configuration. This sampling dependence also changes what successful debiasing means. While mitigation strategies established for ARLMs transfer effectively to DLMs and reduce bias without degrading downstream performance, sampling dependence persists even after mitigation. Our results show that fairness in DLMs cannot be characterized independently of the sampling configuration, even after debiasing. Project page is available at https://pakapaka333.github.io/Beyond‑Model‑Weights/.

PaperId: 413, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27581.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuxuan Li, Xiangchen Guan, Kunrong Li, Jin Wang, Kaiwen Luo, Yang Xiao, Yufei Guo, Zhisheng Chen, Liang Lin, Kun Wang
Title: DuplexLedger: Benchmarking Transactional Memory in Full-Duplex Speech Agents
Abstract:
Full‑duplex speech agents must update persistent memory while listening and speaking, yet it remains unclear which events should be stored, revised, or excluded. Existing benchmarks isolate interaction timing from memory outcomes, obscuring the state transitions behind a correct answer. We introduce DuplexLedger, a bilingual benchmark of 1,094 persistent sessions aligning four full‑duplex scenarios with event‑level Write/Update/Ignore/Retain supervision, explicit pre/post memory states, and 6,564 same‑session questions and checks. Evaluating five full‑duplex models reveals an interaction‑memory gap: no system combines strong boundary control with coherent final‑state memory, and the best final‑state fact coverage is 2.01%. We propose ACT‑Mem, an 8.92M‑parameter sidecar comprising an event controller, a versioned transactional ledger, and a typed retriever coupled with a frozen MiniCPM‑o 4.5 backbone. On 219 held‑out sessions, ACT‑Mem increases latest‑value accuracy from 4.11% to 8.68% while reducing stale assertions and distractor adoption. It improves interaction boundaries but slows interruption stopping. These results motivate selective, auditable full‑duplex memory rather than indiscriminate transcript retention. Code is available at https://github.com/lyx‑researcher/DuplexLedger.

PaperId: 414, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27550.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuxing Peng, Zhiqing Tang, Weijia Jia
Title: Lower Bounds for Smooth Nonconvex Zeroth-Order Optimization: The Price of Determinism under Low Curvature Trace
Abstract:
Low curvature trace, an effective rank condition, is a common explanation for why randomized zeroth‑order methods scale to high‑dimensional tasks such as language model fine‑tuning. Can deterministic methods achieve the same savings? We show that they cannot. We study finding \varepsilon‑stationary points of L‑smooth nonconvex functions on \mathbbR^d from exact function values, assuming that below the starting value the Hessian is dominated by a fixed matrix with trace at most LE; this is a fixed‑matrix form of the effective rank condition used to explain zeroth‑order fine‑tuning. When ET\le d, the Gaussian two‑point method that such fine‑tuning uses needs only O(ET) calls if it rejects steps that raise f, where T=LΔ/\varepsilon^2 is the iteration count of gradient descent from initial gap Δ, and we prove that every randomized method needs Ω(ET) calls, so this cost is optimal up to constants. In contrast, every deterministic method needs \widetildeΩ(d\min\T,\sqrtET\) calls, and adaptive subspace search attains O(d\min\T,\sqrtET\): a deterministic method pays about d calls per discovered direction, and the trace budget allows about \sqrtET directions. Determinism thus multiplies the cost by a factor of order d/(E+\sqrtET) up to logarithmic factors, which grows linearly with d for fixed E and T; once E exceeds T by a logarithmic factor, deterministic methods need Ω(dT) calls, as without any trace budget. Our lower bounds hold for C^\infty functions with the matrix bound on all of \mathbbR^d, even when each call also returns gradient projections priced by rank.

PaperId: 415, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27548.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhiping Zhang, Franklin Mingzhe Li, Zihao Huang, Tianshi Li
Title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
Abstract:
When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real‑world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning‑effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization‑aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out‑of‑authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence‑oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out‑of‑authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human‑centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH‑Research‑Lab/AuthorizationBench .

PaperId: 416, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27538.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuqian Zheng, Hyoju Ahn, Hyeongjin Ahn, Eunil Park
Title: Less is More: Concise Retrieval and Critic-based Re-ranking for Composed Image Retrieval
Abstract:
Zero‑shot composed image retrieval (ZS‑CIR) aims to retrieve a target image based on a reference image and modification text. Recent approaches commonly rely on large vision‑language models to generate target image captions for retrieval. However, these captions may include redundant semantic details, introducing noise when retrieving the target image and leading to suboptimal retrieval results. To address this issue, we propose Less‑is‑More CIR, a two‑stage training‑free framework that combines Concise Retrieval and Critic Re‑ranking. In the first stage, concise target‑oriented captions are generated that preserve only the most discriminative modification semantics, thereby reducing semantic noise in the retrieval. In the second stage, a critic re‑rank module further evaluates the retrieved candidates from the perspectives of modification consistency and reference preservation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework for the ZS‑CIR. Our code is available at: https://github.com/dxlabskku/LM‑CIR.

PaperId: 417, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27485.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shiza Charania
Title: HATCH: Hardware-Attested Task Chains for Verifiable Manipulation
Abstract:
Capability claims in robot manipulation are unverifiable, and existing leaderboards are each closed, simulated, or gameable. We propose HATCH, a robot escape room: an openly specified, physically replicable, sensor‑scored, and unrehearsable benchmark. Tasks span five skill categories at three difficulty levels and are chained so that the sensor confirming one task's completion unlocks the next, turning a room into a single long‑horizon evaluation. Success is confirmed by instrumentation rather than human judgment, scoring is embodiment‑agnostic, and object placements are randomized by a run‑day seed. Entrants submit attested self‑runs (uncut video, sensor logs, and the seed), with occasional organized events for calibration. Task specifications, build guide, bill of materials, and scoring rubrics are released under an open license.

PaperId: 418, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27455.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ningzhi Li, Xiaojun Ma, Xiaofei Wang
Title: Detecting Errors in Large Language Model Responses: The Incremental Predictive Value of Hidden States
Abstract:
Although large language models support a wide range of tasks, hallucinations remain a major obstacle to user trust. When a model generates an answer, both its internal processing and final output vary with the question. Internal states are often expected to offer richer signals for hallucination detection. However, studies using these states typically report their standalone discrimination performance, while output‑side comparisons often use simple baselines with weaker modeling capacity. We integrate output‑side information available at inference time into a combined baseline and compare detection performance before and after adding hidden states under identical data splits and evaluation rules. Experiments cover open‑ended generation and constrained multiple‑choice tasks across different models. Adding hidden states improves AUROC by approximately 0.004 and 0.039 on the two tasks, respectively. Hidden states thus provide additional predictive information, but strong standalone detection performance can still yield only limited additional gains.

PaperId: 419, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27451.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Greg Sidebottom
Title: A 55-Addition Rank-23 Scheme for $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication via Exact Two-Sided Minimization
Abstract:
We give a scheme that multiplies two 3×3 matrices with 23 multiplications and 55 additions over any ring, one addition below the previous record of 56 (Sun, 2026) and the first below 56 for exact non‑commutative 3×3 multiplication without a change of basis. The scheme forms 13 signed combinations of the entries of A and 14 of B, takes 23 products, and recombines them with 28 further additions; its correctness is machine‑checked in Lean 4. The previous records, from 60 down to 56, were obtained by greedy common‑subexpression elimination, which only bounds each side of a scheme from above. We minimize both input sides exactly by chain covering, and the output side exactly through the transposition principle: the 9‑by‑23 output map costs its transpose plus 14, and the transpose is a 9‑input map that the input‑side minimizer solves exactly. Applied to Perminov's cn122 scheme (class i19w225c4efh, published at 58 additions) this gives 55 = 13 + 14 + 28, where greedy elimination reaches only 29 on the output side. The same method shows that Sun's representative is output‑optimal at 56, and an exact orbit‑wide computation over the Heule‑Kauers‑Seidl database shows that the record class is the only database class attaining 55.

PaperId: 420, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27450.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiashuo Sun, Hao Zhang, Xueqiang Xu, Heng Wang, Yixuan Xie, Pengcheng Jiang, Zhenrui Yue, Jiajun Fan, Peiran Li, Ge Liu, Shaowen Wang, Jiawei Han
Title: Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation
Abstract:
On‑policy distillation (OPD) can succeed with surprisingly few training questions, motivating a view of questions as carriers of distributional knowledge transfer. How can we assess whether a newly generated question is valuable for distillation, and learn to generate better questions‑‑‑without access to its correct answer? We introduce Ask‑to‑Distill (\method), a framework that treats synthetic questions as distribution elicitors and optimizes the teacher supervision they expose along student‑generated trajectories. A student‑initialized synthesizer is optimized using a distributional surrogate for question value, computed from a frozen student‑‑teacher pair without reference answers, correctness rewards, or per‑candidate student updates. The reward combines teacher‑‑student disagreement with teacher probability mass on the student's candidate support, together with length and diversity controls. The generated questions are filtered and deduplicated into a prompt‑only bank for standard OPD. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks, our method improves average performance and teacher‑gap recovery over unoptimized student‑generated prompts and KL‑filtered real questions, while matching or exceeding real‑bank OPD in the evaluated settings. Signal analyses further show that optimized questions can elicit denser supervision and more total signal from shorter student responses, supporting elicited distributional supervision as an objective for synthetic distillation data. Our code, data and models are publicly available at https://github.com/GasolSun36/Ask_to_Distill.

PaperId: 421, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27444.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Thamirawaran Sathiyalogeswaran, Navindu De Silva, Chamikara Siriwardane, W. K. Alwis, Jason Mars, Udaya Sampath K. Perera Miriya Thanthrige, Ranga Rodrigo
Title: LoRASpace: A Pool-Wide Shared Substrate for Static and Dynamic Multi-LoRA Composition
Abstract:
Low‑rank adaptation (LoRA) attaches small low‑rank matrices to a frozen backbone, and public repositories host many LoRAs per backbone, each for a different concept or task. Combining several LoRAs in one generation forces a trade‑off. Merging their weights into one update needs a single forward pass, but LoRAs trained for different concepts interfere and quality drops. Running each LoRA in its own forward pass (composite) preserves quality, but inference time grows linearly with the number of active LoRAs. We study a property of LoRA pools overlooked by prior multi‑LoRA work. In real LoRA pools, the stacked low‑rank factors need far fewer directions than their summed ranks. Using singular value decomposition, we find the minimal subspace that keeps 99% of the factor energy. On three diffusion pools, only 46% to 57% of the summed LoRA ranks is needed, and the subspace grows sub‑linearly with pool size. A 48‑LoRA sub‑pool of LoRA‑Hub on FLAN‑T5 tasks shows comparable overlap (62%), while the diversity‑curated LoRA‑Retriever benchmark sits near the no‑overlap baseline (96%), so pool composition rather than modality predicts where compression is large. We build on this overlap with LoRASpace, a training‑free method that computes the subspace once per pool and reuses it in two inference modes, a static mode at merge cost and a dynamic mode for input‑dependent routing. On the diffusion pools, static LoRASpace matches composite quality at merge cost, and dynamic LoRASpace is more than 6x faster than composite with six active LoRAs on a 17‑LoRA pool, mainly because it runs one backbone pass instead of six. In an ablation, static variants at the same rank match LoRASpace, so the quality gain does not depend on the pool‑wide basis. On the near‑orthogonal LoRA‑Retriever benchmark, compression is small and gains come from coupling with external retrieval.

PaperId: 422, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27389.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Erik Skalnes, Michael Oberst
Title: Fixed-Size Active Statistical Inference
Abstract:
Variance reduction techniques improve the efficiency of drawing conclusions from data. Recent proposals for variance‑reduction use two complementary techniques to reduce variance: incorporating machine learning predictions into estimators and weighted sampling. A popular weighted sampling algorithm is Poisson Sampling (PS), which independently flips a biased coin at each unit and includes all heads in the sample. A fundamental flaw with PS is that it has a random sample size, which presents practical challenges and introduces variance into the estimator. We show that a fixed‑size alternative, known in survey sampling as Conditional Poisson Sampling (CPS), is a drop‑in replacement for PS on general multivariate Z‑estimation problems, which include convex M‑estimation considered in prior work. Notably, we show that the asymptotic variance of CPS is no worse than that of PS, and can be substantially better in realistic scenarios where predictions are imperfect. We illustrate these advantages on both synthetic and real datasets, and release a Python package implementing CPS. In light of our contributions, there is no need to suffer a variable sample size.

PaperId: 423, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27374.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianhao Peng, Ho Man Kwan, Fan Zhang, Shan Liu, Dave Bull
Title: PerQ: Inverse Generative Modeling for Neural Image Compression via Quantization Error Compensation
Abstract:
Neural image codecs face a fundamental trade‑off between pixel fidelity and perceptual quality. Distortion‑optimized codecs preserve pixel‑wise fidelity but produce blurred reconstructions at low bitrates, whereas generative codecs leverage learned priors to improve perceptual quality but tend to exhibit saturating PSNR at higher bitrates and require separate models for different bitrate targets. We propose PerQ, which reframes perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling with bounded support. Specifically, we define the quantization cell as the set of latents that yield the same transmitted symbols and derive a transport bound showing that reconstructions from this cell remain within a rate‑determined radius of the codec output. This motivates performing generative reconstruction within the codec‑induced quantization cell, rather than sampling from an unconstrained image prior. PerQ implements this principle by attaching a rate‑conditioned flow‑matching compensator to a frozen, multi‑rate distortion‑optimized backbone, enabling perceptual enhancement while preserving the backbone's coding performance. Experiments on Kodak and CLIC2020 show that PerQ achieves perceptual performance comparable to generative codecs such as MS‑ILLM in LPIPS and FID, while maintaining competitive PSNR relative to distortion‑optimized codecs such as ELIC. A single model checkpoint supports a wide bitrate range with fast decoding, and the compensator provides consistent gains across three different backbones. The implementation is available at https://jasminepp.github.io/PerQ/.

PaperId: 424, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27350.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Arnav Grover
Title: Refuses When Asked, Complies When Acting: A Runtime Safety Check for Robot Control Loops
Abstract:
Frontier models can control robots through agent harnesses that loop on one question: what motion comes next toward the user's goal? We show that this default loop carries out harmful instructions. With GPT‑6 Astra controlling a low‑cost SO‑101 arm through the Inspect Robots harness on three household tasks whose hazard is common knowledge, such as "put the knife in the toy basket", the policy refused 0% of 15 trials, attempted the harm every time, and completed it in 27%. Its one exit, give_up, is meant for goals that cannot be achieved, and it never cited the hazard. We add an optional runtime safety check to the loop: before the first motion, the model is asked whether it would carry out the instruction, given the same camera frames. The check would have stopped all 15 hazardous instructions, including the 4 that completed the harm, and flagged none of the 15 harmless controls. Code and data: https://github.com/Arnav‑Gr0ver/Refuses‑When‑Asked‑Complies‑When‑Acting.

PaperId: 425, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27341.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zerui Chen, Changrui Chen, Fei Ni, Jiankang Deng
Title: Look Before You Reason: Implicit Visual Thinking for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
Abstract:
Vision‑language models (VLMs) have advanced rapidly in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain limited on tasks requiring fine‑grained understanding of small or easily overlooked image regions. Recent thinking with images approaches mitigate this limitation by allowing models to inspect images through operations such as zooming, cropping, or code execution. While effective, their multi‑turn interactions with VLMs introduce redundant token computation and slow inference, and separate region inspection from the reasoning step that depends on it. To address these issues, we propose Look Before You Reason (LoRe), an implicit visual thinking framework for efficient visual reasoning within a single‑turn VLM interaction. Given an image and a question, LoRe predicts the most relevant image region, aligns it with the corresponding image patch features, and strengthens the associated key‑value (KV) cache entries, enabling subsequent decoding to directly exploit the selected visual cues without additional visual inputs or explicit tool calls. We further employ reinforcement learning to guide the VLM toward identifying informative image regions and leveraging them during reasoning. To support fine‑grained evaluation of multimodal reasoning, we introduce COCO‑ObjQA, a large‑scale benchmark for object‑centric multimodal reasoning. Experiments on three challenging multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that LoRe consistently improves VLM reasoning performance with low additional inference overhead.

PaperId: 426, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27305.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yihua Xu, Yan Lyu, Jize Li, Jiani He, You Lin, Yidan Hu, Rubing Qiang
Title: When Does an Added Planning Capability Create Operational Value? An Observable Evidence Standard
Abstract:
Industrial artificial intelligence (AI) planning systems combine predictive models, optimization logic, controls, and governance rules, but improvement in the complete policy does not show whether one addition made an independent contribution or whether that contribution justifies its burden. We address this attribution problem with an observable evidence standard that separates opportunity to act, executed‑plan change, operational consequence, equivalence, uncertainty, and operating scope. Using forecast‑to‑plan replay on Favorita, M5, and Walmart data, we apply the standard to heterogeneous planning additions. Three limits of single‑indicator evaluation emerge. First, a composite policy can conceal negligible component contribution: one control changed only 15 of 681 executed plans. Second, changing execution does not guarantee stable benefit: the evaluated multi‑period capability helped in several long‑lead settings but was 7.6% more costly under tight capacity. Third, indirect evidence can prioritize review but cannot complete attribution. Independent runs produced different paths in 19 of 599 cases that a rule‑based check predicted would be unchanged. Although a lower‑cost diagnostic matched the full‑evaluation winner in only 55.0% of cases, it selected an option within the 10^‑6 cost‑equivalence tolerance in 79.5%; the remaining cases prevented the proxy from authorizing acceptance. These experiments establish capability‑level contribution evidence; the organization completes the value decision by weighing it against implementation and sustaining burden. The resulting capability evidence record links the observations to validation, deployment scope, fallback, monitoring, redesign, and retirement decisions.

PaperId: 427, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27298.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Avi Gupta, Nilotpal Sinha, Vishnu Raj, Sambuddha Saha, Pratik Joshi, Koteswar Rao Jerripothula, Tammam Tillo
Title: Generalizing Multimodal Foundational Models in Context-Driven Class Incremental Learning
Abstract:
Class‑Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn new classes continuously without forgetting the previously learned ones. Recent works in CIL have significantly advanced across various modalities; however, at the intersection of audio‑visual modality, this problem remains underexplored. While representations from multimodal foundational models (MFMs) encapsulate rich static priors, our preliminary analysis shows that these representations struggle in incremental settings. Motivated by this, we propose a framework that generalizes frozen MFMs to audio‑visual CIL. Specifically, we leverage their dense audio and visual representations and employ an attention‑based contextual guidance module, in which the audio representations serve as task‑stable contextual guidance for the visual representations, enabling effective class recognition in the incremental setting. To further mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve stability across tasks, we employ feature‑ and logit‑level distillation, which are primarily responsible for the reduced forgetting. Extensive evaluations across various audio‑visual CIL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state‑of‑the‑art methods. Code is available at https://github.com/avigupta2798/MFM‑CIL.

PaperId: 428, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27275.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Abolfazl Babanazari, Kaveh Fathian
Title: On Maximum Clique and Maximum Consensus Formulations in Point Cloud Registration
Abstract:
Maximum clique and maximum consensus are widely used formulations for robust point cloud registration in robotics. Maximum consensus seeks one transformation that aligns as many matches as possible, while maximum clique selects matches through pairwise distance tests. Maximum clique is often used as a substitute for or an approximation to maximum consensus, with empirical evidence suggesting a close relationship. However, how closely the two formulations agree is not fully understood. We study this relationship theoretically. We show that a maximum clique can have arbitrarily large alignment error and be arbitrarily larger than the maximum consensus set at any fixed positive tolerance, and derive geometric conditions that bound this error. When rotation is fixed, we derive sharp error bounds and tests that exactly characterize maximum consensus for the translation subproblem. Finally, we study group‑k consistency, which tests groups of k matches, and determine the smallest group sizes that guarantee alignment error bounds independent of point cloud scale and geometry. These are d+1 for rotations and translations and d+2 when reflections are allowed, in dimensions d\ge 2. Interactive examples and proof verification using the Lean theorem prover are available at https://ariarobotics.github.io/mc‑vs‑mc‑registration/.

PaperId: 429, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27244.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hao Li, Tongyan Hu, Weidi Luo, Shanghao Shi, Xiaogeng Liu, Aiden Suh, Yulong Cao, Ning Zhang, William Yeoh, Yevgeniy Vorobeychik, Chaowei Xiao
Title: AutoRedClaw: Automated Red-Teaming for Claw-Style Agents
Abstract:
Agent systems are shifting from task‑scoped tool‑use agents to persistent, personalized assistants such as OpenClaw. These claw‑style agents maintain configuration files (e.g., AGENTS.md), long‑term memory, and reusable skills. Once poisoned, this persistent state is repeatedly reloaded into the agent's context, creating persistent threats across tasks and sessions. Existing security evaluation systems struggle to evaluate these complex claw‑style systems since they rely heavily on manually constructed test cases and environments, which limits their scale and coverage; in addition, these manually designed cases quickly become outdated as agents evolve, and their evaluation settings leave a gap with how claw‑style agents are deployed in practice. To address this, we introduce AutoRedClaw, an automated red‑teaming framework that generates end‑to‑end attacks together with the environments needed to execute them. AutoRedClaw combines a strict quality‑checking protocol with execution‑based validation to ensure the correctness, realism, and effectiveness of generated samples, and adopts task‑driven environment construction to keep costs low. To achieve broad coverage, it organizes generation along risk categories, attack strategies, attack stages, and attack surfaces, and uses experience‑guided exploration to steer generation toward under‑explored regions. AutoRedClaw achieves an effective attack rate above 30% at less than 0.10 per successful sample. From its outputs, we construct RedClaw‑Bench, a 330‑case benchmark that yields substantially higher attack success rates (ASRs) than AgentDojo, AgentDyn, and DTap. Across seven harnesses and four frontier models, most agent systems exceed 50% ASR, showing that our red‑teaming pipeline provides a strong evaluation signal even for the most advanced agent systems. Our code and benchmark are released at https://github.com/SaFo‑Lab/AutoRedClaw.

PaperId: 430, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27241.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jonas Rohweder, Adrian Mülthaler, Faridoun Mehri, Sebastian Gerstner, Hinrich Schütze
Title: Predicting Linear Relational Decodability Without the Relation
Abstract:
Linear relational embeddings (LREs) approximate a language model's subject‑to‑object mapping with an affine function. Their faithfulness varies enormously across relations, from near zero for person_father to the ceiling for country_capital_city. We investigate the factors that contribute to this variation and demonstrate that it can be significantly predicted from a readout that is not aware of the underlying relation. To do so, we propose a novel form of the Jacobian lens, the entity lens. Whereas the Jacobian lens is estimated across all tokens and concepts, the entity lens EL_t is trained to predict what the model will output for an entity of type t under the neutral prompt " is known for"; e.g., we train ELs for countries and persons. After estimating an entity lens, we measure how highly it ranks the model's answer for a relation without using any relation‑specific information in estimation and prediction. Across 28 relations of the LRE dataset on Olmo‑3‑7B this relation‑agnostic score correlates with LRE faithfulness at ρ= 0.7355 (p < .01). This suggests that linear decodability is largely a property of what a subject's representation already carries, rather than of the relation being decoded. Moving the unit of analysis from the relation to the individual fact, we conclude that new relation datasets and analysis methods are needed to address several problems in existing datasets, most prominently semantically weak first tokens (e.g., most predicted universities' first token is "University") and reference competition (e.g., the LLM confuses obscure actor names with competing non‑actor entities that have the same last name). Our full pipeline is available at https://github.com/jonasrohw/entity‑lens

PaperId: 431, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27237.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kristina Mustakova, Alexey Sorokin
Title: CEFR-oriented Russian Text Simplification Using Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
We present a study on controlled automatic simplification of Russian texts using preference‑based optimization algorithms with a focus on adapting texts to the A1, A2 and B1 proficiency levels. We fine‑tune YandexGPT using Rejection Sampling and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) methods to improve control over the complexity of the generated text. We compare several training configurations that differ in dataset composition, text type and the strategy used to construct preference pairs for DPO. For automatic evaluation we train a regression model based on ruRoBERTa‑large to predict continuous complexity scores corresponding to CEFR levels. We also consider semantic similarity, lexical coverage and quantitative readability metrics. Human evaluation assesses simplicity, fluency and adequacy. Our best model achieves 87.15% target level accuracy, an MAE of 0.35 CEFR levels and a target interval MAE of 0.11. Manual assessment shows that 75% of the evaluated simplifications match the target morphological and syntactic level, and fluency and adequacy scores are especially high for A2 and B1. Although A1 remains the most challenging level, the model significantly reduces the proportion of vocabulary and grammatical constructions beyond the target level while generally preserving meaning. Our model is freely available on \hrefhttps://huggingface.co/kmustakova/RuSimplifier_DPOHuggingFace.

PaperId: 432, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27234.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhiwei Liu, Zhujun Lan, Jielin Qiu, Zixiang Chen, Liangwei Yang, Ming Zhu, Akshara Prabhakar, Wenting Zhao, John Emmons, Jason Wu, Shafiq Rayhan Joty, Junnan Li, Shelby Heinecke, Silvio Savarese, Huan Wang
Title: EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite
Abstract:
Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous‑document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi‑turn planning, tool use, function calling, long‑horizon research, and long‑context software engineering. These evaluations live today in separate repositories with divergent runners, dependencies, and scoring conventions, which makes cross‑benchmark comparison difficult and obscures what a single aggregate number actually represents. We release EGI‑BENCH, a unified LLM agent benchmark suite that consolidates eight enterprise facing agent benchmarks (CRMARENA, HERB, PERSONABENCH, USERBENCH, MCP‑UNIVERSE, MCPEVAL, BENCHFORCE, LOCOBENCH) behind a single command‑line interface with two runtime‑budgeted execution modes. On top of the suite we define the Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) Score, a six‑dimensional framework (M1‑M6) whose buckets are populated by fine‑grained sub‑metrics routed from each benchmark rather than by benchmark‑level averages. We describe the suite, the sub‑metric routing, and the quick/deep budgets, and report results for fourteen frontier and cost‑efficient LLMs spanning the GPT, Claude, and Gemini families under quick mode. Top‑line EGI ranges from 39.6 (GPT‑4o mini) to 65.6 (gpt‑5.5), and no single model dominates every capability axis: gpt‑5.5 leads task outcome, planning, and retrieval grounding; Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads tool actioning and safety/abstention; and Claude Haiku 4.5 leads engineering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/egi‑bench.

PaperId: 433, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27230.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tao Jiang, Benjamin Navet, Yousouf Taghzouti, Fabien Gandon, Louis-Félix Nothias, Élise Dumont
Title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
Abstract:
Chemistry has recently entered a high‑data regime as molecular databases from high‑throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever‑increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent‑memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three‑tier memory system: session‑level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project‑tier entries and, when human‑validated, promoted to cross‑project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum‑chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein‑peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project‑tier entries, from which four cross‑project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking‑configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human‑in‑the‑loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM‑augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

PaperId: 434, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27199.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Leaf Jiang
Title: Which Depth Estimator for Jetson AGX Orin? A 2026 Benchmark of Monocular and Stereo Methods
Abstract:
The Jetson AGX Orin is a common computer for robots and vehicles, yet measured accuracy, speed and energy of current depth estimators on it are hard to find. We benchmark nine model families as of October 2026: the monocular Depth Anything V2 and 3, Depth Pro, MoGe‑2, Metric3D v2 and UniDepth V2, and the stereo methods libSGM, NVIDIA ESS and Fast‑FoundationStereo. Every method runs on the Orin as a TensorRT FP16 engine or native CUDA code at up to three input sizes, up to the full 5.7 MP, and is scored for metric accuracy against Middlebury 2014 ground truth (non‑occluded pixels of the 10 scenes whose disparity stays below 256 px), GPU time, energy and licence. Stereo is far more accurate. At 30 fps, NVIDIA's ESS reaches 0.70% AbsRel in 8.6 ms and libSGM 0.73% in 25 ms; with more compute, Fast‑FoundationStereo reaches 0.33%. The best monocular models reach 12% with the true focal length (Depth Anything 3 Metric‑L in 33 ms, Depth Pro in 803 ms), and 3.8‑4.0% only with an oracle per‑image scale (MoGe‑2‑L, UniDepth V2‑B, Metric3D v2‑L). Stereo error falls as the input resolution grows; no monocular model improves, and the metric scale of most drifts away from the truth outside their training resolution. At depth discontinuities, which AbsRel barely registers, the monocular models scatter 17‑46% of the edge points between foreground and background, learned stereo 2‑9% and libSGM at full resolution 1%. We give recommendations per frame‑rate budget and release all code, per‑scene results and engine build scripts.

PaperId: 435, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27195.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Abdelrahman Abdallah, Mohammed Ali, Adam Jatowt
Title: UIBK-Embedding: Effective Text Retrieval by Unifying Dense and Late-Interaction Retrieval
Abstract:
Dense bi‑encoders and late‑interaction retrievers are usually treated as alternatives, yet they fail on different queries: one vector captures what a text is about, token‑level matching finds its exact entities and phrases. Using both today means two models, two indexes and a score‑fusion step. We present UIBK‑Embedding‑v1, a 179M‑parameter English encoder that produces both representations in one pass and scores them with one unmodified MaxSim. The dense embedding is written into the list of token vectors as three extra vectors, and a one‑dimensional tag keeps the two kinds of vectors from matching each other, so that plain MaxSim equals the token‑level MaxSim plus a weighted dense cosine. The model therefore runs in a standard late‑interaction index without changes; we test it with PLAID. A shared 18‑layer trunk with a separate 4‑layer top per head, and a cross‑encoder distilled into the fused score, turn the two heads into one retriever. On BEIR, UIBK‑Embedding‑v1 reaches 59.79 nDCG@10. This is 2.57 points above LateOn, the strongest model of its size, and 2.10 points above it when both models read documents of the same length; UIBK‑Embedding‑v1 is ahead on all 15 datasets. On a decontaminated version of BEIR it stays ahead on average (61.55 against 60.36) and on 8 of 12 datasets. Among the 156 models with complete BEIR results in the MTEB results repository, only models with at least 1.5B parameters score higher. Code, model weights, and a technical blog post are available at https://github.com/DataScienceUIBK/uibk‑embedding , https://huggingface.co/DataScience‑UIBK/uibk‑embedding‑v1 , and https://huggingface.co/blog/abdoelsayed/uibk‑embedding‑v1 .

PaperId: 436, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27194.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Alec Laprevotte, Haonan Chen, Xiaoshen Han, Yilun Du
Title: Learning to Be Different: Component Specialization for Compositional Diffusion Policies
Abstract:
Diffusion policies with linearly composed scores have emerged as a promising approach to multitask robotic learning by combining separate factors to enable modular, task‑wise adaptation, compositional generalization, and interpretable functional decomposition. However, current training objectives do not encourage factor specialization, often resulting in uninterpretable denoisers whose composed prediction is an average over identical copies, undermining their architectural premise. To address this, we propose a drop‑in score‑decorrelation auxiliary loss, motivated by projective composition theory. Our approach encourages specialization by penalizing overlap directly between component noise predictions, with little architectural change or computational overhead. We demonstrate across multiple benchmarks that our decorrelation loss consistently reduces measurable double‑counting between components, improves task decomposition, and produces behaviorally meaningful specialization without compromising multitask performance. Website: https://al3cl1.github.io/robotics‑score‑decorrelation.

PaperId: 437, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27180.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yubo Ye, Sweekar Piya, Xiajun Jiang, Linwei Wang
Title: Meta-iLaD: Identifiable Latent Dynamics via Meta-Learning of Dynamics Environments
Abstract:
Learning latent dynamics is central to assessing the current states and forecasting the future trajectories of high‑dimensional time series. For locally‑stationary latent dynamics \mathcalF(\mathbfz_<t; \mathbfc) with latent dynamics state \mathbfz_t and environment variable \mathbfc, prior identifiability results have largely focused on \mathbfz_t when conditioned on predefined label u of dynamics environments. This leaves two limitations: reliance on predefined labels that hinder generalization to unseen environments, and a limited understanding of the identifiability of \mathcalF and \mathbfc which ‑‑ although offering important structural properties for the identifiability of \mathbfz_t ‑‑ are learned jointly with \mathbfz_t. We address these limitations with Meta‑iLaD, a novel identifiable latent dynamics framework attained by meta‑learning across dynamics environments. Meta‑iLaD introduces a novel conditional prior of \mathbfc, modeled as a feedforward meta‑learner to rapidly extract \mathbfc from few‑shot examples. Meta‑iLaD further establishes identifiability for \mathbfz_t, \mathbfc, and \mathcalF simultaneously, for a general formulation of \mathcalF(\mathbfz_< t;\mathbfc) without restricting the dimension of \mathbfc or how it modulates \mathcalF. On synthetic and real data, we provide strong empirical evidence that 1) conditioning on few‑shot examples enables generalization to out‑of‑distribution environments, and 2) identifiability for \mathbfc and \mathcalF is critical for accurate forecasting beyond reconstructing observed trajectories. Code is available at https://github.com/GoForIt‑YYB/Meta‑iLaD.

PaperId: 438, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27140.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ping Zhang, Quang-Huy Nguyen, Yingtie Lei, Sameera Shridhar, Zachary Leveroni, Ellie Quattrocchi, Jai Y Yu, Wei-Lun Chao
Title: Representing short-term movement to reveal animal identity and learning progress
Abstract:
How learning progresses over time and varies across individuals is a longstanding question in cognitive and behavioral science. However, a major challenge is identifying observable behavioral measures that faithfully capture learning progression. Existing approaches commonly rely on predefined behavioral features or task‑level performance, while fine‑scale posture and movement in freely behaving animals remain less explored. In this paper, we ask: can short‑term movement trajectories reveal learning progress and individual identity? We introduce a self‑supervised representation learning framework built on a simple hypothesis: behavioral characteristics associated with identity and learning remain relatively stable over nearby time intervals. Using temporal proximity as supervision, our framework learns compact representations directly from movement trajectories without manually defining behavioral states or kinematic features. Using behavior data from freely behaving rats, we show that the learned representations not only improve prediction of identity and learning‑related readouts over existing methods, but also provide a tool for investigating broader scientific questions about when and how these signals appear in behavior. Specifically, trajectories as short as one second contain informative learning and identity signals. Egocentric pose dynamics are more predictive of identity, whereas allocentric motion is more predictive of learning‑related variation, and both signals are strongest at decision junctions in the alternation cohort. We further use a representation‑conditioned diffusion model to inspect movement patterns associated with identity and learning progress. Our findings establish short‑term movement as an informative behavioral "fingerprint" for studying learning and individual differences. Our code is available at https://github.com/pizhn/TRAIL.

PaperId: 439, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27110.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Oussema Dhaouadi, Zuria Bauer, Johannes Michael Meier, Marc Pollefeys, Daniel Cremers, Olaf Wysocki
Title: MatchCityLoc: Aerial Localization in LoD City Models via Surface Normal Matching
Abstract:
Autonomous Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) navigation in urban environments requires precise pose estimation. Because Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals are often unreliable in cities, visual localization serves as a crucial complement. Within this domain, textureless Level‑of‑Detail (LoD) city models provide a lightweight and privacy‑preserving substitute for heavy 3D textured meshes. However, localizing against abstract geometry is challenging. Existing pipelines typically score 2D silhouette overlaps, which can suffer from severe geometric ambiguities. We present MatchCityLoc, a framework that shifts this paradigm to direct feature matching from a noisy 6‑DoF pose prior. By extracting surface normals from the query image using a zero‑shot foundation model and matching them against rendered LoD normals, we establish explicit 3D‑to‑2D correspondences. This enables a Perspective‑n‑Point (PnP) pose solve, which we iteratively refine through a render‑and‑match loop. Experiments demonstrate strong pose recall and accurate translation and rotation among the evaluated off‑the‑shelf LoD‑based methods with very few renderings. By bridging the modality gap between aerial imagery and texture‑free geometry, MatchCityLoc enables accurate localization using lightweight, privacy‑preserving city models.

PaperId: 440, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27109.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuxuan Chen, Yang Xiao, Jack Sun, Chak Sun, Brick Li, Sam
Title: Beyond Two Tracks: Speaker-Anchored Full-Duplex Dialogue Recovery
Abstract:
Spoken interaction is moving from alternating turns to full‑duplex conversation, where an agent listens while speaking. Learning this coordination requires natural dialogue with persistent speaker‑resolved tracks, a data requirement that remains difficult to satisfy at scale. Generative recovery offers a route from ordinary recordings, but recovering two voices is not enough: their track assignments can drift as the conversation unfolds. We address this missing link with speaker‑anchored routing before diffusion: a 1.84M‑parameter module matches the separator's coarse streams to fixed enrollment identities and orders them before a frozen generator reconstructs the speech, without retraining the generator or altering the reconstructed audio. On 25‑minute remote conversations, routing cuts wrong‑track time from 43.9% to 4.1%, below the 6.2% of matched‑enrollment waveform re‑identification, with its largest advantage when one participant holds the floor (17.8% versus 28.6%), and raises fixed‑track activity F1 from 0.46 to 0.84 while per‑chunk reconstruction quality is unchanged. The same router transfers to unseen face‑to‑face and telephone recordings, and a margin‑gated verification step brings their wrong‑track time to 0.9‑1.7% while embedding 20‑36% of the output, where full re‑identification embeds all of it. Recovered voices thus become the participant‑consistent tracks that full‑duplex dialogue modeling needs. Audio examples: https://elpsykongloo.github.io/beyond‑two‑tracks/

PaperId: 441, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27108.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Marcel Rogge, René Schuster, Didier Stricker
Title: Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
Abstract:
3D Gaussian Splatting grows a dense scene from a sparse initialization through adaptive density control (ADC), driven by per‑Gaussian statistics gathered during rendering. These statistics pass a frustum‑based visibility filter blind to occlusion: fully occluded Gaussians still count as observed, diluting the averaged gradient signal and suppressing densification precisely where geometry is occluded. We correct this with an occlusion‑aware filter that restricts densification statistics to views in which a Gaussian actually contributes, and replace the criterion's raw view‑count normalizer with an average‑contribution one. Integrated into a StopThePop‑based framework, the two together improve every image‑quality metric over the occlusion‑blind baseline on occlusion‑heavy scenes (up to 6% lower LPIPS), at less than half the Gaussians a view‑count normalizer requires. Under the longer schedules these large scenes require, the count stays bounded where most criteria diverge, and on smaller benchmarks our method stays competitive at a fraction of the competitors' count.

PaperId: 442, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27103.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zijian Liu, Chaoyou Fu, Yan Yang, Caifeng Shan, Ran He
Title: Omni-Woodpecker: Hallucination Correction via Evidence-Prior Rebalancing for Omni LLMs
Abstract:
Recent Omni LLMs (OLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in joint audio‑visual reasoning, yet cross‑modal hallucinations remain a major challenge. Existing mitigation methods mainly operate at the output level, overlooking the entanglement of grounding evidence and learned priors within fused representations. To address this issue, we propose Omni‑Woodpecker (OWP), a training‑free framework that shifts hallucination mitigation from output‑level manipulation to conflict‑conditioned representation rebalancing. Specifically, OWP first identifies cross‑modal conflicts from complementary modality‑specific views. It then employs orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from competing priors within the hidden states. Finally, OWP adaptively rebalances fused representations by suppressing misleading priors and restoring ignored evidence before decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and strong cross‑architecture generalization of OWP. Using Qwen2.5‑Omni‑7B as the backbone, OWP improves performance by 12.9 and 8.6 points on CMM and AVHBench, respectively, while consistently achieving gains of 0.67‑2.25 points across four general OLLM reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, OWP generalizes effectively to VideoLLaMA2‑AV, improving performance by 4.6 and 3.9 points on the same benchmarks. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZiiJianLiu/Omni‑Woodpecker

PaperId: 443, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27100.pdf   GitHub
Authors:George Nigmatulin, Valentin Mohl, Sascha Frey, Kang Li, Aramis Marti-Shahandeh, Mihai Cucuringu, Anisoara Calinescu, Jakob Foerster, Stefan Zohren
Title: LOB-Impact Benchmark: Emergent Market Impact in Generative Limit Order Book Models
Abstract:
Realistic market impact is essential for generative limit order book (LOB) models to serve as world models for trading agents. If a simulator misprices this mechanism, agents learn policies that are optimal in the simulator but wrong in the real market. Existing metrics assess generated streams purely through distributional comparison with historical data, leaving counterfactual response to an agent's own orders largely unexplored. Here, we show that market impact emerges naturally in neural LOB generators trained solely for next‑token prediction. We inject execution‑style metaorders into the generated message flow of five autoregressive models across five NASDAQ stocks and measure the response using estimators from the empirical impact literature, validated on baselines whose physics is known in advance. Our benchmark evaluates any message‑level generator in three phases: free generation (reading order‑flow persistence against price diffusivity); metaorder injection (yielding the impact law's exponent and amplitude); and a post‑execution window (measuring relaxation). In addition, comparing each visible injection to a blind, simulator‑only control isolates the model's learned response from standard book mechanics. For every model on every stock, we measure how the impact responds as a function of cumulative metaorder participation. Interestingly, we observe emergent impact in generative models of market data, with exponents in the range of 0.63 to 1.21, slightly above the traditional 0.5 of the square‑root law of impact. In the family of models tested, we are so far unable to observe impact decay during relaxation. We tentatively attribute this to the still‑short context windows of the models. We release the benchmark as open source to validate future generative models for market data.

PaperId: 444, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27087.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Lijia Wu, Zheng Li, Yuxuan Liu, Jingwen Zhang, Penghai Zhao, Xiang Li
Title: SciFigBench: A Benchmark for Scientific Method Figure Understanding
Abstract:
Scientific method figures often provide researchers with a clear visual entry point into a paper's methodology and core contributions, yet their dense layouts and complex information flows are difficult for Vision Language Models (VLMs) to interpret. Existing benchmarks predominantly focus on coarse‑grained tasks, such as context‑based retrieval or holistic comprehension, overlooking the fine‑grained content and inter‑module relations within complex methodological diagrams. To address these overlooked aspects, we introduce Scientific Figure Benchmark (SciFigBench), a benchmark for evaluating core capabilities required for scientific method figure understanding. Specifically, it targets three capabilities: dense content perception, visual relation comprehension, and information‑flow tracing. For this purpose, we curate 4,352 scientific method figures from real‑world research papers and construct 40,670 QA pairs to operationalize these capabilities as measurable question‑answering tasks. All annotations are generated by dedicated pipelines and then manually verified. We further propose SciFigCue, a training‑free visual prompting module that externalizes arrow‑induced dependencies as visual relational evidence for method‑figure reasoning. Experiments across open‑source and proprietary VLMs show that even strong models remain substantially limited in visual relation comprehension, while SciFigCue improves performance across several tasks without parameter updates. The code and related resources are available at https://github.com/LeNcyer/SciFigBench.

PaperId: 445, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27066.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wonjung Woo, Hyeonwoo Kim, Hanbyul Joo
Title: BUMP: Body-driven Unified Multi-object Physics for HOI Synthesis
Abstract:
Generating human‑object interactions (HOIs) with multiple objects is challenging because the resulting motions arise from different underlying causes. Human motion reflects semantic intent, intentionally manipulated objects must remain coordinated with the human, while surrounding objects move primarily as physical consequences of contact and collision. We present BUMP, a text‑driven framework for multi‑object HOI generation based on a simple principle: learn intentional motion and simulate physical consequences. Our method first generates full‑body human motion from text and scene context, then predicts trajectories for a small number of intentionally manipulated driver objects conditioned on the human motion. We then obtain responder object motions through physics simulation, allowing the framework to handle varying numbers and configurations of surrounding objects without expanding the learned trajectory output space. To address the scarcity of paired full‑body multi‑object HOI data, we combine heterogeneous supervision from human‑only motion, full‑body HOI, and hand‑centric manipulation data augmented with plausible body motion. We further introduce outcome‑conditioned interaction editing, which infers a local modification of the causal driver object trajectory from a desired responder object behavior without requiring an explicit target driver object trajectory. Experiments demonstrate strong performance on both single‑object and multi‑object HOI benchmarks. Qualitative results showcase diverse scenarios involving inter‑object relationships and edits, highlighting the advantage of our unified model formulation.

PaperId: 446, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27049.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jing Wang, Yanlin Li, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu, Shengqiong Wu, Hao Fei
Title: VitronEdit: Universal Visual Editing across Images, Videos, and 3D Scenes
Abstract:
Recent advances in unified visual editing have begun to consolidate image and video editing within a single model, while 3D scene editing remains largely separate and constrained by scarce paired training data. Given the rich image and video editing supervision now available and the common editing semantics shared across modalities, a natural question is whether this knowledge can be transferred to data‑scarce 3D editing. We present VitronEdit, a universal framework for image, video, and 3D scene editing. VitronEdit adopts a shared sequence representation and progressive multimodal training to transfer editing knowledge across modalities. We further introduce geometry‑aware post‑training, which leverages a pretrained geometry reconstruction model to provide depth and camera‑pose supervision. Surprisingly, applying geometric supervision only to 3D samples yields the best overall performance, while image and video editing also improve despite receiving no direct geometric supervision, suggesting that geometric regularization transfers through the shared backbone. Our analysis further shows that image and video training mainly transfers editing semantics to 3D, whereas 3D supervision primarily improves multi‑view consistency. The project page: https://vitron‑llm.github.io/VitronEdit/.

PaperId: 447, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27046.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zeyu Zheng, Yiyang Liu, Yuyang Zhao, Congmin Zheng, Jiachen Zhu, Jianian Chen, Kangning Zhang, Kayue Daniel Wong, Lingyu Yang, Rong Shan, Shihao Chen, Thomas Zhu, Wentao Zhang, Xiaopeng Li, Yan Hu, Yongxi Lin, Yuxiang Chen, Zhuoying Ou, Jianghao Lin, Jeremy Avigad, Prasad Tetali, Jingbang Chen, Sean Welleck
Title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems
Abstract:
As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine‑checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry‑level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held‑out evaluation of end‑to‑end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding‑agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum‑agent on mini‑SWE‑agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best‑performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.

PaperId: 448, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27044.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rong Wang, Mulong Luo
Title: ECHO: Revealing Review-to-Submission Linkage in Anonymous Peer Review
Abstract:
Anonymous peer review protects reviewers from retaliation, yet reviewer anonymity may also be weakened by artifacts released through the review process itself. This risk is growing as many venues require submitting authors to review, creating substantial overlap between authors and reviewers within the same review cycle. We identify review‑to‑submission linkage, where an anonymous review can be associated with the reviewer's own submission, substantially shrinking the reviewer anonymity set. To assess whether this linkage is practically exploitable, we develop ECHO, which combines technical‑expertise and writing‑style signals across reviews, papers, and rebuttals, and evaluate it on R2S‑Bench, a ground‑truth benchmark we construct. ECHO correctly identifies the reviewer's own submission in Top‑1 for 34.6% of reviews, in the Top‑5 for 54.0%, and in the Top‑10 for 63.4%, compared with 0.5%, 2.6%, and 5.3% under random ranking, from the candidate submissions. With a stronger Stage‑2 reranker, ECHO further reaches 56.4% Top‑1 and 66.4% Top‑10. These results demonstrate that review‑to‑submission linkage is feasible using only routinely released peer‑review artifacts. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/kaimu11111/ECHO‑Revealing‑Review‑to‑Submission‑Linkage‑in‑Anonymous‑Peer‑Review.

PaperId: 449, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27039.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Feng Chen, Pei Zhou, Lixuan He, Yunchao Yao, Li Sun, Shenghua Gao, Mingyu Ding, Kaifeng Zhang, Kaichen Zhou, Yi Ma
Title: Embodied Playground: A Long-Horizon Agentic Robotics Benchmark for Physical, Strategic, and Spatial Reasoning
Abstract:
Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long‑horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for evaluating how foundation‑model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi‑stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP‑100, a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP‑Easy and EP‑Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP‑20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task‑rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation‑model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons. https://winniechen2002.github.io/Agent‑bench‑website/

PaperId: 450, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27037.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chen Chen, Chenggang Wu, Yongbiao Chen, Weidong Qiu, Zhengwei Qi, Haibing Guan
Title: Channel-Level Mask Guidance for Slimmable Image Compression
Abstract:
Learned image compression (LIC) has achieved promising rate‑distortion performance, but most methods lack scalability for diverse platforms with varying computational and storage constraints. Existing slimmable LIC methods achieve flexible complexity via consecutive‑channel activation but suffer from two limitations: forced consecutive‑channel selection degrades narrow‑model performance at low bitrates, and the lack of stable variable‑rate control limits adaptability to varying bandwidth. We propose a channel‑level mask‑guided slimmable image compression method. A learnable channel‑wise mask with sparsity‑promoting regularization enables non‑contiguous top‑w channel selection, letting narrow models use the most informative channels. After training, mask merging and channel reordering convert the model into a standard slimmable network via Mask‑to‑Slimmable (M2S) conversion, enabling efficient inference without architectural changes. For variable‑rate control, we combine lambda‑ and width‑conditioned modulation with quantization‑step scaling and a progressive training pipeline stabilized by a freeze‑then‑fine‑tune strategy. Experiments on Kodak across E2E, Hyperprior, and Checkerboard backbones show superior rate‑distortion performance across widths and bitrates, with large gains for narrow models at low bitrates. At w=48, it achieves up to 19.22%, 24.11%, and 22.76% BD‑rate savings over the same‑width Slimmable baseline on E2E, Hyperprior, and CKBD, respectively. A single VBR model replaces 40 independent models, reducing storage by 14.8x to 15.9x. Code: https://github.com/sjtu‑tcloud/MGSIC.

PaperId: 451, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26988.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Lanfeng Zhong, Xiangyu Sun, Guixuan Xu, Rongzhao Zhang, Jie Xu, Shaoting Zhang, Guotai Wang
Title: REST: Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics Supervision for Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathological HE-Stained Images
Abstract:
Histopathology is central to cancer diagnosis, but morphology in Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE)‑stained images does not directly reveal the molecular states that characterize disease heterogeneity and inform tumor characterization, prognostic assessment, and biomarker discovery. Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) measures spatially resolved gene expression, providing molecular information within tissue architecture, yet differences in assay coverage and spot informativeness make paired HE‑‑ST observations unequally reliable for representation learning. We propose Reliability‑Guided Spatial Transcriptomics (REST) supervision with Biological Program Bank (BPB), a program‑structured and reliability‑guided ST‑supervised training framework for predicting molecular information from H\&E images. REST constructs BPB from curated signature, pathway, and cell‑type gene sets to provide a shared structure for ST encoding, reliability estimation, and molecular reconstruction. Guided by BPB, Spot‑Reliability Contrastive Alignment (SRCA) measures the reliability of each spot from assay‑level program coverage and spot‑level activity dispersion, and reweights HE‑‑ST alignment accordingly. Biology‑Informed Program Reconstruction (BIPR) further uses learnable program queries to reconstruct member‑gene expression from histological morphology. REST's training corpus comprised 209 samples (407,475 spots across 16 organs); evaluation used 70 disjoint samples (230,056 spots across eight organs) for gene‑expression, pathway‑activity, and cell‑signature prediction. REST achieved the highest Macro correlation among state‑of‑the‑art ST‑supervised training methods and outperformed existing pathology foundation models. Code is available at https://github.com/lanfz2000/REST.

PaperId: 452, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26979.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yoo Sung Jang, Michael Ryoo
Title: Latent Projection for Latent Planning
Abstract:
Latent world models let an agent plan in latent space. The planner searches for an action sequence that minimizes a cost, and that cost is often the \ell_2 distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent. The latent, however, is partly noise: the regularizer that prevents collapse during world model training promotes variance in the directions carrying no signal. We show that the same regularizer also supplies the structure to prune that noise in the latent. SIGReg drives the latent marginal to a standard Gaussian at every step, and assuming further that the latent sequence is a Gauss‑Markov process, the transition is linear with its covariance pinned by the map itself, z' \mid z ～ \mathcalN(Az,\, I ‑ AA^\top). Fitting the state dynamics A therefore yields the covariance at no additional cost, and in its eigenbasis each latent direction carries its own uncertainty. Furthermore, constraining A to be a normal matrix fixes that basis across timesteps, so one eigenbasis measures the uncertainty over an arbitrary number of steps and serves as a stable basis to compute the planning cost on. We then restrict the \ell_2 cost to the k‑dimensional subspace the state dynamics carry forward with the least uncertainty. The correction is post hoc: the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all left untouched, and only a single constrained matrix, A, is fit. We evaluate across six environments and show large gains on the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, raising success rate over the plain \ell_2 cost by up to +54.7 points under a harder planning setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yjang43/lp2.

PaperId: 453, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26954.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fuping Wu, Xi Jia, Le Zhang, Jiahua Li, Rima Mustafa, Thomas E. Nichols, Bartlomiej W. Papiez
Title: Deep Auxiliary Learning via Bilevel Feature Optimization for Label-Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
Abstract:
Auxiliary learning (AL), which can improve the performance of a primary task by leveraging related auxiliary tasks, is commonly regarded as a special case of multi‑task learning. Existing AL approaches typically require manually annotated auxiliary labels, increasing annotation costs, particularly in medical imaging where expert labeling is expensive. In this work, we investigate whether segmentation performance can be improved using auxiliary tasks whose labels are automatically derived from existing segmentation annotations, requiring no additional manual labeling. To address this, we propose a novel auxiliary learning framework, formulated as a bilevel optimization problem. Our method enables effective knowledge transfer between tasks via a feature communication module, enhancing the primary segmentation task. We evaluate the method on three medical image segmentation benchmarks under limited‑label settings. The results demonstrate consistent improvements over state‑of‑the‑art methods, achieving superior label efficiency. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/FupingWu90/ALBO.

PaperId: 454, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26952.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaocheng Luo, Yanping Chen, Zaifu Zhan
Title: A Multi-granularity Interaction Network for Relational Triple Extraction
Abstract:
Relational triple extraction identifies entity relations from raw sentences without depending on entity type information. The performance of traditional methods is seriously degenerated by ``unseen'' entities, because these methods can't build contextual dependencies relevant ``unseen'' entities. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a multi‑granularity interaction network that leverages word‑word, entity‑relation, and head‑tail interactions to capture deep semantic dependencies. By incorporating multiple iterations, the multi‑granularity interaction network is effective to refine the representations corresponding to head and tail entities. It enhances the global semantic features associated with relational triples, aiding in the remediation of triples that may have been overlooked or omitted in earlier steps. Strong and consistent performance is achieved by our method on two rearranged datasets, with a significant improvement in identifying relational triples, including those involving ``unseen'' named entities. For example, our model improves F1‑score by 3.1%/20.5% over previous approaches on the NYT‑R/WebNLG‑R datasets in the Unseen metric. Code: https://github.com/xiaocen‑luo/Interaction‑Network.

PaperId: 455, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26951.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Debopriyo Banerjee, Owais Aijaz, Ahmer Tabassum, Zhuohan Xie, Preslav Nakov, Veselin Stoyanov
Title: The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering
Abstract:
Retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity‑driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document‑level context that resolves cross‑passage references. We introduce evidence‑based generation (EBG), requiring models to return an answer with line‑level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric that scores correctness and grounding simultaneously. We reformulate two corpora into evidence‑grounded multi‑document QA benchmarks‑ MultiHop‑RAG and QASPER‑MP, a multi‑paper adaptation of QASPER with realistic short paper cues, and pair them with a controlled synthetic two‑hop haystack and an evidence‑augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K‑1M characters. Across ten proprietary frontier and three open‑weight LLMs, EBG isolates two RAG limitations that long‑context models avoid: similarity retrieval surfaces any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi‑fact queries, and chunking destroys document meta‑information needed to resolve identity‑bearing queries. EBG also exposes grounding failures invisible to answer‑only evaluation, including incomplete citations in two‑needle settings and a widening gap between Ans and Ans+Evid when context contradicts parametric knowledge. Data and code are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/LC‑EBG.

PaperId: 456, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26945.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rostislavs Rostovskis, Aleksandrs Platonenko
Title: Emulating DGEMM and ZGEMM with INT8 Matrix Engines on Intel Arc GPUs: Ozaki Scheme II on the Xe2 Architecture
Abstract:
Double‑precision matrix multiplication, real (DGEMM) and complex (ZGEMM), dominates the run time of dense linear algebra and electronic‑structure codes. On affordable GPUs, however, FP64 throughput is a small and shrinking fraction of the throughput of the low‑precision matrix engines. Ozaki scheme II closes this gap by reducing a floating‑point matrix product to a handful of exact INT8 products followed by a Chinese‑remainder reconstruction; the number of products sets the accuracy. We present what is, to our knowledge, the first implementation of Ozaki scheme II for Intel GPUs. Written in SYCL on top of oneMKL, it runs entirely on the device and exposes the full BLAS dgemm/zgemm interface. Making the scheme fast on the Xe2 (Battlemage) architecture required keeping FP64 arithmetic out of all memory‑bound kernels, a branch‑free residue computation, an FP32 evaluation of the CRT quotient with a proven safety margin, 16‑bit limb arithmetic in the reconstruction, and work‑arounds for performance cliffs of the vendor INT8 GEMM. On an Intel Arc Pro B60 (24 GB) the emulated DGEMM reaches 17.3, 12.1 and 9.3 TFLOP/s with s=8, 12 and 16 moduli at N=8192, and up to 21.1 TFLOP/s overall, i.e. 12‑28x the native FP64 DGEMM of the same board. The emulated ZGEMM, which uses the 3M form exactly in integer arithmetic, reaches up to 27.4 TFLOP/s and is 13.7‑17.8x faster than native ZGEMM for N\ge4096 at s=16. With s\ge16 the results are correctly rounded for well‑scaled inputs and, using an extended‑width residue path (s=20‑24), also for inputs with wide exponent ranges, whereas native DGEMM rounds only 2‑13% of the entries correctly. We also report worst‑case accuracy, phase breakdowns, energy, an ablation study, a comparison with Ozaki scheme I, and a validated performance model.

PaperId: 457, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26943.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xinping Wang, Jie Ma, Rui Xing, Wensong Guo, Xiayi Zhang, Jianhao Deng, Zihao Zhou, Boqian Yang, Feijuan He
Title: MAMath-Bench: Process-Aware and Robust Evaluation of Multimodal Multi-Agent Mathematical Reasoning
Abstract:
Mathematical reasoning is a fundamental capability for educational applications of Large Language Models (LLMs), where reliable problem solving requires not only correct answers but also coherent and verifiable reasoning processes. Multi‑agent systems (MASs) have shown growing potential in this domain by leveraging collaboration and verification among multiple LLM agents. However, existing evaluations primarily focus on the correctness of final answers in text‑only settings, offering limited insight into multimodal reasoning capabilities, the reliability of intermediate reasoning steps, and robustness against reasoning errors. To address these limitations, we introduce MAMath‑Bench, a process‑aware benchmark designed to evaluate the multimodal mathematical reasoning capabilities of MASs. MAMath‑Bench comprises 1,003 problems spanning 11 mathematical categories, multiple difficulty levels, and several modalities, including text, images, and audio. It features fine‑grained milestone annotations to evaluate systems across three dimensions: problem‑solving correctness, reasoning‑process reliability, and robustness to adversarial reasoning‑chain perturbations. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, multi‑agent collaboration does not consistently improve final‑answer accuracy over strong single LLMs. Second, collaboration can substantially enhance the coverage of intermediate reasoning, but such gains may come at the cost of increased reasoning redundancy.
