Third, current systems remain vulnerable to adversarial reasoning errors, particularly those involving subtle structural perturbations. The dataset is available at https://github.com/mira‑ai‑lab/AgentMath.

PaperId: 458, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26872.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziyun Chen, Yijun Wang, Chuanyi Zhang, Liang Yao, Yuexuan An, Xiang Gu, Wei Zhou, Fan Liu
Title: Commanding at the Speed of Sound: Audio-Centric Referring Expression Segmentation for Aerial Scenes
Abstract:
Referring expression segmentation (RES) aims to localize targets at the pixel level guided by human instructions. However, current models predominantly follow a text‑centric paradigm that treats discrete text as the primary interaction medium for these human instructions. This assumption is especially limiting in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) applications, where rapid response, hands‑free operation, and natural communication are often critical. In this paper, we reconstruct UAV referring expression segmentation through an audio‑centric perspective. Grounded in information theory, we demonstrate that raw audio provides a higher upper bound for extracting rich semantic features than transcribed text. To achieve this, we construct an audio‑driven UAV referring expression segmentation benchmark named Aerial‑AudioRES by augmenting VisDrone with synthesized speech, forming "audio‑text‑image‑mask" quadruples. Specifically, we employ an ambiguity filtering mechanism to ensure referential uniqueness, and incorporate eight distinct timbres alongside 4 realistic noises to simulate authentic environments. To drive the paradigm shift from text‑centric to audio‑centric, we propose the end‑to‑end Audio‑centric Referring Expression Segmentation Network (ARES‑Net). Distinct from discrete text‑visual matching, our approach learns to establish a direct soft alignment between continuous acoustic manifolds and multi‑scale visual representations. Comprehensive experiments show that our method obtains a peak accuracy of 64.23% in oIoU and demonstrates robust generalization on a collected real‑human test set. Furthermore, it significantly reduces total interaction latency to one‑third of the text‑based method. Our code is available at https://github.com/LemonGauss/ARES‑Net.

PaperId: 459, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26868.pdf   GitHub
Authors:TingTing Gu, JinCheng Luo, WenQiu Guo
Title: Multimodal Ambivalence and Hesitancy Recognition with Bidirectional Audio--Text Cross-Attention
Abstract:
Ambivalence and hesitancy (A/H) are subtle behavioural states that can be expressed through both what a person says and how it is spoken. This paper presents an audio‑‑text framework for video‑level A/H recognition. Full‑video transcripts and speech waveforms are encoded using pre‑trained multilingual BERT and wav2vec~2.0, respectively, and projected into a shared representation space. Two stacked bidirectional cross‑attention blocks allow linguistic tokens to attend to acoustic frames and acoustic frames to attend to linguistic context without requiring explicit temporal alignment. The resulting sequences are aggregated through masked mean pooling and combined using concatenation, element‑wise products, and absolute differences for binary classification. We evaluate the model on the subject‑independent split of the Behavioural Ambivalence/Hesitancy (BAH) dataset. The proposed system achieves 72.19% accuracy, 75.00% precision, 81.13% recall, 77.95% A/H F1‑score, and 70.16% Macro‑F1 on the test set. These results demonstrate the potential of jointly modelling linguistic and acoustic information for automatic A/H recognition.code at:https://github.com/DorriG/ECCV.

PaperId: 460, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26865.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiaxuan Luo, Siqi Ouyang, Lei Li
Title: AutoTerm-SST: Adaptive Terminology Memory with Zero Session-Time Setup for Streaming Speech Translation
Abstract:
Retrieval‑augmented speech translation improves rare terminology, but systems such as RASST still assume that users provide a glossary before each session. That assumption is inconvenient for live talks, while merging every domain into one growing glossary eventually places too many irrelevant terms in the same retrieval and prompt competition. We present AutoTerm‑SST, an interactive system that removes session‑time glossary upload and domain selection. It organizes a large offline terminology catalog into topic slices, matches recent streaming translation context to bilingual slice prototypes, and activates a compact multi‑slice working set under fixed retrieval and prompt budgets. On five ACL and five ESO oncology talks, AutoTerm matches a known‑domain reference in terminology accuracy (88.3% vs. 88.1%) and mWER‑resegmented BLEU (45.09 vs. 45.19), while requiring no domain input. Compared with a one‑million‑entry merged glossary, it improves terminology accuracy by 3.9 points and BLEU by 2.30. Routing plus four‑slice retrieval remains lightweight: the complete system runs at 0.406 RTF, and the vLLM host sustains 32 real‑time sessions. The live demo exposes active slices and retrieved terminology as the topic changes, providing zero‑setup terminology‑aware streaming translation.

PaperId: 461, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26854.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiaming Liu, Xinghao Zhu, Yiming Zhang, Shanghang Zhang, Yinxi Wang, Yichu Yang, Zhuoyang Liu, Dantong Niu, Soha Pouya, Juekun Li, Yan Chang
Title: Physical Words: A Vocabulary for Structuring Latent Reasoning in Robot Manipulation
Abstract:
Multimodal reasoning provides robotic foundation models with predictive context needed for reliable action generation. However, language‑based reasoning captures task semantics but struggles to express fine‑grained physical dynamics, while latent reasoning models future state evolution but offers limited structure for organizing these dynamics into reusable reasoning primitives. To bridge this gap, we introduce PhysWord, a reasoning‑before‑acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as shared semantic anchors for continuous representations of physical dynamics. Specifically, PhysWord predicts upcoming atomic action words and directly aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from the corresponding future observations. Building on these primitives, we construct a temporally structured PhysWord space with visual and optional tactile variants of each action word. Autoregressively predicting Physical Words across future timesteps captures transitions between execution stages, providing structured multimodal context for action generation. PhysWord achieves state‑of‑the‑art success rates of 90.3% on visuotactile UniVTAC and 99.6% on vision‑based LIBERO‑Long, and outperforms competing methods on real‑world tasks using bimanual grippers and dexterous hands. Further evaluations demonstrate that our structured latent reasoning framework generalizes to unseen scenarios and enables long‑horizon manipulation. Project page: https://nvidia‑isaac.github.io/video_to_data/physicalword/

PaperId: 462, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26853.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yi-Chuan Huang, Hao-Jen Chien, Zheng-Hui Huang, Yu-Lun Liu, Kaipeng Zhang, Zhixiang Wang
Title: InfiniDream: Open-Ended Photorealistic 3D Worlds Through Procedural Generation
Abstract:
Procedural generation plays a key role in synthetic data creation and game development, offering greater controllability, editability, and diversity than static mesh representations. However, VLM‑based code generation often produces relatively simple 3D assets, while sophisticated photorealistic procedural systems require extensive manual development. Existing VLM‑guided procedural methods remain largely constrained by predefined factories and APIs, limiting their ability to create novel asset types. We introduce InfiniDream, a VLM‑driven framework for open‑ended procedural 3D world generation. First, we propose Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which leverages existing procedural algorithms to create novel, photorealistic assets while preserving editability and seed‑based diversity. Second, we develop an end‑to‑end text‑to‑world pipeline that combines semantic scene planning with Deterministic Frustum‑Guided Grid Placement to construct large‑scale 3D worlds with precise object placement, procedural population, and animation. Extensive evaluations on 100 object and 20 scene generation tasks demonstrate improvements across four perceptual metrics. Diversity analysis, ablation studies, and human preference evaluations further validate the effectiveness of our framework. Project page: https://yichuanh.github.io/infinidream‑page/

PaperId: 463, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26770.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhuoshi Pan, ZhiYuan Feng, Yukuo Cen, Honglin Lin, Junru Lu, Zhongxia Chen, Shuo Yang, H. Vicky Zhao, Jie Tang
Title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
Abstract:
Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self‑improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label‑free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM‑generated tests without access to ground‑truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance‑cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared‑distance selection to provide cost‑focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance‑focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal‑Bench 2, SWE‑Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT‑5.5 with Codex and GLM‑5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT‑5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass‑rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per‑task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM‑5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro

PaperId: 464, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26680.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Akihiro Miki, Shun Hasegawa, Yoshimoto Ribayashi, Yuta Sahara, Kento Kawaharazuka, Kei Okada
Title: Robotic Physical Comparison of Biologically Motivated and Counterfactual Sensory Arrangements using Biomimetic Skin
Abstract:
Human skin contains diverse mechanoreceptors, including Merkel cells and Pacinian corpuscles, each localized in specific regions. Although their spatial organization is known to be shaped by molecular signaling and neural induction during development, experimentally examining its functional significance under controlled conditions in living systems remains challenging. In particular, physically comparing alternative receptor arrangements that do not occur biologically is difficult. In this study, we developed a layered biomimetic robotic skin designed to mimic key structural features of human skin tissue by embedding receptor‑analog sensors within compliant soft media. Using this platform, we implemented both biologically motivated and counterfactual sensory arrangements and quantitatively evaluated their performance across three passive tactile tasks: detection of weak contacts, a two‑point discrimination‑like assessment, and texture identification. Arrangements reflecting key features of the biologically motivated sensory organization exhibited higher performance than the alternative configurations examined. This study addresses a biological question concerning how spatial organization influences tactile function by presenting a biomimetic robotic approach that enables physical and empirical comparison of biologically motivated and counterfactual sensory arrangements that are difficult to investigate in living systems.

PaperId: 465, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26659.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhaoxi Zhang, Hao Liang, Linxuan Wu, Yiming Xu, Yifu Yuan, Kun Liang, Chenming Tang, Meiyi Qiang, Wentao Zhang, Weikang Li
Title: SpatialScout: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore and Map 3D Scenes?
Abstract:
Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three‑dimensional world. Yet spatial question answering offers limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision‑language model (VLM) agents on active object‑level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, camera calibration, and camera poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. The task requires coordinating viewpoint selection, cross‑view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage through object‑scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets exceeding an intersection‑over‑union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 and only 3.25% exceeding 0.9. These results reveal a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at https://github.com/JesseZZZZZ/SpatialScout.

PaperId: 466, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26589.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rohan Menon, Chih-Hong Cheng
Title: Beyond Attack Success Rate: Cost-Aware Metric for Evaluating Iterative LLM Jailbreaks
Abstract:
Attack success rate (ASR) evaluates jailbreaks against large language models without accounting for repeated calls to the victim model. Yet each additional call gives the deployed system another opportunity to detect the attack and intervene. We introduce \mathrmASR_\mathrmSTEP, which penalizes additional victim‑model calls while retaining binary success judgments. Our evaluation considers GCG, PAIR with a step budget, and a single‑step PAP baseline on JailBreakBench across three model families. GCG's scores decrease by 7.0‑8.7 percentage points after discounting, while PAP's remain unchanged. While for PAIR attack, we see a wider discounting range between 3.4‑12 percentage points, showing that the "step" quantity differs per iterative strategy. Reporting both metrics makes the discount due to repeated victim‑model interaction explicit. Code is available here: https://github.com/SuELS‑Group/beyond_asr.

PaperId: 467, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26582.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Arjun Ashok, Mihir Parmar, Palash Goyal, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, Chun-Liang Li, Irina Rish, Alexandre Drouin, Jinsung Yoon, Tomas Pfister
Title: WhatIf-Bench: Benchmarking Intervention-Aware Time Series Forecasting
Abstract:
Recent time series foundation models (TSFMs) can consume covariates in‑context, extending zero‑shot forecasting to problems driven by external factors. This enables scenario analysis: forecasting how a target responds to events that set covariates to chosen future values. Whether they can do this reliably is an open question. We introduce WhatIf‑Bench, a benchmark measuring how well forecasters use covariates to forecast a target's response to future events. WhatIf‑Bench is semi‑synthetic: time series come from mechanistic simulators of data centers, power grids, road traffic, and water networks, with controlled covariate‑target relationships grounded in each system. Each task presents a history of events intervening on covariates, then asks to forecast a future event that either replays seen values (Replay) or sets them to unseen ones (Novel). Varying the number of covariates, historical events, and event length yields 37,665 tasks. Evaluating TSFMs, frontier LLMs, and simple regression baselines, we find the LLMs reach the highest skill (improvement over a naive baseline), ahead of the best TSFMs. Every model forecasts well on Replay futures (48 to 85% skill) but drops to ‑7 to 50% on Novel futures, with the regression baselines falling the most. Skill on Novel futures also falls as events set more covariates jointly. More historical events raise skill on Novel futures across the board, but large differences remain. WhatIf‑Bench reveals generalization to Novel futures as the core challenge, and offers a testbed toward arbitrary scenario analysis.

PaperId: 468, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26538.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaomeng Li
Title: Small Average Error, Wide Individual Error: General-Purpose LLMs Estimating Energy Intake from Meal Photos in a Feeding Trial
Abstract:
Photo‑based estimation of food energy could ease dietary assessment, and general‑purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) make such estimates easy to obtain. Most evaluations use one photo taken before eating and compare with energy served, while dietary assessment needs energy eaten. We evaluated eight models from three vendors (Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5; GPT‑6 luna, 6.1 sol and 6 astra; Gemini 3.8 Flash and 4 Argon) on 802 meals from ACETADA, a controlled feeding trial with weighed intake, with the before photo only, before and after photos in separate calls (subtraction), or both photos in one request. Three results ran against intuition. Subtraction under‑estimated intake for six of eight models, because the models still report hundreds of kilocalories for a nearly empty tray. Scaling the before‑only estimate by the average share eaten (0.87) matched much of the gain from the after photo; beyond that constant, the second photo lowered meal‑level error by only 2.2 to 4.4 points, mainly in meals with food left. With one photo, two models had a near‑zero intake bias only because they under‑estimated the served energy and ignored uneaten food. In ablations, adding the after photo improved accuracy under both prompt formats for seven models, while prompt effects varied across models. Over 148 feeding days, five models kept the 90% confidence interval of their mean error within a pre‑set 10% margin; one model also met the pre‑set 30% limits of agreement, narrowly (‑28% to +27%; limits outside 30% cannot be excluded), and the other seven did not. Protein was under‑estimated by every model, most in protein‑dense meals; repeated calls changed error by at most 1.4 points; a high reasoning effort helped only the smallest model. A low average bias is not evidence of accurate individual intake estimation; such estimates should support, not replace, assessment by a dietitian.

PaperId: 469, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26453.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Guannan Lai, Zi-Yang Bai, Jun-Peng Jiang, Han-Jia Ye
Title: Learning What to Remember: Resource-Efficient Self-Improvement for Lifelong Agents
Abstract:
Self‑improving agents aim to continuously improve their behavior by learning from experience after deployment. However, accumulating and reusing more experience does not necessarily lead to better decisions, particularly when generation, interaction, and memory resources are jointly constrained. Under such stringent constraints, we find that several existing lifelong‑memory methods provide limited benefits over simple retrieval or even no‑memory agents. This reveals a fundamental challenge for resource‑efficient self‑improvement: agents must learn not only which past experiences are relevant, but which are actually worth reusing to improve future decisions. When memory capacity and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving an ineffective experience can consume scarce resources and hinder downstream execution. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight feedback‑driven memory adaptation framework that learns query‑dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback. Without updating the backbone model, TokenWorth uses the learned worth to guide both experience retrieval and bounded memory management, enabling the agent to continually adapt how it reuses accumulated experience. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API‑based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods under the specified resource budgets. These results suggest that effective self‑improvement under resource constraints depends not on accumulating more experience, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth.

PaperId: 470, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26342.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ruotian Peng, Yuanyi Ren, Shuaiqi Liu, Xin Guo, Fang Zhu, Yangyi Huang, Yue Wu, Zheng Wang, Yandong Wen, Zhihang Fu
Title: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement
Abstract:
Recursive self‑improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross‑component co‑design. We introduce VibeTraining‑Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi‑turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. Within each task, research agents start from an identical initial agent system under a fixed resource budget. Guided by validation feedback, they iteratively refine data, trainers, and inference harnesses, then select and submit a final agent system for evaluation on the test set. To prevent reward hacking, we enforce three safeguards: test data isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions for research agents. Our evaluation results show that frontier research agents substantially improve target agent systems. For example, on SWE‑bench Verified, GPT‑6‑Astra raises the target agent system's performance from 32.9% to 53.7%, comparable to the human‑developed instruct model's 55.4%. However, there is still room to improve their ability to co‑design and iteratively refine data, trainer, and harness to achieve cumulative performance gains. We hope that VibeTraining‑Bench will serve as a unified platform for advancing RSI, deepening our understanding of cross‑component optimization for agent systems. Code and data are available at https://github.com/D2I‑ai/VibeTraining‑Bench.

PaperId: 471, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26255.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Michael Glöckler, Timo Ropinski
Title: XGLASS: X-Ray, Gaze and Language Assisted Slice Sequencing for CT Volumes
Abstract:
Vision‑language models (VLMs) achieve remarkable performance on 2D medical images, such as X‑rays or pathology images, while 3D VLMs that directly process CT/MRI volumes lag behind due to limited 3D training data and the predominance of 2D foundation architectures. To leverage powerful 2D VLMs for analyzing medical volumes, which contain hundreds of slices, it is therefore necessary to focus only on those few slices, which are diagnostically relevant. To enable such a prioritization, we propose XGLASS, a method that transfers medical expertise from 2D X‑rays to 3D CT for task‑aware slice prioritization. XGLASS uses disease‑conditioned importance maps derived from language‑aligned radiologist gaze on X‑rays and spatially aligns them with coronal CT projections, bringing gaze priors and CT content into a shared 2D representation. The fused gaze‑prior/CT projection is then used to predict a disease‑specific ordering of axial slices, prioritizing diagnostically relevant slices. XGLASS significantly improves budgeted retrieval over 2D and 3D‑native baselines, achieving a top‑10 hit rate up to 75.9% for the best‑performing disease. In practice, this means that after inspecting only the top 10 slices (4.17% of a 240‑slice scan), XGLASS identifies a diagnostically relevant slice in more than 75% of cases. For downstream slice‑wise finding classification, an XGLASS‑selected 30‑slice candidate set reduces model calls by 87.5% while improving F1 by 11.3 percentage points over all‑slice inference, 4.2 points over the strongest 2D selector, and remains competitive with 3D‑native selectors while requiring up to 130.8 times less time and 10.9 times less GPU memory per finding, supporting its use as a lightweight preselector for volumetric CT analysis. The code and pretrained checkpoint are available on https://github.com/michaelgloeckler/XGLASS.

PaperId: 472, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26096.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Emirkan Burak Yilmaz, Yakup Genc
Title: PnP-Transformer: A Neural Pose Solver for Zero-Shot 6D Object Pose Estimation
Abstract:
We present PnP‑Transformer, a neural pose solver designed as an iterative‑free, differentiable alternative to classical PnP‑RANSAC algorithms. PnP‑Transformer regresses the 6D object pose by processing predicted semi‑dense 2D‑3D correspondence fields alongside confidence scores, while mapping geometric inputs into a continuous latent space. To evaluate its practical utility, we integrate PnP‑Transformer into a zero‑shot 6D pose estimation pipeline, where the correspondence module and pose solver are trained separately. PnP‑Transformer achieves a 41.2% mean AR score with low latency (0.46 s/obj) on seven core BOP benchmark datasets, surpassing all prior baselines (such as RayPose with 39.1% AR) but one (Co‑op with 58.4% AR). When the pose solver is replaced with EPnP‑RANSAC (similar to Co‑op) while keeping the correspondence module unchanged, the RANSAC alternative outperforms PnP‑Transformer on six of the seven datasets by reaching 52.2% mean AR at a cost of an additional 60 ms per object, revealing an accuracy‑latency trade‑off. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/ebylmz/pnp‑transformer.

PaperId: 473, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.26043.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yinghao Li, Tianyu Zhang, Zhuohao Li, Yi-Lin Wei, Fa-Ting Hong, Qing Zhang, Wei-Shi Zheng
Title: OmniInteract: Towards Unified Whole-Body Interaction Control for Dual Humanoids
Abstract:
Physical interaction is a key capability for humanoid collaboration, requiring coordinated whole‑body motion and precise contact. However, learning diverse dual‑humanoid interactions faces two major challenges: (1) human‑robot morphological differences disrupt contact interfaces and spatial relationships during retargeting, and (2) jointly learning motor skills and partner coordination makes it difficult to retain control fidelity as interaction diversity grows. In this paper, we propose OmniInteract to address these challenges through surface‑aware modeling and scalable residual policy learning. First, we introduce Surface Contact‑Aware Retargeting, which leverages dense human‑robot surface correspondences to jointly retarget both humanoids, preserving explicit interaction contact interfaces and their near‑field geometric context. Second, we propose a Scalable Flow‑based Interaction Policy for partner‑conditioned residual generation. It factorizes dual‑humanoid control into a reusable motor foundation and interaction‑specific adaptations: partner‑aware experts learn corrections over a frozen whole‑body motion prior, while conditional flow matching unifies them in a shared residual action space. This enables scalable skill consolidation while retaining pretrained motor capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniInteract improves retargeting fidelity and dual‑humanoid coordination while better retaining interaction performance as skill diversity grows. Real‑world deployment further demonstrates successful contact establishment, stable whole‑body coordination, and recovery from external perturbations.

PaperId: 474, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25964.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kesav Kumar Jayakumar, Karthigeyan Thilak
Title: Token-Set Choice Confounds POPE: A Systematic Audit of Yes/No Extraction in VLM Hallucination Evaluation
Abstract:
We set out to reproduce a recent hallucination‑mitigation result on the POPE benchmark. The LLaVA‑1.5‑7B baseline we measured, 82.21 F1 on the adversarial split, sat 1.21 to 8.67 points above the adversarial baselines we planned to compare against (81.00, 79.30, and 73.54). We looked at the evaluation code and found a readout choice that moves F1 on its own. A two‑token logit readout decides yes versus no by comparing two vocabulary IDs, 3582 ("yes") and 1217 ("no"). Across 9,000 greedy‑decode questions spanning all three splits, neither ID is generated even once. The model emits " Yes" (token 3869) and " No" (token 1939), because SentencePiece prepends a space byte after the prompt suffix "ASSISTANT:". Read with an eight‑token lookup that covers the space‑prefixed surface forms, LLaVA‑1.5‑7B scores F1 0.8221, 0.8498, and 0.8713 on the adversarial, popular, and random splits. That 6.13‑point adversarial shift exceeds the adversarial gain reported by five of the six papers we surveyed. None of them states its readout, and our reference ran under 4‑bit NF4 quantization, so we cannot say how much of any reported gain a matched evaluation would keep. That comparison stays unresolved until readout and precision are matched. On the fixed baseline we run nine inference‑time corrections of our own (none beat it) and dissect why the adversarial split resists logit‑level intervention. In a 3,000‑question probe, wrong predictions draw more image attention than correct ones (Cohen's d=‑0.46, p=1.4×10^‑24), the opposite of what grounding‑based corrections assume. A four‑readout audit across four further VLMs from three tokenizer families confirms the confound is protocol‑level, not model‑specific: porting the LLaVA‑1.5 IDs verbatim drops F1 to 0.00 on the two disjoint‑vocabulary models, whereas a tokenizer‑derived readout holds between 0.80 and 0.92.

PaperId: 475, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25927.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Feiyang Hong, Yujie Wei, Bo Zhao, Xiu Su, Hongxun Yao, Shuo Yang
Title: CondenseVLA: Learnable History Condensation for Efficient Multi-Frame VLA
Abstract:
Robot manipulation often depends on short‑term cues ‑ such as brief contacts, temporary occlusions, and intermediate object states ‑ that are ambiguous in a single frame and can only be resolved by integrating observations over time. However, injecting historical information solely by enlarging the history window is computationally costly and frequently yields limited gains due to substantial redundancy and task‑agnostic, inflexible sampling of observations. We propose CondenseVLA, a multi‑frame VLA policy with a learnable decoder‑side history condensation module for using short‑term visual context in action decoding. Given a sequence of cached per‑frame features from the VLM backbone, CondenseVLA distills observation history into a fixed set of slot tokens using learnable queries and multi‑head cross‑attention. Simple auxiliary regularization penalizes overlap among slot attention maps and decorrelates slot embeddings, encouraging complementary attention and reducing slot redundancy. Across the evaluated tasks, CondenseVLA improves Simpler‑WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8% (+11.1 percentage points), achieves 97.2% on LIBERO, and reaches 52.8% on real‑world tasks. It achieves 21.6% success on memory‑dependent RMBench tasks. These results support selective condensation of bounded recent visual evidence for action decoding, while harder multi‑observation tasks expose the limits of a finite history window. Project page: https://github.com/FeiyangHong/CondenseVLA

PaperId: 476, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25751.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jianhao Zhang, Ou Wu, Yi Du
Title: NADS: Navigator-Guided Data Selection for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning
Abstract:
Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle in single‑stage fine‑tuning of large language models (LLMs) on a new task, especially when the original pretraining data are unavailable. Synthetic data offers a practical mitigation path, but candidate pools are often noisy and redundant, making effective selection essential. Existing methods often rely on indirect proxy signals whose alignment with actual training benefit can be limited, while utility‑‑diversity selection over large candidate pools remains computationally demanding. To address these challenges, we propose NAvigator‑guided Data Selection (NADS), a fine‑tuning framework for LLMs. NADS first follows the target fine‑tuning recipe without preservation regularization to obtain a navigator model, whose deviation from the pretrained model exposes recipe‑induced capability drift. It then uses the predictive divergence between the navigator and the pretrained model to score forgetting‑aware utility for each synthetic candidate, and constructs a constraint set through an efficient utility‑‑diversity selection strategy. Finally, NADS fine‑tunes on the new‑task data while distilling pretrained behavior on the selected constraints to preserve general capabilities. Experiments show that NADS delivers a stronger balance between new‑task performance and general capability preservation, while reducing utility‑‑diversity selection overhead. Code at: https://github.com/zjh‑vinky/NADS.

PaperId: 477, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25716.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiao Ma, Zhonghao Zhan, Yi Tang, Qi Chen
Title: LEVI: Benchmarking Visual Identity Fidelity with Verifiable Low-Entropy Constructs
Abstract:
Modern generative models can produce visually plausible images while violating exact identity constraints. Evaluating such failures requires distinguishing violations of the requested identity from permissible variation in appearance. We introduce Low‑Entropy Visual Identity (LEVI), which characterizes visual identities determined by compact facts and explicit rules. The low‑entropy requirement concerns identity uncertainty, while appearance may remain diverse. We formulate identity fidelity in terms of the probability that a conditional image distribution assigns to the identities permitted by the prompt. Visual Identity Spaces (VIS) formalize this distinction by specifying admissible identity values and which different realizations express the same identity. Building on this formulation, we develop Verifiable Visual Grammar (VVG), a declarative language whose typed primitives and compositional constraints describe identity‑bearing structures. Using this grammar, we build a benchmark for image generation. It assesses each output against the task's identity requirements, drawing evidence from the final pixels. The curated benchmark contains 1,375 tasks spanning 120 base identity spaces across six domains. Among ten evaluated model configurations, the highest whole‑task pass rate is 58.69%. These results reveal a persistent gap between visually plausible images and faithful realization of their specified identities. Project page: https://maxiao0234.github.io/LEVI/.

PaperId: 478, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25649.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Senhe Zhang, Tao Zhang, Yujia Zhang, Zeyu Zhang, Dong Gong
Title: InteractAgent: Agentic Human Motion Interaction with Memory-Augmented Reflection
Abstract:
Long‑horizon human‑scene interaction requires coordinated spatial reasoning, physical feasibility, and the ability to recover from compounding execution errors. Text‑driven motion models are largely scene‑agnostic and lack closed‑loop correction, while geometry‑conditioned approaches depend on paired scene‑motion training or explicit 3D preprocessing that limits generalization to novel layouts and open‑vocabulary goals. We present InteractAgent, an agentic multimodal LLM system for long‑horizon human‑scene interaction that plans, executes, observes, and reflects in a closed loop, using a single MLLM as both planner and evaluator and a frozen MotionLLM as the executor. InteractAgent integrates Online Observation for step‑wise recovery decisions (continue/redo/replan) and Memory‑Augmented Reflection for multi‑round plan refinement with adaptive stopping. On UniHSI, InteractAgent improves task success and reduces penetration compared with training‑free baselines. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/InteractAgent.

PaperId: 479, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25481.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Antonio Scardace, Silvia Ingala, Sebastiano Battiato, Daniele Ravì
Title: Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Models for Spatiotemporal Brain MRI Forecasting
Abstract:
Spatiotemporal forecasting of 3D anatomical changes is a critical generative vision challenge for modeling Alzheimer's Disease (AD) progression. While brain MRI forecasting from single‑modality data has advanced, other key complementary multimodal biomarkers remain underutilized. In this work, we propose the Multimodal‑Conditioned Latent Diffusion Model (MC‑LDM), a novel framework for patient‑specific brain MRI synthesis. MC‑LDM leverages multimodal biomarkers‑‑‑MRI, tau‑PET, Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), and APOE4‑‑‑during training, but relies only on baseline MRI, APOE4, and patient metadata at inference, reflecting realistic clinical availability. Our contributions are threefold: (1) a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) fine‑tuned via Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for data‑efficient learning; (2) a multimodal conditioning that integrates molecular and clinical signals to model heterogeneous disease trajectories; and (3) auxiliary predictors estimating unobserved multimodal biomarkers from MRI features and patient covariates to condition the diffusion model, removing the need for these assessments at inference. Trained on 1,355 visits from 852 subjects in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), MC‑LDM reduces average regional volumetric MAE by 18% over the second‑best baseline on an independent test set of 664 visits. To our knowledge, MC‑LDM represents the first diffusion‑based framework to leverage multimodal priors for MRI forecasting. This conceptual advancement enables patient‑specific trajectory generation that captures aspects of AD heterogeneity not observable from structural anatomy alone, bridging the gap between rich multimodal supervision and the strict constraints of routine clinical deployment. Code is available at: https://github.com/antonioscardace/MC‑LDM.

PaperId: 480, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25479.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wenyi Lian, Zheng Zhao, Thomas B. Schön
Title: Test-Time Scaling of Text-to-Image Flow Matching Models with Noise-Rejuvenated Sequential Monte Carlo
Abstract:
Test‑time scaling of diffusion models with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) has become a promising strategy for sampling under user‑specified rewards, such as human preference scores. However, the standard SMC framework typically relies on stochastic proposals and therefore does not directly transfer to flow matching models, in which inference is governed by deterministic ODEs. In this work, we introduce noise‑rejuvenated SMC, an inference‑time scaling method tailored for text‑to‑image flow matching models. Our key idea is to perturb each resampled particle by changing its source noise and constructing a new intermediate state using its current endpoint estimate. This moves the particle to another state that remains representable under the flow‑matching interpolation form, enabling particle exploration without converting the sampler to an SDE. We further introduce a look‑ahead mechanism to refine resampled particles before weighting. Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1‑dev, and Z‑Image demonstrate consistent improvements in reward‑guided generation, while ablation studies validate the contributions of noise rejuvenation and look‑ahead refinement. Code is available at https://github.com/shermanlian/NR‑SMC.

PaperId: 481, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25404.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Houyuan Chen, Fanzhou Wang, Xiangyu Fan, Zesong Qiu, Yukun Wei, Songlin Yang, Zhitao Yang, Lvmin Zhang, Pei Yang, Hao Zhao, Dahua Lin, Lei Yang, Anyi Rao
Title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
Abstract:
Multi‑turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits. To address these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, a novel training paradigm for multi‑turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion. Specifically, we propose Single‑Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single‑Turn DMD), which supervises student self‑rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual‑quality guidance without recursive error accumulation. Additionally, we introduce Teacher‑Forcing Guidance, which supervises history‑dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross‑turn content consistency beyond what per‑turn distribution matching alone can ensure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi‑turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross‑turn consistency.

PaperId: 482, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25369.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Markus Pobitzer, Chang Liu, Niccolò Biondi, Nicu Sebe
Title: Painting Change Map as guidance for generating painting processes
Abstract:
Digital art generation has undergone a massive paradigm shift, moving from static image synthesis to dynamic video generation that can mimic the human painting process. While existing models can synthesize visually stunning time‑lapses of paintings being created or "unpainted," they largely treat the creative process as a black box. Current conditioning mechanisms are either too rigid, relying on static geometric cues like Canny edges or depth maps, or too holistic, utilizing simple scalar progress variables that offer no localized control. Consequently, users lack the agency to steer how a painting evolves over time. In this work, we argue that true control over the video generation of artwork requires a joint understanding of two fundamental dimensions: where an artist acts, and when those actions take place. To achieve this, we introduce the Painting Change Map, a novel spatio‑temporal control mechanism that explicitly tracks normalized structural changes across a 1,000‑timestep continuum, a resolution sufficient to capture fine‑grained stroke‑level changes while remaining computationally tractable. By mapping localized visual differences into an encoded RGB space, our representation enables fine‑grained guidance for both the forward painting and reverse unpainting processes. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates the efficacy of our approach. We outperform existing control baselines and achieve competitive or superior results compared to state‑of‑the‑art painting methods. Furthermore, under oracle conditions, our method surpasses all baselines by a significant margin. Code is available at https://github.com/Markus‑Pobitzer/painting‑change‑map.

PaperId: 483, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25276.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yushi Lan, Zeren Jiang, Koichi Namekata, Xingang Pan, Chuanxia Zheng, Andrea Vedaldi
Title: Holo4D: Holistic 4D Reconstruction as Geometric Control for Video Diffusion
Abstract:
Synthesizing a monocular video from a new camera trajectory requires preserving the observed scene geometry and motion while completing regions that become newly visible. Feed‑forward 4D reconstructors recover the structure of the observed scene, whereas video diffusion models provide a generative prior for completing unseen content. We introduce Holo4D, a video reshooting framework that uses reconstructed 3D trajectories as a holistic source‑view 4D scaffold. We project these trajectories into the requested views and encode their geometry and source appearance to guide a pretrained video diffusion model. Together with the source video and target cameras, the scaffold grounds generation in reconstructed observations while leaving unsupported regions to the generative prior. Experiments demonstrate the value of trajectory‑based conditioning for camera control and novel‑view synthesis. The framework accommodates different 4D reconstructors without retraining the video generator, allowing it to benefit from future advances in source reconstruction. More details can be found in our project page.

PaperId: 484, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25261.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Boxin Bu, Simon Boche, Haoming Zhang, Jaehyung Jung, Jiaxin Wei, Hannah Schieber, Daniel Roth, Angela P. Schoellig, Stefan Leutenegger
Title: GOFusion: Real-Time Gaussian-Occupancy Submap Fusion for Fisher-Informed Autonomous Robot Navigation
Abstract:
In this letter, we present GOFusion, a real‑time visual mapping system for autonomous robot navigation that anchors Gaussian primitives to local occupancy maps, providing both spatial awareness for path planning and high‑fidelity appearance that enables information‑driven robot navigation. GOFusion builds 3D Gaussian maps from pose estimates and local occupancy maps obtained via visual‑inertial SLAM and enables pose corrections to maintain both geometric and visual consistency. Furthermore, it restricts the 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to active submaps to bound GPU memory usage. Building on the appearance‑rich Gaussian map, we introduce a rasterizer‑integrated Fisher approximation that quantifies per‑primitive sensitivity online, serving as an information‑driven heuristic for Gaussian pruning and next‑best‑view planning. We evaluate GOFusion on public datasets and in real‑world drone flights. It not only outperforms several baselines in mapping quality, but also achieves real‑time, high‑fidelity and uncertainty‑aware mapping at scale. Finally, we demonstrate fully autonomous drone exploration for Gaussian map refinement using the proposed Fisher‑informed heuristic. Code is available at https://github.com/Bennnoo/GOFusion. We provide a supplementary video demonstration at https://youtu.be/pLQKbxQvb6I.

PaperId: 485, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25259.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kaidi Wang, Wenhao Guan, Peijie Chen, Weijie Wu, Xuetao Lin, Lin Li, Qingyang Hong
Title: VoxDub: A Bilingual Lip-Synchronized Audio-Visual Dataset for Automatic Video Dubbing
Abstract:
Automatic video dubbing (AVD) requires temporally aligned speech, transcripts, and video, yet existing corpora vary in audio quality, transcription reliability, and speaking‑face visibility. We introduce VoxDub, a bilingual lip‑synchronized audio‑visual dataset containing 766K clips and approximately 1.58K hours of in‑the‑wild Chinese and English recordings, covering varied speakers, scenes, speaking styles, and linguistic content. Its curation pipeline combines speech‑centered segmentation with dual‑ASR transcription checking, speech quality filtering, face visibility checks, and lip‑speech synchronization verification. Text‑to‑speech (TTS) experiments show that training on VoxDub yields lower word error rates and higher speaker similarity than training on the compared audio‑visual corpora, LRS3 and CN‑CVS. AVD experiments show broadly comparable speech quality and subjective synchronization. These results support the utility of VoxDub for TTS and AVD training. More details are available on the project website (https://voxdub‑dataset.github.io/VoxDub/).

PaperId: 486, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25245.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuchen Xi, Yuhan Guo, Chenwei Hou, Zixu Liu, Jin Fang, Jason Liu, Ruigang Yang
Title: GeoV2V: Geometry-Grounded Video Diffusion Model for Driving Scene Generation
Abstract:
Novel view synthesis under trajectory changes is essential for autonomous driving simulation, yet existing methods struggle to generate consistent videos when extrapolating to unseen viewpoints such as lane shifts. Reconstruction‑based approaches maintain geometric consistency but degrade in visual quality under large viewpoint changes, while reconstruct‑then‑restore methods often produce visually plausible frames yet suffer from geometric and temporal inconsistencies. We present GeoV2V, a geometry‑grounded video‑to‑video diffusion framework that synthesizes temporally coherent driving videos along novel trajectories by integrating LiDAR and depth‑derived geometric priors with full‑video conditioning in the Wan 2.1 backbone. A key challenge in learning cross‑lane transformations is the lack of synchronized multi‑trajectory supervision in real‑world datasets. To address this, we also introduce Para4D, a synthetic dataset capturing synchronized multi‑lane driving videos within dynamic scenes, which provides explicit supervision for lane‑shift generation and serves as a strong training prior for geometry‑consistent view synthesis. Experiments on Waymo, nuScenes, and Para4D demonstrate state‑of‑the‑art performance in visual quality, geometric consistency, and robustness to complex lighting dynamics under large trajectory shifts. Project page: https://xiyuche.github.io/GeoV2V/

PaperId: 487, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25208.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haotian Gan, Weidong Tang, Hanbin Sun, Yi Luo, Xintian Li, Jiayong Wang, WanYue Li, Yudong Li
Title: BrandEval: A Two-Track Multi-Agent Benchmark for Risk-Sensitive LLM Crisis Communication
Abstract:
Evaluating LLMs for crisis communication requires more than judging isolated responses, because public feedback and competitor actions can reshape trust over time. Existing benchmarks remain largely static and single‑turn, offering limited evidence about long‑horizon risk‑sensitive communication. We introduce BrandEval, a two‑track benchmark for product‑crisis communication, focusing on public brand responses to product‑related safety, quality, service, and trust incidents. BrandEval‑Static evaluates stakeholder‑aware strategic analysis, while BrandEval‑Dynamic stress‑tests response policies in BrandPolis, a controlled multi‑agent sandbox with consumer feedback, competitor responses, and trust‑risk trajectories. We also construct BrandSRD, a Chinese crisis‑response dataset, and instantiate a reference Strategic Agent using Strategic Rationale (SR). Across proprietary and open‑source models, we find that static strategic quality is informative but incomplete: it aligns with some end‑state outcomes but does not reliably predict volatility and delayed recovery; dynamic stress tests further expose tail‑risk failures under manipulative or weakly grounded policies. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/htgan‑ai/BrandEval.

PaperId: 488, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25202.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haotian Gan, Yudong Li, Xintian Li, Jiarui Han, Weidong Tang
Title: ViCoR: Estimating Visual Necessity via Counterfactual Residuals for Multimodal Medical Data Selection
Abstract:
Medical vision‑language models often exhibit hidden stratification, where high overall performance masks failures on subtle visual findings and overlapping clinical conditions. We trace this failure mode to modality imbalance during fine‑tuning, where strong linguistic priors can suppress visually grounded learning and induce plausible but weakly grounded rationales. Existing data selection methods usually score image‑text pairs as holistic units, without separating visually necessary samples from shortcut‑solvable ones. To address this problem, we propose ViCoR, a counterfactual‑residual‑based data selection method for Med‑VLM fine‑tuning. ViCoR estimates visual necessity through image‑dependent optimization residuals, calibrates the resulting scores with medical supervision compatibility, and constructs a diversity‑aware fine‑tuning subset. Across two backbones, four external generalization benchmarks, and one multi‑disease robustness benchmark, ViCoR‑selected 20% subsets achieve the strongest average performance compared with full‑data fine‑tuning and selection baselines. Gradient‑level analysis and perturbation audits further show that ViCoR enriches image‑dependent training signals and strengthens image‑level and evidence‑region dependence. The code will be available at https://github.com/htgan‑ai/ViCoR.

PaperId: 489, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25184.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Simon Josef Durstewitz
Title: Concept Representations in Vector Space: Toward an Interdisciplinary Study of Meaning Variation
Abstract:
An increasing number of disciplines recognize the explanatory potential of meaning‑bearing mental structures through which individuals interpret the world and guide their behavior. Concept representations constitute a core class of these structures, emerging from individuals' experiences with concept referents and encoding and organizing their understanding of them. Recognizing a private level of meaning, where concepts are not objectively defined by rules in the world but constitute subjective structures in individuals' minds, raises a fundamental question: do different individuals actually mean the same thing when they invoke the same concept? As latent structures, concept representations are difficult to access and model empirically. The present study introduces a measurement framework that makes such representations empirically accessible through textual traces elicited under standardized conditions. Using transformer‑based sentence embeddings, the framework maps standardized responses elicited for concepts into a high‑dimensional shared vector space, opening concept representations to the systematic analysis of interindividual variation. It develops three analytical avenues: (1) comparing representational sharedness across concepts, (2) identifying variables that correlate with representational variation, and (3) examining how focal actors or subpopulations deviate from a reference population. Each avenue is illustrated through an empirical proof‑of‑concept drawing on a large‑scale free‑association dataset. Together, the demonstrations show how researchers from across disciplines can move from a research question and data source to analysis and interpretation. An accompanying GitHub repository provides a ready‑to‑use implementation of the framework for existing and custom datasets.

PaperId: 490, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25170.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Karthik Iyer, Madan Dabbeeru
Title: World Models, Trees and Foundation Models for Retail Forecasting: Evidence from Four Public Data Sets
Abstract:
A retailer makes different decisions at different grains of the product, store and time hierarchy: store orders for an item in a store, supplier funding for an item across stores, category performance by store, and the financial plan for the chain. Which forecasting model to use depends on the grain. This paper compares models at each grain on four public data sets (M5, six Dominick's categories, Breakfast at the Frat, and Corporación Favorita, the last kept out of all development), over rolling forecast origins with paired tests and model confidence sets. It covers price and promotion through the plan inputs these data record, not product, assortment or place. The models are a world model that carries each item's state forward under the price and promotion plan, the same network without that state, LightGBM, the Temporal Fusion Transformer, TimesFM, Chronos‑Bolt, Timestral, seasonal naive, and an equal‑weight average of the world model, LightGBM and TimesFM given the plan. The answer changed with the grain. For an item by store and an item across stores, the average had the lowest error on seven and eight of nine data sets, and the 90% confidence set held a median of 1 and 2 models. For a category by store, a category and the chain total, the lowest‑error model differed between data sets and a median of 4 of nine models were not separated by the four to six windows available. For category‑by‑store planning cost, the average or LightGBM was lowest on seven of eight data sets, and the world model was lowest only on M5; it was behind LightGBM item by store on six of eight. Every trained model used the plan, and on the weekly promotion‑driven data pretrained models were less accurate without it. These results hold for these data sets; a forecast solved across all four Ps, or a retailer's own data, may give different results. Every model, test and change that lost is reported.

PaperId: 491, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25159.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Amirreza Mohseni, Gerasimos Spanakis
Title: Legal Guidance in the Wild: How Users Seek Legal Help in Real-World LLM Conversations
Abstract:
People ask conversational AI models about their legal rights, obligations, procedures, and personal situations that may have legal consequences. To study this behavior, we first need to distinguish requests for legal guidance from other legally themed discussions and unrelated conversations. We contribute a multi‑axis taxonomy of legal queries capturing whether legal guidance is sought, how a request is formulated, and which legal domains it concerns; apply it to 2,122 naturally occurring WildChat‑1M conversations; and create a human‑reviewed gold evaluation set of 200 conversations. All annotations, model checkpoints, and evaluation code are publicly available. In this enriched sample, 71.1% of conversations containing legal content seek personalized or practical guidance. Rights‑and‑options advice is the most common primary request type among legal‑content conversations, and 25.3% of guidance‑positive conversations span multiple legal topics. The gold evaluation set supports a two‑stage comparison of ModernBERT‑base and ModernBERT‑large against a TF‑IDF cascade. Our framework supports large‑scale studies of legal guidance in conversational AI, and the public release of the annotated data facilitates reproducible research and future model development.

PaperId: 492, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25149.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yakiv Shavidze
Title: panvram: GPU-resident random access to a human pangenome cohort
Abstract:
Repeatedly sampling short sequence windows from a human pangenome requires an access representation as well as compression. panvram stores each assembly as a reference‑relative block archive and pools these archives on a GPU. For 558 haplotype assemblies, the default q4k representation occupies 16.642 GB of persistent pools including the decoded reference; a packed‑reference, compact‑directory representation occupies 11.634 GB. These quantities are not peak application memory. In the C1 experiment, default and fully compact forms delivered 743,271 and 736,762 windows/s; a separate public Colab run delivered 741,931 and 680,760 windows/s. All are batch API measurements and must not be pooled as repeated trials of an identical environment. Full‑decoding checks compared reconstructed FASTA checksums with the manifest. On the CPU, the M6 shuffled‑window workload at the same cohort cardinality reported 26 requests/s for AGC and 145,222 requests/s for refrel3 q4k. This comparison concerns one‑thread requests of 4 KiB on the recorded warm‑cache workload, not all genome‑access patterns. AGC provides the smaller incremental archive: 5.40 MB/assembly versus 13.04 MB/assembly for refrel3 q16k, with different exclusions; the size pair is not the same refrel3 configuration as the q4k timing pair. We derive an expected‑work expression for fixed independent granules and distinguish it from an empirical median‑latency predictor. Cohort‑scale counter and DRAM measurements motivate a locality hypothesis, but do not establish a causal per‑miss latency or independently reproduce a model‑failure verdict. The window‑cost verdict at N=558 is published with its harness and raw timings.

PaperId: 493, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25140.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Amirhossein Ghaffari, Susanna Pirttikangas, Ekaterina Gilman
Title: Spectral Adaptive Graph Transformer for Efficient and Scalable Traffic Forecasting
Abstract:
Traffic forecasting models based on spectral graph convolution offer an interpretable account of how information is mixed between sensors, but they rely on an eigendecomposition of the graph Laplacian. It costs cubic time, is fixed by the road network, and provides a symmetric operator that cannot represent the directed propagation of traffic congestion. Attention‑based spatio‑temporal transformers remove these limitations but generate a dense sensor‑by‑sensor attention map at each layer and time step, so memory, rather than accuracy, becomes the binding constraint on large networks. We introduce the spectral adaptive graph transformer, whose spatial operator is learned rather than derived from the Laplacian, directed rather than symmetric, and conditioned on the current traffic state rather than a static state, at a cost linear in the number of sensors. A sparse road graph diffusion branch provides the strictly local propagation that a low‑rank operator cannot express, and a zero‑initialized gate learns the balance between the two. Before spatial mixing, a unit‑mean‑gain frequency‑bin attention module reweights each sensor's short‑term periodicities according to its identity and current context. Across six public benchmarks spanning 170 to 1843 sensors, evaluated over three random seeds, the proposed model attains the lowest error of any single end‑to‑end model on one benchmark and remains competitive with the strongest current attention models on the others, while using about a quarter of their memory and training about twice as fast.

PaperId: 494, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25139.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shuo Xu, Hanrui Ying, Debin Liu, Jianjun Li, Zhiyuan Ma
Title: Reflection-Guided Dynamics Rectification for Text-to-Image Generation
Abstract:
Fine‑grained rectification of existing generations under a limited additional budget remains a key problem in test‑time optimization (TTO) for image generation. As for prior approaches, they could identify residual errors, but could not directly ensure that the model acts on the feedback during reasoning. Such errors stem from multiple sources, such as the initial noise or text prompt, and ultimately induce an execution gap of failing to handle potential deviations along the trajectory generating. However, classic models generally cannot remedy this gap. To narrow it, we propose Reflection‑Guided Dynamics Rectification (RGDR), which turns reflections on completed outputs into corrective interventions on the process of sampling dynamics at the trajectory level. Specifically, RGDR could impact every sampling step by adapting to instantaneous intervention. Moreover, RGDR generates flexible candidates while adjudicating between them and the reference. As experiments show, rectification from RGDR starts from the existing base trajectory and reflection, and RGDR is substantially more effective than former trajectory exploration. Under matched budgets for additional image generation, RGDR's gain in the cross‑model average final checklist score over the reference is 1.51× that of TIR prompt refinement and 1.81× that of Dynamic CFG.

PaperId: 495, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25137.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Faisal Mohammad, Mohamed Younis
Title: HullProbe: Measuring Interventional Part Reliance in Maritime Vessel Classifiers
Abstract:
Recognizing a vessel's type from an image supports maritime surveillance and sanctions monitoring, but a classifier can reach high accuracy by leaning on the generic hull instead of the more distinctive superstructure, and is then fooled when a vessel is re‑hulled or occluded. De‑biasing methods claim to remove such reliance, yet the field certifies them with worst‑group accuracy, a proxy that needs group labels and only infers reliance from accuracy. We measure the reliance directly. HullProbe swaps a registered anatomical part of a vessel for another instance's and reads how much that part drives the decision, using a same‑class swap to control for compositing artifacts. Because a surface vessel is a hull and a superstructure arranged along one axis, its parts form a 2x3 grid whose 2^6 = 64 swaps we evaluate exhaustively, and a single Walsh transform returns each part's interventional influence and its interaction spectrum. On planted shortcuts, where the true reliance is known, the measure tracks worst‑group accuracy (r = ‑0.94 over 45 configurations), and replacing its learned segmenter with human annotations changes the hull‑share by less than the audit's resolution. On the 26 vessel types of MARVEL, the classifier places about 46% of its corrected sensitivity on the generic hull yet follows the superstructure when the two conflict, and the group‑label‑free de‑biasers available there do not detectably reduce the hull's share. The findings hold across three architectures and a second maritime dataset, and the method extends to fine‑grained vehicle recognition on Stanford Cars.

PaperId: 496, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25126.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xi Zhu, Yuanlin Duan, Changyi Yang, Kai Mei, Riyang Bao, Shichao Zhu, Dimitris N. Metaxas
Title: Trackable Skill Library Lifecycle Management for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
Skill‑augmented agentic RL has emerged as an effective approach to improving LLM agents on long‑horizon tasks. Despite this progress, individual skills may follow distinct trajectories as the policy evolves, with some becoming redundant after the model internalizes their capabilities, others remaining valuable as external scaffolding, and still others turning harmful. However, existing skill library systems fail to identify each skill's true contribution due to free‑riding among co‑retrieved skills, difficulty confounding across tasks, and the absence of skill‑specific counterfactual evidence, which prevents reliable skill lifecycle management. We propose TrackRL, an agentic RL framework where skill tracking drives skill library full lifecycle management. Specifically, within each GRPO group, we turn grouped sampling into online randomized controlled experiments. Independent random injection and within‑group contrasts on the same task isolate each skill's true contribution, and reliability‑weighted aggregation accumulates evidence across groups. As evidence accumulates, we continuously track skill utility, which measures the skill's causal contribution as external scaffolding, and model mastery, which reflects how far the corresponding capability has been internalized. Along this line, we formulate skill lifecycle management as an evidence‑gated state‑transition process that governs each skill from generation and admission through protected incubation to retention, retirement, or removal, while a soft capacity bound controls library growth. Experiments show that TrackRL outperforms recent skill‑augmented RL baselines in both library‑assisted and skill‑free evaluation, with further analyses revealing how skill value shifts during policy learning and how evidence‑driven state transitions shape skill library evolution. Our code is available at https://github.com/xizhu1022/TrackRL.

PaperId: 497, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25121.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yanyan Wu, Guanyu Zhu, Changbin Zhao, Jin Zhang, Dexu Yu, Tianmin Sun, Jining Luan, Chunxiao Li, Hanwen Du, Youhua Li
Title: ClinSDT: LLM-Encoded Clinical Semantic Guidance for Sepsis Treatment via Decision Transformer
Abstract:
Offline sepsis treatment aims to learn treatment policies from retrospective ICU trajectories. Decision Transformer‑based methods provide a natural sequence modeling framework for this task, but they mainly rely on raw physiological states and historical clinician actions. Such raw trajectory tokens may not explicitly capture clinical semantics that clinicians use in practice, such as patient severity, recent treatment response, and current risk priorities. To address this limitation, we propose ClinSDT, an LLM‑assisted Decision Transformer framework for offline sepsis treatment. ClinSDT uses a frozen LLM as a semantic bridge rather than a treatment decision maker. It constructs three clinical semantic views from ICU trajectories, namely Profile, Context, and Advisory, and inserts their encoded representations as independent tokens into a Decision Transformer policy. To support policy refinement and rollout, ClinSDT further trains a Treatment‑Response Forecaster to estimate the next physiological state, SAPS‑II change, and predictive uncertainty from state‑action inputs. In the second training stage, the forecaster screens local counterfactual treatment candidates, and only low‑uncertainty candidates with lower predicted SAPS‑II increase are distilled into the policy after semantic regeneration. During inference, ClinSDT performs closed‑loop treatment rollout by refreshing semantic inputs from the currently available patient state. Experiments on MIMIC‑III and MIMIC‑IV show that ClinSDT achieves consistent relative improvements over representative imitation learning, offline reinforcement learning, and Decision Transformer baselines under the same rollout protocol. Code and data are available at https://github.com/KAG778/ClinSDT.

PaperId: 498, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25114.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jingwen Bai, Guochao Bai, Canbo Zhang, Shuangqi Li, Minchao Hu, Weichun Huang, Shuang Liu
Title: Compile Once, Run Cheap: Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents, and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds
Abstract:
Embodied AI lacks the data‑rich pretraining that gave language models their agents and skills, so new manipulation capability costs demonstrations per task or a frontier model in every episode. We study a third route: a strong general model acts only as an offline author that writes, runs, diagnoses and repairs a manipulation skill in simulation until it passes an exam on layouts drawn after freezing; the frozen skill then runs as code alone or under a cheap caller that reads only its description. We call this skill‑level recursive self‑improvement Skill‑RSI and specify a compile protocol (isolated, audited author; hidden validation layouts; no‑feedback and inherit‑only controls; tamper‑evident ledger) and a reuse protocol that runs the identical files with executors from another model family. On 7 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with cluttered tables, Claude Code compiled 4 tasks into 7 frozen skills, 5 from a first draft needing only qualification, at USD 4.29‑8.22 of author cost each (USD 55 per skill counting the 13 failed campaigns). The other three tasks did not compile in 18 campaigns, including five with GPT‑6 and a pre‑registered 150‑layout run: on the hardest task every campaign scored 78‑95 of 100 but had 3‑16 safety aborts, failing the gate of 95% success with zero aborts; a 100‑episode exam bounds an abort rate only to 3.6%. On hidden layouts, repair that inherits the previous version beat from‑scratch rewriting in 8 of 8 controlled campaigns (sign test p = 0.004); an inherit‑only lineage attributes most of the gap to inheritance, with development feedback adding a little (3 of 3, p = 0.125). Write‑once campaigns found no detectable first‑draft effect of practice (minimum detectable effect 14 points). The frozen skills kept 148/150 successes on new layouts with no model and 147/150 with a DeepSeek‑flash caller at USD 0.00028‑0.00054 per episode; no direct‑control baseline was run.

PaperId: 499, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25113.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Galen J. Wilkerson
Title: Self-organizing reinforcement learning: a learner-free swarm approaches the explore-exploit optimum
Abstract:
The explore/exploit trade‑off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). We show that a minimal foraging swarm approaches its optimum ‑ the ideal‑free / Nash allocation of a multi‑agent resource‑sharing game (an equilibrium, not a return maximum) ‑ with no learner and no reward signal. Agents explore by heavy‑tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; this cascade cycle balances exploration and exploitation and drives foragers toward the ideal free distribution. The swarm attains the shape of this optimum (committed foragers track richness with slope 0.94) but not its exact equilibrium ‑ it stays measurably exploitable ‑ reaching it dynamically (~150 steps) through the coupling of recruitment to movement: remove the coupling and matching collapses (0.94 ‑> 0.08). The RL sits at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro‑rule: no step evaluates payoff (reward‑free by construction, though the crowd signal is informationally tied to payoff), and the swarm reaches the allocation without learning it (quality plateaus and re‑settles after resources move, no cumulative gain). Against a trained baseline the comparison is two‑sided: in an easier, disembodied game a learner is more precise, while in the same embodied environment the reward‑free swarm reaches ~65% of a validated oracle ceiling at zero training and leads until trained PPO and centralised‑critic (CTDE) learners overtake it (~74‑75%, 16 seeds, all above the swarm mean) after ~4,000 of 15,000 training steps ‑ its advantage is in budget, not asymptote. In this one setting we read it not as beating RL but as a strong zero‑shot, reward‑free operating point: a demonstration that the self‑organizing physics of a minimal swarm can carry a collective close to the optimum RL seeks, with none of RL's machinery.

PaperId: 500, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25111.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Abdul Karim, Matt Keon
Title: Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise
Abstract:
As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re‑testing it. We measure that choice in Wellocate, a simulated assay campaign with known true values. It is built on a generated landscape and on two real protein datasets, GB1 and PhoQ, scrambled so no model can answer from memory. We test five language models as minimal agents, with no tools and no memory beyond the history in each prompt. They misallocate in both directions. Three over‑confirm, spending most of the budget re‑testing. On the generated landscape one under‑confirms, trusting single readings, and there every model ends with a worse final pick than a basic scripted strategy. Each failure has its own cause. The over‑confirmers run short of new candidates worth trying: a list of untried candidates cuts their re‑testing and, on real protein data, makes two of them pick much better. A running summary of their readings or a description of the landscape changes it by at most five percentage points. For the under‑confirmer, re‑testing its top candidates in a final round, replayed on its own campaigns, recovers only about a quarter of what it loses by picking the wrong candidate. This suggests confirmation has to run through the whole campaign. We release Wellocate as a benchmark and reinforcement‑learning environment with frozen splits and scripted baselines. With it, anyone can measure how an agent splits its budget before trusting it with real experiments, and train agents to split it better. Code, data and the environment are available at https://github.com/Xstendyl/wellocate.

PaperId: 501, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25096.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jeonghwan Choi, Jibin Hwang, Hayoon Park, Hyeonjae Cheon, Hwanjun Song
Title: Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources
Abstract:
Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona‑driven simulations. Its questions are constructed by linking entities and intermediate answers across heterogeneous sources, requiring agents to identify the relevant sources, carry evidence between them, and produce a grounded answer. To systematically evaluate LLMs on these retail workflows, we develop RetailRAG, a retail‑aware framework equipped with auto‑schema briefing, source‑routed plan chaining, and diagnostic plan revision. RetailRAG consistently outperforms existing agentic RAG baselines across all evaluation axes, serving as a strong reference system for assessing LLM agents on retail workflows. On RetailBridge, evaluating ten LLM backbones with RetailRAG reveals multi‑source chaining as the dominant bottleneck across providers and model scales, suggesting that reliable retail agents require explicit cross‑source orchestration rather than scaling alone. Code and data are publicly available at \urlhttps://github.com/DISL‑Lab/RetailBridge.

PaperId: 502, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25093.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kaiwen Wei, Kejun He, Jie Zhang, Xiaomian Kang, Yuming Yang, Aijia Zhou, Xie Zhou, Yining Wang, Nayu Liu, Li Jin, Zhenyang Li, Jiang Zhong, He Bai, Jingxuan Wei, Junnan Zhu
Title: Structure-Aligned History Learning with Subspace-Structured Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
Abstract:
Generative recommendation constructs semantic IDs for catalog items and predicts the next ID from user interaction histories. However, existing methods face limitations in both stages. First, conventional quantizers may produce imbalanced code assignments and lack coherent intermediate semantic units between individual tokens and complete items, limiting history reconstruction. Second, recommendation models remain dominated by next‑item prediction, treating historical interactions mainly as conditioning context and providing limited supervision for recovering persistent preferences across the historical path, particularly when relevant preference signals are distributed over distant interactions. To address these limitations, Structure‑Aligned History Learning (SAHL) reconnects the two stages by using the structure created during quantization directly for history reconstruction. Its Semantic Residual Balanced Quantization (SRBQ) forms a balanced token‑subspace‑item hierarchy, and SAHL reconstructs history at these same granularities. Predictive entropy prioritizes uncertain transitions, while curriculum optimization progressively shifts training to inference‑aligned next‑item prediction. On four Amazon Review categories, SAHL improves NDCG@10 by 18.6%‑30.0% over RPG and 2.7%‑6.0% over strong method MHL. Controlled analyses verify balanced code use, the benefit of following quantizer‑defined groups during reconstruction, and dependence on user history. The relevant code is available at https://github.com/CQU‑MM‑Intelligent‑Lab/SAHL.

PaperId: 503, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25090.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Junwei Wen, Deshui Miao, Guangming Lu, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Xin Li, Wenjie Pei
Title: Think Visually Across Space and Time: Grounded Reasoning for Video Segmentation
Abstract:
