Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) requires a model to identify an implicitly described target and predict its pixel‑level mask trajectory, while resolving the spatial relations and temporal events that determine the answer. Text‑only Chain‑of‑Thought (CoT) can explain a target choice without making the underlying visual references explicit, leaving a \emphvideo reference gap between linguistic inference and the evidence distributed across frames. We introduce Temporal Chain of Video Primitives (TCoVP), a spatiotemporally grounded form of Video CoT that organizes query‑relevant observations into a chronological reasoning chain. Each primitive associates an entity reference with temporal support and timestamped spatial evidence, and the chain interleaves these references with language to guide reasoning about which entity is relevant, when the queried event holds, and where its evidence appears. The selected target primitives then provide box prompts and temporal support for video mask prediction. We construct TCoVP‑SFT‑15k and TCoVP‑RL‑13k to learn this representation through supervised fine‑tuning and chain‑aligned reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones demonstrate the strong performance of TCoVP, highlighting the effectiveness of organizing spatial and temporal evidence within the reasoning process. All models and code will be publicly released. Project page: \urlhttps://victor‑wjw.github.io/TCoVP/

PaperId: 504, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25089.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Dengyuxing Wang, Yonggang Zhang, Qianshu Cai, Huajiang Zheng, Jun Song, Yangqiu Song, Yike Guo
Title: DAGLoop: Aligning Method Design with Experimental Feedback in Automated AI Research
Abstract:
Automated AI research agents aim to improve machine learning methods by iteratively proposing, implementing, and evaluating candidate methods. Existing work uses the outcome of each evaluation to determine how the next candidate should be revised for performance improvement. However, a candidate often combines multiple design decisions, and its overall outcome alone does not reveal which decisions produced their expected effects, whether their required conditions were satisfied, or which decisions should be retained or revised. Inspired by ablation studies in the machine learning community, we propose DAGLoop to test the expected effect of a design decision by comparing implementations with and without that decision while preserving the other decisions it requires. Specifically, DAGLoop translates each design decision's rationale into a testable expectation and pairs it with a targeted experiment, forming an experimental specification for assessing the expected effect under its required conditions. Using these specifications, we formulate ablation planning as the construction of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from the candidate method's design: nodes associate decisions with tests, and edges encode dependencies. The DAG specifies which decisions each experiment must retain and supports joint tests when an expected effect requires several decisions to act together. Outcomes are recorded with the tested decisions, expectations, and conditions to form structured research memory. This memory guides the agent in retaining experimentally supported decisions, revising unsupported ones, and planning further experiments when the evidence is unresolved. Experiments on dozens of research tasks demonstrate substantial performance improvements achieved by DAGLoop across diverse executable research settings. Code and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/deng34567/DAGLoop.

PaperId: 505, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25087.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sunghoon Kim, Sangyeop Kim
Title: Beyond Factual Accuracy: A Benchmark for Evaluating Perspective Alignment in LLMs
Abstract:
Large Language Models often generate factually correct responses that fail to maintain user‑requested perspectives, blending multiple perspectives and forcing users to filter through unwanted information‑‑‑a perspective control failure that factual accuracy metrics cannot detect. We introduce PerspectiveBench, a benchmark quantifying perspective alignment by constructing scenarios where multiple valid reasoning paths coexist, and propose the Perspective Alignment Score (PAS) to measure adherence to specified perspectives. Experiments reveal that state‑of‑the‑art models successfully include target content but fail to exclude non‑requested perspectives. Providing documents through RAG improves factual grounding but does not resolve perspective drift, as models prioritize comprehensive coverage over strict user constraints. Code and data are available at https://github.com/sunghoon014/PerspectiveBench.

PaperId: 506, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25085.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Pavel Sokolov, Alexander Kuklev
Title: A sound pure type system with ranks as sorts and Type-in-Type
Abstract:
We present a dependently typed pure type system that contains a circular axiom s : s for a certain sort s and is nonetheless strongly normalizing. Girard's paradox is avoided because our sorts are not closed under a Π‑former: function types are placed in sorts according to their rank. Turns out that this system has a unique set of characteristics: it has similar normalization behaviour as STLC (so complexity of normalization is TOWER‑complete) while at the same time allowing non‑uniform representation of arbitrary elementary recursive functions; furthermore, it has a nontrivial set‑theoretical model in ZF+GCH and allows to carry out nontrivial proof developments. Base normalization proof is surprisingly simple (modulo general metatheoretical properties of pure type systems) and has been fully formalized in vanilla Rocq (formerly Coq) without additional axioms.

PaperId: 507, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25069.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shenqi Zhou, Qiran Zou, Wenhao Zhao, Zhenyu Liao, Dianbo Liu
Title: Auto-MD-bench: Evaluating Autoresearch Agents for Real-World Medical Tasks
Abstract:
Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of developing machine learning (ML) models end to end. In medical practice, however, strong performance on the target metric does not fully characterize how good the models are in real‑world use cases. For example, medical ML models should also provide well‑calibrated risk estimates and remain robust across patient populations. Yet autonomous model development is typically guided by task objectives that emphasize simple predictive discrimination (e.g. AUROC). This raises a key question: are these objectives sufficient to guide agents toward models that meet the broader requirements of real‑world medical use? In this study, we introduce Auto‑MD‑bench, a benchmark of 15 real‑world medical tasks from 10 clinical datasets, spanning survival analysis, classification and sequential prediction, with external validation across cohorts, hospitals and time periods. We evaluate four agents: AIDE, AI Scientist v2, Codex, and Autoresearch. The strongest agents achieve competitive primary scores, yet their predicted risks are less calibrated than those of the simple baseline models, which could lead to severe medical accidents. Moreover, models with nearly identical primary scores can exhibit markedly different calibration, while performance varies substantially across population shifts. These findings show that primary task performance alone is insufficient to assess autonomous clinical modeling and multiple different metrics widely used in healthcare practice need to be taken into consideration.

PaperId: 508, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25066.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tao Zhang, Bin Liao
Title: Ineffective Occupancy in Heterogeneous GPU Clusters: Prediction, Contribution Analysis, and Readiness-Aware Scheduling
Abstract:
In heterogeneous GPU clusters, GPUs are costly and scarce, yet placing a job on a machine does not mean that the job becomes ready to run. A large amount of allocated capacity can remain occupied for long periods without producing useful computation, further aggravating the waste of compute resources. On the Alibaba GPU cluster trace we find that, even when GPU capacity is sufficient and placement is complete, 52.70% of execution records never became ready. We term this phenomenon ineffective occupancy. Building on this diagnosis, and keeping the placement policy fixed, we propose Readiness‑Aware Scheduling (RAS): it uses only nine attributes observable at admission time to predict readiness probability and reorders admission accordingly. Under a five‑fold split grouped by machine, the gradient‑boosted model reaches an ROC‑AUC of 0.8187. A feature‑group contribution analysis shows that the model's score is driven mainly by job profile, duration, and GPU model, with the request‑size group contributing least, followed by the scheduling and concurrency group. In GPU terms, RAS reduces the ineffective‑occupancy ratio (the share of cluster GPUs held under ineffective occupancy) from 43.64% to 27.15% and raises the effective coverage of large requests (eight GPUs or more) from 46.11% to 63.18%, without sacrificing capacity utilization. Relative to the upper bound obtained by ordering with ground‑truth labels, RAS captures 65.1% of the attainable improvement, well above the interpretable rules built only from the contribution‑analysis conclusions; the gain therefore comes mainly from predicting with all nine attributes jointly rather than from combining rules built on any single attribute group. These results indicate that readiness status is a measurable, predictable, and optimizable dimension of admission decisions in heterogeneous GPU clusters.

PaperId: 509, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25064.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Parsa Razmara, Seyedarmin Azizi, Ardalan Aryashad
Title: One Skill Takes Over: Clashing Agent Skills and a One-File Fix
Abstract:
Agent Skills are instruction files that tell a coding agent how to do one job. Users install skills from many authors, so two skills for the same job can be active at the same time. We ask what a model does when both skill files are in its context: does it combine their compatible rules, or follow one skill and drop the other? We build SkillClash, 16 pairs of same‑job skills in which code checks every rule and a reference output shows the best result that can be reached. On seven models from five families, from 4B open models to Qwen3‑235B and GPT‑4.1, a skill's rules are followed 93 to 99% of the time when it is loaded alone and 61 to 62% when a same‑job skill is loaded next to it. Most outputs show takeover: every rule that only one skill asks for is followed, and every rule that only the other skill asks for is dropped. The worked examples inside the skills drive this. When each skill file instead ends with one example that follows both skills, takeover falls to 1 to 15% on the six models we tested. Telling the model which skill has priority does not bring the dropped skill back, and telling it to apply both skills brings the dropped skill back only on the two strong models and leaves the interacting rules broken. One merged skill file written by the strongest model we used, Claude Opus 5.5, lets all seven models follow 96 to 99% of the achievable rules. Most of its gain over a plain list of both skills' rules comes from its one worked example, and such an example helps only when it is correct. Code and data: https://github.com/prazmara/skillclash

PaperId: 510, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25059.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shyam Sundar Saravanan, Tie Luo, Sanjay Madria
Title: HCFM: Helmholtz Component Flow Matching for Time Series Anomaly Detection
Abstract:
Flow Matching (FM) is an efficient simulation‑free approach for training flow‑based generative models, making it a promising foundation for scalable time‑series anomaly detection (TSAD). However, standard FM learns a monolithic vector field in which nominal transport and local density‑changing behavior are entangled. This creates a central challenge for TSAD; local expansion and contraction carry crucial anomaly‑sensitive information, yet isolating this signal requires expensive Jacobian‑trace estimation over the entire field. We propose \emphHelmholtz Component Flow Matching (HCFM), an unsupervised TSAD framework that parameterizes the vector field prediction network with separate transport, compression, and residual heads. The transport head is constrained to be divergence‑free, so divergence estimation is restricted to the compression head, while a lightweight residual head absorbs the remaining mismatch. This structured parameterization improves scalability and detection performance by separating volume‑preserving nominal transport from density‑changing compression, yielding cleaner anomaly signals from distinct deviations of nominal behavior. Experiments on large‑scale univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks show that HCFM consistently improves detection accuracy while maintaining efficient inference compared with 16 baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/TrustAIoT/HCFM__time‑series‑anomaly/

PaperId: 511, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25058.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sinan Ekmekçibaşı, James D. Trotter, Johannes Langguth, Xing Cai, Didem Unat
Title: Triple Overlap in Pipelined Krylov Methods on Multi-GPU Systems
Abstract:
We introduce a novel triple‑overlap implementation of the pipelined preconditioned conjugate gradient (Pipe‑PCG) and pipelined stabilized biconjugate gradient (Pipe‑BiCGStab) solvers, methods widely used in scientific applications. By leveraging a collective communication library, our approach extends conventional computation‑communication overlap to concurrently execute collective operations, irregular P2P communication, and compute kernels, enabling computation‑communication‑communication overlap across multiple GPUs. We evaluate the design on the MareNostrum 5 (H100) and Leonardo (A100) supercomputers, comparing against PETSc and the state‑of‑the‑art two‑stream NCCL implementation using SuiteSparse matrices and three massive instances scaled up to 512 GPUs. The three‑stream design outperforms the two‑stream baseline on every instance, with the margin widening from 2‑6% at 4 GPUs to 18‑47% at 64 GPUs. At 64 GPUs, the geometric‑mean speedup over the two‑stream baseline is 1.33x on MareNostrum 5 and 1.23x on Leonardo for Pipe‑PCG, and reaches 1.30x for Pipe‑BiCGStab. In large‑scale experiments, we observed a speedup up to 35% in Pipe‑PCG and up to 33% in Pipe‑BiCGStab compared to the two‑stream design. For PETSc, the margin is even wider, up to 3.27x speedup in both Pipe‑PCG and Pipe‑BiCGStab. Related code for the proposed method is available online: https://github.com/ParCoreLab/aCG

PaperId: 512, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25052.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hamin Chang, Fei Teng, Gyu-Sub Lee, Jae-Won Chang
Title: Generalized and Unified Power Flow Framework for Converter-Dominated AC/DC Power Grids
Abstract:
Modern power grids increasingly rely on power electronic interfaces, requiring steady‑state power flow analysis to accommodate diverse operating modes and network structures. Conventional approaches often rely on system‑specific formulations and sequential approaches to handle such complexity. However, these approaches may limit applicability to diverse grid configurations and lead to convergence and computational issues. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a generalized and unified Newton‑Raphson (NR) power flow framework for AC/DC hybrid grids. For generalized operational modeling, conventional and droop operating modes of generators and interlinking converters are represented through a common set of coefficients. For generalized structural modeling, models of AC transformers and DC/DC converters accommodate different transformer winding configurations and converter operating modes. For a unified solution, augmented variables are introduced to incorporate droop deadbands, output limits, and converter station losses into a single NR formulation, eliminating the need for sequential outer loops. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, its results are compared with those obtained from existing power flow methods and electromagnetic transient simulations across transmission networks, distribution networks, and microgrids. The implementation is made publicly available to facilitate its use in analyzing AC/DC hybrid grids.

PaperId: 513, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25045.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhenyue Peng, Lin Yang, Jie Wang, Xiaoqi Ni, Hanzhu Chen, Xize Liang, Yanjun Wu, Rujing Wang, Kaiwen Zhou, Jianye Hao
Title: SteadyThought: Mitigating LLM Under-Thinking via Thought-Level Preference Optimization
Abstract:
Flexible switching between reasoning trajectories (i.e., thought switching) has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). However, existing models often switch excessively yet fail to sustain promising reasoning thoughts, a phenomenon termed "under‑thinking". While recent efforts suppress switching to mitigate this, such over‑correction may discard valuable trajectories. To address this challenge, we propose Steady Thought (ST), a novel thought‑level preference optimization framework. ST formalizes under‑thinking as a preference issue at switching points, forcing single‑path continuations from identified points to yield high‑quality reasoning. Then, ST performs thought‑level preference optimization by treating the newly generated response as preferred and the original one as dis‑preferred. Experiments across multiple models and datasets show that ST effectively reduces token consumption, achieving reductions of up to 63.8%, while maintaining strong reasoning accuracy. Further analysis suggests that ST helps models acquire a generalizable ability to reduce redundant switching across domains and languages. Code is available at https://github.com/MIRALab‑USTC/SteadyThought.

PaperId: 514, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25043.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sicheng He, Yi Pan, Qiuting Yu, Jiaming Huang, Qi Lu, Shuyan Wu, Hongyan Feng, Xuanyu Liu, Jun Zhang, Jie Zhang, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang, Jianwei Yin
Title: VLA-Rolling: Fewer Denoising Steps, Better Control via Adaptive Action Reuse
Abstract:
Flow‑matching vision‑language‑action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding‑horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder‑‑‑the action tail‑‑‑is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action‑tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10‑step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment. Based on this observation, we introduce VLA‑Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action‑tail inheritance, per‑action confidence estimation, and confidence‑guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen. Across π_0.5, SmolVLA, X‑VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO‑Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA‑Rolling reduces action‑chunk inference cost in all 16 model‑‑benchmark pairs, achieving up to a 1.48× speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to 15.08 percentage points. These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA‑Rolling/.

PaperId: 515, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25034.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jike Zhong, Ming Li, Yuxiang Lai, Xi Xiao, Sheng Zhang, Ritwick Chaudhry, Tianle Chen, Jingyu Xie, Zheda Mai, Shao-Yuan Lo, Konstantinos Psounis, Yuanyuan Lei
Title: Beyond the Teacher: Understanding and Preserving Distillation Overshoot in Agentic On-Policy Distillation
Abstract:
On‑policy distillation (OPD) trains agents on their own trajectories using supervision from a stronger teacher. We uncover a counterintuitive phenomenon in multi‑turn agentic tasks: a smaller, initially weaker student can substantially outperform its teacher during training, only to regress as distillation continues. We term this phenomenon distillation overshoot. Through decision‑ and task‑level analyses, we trace overshoot to two competing effects of OPD: repairing weak student decisions and eroding successful student choices that the teacher disfavors. Early in training, repair outpaces erosion, allowing the student to combine the teacher's corrections with its own strengths and surpass the teacher. As training continues, erosion overtakes repair, causing these gains to vanish. Motivated by this finding, we propose Success‑Preserving On‑Policy Distillation (SPOD), which selectively masks conflicting teacher supervision on successful student choices and introduces a soft probability floor to counteract their erosion, while retaining teacher guidance elsewhere. SPOD requires only binary episode success and model probabilities already available during OPD. Across two model families and three agentic benchmarks, SPOD consistently outperforms ordinary OPD and evaluated variants, improving final success by up to 15.2 percentage points and surpassing the teacher by up to 20.0 points. Moreover, SPOD's final checkpoints outperform even ordinary OPD's best intermediate checkpoints in all six settings, demonstrating that beyond‑teacher gains can be not only preserved but further extended. Code: https://github.com/Jike338/SPOD

PaperId: 516, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25026.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiwon Jeong, Anjelo Jann Laroza, Chaewoon Yoon, Arjun Pillai, Pranav Kokati, Christian Hoang, Seunghyeok Hong
Title: One Head Away from Language Confusion: Single Attention Heads Across Model Families
Abstract:
Large language models sometimes reply in an unexpected language, a failure known as language confusion. We ablate individual attention heads in 12 model checkpoints spanning seven model series, using FLORES‑200 continuations in five languages and Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB) chat replies. In ten models, zeroing one head causes substantially more departures from the expected language than zeroing any other head in its layer; its LCB pass‑rate drop persists, though reduced, under mean ablation. Seven heads move 8.0 to 51.5 percent of all FLORES continuations out of the prompt's language, versus at most 1.4 percent for other same‑layer heads; the other three mainly affect explicitly requested languages. These seven heads matter less in base models given plain text. In two models, replacing the values a head reads at the requested‑language name with another language's mean makes replies fail and shifts some into that language, unlike a random change of equal size. Replacing a head's output with another language's mean redirects 84 to 99 percent of scored non‑English monolingual LCB replies into that language in five models. Yet the requested language's mean improves crosslingual replies beyond every control head only in the two Gemma models, whose baselines are low. Code and results are available in the public repository at https://github.com/christian‑hoang‑04/anonymous‑release.

PaperId: 517, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24999.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Stavros Damianakis, Konstantinos Psounis
Title: SoK: PIAtlas: Decomposing the Unbounded Prompt Injection Attack Space
Abstract:
Prompt injection is the dominant security risk for large‑language‑model (LLM) applications and agents, yet the field still lacks a coherent map of how these attacks are constructed. More than twenty public datasets describe prompt injection using incompatible vocabularies, often organized around delivery vector, attacker goal, or generation method. In this Systematization of Knowledge, we present PIAtlas, a taxonomy organized instead around how the injected instruction is constructed to subvert the underlying model. Its six classes, one per subversion mechanism, form the roots of a hierarchy of techniques and sub‑techniques that researchers can use to describe attacks consistently and design more systematic evaluations. We derive the taxonomy from how LLMs are trained, prompted, and influenced by human‑like framing, and compare it with historical attack data. To ground this comparison, we release PICorpus, to our knowledge the largest license‑clean collection of public prompt‑injection datasets, and map thousands of its records to PIAtlas under a human‑verified protocol. The mapping shows that attacks usually combine several techniques drawn from only a few mechanisms. It also reveals gaps that existing labels obscure: widely used agent benchmarks test only part of the attack space, and adaptive attackers favor mechanisms that curated benchmarks underrepresent. PIAtlas thus provides a common foundation for understanding this attack space, improving benchmark coverage, and guiding red teaming and defenses.

PaperId: 518, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24998.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Josep Marques, Hyunyoung A. Cho, Youngeun Kim, Youjia Zhang, Aecheon Jung, Kyuhong Shim, Sungeun Hong
Title: Block Recursive Transformers for Structured Parameter Sharing
Abstract:
Recursive Transformers depend not only on how many parameters are shared, but also on how shared parameters are organized across depth. Existing static schemes adopt two extreme reuse topologies: layer‑wise repetition, where each layer is reused independently, and global cyclic reuse, where the entire stack is repeatedly applied as a single shared function. We argue that sharing granularity is an important factor in recursive parameter sharing. This study proposes Block Recursive Transformers (BRT), which partition layers into contiguous blocks and recursively reuse each block before moving to the next. This intermediate topology enables local refinement within blocks while preserving depth‑wise transitions, without adding routing modules, auxiliary states, or extra training objectives. Across decoder‑only models up to 1.7B parameters, with additional encoder‑decoder and encoder‑only studies, BRT improves validation negative log‑likelihood and downstream accuracy over static recursive sharing baselines. Ablations and representation analyses further show that intermediate block granularity better balances local refinement and depth‑wise differentiation. Project website: https://aim‑skku.github.io/BRT/

PaperId: 519, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24993.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yongchao Long, Chunrui Zheng, Yuxuan Zhou, Guangkun Nie, Tian-Chi Ma, Chao Pang, Shuohuan Wang, Yuchen Ding, Xianbin Wen, Dianhai Yu, Junyuan Shang, Yuxi Zhou, Shenda Hong
Title: When Does Better Acceptance Pay? A Controlled Study of Speculative Decoding
Abstract:
The throughput gains of speculative decoding depend on the trade‑off between acceptance length and execution latency. We ask when additional acceptance is worth the cost of obtaining it. We establish a comparison protocol spanning training, inference, and evaluation, remeasuring released checkpoints and retraining six drafter recipes on shared target‑generated data across ten benchmarks and two target models. Alignment changes the picture: gaps that appear large in published comparisons shrink substantially under shared training and inference conditions. This narrowing motivates two deeper questions: how is acceptance improved at different costs, and when do these gains improve throughput? We find that acceptance can be improved through nearly free objective and context changes or more expensive token‑to‑token conditioning. DCore illustrates the former route as a strong baseline with little additional measured drafting overhead. The payoff is conditional: task uncertainty and serving conditions affect acceptance returns, execution costs, and the preferred drafter and budget. These findings inform future drafter design and deployment choices.

PaperId: 520, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24981.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chongkai Gao, Wenlong Huang, Haonan Chen, Lin Shao, Yilun Du, Jiajun Wu, Ruohan Zhang, Li Fei-Fei
Title: Dream What I Can: Sparse Visual Planning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
Abstract:
Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. We introduce DreamCan, a hierarchical policy that grounds video models through sparse visual planning: a high‑level planner adapted from a pre‑trained video model and a low‑level visuomotor policy. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, the high‑level planner generates sparse visual subgoals that balance reachability and task utility. From offline, action‑free robot videos, we estimate these quantities and use dynamic programming to select subgoal sequences without manual annotations. The resulting subgoals are more reliably attained than uniformly spaced alternatives, and the full system outperforms language, dense‑video, and uniform‑subgoal planners, reaching high planning success rates on Language‑Table tasks and 91.2% success on LIBERO‑Long with a 0.1B‑parameter low‑level policy. Additional suboptimal videos and test‑time compute further improve success. The system also performs challenging real‑world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations. More results are available at https://dreamcan.github.io/.

PaperId: 521, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24965.pdf   GitHub GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yerin Jung, Jongheon Jeong
Title: Meta Inverse Prompting for Video Generative Models
Abstract:
Recent advances in video generative models have enabled flexible conditional generation and editing pipelines, such as text‑to‑video, image‑to‑video, and reference‑guided synthesis. However, these workflows are inherently one‑directional, mapping conditions to videos without providing a mechanism to invert this process. In complex media production settings, the ability to recover controllable textual conditions from a given video is highly desirable, yet remains underexplored. While inverse prompting has been studied for image generation, directly extending these approaches to video is challenging due to the need to capture temporal dynamics beyond static appearance, as well as the substantial computational cost of per‑video optimization. In this work, we propose the first practical framework for efficient video inverse prompting. Specifically, we formulate inverse prompting as a meta‑learning problem and introduce Meta Video Inverse Prompting (MVIP), which learns a meta‑prompt optimized over temporal dimensions to enable fast and effective prompt inference. Our approach amortizes the inversion process, eliminating the need for costly iterative optimization at test time. Experimental results demonstrate that MVIP recovers higher‑quality inverse prompts with significantly improved reconstruction fidelity compared to image‑based inversion and iterative captioning baselines, while achieving substantial gains in efficiency. Code and video results are available at https://ueriniuno.github.io/mvip‑page/.

PaperId: 522, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24963.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Changho Lee, Janghoon Han, Rajdeep Mukherjee, Yeda Song, Lening Nick Cui, Xinya Du, Honglak Lee
Title: DeGMatch: Target-Aware Reasoning Data Selection via Deconfounded Gradient Matching
Abstract:
Reasoning post‑training on long trajectories has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but scaling such training to large datasets is increasingly expensive. We study target‑aware reasoning data selection, where a small reference set specifies a target capability and guides the selection of training trajectories for specialization. We find that existing target‑aware methods can exhibit limited target discrimination on long reasoning trajectories, while dominant population‑level structure in candidate gradients can obscure finer target‑dependent variation during gradient matching. To address these limitations, we introduce Deconfounded Gradient Matching (DeGMatch), which first constructs a target‑relevance gate and then reranks candidates using model‑specific gradients. DeGMatch centers gradients using the candidate‑population mean and removes leading principal directions before target matching, reducing the influence of dominant population‑level structure and improving target discrimination. Across mathematics, science, and code, DeGMatch outperforms strong heuristic, target‑aware, and reasoning‑specific data selection baselines, while remaining effective across selection budgets, model families, and scales. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/CHLee0801/degmatch.

PaperId: 523, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24957.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kazem Faghih, Yize Cheng, Shoumik Saha, Mobina Pournemat, Armin Gerami, Soheil Feizi
Title: Revealing what benchmark scores hide: Jointly measuring the breadth and reliability of LLM capabilities using accessibility profiles
Abstract:
Language model benchmarks assign each question a single outcome from one fixed wording, even though the same underlying request can be expressed in many equivalent ways. We argue that the quantity of interest should therefore not be correctness on one wording, but the accessibility of an inquiry, which we define as the probability that a model succeeds across meaning‑preserving formulations. The distribution of accessibility across inquiries reveals a structure that accuracy and existing best‑, worst‑, or average‑case prompt scores collapse: how broadly a model's capabilities extend across inquiries and how dependably those capabilities can be elicited. Two models can have the same average performance while one succeeds across more inquiries unreliably and the other succeeds across fewer inquiries but more consistently, leading to opposite preferences depending on whether the task allows multiple retries until one success or when repeated consistent success is required. Across six benchmarks and more than twenty models, this tradeoff is common: for about half of the model pairs with nearly equal mean accessibility, which model looks better depends on whether one success across five formulations is enough or all five must succeed, quantities we call Access@5 and Reliable@5, respectively. For some pairs the two measures diverge significantly, by up to 10 points in opposite directions. Accessibility also reveals that scaling, reasoning, and prompt optimization can redistribute capability across inquiries in ways aggregate accuracy obscures, sometimes broadening the set of inquiries a model can succeed on while making success on them less repeatable. Accessibility turns formulation sensitivity from a nuisance into a measurable property of capability, distinguishing what a model can sometimes succeed on from what users can actually depend on.

PaperId: 524, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24951.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Thai-Khanh Nguyen, Nhi Y. Pham, Uyen N. B. Vo, Thieu N. Vo, Cuong Pham, Tan M. Nguyen
Title: ControlJEPA: Principled Trajectory Regularization via Lyapunov Tube Loss
Abstract:
Next‑token prediction leaves hidden‑state trajectories largely unconstrained, while existing geometric regularizers primarily control the direction rather than the magnitude of trajectory deviations. We introduce \emphControlJEPA, a trajectory regularization framework based on a discrete‑time Lyapunov contraction condition from practical Input‑to‑State Stability theory. Its Lyapunov Tube Loss penalizes violations of this condition on a normalized, scale‑invariant measure of transversal deviation. When the contraction condition holds at every step, the hidden‑state trajectory remains within an explicit tube around the reference secant. In the partial‑ISS regime, we bound mean transversal energy, temporal variance, and average tube width using the Lyapunov loss and contraction parameters, with horizon‑independent variance bounds under uniformly bounded violations. ControlJEPA requires no architectural modifications. Across six benchmarks and six model families, it consistently improves accuracy and data efficiency over standard fine‑tuning and prior trajectory regularizers. The resulting smoother transversal profile also persists empirically during inference, when the regularizer is inactive. The code is publicly available at: \urlhttps://github.com/t‑khanusa/ControlJEPA

PaperId: 525, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24949.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Hanjun Luo, Xuecheng Liu, Xiucheng Zhang, Zhuoning Xu, Yingbin Jin, Yankai Chen, Xue Liu, Hanan Salam
Title: Over-Defense in Coding Agents Begins at Silent Forks
Abstract:
Language models behind coding agents are post‑trained with outcome rewards, and recent methods concentrate credit on the turns that decide the outcome. We find that defensive actions beyond what a task requires escape both. They begin at silent forks, the turns where every next action leads to the same outcome. Such actions leave the success rate unchanged, and frontier models take the disproportionate branch there in up to 91% of decisive actions under implicit budgets. The most direct fix, a checker in the trajectory reward, reaches these forks only through fully proportionate trajectories, leaving 74% of GRPO groups with identical rewards and behavior unchanged. This motivates a rethink of where learning signals belong, namely where behavior diverges, which a behavioral checker can locate and the outcome cannot. Our method, ForkDPO, contrasts a proportionate and a disproportionate action at the same prefix, at silent forks on both sides of the required behavior. On a test set of unseen repositories, it lowers a 4B model's disproportionate behavior from 70.3% to 58.9%, against 67.7% for DPO at randomly chosen turns, establishing behavioral divergence as a learning signal for how agents act beyond whether they finish. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Astarojth/silent‑forks.

PaperId: 526, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24937.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Quan Wang, Yiran Mao
Title: MLFont: Machine Learning-Driven Font Subsetting and Range-Compact Unicode-Range Slicing for Low-Latency Web Typography
Abstract:
CSS3 @font‑face rules with unicode‑range descriptors partition web fonts into downloadable slices. While Latin fonts need ~20 KB in WOFF2, Pan‑European (LGC) and East Asian (CJK) fonts contain 2,297‑30,759 codepoints (158 KB‑5.9 MB in WOFF2), where heuristic partitioning causes unused‑glyph downloads, high HTTP RTT, CSS bloat, or missing‑glyph fallbacks. We present MLFont, a machine learning and optimization framework that learns font slicing strategies from corpora via three stages: (1) a Zipfian High‑Frequency Tier (most) isolating top‑frequency codepoints; (2) a Latent Co‑Occurrence Topic Tier using Online Variational Bayes LDA (Online LDA) or a Deep Neural Network Topic Model (DNNTM) with Shannon Entropy Difference Loss and Sinkhorn‑Knopp normalization; and (3) a Memetic Range‑Compact Genetic Algorithm (GA) with Potts‑Viterbi dynamic programming and island bridging that minimizes topic discrepancy and CSS fragmentation. Across five Google Noto fonts (LGC, KR, JP, TC, SC), MLFont cuts 3G per‑glyph latency by 56.7%‑75.3% over single‑file delivery and 46.1%‑66.3% over equal‑bin baselines on CJK with 100% coverage, reduces CSS intervals by 17.9%‑41.7%, and achieves 1.56x‑6.09x cold‑cache speedups (65.4%‑84.9% CJK and 44.7% LGC bandwidth savings) across 20 websites in simulator and Headless Chrome benchmarks (45/45 exact slice‑set parity). Code: https://github.com/wq2012/mlfont Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/wq2012/mlfont

PaperId: 527, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24926.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sen Fang, Liwei Che, Dimitris N. Metaxas
Title: Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production
Abstract:
We present Stable Signer V3, an interactive high‑resolution sign language avatar system built on 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting. It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity‑specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. Shared Face Primitive Splatting adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; Test‑Time Body Primitive Splatting learns an identity‑specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and Test‑Time Tunneling Super‑Resolution uses TunnelingNet to recover identity‑specific high‑resolution details. Both test‑time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters. Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body‑boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high‑resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held‑out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.

PaperId: 528, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24921.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yulin Sun, Shenghua Li, Yong Dou, Xinwang Liu, Cheng Yang, Kele Xu
Title: DF-PALM: Dynamic Fusion Prompt Learning for Audio--Language Models
Abstract:
Few‑shot audio classification requires audio‑‑language models to distinguish variable acoustic events from limited labeled data. PALM's main formulation adapts encoded class representations without changing pretrained encoders, but its class representations remain input‑independent and classification uses audio features without class‑conditioned refinement. We introduce DF‑PALM, a dynamic feature‑space prompting framework that combines audio‑conditioned class representations with asymmetric cross‑attention for audio refinement. Class representations are conditioned after text encoding, held fixed across fusion layers for each input, and reused for final scoring. Both pretrained encoders remain frozen, avoiding audio‑conditioned text‑encoder passes. With PENGI as the frozen backbone, the main 16‑shot evaluation covered 11 benchmarks and six baselines. DF‑PALM achieved 80.69% mean accuracy and 80.32% macro‑averaged F1, exceeding PALM by 4.11 and 4.30 percentage points, respectively. Paired benchmark‑level tests supported both gains after Holm correction. Across four shot settings, DF‑PALM achieved the highest mean accuracy and macro‑averaged F1 among the four evaluated prompt‑learning methods. The gains extended to LAION‑CLAP and OpenFLAM, with significant improvements over PALM in both metrics. At 50 candidate classes, operator‑counted inference floating‑point operations increased by 0.39% relative to PALM. These results support instance‑conditioned feature‑space adaptation as an effective approach to few‑shot audio classification. Our code is publicly available at GitHub https://github.com/sunyulin0421/DF‑PALM.

PaperId: 529, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24888.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Cantao Su, Anna Wegmann, Esther Ploeger, Dong Nguyen
Title: Measuring Data Diversity with Embeddings: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Diversity Measures
Abstract:
Diversity is a critical property of text corpora, with direct implications for training data curation, test set design, and model generalization. However, its measurement remains fragmented and poorly understood. Existing embedding‑based diversity measures vary widely in how they are computed and can yield substantially different diversity scores on the same data, yet no systematic comparison of their empirical behaviour exists. We make two contributions toward addressing this gap. First, we present a taxonomy of 21 embedding‑based diversity measures, organizing them into four families based on their underlying computations. Second, we introduce EmbDivBench, a benchmark that evaluates these measures along three conceptually distinct components (variety, balance and disparity) on both simulated and natural text data. Although Mean Pairwise Distance is the most commonly used measure, our experiments show that it is outperformed by several alternatives on the three diversity components, with Graph Entropy being the best choice overall. Lastly, we distil these findings into practical recommendations for diversity measure selection.

PaperId: 530, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24885.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Riddhi Chatterjee, Ritish Shrirao, Kushagra Mehrotra, Viswanath Gopalakrishnan
Title: Goal Images Are Control Targets: Spatially-Grounded Goal-Image Synthesis for Robotic Manipulation
Abstract:
Goal‑conditioned manipulation policies are steered by a goal image, a picture of the desired post‑manipulation scene synthesized from the current observation and a language instruction. The prevailing assumption is that better image‑editing quality yields better goals, so goal generators are built and compared using general image‑editing metrics. We show this assumption is false. Across two independent goal‑conditioned policies on CALVIN, the image editors that top aggregate editing‑quality leaderboards (Gemini 3 Pro Image and GPT Image 1.5) produce worse control targets than our proposed far smaller finetuned open models, and the gap widens sharply for the multi‑step (long‑horizon) tasks robots actually face. A per‑dimension analysis explains why. Downstream policy success is governed almost entirely by manipulation adherence (selecting the right object and the right final state; Spearman ρ\approx 0.9 with success), while photorealism and aesthetic fidelity, precisely where large proprietary editors excel, are uncorrelated with success (ρ\approx 0). This dissociation holds on both CALVIN and the real‑world‑aligned SIMPLER‑Bridge benchmark. We then present SGE‑Goal, a spatially‑grounded decomposed editing framework that predicts initial and final 2D edit‑region masks before goal‑image synthesis. SGE‑Goal turns open base models (FLUX.1 Kontext, FLUX.2 klein) into the strongest goal generators we evaluate on CALVIN, and second only to Gemini 3 Pro Image on SIMPLER‑Bridge. Base models fine‑tuned with SGE‑Goal also hold up under chaining far better than the best proprietary editor, sustaining roughly seven times the success rate at the longest (five‑step) chains. We release code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human‑aligned diagnostic evaluator. Our results argue that goal generators must be selected by downstream utility, not by editing‑quality leaderboards.

PaperId: 531, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24871.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Adarsh Vatsa, William Eiers
Title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents
Abstract:
A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re‑derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state. On τ^2‑bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8‑27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.

PaperId: 532, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24865.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Galen J. Wilkerson
Title: A mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy field
Abstract:
Foraging recruitment is a contagion: an agent that finds a resource triggers a linear‑threshold cascade, the model built for rumour and adoption spread on social networks, now embedded in space. Because activation is degree‑normalized, the same rule that spreads the cascade also stifles it as neighbourhoods crowd, so the swarm aggregates on a resource and then releases to explore again. The cascade runs on the communication network, but acting on it moves agents in physical space, and that motion rewires the network: network and space are one coupled system, and this feedback, not any tuning, makes the coordination self‑limiting. Because recruitment chains along the graph rather than reaching near neighbours alone, whether a discovery stays local or spans the swarm is a question of percolation. The swarm holds itself in a cascade window that is locally near‑critical though globally subcritical, a self‑organized, self‑limiting drive‑release cycle, sandpile‑like but non‑conservative. Nothing is tuned, yet behaviours that foraging biology documents separately emerge together: recruitment to discoveries, marginal‑value patch‑leaving, and Levy search with a switch to local exploitation. These follow from one least‑committal principle, the resource field and the search both as maximum entropy, with Levy search matched to the field's sparsity and recruitment to its clustering, so active‑matter order and optimal foraging appear as one system seen in two domains. The gains are real but conditional: up to 7.6x the harvest of solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, shrinking to nothing when search is already easy. That sparse, clustered field is also the generic one, because resources almost inevitably aggregate, so one untuned rule should recur widely.

PaperId: 533, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24791.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Kien T. Pham, Yuhao Liu, Chong Hou Choi, Zhenqi He, Yanghao Wang, Chenyang Lei, Rui Liu, Qifeng Chen, Long Chen
Title: UniAVC: Unified Audio-Video Creation via Progressive Training and Asymmetric Scheduling
Abstract:
Unified audio‑video creation requires a single model capable of text‑conditioned joint synthesis, bidirectional cross‑modal generation, and instruction‑guided editing across both modalities. Existing methods rely heavily on paired corpora, which are scarce for joint generation and even rarer for editing. Consequently, they are spent learning single‑branch generative and editing capabilities that abundant unimodal data could readily teach, rather than on the cross‑modal coupling. Furthermore, prevailing systems apply a single shared noise schedule to both modalities, neglecting two critical limitations. First, due to the significant discrepancy in information density, video requires prolonged high noise to organize spatial and motion structure, whereas the sparser audio signal can settle earlier during the synthesis process, the dynamics a uniform schedule might compromise. Second, lockstep denoising leaves asymmetric workflows, such as conditioning on one modality to synthesize or edit another, untrained. We present UniAVC, which addresses both obstacles. It first trains each branch on unimodal dataset to full generative and editing competence, and subsequently dedicates paired data to exploit cross‑modal correspondence. Modality‑decoupled schedulers meanwhile warp the noise schedule independently from a shared timestep, while subtasks with one clean modality directly supervise asymmetric configurations. These settings respectively enable intent‑aware editing, which preserves one modality intact while enlisting it to constrain the other, and post‑inference self‑refinement, which regenerates only an unsatisfactory branch against an accepted one. UniAVC thus spans multiple creation tasks from a single set of weights without task‑specific adapters.

PaperId: 534, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24783.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hamidreza Dastmalchi, Ali Cheraghian, Aijun An, Abdelwahed Khamis, Lars Petersson
Title: ATLAS: Learning to Adapt LVLM Attention for Reasoning Video Segmentation
Abstract:
Reasoning Video Object Segmentation (RVOS) aims to localize and segment objects referred to by natural‑language expressions throughout a video. Although large vision‑language models (LVLMs) implicitly encode localization cues in their attention maps, these attentions are often noisy, diffuse, and scattered across layers, heads, and modalities, limiting their direct use for segmentation. Existing methods typically rely on handcrafted attention‑selection heuristics or computationally expensive attention refinement. We propose ATLAS, an attention adaptation framework that learns to transform raw LVLM attentions into object‑centric localization cues. ATLAS treats attentions from all layers, heads, and modalities as structured features, combining high‑resolution frame‑level attentions that capture spatial information with low‑resolution video‑level attentions that encode temporal context. A lightweight U‑Net equipped with temporal attention and FiLM‑based modulation fuses these complementary representations to generate coarse segmentation heatmaps, which are propagated across the video using SAM2. Extensive experiments on challenging referring and reasoning video segmentation benchmarks show that ATLAS outperforms existing frozen‑backbone methods. Code and models are available at \urlhttps://hamidreza‑136.github.io/atlas/.

PaperId: 535, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24777.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sjoerd van Straten, Alessandro Padella, Marwan Hassani
Title: Process-Aware Event Log Augmentation for Process Prediction under Labeled Data Scarcity
Abstract:
Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) forecasts future events of ongoing business processes based on event logs. However, deep learning PPM approaches are often limited by labeled data scarcity and the low variability of real‑world logs. To address this, we introduce SiamSA‑PPM, a self‑supervised framework combining Siamese learning with statistically grounded data augmentation. It employs novel transformation methods that leverage control‑flow semantics and frequent behavioral patterns to generate realistic, semantically valid trace variants, learning generalizable prefix representations without labeled supervision. Extensive experiments on real‑world event logs with a wide range of variability, incorporating exhaustive hyperparameter tuning, demonstrate the value of this process‑aware augmentation. Compared to state‑of‑the‑art baselines, SiamSA‑PPM achieves competitive or superior predictive performance in both next activity and final outcome prediction tasks. An open source implementation of our method is publicly available under https://github.com/SvStraten/SiamSA‑PPM‑Extension..

PaperId: 536, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24764.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sumit Anthony Gomes, Yasin Rahman, Taeeba Tasnia, Faiza Nooren Suhita
Title: BanglaBBQ: A Bias Benchmark for Question Answering in the Bangladeshi Context
Abstract:
This paper introduces BanglaBBQ, a question‑answering bias benchmark designed to capture stereotypes grounded in the Bangladeshi context, in both Bangla and English. Following KoBBQ and PakBBQ, BanglaBBQ adapts the original Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) by classifying its templates into three groups: directly translated (DT), modified to align target groups or contexts with Bangladesh (TM), and removed when deemed unsuitable for the Bangladeshi context (SR). This process retains 140 templates across six categories, comprising 76 DT and 64 TM templates. Five newly authored (NA) categories, based on stereotypes common in Bangladeshi society, are then added: marital status, age and political perception, regional origin, educational background, and mental‑health status. Native Bangladeshi annotators judged all 466 newly authored templates, and 372 were retained because a strict majority of English annotators identified the intended target and rated the attitude as common enough. Each newly authored template is linked to a documented source and a verbatim quote from it. Each evaluated template also has a counter‑stereotypical version of its disambiguated context. The dataset was evaluated using two open‑weight models (Qwen3‑4B and Qwen3‑8B) and two closed models (GPT‑4.1‑mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash). All four lean towards the stereotyped person when the context is ambiguous, in both languages, and the effect of language differs by model, so English results do not predict behaviour in Bangla. On the adapted BBQ templates, both Qwen3 models are also less accurate when the context contradicts a stereotype than when it confirms it. On the newly authored templates, the closed models follow counter‑stereotypical evidence almost perfectly, and all four models are more biased on the templates that annotators validated than on those they rejected.

PaperId: 537, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24758.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chris Dzoba
Title: Optimal single-track Gray codes from Gray-ordered necklaces
Abstract:
A single‑track Gray code of length n is a cyclic Gray code of n‑bit words in which every column is a cyclic shift of the first. For prime n the longest possible period is 2^n‑2. Whether it is attained for every prime has been open since Hiltgen, Paterson and Brandestini introduced these codes in 1996, and optimal codes were known for primes n\le 19. We show that a conjecture of Degni and Drisko (2007) on the reflected Gray code order of necklaces implies optimal single‑track Gray codes for every prime. Their list of necklaces, conjecturally a Gray path for prime n, closes into a Hamilton cycle of the necklace graph after (n‑3)/2 explicit Pósa rotations, and such a cycle lifts to an optimal code. This implication is formalized in Lean 4. Together with computation it gives optimal single‑track Gray codes for every odd prime n\le 47: for n\le 37 explicit codes checked word by word by a program independent of the generator, and for n=41, 43 and 47 codes obtained from the implication after the Degni‑Drisko property was verified at these lengths by two independently written programs.

PaperId: 538, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24757.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dengke Zhang, Fagui Liu, Quan Tang, C. L. Philip Chen
Title: CorrCLIPv2: Harnessing Unlabeled Images for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation
Abstract:
Open‑vocabulary semantic segmentation aims to classify pixels without being restricted to a fixed set of categories. Although Contrastive Language‑Image Pre‑training (CLIP) demonstrates remarkable potential for open‑vocabulary recognition, its segmentation capability is impaired by noisy inter‑class patch interactions. To this end, this work proposes a unified training‑free object‑centric framework, named CorrCLIPv2, from three complementary aspects of patch correlation, feature representation, and output regularization. Specifically, for patch correlation, we leverage class‑agnostic mask generators to explicitly disentangle inter‑class interactions. Moreover, we utilize spatially‑coherent features from self‑supervised models to compute attention scores to mitigate mask inaccuracies. Regarding feature representation, we devise a refinement mechanism to simultaneously strengthen spatial details and semantic representation. Within the output space, we unify predictions via voting in each mask to enhance spatial consistency. To mitigate contextual bias and enhance prediction accuracy of objects, we further extend the framework by incorporating a cross‑image object retrieval paradigm, which incurs minimal computational overhead. We build a memory bank of CorrCLIP‑enhanced features from unlabeled images and implement a regime of multi‑CLIP ensemble. By aggregating semantically consistent object features across diverse contexts retrieved from the memory bank, CorrCLIPv2 mitigates context‑induced interference and obtains more robust predictions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach establishes a new state‑of‑the‑art on 10 standard benchmarks. Remarkably, it even surpasses fully supervised open‑vocabulary methods across 22 multi‑domain datasets. Code is available at: https://github.com/zdk258/CorrCLIP.

PaperId: 539, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24750.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hangwei Zhang, Nathan Rouillé, Chuanxia Zheng
Title: CorrFlow: Self-Correcting Flow Matching
Abstract:
Flow‑matching models generate samples through iterative velocity predictions, but typically do not revisit these predictions using the intermediate representations that produced them. We introduce CorrFlow, a self‑correcting flow‑matching framework that reuses this information through a lightweight refiner. Under rectified‑flow interpolation, the error of the one‑step clean prediction equals the realized velocity residual scaled by the noise level. Motivated by this identity, the refiner learns to predict residual corrections from the base model's clean prediction, conditioning, noise level and hidden states from the same forward pass. The correction is added to the base velocity before each sampling update, so subsequent predictions are made from the corrected state. This requires no additional base‑model evaluations and only one lightweight refiner evaluation per step. Our theoretical analyses establish conditions under which feature reuse outperforms raw‑input affine predictors and refiner training achieves greater residual‑risk reduction than continued base‑model training under a matched training compute budget. Experiments on class‑conditional image generation, text‑to‑video generation and image‑to‑video generation show consistent improvements over the corresponding base models, including gains in visual quality and physical consistency. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/corrflow‑project

PaperId: 540, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24730.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mich-Seth Owusu, Stephen E. Moore, Akwasi Asare, Lawrence Adu Gyamfi, Paul Azunre, Joel Budu, Jonathan Asiamah
Title: GLOSS-MT: Controllable Low-Resource Machine Translation with an Editable Dictionary
Abstract:
Adapting a pretrained machine translation (MT) model to new terminology usually requires new parallel data and another round of fine‑tuning, which is costly for low‑resource languages. We ask whether controllability can be added to MT, and the fine‑tuning burden reduced, without degrading the pretrained model. GLOSS‑MT looks up the source's noun phrases in an offline English‑Twi dictionary, replaces every phrase found by its Twi translation in place, and fine‑tunes a translation model once to translate these mixed inputs. We apply the same data and pipeline to NLLB‑200 (600M, 1.3B, 3.3B), OPUS‑MT en‑tw and TranslateGemma 4B. On a document‑level English‑to‑Asante Twi benchmark (84 documents, four domains), every fine‑tune scores above its pretrained base in chrF2 (+2.85 to +5.48), and the three NLLB fine‑tunes are the best open systems (50.12‑50.80). A direct controllability test on human‑translated Bible passages shows that the three fine‑tunes tested write 79‑97% of the dictionary terms, and that replacing every dictionary entry by a different term changes the output accordingly (70‑97% of the new terms appear) with no retraining. We release the models, data and code.

PaperId: 541, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24723.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Meng Shu, Wei He, Hang Zhou, Runke Liu, Kai Han, Yunhe Wang
Title: Where Natural Language Ends in Agents: Executable Skill Composition with MetaSkill
Abstract:
Agent Skills express open‑ended task knowledge in natural language, but composing them requires persistent execution order and upstream‑output handoffs. We propose selective formalization at Skill boundaries: coordination relations with stable references and machine‑checkable constraints become executable, while substantive task judgments remain within Skills. We introduce MetaSkill, a hybrid representation that preserves complete Skill packages and local instructions while making invocation dependencies and predecessor‑text bindings executable through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) runtime. This interface supports explicit coordination without prescribing how each Skill performs its local task. Across 20 multi‑Skill artifact tasks and two LLMs, we compare natural‑language procedures, prompt‑visible graphs, and MetaSkill derived from a common frozen plan per task, using the same designated Skill packages. Additional comparisons evaluate AgentSkillOS with the same available Skill packages as MetaSkill, as well as agent systems using their configured tools. Blinded artifact judgments yield favorable preference point estimates across all reported comparisons, with 95% task‑bootstrap intervals excluding parity against Prompt Graph under DeepSeek‑V4‑Flash and OpenClaw under GLM‑5.2. In audited GLM‑5.2 execution traces, all planned nodes complete and all declared precedence constraints are satisfied. Together, these findings support MetaSkill as a practical interface for composing open‑ended Skills, combining local linguistic flexibility with executable dependencies, explicit predecessor‑text bindings, and auditable coordination. Code is available at: https://github.com/TokenRhythm/opensquilla/tree/paper/metaskill‑lp4fm‑2026

PaperId: 542, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24717.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qisheng Zhou, Zhen Xiong, Qiaoyu Tan
Title: DiffuPlan: Editable Planning State for Diffusion Language Model Agents
Abstract:
Diffusion language models (dLLMs) are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, yet dLLM agents largely inherit an interaction protocol designed for AR generation: once intermediate state is written, later observations can only be incorporated by appending more text. This is a poor match to a defining capability of dLLMs ‑‑ reconstructing earlier text conditioned on context that appears both before and after it. We ask whether this capability can support a different agent‑state paradigm in which intermediate planning state is directly revisable as evidence arrives. We introduce DiffuPlan, a diffusion search agent that maintains a single editable planning state and reconstructs only the affected steps when later evidence resolves an entity or changes the search route. To support variable‑length revisions, we introduce Expansion‑Partition Marginalization (EPM), which marginalizes over equivalent expansion paths. We further adapt diffusion trajectory RL to multi‑turn search. Across four multi‑hop QA benchmarks, DiffuPlan achieves 50.24 average F1, outperforming strong AR search agents. More importantly, under identical data and training, editable planning state improves the diffusion agent by 2.44 F1 versus only 0.47 for its AR source model. These results show that dLLMs need not imitate append‑only AR agents: revising committed state is a distinct agentic advantage.

PaperId: 543, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24680.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Ruodai Cui, Shuaizheng Liu, Rongyuan Wu, Lei Zhang
Title: MESS: Multi-Exposure Sequence Synthesis for Generalizable Image Enhancement
Abstract:
Despite the significant progress in image enhancement under adverse illuminations, such as low‑light image enhancement, exposure correction, and backlit image enhancement, existing models show limited generalizability to different scenarios. A major bottleneck lies in the lack of large‑scale and diverse training data, as these tasks typically rely on manually captured, precisely aligned image pairs that are expensive to scale up. Although synthetic data have been explored as an alternative, existing synthesis methods are limited in modeling complex adverse illumination conditions and camera imaging pipelines. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework to synthesize realistic training pairs for generalizable image enhancement in the wild. Specifically, we first derive multi‑exposure sequences (MES) from high‑bit RAW images by rendering them under different exposure settings through an emulated ISP pipeline. Using these RAW‑derived MES as supervision, we train a diffusion‑based RGB‑to‑MES generator to synthesize plausible exposure sequences from a single 8‑bit RGB image, extending the synthesis pipeline from limited RAW collections to large‑scale in‑the‑wild RGB data. For each source image, we randomly sample one synthesized exposure variant as the degraded input and use the original high‑quality RGB image as the target. With the proposed MES Synthesis (MESS) approach, we construct a dataset of 500K training pairs and train a lightweight network, which demonstrates significantly better generalization performance than existing models across various image enhancement tasks. Code and data are available at https://github.com/PolyU‑VCLab/MESS.

PaperId: 544, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24676.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Qijian Tian, Jiayu Ying, Ke Fan, Lizhuang Ma, Xin Tan
Title: From Views to Worlds: Active Exploration over 3D Worlds for Vision-Language Models
Abstract:
Vision‑language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in 2D visual understanding tasks, yet the passive view‑centric perception paradigm limits their capacity for 3D spatial reasoning. Such reasoning often requires actively acquiring spatial evidence beyond the currently visible views, such as camera poses and cross‑view spatial relationships, to infer 3D relationships that are not explicitly represented in 2D images. However, existing methods either lack active exploration or merely provide additional views during inference, without explicitly acquiring such spatial evidence beyond 2D images. In this paper, we propose View‑to‑World (V2W), an active exploration framework that enables VLMs to actively explore 3D worlds and lifts VLMs from passive view‑centric perception to active world‑centric spatial reasoning. Given a spatial reasoning task with multi‑view images, V2W first reconstructs an explicit 3D world with geometry, camera poses, and language‑grounded semantics, and exposes it to VLMs through visual and linguistic interfaces. Through multi‑turn interaction with these interfaces, VLMs iteratively acquire spatial evidence from the constructed 3D world, enabling active world‑centric spatial reasoning. V2W can be integrated with existing VLMs in a training‑free manner and can be further enhanced by optimizing the exploration policy via reinforcement learning. Experiments on spatial mental modeling benchmarks demonstrate that V2W substantially improves VLM baselines in the training‑free setting and achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance with the learned exploration policy, highlighting the importance of active exploration for spatial intelligence. Project page: \urlhttps://fangzhou2000.github.io/projects/v2w.

PaperId: 545, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24663.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Siyu Zhang, Yuquan Lu, Yoshua Y. Li, Yifan Ding, Kun Zeng, Yu Huo, Yifu Guo, Rongxiang Weng, Xunliang Cai, Xiaoying Tang
Title: What RL Brings to Reasoning: A Few Decisions the Base Model Would Not Make
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) substantially improves mathematical reasoning, but what it adds to the base model remains unclear. We investigate this through a sequence of generation‑time interventions on Qwen3‑4B‑Base, measuring how much of its RL‑trained counterpart's gain each intervention recovers on 120 AIME problems. Power sampling with the same 8,192‑token output limit brings no gain beyond greedy decoding. Yet borrowing the RL model's token only where the two models' greedy choices differ, roughly 4% of generated positions, recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 gain, with similar recovery across three model pairs on MATH‑500. We find that even a single opening token has a substantial effect: forcing the base model to begin with "Alright" recovers 35% of the RL gain. The opening alone is insufficient, however. Later replacements after the same opening add another 5.2 percentage points to pass@1, and the fixed rules we test for inserting reflective words such as "Wait" do not reproduce this benefit. Sparse replacement also retains much of the base model's diversity while staying close to the RL model at pass@1. At k=256, it solves 67.5% of the problems, significantly more than the RL model (61.4%) and a mixture of whole responses matched in pass@1 (61.45%). The comparison is at equal attempt counts rather than equal compute, since rl‑replace consults both models at every decoding step. These results show that the opening can recover a meaningful part of the RL gain, but a larger contribution comes from later choices, which can be borrowed while retaining much of the base model's diversity. Code is available at https://github.com/CyrusZhang04/WhatRLBrings.

PaperId: 546, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24659.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Omar El Bachyr, Saad Ezzini, Tegawendé F. Bissyandé, Jacques Klein
Title: RAGit: Turning Document Preprocessing into an Experimental Variable for RAG
Abstract:
Document preprocessing choices can substantially affect retrieval in Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, yet they are often selected heuristically and are difficult to compare under consistent conditions. We present RAGit, an open‑source experimentation workbench for the systematic and reproducible evaluation of document preprocessing choices through downstream retrieval. RAGit represents parsing, chunking, indexing, retrieval, and evaluation as configurable experimental stages, enabling controlled comparisons while the remaining downstream settings are kept fixed. It preserves provenance from retrieved chunks to source pages and maps heterogeneous retrieval units to a common page‑level ranking for evaluation. The current implementation supports multiple parsers and chunking strategies, dense and late‑interaction retrieval, reusable intermediate artifacts, and multi‑configuration benchmarking. We demonstrate RAGit through controlled experiments comparing alternative preprocessing configurations under a fixed retrieval setup, illustrating how preprocessing can be treated as an explicit experimental variable. RAGit and its documentation are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/OmarElbachyr/ragit). A demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/tsst‑Bhfz4I.

PaperId: 547, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24649.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Naman Vats
Title: Good Judgment, Bad Advice: Decision-Model Controllers Raise Agent Cost Without Improving Success
Abstract:
Agent scaffolds increasingly delegate small decisions (whether to stop, verify, or change approach) to cheaper models. We ask whether a typed decision model, Jev 1.13, consulted only at deterministic decision points, makes a Claude Sonnet 5.5 terminal agent cheaper without making it worse. In a pre‑specified study on Terminal‑Bench 2.1, we hold one agent loop fixed and vary only the controller: none, deterministic rules, a small LLM (Claude Haiku 5.5) answering the same questions, Jev, and a placebo that samples Jev's development‑phase choice frequencies at the same moments. On 21 held‑out tasks (315 trials), Jev raised cost per attempt by 19% (geometric‑mean ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.02‑1.36) at an identical pass rate (73.0% vs. 73.0%). Jev was cheaper than the small‑LLM controller (ratio 0.81) but 22% more expensive than the placebo, and no pass‑rate difference between arms was detectable. Offline, Jev ranked finish requests better than the alternatives (AUROC 0.78 vs. 0.62 for rules and 0.60 for the small LLM) but was poorly calibrated: its mean probability that a run was complete was 0.50 when 87% of those runs passed, so it asked the agent to verify work that was already correct. No controller ever chose to abandon a run. Informative decision signals did not become useful interventions; we discuss what that would require.

PaperId: 548, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24648.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuhua Zheng, Xueyi Chen, Xinze Zou, Xin Li, Haoji Hu, Huan Wang
Title: EdgeKernelBench: Unified LLM-Driven Kernel Generation for Edge Backends
Abstract:
Recent works show that LLMs can generate kernels with strong performance on server GPUs. Edge deployment presents distinct challenges because the hardware is heterogeneous, the software stacks are fragmented, and the resource budgets are tight. LLM kernel generation across diverse edge backends has yet to be studied systematically. We introduce EdgeKernelBench, which combines a unified IR deployment framework with a hierarchical benchmark for edge workloads. The unified IR captures reusable computation, scheduling, and memory decisions and connects to each target backend through a compiler interface. The benchmark spans progressively larger program scopes, from individual operators to compact model graphs, across representative edge application domains. We instantiate the design with TVM as a reference compiler and validate it across heterogeneous edge backends. With a single generation attempt, the best model achieves 64.5% Correct@1 but only 25.5% Fast@1.0. This gap shows that functional correctness does not consistently translate into performance gains. We therefore introduce the Layered Edge Kernel Agent (LEKA), which organizes optimization through a layered IR. On the agent evaluation subset, LEKA achieves 43.5% Fast@1.0, compared with 13.0% for direct generation and 26.1% for Claude Code. LEKA and Claude Code use the same base model and optimization budget. Together, EdgeKernelBench and LEKA support unified evaluation and layered optimization of kernels generated by LLMs across edge backends.

PaperId: 549, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24646.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Megh Shukla, Edo Collins, Prashanth Chandran, Karel Petránek, Sergio Orts-Escolano, Mathieu Salzmann, Alexandre Alahi
Title: Modeling Uncertainty Propagation in 3D Morphable Models
Abstract:
We study the problem of mapping parameter‑space variance of a 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) to per‑vertex variance. Traditionally, per‑vertex variance has been used to visually interpret the learnt parameter uncertainty. However, mapping parameter‑space variance to per‑vertex using sampling or error propagation is computationally expensive. We address this limitation with Closed‑form Local Uncertainty Estimation (CLUE), which transforms the parameter‑space distribution of 3DMMs to per‑vertex through a closed‑form approximation. CLUE emerges from applying the law of total variance to the 3DMM formulation and is modular, computationally inexpensive, and accurate. Subsequently, we study integrating CLUE for in‑the‑wild human mesh recovery training and inference. We note that CLUE uses the geometry of the mesh as an inductive bias when predicting the variance, leading to improved accuracy. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that when used in training, CLUE (1) outpeforms probabilistic and deterministic baselines on metrics evaluating joints, mesh and uncertainty, and (2) has the highest uncertainty‑to‑error spearman correlation, with applications including data mining and interpretable uncertainty.
