Finally, we share SAM 3D Body (CLUE) which augments the regressor with high resolution uncertainty maps. We make our code available at https://github.com/vita‑epfl/CLUE

PaperId: 550, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24624.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yunhui Liu, Xudong Jin, Qizhuo Xie, Chunhui Zhao, Xiao Luo, Tao Zheng, Bin Chong, Tieke He
Title: Uncovering Semantic Hierarchies in Text-Attributed Graphs via Variational EM-based LLM-GNN Synergy
Abstract:
While hierarchical structures are intrinsic to organizing human knowledge, current representation learning on text‑attributed graphs predominantly operates on flat semantic spaces, overlooking the rich coarse‑to‑fine granularity inherent in real‑world data. To bridge this gap, we propose SHiFT, which synergizes the reasoning power of LLMs with the structural representation capability of GNNs within an Expectation‑Maximization (EM) paradigm. In the E‑step, we harness LLMs as expert taxonomists to induce an explicit semantic tree, introducing a lightweight Mapping & Diagnosis strategy that reduces inference costs by surgically updating the hierarchy only when anomalies are detected. In the M‑step, we align the GNN encoder with this induced hierarchy from complementary perspectives, including clustering partition, topological skeleton, and semantic concepts. Theoretical analysis interprets SHiFT as a generalized Variational EM algorithm. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SHiFT not only achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance but also uncovers high‑quality, human‑readable taxonomies. Our code can be found at https://github.com/Cloudy1225/SHiFT.

PaperId: 551, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24622.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Matteo Spanio, Antonio Rodà
Title: Fluxion: A Differentiable DSP Runtime from Training GPU to Real-Time Edge
Abstract:
Native real‑time audio engines meet audio deadlines but are hard to connect to machine‑learning workflows, while tensor frameworks integrate with machine learning but process audio as offline batches without timing guarantees; runtime layers built on them inherit the host's scheduling and deployment footprint. This paper presents Fluxion, a Rust audio DSP runtime for cascaded second‑order sections, FIR filters, and delay‑line effects. Fluxion implements the parts that are specific to DSP: closed‑form filter design, forward kernels, analytic adjoints for the recursion, and stability checks. It relies on existing libraries for the autodiff graph, GPU code generation (tested here on CUDA), and array interchange. One graph algebra is lowered to a differentiable training engine and to an allocation‑free real‑time engine; between them, a trained graph is checked for stability and frozen into a versioned artifact that an edge device checks again before playback. We compare Fluxion with six framework‑hosted and native baselines under one float32 protocol. Among the systems that compute the exact recursion, Fluxion has the highest GPU throughput when data stays on the device and the highest throughput on most CPU workloads, while its CPU training step is slower than those of torchaudio and GRAFX. Its test suite checks the audio thread for allocations with an instrumented allocator, and we report measured latency tails. Fluxion is open source at \urlhttps://github.com/matteospanio/fluxion.

PaperId: 552, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24619.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qibin Gu, Yunfeng Yan
Title: Beyond Geometric Closure: Measuring and Diagnosing Mechanical Consistency in Visual Dynamics
Abstract:
Visual accuracy, geometric validity, and agreement with applied forces are distinct requirements for visual dynamics. We introduce a diagnostic framework that connects reaction‑free SI measurements to controlled interventions on coordinate readout, training integration, and actuator response. Reference replay calibrates the measurement path, while continuous scoring exposes progress against fixed engineering targets. With three seeds per setting, we evaluate KeyCLD and CON across 343 planar assemblies at 64/256 pixels and V‑JEPA + AC and LingBot‑VA on 100 shared spatial test assemblies. CON reduces image MSE by 37.6%/37.2% relative to persistence, yet neither planar model attains valid native geometry. At 256 pixels, calibrated RGB replay places forecast errors far above the reference measurement floor. Exact‑state KeyCLD has identical geometric pass rates under Euler and RK4 training, yet its score rises from 52.65 to 64.30 as force and energy errors decrease. In both spatial pathways, CAD/IK reconstruction restores geometry while mean actuator residuals exceed five times the engineering targets. These diagnoses distinguish coordinate correction, numerical improvement, and persistent force‑response errors, guiding targeted improvements to visual dynamics.

PaperId: 553, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24610.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Lukas Amiet, Gabriel Sánchez-Blanco Repgen, Mayank Mittal, Victor Klemm, Andrei Cramariuc, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
Title: Solving a Giant Rubik's Cube with a Quadruped Robot
Abstract:
Pedipulating a freestanding articulated object requires controlling its pose and internal configuration while maintaining balance. We demonstrate this capability by autonomously solving a giant Rubik's Cube with a quadruped using only its feet. The task demands repeated precise interactions, since unintended layer motion can invalidate subsequent operations. We develop an onboard RGB‑D perception pipeline that estimates the cube's metric pose and its full color state from partial views acquired through locomotion and flipping. A planner converts the computed solve into robot‑executable skill sequences. Learned whole‑body skills reorient the cube while preserving its layer configuration and turn its layers with one foot pinning the cube as the other pushes. We train these skills using reinforcement learning with privileged observations and distill them into policies that map onboard depth and proprioception to joint targets. The deployed policies tolerate variations in relative robot‑cube placement and recover from external disturbances. The system completes three autonomous hardware solves, each about 30 steps over 8‑9 minutes. These results show that combining onboard perception with coordinated pedipulation enables a quadruped to complete extended multi‑step physical tasks. Additional material can be found at: https://leggedrobotics.github.io/rubik‑skills/

PaperId: 554, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24604.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Gengyu Liao, Yechun Yong, Zheng Chen, Jianze Li, Ziqing Zhang, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
Title: SCOPE-VSR: A Broad-Coverage Training Dataset for Video Super-Resolution
Abstract:
Open‑domain video super‑resolution (VSR) requires temporally coherent details across widely varying scenes and subjects. However, existing training datasets are often semantically imbalanced and insufficiently diverse. We address this data bottleneck with a structured curation pipeline for open‑domain VSR, SCOPE. In this pipeline, we combine task‑oriented video selection with hierarchical semantic rebalancing. Applying this pipeline to a large‑scale collection of data sources, we construct the SCOPE‑VSR dataset for training and SCOPE‑test for testing. SCOPE‑VSR has approximately 27k videos and provides balanced and diverse coverage of various real‑world scenarios and subjects. We further develop GraCo‑VSR, a novel framework for one‑step video restoration. GraCo‑VSR adopts a reliability‑aware design with explicit supervision to reduce degradation‑induced distortions in motion and texture guidance, allowing the model to benefit more effectively from the diverse training content in SCOPE‑VSR. Evaluations show that our model achieves strong reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality. Our code is available at: https://github.com/gyliao2768/SCOPE‑VSR.

PaperId: 555, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24601.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yanlan Kang, Ruiqi Liu, Xinpei Gu, Tzu-Yi Lei, Shuai Xu, Xukun Zhang, William Cheng-Chung Chu
Title: TCMScience: An Autonomous Scientist for Traditional Chinese Medicine
Abstract:
Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) research connects classical texts, medicinal entities, molecular assays, computational predictions, and clinical studies. An autonomous research agent must preserve the inferential boundaries between these evidence types while coordinating analysis across heterogeneous resources. We introduce TCMScience, a scientific knowledge‑discovery agent that separates language‑model proposals from execution and release authority. Its architecture combines a trusted kernel, a scientific compiler, and claim‑support contracts: plans are compiled into typed operations, execution is bounded by explicit permissions, and candidate findings are checked against source provenance, study design, and claim scope before release. The full capability registry contains 117 public‑source connectors with 444 typed operations across 29 domains and 150 native tools across 12 domains; the TCM data hub catalogs 136 databases, 76 dataset specifications, and 84,294 formula‑source records. These resources support model‑independent workflows through browser and local execution interfaces. In a network‑pharmacology analysis of Gegen Qinlian Tang, replacing the whole‑proteome background with the assayed‑protein background changed the number of significant pathways from 66 to zero; incorporating inactive screening records identified nine pathways, including drug‑metabolism signals retained as mechanistic hypotheses. A governance ablation over 121 constructed erroneous outputs spanning 26 classes released 121 errors without governance, 57 with the domain layer, seven with the kernel, and zero with both layers. All 10 compliant controls were retained. These results establish complementary control of known failure modes and show how explicit evidence contracts change the conclusions an agent is permitted to report.

PaperId: 556, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24599.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Abdullah Al Shafi, Kazi Saeed Alam, Sumaiya Rahim Suma, Sk. Imran Hossain
Title: Severity-Channel Conditioning: An Injection-Level Study for Consumer-Device Deblurring
Abstract:
Motion‑deblurring models lose substantial accuracy when transferred from professional cameras to smartphone‑derived imagery. This paper studies whether a severity descriptor, partly derived from the paired sharp target, helps adaptation on the iPhoneBlur consumer‑device benchmark. Under a shared update budget, input concatenation of a severity map is compared with global feature modulation by capture metadata, spatial feature modulation by the severity map, and a tier‑contrastive output objective, together with an unconditioned spectral‑loss control, all fine‑tuned from the same domain‑adapted latent‑diffusion baseline. The primary experiment is an oracle diagnostic: target‑derived information is supplied at inference. For the evaluated model pair, input concatenation improves overall peak signal‑to‑noise ratio from 31.23 to 31.30 dB, whereas feature modulation, the contrastive objective, and the spectral‑loss control do not exceed the baseline. The gain is positive on 87.2% of test images and on 14 of 15 held‑out source videos; this video‑level analysis describes the evaluated checkpoint pair and does not establish robustness to retraining, and three training seeds are reported separately. The input‑level gain recurs on a transformer backbone. In one exploratory run, zeroing the channel at inference retains most of the gain in peak signal‑to‑noise ratio but lowers structural similarity below the baseline. A normalized‑step diagnostic does not support the expected larger‑gradient explanation. The results characterize the evaluated configurations and do not establish injection location as the sole cause, a spatial‑locality mechanism, or a reliable deployment advantage.

PaperId: 557, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24598.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaowei Ji, Lishan Xu, Jianing An, Jie Luo, Wenjun Wu, Lei Huang
Title: AdamPM: Memory-Efficient LLM Optimization via Moment Pooling
Abstract:
Adam is widely used for training large language models (LLMs) owing to its strong optimization performance and training stability, but its element‑wise estimation for the first and second moments incur substantial memory overhead. Although numerous memory‑efficient optimizers have been proposed, many incur additional computational overhead or require additional tuning of hyperparameters. Consequently, Adam remains a dominant and reliable choice for LLM pre‑training. We propose AdamPM (Adam with Pooled Moments), a simple and memory‑efficient variant of Adam that groups adjacent moment entries along the row or column dimension and represents each group by a single shared mean. AdamPM can well inherit Adam's hyperparameter settings and is readily integrated into existing Adam optimizer implementations, with less memory overhead. We systematically investigate pooling of both first and second moment estimates and identify second moment pooling as the effective design. With a group size of s, AdamPM reduces second moment memory to 1/s of the original requirement. Extensive experiments on language model pretraining, fine‑tuning and multimodal learning demonstrate that AdamPM maintains model performance and training speed while substantially reducing optimizer‑state memory. Our code is available at \urlhttps://github.com/jixiaowei95/AdamPM.

PaperId: 558, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24588.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hangyu Li, Yiming Meng, Zhaohui Liang, Yunqing Xiao, Yuxuan Chen, Bofeng Cao, Shixiao Liang, Jiaxi Liu, Haotian Shi, Xiaopeng Li
Title: Physics-Informed Koopman Learning for Data-Efficient System Identification of Automated Vehicle Dynamics
Abstract:
Understanding how a particular automated vehicle reacts to nearby traffic can improve motion prediction, control development, traffic simulation, and safety evaluation. However, commercial automated driving systems are proprietary, and single encounters may provide only a few seconds of noisy data. Standard physical models are interpretable but inflexible, whereas neural models are often data‑hungry. We propose a physics‑informed Koopman framework that combines a calibrated car‑following law with a correction learned from the observations. A weak‑form estimator learns this correction from velocity measurements integrated over time, avoiding noise‑sensitive numerical differentiation. The resulting continuous‑time model predicts the follower's response and provides interpretable measures of driving behavior. Experiments on OpenACC and CATS‑CF evaluate 5‑, 7‑, and 11‑second histories. Averaged over these histories, the constant‑time‑headway branch reduces speed prediction error by 16.0% and 15.4% on OpenACC and CATS‑CF, respectively, relative to the best neural baselines. The PI‑Koopman branches achieve the lowest mean speed and gap errors among the physical and neural comparators. Weak‑form estimation reduces acceleration‑field reconstruction error by 74.5% in noisy known‑law simulations and noise‑induced field perturbation by 91.6% in paired real‑vehicle measurements. The same PI‑Koopman system identification supports following‑mode recognition with an approximately eleven‑fold difference in median residual variance between human drivers and automated vehicles, and a single residual threshold achieves 85.4% balanced accuracy. The branch informed by the intelligent driver model takes a median 17 to 26 ms for identification and forecasting on the tested central processing units, supporting frequent target adaptation.

PaperId: 559, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24586.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Agus Sudjianto, Denis Burakov
Title: Conditional Weight of Evidence for Gradient-Boosted Credit Models: Estimation, Additivity and Its Relation to Adverse Action Reasons
Abstract:
Traditional weight of evidence assigns a credit characteristic a value based on its association with default across a population. Credit analysis also requires an assessment of that characteristic in the context of an individual applicant's record. We study conditional weight of evidence for this purpose. It measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known. Its sign identifies whether the characteristic adds adverse or favorable information for that applicant, and its magnitude measures the strength of that information. The same characteristic value can therefore receive different assessments for applicants with different payment histories or other credit attributes. We develop estimators using gradient‑boosted trees and evaluate their accuracy in a bureau‑style simulation. Regressions of the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence more accurately than separate models fitted to default outcomes, provided the full model is accurate. They also recover a deliberately constructed file‑age effect whose direction varies with utilization and is often missed by marginal weight of evidence. Local class‑frequency estimates improve on marginal weight of evidence but remain inaccurate for some weak effects. An application to FICO HELOC data illustrates estimation when the population evidence is unknown. Conditional weight of evidence provides an applicant‑specific interpretation of the information in a credit characteristic; its population summary, a conditional information value, splits the joint information in the record across blocks when averaged over orderings. Neither is an adverse action reason, which explains the fitted score difference between the applicant and chosen passing records.

PaperId: 560, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24556.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dmitry Scherbakov, Oleg Chernikov, Victoria Khamash, Kirill Afendulev, Alexey Dontsov, Ivan Oseledets, Elena Tutubalina, Anton Korznikov
Title: From Stories to Features: Scaling Concept Vectors for AI Alignment & Interpretability
Abstract:
We study feature vectors: directions in a language model's activation space that correspond to human‑interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept‑antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment‑relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.

PaperId: 561, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24540.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ahad Bin Islam Shoeb, Jamal Uddin Tanvin, Kamrul Hasan, Alve Reduan, Imtiaz Ahmed
Title: Theory-Guided Instance-Dependent Early Stopping via Second-Order Loss Dynamics
Abstract:
Instance‑dependent early stopping (IES) reduces training computation by skipping backpropagation for examples whose losses have stabilized, but the second‑order loss‑difference criterion used by IES lacks a theoretical justification. We develop Theory‑Guided Instance‑Dependent Early Stopping (TG‑IES), which analyzes this criterion under explicit assumptions and derives a noise‑calibrated mastery threshold and a conditional stability bound for instance exclusion. We show that second‑order differencing has a favorable bias‑variance trade‑off over first‑ and third‑order differences in a specific signal‑to‑noise regime, and that its signal contains both gradient‑drift and curvature terms. TG‑IES derives its stopping threshold and patience from training‑run statistics rather than using the manually selected threshold of IES. Across CIFAR‑10 and CIFAR‑100, TG‑IES saves 53‑58% of backpropagation instances in its main convolutional settings while keeping accuracy within 0.1‑0.9 percentage points of full training; in the primary ResNet‑18/CIFAR‑10 setting, this corresponds to 35.7% FLOP‑normalized savings. The method also transfers to ViT‑Tiny, where it achieves smaller savings and incurs a modest accuracy cost. These results provide a theoretical basis for second‑order instance‑dependent early stopping and show that theory‑guided calibration can substantially reduce training computation under the assumptions and experimental settings studied.

PaperId: 562, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24530.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jin-Shiang Hu, Bo-Yuan Cheng, Li Su
Title: An Optical Music Recognition Tool for String Quartets
Abstract:
This paper presents an optical music recognition (OMR) system tailored for PDF scores of string quartet pieces. The approach begins with a SegNet‑based segmentation model to localize musical regions, followed by convolutional neural networks and image processing techniques to classify and extract musical symbols. To improve rhythmic precision, dynamic programming methods enforce time signature constraints and explicitly handle tuplets. Evaluation using a longest common subsequence metric across multiple feature matrices demonstrates robust accuracy in recognizing pitch, onset, duration, and accidentals on a benchmark dataset. Code and data are available at https://github.com/lattellie/25‑omr.

PaperId: 563, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24512.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Jeannette Bohg, Wenzhen Yuan
Title: ContactBench 1.0: A Benchmark for Everyday Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
Abstract:
Contact‑rich manipulation underlies many everyday human activities, yet evaluating robots on such tasks remains difficult: the tasks involve diverse contact behaviors and are hard to reproduce across laboratories. Drawing on observations of everyday human manipulation, we identify eight essential skills that provide a practical framework for studying contact‑rich manipulation. We introduce ContactBench 1.0, an extensible benchmark that instantiates these skills through 36 reference tasks and more than 40 object assets. The assets capture task‑relevant geometry and contact behavior, can be fabricated reproducibly on consumer‑grade 3D printers, and are each paired with a matching simulation model. Controlled task variations in both the real world and simulation enable evaluation of how well robot systems generalize. We evaluate recent representative vision‑only and visual‑tactile policy learning methods on six benchmark tasks. The results reveal that while vision‑only policies struggle to perceive or react to contact events, visual‑tactile policies do not meaningfully improve their performance, highlighting that contact‑rich manipulation remains a significant challenge for current policy learning methods. By providing common task definitions alongside physical and simulated assets, ContactBench 1.0 offers a shared testbed for developing, evaluating, and comparing contact‑rich manipulation systems. The benchmark will be open‑sourced at https://jingyi‑xiang.github.io/contactbench.

PaperId: 564, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24498.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qingyue Chen, Huaiyuan Yao, Wanpeng Xu, Varun Shourie, Qianwen Wang, Hua Wei
Title: MAVE: A Multi-Agent Framework for Grounded Pedagogical Feedback from Online Class Videos
Abstract:
Timely pedagogical feedback is difficult to scale in online classes, where long and noisy videos make student responses hard to locate and automated systems often produce generic advice weakly grounded in actual classroom behavior. The key challenge is to connect the instructional goal of a specific lesson segment with temporally aligned multimodal evidence of student responses, and then translate the observed gap into an actionable teaching move. We introduce MAVE (Multi‑Agents for Video‑based Educational Feedback), a multi‑agent framework for grounded pedagogical feedback from online‑class videos. MAVE decomposes feedback generation into four roles: the Curator structures the lesson and infers expected student activity; the Observer extracts aligned speech, visual, and interaction evidence; the Assessor estimates the activity supported by student behavior; and the Advisor generates gap‑conditioned teaching recommendations. To evaluate this capability, we introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark designed to measure whether feedback systems can ground diagnoses in multimodal student evidence, and generate actionable pedagogical feedback. MAVEBench contains 173 knowledge‑point segments from approximately 20 hours of authentic online‑class videos across STEM and Humanities, together with comprehensive simulation. Experiments show that MAVE outperforms direct prompting, Reflexion, and TextGrad in diagnostic correctness, instructional alignment, and actionability. Our code is available at https://github.com/DaRL‑GenAI/MAVE

PaperId: 565, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24480.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kahim Wong, Kemou Li, Yiming Chen, Haiwei Wu, Jiantao Zhou
Title: RiSE: Residual Subspace Expert for Generalizable Text-Centric Image Forgery Localization
Abstract:
As AI‑assisted image editing becomes increasingly prevalent, Text‑Centric Image Forgery Localization (TFL) is essential for protecting trust in financial and legal records. However, we observe that existing TFL detectors predominantly rely on Full‑Parameter Fine‑Tuning (FPFT) and fail to generalize to unseen forgery types because FPFT can induce low‑rank feature collapse and overfit training artifacts. Meanwhile, prior detectors capture diverse forgery traces with a single unified representation, making subtle traces entangled and difficult to learn. To address these challenges, we propose RiSE, a Residual Subspace Expert model that preserves pre‑trained priors by freezing principal SVD components and adapting only the residual subspaces with a ViT‑only segmentor to avoid feature collapse. RiSE introduces forgery‑aware residual experts, where each expert is trained independently on a training subset with a particular forgery type, and we show that cross‑domain localization performance improves consistently as more experts are added. At inference, we introduce Latent Perturbation Confidence (LPC), which selects the most confident expert by analytically computing the latent‑perturbed output. LPC enables efficient confidence estimation with a single forward pass, avoiding repeated forward passes on perturbed samples and improving expert selection. By training on synthetic forgery data, RiSE with 1 expert outperforms prior methods on real‑world forgery images by 20.4% while reducing training steps by 10 times. Scaling the number of experts to 9 yields a 35.8% gain. RiSE remains effective with DCT feature, even when the majority of the parameters is frozen with RGB‑only pretraining. Code: https://github.com/KahimWong/RiSE.

PaperId: 566, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24467.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tongshun Zhang, Zixuan Zhong, Pingping Liu, Jin Kuang, Yubing Lu, Dong Liu, Qiuzhan Zhou
Title: Unifying Amplitude-Phase Coupling and Reliable Endogenous Priors for Low-Light Image Enhancement
Abstract:
Frequency‑domain methods have shown strong potential for low‑light image enhancement (LLIE) because they can effectively regulate global illumination. However, most existing methods assume that amplitude and phase can be restored independently, while overlooking their inherent spectral coupling. This artificial decoupling often leads to information inconsistency and structural distortions. To address this issue, we propose a frequency‑spatial framework that jointly models spectral interaction and reliable prior guidance. We first empirically analyze the coupling between amplitude and phase and develop an Amplitude‑Phase Adaptive Compensation Fusion (APACF) module. Instead of enforcing a hard separation between the two components, APACF enables their bidirectional interaction, resulting in spectrally coherent restoration. In addition, directly extracting priors from raw low‑light inputs is unreliable, since severe noise and underexposure destroy critical visual content. To alleviate this problem, we introduce an Endogenous Reliability Prior (ERP). Specifically, we treat an intermediate result, preliminarily restored in the frequency domain and already close to the ground‑truth illumination, as a high‑fidelity source for extracting complementary pseudo‑infrared and gradient cues. Based on ERP, we further design a Dual‑Modal Guided Refinement Network (DGRN) to inject these purified structural cues into the decoder, thereby recovering missing fine textures more accurately. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that our method achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance and consistently surpasses existing methods in both quantitative metrics and visual quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/bywlzts/Amplitude‑Phase‑Coupling‑Net.

PaperId: 567, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24462.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chamuditha Jayanga Galappaththige, Jason Lai, Lloyd Windrim, Timothy Patten, Donald G. Dansereau, Niko Suenderhauf, Dimity Miller
Title: O-SCD++: Replay-Free Online Scene Change Detection via Recursive Evidence Fusion
Abstract:
Online scene change detection requires an agent to detect what has changed in a previously mapped environment while it is still on site, observing from unconstrained viewpoints and without access to future observations. This causal setting is strictly harder than its offline counterpart, and online methods have consistently trailed offline accuracy. O‑SCD closed that gap by treating change as a persistent property of a 3D Gaussian splatting map of the reference scene, surpassing the strongest offline methods in change detection accuracy while operating at over 10 frames per second. O‑SCD optimizes a change field over the Gaussians of the reference map, refitting it to all past cue maps at every frame, a step that consumes more than half of the per‑frame budget and forces accuracy to be traded against speed. We present a replay‑free formulation that eliminates this trade‑off. Because the reference map stays fixed, rendering the change field is a linear operation. Each new observation can therefore be carried onto the map's Gaussians directly, by a single backward pass of the renderer, which reduces multi‑view fusion to an exact two‑scalar recursion per Gaussian. Past observations are never stored or revisited. The self‑supervised objective that O‑SCD minimizes by descent also determines the decision threshold exactly, by sorting, yielding a label‑free per‑frame cutoff whose margin provides a selective‑prediction signal. On PASLCD, our method improves mean intersection over union from 0.489 to 0.575 and throughput from 11.8 to 25.6 frames per second, even exceeding O‑SCD's offline result while remaining strictly causal.

PaperId: 568, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24461.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ishir Garg, Vivek Myers, Qiyang Li, Catherine Ji, Benjamin Eysenbach, Sergey Levine
Title: Measuring Empowerment from Offline Data for Intrinsically Motivated Exploration
Abstract:
Large, unlabeled datasets of prior experience have become increasingly available for agentic tasks in domains such as robotics and coding. A common recipe for these tasks is to train a policy using the prior data, and then further improve it with online rollouts. But while much work has studied how to use both the offline and online data for policy extraction, far less work has been done to understand how the prior data can be used to efficiently explore during the online learning phase. Previous work has attempted to formalize this idea by defining the empowerment, a measure of how many future states an agent can realize; states with higher empowerment require more exploration as there are more futures to explore. However, existing methods for estimating empowerment require online policy rollouts in the environment. We propose the first method for estimating empowerment from unlabeled prior data, without any environment interaction. By jointly learning an empowerment‑maximizing policy together with its discounted state‑occupancy measure, our estimator can be trained on unlabeled trajectories generated from any unknown policy. We demonstrate that our empowerment estimator qualitatively gives intuitive empowerment measures and show that the pretrained estimator can be used to improve exploration in the online goal‑conditioned reinforcement learning setting. Code is available at \urlhttps://github.com/ishirgarg/offline‑empowerment.

PaperId: 569, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24452.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Junsu Kim, Naeun Kim, Dongyoon Han, Seungryul Baek
Title: HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars in Space and Time
Abstract:
We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine‑grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill‑4D, a training‑free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body‑part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human‑annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill‑4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.

PaperId: 570, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24451.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qiang Zou, Jiajun Shen, Zhijie Yang, Yuhao Wang, Shitianyi Leng, Dongshuo Yin
Title: Assessing the CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models: A Case Study of GPT-6 Astra
Abstract:
Recent advances in general‑purpose AI models and agentic systems have enabled them to perform some CAD tasks. A systematic assessment is now needed to establish what these systems can accomplish and how well their outputs meet engineering requirements. This paper presents an empirical study of GPT‑6 Astra, a SOTA general‑purpose AI model, across four basic CAD tasks: model understanding, generation, editing, and evaluation. We design test cases spanning different levels of complexity and engineering requirements. The results show that GPT‑6 Astra can support multiple stages of CAD workflows, with successful outcomes in cases involving nontrivial geometric complexity. This suggests that general‑purpose AI is beginning to offer practical value in almost all steps in CAD workflow. However, gaps remain between generating visually plausible geometry and producing valid, functional, and editable CAD models. Recurring errors in freeform geometry, parameter dependencies, and mating relationships between parts limit engineering usefulness. Agentic iterative refinement can improve results but does not consistently resolve critical errors; long completion times further constrain practical use.

PaperId: 571, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24414.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Weiqiang Zhao, Xian Li, Yuzhe Gui, Tianzhu Liu, Yanfeng Gu
Title: S3D-Mosaic: Subgradient-Guided Cross-Band Structure Transfer for Spectral Demosaicing
Abstract:
Multispectral filter array (MSFA) imaging enables snapshot spectral acquisition, but its per‑band sparse sampling causes severe spatial aliasing. Although missing spatial structures can be inferred across bands, wavelength‑dependent contrast variations make direct cross‑band transfer unreliable. Existing model‑based methods lack explicit magnitude‑invariant mechanisms, and learning‑based methods require layout‑specific training or per‑image tuning, limiting generalization. To address these issues, we propose S3D‑Mosaic, a model‑based spectral demosaicing method built upon a subgradient‑guided cross‑band structure transfer framework. We first establish a subgradient‑guided regularization framework with a generalized cosine‑similarity interpretation, providing a convex mechanism for magnitude‑invariant information transfer. Then we design a compact Directional Sparse Equivariant Difference Convolution (DSE‑DConv) for band‑level extraction of orientation‑selective, high‑frequency structure features at low computational cost. Instantiating the framework with DSE‑DConv on spectrally adjacent bands yields a cross‑band self‑structure similarity regularizer for spectral demosaicing, which we optimize via a dual‑scan ADMM algorithm that decouples the bidirectional dependency while propagating magnitude‑robust structural information across bands. With DSE‑DConv's two parameters trained once via self‑supervision, S3D‑Mosaic outperforms state‑of‑the‑art unsupervised methods on CAVE and NTIRE 2022, and generalizes robustly to varying MSFA layouts, pan‑mosaic fusion, and real‑world UAV data with fixed reconstruction hyperparameters. The source code is available at \urlhttps://github.com/bestwishes43/S3D‑Mosaic.

PaperId: 572, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24409.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jaeyeon Kim, Chao-Han Huck Yang, Luoyi Zhang, Chan-Jan Hsu, Fernando Ruiloba Portilla, Jinchuan Tian, Shinji Watanabe, Carlos Busso
Title: Long Listening Thoughts: Eliciting Open Auditory Reasoning with Deliberative Perception and Cognitive Refinement
Abstract:
We introduce Long Listening Thoughts (LLT), a framework for constructing post‑training datasets that improves audio reasoning by pairing deliberate perceptual grounding with explicit cognitive behaviors. On audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, large audio‑language models (LALMs) are limited primarily by perceptual errors, yet existing post‑training datasets rely on audio descriptions of limited diversity. Through a four‑stage pipeline, LLT (1) builds multi‑aspect dense audio descriptions spanning semantic, acoustic, and temporal information, (2) generates more challenging questions, (3) synthesizes incorrect reasoning traces, and (4) extends short reasoning traces into long ones via a thought‑continuation strategy that elicits cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. Using LLT, we synthesize 1.6M reasoning traces and train Qwen2.5‑Omni‑7B with a two‑stage pipeline of supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). This improves accuracy on MMAU Test‑mini (71.5 to 78.2), MMAR (56.7 to 63.7), and MMSU (60.6 to 66.0).

PaperId: 573, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24395.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xinyu Chen, Liangjian Wen, Jiang Duan, Dongkai Wang, Yong Dai, Jiayu Bai, Jianzhuang Liu, Zhen Tian, Guoping Qiu, Zhao Kan
Title: MSCR: Jointly Balancing Utilization Across Modalities and Discovering Synergistic Information
Abstract:
In multimodal learning, modality imbalance often lets one modality dominate optimization and keeps the model from fully exploiting cross‑modal interactions. Balance‑oriented methods such as the Multimodal Competition Regularizer (MCR) perform well by alleviating this imbalance during training. These dynamic balancing methods, however, mainly adjust modality contributions and do not consider how imbalance affects the formation of synergistic information during fusion. Synergy is a major source of multimodal advantage, because it is predictive gain that cannot be recovered from unimodal evidence alone. We propose the Multimodal Synergistic Competition Regularizer (MSCR), a fusion method that jointly promotes balanced modality utilization and the discovery of synergistic information. MSCR has two complementary objectives. An anti‑dominance objective suppresses excessive unimodal influence and leaves room for synergistic information, and a synergy objective encourages the fused predictor to outperform a non‑synergistic unimodal reference. An adaptive gate further concentrates the regularization on samples that need stronger collaborative modeling. Experiments on five benchmarks show that MSCR consistently improves performance over MCR and strengthens synergistic capability. It raises conditional recovery, the accuracy of the fused prediction on samples that the unimodal predictors misclassify, as well as the share of the model's output that InterSHAP attributes to cross‑modal interactions. Its gain in conditional recovery persists when the fusion module is Transformer‑based. Code is available at https://github.com/chenxinyu991‑collab/MSCR.

PaperId: 574, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24379.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wonjun Lee, Vaidehi Patil, Zaid Khan, Yue Zhang, Hyunji Lee, Suhyun Kim, Mohit Bansal
Title: Defending Against Dormant Poisoning Attacks Across Language and Multimodal Agents
Abstract:
Recent work shows that attackers can implant dormant malicious behaviors that remain hidden at release but emerge after benign fine‑tuning. As foundation models are used as agents, whether dormant poisoning extends to harmful agent actions and multimodal settings remains unclear. We show two agentic risks: (1) harmful behaviors activated by benign fine‑tuning can extend to unseen actions; (2) multiple harmful behaviors can coexist and be jointly activated by benign downstream fine‑tuning. Existing defenses often rely on external safe responses, which are hard to obtain for agent actions, or a trusted clean reference model. We exploit a key property of dormant poisoning: the attacker must preserve safe behavior at release to conceal poisoning, and this behavior can serve as a safety reference. Leveraging this property, we automatically construct a Safety Buffer pairing harmful inputs with the released model's responses and benign versions generated by the same model to remove harmful intent. The Safety Buffer can replace external safe responses in existing defenses, but these defenses do not distinguish updates that weaken safety from those that preserve it, often increasing over‑refusal or reducing utility. To address this limitation, we introduce LookAhead Defense, which previews benign fine‑tuning updates using the Safety Buffer and penalizes only updates predicted to weaken safe behavior on harmful inputs or increase the likelihood of refusals on benign versions in the Safety Buffer. Across language models, language agents, and multimodal agents, LookAhead Defense reduces harmful behavior in agents from up to 93.9% to at most 14.2% and harmful responses in language models from up to 92.5% to at most 2.0% versus vanilla fine‑tuning, while maintaining competitive utility and low over‑refusal. It remains effective against other poisoning methods.

PaperId: 575, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24378.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shidu Ren, Rong-cheng Tu, Hang Zhou, Xiao Luo
Title: PACE-Mem: Prefix-Aware Complementary Evidence for Multimodal Agents
Abstract:
As multimodal agents accumulate experience, their long‑term memories contain many similar observations of recurring scenes, actions, and entities. Answer quality depends on the evidence retrieved from these memories into the model's context. However, query‑relevant memories may contain overlapping information, and a fixed retrieval depth may return too little or too much evidence for a given question. To address these challenges, we propose PACE‑Mem, Prefix‑Aware Complementary Evidence, which constructs a complementary evidence sequence and determines its length from the same selection trajectory. For structured memories, query‑guided pooling combines records within each clip to obtain relevance scores and representations. Using these relevance scores and representations, maximal marginal relevance (MMR) selection balances query relevance against overlap with previously selected evidence. From the resulting score trajectory, a prefix‑length selection algorithm determines retrieval depth by comparing length‑normalized adjacent declines, accounting for both score changes and the amount of evidence accumulated. PACE‑Mem is a training‑free, plug‑in retrieval method for clip‑based agent memory systems, leaving memory construction and answer generation unchanged. Across three long‑video benchmarks and two agent frameworks, PACE‑Mem improves question‑answering accuracy by an average of 1.6% over Adaptive‑k, the strongest baseline at comparable mean retrieval depths. Further analysis reveals that jointly adding and removing evidence is associated with larger net accuracy gains than either change alone.

PaperId: 576, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24365.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jeff Shen, Zhejian Zhou, Ryan Lee, Jonathan May, Shirley Ho
Title: FlashMap: Flow Map Speculative Decoding
Abstract:
Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose a block of tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass. Autoregressive drafters generate this block one token at a time, whereas block diffusion drafters such as DFlash generate it in one pass, making drafting faster. However, these diffusion drafters predict each token independently, ignoring dependencies between tokens in the block. We introduce FlashMap, a continuous flow drafter that conditions a flow map language model on the target model's hidden states and generates the whole block in one forward pass while capturing inter‑token dependencies. On Qwen3‑8B, FlashMap is faster than a matched DFlash baseline on every benchmark, with 7% higher average speedup and up to 6.1x lossless acceleration.

PaperId: 577, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24349.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Liang Su, David Chen, Jason Li, Kevin Guo, Teresa Lv
Title: FlashRT-PAI: Fast Kernels Are Not Fast Pipelines for Physical AI Inference
Abstract:
Vision‑language‑action (VLA), video‑action (VA), and world action models (WAMs) form the backbone of modern physical AI systems, yet their real‑time single‑batch inference remains a defining bottleneck. Latency is dominated not by individual kernel computation, but by system‑level overhead: thousands of short kernel launches, intermediate data movement across operator boundaries, and redundant recomputation across consecutive decisions. General‑purpose graph compilers cannot address these costs, as they optimize individual calls in isolation and lack visibility into cross‑call state semantics and global pipeline structure. We present FLASHRT‑PAI, a low‑latency inference engine built around model‑hardware pipeline co‑design rather than isolated kernel optimization. FLASHRT‑PAI combines three core mechanisms: deep kernel fusion with launch overlap eliminates inter‑operator boundaries and launch gaps; an execution contract formalizes the pipeline's stage DAG, update rates, and named buffers to enable cross‑decision state reuse and selective refresh; and execution‑state capsules enable fast snapshot, restore, and fork of persistent pipeline state. The system also supports drop‑in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models via parity‑ and latency‑gated kernel replacement. Evaluation covers six policies on RTX 5090 and four on Jetson AGX Thor. At matched 16‑bit precision, FLASHRT‑PAI is 1.3‑3.7x faster than official compiled paths. Combining pipeline co‑design with reduced precision delivers 3.38‑12.66x speedup over official eager implementations. In LIBERO‑10, four‑bit pi0.5 achieves 94.04% success on Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, compared with 92.4% for the measured official FP16 reference. FLASHRT‑PAI is open source, distributed via Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and its opt‑in pi0.5 kernels have been adopted into the LeRobot framework.

PaperId: 578, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24341.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Iris Ma, Zahra Shekarchi, Stuart Mcilroy, Mahtab Farrokh, Fattane Zarrinkalam, Joel Stremmel
Title: Optimal Fusion Weights Form Intervals, Not Points: A Latency-Aware Study of Query-Adaptive WRRF
Abstract:
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is widely used to combine sparse and dense retrievers in hybrid information retrieval, but a critical limitation is that it assigns a fixed, uniform weight to each retriever regardless of the query. Query‑aware methods treat the per‑query optimal weight as a single point, an assumption whose empirical validity has not been examined. We present an empirical study of eight dynamic fusion weight prediction strategies across four datasets and four sparse‑‑dense retriever pairs. When we compare these approaches to static fusion and a per‑query oracle that bounds achievable performance, several findings emerge. First, the per‑query optimal fusion weight is typically an interval rather than a point. Queries can have multiple optimal intervals, and these can take on a variety of shapes. Second, 74 of 128 dynamic fusion methods tested were significantly better than standard RRF after false discovery rate correction. Third, dynamic fusion methods exhibit differing quality and latency characteristics that should be considered when choosing an appropriate fusion method. To address this last finding, we present a tiered decision framework that maps practitioner constraints, dataset properties, label availability, hardware, and latency budget to an appropriate method class. We release the code for our experiments at https://github.com/thomsonreuters/query‑based‑rrf.

PaperId: 579, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24329.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Minbo Ma, Honglin Zhang, Bangtao Zhou, Chunguang Yu, Dasheng Ju, Yichen Shen, Fengli Xu, Yong Li
Title: VERAS: Verification-Guided Adaptive Search for Reliable Operations Research
Abstract:
Advances in reasoning, coding, and tool use enable LLM agents to solve operations research (OR) problems through iterative problem modeling, program construction, and verification. Yet passing self‑authored verification does not ensure that the solutions satisfy task constraints and meet optimization quality. This gap can arise from correlated specification errors, where the generated program and its checks share omissions or misinterpretations of task requirements, alongside incomplete verification coverage and ineffective optimization strategies. We propose VERAS, a verification‑guided adaptive search harness for reliable OR that uses verification evidence to prioritize feasibility repair, constraint‑coverage review, and solution‑quality improvement. VERAS combines task‑specific solution checkers with a separate verification agent to examine candidate solutions against the task requirements. It uses verification feedback to guide feasibility repair, additional constraint checking, and objective improvement, while candidate acceptance criteria screen revisions for deterioration in output validity or constraint satisfaction. On ORAgentBench, VERAS achieves a 42.99% pass rate, exceeding the reported 35.51% of Codex using the same LLM. Across two industrial‑scale OR problems, VERAS reduces inter‑datacenter peak bandwidth by 10.34% relative to native Codex and lowers annualized distribution network planning costs by 6.28% compared with expert‑designed solutions. Code and evidence are available at https://github.com/holimario/VERAS.

PaperId: 580, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24328.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Javid Baydamirli, Didem Unat
Title: SigmaTrace: Library-Agnostic Observability for CPU/GPU-Initiated RDMA Communication
Abstract:
RDMA networking enables low‑latency, high‑bandwidth communication on large systems. Despite its adoption, however, observability is lacking. Existing tools target specific communication libraries or only report aggregated data, missing per‑operation behavior. The gap is widest for GPU‑initiated networking, whose in‑kernel RDMA operations are invisible to the host. We present SigmaTrace, a library‑agnostic RDMA profiling framework providing fine‑grained, per‑operation visibility for CPU and GPU‑initiated networking. It traces operations at the libibverbs/mlx5dv layers, the common denominator beneath communication libraries on InfiniBand and RoCE, and employs a low‑overhead memory interposition technique that, to our knowledge, gives the first observability into GPU‑initiated RDMA without source patching or binary instrumentation. Host‑side tracing adds 1.3% overhead on NCCL AllReduce at 128 GPUs and under 2% on RCCL at 1024 GPUs. On a persistent‑kernel BFS and Mixture‑of‑Experts inference, SigmaTrace exposes an in‑kernel barrier spread and 2.13x inter‑node traffic skew invisible to existing profilers.

PaperId: 581, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24311.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuntao Du, Harsh Chaudhari, Yuetian Chen, Ron Heichman, Ashish Jayamohan, Kumar Pallav, Mahim Patel, Kaiyuan Zhang, Kyle Polley, Jerry Ma, Ninghui Li
Title: RATION: Towards Quantitative Risk-Based Access Control for AI Agents
Abstract:
AI agents increasingly interact with external environments to complete complex user tasks. These interactions can lead to unexpected behavior and expose agents to security threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current agent security systems largely protect agents by restricting their actions, which can result in a substantial security‑utility trade‑off for complex, open‑ended tasks. To address this, we propose a quantitative risk‑based approach to access control for AI agents that regulates measurable risks accumulated during task execution. As a concrete realization of this approach, we introduce RATION, a security framework that tracks measurable risks associated with agent actions and enforces quantitative constraints throughout execution. RATION first constructs a task‑specific policy by combining explicit constraints derived from the user request with implicit risks calibrated from historical executions of similar tasks. During task execution, RATION continuously tracks the accumulated risks and applies different enforcement strategies depending on the type of risk. Extensive experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION provides strong security while maintaining high task utility across diverse models and environments.

PaperId: 582, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24305.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Niko Covic, Baraq Lipshitz, Alexander Padula, Stefan Visnjic
Title: Muon Operates Beyond the Edge of Stability
Abstract:
We study the Muon optimizer using sharpness and provide the first empirical evidence that the Flat Minima Hypothesis also applies to Muon. Further, we derive Muon's implicit preconditioner to analyze its potential Edge of Stability behavior. Experiments on CIFAR‑10 show sharpness strongly correlates with generalization gap within each optimizer (Pearson r = 0.45‑0.69, p \leq 10^‑4), confirming the hypothesis holds for Muon similarly to Adam and SGD. However, Muon operates above the classical sharpness‑based Adaptive Edge of Stability threshold that bounds diagonally‑preconditioned optimizers like Adam and RMSprop, yet remains stable. Our findings suggest Muon operates in a fundamentally different regime than diagonally‑adaptive methods. Defining the exact stability boundary for Muon remains an open question. All code is available at https://github.com/NikoCovic/DL‑project.

PaperId: 583, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24293.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sho Sonoda, Luca Galimberti, Yuanchao Xu, Isao Ishikawa, Masahiro Ikeda
Title: Constructive Universal Approximation by Infinite-Dimensional Neural Networks via Gaussian-Weighted Ridgelet Transform
Abstract:
Neural networks whose inputs are functions, as in operator learning, are usually shown to be universal by existence arguments, either by reduction to finite‑dimensional networks or by Stone‑‑Weierstrass‑type density; these prove that approximants exist but say little about how the parameters depend on the target. We take a constructive route. We extend the ridgelet transform, an integral transform related to the Fourier, Radon, and wavelet transforms, to continuous maps on a separable infinite‑dimensional Hilbert space, replacing the Lebesgue measure that is unavailable in infinite dimensions by Gaussian weights with a homogeneous mixture on the direction space. The resulting transform has a Plancherel identity and reconstruction formulas incorporating the frame operator, the correction induced by the weights, and it assigns to each target an explicit coefficient measure, one for every admissible analysis filter. From these representations we obtain uniform approximation on compact sets for all continuous non‑polynomial activations of polynomial growth, including ReLU, and, by Monte Carlo sampling of the coefficient, finite‑width networks with a dimension‑free O(N^‑1/2) error in the width N for globally Lipschitz activations and coefficients with finite variation and second moments. Explicit examples include Gaussian targets and neural‑operator layers. A companion Lean~4 formalization provides machine‑checked proofs, with its correspondence to the manuscript documented at https://shosonoda.github.io/lean‑operator‑ridgelet/ .

PaperId: 584, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24288.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mohsinul Kabir, Md. Tariquzzaman, Mohammad Rashidujjaman Rifat, Tharindu Ranasinghe, Nishat Raihan
Title: BanglaShield: A Script-Robust Safety Classifier and Benchmark for Bangla Native, Romanized, and Code-Mixed Prompts
Abstract:
Safety classifiers for large language models (LLMs) are typically built and evaluated on standard‑script text, yet Bangla, like many lower‑resource languages, is routinely written in native script, in Latin‑script romanization, and code‑mixed with English, Hindi, or Urdu. We introduce BanglaShield, a resource and model for graded prompt‑safety classification across these written forms. We consolidate 10,245 Bangla prompts from six sources under a four‑level taxonomy (Safe, Offensive, Harmful, Severe) and render each prompt in three aligned forms that share labels and a group‑aware split, enabling strictly paired comparisons. Benchmarking six contemporary LLMs, including a Bangla‑specialized one, on 36,882 classification queries and 24,318 judged responses, we find that LLM classifiers label 47.0% of unsafe native‑script prompts as Safe, rising to 63.4% under romanization, while response‑level safety accuracy drops by 10.3 points. Three multilingual guard models also pass 30.3‑57.3% of unsafe native‑script prompts. Using a model's own classification as an input filter reduces harmful compliance by only about five points. In contrast, BanglaShield, a compact fine‑tuned encoder, reaches 87.8 macro‑F1 on native‑script and 84.4 on romanized prompts, outperforming the best LLM on each form by 42.8‑46.1 points with ~130x fewer parameters than Gemma 4 31B. We release the corpus, splits, judgments, and model.

PaperId: 585, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24278.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dariush Wahdany, Jesse Cresswell, Naiqing Guan, Atiyeh Ashari Ghomi, Franziska Boenisch, Adam Dziedzic
Title: Dataset Inference for Data Provenance and Privacy Auditing in Tabular Foundation Models
Abstract:
Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly deployed through black‑box APIs and trained on large collections of real‑world tabular datasets. As this training paradigm becomes more widely adopted, private or proprietary datasets may be incorporated into pre‑training corpora, yet there are currently no dedicated methods for determining whether a given tabular dataset was used to train a TFM. As a solution, we introduce the first dataset inference method for TFMs, aiming to infer whether a suspect dataset was part of a model's pre‑training data. We systematically analyze a broad collection of candidate signals that can be observed from a black‑box TFM via input manipulation and find that individual signals provide only weak evidence of training data membership. However, by combining multiple complementary signals, we can infer dataset membership for several state‑of‑the‑art TFMs trained on real tabular data, achieving up to 0.99 ROCAUC dependent on the TFM. We then study factors that influence dataset identification, including pre‑training data composition, model capacity, and the use of real vs. synthetic data. Our results show that our dataset inference method is a practical auditing tool for detecting privacy leakage and the use of proprietary datasets in TFMs.

PaperId: 586, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24277.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Egor Zverev, Juhee Kim, Leon Trampert, Boris Köpf, Aashish Kolluri, Shruti Tople, Santiago Zanella-Béguelin
Title: SPIDES: Information-Flow Control for Browser Agents
Abstract:
Browser agents automate complex workflows by reading and acting on arbitrary page content, but this flexibility exposes them to prompt injection attacks and unintended data exfiltration. Recent work argues that LLM‑driven browser agents erode traditional web security boundaries such as the Same‑Origin Policy (SOP) by acting across origins with the user's authority and no built‑in isolation. We argue that restoring SOP is neither sufficient (a same‑origin public sink can leak private data) nor necessary (legitimate tasks require authorized cross‑origin flows) for protecting the security of users. We propose SPIDES, which instead enforces information‑flow control by gating primitive browser actions such as typing, clicking and navigating on labels propagated from element‑level HTML confidentiality and integrity annotations. Untrusted and confidential content is masked from the agent's context, while policies block unauthorized flows, providing security guarantees against both prompt injection and data exfiltration that hold independently of the model driving the agent. To evaluate SPIDES and baseline defenses under a common threat model, we build MicroNet, a closed ecosystem of 28 interlinked websites with element‑level ground‑truth labels and paired benign/adversarial tasks. SPIDES achieves 0% attack success rate by design while retaining high task completion rate and autonomy. Our findings demonstrate that information‑flow control is an effective technique to extend web security to browser agents, gaining on autonomy and utility against state‑of‑the‑art baselines. The source code and data are openly accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/SPIDES.

PaperId: 587, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24264.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Eric Zhang, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Chijioke Ugwuanyi, Jerick Shi, Bernhard Schölkopf, Zhijing Jin
Title: AM-Bench: A Unified Taxonomy and Evaluation Suite for Agentic Misalignment
Abstract:
As LLM‑based agents are deployed with increasing autonomy in real‑world environments, a critical failure mode emerges: agentic misalignment, where agents choose harmful actions over failure. However, existing safety benchmarks primarily evaluate whether agents comply with explicitly harmful instructions, leaving the conditions that cause agents to choose harmful actions poorly understood. To address this limitation, we propose AM‑Bench, a unified taxonomy and 35 scenario evaluation benchmark spanning seven industries for agentic misalignment grounded in the fraud triangle, a well‑established criminological framework explaining goal‑directed misconduct. We adapt this framework to agentic environments and construct our evaluation suite and detection systems along three dimensions: perceived threat, perceived opportunity, and reasoning. We operationalize each dimension into structured subcategories rooted in prior theory: five threat categories derived from the instrumental convergence thesis, seven opportunity categories drawn from the Emergent Strategic Reasoning Risks (ESRR) taxonomy, and a novel four‑question binary reasoning framework synthesized from prior literature. Our evaluation of 10 frontier models reveals a 62‑percentage‑point gap in misalignment across scenarios, with Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro exhibiting the highest levels of agentic misalignment while Claude Sonnet 4.6 displays near‑zero rates across all conditions. Our reasoning framework further reveals that models may exhibit harmful behaviours without explicit situational awareness or explanation, complicating both mitigation and detection. AM‑Bench scenarios and code are available at https://github.com/AI4Collaboration/Agentic‑Misalignment‑Bench

PaperId: 588, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24236.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wen-Zhi Li, Sainyam Galhotra, Claire Cardie
Title: Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay
Abstract:
Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but often reduces the diversity of their reasoning behaviors. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of finite‑sample learning dynamics and show that limited on‑policy rollouts can progressively suppress semantically distinct but equally rewarded reasoning modes. Once a mode becomes sufficiently under‑sampled, standard on‑policy RLVR rarely recovers it. Motivated by this observation, we propose TAR, a Targeted Adaptive Replay framework that preserves diverse correct reasoning behaviors already present in the base policy. TAR constructs a compact memory bank of diverse base‑model solutions and selectively replays them through an adaptive mechanism that activates only when stored behaviors are being suppressed during RLVR. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 model scales, TAR consistently achieves a better balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation than existing diversity‑preserving post‑training methods, while substantially reducing the forgetting of correct base‑model solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/wenzhilics/tar.

PaperId: 589, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24177.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hyunwoo Ryu, Eric Ming Chen, Max Wilcoxson, Vincent Sitzmann
Title: Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models
Abstract:
Video generative models are an emerging tool for embodied agents: they can serve as scalable visual planners, generating videos that depict how to complete previously unseen tasks. However, executing these plans typically requires a video‑to‑action or "inverse dynamics" model trained on large, human‑collected video‑action datasets, severely limiting scalability. We introduce Mirror, a self‑supervised approach that learns video‑to‑action mappings through environment interactions, without prior action data or hand‑crafted rewards. Mirror learns by attempting to follow a visual plan by executing its best guess of the underlying actions in the environment. Mirror then trains on the resulting video‑action pairs, incrementally self‑improving and following the visual planner more closely. Across Atari, OGBench, and DeepMind Control, Mirror outperforms leading learning‑from‑observation methods with learned video plans, and achieves near‑expert performance with oracle plans. On Minecraft BASALT, it outperforms methods with access to expert actions or hand‑engineered task knowledge. In Minecraft survival, it is the first method to acquire an iron pickaxe through self‑improvement alone, without rewards or expert action labels. In the offline setting, with expert action labels but no environment interaction, it sets a new state of the art in obtaining diamonds. Our results suggest that advances in video models can translate into increasingly capable agents without a corresponding need for hand‑crafted rewards or large collections of expert action data.

PaperId: 590, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24173.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Amreen Hasheem Siraj, Alireza Javanmardi, Pragati Jaiswal, Didier Stricker, Alain Pagani
Title: SERO: Semantic Prediction for Single-Step Object Removal
Abstract:
Object removal and semantic inpainting of missing regions remain inherently ill‑posed, as multiple plausible completions may exist for a given scene. Recent diffusion‑based methods have demonstrated strong potential for high‑quality object removal; however, they still face two key limitations. First, although they can synthesise sharp and high‑resolution images, they often struggle to complete removed regions in a semantically consistent and contextually meaningful manner, where the generated content should agree with the surrounding scene layout and object relationships rather than merely appear visually realistic. Second, their iterative denoising process makes them computationally expensive, limiting their practicality for downstream applications. We propose SERO, a semantic prediction framework for single‑step object removal. Our model predicts a hidden‑region semantic prior in embedding space, which guides a latent bridge‑matching generator toward plausible scene completion by providing both where to edit and what structure is likely to exist behind the removed object. This enables visually realistic and contextually coherent completions in one forward pass. Experiments on the RORD and OBER datasets show that SERO achieves competitive or state‑of‑the‑art performance while requiring only a single generation step.

PaperId: 591, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24149.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mani Amani, Hesam Mojtahedi, Reza Akhavian, Nikolay Atanasov, Ki Myung Brian Lee
Title: FLASH-CBF-RRT: Fast Lipschitz-Adaptive Safe Horizon CBF Steering for Certified Motion Planning
Abstract:
Fast motion planning requires both sample‑efficient exploration and computationally efficient local steering. Conventional straight‑line steering is inexpensive but wastes samples by rejecting colliding extensions. Quadratic program controllers with control barrier function (CBF) constraints can be used to achieve effective local steering but can increase the planning time due to the expensive sequential evaluations. We develop a method to accelerate CBF steering by computing a time horizon within which CBF‑filtered velocity may be applied constantly using closed‑form kinematic bounds on collision‑clearance. Our method, FLASH‑CBF‑RRT, significantly reduces the number of evaluations compared to prior CBF‑RRT approaches because the planner can take adaptive steering step sizes that are shorter near obstacles and longer in open space. We implement this steering procedure as an extension of RRT‑Connect in OMPL. Across 689 MotionBenchMaker problems, FLASH‑CBF‑RRT matches RRT‑Connect's 100% success rate while reducing median planning time by 3.82x, and is 3.88x faster than fixed‑step CBF‑RRT. Hardware experiments on a 17‑DoF mobile manipulator demonstrate 2.2x faster planning and 4.2x fewer evaluations. Videos and results are available at: https://mamani828.github.io/FLASH‑CBF‑RRT/.

PaperId: 592, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24147.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Danilo Augusto Sarti
Title: lepidoptera: A Domain-Agnostic Engine for Causal Simulation with Mixed Variable Types, Vine Copula Dependence, and Individual-Level Counterfactual Propagation
Abstract:
lepidoptera is an open‑source R and Python package for simulation from structural causal models with heterogeneous variable types. The package is built around a typed mechanism architecture, which separates the causal graph from the generating rule at each node and exposes each rule as an inspectable, serialisable object. A pre‑built mechanism library covers all nine combinations of continuous, categorical, and ordinal parent and child types, removing the need for users to implement type‑specific sampling from scratch. A vine copula mechanism estimates the full joint dependence structure from observed data using pair‑copula constructions and the Rosenblatt conditional‑simulation algorithm, supporting over twenty copula families. Individual‑level counterfactual queries are supported through partial propagation, which freezes the random draws of unaffected nodes and replays only the downstream consequences of an intervention, thereby separating the individual treatment effect (ITE) estimand from the population‑level average treatment effect (ATE) without additional model assumptions. An extension layer allows any pre‑fitted predictive model to serve as a generative mechanism via a unified callable interface. Three worked illustrations spanning clinical trial planning, emergency‑ward capacity analysis, and epidemiological mediation analysis demonstrate the package's scope.

PaperId: 593, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24135.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Magnus Sesodia, Juil Sock, Philip Torr, Christian Schroeder de Witt
Title: Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Weight-Tied Transformers on Depth-Bound Algorithmic Tasks
Abstract:
Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain‑of‑thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference‑compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows H hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four‑layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically‑trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically‑trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus‑sesodia/insidetheloop.

PaperId: 594, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24130.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zheng Qu
Title: Reducing double-dipping in single-cell topic models with three-way count splitting
Abstract:
Topic models learn gene programs from single‑cell RNA sequencing (scRNA‑seq) data, and the same counts are then used to test which genes and donors are associated with those programs. Count splitting is the standard remedy for this reuse, but it has not been tested when an encoder reads each cell's counts. On a 104,400‑cell lupus cohort with 300 permuted null genes per run, naive tests rejected 36% of null gene‑topic pairs at a nominal 5% level, and the usual two‑way split rejected 38%, because the encoder sees the tested gene's own held‑out count. Encoding topic usage on a separate third of the counts, with beta‑binomial thinning, lowered this to 7.7% (6.7% for genes outside the model); for two other models, LDVAE and scETM, the rate was 7.0‑7.3% (naive 51‑59%). A label‑free interferon program shifts in held‑out counts in the lupus cohort and in a pre‑specified COVID‑19 cohort, and donor‑level topic usage predicts disease (AUROC 0.96) beyond cell‑type proportions (0.86 and 0.58 in the two cohorts). Calibration and prediction did not depend on the model. We do not claim better clustering, prediction or topic stability. Code, figures and result tables are public (MIT license; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23307193).

PaperId: 595, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24128.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mustafa Umut Ozbek, Khalil El-Khatib, Li Yang
Title: Recording-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal OT Intrusion Detection
Abstract:
Machine‑learning‑based intrusion detection systems (IDSs) for operational technology (OT) are commonly evaluated on benchmark datasets in which normal and attack data are collected in separate recordings. In such settings, high performance may reflect recording‑associated differences as well as attack behavior. We introduce a recording‑aware evaluation procedure that compares attack windows with background from the same recording, uses prior data for model fitting and calibration, tests temporal alignment against randomized event schedules, and reports event coverage together with alarm burden. On the ProvICS multimodal dataset, cyber modalities strongly distinguish the benign and attack recordings before the first labeled attack. Same‑recording evaluation reverses the apparent modality ranking across all studied window sizes: the physical view becomes the strongest individual modality, while cyber‑only fusion shows the largest difference between cross‑recording and same‑recording AUC, reaching 0.54. Operational analysis further shows that permissive event‑overlap metrics can overstate detection when a small number of long alarm episodes cover multiple actions. An external analysis on HAI shows smaller and reference‑dependent recording sensitivity. These findings show that cross‑recording benchmark performance should be interpreted alongside same‑recording, forward, temporal, and operational evaluations.

PaperId: 596, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24124.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ella Miray Rajaonson, Jungyoon Lee, William Chau, Alan Aspuru-Guzik, Benjamin Sanchez-Lengeling, Dominique Beaini, Kirill Neklyudov, Marta Skreta
Title: On the Selectivity of Generative Models in Structure-Based Drug Design
Abstract:
Designing small‑molecule drugs that selectively bind to a target protein while avoiding unintended interactions with other proteins is essential for reducing side effects that contribute substantially to clinical attrition. Although structure‑based drug design (SBDD) has advanced rapidly with deep learning, most generative models still optimize binding to a single target and disregard selectivity due to limited training data and unknown off‑target interactions. Motivated by this gap, we introduce SELECTBENCH, a comprehensive benchmark assessing the selectivity of generative SBDD models. SELECTBENCH provides three curated evaluation tasks reflecting different real‑world drug discovery scenarios: literature‑based case studies, safety screening panels used in pharmaceutical development, and large‑scale structure‑based evaluation sets. We further introduce a suite of metrics to quantify selectivity and conduct a systematic evaluation of nine representative SBDD models, including methods explicitly trained for selectivity and widely‑used inference‑time guidance techniques. Our results show that even selectivity‑trained models achieve only modest off‑target discrimination and inference‑time guidance provides limited gains, underscoring the need for method improvement. SELECTBENCH provides both a characterization of where current generative SBDD stands on selectivity and an open, extensible platform to accelerate progress. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/lovetaro/selectbench.

PaperId: 597, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24123.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Peter Cho-Ho Lam, Ziyi Wang, Zirui Zhou
