Title: Prefix-Tuning for Arbitrary Output Sequences on Pretrained Transformers
Abstract:
Prefix‑tuning is a parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning method for large language models (LLMs) that steers model outputs by prepending task‑specific prefix representations to the input sequence. Despite its practical success, the theoretical understanding of the expressiveness of prefixes remains incomplete. In particular, the following question remains open: Given a pretrained autoregressive Transformer, for any input‑output sequence pair (\mathttx,\mathtty), does there always exist a prefix \mathcalS such that prepending \mathcalS to \mathttx induces the model to generate the target output \mathtty? In this work, we prove that under the assumption that \mathtty is in the range of the pretrained Transformer, such a prefix \mathcalS exists and can be explicitly computed by solving multiple linear systems. We further show that this assumption is necessary, in the sense that such a prefix may not exist when the assumption fails, thereby providing a complete answer to the above question. Our analysis is constructive and the obtained theoretical results hold under fairly general assumptions on model architecture. Extensive experiments on GPT‑2 and Qwen3‑4B demonstrate that our algorithm produces prefixes with strong control over model outputs.

PaperId: 598, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24122.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dongzhihan Wang, Yi Du, Chen Wang, Xiuxian Li, Liang Xu
Title: HAVANA: A Hierarchical Video-Action Model for Vision-Language Navigation
Abstract:
Vision‑Language Navigation (VLN) requires long‑horizon instruction‑consistent planning and short‑horizon local planning in current geometry. Video‑action models (VAMs) offer a promising way to learn predictive representations for navigation. However, existing VAMs jointly predict visual futures and local trajectories in a single process, even though they operate at different paces: future prediction remains stable across multiple updates while local trajectories must react to fresh observations. To bridge this gap, we introduce HAVANA, a dual‑system VAM that decouples predictive reasoning from reactive local planning. A slow system produces a compact language‑conditioned latent plan from observation history, while a fast system combines the latest plan with the current observation to generate local trajectories. Their asynchronous execution enables rapid adaptation without repeated future prediction, and no future video is generated during inference. Experiments on OmniNavBench demonstrate state‑of‑the‑art navigation performance over prior baselines, while real‑world deployments further show robust generalization to unseen environments across different robot embodiments. Our code and checkpoints will be available at https://github.com/Anastasiawd/HAVANA.

PaperId: 599, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24109.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Youngmin Kim, Seoyeong Hwang, Sujung Hong, Seong Jae Hwang
Title: BLANC: Adaptive Temporal Scheduling for Sign Language Production
Abstract:
Sign language production (SLP) aims to synthesize expressive signing motion from written text. Modeling signing motion presents two key temporal challenges. First, fine‑grained hand articulations demand higher temporal resolution than relatively slower body movements. Second, signing events unfold over variable durations, calling for adaptive temporal scheduling during generation. To address these challenges, we first introduce a Multi‑Rate Vector Quantizer (MRVQ), an articulation‑decoupled motion tokenizer that represents the body and both hands as separate discrete streams at distinct temporal resolutions. Building on this representation, we propose BLANC (BLock‑wise Adaptive diffusioN with Articulatory Clock), a gloss‑free SLP framework that generates variable‑duration motion blocks causally while denoising tokens in parallel within each block. At its core, a Latent Articulatory Clock (LAC) learns temporal structure from multi‑scale motion‑derived partitions to predict block durations and sequence termination during generation. We further introduce inference‑time body‑conditioned hand refinement to improve coordination across articulators. Extensive experiments on PHOENIX‑2014T and CSL‑Daily demonstrate that BLANC achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance in sign language production.

PaperId: 600, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24087.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Peisong Wang, Feixue Liu, Yize Meng, Bowen Liu, Ruoyu Chen, Gaoyang Dai, Xing He, Aiqian Li, Fengchi Yuan, Aochuan Chen, Chenyi Zi, Yuhan Li, Hongchuan Zeng, Yimo Yan, Nuo Chen, Jie Fu, Zuo-Jun Max Shen, Yong-Hong KUO, Jia Li
Title: OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners
Abstract:
Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert‑level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation? Existing OR benchmarks typically begin with self‑contained descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, underrepresenting the translation of original business materials into professionally validated solutions. We introduce OR‑License, an end‑to‑end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios from paid OR engagements totaling USD 3.68 million. It preserves original requirements, input data, deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de‑identification. To study information acquisition, we introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business facts without supplying OR expertise. Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction. Deployment‑Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert‑relative quality across instances, assigning zero to infeasible deliveries. Across 11 frontier LLMs using coding‑agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1. Client information acquisition extends beyond clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages showing higher confirmed issue‑resolution proportions. Trajectory analysis identifies formulation and implementation failures, while task‑equalized research‑chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks. These findings motivate sustained information‑gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and evidence‑linked self‑improvement for reliable long‑horizon agents.

PaperId: 601, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24074.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Seth K. Asante
Title: QRecoupling.jl: numerical and exact computation of classical and quantum recoupling coefficients
Abstract:
QRecoupling.jl is a Julia package for numerical, exact and symbolic evaluation of classical and quantum recoupling coefficients and generic finite sums of quantum factorials, with one interface across the classical limit, principal unitary levels and real or complex deformation. A compact factorial rule and its cyclotomic exponents expose factor cancellation, polynomial structure and level support. The package covers quantum Clebsch‑Gordan coefficients, 3j and 6j symbols and user‑defined sums. Its adaptive numerical evaluation is combined with exact decisions for sums that cancel to zero. Classical 3j and 6j symbols are evaluated at a speed comparable to that of WIGXJPF, which is based on prime factorization tables, at the smallest spins, and about 6 and 10 times faster at spin cutoff 500. Under real, root‑of‑unity and complex deformation, the largest relative error measured against independent high‑precision references is 3.5 × 10^‑14 for spins up to 400. Fusion matrices with 401 channels are computed about 100 times faster than by loops over their entries.

PaperId: 602, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24045.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yujie Lu, Da Yan
Title: What Remains Without Test Labels? Re-evaluating a Graph-Level Anomaly Detection Benchmark
Abstract:
Graph‑level anomaly detectors are trained only on normal graphs, yet benchmarks may use test labels for model selection. We examine whether UB‑GOLD results reused by later papers support label‑free detection. We audit UB‑GOLD and 14 GLAD code bases, re‑run 21 detectors on UB‑GOLD's folds under selection rules with and without test labels, and evaluate sensitivity to known structural changes. Test labels select checkpoints in UB‑GOLD's shared training loop and checkpoints or hyperparameters in 8 of the 14 code bases. UB‑GOLD also evaluates its kernel baselines against misaligned labels. Across nine datasets, selecting checkpoints by test AUROC adds an average of 5.12 AUROC points [3.97, 6.24] for the 12 UB‑GOLD detectors relative to the final checkpoint and 4.13 [3.32, 4.79] relative to held‑out normal graphs. In a post hoc permutation analysis with no truly better checkpoint, picking the best of noisy test evaluations still yields a gain more than half as large as the one observed against the final checkpoint. Configurations tuned on test labels score a further 1.53 points [0.64, 2.42] above repository defaults, a gap that mixes the value of test labels with that of tuning itself. With tuned hyperparameters and label‑free checkpoint selection, the two strongest detectors retain their lead, while comparisons below them are less stable. Six of eight detectors evaluated out of sample miss size‑preserving composition changes that graphlet counts detect. We recommend reporting results selected without test labels as the main comparisons and release per‑run outputs that allow verification without retraining.

PaperId: 603, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24038.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Elena Raikova
Title: Merge Hulls Without Copying Vertices: GPU Isotonic Regression
Abstract:
Isotonic regression finds the monotone sequence closest to the data in weighted least squares. It is used to calibrate probabilities and inside differentiable ranking. Its standard algorithm, pool adjacent violators, is sequential within a sequence, and torchsort, the exact GPU solver of differentiable sorting libraries, runs it with one thread per sequence, which is slow on long ones. The fit is the slope sequence of the lower convex hull of cumulative sums, and hulls of sorted points can be merged in parallel. Merging partial hulls level by level, however, copies the surviving vertices at every level, which moves Θ(n \log n) data when most points survive. We store each chunk's hull once and represent a merged hull as a list of segments of these chunk hulls, at most one per chunk; a merge then updates the list. We prove the representation correct, bound the work and depth of the merge phase, and measure a CUDA implementation on four NVIDIA GPUs against a control that copies the surviving vertices with the whole GPU at every level. On dense hulls the merge phase is 17 to 276 times faster with segment lists and the whole operator 3.9 to 19 times; on noisy data, where few vertices survive, the difference is small. In a differentiable soft rank, replacing torchsort's isotonic solver makes forward and backward 2.3 to 230 times faster on a T4, and the training step of a compact model with a Spearman loss 1.6 to 9 times.

PaperId: 604, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24029.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Parsa Rahimi, Azim Dehghani Amirabad
Title: Do Knowledge and Reasoning Oriented Benchmarks Induce Stable Representation Signatures in LLMs?
Abstract:
Internal signatures could support monitoring, adaptive computation, and mechanistic analysis, but benchmark prompts can be separable without any shared computational distinction. We test whether a prespecified knowledge/reasoning label defines a reusable internal signature in five contemporary 7B to 31B models. We treat the task as the unit of inference probes hold out complete tasks, labels are permuted across tasks, and the best layer and stream are reselected for every permutation. Raw probes recover an eight‑versus‑eight‑subject MMLU partition in all five models (macro‑F1 0.78‑‑0.81), but prompt text predicts it nearly as well: under an identical probe configuration, the activation advantage is only 0.017‑‑0.070 macro‑F1 and is not significant. At the prespecified 0.01 level, lexical adjustment removes significance while the adjusted states still identify individual subjects, and the selected site changes across task panels and selection rules. Additionally, two released base‑training trajectories show no common direction. These pooled layerwise measures recover the task label but identify no transferable knowledge/reasoning signature at the tested sensitivity, which cannot exclude moderate effects. The resulting protocol gives future internal monitors and intervention studies a sequence of tests to pass. Project page: \urlhttps://parsa‑ra.github.io/lmbehave/.

PaperId: 605, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24023.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Iori Azuma, Hiroyuki Kusuhara, Tadahaya Mizuno
Title: ProtoGTX: Prototype-Aligned Graph Transformer for Explainable Whole-Slide Image Analysis
Abstract:
Deep learning has achieved strong performance in computational pathology, but explaining whole‑slide image (WSI) predictions remains challenging. Existing explanation methods often highlight important regions without identifying their morphological patterns, leaving a gap between patch‑level computational evidence and slide‑level pathological interpretation. We propose ProtoGTX, a graph‑based framework that combines spatial contextualization with a flexible morphological prototype vocabulary. ProtoGTX separates the reference prototypes used to define morphological concepts from the predictive model: the reference vocabulary can be generated from training data by unsupervised clustering or supplied externally, and remains fixed during classifier training. Patch features are first contextualized over a spatial graph, after which learnable prototypes representing morphological concepts are optimized through cross‑attention. Their slide‑level activation profile is aligned with the morphological composition induced by the fixed reference prototype bank. On the CPTAC and BRACS datasets, ProtoGTX outperforms the evaluated MIL, prototype‑based, and graph‑based baselines, with particularly pronounced improvements on BRACS. Qualitative analyses further show that spatial contextualization transforms fragmented patch‑level prototype assignments into more coherent tissue regions. In BRACS, prototype maps also co‑localize with pathologist annotations and regions relevant to slide‑level prediction. These results demonstrate that ProtoGTX provides complementary semantic and spatial explanations while retaining a prototype vocabulary that can be defined independently of the predictive model. Code is available at https://github.com/mizuno‑group/ProtoGTX.

PaperId: 606, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24001.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mathias Lowes, Kurt Butler, Kristine Aavild Sørensen, Klaus F. Kofoed, Sotirios A. Tsaftaris, Rasmus R. Paulsen, Steven McDonagh
Title: Causal Spatio-Temporal Neural Distance Fields for Counterfactual Cardiac Anatomy
Abstract:
Counterfactual cardiac anatomy can support risk modelling and intervention planning, by predicting how a patient's heart would change under altered clinical conditions. However, current shape generative models are conditional on clinical variables and disregard causal links between these variables. Thus, they cannot answer counterfactual questions about how a given subject's anatomy would change under a different clinical profile. Modelling the heart's continuous movement over the cardiac cycle requires a representation that is itself continuous in space and time. Spatio‑temporal neural distance fields provide this while separating clinical conditioning from subject‑specific shape. We place a structural causal model (SCM) over the set of clinical variables (age, sex, smoking, BMI, heart rate, systolic blood pressure), before the condition encoding of the spatio‑temporal neural distance field which represents the left atrial complex over a cardiac cycle by signed distance fields. An intervention of the clinical variables, propagated through a SCM before the 4D counterfactual, is constructed from the neural distance field. The generated counterfactuals follow dose‑response under age interventions and transforms the male distribution to closely match the female distribution under the intervention \mathrmdo(\mathrmfemale=1). By doing inverse interventions the model also approximates the original anatomy with sub millimeter precision. To our knowledge, this is the first counterfactual generation of 4D cardiac anatomy and the first integration of an SCM with an implicit neural representation as its imaging mechanism.

PaperId: 607, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23988.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Patrick Wienholt, Frederik Hauke, Christiane Kuhl, Jakob Nikolas Kather, Sven Nebelung, Daniel Truhn
Title: Single-Pass Decision Scores Enable Rapid Classification with Adjustable Thresholds in Medical Multimodal Large Language Models
Abstract:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer binary clinical questions with a yes or no token, leaving the decision threshold implicit and fixed. We derive a continuous score from a single forward pass by renormalizing the probabilities of the yes and no tokens, allowing the threshold to be adapted to clinical needs without retraining. We evaluated this approach with MedGemma and Gemma‑3 (4B and 27B) on six medical imaging datasets. The default threshold was frequently misaligned with the task: for identifying normal chest radiographs, MedGemma‑27B labeled every image as abnormal, whereas a validation‑selected threshold yielded a sensitivity of 0.945 and a specificity of 0.696. Normalization achieved the highest AUROC on four of six datasets (CheXpert: 0.819 vs. 0.777 for raw and 0.743 for text‑elicited probabilities), and a single decision required 53‑79 ms on one GPU. This simple post‑hoc method turns medical MLLMs into fast classifiers with adjustable operating points. Code: https://github.com/TruhnLab/llm‑threshold‑calibration

PaperId: 608, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23982.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shenyi Li, Ziyang Zhang, Wen Wu, Ming Liu, Chao Zhang
Title: Time-JEPA: Grounding Video World Models with Physical Time Series
Abstract:
Video world models learn how visual environments evolve by predicting missing or future content. However, physical‑state information can provide useful context for predicting how environments evolve. Prior work incorporates this information through different mechanisms: domain‑specific physical laws can complicate multi‑domain training, while supervision on individual frames or frame pairs gives limited attention to how physical state evolves over time. We introduce Time‑JEPA, which fine‑tunes a video world model using low‑dimensional, temporally aligned physical time series as auxiliary supervision. Physical time series connect video representations with physical state at corresponding temporal positions, encouraging the model to preserve how physical state evolves. In multiple domains including autonomous driving, robot manipulation, and human motion, Time‑JEPA improves current‑state decoding, multi‑horizon future‑state prediction, and kinematic reconstruction over matched video‑fine‑tuned controls across both condition and state‑variable distribution shifts. Multi‑domain training provides aggregate gains over matched single‑domain training in all three tasks. External evaluations further suggest that time‑series supervision improves sensitivity to physical anomalies and the representation of physical interactions, including in unseen scenarios. Aggregate gains on a second video backbone indicate that the method can be applied to more backbones. These results suggest that physical time series help video world models better understand the physical world.

PaperId: 609, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23975.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haonan Hu, Shuhao Chen, Weisen Jiang, Lizhao Gao, James Kwok, Yu Zhang
Title: FrameScout: Scouting Query-Relevant Frames for Long Video Understanding
Abstract:
Long video understanding requires VideoLLMs to answer queries about videos spanning tens of minutes to hours, but such long videos produce far more visual tokens than current VideoLLMs can process. To address this issue, keyframe selectors are proposed to select the most query‑relevant frames by computing the similarity between frame and query embeddings. Existing selectors either encode frames independently without temporal context or process chunks in isolation with ranking objectives that are difficult to optimize. To alleviate those limitations, we propose FrameScout with two core designs: (i) a streaming selector architecture that leverages a sliding‑window KV cache and successor aggregation to produce temporally‑contextualized frame embeddings; (ii) a frame‑query contrastive objective that aligns frame and query embeddings in a shared space, directly training the selector to distinguish relevant frames from irrelevant ones. Extensive experiments on three long‑video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs demonstrate that FrameScout consistently achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Hubert‑1102/FrameScout.

PaperId: 610, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23967.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Usef Faghihi, Amir Saki, Serge Jonathan Kogbeti-Wongo
Title: Geo-vision: Native-Resolution Geometry and Sampled Topology for Vehicle-Part Damage Classification
Abstract:
Geo‑vision classifies vehicle‑part damage using a fixed representation combining appearance, multiscale geometry, orientation, and sampled digital topology. Connected components, holes, Euler characteristics, and spatial arrangement complement amplitude‑sensitive pooling and a supervised tree classifier. We establish amplitude preservation, axial sign invariance, and conditional operator stability. Retrospective checkpoint evaluation on 55,303 crops from 4,916 source groups yields average precision 0.7577, exceeding 0.7458 for an ImageNet‑pretrained frozen YOLO11n comparator on identical crops. The complete added structural block, comprising topology, occupancy, and component location, improves average precision by 0.00493 beyond appearance and geometry. Geo‑vision uses no external encoder pretraining and has higher AP point estimates at every matched label budget. With approximately 25% fewer task labels, its AP point estimate exceeds full‑data YOLO, although the adjusted interval includes zero. Complete serial CPU inference requires 26.98 ms per crop versus YOLO's 11.20 ms, with peak memory 185 versus 437 MiB. Independent external validation remains necessary.

PaperId: 611, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23931.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kuizhi Liu, Junying Zhang, Xindi Ma, Xiangyu Wang, Qi Jiang, Sheng Gao, Chen Gong, Jianfeng Ma
Title: STLQ: Spatio-Topological Linkage Quantization for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
Abstract:
Vector quantization is widely used for large‑scale data compression and approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS). Multi‑codebook quantization (MCQ) is a practical paradigm that represents database vectors with compact codes and supports efficient retrieval through asymmetric distance computation (ADC). However, existing shallow MCQs encode vectors independently within each inverted file (IVF) cluster, without exploiting local references. Therefore, we propose Spatio‑Topological Linkage Quantization (STLQ), a topological shallow MCQ method that organizes each IVF cluster as a directed‑forest with compact codes and scaling coefficients. Its basic encoding phase first quantizes vectors independently, while the linked encoding phase re‑encodes relative residuals with respect to selected reconstructed parents, reusing local reconstruction information to obtain finer representations. The corresponding linked‑ADC preserves linear scanning complexity. STLQ further compresses the scaling coefficients and directed‑forest structure to control the additional topology overhead. Extensive experiments show that STLQ achieves higher recall than the evaluated shallow MCQs at comparable bit budgets, although at a higher offline construction cost. Meanwhile, it has a competitive recall‑QPS tradeoff against deep MCQs. The code is available at https://github.com/ighxiy/STLQ.

PaperId: 612, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23929.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hoyeon Shin, Jeongyeon Kim, Yeong Jun Koh, Yeoneung Kim, Hanul Kim
Title: Unbalanced Optimal Transport for Efficient Visual Document Retrieval
Abstract:
Vision‑Language Models(VLMs)have advanced Visual Document Retrieval (VDR) by enabling OCR‑free, multi‑vector representations. However, these models generate excessive tokens to preserve dense visual details, which severely limits retrieval scalability. Existing compression methods mitigate this overhead but rely on isolated heuristics that fail to balance token importance, semantic redundancy, and coverage capacity. We propose a visual token compression framework formulated as an Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) problem. Our approach unifies these three objectives into a single alternating optimization process. Furthermore, we theoretically show that minimizing the transport cost upper‑bounds the MaxSim retrieval error, ensuring ranking stability. Extensive experiments on the ViDoRe V1 and V3 benchmarks demonstrate that our method preserves fine‑grained document semantics and improves the efficiency‑effectiveness trade‑off over state‑of‑the‑art base‑lines. Code is available at https://github.com/shhhhhyy/Unbalanced‑Optimal‑Transport‑for‑EVDR.

PaperId: 613, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23921.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Ritvik Garimella, Biplav Srivastava, Amit Sheth
Title: Doing Less with More: A First-Principles Exploration of the Suitability of Agentic Computing over Alternative Architectural Choices
Abstract:
There is growing interest in automating business activities with Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) due to latter's seeming ease of use. Never has it been easier, or costlier, to do less with more. However, little is known about when agents are preferable to established alternatives such as local computation, Representational State Transfer (REST), the Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), particularly when development speed, performance, and operational cost are considered. We investigate this question using a controlled mathematical task that compares seven methods on a benchmark of 1,000 arithmetic expressions where semantics of operator precedence has to be preserved. We ran this setup across a native Function Calling baseline (Python library), REST, SOAP and MCP microservice architectures, direct responses from large language models (LLMs) using a Groq cloud API and five locally deployed Ollama models, and agentic systems in which five local LLMs invoke MCP tools. The deterministic methods achieve 100% accuracy with negligible latency. Direct LLM evaluation achieves at most 92.9% accuracy at over 22,000x the latency of a native function call. With MCP tools, the best agent reaches 99.9% accuracy, but incurs nearly 1,000,000x the baseline latency. These results demonstrate that LLMs approaches are poorly suited for exact arithmetic evaluation and motivate an informed architectural decision framework (ADF) for choosing an architecture based on accuracy and throughput requirements. We recognize that an actual interaction with an agent may span both reasoning and linguistic tasks. Hence our recommendation is to explore multiple architectural choices (based on task type) rather than one‑size‑fits‑all solution (LLMs). Code is available at ‑ https://github.com/Ritvik‑G/adf/

PaperId: 614, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23909.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xianmin Ye, Zhiyuan Fan, Tianju Liu, Yuhang Wang, Zhenxing Niu, Haichang Gao
Title: When the Editing Intent Is Split: A Cross-Modal Jailbreak Attack for Large Image Editing Models
Abstract:
Large image editing models increasingly infer editing intent from both textual and visual inputs, creating an underexplored safety risk when harmful intent is distributed across modalities. In this work, we formalize this split‑intent vulnerability and propose the Split‑Intent Jailbreak Attack (SIJA), which asymmetrically distributes an unsafe editing intent by specifying the editing referent in text while concealing the safety‑critical action and specification through graphical visual semantics in an auxiliary cue. To systematically study this threat, we introduce the Split‑Intent Image Editing Safety Benchmark (SI2ESBench) for evaluating image editing models under split‑intent inputs. Extensive experiments on representative commercial and open‑source models demonstrate that SIJA effectively compromises state‑of‑the‑art image editing systems, achieving ASRs of 68.28% on GPT Image 2 and 91.38% on Qwen‑Image‑3.0‑Pro. Our results expose a mismatch between multimodal editing and safety assessment: the distributed intent can be recovered to execute the requested transformation, yet its harmfulness often remains undetected by existing safeguards. To mitigate this vulnerability, we propose editing‑intent reconstruction, a defense principle that explicitly evaluates the complete transformation implied by the joint multimodal context and substantially improves rejection of split‑intent attacks. Our findings expose a cross‑modal safety gap in modern image editing systems and highlight the need to assess the jointly inferred transformation rather than individual inputs in isolation. https://github.com/yexianmin/SIJA

PaperId: 615, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23903.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Bernhard Egger, Hans Furer
Title: AI-Experiment: an augmented reality art project co-created with artificial intelligence
Abstract:
We describe the creation of a physical artwork that was performed in synergy between an artist, a computer scientist and generative AI tools. A latent diffusion model was finetuned on photographs of the artwork of the specific artist and the generative model then generated synthetic artworks in a similar style. From the generated artworks a subset was selected to be painted again with acrylic on canvas by the original artist. In addition to the physical artifact an augmented reality component was added which brings the artwork to life with a set of generative video models. Together with this paper we release part of the artwork (training data), the code that was deployed to generate the artwork as well as the augmented reality experience for arts, research and education under https://github.com/BernhardEgger/ARTimate

PaperId: 616, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23896.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Siming Zhou, Bowen Ma, Ruiran Du, Pengcheng Zheng, Sheng Zheng, Dongshen Han, Zhijie Li, Wei Dong, Fan Mo, Chaoning Zhang
Title: InJePA: Intention-First Latent Planning with Coupled JEPA World Models for Visual Navigation
Abstract:
Visual navigation requires goal directed planning informed by predictions of environment dynamics. Representative navigation world model methods propose complete action candidates before predicting consequences for selection or search updates. For each candidate, predictions primarily evaluate proposed actions rather than guide its stepwise construction. To this end, we propose InJepa, an intention first planning paradigm centered on latent states. A goal conditioned JEPA proposes latent intentions, and an action conditioned JEPA continually predicts future latent states. Both operate in a shared latent space to align their predictive representations. Within each candidate, predicted consequences feed into the next intention proposal and action inference, forming a closed loop of intention, action, and consequence. This extends the world model's role beyond evaluation to leading candidate construction through latent intentions. We evaluate InJepa through closed loop image goal navigation in Habitat MP3D. The results show effective multistep navigation through intention guided action generation and consequence feedback. Experiments across encoders further support applicability across visual representations. These findings support latent intentions as the central planning object and show that world models can directly guide plan construction through coordinated reasoning about intentions and consequences. Code is available at https://github.com/zhuxun132/InJepa.

PaperId: 617, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23892.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ruochen Zhao, Jiazheng Kang, Gezi Li, Dongying Lin, Ting Bai
Title: EMMA: Event-Driven Multimodal Memory System with Multi-Agent Retrieval
Abstract:
Long video understanding requires reasoning over hours of content that far exceed the context window of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Existing approaches compress video into fixed‑length clips, yet events are fragmented and unrelated content is merged, yielding noisy retrieval. To overcome this challenge, we propose EMMA, an Event‑driven Multimodal Memory system with Multi‑Agent retrieval, which organizes memory around semantic events in three stages: (1) Event segmentation: a dual‑stream detector adaptively locates event boundaries by fusing visual semantic drift with spoken transitions, rather than fixed windows. (2) Memory construction: built on the detected events, a three‑level hierarchy of raw video, clip‑level memory, and event‑level memory stores content at progressively higher semantic abstraction. (3) Memory retrieval: a multi‑agent framework collaboratively queries this hierarchy through query decomposition, tiered search, evidence validation, and answer generation, narrowing evidence from coarse events to precise clips. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements, showing the effectiveness of our event‑aligned memory system. Code, prompt templates, and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/BAI‑LAB/EMMA.

PaperId: 618, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23888.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Jing Xiong, Jiale Xie, Haoqi Yuan, Chaoyi Xu, Zongqing Lu
Title: MoDex: Towards Universal Multi-Object Dexterous Grasping
Abstract:
Multi‑object grasping is a fundamental yet challenging problem, constrained by data collection costs, varying spatial layouts, and the need for broad generalization. To address these challenges, we propose MoDex, a data‑efficient framework that provides the first unified solution for universal multi‑object dexterous grasping across diverse spatial layouts. MoDex accomplishes this by formulating the task as a single‑step decision problem of learning residual corrections to a reference trajectory, and introducing a spatially adaptive dual‑strategy that performs single‑shot grasping for proximal objects and sequential interaction for separated objects. Extensive evaluations show that MoDex significantly outperforms baselines in proximal configurations, achieving 61.24% success on unseen objects, and achieves high success rates in separated layouts. Further experiments demonstrate its generalization across robot embodiments, scalability and zero‑shot sim‑to‑real deployment through a vision‑based policy trained solely on simulation data. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/Aurora‑Xiong/MoDex.

PaperId: 619, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23884.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hong Wu, ChaoXuan Liu, ShuJie Wang
Title: PrismPlan: A Shared GPU Substrate for Motion Planning Across Paradigms
Abstract:
GPU acceleration has made motion planning one to two orders of magnitude faster, but it has not made the three paradigms‑‑‑sampling, search, and optimization‑‑‑comparable to one another: every GPU‑accelerated planner is built around a single paradigm, so comparing across libraries also compares their collision checkers. All three, however, bottleneck on the same GPU primitive: batched collision detection and the batched forward kinematics beneath it. PrismPlan builds that primitive once, as a shared substrate of per‑sphere collision‑‑kinematics device code that every planner consumes. Because they all execute the same device code, the backend is held fixed by construction and the paradigms can be compared head‑to‑head. We run six planners over 1800 MotionBenchMaker problems on three robots (7‑‑14 DoF, one a dual‑arm whole‑body composite) at an equal 2s budget. On the 7‑DoF Panda, sampling (pRRTC) is the most reliable paradigm at 98%, while parallel search (wPASE) follows within four points at a 3‑4 times lower median latency, and the local optimizers trail well behind when made to solve from scratch. On the 14‑DoF dual‑arm composite, sampling still solves about 90% of feasible problems, while no search or optimization planner clears a third of them. Our open‑source code is available at https://github.com/XiaoyubotMotionTeam/PrismPlan.

PaperId: 620, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23858.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Md Sajid, Shreeyut Maheshwari, Akshat Mishra, Ritik Mishra, Mohammad Tanveer
Title: I$^2$-Med: Interpretable Medical Inference through Visual-Guided Dynamic Logits Calibration
Abstract:
Medical vision language models have demonstrated strong potential for medical image understanding and reasoning. However, their interpretability and reliability remain limited because medical vision language tasks require precise visual grounding and clinically coherent explanations. This is particularly challenging due to complex imaging patterns and scarce expert annotations. These challenges reduce the effectiveness of conventional reasoning methods and lead to visual hallucination, defined as the generation of text that is not grounded in the given visual input, which further limits their applicability in clinical practice. To mitigate these challenges, we propose an interpretable medical inference (I^2‑Med) framework that enhances visual faithfulness during inference without additional training to improve reasoning and explanation faithfulness in medical vision language models. During text generation, I^2‑Med uses a visual guidance module to check whether each candidate word is supported by the medical image and consistent with the current reasoning. Based on this guidance, the model's output scores are adjusted to favor visually grounded words, without changing the model parameters. Extensive experiments on the OmniMedVQA benchmark, covering eight medical imaging modalities and five clinical question types, demonstrate that our proposed I^2‑Med framework generates more clinically meaningful and visually faithful reasoning chains and reduces visual hallucination under standard medical VQA evaluation metrics. The source code is publicly available at \urlhttps://github.com/mtanveer1/l2‑med.

PaperId: 621, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23856.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Weijie Lyu, Tiancheng Shen, Jason Li, Yujing Wang, Xiaoyuan Wang, Haobo Yuan, Yizhou Zhao, Ming-Hsuan Yang
Title: Learning to Correct Geometry in Generated Videos
Abstract:
Generated videos often lose geometric consistency under camera motion: structures warp under viewpoint change, parallax becomes inconsistent, and smooth camera movement may collapse into shot‑like transitions. We argue that this failure is largely a data problem. In web‑scale video corpora, most visible motion comes from dynamic objects captured by static or weakly moving cameras, leaving only sparse supervision for viewpoint‑induced appearance changes. To address this, we propose Video Geometry Corrector (VGC), a post‑hoc video‑to‑video model trained on synthetic paired supervision. Starting from real videos with diverse camera motion and pose annotations, we construct VG‑Pairs with a synthetic paired‑supervision data generation pipeline. Each video clip is treated as a geometry‑consistent target and paired with a distorted counterpart synthesized by a pretrained image‑to‑video inpainting model using trajectory‑adaptive keyframes. VGC learns to map the distorted input to the geometry‑consistent target without modifying the source generator, and uses optical flow as an auxiliary cue to help disentangle camera motion from object motion. Experiments on pose‑conditioned and prompt‑driven benchmarks show that VGC improves geometric consistency across multiple source generators, and scaling to a larger backbone further extends the framework toward more general video refinement.

PaperId: 622, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23854.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Soumik Mukhopadhyay, Long Mai, Abhinav Shrivastava, Aniruddha Mahapatra
Title: Rethinking the design space of Vanilla Pixel Diffusion Transformers
Abstract:
Pixel‑space diffusion models have recently re‑emerged as a compelling alternative to latent diffusion, avoiding the lossy latent bottleneck and separately trained autoencoder. JiT shows that a vanilla diffusion transformer can generate directly in pixel space by replacing the commonly used velocity prediction (\boldsymbolu‑prediction) with clean image prediction (\boldsymbolx_0‑prediction). In this work, we revisit this choice and introduce MFlow, an adaptive parameterization that learns to interpolate between \boldsymbolx_0‑ and \boldsymbolu‑prediction across principal directions of the data, learned end‑to‑end with diffusion training. We find that the preferred parameterization varies systematically with the data representation and model capacity ‑‑ notably, increasing model capacity shifts preference toward velocity prediction. We evaluate MFlow across ImageNet, UCF‑101 video, and large‑scale text‑to‑image generation, demonstrating competitive or improved generative performance across diverse settings. In addition, we find that vanilla pixel diffusion transformers, irrespective of parameterization, retain a persistent high‑frequency deficit relative to real images. To address this, we introduce ConvRefiner, a lightweight convolutional module trained post‑hoc with an adversarial loss while keeping the diffusion backbone frozen. With only a small amount of additional training, ConvRefiner restores the high‑frequency statistics of generated images while preserving FID. Project webpage: https://soumik‑kanad.github.io/mflow‑diffusion/.

PaperId: 623, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23839.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jianyuan Zhong, Chenwei Wu, Zhaochen Yu, Xixian Jiang, Xuewei Li, Hao Xiao, Xilin Dai, Junyang Wang, Jiaru Zou, Zhiqing Cui, Boyuan Zheng, Jing Xiong, Zhen Zhang, Qiang Gao, Michael Morley, Luis Nakayama, Qiang Xu, Liyue Shen, Tao Gui, Leo Anthony Celi, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu, Ling Yang
Title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses
Abstract:
Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence‑grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi‑agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM‑Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life‑science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self‑improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI‑27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI‑27B scores higher than GPT‑6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence‑bounded. DiscoveryRSI‑27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT‑6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human‑rated improvement along research paths.

PaperId: 624, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23830.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rama AlHamidi, Rasul Khanbayov, Erchin Serpedin, Hasan Kurban
Title: Waiting Buys Exactly Two Moments: Endogenous Identification in Prediction-Driven Allocation
Abstract:
A planner with a fixed budget of preventive help must decide whom to help and when. Waiting reveals risk but removes intervention opportunities as higher‑risk individuals leave first. We characterize this tradeoff under repeated noisy signals and risk‑dependent attrition: in the canonical model, a length‑τ observation prefix identifies exactly the latent risk moments m_j=\mathbb E[p^j] for j=0,\ldots,2τ‑1, buying two new moments per additional period. These identify average next‑period attrition among survivors but need not identify allocation welfare or attrition among those prioritized for treatment. Our observationally equivalent constructions establish unavoidable timing regret at any sample size for a fixed observation length, while exact certificates determine whether all compatible populations share a unique optimal date. Matched experiments separate the effects of estimation, bootstrap averaging, and regret weighting. Longer observation often resolves timing ambiguity, but the optimal date may already have passed. In our experiments, bootstrap averaging and early stopping improve decisions, while regret weighting adds no improvement in pooled mean squared regret: better statistical fit need not yield better allocation welfare. The code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/waiting‑buys‑two‑moments.

PaperId: 625, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23795.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuze He, Bin Tan, Zelin Gao, Yujun Shen, Yong-Jin Liu, Nan Xue, Yinghao Xu
Title: Persistent Planar Memory for Video World Models
Abstract:
Video world models that generate and explore environments at scale need a persistent 3D memory of what they have produced. Plane primitives offer a natural candidate: a compact set of oriented planes captures the dominant structural elements (e.g., walls, floors, facades) of indoor and outdoor scenes, while requiring only 7 parameters per primitive. We present PPMem, a video world model that adopts plane primitives as its persistent 3D memory. PPMem augments a video diffusion transformer with a planar prediction head and a Depth Token Fusion (DTF) module: each autoregressive chunk jointly produces RGB video and planar geometry, which merges into a persistent plane memory that conditions subsequent chunks via rendered depth. The resulting memory is three orders of magnitude more compact than per‑pixel point clouds (~100K primitives, 5MB for a full scene), geometrically explicit (metric depth, normals, exportable surfaces), cross‑view consistent (jointly predicted by the shared backbone), and adaptive (refined by the merging procedure as generation proceeds). On DL3DV and RealEstate10K, PPMem outperforms prior 3D‑grounded world models in video quality while jointly producing metric‑scale depth, surface normals, and exportable planar geometry, sustaining coherence across hundreds of frames under large viewpoint changes. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/ppmem.

PaperId: 626, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23788.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Maxime Baelde
Title: Parametric Resonance in Primal-Dual Learning for Slowly Non-Stationary Constrained MDPs
Abstract:
Primal‑dual methods for constrained Markov decision processes are analyzed under a two‑timescale assumption, with non‑stationarity entering through two channels. In the additive channel, where the constraint level oscillates, the dual oscillation saturates at a floor set by the moving optimum and is amplified linearly by the timescale ratio. In the parametric channel, where the constraint sensitivity oscillates, a coherent modulation carries no resonant forcing at any depth: the dual update's stiffness modulation cancels the primal update's damping modulation. Instability instead comes from a mismatch between the constraint estimate used by the primal update and the measurement used by the dual update, producing a parametric resonance at twice the pair's natural frequency. The tolerated mismatch grows with the square root of the forcing bandwidth and collapses with the square root of the dual‑to‑primal step‑size ratio. These results hold on the tangent linear‑quadratic reduction around an active saddle, for one constraint and for K constraints under a common modulation and an isotropy condition. Driving both updates from the same estimate removes the resonant forcing but introduces a stationary offset equal to the estimator's bias. In a Lagrangian soft actor‑critic agent, the multiplier locks onto the sub‑harmonic at the timescale ratios its identified linear loop predicts and a coherent cost critic suppresses the lock‑in, while a proportional (PID) term, predicted to leave the lock‑in in place, suppresses most of it through the projection of the multiplier.

PaperId: 627, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23772.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Simon Giebenhain, Tobias Kirschstein, Liam Schoneveld, Davide Davoli, Zhe Chen, Matthias Nießner
Title: Video Diffusion Avatars: Taming Video Diffusion Models into Controllable 3D Avatars
Abstract:
Video diffusion models (VDMs) trained on internet‑scale data encode a rich prior on appearance, motion, and physics that is difficult to replicate with explicit 3D rendering and costly 3D data capture. We introduce Video Diffusion Avatars (VDAs), a method that creates photo‑realistic, multi‑view consistent avatars from a single image by fine‑tuning a VDM for precise control over camera viewpoint, facial expression, and upper‑body pose. Departing from 3D morphable models (3DMMs), VDAs use a learned expression space that lifts the expressiveness ceiling of 3DMMs, e.g., for the tongue and mouth interior. However, learned expression codes exhibit heavy viewpoint bias, as our DISTRACT benchmark reveals. We show that this bias can be removed through disentanglement, enabling their use as driving signals for multi‑view consistent avatars. Camera and upper‑body pose are controlled jointly via proxy‑mesh renderings, giving independent control over expression, pose, and viewpoint. A camera‑triplet training strategy makes the approach efficient: our models train for 34 hours on a single A100 using only public multi‑view data. VDAs outperform state‑of‑the‑art single‑image 3D avatars on novel‑view reenactment, reducing face LPIPS by 29% and improving perceptual quality (JOD) by 66% on BecomingLit. A static 3DGS reconstruction probe further confirms that our generations are the most multi‑view consistent. Built on a video prior, VDAs produce effects beyond the reach of explicit renderers, including physically plausible hair dynamics, shadows, reflections, and refractions.

PaperId: 628, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23765.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Siyu Zhou, Yuqin Xie, Hao Yuan, Yingjie Zhou
Title: Universal Semantic Enhancement for Weakly Supervised Anomaly Detection
Abstract:
Weakly supervised anomaly detection on tabular data is an essential task in many label‑scarce applications, since tabular data is widely encountered and it is commonly observed in practice that only a limited number of labeled anomalies are available alongside abundant unlabeled samples. Most existing methods try to learn features that capture the inherent distribution patterns in the target domain. However, such features often struggle to provide a complete description of possible abnormal characteristics and are highly susceptible to overfitting the extremely scarce labels. To address this challenge, we propose a weakly supervised anomaly detection method based on universal semantic enhancement for tabular data, which fuses the universal knowledge from a pre‑trained tabular foundation model with the domain‑specific knowledge learned on the target dataset. The two types of knowledge are naturally complementary: universal semantics describe the common patterns of tabular data across domains, while the domain‑specific features capture the inherent distributions of normal and anomalous behaviors in the target dataset. A prototype‑conditioned modulation mechanism is then designed to effectively integrate the two types of features, allowing them to reinforce each other for improved anomaly detection. Extensive experiments on public datasets show that the proposed method outperforms competitive methods when only eight labeled anomalies are available in the training procedure.

PaperId: 629, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23716.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chashi Mahiul Islam, Samuel Jacob Chacko, Mao Nishino, Canlin Zhang, Xiuwen Liu
Title: Neural Expansion: A Unified Mechanism for How Deep Neural Networks Generalize
Abstract:
Deep neural networks demonstrate remarkable generalization despite being highly over‑parameterized, challenging traditional statistical learning theories. While several theoretical paradigms such as margin‑based bounds, PAC‑Bayesian analyses, and neural tangent kernels provide global explanations, they often lack mechanistic insight into how generalization emerges from training dynamics. We introduce Neural Expansion, a unified geometric framework that characterizes generalization through the expansion of directionally‑selective ray coverage in the input space. Using Generalization Intervals (GIs), we quantify direction‑specific regions around training samples where the model's predictions remain stable. Our extensive empirical studies across diverse architectures and datasets reveal that training leads to progressive expansion of ray coverage, particularly along directions with low Jacobian singular values. This mechanism helps explain a large fraction of correctly classified test inputs, adversarial examples, and even mislabeled or out‑of‑distribution samples through the geometry of ray coverage rather than instance‑level memorization. By connecting input‑space curvature to predictive behavior, our framework provides a mechanistic foundation that complements existing global theories of deep learning.

PaperId: 630, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23700.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dmytro Knopov, Nadiya Shvai
Title: Equivalence testing and run-count design for stochastic machine-learning experiments
Abstract:
Claims that two training methods perform equally well often rest on a non‑significant difference between two or three runs per method. We develop a protocol, with its power theory, for certifying practical equivalence in per‑run metrics such as the AUROC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve). It rests on a two‑level (seed x item) variance model separating between‑run dispersion from item‑level noise. Equivalence within a pre‑specified margin is tested by two one‑sided tests (TOST), equivalently by a confidence interval inside the margin; a two‑level bootstrap covers composite statistics. A closed‑form formula converts a margin and a target power into runs per method; its shifted‑t refinement is calibrated against the realised two‑level process. Simulations on a 270‑cell grid and under non‑Gaussian seed laws confirm the formula within its design‑relevant range, from five runs per method. For four published runs of a joint energy‑based model, the failure to certify equivalence was largely decided by design: with the variance calibrated to those runs, two per method certify with probability near three per cent, whereas certifying 0.01 AUROC at 80 per cent power needs twelve even under exact equality. A second case study on a thousand‑seed CIFAR‑10 zoo and the MultiBERTs checks the formula against real seed laws (within 0.05 in that range) and resolves comparisons that two or three runs leave undecided. In a two‑stage design (pilot, then formula), our experiments suggest that an upper confidence bound on the pilot variance substantially reduces the undersizing seen with its point estimate.

PaperId: 631, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23685.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Manohar Vellala, Soumya Banerjee, Sandip Roy, Ross Gore, Sachin Shetty
Title: HardEval: An Execution-Verified Benchmark for AI-Driven Security Hardening and Compliance Remediation
Abstract:
Implementing Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) controls remains a demanding operating‑system administration task. Each natural‑language security requirement must be translated into a precise and persistent configuration change. These changes span Secure Shell (SSH) configuration, authentication policy, audit rules, and kernel parameters. Existing benchmarks do not measure whether a model can perform this task on a live system. Code benchmarks evaluate isolated programs without persistent system state, while agent benchmarks largely focus on applications rather than operating‑system configuration. In this paper, we introduce HardEval, an execution‑verified benchmark for evaluating language‑model‑assisted security hardening. HardEval is built from Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 STIG controls that fail on an unhardened baseline system. Expert‑written reference remediations and Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL) checks serve as hidden ground truth for grading; they are never shown to the model, and each task states only the required security outcome while withholding the implementation. The model produces a Bash script, which is executed on a live virtual machine and graded from fail to pass using the corresponding OpenSCAP/OVAL compliance check. Evaluation of fourteen frontier and open‑weight configurations reveals large and uneven capability differences across security domains. A recurring failure mode is plausible security code that does not satisfy the exact compliance condition. For four open‑weight configurations, multi‑run Wilson confidence intervals preserve the observed ordering. HardEval is publicly available.

PaperId: 632, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23677.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xikang Guan, Shaocong Yang, Yanqi Bao, Can Wang, Zheng Gu, Zhengqing Chen, Kai Chen, Jing Huo, Yang Gao
Title: Agentic Physics-Grounded Video Generation via Memory-Augmented In-Context Reasoning
Abstract:
Physical plausibility is essential for realistic video generation. Existing methods impose physical guidance before synthesis via simulations or refined prompts, but this can limit dynamic diversity, miss errors that emerge only after generation, and require repeated regeneration when inconsistencies remain. We therefore study a generate‑diagnose‑repair paradigm that preserves the original generation capability and selectively repairs physical inconsistencies afterward, raising two key questions: what to repair and how to repair? To address them, we introduce PhysRepair, an agentic video generation framework that combines causal reasoning over the observed physical failure with prior repair experience to enable localized and adaptive correction. Specifically, Spatiotemporal Causal Constraints identify the first invalid physical state and its causally affected states, producing a repair specification that guides physically plausible local regeneration while preserving unaffected content. Experience‑augmented In‑context Learning combines the ongoing repair context with relevant experience from previous repairs, allowing the agent to adapt its repair decisions across diverse physical failures and accumulate completed trajectories for future cases. Experiments on Physics‑IQ Verified across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism demonstrate that PhysRepair consistently improves the physical plausibility of generated videos over existing methods. Our project page is available at https://xxkkxxx.github.io/PhysRepair‑Website/.

PaperId: 633, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23663.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rui Liu, Lin Gu, Hesong Li, Ying Fu
Title: PCDFusion: Proposal-Context-Detail Bayesian Rendering for Infrared-Visible Image Fusion
Abstract:
Infrared‑visible image fusion (IVIF) aims to combine visible and thermal infrared observations for human perception and downstream vision tasks. Visible and thermal infrared observations are physically complementary but unreliable in different ways. Existing deep IVIF methods mainly improve feature interaction and reconstruction, but often lack an explicit local rule for deciding when visible appearance should dominate and when thermal responses should contribute. To address this issue, we reformulate IVIF as local Bayesian posterior rendering, where fusion is controlled by posterior action weights rather than direct modality mixing. In this paper, we propose Proposal‑Context‑Detail Fusion (PCDFusion), a visible‑anchored framework that implements this formulation through three rendering stages. PCDFusion preserves potentially useful thermal responses, updates exposure‑degraded visible regions, and renders reliable band‑limited infrared structures into the final luminance. Extensive experiments on public IVIF benchmarks show that PCDFusion improves fusion quality, target recovery, and downstream detection and segmentation performance under challenging illumination. The code is available at https://github.com/BIT‑RuiLiu/PCDFusion.git.

PaperId: 634, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23662.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Lorenzo Magnino, Antonio Marino, Michael Amir, Daigo Shishika, Amanda Prorok
Title: Learning Robot Metareasoning: Adaptive Computation Budgets for Real-Time Control
Abstract:
Planning while moving faces an historical trade‑off between deliberation and reactivity. A planner running concurrently with execution needs time to compute, so the robot must commit to an open‑loop action chunk for that duration: a longer commitment buys a better plan at the cost of feedback frequency. Existing controllers fix this action commitment, and consequently the computation budget, before deployment. However, the optimal computation time is highly state‑dependent (due to factors such as unmodeled dynamics, safety constraints, and marginal optimisation gains), i.e. dynamic, therefore offline static tuning risks leaving systems blind during critical maneuvers or unable to find global effective solutions. We cast the identification of the optimal computation budget as a semi‑Markov decision process (SMDP) in which a single decision defines both the robot action commitments and the time allocated to the solver. To solve this, we train a reinforcement‑learning policy conditioned on the current state, the executing plan, and inexpensive planner statistics. Across ground‑robot navigation, agile quadrotor flight, and contact‑rich manipulation, the learned policy changes its budget with the demands of the scenario, discovering efficient reasoning patterns that outperform fixed‑budget baselines. https://lorenzomagnino.github.io/learning‑robot‑metareasoning‑review/

PaperId: 635, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23623.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Juho Jung, Seongjae Kang, Jinyoung Han
Title: Deconstructing Multi-Task Active Learning: The Paradox of Gradient Conflict and Orthogonal Decomposition
Abstract:
Existing multi‑task active learning (MTL‑AL) methods predominantly rely on linear scalarization of heterogeneous objectives such as uncertainty, diversity, and gradient conflict. We argue that this entangled formulation is fundamentally limited, as linear combination fails to capture Pareto‑optimal trade‑offs under conflicting objectives. We propose a shift from combination to deconstruction and introduce a principled framework that rethinks MTL‑AL along three orthogonal dimensions. First, we identify the Conflict Paradox: although the optimization literature treats gradient conflict as interference to be suppressed, penalizing conflict when ranking candidates is measurably worse than not scoring it at all. We therefore decouple the two concerns: the acquisition function does not score conflict, and the resulting interference is resolved by gradient surgery during training. Second, we introduce Orthogonal Decomposition, separating acquisition into Informativeness and Exploration. This two‑stage process, informativeness filtering followed by coverage maximization, prevents "diversity dilution" by excluding uninformative outliers before enforcing diversity. Third, we propose Cross‑Task Mutual Information (CTMI), a covariance‑based statistic of cross‑task dependency computed from MC‑dropout task entropies. Extensive experiments on COCO, Cityscapes, and NYUv2, including comparisons against recent MTL‑AL and data‑selection baselines, demonstrate consistent improvements over state‑of‑the‑art methods, highlighting that structural rethinking of acquisition yields larger gains than incremental heuristic design. Code is available at https://github.com/Juho‑Jung/multitask_active_learning_official.

PaperId: 636, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23609.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Piper Powell, Robert Franz, Amos Smith, Isaak Ihorst, Joachim Hertzberg, Martin Atzmueller
Title: ADA 2025: A Multimodal Dataset for Water-Deficit Stress Detection in Sugar Beets
Abstract:
Research and development into artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applications in crop management are hindered by a lack of suitable public datasets. Whereas applications in disease and pest detection benefit from a comparatively higher amount of available data, applications like water‑deficit stress detection often have very few if any public datasets available. Moreover, most datasets that are available are single‑modality and frequently RGB‑only, leaving the early detection and enhanced performance offered by other methods, and particularly by multimodal approaches, out of reach. Datasets with accurate metadata, higher numbers of plants, and smaller intervals between data points are also scarce. To address this, we publicly release ADA 2025, a >500 GB comprehensive multimodal dataset of young sugar beet plants under healthy and water‑deficit conditions combining thermal, hyperspectral, RGB, and depth imagery along with relevant environmental and metadata and both relative water content (RWC) and leaf thickness as ground truth sources. Exemplary results showcase the dataset's validity in terms of differences detectable between stressed and healthy plants.

PaperId: 637, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23587.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Manthan Gadhia, Alexander Hoyle, Karolina Stańczak
Title: Analyzing Occupational Gender Bias across the LLM Training Lifecycle
Abstract:
Post‑training is widely assumed to reduce the social biases language models inherit from pretraining, yet direct evidence for this assumption remains mixed. In this paper, we examine how gender disparities evolve across the language modeling pipeline. In particular, we study occupational gender bias in OLMo 3, a fully open language model family, across its post‑training stages by prompting each checkpoint to generate open‑ended narratives about synthetic personas given their occupation and education. We consider two settings, a gender‑given setting in which the profile states the persona's gender explicitly and a gender‑assumed setting in which it must be inferred by the model. We find that when gender is stated, post‑training increases semantic diversity for male‑coded profiles, whereas for female‑coded profiles the increase is smaller after SFT and not significant after DPO and RLVR. When gender is assumed by the model, post‑training affects narratives about female and male personas similarly. The model's own gender assumptions, however, show a consistent female‑preferential skew relative to United States labor‑force demographics, except for heavily male‑dominated occupations. Every successive post‑training stage monotonically increases the odds of attributing a female label over the base model. A provenance analysis of the supervised fine‑tuning corpus finds only a modest 7.7% female‑token surplus, too small to explain the size of these downstream effects. The project code is available under: https://github.com/manthangadhia/llm‑lifecycle‑bias.

PaperId: 638, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23577.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yan Zeng, Changlu Guo, Oskar Kristoffersen, Anders Nymark Christensen, Morten Rieger Hannemose, Anders Bjorholm Dahl
Title: CLEAR: Cooperative Latent Flow for Visual Counterfactual Explanations with Accurate Region Preservation
Abstract:
Visual counterfactual explanations (VCEs) should alter a classifier's prediction while remaining realistic and preserving decision‑irrelevant content. Image‑space methods provide high‑quality counterfactuals but are computationally costly, whereas latent‑space methods are more efficient but often less faithful. We identify two sources responsible for this gap. First, latent generation recovers a natural sample from a perturbed representation, whereas classifier guidance pushes it toward a target class, so their update directions may oppose. Second, VAE reconstruction can alter regions that should remain unchanged. We introduce CLEAR, a latent Flow Matching framework for VCEs. CLEAR uses Flow Matching's explicit instantaneous velocity as a reference for the generative direction to decompose classifier guidance into cooperative and conflicting components. It preserves the cooperative component and adaptively attenuates only the conflicting one according to conflict strength. We further analyze conflict frequency and strength throughout generation to reveal how classifier guidance interacts with the generative process. CLEAR also dynamically identifies editable regions, constrains latent modifications, and directly preserves factual content outside them to reduce VAE‑induced changes. Across five bidirectional tasks on two datasets, CLEAR retains latent‑space efficiency while achieving counterfactual quality comparable to or better than strong image‑space baselines, with a 2.5x speedup over the strongest baseline. Project page: https://yan‑zen9.github.io/CLEAR/

PaperId: 639, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23551.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sukhvansh Jain, Anurag Maurya, Shivam Vats, Narendra Kumar Dhar, Ravi Prakash
Title: Embodiment-Aware Planning for Heterogeneous Bimanual Manipulation
Abstract:
Many manipulation tasks that are effortless for dexterous human hands remain challenging for robotic systems equipped with simple, task‑specialized grippers. Industrial platforms commonly rely on end‑effectors such as suction cups or parallel‑jaw grippers, yet no single mode can reliably satisfy the diverse constraints encountered across different phases of complex manipulation tasks, including pickup, reorientation, insertion, and constrained placement. In this work, we investigate whether complementary simple grippers within a heterogeneous bimanual setup can collectively realize tasks that exceed the capability of any individual gripper alone. Given a single human demonstration specifying the desired object motion, we formulate embodiment‑aware execution as a finite‑horizon optimization over arm‑trajectory assignments. At each segment, the planner determines whether single‑arm manipulation or a coordinated dual arm handover is required, jointly reasoning over heterogeneous grasp feasibility, motion constraints, manipulability, and cross‑gripper compatibility. Exploiting this formulation, we compute globally consistent assignments with explicit switching regularization. Experiments on a dual Franka FR3 platform equipped with suction and parallel‑jaw grippers demonstrate improved feasibility and reliability in tasks that are infeasible under single‑gripper execution.

PaperId: 640, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23542.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Weiyang Jin, Jiwen Yu, Sihan Xu, Yuwei Niu, Xihui Liu
Title: Execution Before Memory: Diagnosing Memory Failures in Video World Models
Abstract:
A memory test for a video world model should say whether the scene was set, whether the asked change was carried out, and whether the last frame shows the result. Current tests fold these into one number, so a low score is easy to read as forgetting. When the change is not carried out, the hidden state transition cannot appear, so the test is not really a test of memory. We introduce MIST, an evaluation that separates the change from the memory it should leave behind. The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it, with leakage before that point kept under control. This separation locates the bottleneck: the model sets the scene but does not carry out the instructed change. The same gap appears in general memory evaluations. On that basis we propose M3‑Agent (Make the Missing Move), which recursively revises the details of the input instruction so that the model successfully carries out the requested instruction. Relative to the baseline, it more than triples the MIST reveal score. On the benchmarks, WRBench's score T rises by 26.1% and MBench‑T's score U by 52.7%. The method meets the problem from the execution side: it shows what the frozen model can do once the move is stated, and it sets a stricter baseline.

PaperId: 641, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23531.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Julius Erbach, Dominik Narnhofer, Bernt Schiele, Jan Eric Lenssen, Konrad Schindler
Title: PONDER: Learning to Generate in the Right Order
Abstract:
We introduce PONDER, a method that learns in which order an image generator should fill in content and which of its earlier predictions to revise. Masked generative models construct a sample by repeatedly filling in subsets of missing variables. The order of these partial predictions determines the context available in subsequent steps and therefore affects the quality of the final sample. Common strategies are to choose the order randomly or based on local confidence estimates. Conditioned on the partially generated sample and the generator's features, our policy chooses which positions to fill next and/or which previously filled positions to mask for later regeneration, a mechanism we call rethinking. In this way, the generation process is able to adapt to the evolving context and also to revise earlier predictions. We optimize the policy using group‑relative policy gradients, with rewards that measure constraint satisfaction, human preference, or distribution quality. For the latter, we introduce FIDgrad, an image‑level reward derived from the (first‑order) change in Fréchet Inception Distance caused by adding a generated sample to the current feature distribution. With the generators frozen, learned ordering reduces MAR‑B ImageNet FID from 4.09 to 2.78 and raises the accuracy on hard visual Sudokus from 3.9% to 56.6%, surpassing uncertainty‑based greedy ordering (38.7%). Rethinking further improves these results to 2.70 FID and 96.7% accuracy, while increasing the rethinking budget of a fixed policy yields continued improvements at inference time.

PaperId: 642, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23503.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jinheng Li, Guosheng Wang, Hongchao Du, Shangyu Wu, Qiao Li, Chun Jason Xue
Title: HBFSim: A Simulator for Exploring HBF in Memory Hierarchies for LLMs
Abstract:
High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising technology that provides terabyte‑scale accelerator‑local capacity at bandwidths approaching HBM, with a potential cost‑per‑bit advantage over HBM. However, its NAND foundation brings long latency, out‑of‑place updates, and finite write endurance directly into the accelerator memory hierarchy, making its effects on performance and lifetime difficult to predict. To study this emerging design space, we present HBFSim, an LLM‑aware event‑driven simulator for heterogeneous HBM+HBF memory systems that preserves application‑level memory semantics while modeling flash‑internal behavior. HBFSim models HBM, HBF with host‑managed flash translation, and conventional capacity tiers in one simulation driven by a calibrated serving frontend. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama‑3.1‑70B and Qwen3‑235B‑A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. HBF serves data that does not fit in HBM 11.0‑‑19.0× faster than host DRAM; HBM is better used to hold the running sequences' KV cache than as a cache for HBF; and at a published peak load of Llama‑3.1‑70B, HBF lasts 2.0 to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share the KV writes. The artifact is available at https://github.com/FlashLabAE/HBFSim and will track public HBF device data as it becomes available.

PaperId: 643, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23480.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Markus Fischer, Jens Meiler, Matthias Elgeti
Title: MuninAI: A Self-Hosted Agentic Framework for Independent Research Groups
Abstract:
Research groups that want a language model grounded in their own literature face a choice between hosted services that receive their unpublished work and self‑hosted deployments that keep the data local but give the model no access to the corpus. Munin is an open‑source framework for a self‑hosted scientific assistant that indexes a group's corpus and its citation graph, and wraps whichever open‑weight model the group can serve in an agent harness with specialised reading, search, and computation tools. We claim that the harness, rather than the specific model, is what makes the system useful on domain literature, and we ship the evaluation suite that tests this claim with the software. On 199 paired literature questions, the harness more than doubles the accuracy of the base model, from 0.387 to 0.874 (+0.487, 95% CI [0.407, 0.568]), while naive retrieve‑then‑answer scores below the unaided model on every backbone tested. Under the harness, roughly twice as many answer claims trace to a passage the model read itself as with fixed top‑5 retrieval. When the source paper for a question is removed from the corpus, the system abstains on about nine in ten of the questions it had answered correctly on the Qwen backbones and eight in ten on gpt‑oss‑20b, and it produces no fabricated local citation across 300 fabricated references. The pattern holds on three backbones from two developers, including a 20‑billion‑parameter model that runs on a single consumer‑grade GPU. With all outbound network access disabled, both Qwen backbones still exceed the published PaperQA2 accuracy. The evaluation suite runs as a single command, so an adopting group can re‑run it on its own corpus and model.

PaperId: 644, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23479.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Hongcheng Gao, Alex Zhou, Jay Zhu, Zelin Zheng, Shijia Ge, Xiping Li, Di Wu, Yazhe Wang, Jianshu Zeng, Xuan Shangguan, Yongli Wang, Yexing Wan, Lingyu He, Zhiqi Jia, Sihang Wu, Xiao He
Title: HexaShell: A Thin Harness for Exploring the Limits of VLM Agents as Robot Coding Agents
Abstract:
Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now compete with learned policies on robot manipulation leaderboards. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it controls a robot instead of a computer, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, gives the agent a thin harness: one command line that turns its commands into robot motion and makes no decisions of its own. On the robot, the agent keeps doing what it does best: it reads output, writes code and runs tests. Two agents of the same model share the work. An acting agent runs each episode.
