After a failure, an optimizer agent reads the full record of the episode, with every command, image and message, finds the cause, and writes or fixes small programs called tools, each with its own tests. What the agents learn stays as code, and no demonstrations or training are needed. At run time, the tools use only what a real robot also has: RGB images, camera calibration and the state of the arms. They find objects by triangulation between camera views. Because these inputs are the same in simulation and on hardware, the tools move to a real robot with a different arm after only a small change for the arm. We build the tools on ten layouts of one seed per task with Codex and GPT‑6‑Astra and freeze them; the eight Open tasks share one set of tools. In RoboDojo's official evaluation on a hidden seed, 50 episodes for each of the 42 tasks, HexaShell reaches 46.9% success and a progress score of 53.2, the state of the art on the official RoboDojo leaderboard. The limit is contact, not reasoning: memory tasks reach 81.0%, but precision tasks only 32.0%. We open source the tools evolved so far at https://github.com/HexaFuture/HexaShell.

PaperId: 645, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23448.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Deming Song, Chi-Kin Lam, Kefeng Li, Hui Yu, Xilin Li, Huagang Lin
Title: Regularized free deconvolution for spectral repair of resampling distortion in high-dimensional particle filters
Abstract:
Resampling is the standard remedy for weight degeneracy in particle filters, but in high dimensions it distorts the spectrum of the ensemble covariance in a way that is computable from the importance weights. This paper studies the inverse problem: recovering the pre‑resampling spectrum from the observed weights and the empirical spectrum alone, and using it without biasing the filter. We first show that the forward spectral law extends to random importance weights once one conditions on the weights together with the realized offspring counts, rather than on the weights alone. We then construct a regularized free‑deconvolution estimator, prove its consistency with an explicit error budget at a fixed resolution scale, and certify model mismatch through a computable forward residual. The repaired spectrum enters the filter only as the preconditioner of a Metropolis‑adjusted rejuvenation move, so that spectral error affects mixing efficiency but not the invariant target. For the full filtering cycle, we derive a geometrically summable error recursion under stable scalar dynamics and an explicit law for the cost of abstaining from repair. Pre‑registered simulations show that the inversion reduces the spectral error by an order of magnitude, that the corrected preconditioner recovers about 90% of the oracle's sampling efficiency in an anisotropic regime, and that the cost of abstention depends on when abstentions occur rather than on how many. The repair recovers eigenvalue laws, not eigenvectors, and is certified only within an explicitly stated exogenous‑weight regime.

PaperId: 646, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23446.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Liang Yue, Eric A. Vance
Title: "You" Is Not Toxic: How LLM Labelers Rewrite the Web's Conversation Laws
Abstract:
What the Web community believes about toxic conversations, such as that toxicity rises in longer and deeper threads, was measured mostly with Google's Perspective API, which is shutting down; large language models (LLMs) will make the next measurements. We find that LLM labelers mistake second‑person address for toxicity, and that this one bias manufactures laws that human labels do not show. On 1.25 million news comments with crowd labels, Claude Haiku flags 12% of the non‑toxic comments that contain no "you" and 51% of those with four or more; a single crowd rater flags 6% and 10%. Deeper replies address someone more often, so under Haiku toxicity rises with reply depth (+0.93 percentage points per level), while under the crowd's labels it slightly declines (‑0.12). Rewriting "you" in the third person removes two thirds of the false rise; flagging only as many comments as the crowd does not remove it, and showing Haiku the parent comment enlarges it. All seven LLMs we test over‑flag "you", and at the crowd's flag rate, without the parent, any false rise of the open ones vanishes at a fixed number of second‑person words; Haiku also over‑flags "you" on Reddit, Gab and Wikipedia talk pages. Agreement with human labels does not reveal the bias: we prove that a fixed Cohen's kappa leaves a law nearly unconstrained. We therefore certify the law instead of the labeler. Threadsafe uses the labeler's scores to choose which comments human raters label and to predict the others, and corrects the predictions with the human labels; linear laws are estimated without bias whatever the labeler does. In simulated audits its intervals for the laws keep nominal coverage from 250 labels on, where uniform‑sample methods such as PPI++ fall short, and at 1,000 to 8,000 labels are 0.75 times as wide as those of design‑based supervised learning (DSL); a thousand human labels rule out Haiku's rising law.

PaperId: 647, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23416.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Cheng Fan, Han Wu, Tingzhang Luo, Minjing Dong, Yehui Tang, Jianyuan Guo
Title: GeoReason: Bridging Logical Reasoning and Spatial Fidelity in Remote Sensing Segmentation
Abstract:
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly advanced instruction‑driven perception through the "Embedding‑as‑Mask" paradigm. However, extending this capability to Remote Sensing (RS) reasoning segmentation remains exceptionally challenging under cluttered geographical contexts and extreme scale variations, often leading to Spatial Fidelity Degradation and Target Misidentification. We identify a critical yet underexplored bottleneck: the sequential alienation of the segmentation token [SEG] from its initial visual grounding within the autoregressive generation paradigm. Produced only at the end of long reasoning chains, [SEG] relies on visual evidence that has been progressively diluted by linguistic abstraction and autoregressive noise. This information decay is particularly catastrophic for RS targets with minuscule pixel footprints, where even marginal fidelity loss leads to localization failure. To address these bottlenecks, we propose GeoReason, a novel framework designed to fortify logical deduction and preserve spatial integrity. First, we introduce an Anticipatory Prior mechanism that injects the [SEG] token directly into the initial user query, shifting it from a terminal output to a primary condition. This paradigm shift transforms the token into a persistent spatial anchor, preventing information decay during long‑form linguistic inference. Second, we enhance visual reasoning via a Location‑aware Chain‑of‑Thought (CoT) that enforces coarse‑to‑fine localization using bounding boxes, coupled with a Latent Patch‑to‑Token Alignment (PTA) Loss that explicitly aligns the latent segmentation token with physical RS textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GeoReason consistently outperforms state‑of‑the‑art methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS‑D benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanc0126/GeoReason.

PaperId: 648, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23404.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Alberto Foresti, Giulio Franzese, Pietro Michiardi
Title: Information Estimation with Discrete Diffusion
Abstract:
Information‑theoretic measures, such as Mutual Information (MI), play a crucial role in understanding non‑linear relationships between random variables and are widely used across scientific disciplines. Yet, their use on real‑world discrete data remains challenging. Existing methods typically rely on embedding discrete data into a continuous space and apply neural estimators originally designed for continuous distributions. This process requires careful engineering for both the embedding model and estimator architecture, but suffers from issues related to high data dimensionality. In this work, we introduce InfoSEDD, a discrete diffusion‑based approach that bridges information‑theoretic estimation and generative modeling such that they can be used to compute Kullback‑Leibler divergences. Backed by Continuous Time Markov Chains theory principles, the design of InfoSEDD is lightweight and scalable and allows seamless integration with pretrained models. We showcase the versatility of our approach through applications on motif discovery in genetic promoter data, semantic‑aware model selection in text summarization, and entropy estimation in Ising models. Finally, we construct consistency tests on real‑world textual and genomics data. Our experiments demonstrate that InfoSEDD outperforms alternatives that rely on the "embedding trick". Our results position InfoSEDD as a robust and scalable tool for information‑theoretic analysis of discrete data.

PaperId: 649, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23377.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chengyang Zhang, Zhihao Wang, Zhiyu Long, Xueqian Wang, Quanming Yao, Wei Wu, Gang Li
Title: FloodVLM-Pix: Language-Guided Pixel-Level Flood Understanding
Abstract:
As climate change intensifies, floods are becoming more frequent and destructive, making accurate flood understanding an urgent priority. However, existing vision‑language models perform poorly on flood‑related tasks, suffering from attentional bias and inaccurate descriptions of flood magnitude. To bridge this gap, we construct the first large‑scale remote sensing flood multi‑modal benchmark that supports language‑level flood understanding and pixel‑level flood segmentation. The benchmark contains 131,200 flood image patches and corresponding 443,100 textual descriptions for flood severity and evolution. Based on this benchmark, we propose FloodVLM‑Pix, a language‑guided pixel‑level flood understanding model that includes a flood prior module and a multi‑temporal flood pixel decoder to achieve accurate flood understanding. The flood prior module automatically distills sub‑region flood spatial priors and inputs priors into FloodVLM‑Pix, solving the attentional bias problem in flood language understanding. The flood pixel decoder introduces a novel general‑specific feature fusion mechanism to address performance degradation caused by interference (e.g., clouds or mountain shadows) during flood segmentation. Experiments on FloodVL‑Pix demonstrate that FloodVLM‑Pix improves both flood description quality and pixel‑level flood segmentation performance compared with state‑of‑the‑art VLMs and flood segmentation models. Our code and data will be released at https://github.com/Haomiaoyanmeng/FloodPix.

PaperId: 650, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23374.pdf   GitHub
Authors:MOSI. AI
Title: MOSS-Image Technical Report
Abstract:
Recent closed‑source image generation systems can produce diverse visual content from simple compositions to information‑dense graphics, yet open‑weight text‑to‑image models still struggle with dense text and intricate layouts. To narrow this gap, we introduce MOSS‑Image, an open generation system that combines high‑fidelity visual synthesis with intent‑aware composition. First, we pretrain a 5B single‑stream diffusion transformer (DiT) from scratch with a carefully designed recipe, enabling bilingual long‑form text rendering and precise layout control. Second, we develop an intention‑aware agentic prompt enhancement (PE) module that translates diverse user requests into detailed content and layout specifications. Together, they enable MOSS‑Image to generate text‑rich and layout‑coherent images. We further introduce LongLongTextBench (LLTB) for evaluating long‑form English and Chinese text rendering, and RealLayoutArena (RLA) for end‑to‑end layout‑rich generation. MOSS‑Image achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance among open‑weight models on LLTB, with an average text coverage of 96.3%. On RLA, MOSS‑Image ranks second in the end‑to‑end system comparison, while its backbone ranks first among generators evaluated with shared enhanced prompts. We will release the model, training recipe, and evaluation framework to support further research and promote the text‑to‑image community.

PaperId: 651, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23345.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kwangryeol Park, Seulki Lee
Title: OliO: ODE-based Linear Transition Operator for Self-Supervised Time Series Forecasting
Abstract:
Self‑supervised representation learning has advanced time series forecasting by capturing robust features from unlabeled data. However, existing contrastive and masking‑based methods often struggle to explicitly model the underlying temporal flow, either by treating time lag as noise or by disrupting the inherent temporal dynamics essential for forecasting. To address these limitations, we propose OliO (ODE‑based Linear Transition Operator), a plug‑and‑play self‑supervised learning method that learns bidirectional temporal flows as a continuous and structurally consistent dynamical system. OliO introduces a transition operator derived from linear Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) to align latent representations across arbitrary time shifts. By imposing a strictly upper triangular constraint on the transition matrix, we mathematically ensure numerical stability and enforce a robust polynomial boundary that effectively captures long‑term dependencies while preventing the exponential divergence typically found in unconstrained ODE‑based models. This structural constraint induces a temporally coherent representation space that preserves the underlying flow essential for accurate forecasting. Extensive experiments across various backbone architectures and benchmarks demonstrate that OliO achieves significant performance gains, providing Mean Squared Error (MSE) reductions of up to 5.75% over the most competitive grid‑searched SOTA baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/eai‑lab/OliO

PaperId: 652, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23324.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Eunju Park, Uiwon Hwang
Title: CatchUp: Depth-Aware Re-Admission of Visual Tokens for Efficient Large Vision-Language Models
Abstract:
Large Vision‑Language Models (LVLMs) repeatedly process hundreds of visual tokens across decoder layers, incurring substantial computation and memory costs. Existing visual‑token reduction methods often irreversibly discard tokens despite depth‑varying query relevance. Although recoverable routing allows excluded tokens to return, re‑admitted tokens retain stale hidden states after bypassing intermediate decoder transformations. Thus, token recoverability does not guarantee representation readiness at the current decoder depth. Under a fixed routing trajectory at a 64‑token budget, replacing stale re‑admitted states with current‑depth oracle representations improves average RefCOCO Acc@0.5 from 18.96 to 23.18, revealing the impact of representation staleness. We propose CatchUp, a training‑free framework combining reversible visual‑token routing with Local Transition Correction (LTC). CatchUp repeatedly re‑evaluates query‑conditioned relevance over the complete visual‑token set, preserving deferred tokens for later re‑admission. LTC approximates their skipped representation evolution by transferring reference‑to‑current hidden‑state transitions from semantically and spatially related active anchors. This correction improves alignment with current‑depth oracle representations without recomputing the skipped decoder layers. Across three referring‑expression grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the best grounding performance across all eight splits and the highest average multimodal retention among evaluated efficient methods at 64‑, 128‑, and 192‑token budgets. At a 64‑token budget, CatchUp processes 88.9% fewer active visual tokens per post‑routing decoder interval, retains 92.17% of dense‑model multimodal performance, and reduces end‑to‑end latency by 8.0%. Code is available at https://github.com/pej0918/CatchUp

PaperId: 653, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23297.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Ching-Heng Cheng, Chia-Ming Lee, Ming-Ching Chang, Xin Li, Yu-Lun Liu, Chih-Chung Hsu
Title: FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds
Abstract:
Single‑image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. It is inherently interactive: users try many focal points and blur strengths on one image, so each edit should be fast and change only the blur. Recent generative methods, however, rerun large diffusion models for every edit. We observe that the two sub‑problems differ in kind: recovering the all‑in‑focus image is ill‑posed and needs a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders every edit with a lightweight network. To address the ill‑posed restoration, a one‑step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. For precise control, the renderer is conditioned on an explicit defocus map and uses defocus‑bias attention, which lets pixels at similar defocus share information without interference from pixels at other depths; in‑focus content stays unchanged, and editing the map yields tilt‑shift and two focal planes. To further test generalization to unseen cameras, we collect 3CReal, a three‑camera benchmark of 89 pairs. FlashReFocus achieves the best perceptual fidelity for zero‑shot bokeh rendering on EBB! and 3CReal, refocuses 148.3x faster than GenRefocus, and takes about half a second per further edit, 462x faster.

PaperId: 654, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23274.pdf   GitHub
Authors:TianLiang Ma, Ting Ma, ZhongYuan Ma
Title: LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300: Prediction-Guided Action Selection with a Graph Dynamics Model
Abstract:
We present LY‑GWM‑RoboCasa‑Human300, a policy that combines a Human300‑fine‑tuned GR00T‑N1.5 action generator, an action‑conditioned graph dynamics model, and a learned binary state‑reward scorer. At inference, the policy samples four action chunks, predicts the future latent features and robot state for each, and executes the candidate with the highest predicted‑state reward logit. Predictions therefore influence the actions sent to the environment. The evaluated system uses a 16‑step prediction horizon and keeps all three components frozen during evaluation. In the local evaluation on 50 RoboCasa 1.0.1 tasks in the pretrain kitchen split, with 50 episodes per task, the system records 207/2,500 successes (8.28%), compared with 181/2,500 (7.24%) in the historical self‑trained GR00T‑N1.5 baseline. The observed difference is 26 successes, or 1.04 percentage points. The atomic group improves from 141/900 to 150/900. Separately, the RoboCasa maintainers re‑evaluated the submission and reported 354/1,500 successes (23.6%) across 50 tasks, with leaderboard rates of 48.3%, 16.3%, and 3.1% for Atomic‑Seen, Composite‑Seen, and Composite‑Unseen. The local and official results are reported separately; their difference is not attributed to a model improvement. Recorded local audits identify 212,700 changed environment‑input chunks, including 28,223 in atomic tasks. We describe the actual training stages, implemented inference mechanism, evaluation provenance, and public reproduction entrypoints. These results document an active prediction‑and‑selection system and a positive historical difference.

PaperId: 655, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23271.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Guodong Du, Wanyu Lin
Title: NestedVLA: Learning to Consolidate and Generate Skills for Vision-Language-Action Models
Abstract:
Vision‑language‑action (VLA) models can learn a wide range of robotic skills, but combining separately trained skills remains challenging. The original training data may be unavailable for joint retraining, while directly merging model weights can cause interference. We propose NestedVLA, which consolidates independently fine‑tuned VLA policies without access to their original training data. Instead of merging all updates into one checkpoint, a hypernetwork embedded in the VLA generates action‑expert weight updates for a selected task. Each task's compressed vision‑language model update is stored separately, and both updates are added to a frozen base VLA to instantiate the corresponding policy. We evaluate NestedVLA by consolidating three policies fine‑tuned with reinforcement learning on MetaWorld, ManiSkill, and CALVIN. It achieves 66.7% average success, improving on the strongest model‑merging baseline by 41.1 percentage points. It performs within 1 percentage point of per‑task fine‑tuning on ManiSkill and substantially narrows the gap on CALVIN. In this three‑policy setting, total storage is 1.5x that of a single full checkpoint. Code is available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026‑NestedVLA.

PaperId: 656, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23269.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yifan Li, Bowen Qin, Kun Zhou, Haochen Zhao, Zikang Liu, Zheng Li, Minsheng Hao, Yuhao Cheng, Haosheng Zou, Jeff Chen, Wayne Xin Zhao
Title: Agentic Image Generation in the Wild
Abstract:
Agentic image generation pairs an image generator with a search agent that retrieves references from the web, extending generation beyond the generator's training data. Real‑world requests, however, often concern entities that appeared only days ago. We call this setting Image Generation in the Wild. In this setting, the web offers limited visual evidence, search results are crowded with easily confused entities, and the target is rarely shown on its own. To study this setting, we build an automated pipeline that synthesizes prompts from recent headlines and keeps only those whose real search results are highly confusing, yielding requests that are hard to solve yet natural to ask. With it, we construct Savanna, a benchmark of 500 prompts across 16 subcategories. On Savanna, even harness frameworks built on the frontier models retrieve a correct reference for only about half of the prompts. We then propose Locate‑Corroborate‑Isolate, a paradigm in which the agent first pins down the target's identity through text search, then verifies candidate images against multiple sources, and finally crops a clean reference for the generator. Trained on 15K trajectories that follow this paradigm, Ranger‑8B achieves a search score of 67.2, outperforming harnesses equipped with frontier models. It also achieves the best generation quality with every generator we test, and surpasses prior agentic methods on other image generation benchmarks. We release the pipeline, benchmark, training data and model at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Agentic‑ImageGen‑Wild.

PaperId: 657, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23263.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiwan Hur, Dong-Jae Lee, Dongyeun Lee, Gyojin Han, Junmo Kim
Title: SCALE: Improving Guidance-Free Visual Generation via Self-Contrastive Alignment for Likelihood Estimation
Abstract:
Classifier‑free guidance (CFG) is essential for improving sample quality in visual generation, but it incurs substantial sampling overhead. Existing guidance‑free approaches halve this cost by approximating the CFG with a single model inference, but their performance is bounded by the CFG and inherits its limitations. In this paper, we propose self‑contrastive guidance (SCG), which contrasts the model's prediction on real and self‑generated samples to obtain a direct, model‑based signal that pushes generation toward the true data manifold. Integrating SCG into the standard likelihood objective via reparameterization yields Self‑Contrastive Alignment for Likelihood Estimation (SCALE), a guidance‑free training framework that produces SCG‑enhanced predictions in a single forward pass. Across class‑conditional and text‑to‑image generation on diffusion and autoregressive models, SCALE consistently outperforms CFG‑mimicking guidance‑free baselines and improves further when combined with DPO, demonstrating that the self‑contrastive signal yields gains complementary to both CFG and preference‑based fine‑tuning.

PaperId: 658, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23262.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fabian Schmidt, Karol Fedurko, Markus Enzweiler, Abhinav Valada
Title: Expand-and-Prune: Test-Time Candidate-Space Adaptation for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
Abstract:
Candidate‑based end‑to‑end driving planners reason over a finite set of trajectory hypotheses. However, for sparse planners, a limited candidate set may provide insufficient support for scene‑relevant maneuvers, while fixed downstream candidate budgets do not account for prediction uncertainty. To address these challenges, we introduce Expand‑and‑Prune, a test‑time framework that jointly adapts candidate support and capacity without updating learned parameters. The framework expands the native candidate set using semantic driving intent and temporally propagated predictions and then uses uncertainty in intermediate trajectory scores to adaptively prune the resulting candidates. Across four heterogeneous candidate‑based planners and four benchmarks, Expand‑and‑Prune consistently improves planning performance. It achieves state‑of‑the‑art results on LangAuto, increasing the Driving Score from 68.2 to 75.9, while providing further improvement on Bench2Drive, Fail2Drive, and NAVSIMv2, with particularly strong improvements in out‑of‑distribution scenarios. Moreover, in its full instantiation, 72.5% of selected trajectories originate from the newly introduced intent‑guided or temporal candidates, confirming that candidate‑space expansion provides useful hypotheses beyond those generated natively by the planner. The code is available at https://github.com/iis‑esslingen/Expand‑and‑Prune.

PaperId: 659, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23257.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Uriel Dolev, Idan Schwartz, Yoav Goldberg
Title: Reasoning Models Can Control Their Chains of Thought When They Tell Themselves To
Abstract:
Chain‑of‑thought (CoT) controllability, the ability of reasoning models to control properties of their CoT, is consequential for both their usefulness and reliable oversight. Recent work evaluates this capability by measuring whether models follow CoT constraints given in the user prompt, and reports very low controllability across models. We argue that this low controllability may not reflect an inherent inability of reasoning models to control their CoT, but instead result from naively specifying constraints in the user prompt. To test this, we introduce Self‑Instructed CoT Controllability: a complementary evaluation that places the constraint as a self‑instruction inside the model's CoT and measures its ability to follow it. We show that, under self‑instruction, models achieve significantly higher controllability than with standard user instructions. Even a generic reminder to follow the user's constraint substantially improves controllability. Moreover, effective self‑instructions can be bootstrapped into the reasoning through a simple instruction in the user prompt, enabling improved control even without access to the reasoning channel. Finally, using self‑instruction, we demonstrate in a realistic monitoring setup that CoT controllability can be leveraged for monitor evasion, posing a risk to CoT monitorability.

PaperId: 660, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23249.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Md Sabbir Hossen, Anichur Rahman, Pabon Shaha, Airin Afroj Aishi, Andrew H. Sung, Md Shohel Rana
Title: Who Pays for Efficient Inference? Confidence-Based Small-to-Large LLM Routing Across Tasks and Languages
Abstract:
Small‑to‑large language model routing can reduce inference cost by escalating difficult inputs while retaining easier ones on a smaller model. Its success, however, depends on identifying examples that benefit from escalation, and the reliability of confidence across multilingual tasks remains unclear. We present a systematic evaluation of confidence‑based routing across three model families, four languages, and three task types, covering 72 model, dataset, language, and scale configurations and 42,288 predictions. We compare global confidence routing with random routing, equal‑quota confidence routing, and an oracle upper bound. Confidence identifies beneficial escalations on the Belebele reading comprehension and SIB‑200 topic classification datasets, with mean correction‑detection AUCs of 0.612 and 0.705. At 50% escalation, it improves over random routing by 1.40‑‑4.67 percentage points on Belebele and 2.54‑‑5.63 points on SIB‑200. In contrast, the mean AUC on the MMLU‑ProX‑Lite knowledge and reasoning dataset is only 0.510, and routing provides no consistent improvement over random selection because small models often remain highly confident while incorrect. Global confidence routing also creates language escalation gaps up to 30.33 percentage points, whereas equal‑quota routing removes this disparity with little aggregate accuracy cost. These results show that confidence routing is task‑dependent and can allocate computation unevenly across languages. Code is available at https://github.com/sabbir5622r/multilingual‑llm‑routing

PaperId: 661, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23237.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wangze Xu, Chu Zhou, Mae Yamaguchi, Linrui Dai, I-Chao Shen, Takashi Ijiri, Imari Sato
Title: X-Splat: Unified Gaussian Splatting for Joint RGB and X-ray 3D Reconstruction
Abstract:
Jointly reconstructing RGB and X‑ray provides new insights by connecting external appearance with internal structure, enabling a more complete understanding of real‑world objects than single modality. Yet existing methods train separate models per modality and suffer from redundant geometry, alignment artifacts, and loose coupling that limits cross‑modal insight discovery. We propose a unified representation in which all Gaussian primitives share a single set of geometric parameters, with only surface‑proximal primitives additionally carrying appearance attributes. We perform cross‑modal registration through clean multi‑view stereo and X‑ray geometric proxies instead of aligning two sets of optimized Gaussians, improving alignment stability. We then jointly optimize the unified representation via supervision from both modalities, complemented by a surface‑depth consistency loss derived from X‑ray geometry to guide RGB reconstruction. Experiments on the InsideOut dataset and our Flower & Insect dataset show that our framework achieves more robust cross‑modal alignment, higher RGB rendering quality without compromising X‑ray reconstruction, and a more compact representation than maintaining two independent geometries.

PaperId: 662, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23230.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haonan Han, Yukang Lin, Minliang Lin, Haoxian Tan, Jun-Yan He, Rui Yang, Zhi-Qi Cheng, Jie Hu, Guanglu Wan, Xiu Li
Title: RAP: A Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars
Abstract:
Making a conference poster is visual coding in miniature: an entire paper must be compressed onto a single page, which exercises summarization, visual design, and code implementation at once, using nothing beyond the paper itself. Yet benchmarks for this task in the context of visual coding remain scarce: existing resources are small and annotated only with layout boxes, so evaluation must fall back on VLM‑as‑judge or human checklists rather than objective render‑and‑compare, and the generation methods they support design layouts from scratch, leaving human‑crafted posters unusable as either a retrievable design library or as verified supervision. We introduce RAP (Reconstruct A Poster), a dataset and benchmark for paper‑to‑poster generation as a visual coding task. RAP contains 25K+ verified paper‑poster pairs from various machine learning conferences held between 2022 and 2026, annotated with a three‑level content taxonomy, plus a held‑out benchmark of 150 test papers each paired with its human poster. A fully automated derendering pipeline turns each poster into styled HTML/CSS of typed, refillable slots, so every sample is a paper‑poster‑markup triplet verifiable by rendering against the source poster. The corpus serves both inference and training: PosterRAG, a training‑free multi‑agent pipeline, retrieves an exemplar and refills its slots without touching layout or styling, while an SFT+RL recipe trains a dedicated model from the same triplets. An online demo is available at https://reconstruct‑a‑poster.github.io/.

PaperId: 663, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23225.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuki Otsuka, Daisuke Oba, Naoaki Okazaki
Title: ReLaDrift: Recurrent Language Generation via Drifting for Test-Time Scaling
Abstract:
Drifting Models generate a sample with a single function evaluation, making them attractive for fast parallel language generation, but their one‑step formulation does not support iterative refinement. We propose Recurrent Language Generation via Drifting (ReLaDrift), which uses a shared Drifting Model to generate an initial draft from noise and iteratively refine it in a continuous latent space. We train this recurrence by sampling the number of rounds and applying the drifting loss only at the final round, stopping gradients through preceding rounds so that only one round requires backpropagation. Unlike the one‑step Drifting Model, whose accuracy does not improve when iterated, ReLaDrift enables a trade‑off between test‑time computation and generation quality, as diffusion and flow language models do. On Sudoku Hard and GSM8K, it achieves competitive or superior performance compared with these iterative‑generation approaches across a range of inference budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yuki‑Ots/ReLaDrift

PaperId: 664, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23186.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaoyong Li, Haolong Li, Dongliang Xu, Haoyu Li, Yifan Wang, Jingyuan Shi, Yanghua Wang, Yanbin Sun, Shidong Pan, Yue Yao
Title: Code Skill Server: A Large-Scale Search Engine for Code Generation Skills
Abstract:
Agent skills have proven to be an effective technique for improving agent ability on specific tasks, including software engineering, natural science, and mathematics. During such a process, using agent skills often involves manually discovering and organizing skills from heterogeneous sources, while existing skill retrieval methods mainly focus on selecting relevant skills from established skill libraries. However, with the rapidly increasing number and variety of reusable agent skills, manually searching for relevant skills across heterogeneous sources is becoming impractical at scale. In this paper, we introduce the Code Skill Server (CSS), a large‑scale search engine for finding the most useful code generation skills for a target task. CSS consists of a skill server that incrementally collects and indexes publicly available code generation skills from multiple sources, with 993 skills included in the corpus used in this work. Extensive experiments across different retrieval methods and code generation benchmarks show that the best CSS configuration improves Pass@1 by up to 13.91% and consistently improves all evaluated models by at least 4.21% in the cross‑model evaluation. These results demonstrate that CSS can effectively search for and serve relevant skills, improving code generation quality and enhancing models' code generation capabilities. Code and the CSS‑993 corpus are available at https://github.com/haoyuli‑sdu/CodeSkillServer.

PaperId: 665, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23170.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qiang Yan
Title: Chinese Decision: A Family of Language Models for Single-Pass Probabilistic Decision-Making
Abstract:
Many language‑based applications need a probability distribution over a small set of decisions rather than an open‑ended response. We present Chinese Decision, a family of Chinese‑language decision models that adapts pretrained causal language models to this interface. Each question is compiled into a shared instruction‑and‑candidate prompt; a single forward pass reads the final‑position logits of the candidate letters and normalizes them over the valid options, without autoregressive answer generation. The interface covers Boolean judgments, categorical choices, and ordinal scores. We report three completed members built on Qwen3.5 0.8B, 2B, and 4B backbones, each trained for one epoch on the same 13.048 million decisions and released with a validation‑fitted temperature and a Q8_0 quantization. On the full 307,900‑decision CJ‑Bench, the 4B model reaches 85.97% overall accuracy, 75.69% general‑domain accuracy, and 84.00% average accuracy across medicine, law, and finance with a single checkpoint, above every reported baseline in each domain, at 1.00% expected calibration error. Between the 2B and 4B members, which share data, objective, and minimum batch, parent‑clustered paired bootstrap intervals show gains in all four domains, largest in the two low‑resource domains (+8.5 and +7.1 points), whereas the 2B gain over 0.8B in law is not statistically resolved. Analyses of the stored predictions further show that a single global temperature lowers pooled calibration error while worsening some domains, that larger members rank their own errors better for selective prediction, and that merging and quantization each change 0.4‑1.1% of top‑1 predictions while leaving aggregate metrics nearly unchanged. All comparisons rest on single training runs and imported baselines.

PaperId: 666, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23149.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Semra Guven, Tobias Gårdhus, Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen, Anna Rogers, Hjalmar Bang Carlsen
Title: Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
Abstract:
Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI‑interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI‑led and human‑led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non‑expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI‑interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per‑question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple‑testing correction; only AI‑condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on‑topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open‑weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI‑interviewing for large‑N qualitative data collection.

PaperId: 667, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23134.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Donghoon Kim, Seunghyuk Oh, Kevin Galim, Minseo Kim, Minjae Lee, Younghyun Kim, Wooseok Seo, Hyung Il Koo, Wonjun Kang
Title: MetaCurate: Evolving Curation Filters for High-Quality Agentic Coding Data
Abstract:
Supervised fine‑tuning on agent trajectories is an effective way to improve coding agents, but selecting useful training examples requires more than identifying successful runs. A resolved patch may follow inefficient reasoning or unnecessary tool use, while a failed run may still contain useful intermediate steps. Training pipelines therefore rely on rules and qualitative assessments to filter trajectories, yet designing these filters typically requires substantial human expertise, and validating improvements through repeated training and evaluation is expensive. We introduce MetaCurate, a training‑free framework that evolves executable trajectory curation filters using pairwise LLM judgments. Disagreements between the filter's rankings and the judge's preferences provide targeted feedback for jointly revising its rules, rubric, and aggregation policy. The resulting filter scores trajectories independently, so pairwise comparisons are required only during search. Starting from a blank filter, MetaCurate autonomously discovers a curation strategy that achieves competitive downstream performance without task‑specific handwritten criteria. We validate downstream utility through controlled SFT experiments on our uncurated trajectory pool and the Nemotron v3 SWE dataset, with random selection and hand‑authored filtering as baselines. In our experiments, MetaCurate achieves the highest mean SWE‑Verified score among the compared methods, including hand‑authored rule‑based filtering and a training‑loop baseline whose search costs 3.5x as much.

PaperId: 668, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23128.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Junyang Shu, Bingqing Wei, Jishuo Li, Zheqi He, Yongtao Wang
Title: SCOPE: Selective Certification of Program Edits for Embodied Heuristic Learning
Abstract:
Embodied heuristic learning must balance strategic adaptation with the preservation of previously successful behavior. Local repairs may leave structural failures unresolved, whereas broader revisions can introduce regressions that are costly to detect through repeated environment interaction. We introduce SCOPE (Selective Certification Of Program Edits), which uses failed and successful executions as complementary evidence for program revision. Frontier‑guided program search annotates a shared diagnostic graph with execution evidence to distinguish supported progress from unresolved checks. Selective behavioral certification uses stateful API replay to restore recorded responses and mutations, checking whether edits preserve selected historical successes. Diagnosis and certification feedback, supplemented by sparse environment diagnostics, guide consecutive repairs across configurations. SCOPE outperforms the strongest baseline in both simulation and real‑world tasks. On LIBERO‑PRO and Robosuite, it achieves mean success rates of 80.66% and 84.48%, with respective gains of 6.51 and 3.48 percentage points. Our code is available at https://github.com/VDIGPKU/SCOPE.

PaperId: 669, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23127.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Liyun Yan, Haoyang Li, Yang Zhang, Jialing Zhu, Zhanxiang Cao, Zihao Zhou, Keqi Zhu, Yizhi Chen, Huang Chuxuan, Shengcheng Fu, Zhong Jiangwei, Qiao Sun, Chen Zhang, Yue Gao
Title: BeJEPA: A Goal-Conditioned Humanoid Behavior World Model via Unsupervised RL
Abstract:
Humanoid control requires coordinating whole‑body posture with position and heading in the world frame. Mainstream controllers imitate trajectories in the root frame, but struggle to regain the target world pose after displacement. We introduce BeJEPA, a goal‑conditioned Behavior World Model learned through unsupervised reinforcement learning from human motion priors and robot interaction. BeJEPA learns a shared representation of body configuration and world placement through a joint‑embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). A Dynamic Predictor predicts the next state embedding under an action, while a Successor Predictor summarizes a goal‑conditioned policy's expected discounted future state embeddings in a single vector. During joint training, Dynamic grounds the initial representation in observed physical transitions, while Successor increasingly organizes it around long‑term behavior. Their composition guides policy improvement through one physical prediction and one behavioral summary, without long imagined rollouts. In 20‑second motion‑tracking experiments, BeJEPA with online action refinement using Dynamic outperforms all evaluated baselines in global body‑position error, reducing it on AMASS by 61.7% relative to BFM‑Zero with world‑pose inputs and 58.7% relative to SONIC. Physical deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates joint attainment of posture, world position, and heading goals, recovery from the ground, and closed‑loop return after disturbances and goal changes. Project page: https://ylyem9x.github.io/BeJEPA‑project.

PaperId: 670, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23104.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zijun Dou, Zhen Yang, Xijun Liu, Dongzhuoran Zhou, Aohan Zeng, Jie Tang
Title: WebCoder: Scaling General Frontend Development with Artifact-Grounded Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
Real‑world frontend development requires agents to compose reproduction, generation, modification, and repair over an evolving application state. Learning a general policy for this process requires translating heterogeneous execution feedback into task‑aligned rewards and effective credit assignment across long sequences of interdependent actions. We introduce WebCoder, a general frontend development agent trained with artifact‑grounded agentic reinforcement learning. Our key idea is to assess diverse development activities through their effects on a shared executable artifact and its satisfaction of task requirements. We build Webdev‑World, an executable environment that integrates code editing, application execution, browser inspection, and on‑demand skills while preserving project state across interactions. An independent verifier evaluates the final application against task requirements to provide terminal rewards, while changes in intermediate artifact progress redistribute the resulting rollout advantage across development segments. Context compaction and message‑tree sample construction support training on trajectories beyond a single context window while avoiding repeated loss computation on shared generated history. We further introduce Webdev‑Bench to evaluate composed development requirements within a single project. On Webdev‑Bench, WebCoder‑27B raises requirement satisfaction from 64.8 for its Qwen3.8‑27B base model to 72.8, exceeding Claude‑Opus‑4.8 (65.1) and GPT‑5.4 (59.6); on Vision2Web, it improves the average visual and functional score from 41.1 to 62.4, on par with Claude‑Opus‑4.8. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of artifact‑grounded credit assignment and long‑horizon training.

PaperId: 671, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23036.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Benhao Huang, Chufan Shi, Junlin Chen, Shicheng Wen, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric Xing, Xuezhe Ma
Title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part I: Topology, Input Injection, Recurrent-State Design
Abstract:
Looped language models reuse physical Transformer blocks across logical depth, but established architectures entangle recurrence placement, input injection, and recurrent state organization. We isolate these axes in models trained from scratch at matched parameter scale, logical depth, and token budgets, and then test whether the resulting design principles transfer to resident‑ and active‑parameter‑matched Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) models. The prelude‑recurrent block‑coda sandwich architecture consistently improves performance on context extraction and reasoning‑intensive tasks. Input injection primarily enhances knowledge retrieval and context utilization, whereas random initialization and separate H/L recurrent states provide mixed or negative returns. Taken together, these results favor the Huginn‑style design: at the 730M‑parameter and 336B‑token scale, the complete Huginn architecture outperforms Ouro across all ten benchmarks. The advantages of Huginn over Ouro transfer to MoE models. At the 8BA0.8B (32BA3B when unrolled) scale trained on 500B tokens, Huginn outperforms Ouro on nearly all benchmarks spanning knowledge, reasoning, and coding, while also exhibiting more balanced expert routing. Under matched training and inference FLOPs, the Huginn‑style model uses 75% fewer resident parameters than a 112‑layer feedforward MoE baseline. Despite its smaller physical parameters, it outperforms the feedforward baseline on DROP and GSM8K, matches it on MATH500, and remains competitive on the other benchmarks.

PaperId: 672, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23030.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuanwei Wu, Lingdong Huang, Yunlong Mao, Kanye Ye Wang, Jingyu Hua, Sheng Zhong
Title: ECHO: Replacing the Compliance Proxy with Response Harmfulness in Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attack
Abstract:
Despite extensive safety alignment, large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing optimization‑based attacks share a single objective: maximize a token‑level proxy of victim compliance‑‑‑such as the likelihood of an affirmative prefix‑‑‑computed on the prompt rather than the decoded reply. This proxy cannot distinguish a cautious hedge from a fully actionable harmful answer, leaving the search blind to what the model actually says. We propose ECHO (Evaluation‑Conditioned Harmfulness Optimization), which replaces the compliance proxy with response‑level, continuous harmfulness scores from HarmSig, a 1.7B regressor grounded in actual harmful capability. ECHO couples HarmSig with five word‑level perturbation operators and Keyword‑Anchored Beam Search with global top‑m memory, under a strict black‑box threat model. Across five open‑weight victims on AdvBench, ECHO achieves up to 0.898 StrongREJECT mean score and 89.23% HarmBench success. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/STANWYW/echo.

PaperId: 673, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23012.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Chulhoon Yoon, Kyungri Park, Jinyeong Yun, Daeyun Jeong, Sukmin Yun, Woohwan Jung
Title: Adaptation of Computer Use Agents to New Software with User Manuals
Abstract:
Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have significantly improved the ability to operate real‑world software through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) using visual observations and natural language instructions. However, maintaining strong performance on unseen applications remains challenging, as practical tasks often require long‑horizon procedural knowledge and application‑specific operation patterns. In addition, constructing executable tasks and collecting corresponding trajectories for training still heavily rely on human‑annotated data, incurring substantial cost. In this paper, we propose MAGE (Manual‑augmented computer use AGent Execution and learning), a framework that leverages user manuals as a scalable source of procedural knowledge to improve both inference and training. During execution, MAGE retrieves task‑relevant manual content and uses a planner to generate explicit procedural guidance for CUAs. To further account for the discrepancies between manuals and actual GUI environments, such as version differences or user settings, MAGE also adapts the agent policy through environment interaction. During training, MAGE converts manuals into executable task‑plan pairs and uses the plans to guide environment rollouts toward task‑relevant states; the resulting trajectories are then used to optimize the policy without human‑authored demonstrations. This unified design enables effective utilization of manuals for both task execution and training, reducing reliance on human‑authored training data. Experimental results across six applications demonstrate improvements in task success rates over strong baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of manual‑guided planning and policy adaptation in new software environments. We provide the code and reproduction scripts at https://github.com/ku‑autoai/MAGE.

PaperId: 674, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22992.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qi Si, Xuyang Liu, Penglei Wang, Shuo Su, Limei Han, Mengzhu Li, Xin Guo, Yuan Qi, Yuan Cheng
Title: GOLD: Geometric Optimized Latent Diffusion for Structure-Aware RNA Inverse Folding
Abstract:
Designing RNA sequences that fold into specific 3D structures is a fundamental challenge in therapeutics. Current RNA inverse folding methods typically condition on 3D backbone coordinates but the generation is limited to 1D discrete sequences. This ignores the continuous side‑chain orientations, which are essential for overall structural stability. To address this issue, we explicitly introduce side‑chain geometry into the RNA generative process. Unlike co‑design frameworks that diffuse across separate raw spaces, we propose Geometric Optimized Latent Diffusion (GOLD), which project sequence and structure into a unified latent manifold. GOLD employs a novel GeoVAE to elegantly integrate discrete RNA sequences with continuous side‑chain angles. By mapping these modalities into a single, smooth latent manifold, GOLD naturally facilitates a synergistic co‑diffusion process. To enhance structural validity, we further introduce a training‑free, gradient‑guided sampling mechanism. By decoding the generated sequence probabilities and side‑chain geometries into structures during the sampling process, we compute analytical gradients from physical constraints. This dynamic feedback actively guides the generated sequence to a physically stable state. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of GOLD, achieving state‑of‑the‑art performance across sequence recovery, secondary structure validity, and 3D foldability metrics. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/darkflash03/GOLD.

PaperId: 675, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22990.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haoming Li, Defu Cao, Xu Hu, Yingtao Luo, Yiyang Wang, Xianghe Xu, Jiashu He, Wanting Jiang, Yifan Zhang, Yunhan Zhao, Siyang Wu, Chen Yang, Haixin Wang, Zheyuan Deng, Taoran Li, Jingwen Zhang, Zhejian Peng, Shushu Liang, Yue Zhao, Bingzhe Li, Feng Chen, Yifan Wang, Jintao Huang, Yijun Wang, Yuexing Hao, Xiaomin Li
Title: PersonaCUABench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents Serving Diverse Personas
Abstract:
Computer‑use agents (CUAs) are commonly evaluated against fixed task specifications, but users may omit requirements, add constraints, or require approval before consequential actions. Completing the benchmark instruction does not guarantee serving the person who asked. We introduce PersonaCUABench, which holds 74 tasks across 11 domains fixed and varies only who asks. A persona agent, playing one of 44 personas in four groups, rewrites each instruction in that user's own words and answers the CUA's questions, while the CUA sees only the dialogue, never the profile or the original instruction. Across nine backbones (3,330 runs), mean task completion falls by 36% relative to the original requests. The losses have two sources: in 59.9% of cells that lose points, the agent engages with what the user asked for and still gets it wrong, and 11.2% are stops the user requested that the checker scores as failures. Even when a persona request is fully completed, the user gives the top satisfaction rating in only 62.7% of cells, against 84.1% for the original requests. CUAs should therefore be evaluated not only on task completion but also on whether they meet the requirements and constraints users express. Code: https://github.com/MatrAIx‑ai/PersonaCUABench. Project page: https://matraix.ai/research/persona‑cua.html

PaperId: 676, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22982.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yiyang Lin, Chenhui Wang, Tianliang Yao, Pengli Zhu, Shuaibo Li, Zijun Sun, Yiming Deng, Yixuan Yuan
Title: UniField++: A Unified Agentic Framework with Loop Reasoning for MRI Field-Strength Enhancement
Abstract:
MRI field‑strength enhancement seeks to combine the accessibility of low‑field scanners with the image quality of high‑field scanners. Yet, existing methods remain prone to anatomical hallucinations, as uniform processing leaves difficult brain regions insufficiently examined and scarce paired data limit their learning of how tissue contrast and anatomical visibility change across field strengths. To address these challenges, we propose UniField++, a two‑agent framework that unifies enhancement tasks across multiple field‑strength transitions, including 64mT‑to‑3T and 3T‑to‑7T. Unified learning allows both the VLM‑based planner and the flow‑matching‑based enhancer to draw on field‑dependent image characteristics observed across tasks, rather than relying on a single transition. Trained with radiologists' annotations of hallucination‑prone regions and corresponding correction plans, the planner predicts regional risk and formulates targeted restoration strategies. Guided by these plans, the enhancer performs loop reasoning along the flow‑matching trajectory, repeatedly processing high‑risk regions for additional refinement. Together, cross‑transition learning and risk‑guided refinement support anatomically faithful enhancement across field strengths. Across the evaluated tasks, UniField++ improves PSNR by an average of 2.74 dB and SSIM by 14.05 percentage points over comparison methods, with corresponding gains of 3.97 dB and 13.92 percentage points over the ablation baseline. It also maintains enhancement quality on an external cohort with an unseen field strength and improves downstream whole‑brain segmentation Macro Dice by an average of 0.1457 over the original low‑field images. Code is available at https://github.com/CUHK‑AIM‑Group/UniField_plusplus.

PaperId: 677, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22973.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiayuan Wang, Tongyao Pang
Title: DiffusionRVGE: Reinforcement Learning via Regression-Based Value Gradient Estimation
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning improves diffusion models using rewards on generated images, but repeated denoising and gradient estimation make training expensive. We introduce \method, an efficient method that constructs useful update directions by regressing centered rewards on centered final denoised images. It requires neither reward derivatives nor adjoint backpropagation through the sampling trajectory. A unified first‑variation formulation identifies the value‑gradient target with or without a trajectory‑KL penalty. A population analysis under Gaussian noising explains the regression geometry, while a subspace analysis motivates clean‑image coordinates. The implementation adapts rollout bandwidth and query weights to reward continuity: local rollouts suit smooth rewards, whereas broader groups provide informative contrasts for discrete rewards. Trained jointly on five rewards, one SD3.5‑Medium model matches or exceeds DiffusionNFT's joint model on seven of eight metrics, reaching GenEval 0.94, OCR 0.92, and PickScore 23.82 at about one fifth of its estimated training compute. In single‑reward training, \method reaches matched reward thresholds 2.1‑‑6.7× faster than reproduced DiffusionNFT on identical hardware. Ablations support the clean‑image estimator, direct direction transfer, and reward‑dependent rollout choices. Code is available at https://github.com/jy‑wang‑tsinghua/DIFFUSIONRVGE.

PaperId: 678, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22962.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Byunghoo Park, Jayeon Yi, Minje Kim
Title: Rethinking Magnitude Compression in Spectral Losses for DDSP Parameter Estimation
Abstract:
Spectral losses for differentiable digital signal processing (DDSP) commonly compress magnitudes, for example by using log‑magnitude terms. Such compression mimics human perception, but whether it helps the optimization is less clear, and is usually found only by comparing trained models. In this work, we show that whether compression helps depends on the system's informative region: the region of its dynamic range that carries the information pointing toward the target. To indicate where this region lies without having to train, we introduce concordance, which measures how well a loss orders candidate parameter settings by their distance from the target. We then compare uncompressed, compressed, and combined losses by fitting a modal plate reverb and a subtractive synthesizer model to target sounds. A third system, selected for its low‑energy informative region, tests the relationship in the opposite direction. In every system, the loss that matches the informative region performs best: the uncompressed one where the region lies at high energies, and the compressed one where it lies low. Surprisingly, the common combination of both log‑magnitude and linear‑magnitude terms performs best in none of the systems. Code and audio examples are available at https://github.com/superstem000/compression‑analysis

PaperId: 679, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22959.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haoming Li, Dingyi Kang, Xu Hu, Jinxin Yang, Zhu Xu, Chenru Wang, Yi Ge, Miao Yin, Guanpeng Li, Feng Chen, Bingzhe Li
Title: SAFE-Mem: Secure Agentic Memory with Fine-Grained Authority and Governance-Aware Retrieval
Abstract:
Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on persistent memory to support long‑term reasoning and personalized interactions. However, information collected from external sources can introduce security risks when untrusted claims (i.e., atomic statements) are later treated as authorized preferences, policies, or permissions. Existing defenses typically rely on content‑based filtering or coarse‑grained provenance tracking, which either fail to prevent unauthorized memory use or block legitimate information, sacrificing memory utility. To address these limitations, we propose SAFE‑Mem, a fine‑grained memory governance framework that improves security while preserving legitimate memory use. First, SAFE‑Mem annotates each claim with three governance labels (i.e., kind, authority, and scope) to capture its provenance and permitted use. Second, governance‑aware retrieval matches query requirements with claim permissions to block unauthorized influence while retaining legitimate information. Third, a governance‑enabled memory graph connects source sentences, claims, and entities to support provenance tracking and efficient retrieval. Across four LLM backbones on MPBench and LoCoMo, SAFE‑Mem attains the lowest attack success among defenses that retain legitimate memory, at least 77% below the strongest of them, and the highest answer accuracy of all evaluated defenses, improving it by up to 15 points. The code is available at https://github.com/LVenum/SAFE‑Mem.

PaperId: 680, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22951.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Khuyen Pham, Tran Nguyen Le, Edoardo Fazzari, Cesare Stefanini
Title: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models
Abstract:
Vision‑language‑action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real‑time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow‑matching VLAs such as π_0.5, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow‑matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual‑language prefix encoder of π_0.5, while replacing its transformer‑based action expert with a compact Mamba‑based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous‑action sequence. To preserve visual‑language conditioning without repeated token‑level cross‑attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision‑language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a 10× smaller action expert and reduces flow‑matching denoising latency by 64.8% on LIBERO and 58.8% in real‑world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by 1.08 percentage points across three independent fine‑tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO‑Plus and real‑world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.

PaperId: 681, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22929.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Meng Wang, Wu Zeng, Mei Li, Chao He
Title: DICL-Qwen3VL: Decoupled Confidence Calibration for Interpretable Workwear Detection
Abstract:
Poor illumination and occlusion obscure clothing cues in indoor work sites, while diverse clothing styles complicate workwear compliance judgments. Although vision‑language models (VLMs) support localization and semantic reasoning, their predictions often lack explicit supporting evidence, and a single confidence score cannot distinguish visual uncertainty from ambiguity in compliance judgments. We propose DICL‑Qwen3VL, a decoupled interpretable VLM that integrates structured workwear detection, evidence generation, and separate visual and reasoning confidence estimates. First, low‑rank adaptation (LoRA) adapts Qwen3‑VL to localize visible upper‑body clothing and identify workwear. Second, decoupled calibration separates visual observations from compliance reasoning and assigns a confidence score to each. Token entropy and sensitivity to image perturbations provide supervision for visual confidence, linking confidence estimation to the generated observations and their dependence on image content. Finally, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) jointly optimizes detection accuracy, output validity, and confidence calibration. Experiments on the company‑collected Indoor Construction Site Workwear Dataset (ICSWD) and the web‑collected Indoor Construction Workwear Dataset (WICWD) yield mAP@50 values of 0.730 and 0.753, respectively, outperforming the evaluated LoRA‑adapted VLM baselines, including Qwen3‑VL. The framework also provides explicit evidence and separate confidence scores to support manual review in industrial safety monitoring. WICWD is publicly available at https://github.com/DaErwen1/WICWD.

PaperId: 682, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22889.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Lijia Liu, Kyohei Atarashi, Jiyi Li, Koh Takeuchi, Shunji Umetani, Hisashi Kashima
Title: NLData2Opt: Benchmarking Parameter Derivation and Prediction for Modeling Optimization Problems from Natural Language and Data
Abstract:
Formulating optimization problems from raw inputs of problem descriptions and data is time‑consuming and costly. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising way to automate this process, existing benchmarks overestimate their capabilities by relying on idealized inputs where all data is relevant and complete. This diverges from reality, where data‑centric reasoning is required to extract, compute, and predict parameters from noisy sources. To address this, we introduce NLData2Opt, a benchmark to evaluate LLMs on the multi‑stage reasoning inherent in practical optimization workflows. NLData2Opt decomposes problems into problem descriptions and data, and requires models to (1) extract relevant parameters from data containing misleading attributes, (2) compute missing parameters derived by transforming existing data attributes, and (3) predict unavailable future values from historical observations. Evaluation results show substantial performance decline relative to existing benchmarks, indicating that benchmark progress does not directly translate to formulation accuracy in practical optimization workflows. NLData2Opt is available at https://github.com/sumarivyn/NLData2Opt.

PaperId: 683, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22885.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Haoming Liu, Junhao Zhu, Shaoyi Zheng, Yuanhe Guo, Jinnuo Liu, Shenji Wan, Hongyi Wen
Title: Learning to Be Guided: Shaping Latent Geometry for Classifier-Free Guidance
Abstract:
Classifier‑free guidance (CFG) is a standard component of conditional diffusion models, and guided generation performance has become the de facto measure of state‑of‑the‑art models. Recent work on latent diffusion models seeks to learn latent spaces that are easier to model with diffusion. However, under CFG, generation additionally depends on how conditions are arranged in the latent space. We study this arrangement under discrete class conditions, termed \emphclass geometry, and investigate what class geometry allows a latent space to work well with CFG. Under a Gaussian class model, we show that shifting variance from intra‑ to inter‑class at fixed total variance makes classes more distinguishable under noise, and derive a noisy posterior objective whose per‑sample descent direction is proportional to the oracle CFG correction. Based on the analysis, we propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a lightweight surrogate for the intractable noisy posterior objective, which applies a cosine prototype classifier to spatially pooled latents. With a controlled training budget (20 epochs for VAE, 80 epochs for DiT), adding PR to an LDM baseline reduces guided gFID on ImageNet from 3.31 to 2.28, surpassing a DINOv3‑aligned VA‑VAE (2.44) with negligible overhead. We further demonstrate that PR generalizes to pseudo‑labels derived from clustering, continuous text‑embedding conditions, and video latents. Together, our findings highlight class geometry as a critical factor in guided generation and take a first step toward CFG‑compatible representation learning. Our project page is available at: https://maps‑research.github.io/cfg‑geometry/.

PaperId: 684, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22874.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zesheng Shi, Xue Li, Chenrui Dai, Jing Li
Title: Identify, Classify, Act: Per-Instruction Controlled Compliance for LLMs over External Data
Abstract:
LLMs over external data face a per‑instruction tension: a single document or tool return often interleaves legitimate directives with adversarial prompt injections, and the model must follow the former while rejecting the latter. Existing defenses suppress or trust all external instructions, collapsing the safety‑utility frontier and forcing a choice between over‑refusal and over‑compliance. We argue the missing capability is per‑instruction credit attribution and formalize it as External‑Data Instruction Classification, an identify‑classify‑act decision over each embedded directive. We propose EDIC, a decomposed reward framework for per‑instruction compliance. A scene‑grounded pipeline injects mixed beneficial and harmful instructions with counterfactual filtering, while a generative judge is initialized by SFT and refined with GRPO to attribute compliance at the instruction level. The judge then produces a reward that separately encourages beneficial compliance and penalizes harmful compliance for RL training. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, EDIC improves both safety and utility over the strongest prior defense, lifting harmful‑rejection by up to 7.7% and Arena‑Hard‑Auto utility by 12.5% on Qwen3‑4B. The code repository is hosted at https://github.com/yingyingxia666/EDIC.

PaperId: 685, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22869.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Bowen Ding, Qixin Wang, Lexing Ruan, Weiyi Lu, Qiwei Ge, Ruishan Fang, Tao Lin
Title: MS-Eval: Benchmarking Sub-Agent Delegation and Orchestration in MCP-Intensive Working Scenarios
Abstract:
LLM agents are increasingly integrated into real‑world works, yet they must handle diverse domain‑specific tools and complex multi‑sub‑task problems that sequential tool invocation resolves inefficiently and with severe context bloat. The Main‑Agent Delegation and Sub‑Agent Execution (MAD‑SAE) paradigm addresses these issues by delegating sub‑tasks to specialized sub‑agents for parallel execution in isolated contexts, but its delegation and orchestration quality remains unquantified. We introduce MS‑Eval, a unified evaluation kit comprising an MCP‑intensive benchmark, a controlled execution harness, tailored delegation and orchestration metrics, and the MSQ index for comprehensive assessment. Evaluating four MAD‑SAE variants and eight frontier models reveals that (1) sub‑agent specialization (Spec) is the best practical practice; (2) open‑source models are largely competitive with few exceptions; and (3) MAD‑SAE generally raises cost with contingent payoff, benefiting most open‑source models in both performance and efficiency while leaving closed‑source models with higher cost and degraded performance. Our case study further traces these gains to better single‑agent solutions, effective context offloading, and genuine sub‑task parallelism, whereas unnecessary or redundant delegation turns the same cost into pure overhead. Codes: https://github.com/LINs‑lab/MS‑Eval

PaperId: 686, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22822.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Noé Mosca, Mohamed Rayan Barhdadi, Muhammad Hamza, Joshua Yeh, Suryodaya Bikram Shahi, Zhiyan Li, Selim-Antoine Lali, Weiyue Li, Hasan Kurban, Erchin Serpedin, Gang Luo, Yue Zhang, Minghan Li, Mengyu Wang
Title: VISTA: A Multimodal Egocentric Benchmark for Goal-Oriented Perception and Assistance to Blind and Low-Vision Users
Abstract:
Blindness and low vision limit many people's ability to complete daily tasks, motivating AI assistants that provide useful guidance. Yet, existing benchmarks do not adequately test whether vision models can provide effective everyday assistance. In particular, i) existing benchmarks primarily rely on visual and textual inputs, with limited support for other modalities that are increasingly available in egocentric wearable devices such as gaze, inertial measurements, spatial trajectories, and others; and ii) existing evaluations emphasize scene understanding and question answering, with limited coverage of goal‑conditioned guidance for blind and low‑vision users across everyday tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce VISTA (Visually Impaired Scene and Task Annotations), a multimodal egocentric benchmark for goal‑oriented assistance for blind and low‑vision users. VISTA contains ～1,000 egocentric recordings captured with Project Aria glasses; each recording provides synchronized sensor streams, six of which serve as model inputs, and three different types of annotation, covering ten task categories (TC), from object localization to hazard detection. We evaluate 14 representative vision‑language models zero‑shot on VISTA and design a lightweight multimodal model baseline that integrates all six modalities. Experimental results show that, although existing models can often describe egocentric scenes, they remain limited in generating goal‑directed assistive guidance. VISTA thus provides a benchmark for evaluating multimodal models that could improve everyday accessibility.

PaperId: 687, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22820.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Louis Robinson
Title: Causal Edit Serialization
Abstract:
Standard autoregressive language models generate text sequentially, but revision requires referring back to tokens in the input context or those already generated. Causal Edit Serialization (CES) is introduced as a framework for expressing such revisions within the same causal token stream. Special pointer tokens are paired with predicted source addresses, allowing insertion, deletion, replacement, copying and movement to be localized explicitly. A lightweight localization head and dual‑index rotary position encoding support both address prediction and conditioning on previously emitted pointers, while retaining a standard causal attention mask. A pretraining procedure combines ordinary language modeling with serialized repairs derived from random corruptions, model‑generated edits and repeated text. Across model scales and editing baselines, CES models demonstrate complete applied edits with modestly higher clean‑text bits per byte than clean autoregressive models. Supervised and reinforcement‑learning post‑training provide a grammatical‑error‑correction proof of concept, producing more beneficial than harmful changes under reference‑blind model judging. Correct repair programs also improve subsequent text prediction while the original context and its cached states are retained. CES provides a common interface for generation and localized revision, with potential extensions to iterative refinement and additional pointer‑addressed transformations.

PaperId: 688, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22810.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zewei Deng, Mohamed Seif, Liyan Xie
Title: Watermarkability: Measuring and Improving Language-Model Compatibility with Logit-Based Watermarks
Abstract:
Language‑model watermarks can help identify model‑generated text, encode provenance information, and detect post‑generation edits. A broad class of logit‑based watermarks increases the logits of a designated token set at each decoding step. Because a base model's native probability mass on this set varies across contexts, models, and watermark rules, the same logit bias can yield different adherence rates and increases in perplexity (PPL). We introduce watermarkability to characterize the compatibility between a model and the token sets requested by a watermark. At a target mass τ, we quantify this property through a watermarkability cost: the expected minimum KL divergence from the base‑model distribution required to assign probability at least τ to the requested set. A lower cost means that the model is more watermarkable for that request distribution. To reduce this cost, we propose a two‑stage method. In the first stage, we train a target‑set‑conditioned low‑rank adapter on unions drawn from a 16‑way vocabulary partition to increase the requested set's probability mass. In the second stage, a closed‑form controller applies the smallest remaining uniform logit bias needed to reach the target mass. We evaluate the method on six watermark schedules using OPT‑125M and Qwen3‑8B. Across the 12 model‑schedule pairs, the pre‑adaptation watermarkability cost correlates with the log‑PPL increase under a near‑hard fixed‑bias baseline (pooled Pearson r=0.929). For every schedule, at least 99.80% of sampled tokens fall in the target set requested at their decoding step. At this reliability, the adapter and controller reduce average per‑schedule prompt‑conditional PPL by 46.3% on OPT‑125M and 5.2% on Qwen3‑8B relative to the fixed‑bias baseline.

PaperId: 689, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22797.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhenwei Tang, Jintao Liu, Di Bai, Xidong Wu, Xinwu Cheng
Title: Reasoning Reranking with Semantic IDs as the Sole Item Representation
Abstract:
Reasoning rerankers write a rationale before ranking a candidate slate, and existing systems read item metadata to do so, even though generative recommenders increasingly represent items as compact Semantic IDs (SIDs). Ranking from SIDs alone has two appeals: SID prompts are far shorter than the matched item text, and although item codes are fixed from content, the backbone learns their token embeddings in part from user‑item interaction sequences, so the tokens can carry behavioral signal that item text lacks. That training targets next‑item generation, and whether it supports ranking a supplied slate from SIDs alone is untested. We build ReRankID, a controlled testbed in which models reason and rank from a history and slate shown only as SIDs, varying item rendering, history length, and slate size one at a time. On this testbed, such models often copy the input order instead of reranking, and readable metadata does not repair the failure. We compare supervised fine‑tuning, rejection‑sampled self‑training, on‑policy distillation, and verifier‑based reinforcement learning as post‑training methods and find that they elicit the missing behavior. The strongest post‑trained model, the 8B model trained with a graded ranking reward, gives the best SID‑only ranking and matches strong text‑reading LLMs whose prompts are about 20x longer. It ranks above random with no history at all, where a caption‑reading reference does not, and it keeps its gains at long histories, where text prompts pass 50k tokens and the caption‑reading reference stops improving. In a paired rationale audit, this model argues trade‑offs better than that reference but describes items less accurately. The common post‑training methods we test thus elicit ranking from SIDs but not faithful item descriptions, which calls for post‑training that improves the reasoning itself, not only the ranking it produces.

PaperId: 690, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22796.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ilia Zaznov
Title: Causal Latent Workspaces for Looped Transformers
Abstract:
