Reusing a Transformer block across depth increases computation without replicating its parameters, but successive passes have no dedicated state through which positions can exchange compact summaries of their causal prefix. We introduce the causal latent workspace Transformer: an anchored, four‑round shared‑depth architecture in which each position writes gated vectors into prefix‑specific latent slots and retrieves a content‑addressed summary before the next shared block application. This path complements causal self‑attention while the original input embedding remains accessible at every round. Across three byte‑level corpora, three seeds, and two matched parameter budgets, the proposed model achieves the best mean held‑out perplexity in five of six settings against five Transformer controls. At 101.71M parameters it leads on WikiText‑103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories, reaching perplexities 2.7820, 2.7843, and 1.6823; these improve upon the strongest non‑workspace control on each corpus by 1.06%, 0.73%, and 1.01%. All nine seed‑labelled comparisons at this budget favor the workspace. At 0.918M parameters it leads on WikiText‑103 and TinyStories, whereas a conditioned loop is stronger on enwik8. Architectural ablations show that adding the workspace improves upon the anchored loop in all six settings and support refreshing its causal summaries at each round. Together, these results identify a causal, content‑addressable prefix workspace as an effective structural augmentation of looped Transformers.

PaperId: 691, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22795.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Lieqi Liu, Rui gao, Jia-Chen Gu, Wenbo Hu, Zhaobin Mo, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar, Wei Wang, Nanyun Peng
Title: STRIDE: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Driving Edge Cases
Abstract:
In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision‑language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object‑centric benchmark for long‑tail, safety‑critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene‑context awareness. It pairs multiple‑choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free‑form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language‑model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open‑weight, and driving‑specialized models, even the best performer, GPT‑6‑Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple‑choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random‑choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety‑critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.

PaperId: 692, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22778.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhongpai Gao, Benjamin Planche, Van Nguyen Nguyen, Meng Zheng, Anwesa Choudhuri, Arun Innanje, Terrence Chen, Ziyan Wu
Title: Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting
Abstract:
N‑dimensional splatting extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with view direction and time to model view‑dependent and dynamic effects. Each primitive is lifted into a joint distribution over position and conditioning variables, then conditionally sliced at each rendering query. N‑DGS and UBS share this step across Gaussian and Beta kernels: recovering the conditional mean, opacity, and covariance requires per‑primitive matrix inversions and regression products in every forward pass. We introduce direct conditional parameterization, replacing this covariance‑derived readout with explicit per‑effect parameters: a Cholesky precision factor for opacity and a factorized query‑to‑position regression operator with learnable per‑dimension coupling. Unrestricted conditional coordinates recover a valid joint covariance; our factorization adds spatial‑scale and coupling priors. Applied to both kernels, the parameterization yields dGS (Gaussian) and dBS (Beta). Across five static and dynamic benchmarks, they match or exceed their covariance‑derived counterparts on quality, with gains up to +1.26 dB in the main MCMC evaluation. Production slicing is 6.9‑7.7 times faster than on‑the‑fly covariance‑derived conditioning; complete‑render profiling gives 1.25‑1.91 times speedups on four trained scenes. Direct conditioning provides a structured, kernel‑agnostic alternative for N‑dimensional splatting. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/dgs/.

PaperId: 693, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22770.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Gabe Schulman, Lucius E. J. Bynum, Yoav Wald
Title: Unit-level aggregation breaks coverage in causal foundation models
Abstract:
Causal foundation models (CFMs) show promising results for treatment‑effect estimation, with unit‑level estimates that are competitive on standard benchmarks. Many causal analyses, however, inform decisions through effects averaged over groups of units, such as the full sample, the treated units, or a subgroup, and for such decisions a CFM is useful only if its credible intervals are calibrated. We examine these intervals and find that their coverage degrades, both in simple synthetic settings and on standard benchmarks. On ACIC 2016, for example, temperature‑calibrated 95% intervals from CausalPFN fall below nominal coverage beyond groups of 30 out of 4802 units, and intervals for the full‑sample average contain the true value in only 20% of datasets. We trace this problem to how these models are trained and how their intervals are formed. They output a predictive distribution for one unit at a time and, at inference time, combine the unit‑level variances as if the errors on different units were independent. We show formally that posterior uncertainty over the data‑generating process makes these errors correlated. As a result, the combined variance is too small by a factor that grows with the size of the group. Empirically, this factor predicts where coverage fails and by how much. We then show that two neural process models, which make joint predictions for a group of units, account for this correlation and substantially improve coverage on synthetic tasks and, as heads on a frozen CausalPFN, on all six benchmarks.

PaperId: 694, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22765.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Nitin Rai, Won Suk Lee, Hongyoung Leon, Heping Zhu
Title: Pedicel-Targeted Strawberry Harvesting via Imitation Learning on a Low-Cost Teleoperated Robotic Arm
Abstract:
Precise pedicel‑targeted grasping in strawberry harvesting remains a critical bottleneck due to the pedicel's small diameter (1.3‑3 mm), color similarity with surrounding foliage, and precise force control required for clean abscission zone detachment. As a market‑grade crop, strawberry aesthetic value makes bruise‑free pedicel detachment essential over direct fruit grasping. Classical approaches struggle to unify vision models, motion planning, and contact manipulation into a robust framework, particularly in occluded canopy environments. Therefore, this work presents a visuomotor imitation learning pipeline for pedicel‑targeted strawberry harvesting that unifies perception, motion planning, and contact manipulation from collecting human teleoperation demonstrations, training an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy with a ResNet‑50 visual backbone, and deploying the learned policy autonomously on a Jetson AGX Orin edge platform at 15 Hz. The trained policy achieved consistent loss convergence from 2.84 to 0.091 over 100K gradient steps on 130 demonstrations. We have also established a reproducible open‑source pipeline with publicly released dataset and model weights for the agricultural robotics community. Full dataset is available at, https://huggingface.co/datasets/nitindominicrai/strawberry_pedicel_grasp_teleoperation and trained policy at, https://huggingface.co/nitindominicrai/act_strawberry_pedicel. To replicate this work, all code, configurations, and deployment instructions are publicly available at, https://github.com/nitin‑dominic/autonomous_strawberry_pedicel_harvesting.

PaperId: 695, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22760.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuanzhe Liu, Bastian Lipka, Avraham Shinnar, Jatin Ganhotra, Yao Ma, Martin Hirzel
Title: Between Spoilers and Guesswork: Avoiding Over-Specification in Coding Benchmarks
Abstract:
Benchmarks drive AI progress, but are hampered by task under‑specification and over‑specification. Task under‑specification causes guesswork, where solutions have to make things up, or worse, resort to contamination or reward hacking. Task over‑specification causes spoilers, where solutions can bypass some of the harder steps the benchmark was supposed to measure. Since future‑looking benchmarks should be difficult, over‑specification reduces a benchmark's shelflife of community adoption. Repository‑level coding benchmarks have helped the field progress but experience unnecessary churn due to both over‑ and under‑specification. For instance, SWE‑bench Pro, FEA‑bench, Doc2Feat‑bench, and Multi‑SWE‑bench all tackle under‑specification by augmenting task statements with hints derived from ground truth. We show that leaking ground‑truth information into the task statement causes over‑specification in some of these benchmarks. We experiment with various specification levels, trying to thread the needle between spoilers and guesswork. Based on these results, we recommend techniques for deriving parsimonious hints. We will release our hints so the community can obtain more reliable signals from popular benchmarks.

PaperId: 696, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22746.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Edrees Al-Edreesi, Ghaleb Al-Gaphari, Muneer Alsurori, Mohammed Edrees, Fouad Al-Hamdani
Title: Cross-Person Identity Change Under Source-Coupled Multi-Human Generation: A Controlled UniPortrait Study
Abstract:
Multi‑human personalization must account for identity changes in people outside the nominal target of a generative operation. We characterize this behavior in UniPortrait, without introducing a new preservation algorithm. Two sequential studies use 119 accepted two‑person baseline scenes and three fixed output seeds, measuring continuous reference‑based facial similarity with InsightFace \buffalo. In Study~1, source‑coupled single‑ID target‑only generation (A1) produces negative mean transitions for both the protected person (‑0.567904) and target (‑0.236904), indicating broad perturbation rather than established successful repair with collateral loss. In Study~2, native dual‑ID generation (A2) yields more positive paired contrasts: protected +0.512918 (95% case‑cluster CI [0.471434,0.550259]) and target +0.158853 ([0.118903,0.197523]), across 287 jointly measurable pairs from 111 cases. Shared baseline similarity cancels algebraically in these paired contrasts, leaving a matched POST comparison. Validation designed after the primary result freeze finds directional agreement with an independent identity evaluator and blinded human judgments; within‑\buffalo\ nuisance models provide supportive sensitivity evidence. The findings characterize intact native regimes, whose references, routing, adapters, and token counts co‑vary. They do not establish component causality, categorical identity preservation, successful localized editing, or generalization beyond the evaluated implementation and measurable cohort.

PaperId: 697, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22744.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaoyan Cong, Tianyu Wang, Hyeonho Jeong, Zhifei Zhang, Yuqian Zhou, Yijun Li, Shaoteng Liu, Zhe Lin, Srinath Sridhar, Soo Ye Kim
Title: OmniXRef: A Unified Framework for Multimodal Multi-Reference Video Editing
Abstract:
Creative intent in video editing can be expressed through text instructions (e.g., "remove the people"), image references (e.g., subject appearance), video references (e.g., camera movement), or a combination of the above. We introduce OmniXRef, a unified framework for multimodal multi‑reference video editing that allows users to combine variable numbers of text, image, and video references to control diverse attributes of a source video. We first devise a unified input design with a reference‑bank interface and introduce R^2‑RoPE to support generalization to more references. Then our model, OmniXRef‑Model, uses a single‑stream diffusion transformer to jointly process the source video and multimodal context from an MLLM in an interleaved sequence. To address the scarcity of training data for video‑reference editing, we construct OmniXRef‑Data using synthesis pipelines for different editing tasks and combinations of references. We use curriculum learning to progressively increase task complexity and resolution. To support systematic evaluation of video as a control modality, we introduce OmniXRef‑Bench, a benchmark for video‑reference attribute transfer across Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and Visual Effects (VFX). Comprehensive evaluations show that our OmniXRef‑Model outperforms task‑specific baselines and commercial models.

PaperId: 698, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22740.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mingda Zhang, Yun Huang, Qiang Huang, Yanjin Li, Rui Qian, Qichao Zhao, Tiesunlong Shen, Na Zhao, Jian Wang, Xiaoying Tang
Title: R$^2$Orch: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Orchestration via Self-Play within a Skill-Internalization Loop
Abstract:
In recent years, agentic orchestration has been widely applied to solve complex human tasks. However, existing orchestration learning still faces key challenges, including hand‑designed curricula, advantage collapse when a task's rollouts all reach the same outcome, and unreliable evaluation signals that judge each skill by one noisy score. To address these challenges, we propose R^2Orch, a new paradigm of Recursive Self‑Play Orchestration: an inner loop of self‑play that improves the orchestrator on self‑chosen tasks, and an outer loop that improves how the inner loop improves. To support this paradigm, we introduce Recursive Learnability, a training objective that rewards a Proposer for choosing tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn. Built on this objective, we further propose Skill Withdrawal, in which the outer loop withdraws each skill once a controlled evaluation within self‑play shows that the orchestrator performs as well without it. Moreover, the two loops form one cycle: failures are distilled into skills, skills into parameters, and withdrawals lead the Proposer to new failures, so the orchestrator moves toward zero‑skill deployment. Experimental results on twelve datasets show that R^2Orch consistently outperforms baselines across question answering, math, code, and interactive tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/R2Orch.

PaperId: 699, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22736.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qianwei Wang, Ce Zhang, Zhanpeng Luo, Pengpeng Su, Shuo Yang, Hao Xu
Title: Spatial Memory by Agents, for Agents
Abstract:
Spatial memory enables robots to reuse past observations for localization, navigation, and question answering. Designing such memory involves jointly deciding what to retain and how to retrieve it for diverse semantic, metric, and temporal needs. We investigate whether coding agents can automate this design process through iterative implementation and evaluation. Under a fixed development budget, a Designer Agent writes and revises code for memory construction and retrieval using feedback from a fixed Query Agent. The resulting implementations are frozen before building memories from held‑out observation histories, without access to downstream questions, and evaluated across five complementary task tracks using the same Query Agent. Across three independent design searches, Codex / GPT‑6 Astra averages 44.23 on the equally weighted five‑track score, versus 29.32 for ReMEmbR, the strongest evaluated baseline supporting all five tracks, a 50.9% relative improvement. Qualitative analysis relates performance differences to evidence retention and retrieval, while identifying grounding and evidence‑use failures. These results demonstrate the potential of coding agents to automate spatial memory design, while revealing task‑dependent trade‑offs in performance and computational cost. Project page: https://ba‑fa‑3344.github.io/.

PaperId: 700, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22726.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Nuzhat Khan, Ab Al-Hadi Ab Rahman, Mohamad Anuar Kamaruddin, Muhammad Paend Bakht, Sana Fatima, Farhad Khodadadi, Ibrahim Yousef Alshareef
Title: Improving OCR Accuracy Through Multi-Classifier Verification of Visually Similar Characters
Abstract:
Distinguishing visually similar characters is a persistent challenge for optical character recognition (OCR) systems, causing errors in critical applications of text digitization. While preprocessing techniques improve image quality and word‑level post‑processing corrects spelling errors, neither addresses character‑level visual ambiguity, an intrinsic property of certain character pairs that limits even state‑of‑the‑art OCR models. We present the Character Verification Model (CVM), a character‑level post‑processing framework that verifies and corrects ambiguous characters in OCR outputs using specialized binary classifiers trained on visually confusable pairs such as 'O'/'0', 'Z'/'2', and 'S'/'5'. CVM operates independently of dictionary validation, making it suitable for non‑lexical data including serial numbers, alphanumeric codes, and license plates. Experiments on three OCR engines (Tesseract, EasyOCR, TrOCR) and ten fonts with low to high complexity demonstrate accuracy improvements of 3.95‑14.81 percentage points, with an 87.3% correction rate for visually similar character errors and a false‑correction rate of only 2.3%. The modular architecture integrates with existing OCR pipelines without modification to underlying recognition models.

PaperId: 701, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22708.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Nicholas Saban, Charvi Bannur, Mariya Vasileva, Darshan Deshpande
Title: GlobeBench: Evaluating Text-Based World Model Capabilities for Scalable Environment Simulations
Abstract:
Text‑based world models have recently shown potential to simulate complex RL environment state transitions for a diverse set of use cases. However, no standardized benchmark exists to compare, study and improve these models. Through this paper, we attempt to solve this problem by building GlobeBench, a novel benchmark with 1,632 tasks across five separate domains and nineteen simulation skills. The tasks check whether models can predict the environment's response to a specific action given the full agent trajectory by understanding earlier state changes, following environment rules, and predicting the effects of actions on both related and unrelated objects. We compare the predicted environment response with an execution‑derived reference, using a hybrid architecture with both deterministic gates and a semantic judge. Among 20 general‑purpose LLMs and specialized text world models, GPT‑6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate at 49.57%. We find that model accuracy decreases as actions affect a larger portion of the environment. Specifically, when the agent's changes must propagate to dependent objects, task success drops to an average of 5.1% across all 20 models. Although model strengths differ across tasks, 631 tasks remain unsolved by any model, suggesting a significant gap in general LLM capabilities as a world model.

PaperId: 702, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22682.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yinyi Luo, Haoyue Bai, Yi Ge, Nilton Cesar Rojas Vales, Marios Savvides, Jindong Wang
Title: FlexUMM: Flexible Representation Learning for Unified Multimodal Models
Abstract:
Unified multimodal models (UMMs) can integrate understanding and generation within a single backbone. However, it is commonly known that these two capabilities can cause conflicting representations, leading to a central question: how representation and computation should be shared across functionalities? Existing UMMs often rely on a largely fixed structure, where different inputs and functionalities follow the same depth and parameter‑sharing pattern. We argue that this assumption is too restrictive: more effective unification requires sharing the computation that supports cross‑functional communication while specializing the capacity that becomes task‑ or input‑specific. We introduce FlexUMM, a flexible UMM framework that dynamically decides when to preserve shared computation, when to route specialized capacity, and when to stop further processing. Evidence shows that this flexible allocation improves UMMs along two complementary axes. It improves accuracy by reducing harmful competition between functionalities, and it improves efficiency by avoiding unnecessary computation once an input representation is sufficiently mature. Beyond simple architectural unification from the pre‑trained models, FlexUMM works as a model‑agnostic, functional plug‑in to make existing UMMs more unified, stronger, and efficient. Code is available at: https://github.com/AIFrontierLab/TorchUMM/tree/main/src/umm/post_training/flexumm.

PaperId: 703, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22675.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yupeng Zhou, I-Chia Chang, Ziran Wang, Bin Yao
Title: Online Constraint Optimization-Based Indirect-Adaptive Robust Control for Autonomous Vehicles with Unknown Friction
Abstract:
Friction uncertainty is a significant challenge for autonomous vehicle control, undermining feasibility and performance. This paper proposes a novel two‑layer control framework to achieve vehicle motion control under large friction uncertainty by combining optimization‑based planning with indirect adaptive robust control (IARC). The upper layer solves a constrained optimal control problem to generate a feasible trajectory that satisfies all the constraints in a time‑optimal manner along the desired path. The lower layer, IARC, adapts the unknown parameters related to friction uncertainty and combines model compensation with robust feedback to ensure transient and steady‑state tracking performance. An estimation monitor is designed to prevent poor learning when data indicate a model mismatch, while a smooth parameter reset reduces the estimated tire capacity and limits abrupt tightening of constraints. The updated parameters are fed back into the model and constraints in the planner, enabling trajectory replanning as friction conditions change. Simulation results indicate that the proposed method achieves accurate tracking of the desired trajectory and online friction adaptation under large friction uncertainty while ensuring time‑optimal vehicle motion. The simulation results demos are available at https://github.com/TedZhou0603/CO‑IARC.

PaperId: 704, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22619.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Narayanan Palghat Parameswaran, Dong-Ki Kim, Jay Patrikar, Santiago Gutierrez, Harshad Zade, Shayegan Omidshafiei, Harmish Khambhaita
Title: FCTS: Failure-Guided Curriculum Tree Search Over Generated Terrain for Legged Parkour
Abstract:
Quadruped parkour policies handle canonical obstacles well, but their training curricula often miss the irregular, compound geometry of industrial and disaster‑response sites, where agile locomotion matters most. Such environments pose a hard generalization problem: even training directly on reconstructed geometry from the target site does not reliably yield policies that traverse it. Hand‑designed curricula span only a few terrain families, and recent LLM‑generated curricula offer little control over which policy weaknesses they target. We propose FCTS, a failure‑conditioned terrain curriculum framework that uses localized traversal failures to automatically generate the terrains a policy should train on next. Each failure's location, termination mode, robot state, and surrounding terrain geometry condition this generation, and Monte Carlo Tree Search explores alternative curriculum trajectories under a fixed training budget. On terrains built from scanned real‑world construction sites, FCTS raises success rate from 28.4% to 85.8% on a medium‑difficulty course and from 14.9% to 44.7% on a hard course relative to the strongest parkour or LLM‑curriculum baselines, and maintains higher progress on extreme terrains where full traversal is rare. Hardware experiments on a quadruped robot confirm that the learned FCTS policies transfer to the real world.

PaperId: 705, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22606.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jae Joong Lee, Bedrich Benes
Title: Three LiDARs, Twenty-Five Datasets: Cross-Source Generalization in Tree-Species Recognition
Abstract:
FOR‑species20K is the largest public LiDAR benchmark for tree‑species classification, pooling 25 independently collected terrestrial, mobile, and airborne laser‑scanning datasets across 33 species. We introduce a multi‑resolution, multi‑view ConvNeXtV2 model that improves official hidden‑test accuracy from 79.5% to 85.0%, ranking first at the time of submission. We then examine what this score measures. Because the hidden test is species‑balanced, its overall accuracy is more comparable to a macro metric than to accuracy under the public set's long‑tailed distribution. Moreover, the official random split places every source dataset in both training and evaluation. A logistic probe recovers source identity from out‑of‑fold model probabilities with 69% accuracy, while geometric features identify the source above 90% within two widely shared species; 18 of the 33 species occur in only one source. Under a source‑species‑cell holdout, evaluated on 5,566 trees from eight eligible species that retain the same LiDAR‑type training support in other sources, the unweighted species mean falls from 82% to 36%, and tree‑weighted accuracy falls from 95% to 60%. Count‑matched retraining and experiments with two alternative backbones indicate that this gap is not explained by reduced training support alone, while an external PureForest experiment shows a smaller but consistent grouped‑split effect. These results establish the 85% leaderboard score as strong in‑distribution performance, but not as an estimate of source‑disjoint generalization, motivating balanced metrics and source‑aware evaluation. The code is available at: https://github.com/JaeLee18/FOR20K‑lidar‑tree‑species

PaperId: 706, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22599.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ayush Bansal, Aldo Pareja, Sean Klein, Serge Didenko, Artem Lukoianov
Title: Can LLMs predict the outcomes of machine learning experiments?
Abstract:
Recent advances in AI make Recursive Self‑Improvement (RSI) increasingly plausible. Large Language Models (LLMs) can already propose, select, and run Machine Learning (ML) experiments. However, the space of possible design choices in ML is vast. An LLM that proposes an experiment needs a reliable intuition of whether it is worth running given the timing constraints of long training runs. In this work, we measure such intuition in current frontier LLMs by evaluating how accurately they predict the impact of self‑generated ML experiment ideas before these are put into training runs. To this end, we construct a dataset of 288 LLM‑proposed ideas on eight MLE‑bench tasks. We then prompt five frontier LLMs (GPT‑6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and GLM‑5.3) to predict the impact of each idea and compare their predictions with the actual outcomes after training. We report four main findings. First, LLM predictions are substantially better than random chance but far from accurate: even the best model, Claude Opus 5.5, explains only half of the variance in outcomes (R^2 = 0.49). Second, we notice that all tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of the changes. Third, prediction quality varies widely across tasks. Finally, the choice of the coding harness that actually implements the ideas has little effect on outcomes, and we find no evidence of self‑preference. Higher reasoning settings and additional context lead to modest gains. Overall, our results show that current LLMs have useful but limited intuition about which ML ideas will work. We release our dataset to support further study.

PaperId: 707, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22593.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Akash Kumar, Karthik Sankaranarayanan
Title: Flat Loss, Evolving Features: Grokking in Modular Addition
Abstract:
Can a network keep learning while its training cross‑entropy stays nearly flat at a positive level? We show that it can. On modular addition, a standard testbed for grokking, ReLU networks trained with supported‑Polar hidden updates, normalized output‑layer updates and weight decay can keep 100% training accuracy while their hidden features change and held‑out accuracy rises from zero to above 90%, at relatively flat training cross‑entropy. Correct classification need not minimize cross‑entropy, which still depends on prediction confidence. We prove this coexistence for one‑hidden‑layer networks in two finite‑window theorems from constructed initializations: one gives a constant gain in the Fourier fraction of the hidden features, and the other holds at arbitrarily low positive loss, where a readout refitted on the training data generalizes before the network. Experiments from random initialization show the same coexistence on a window fixed in advance, and in deeper networks held‑out accuracy also rises over post‑hoc windows with a net increase in training cross‑entropy. With a last‑layer rate set per training fraction and head decay scaled with the prime, deeper networks at p=47 and 61 meet a criterion on post‑hoc windows, fixed in advance, in nearly all fresh runs. A one‑block transformer trained with the same updates and a slowly decaying output gain keeps every training pair correct at every logged checkpoint while its training cross‑entropy rises and its held‑out accuracy approaches one; with two blocks this holds through the held‑out rise, after which training pairs begin to flip. A plateau in training loss need not be a plateau in learning. Code: https://github.com/akashkumar‑d/flat‑loss‑evolving‑features.

PaperId: 708, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22581.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kaan Baydemir, Sajjad Baghaee, Ilkay Ulusoy
Title: VesperCSI: A High-Performance and Extensible CSI Acquisition Framework for Edge Wi-Fi Sensing
Abstract:
Channel State Information (CSI) captures fine‑grained changes in Wi‑Fi channel propagation and provides a foundation for device‑free sensing applications such as activity recognition, localization, and occupancy detection. The development of such applications depends on an acquisition system that can handle high‑rate CSI streams while remaining extensible to the requirements of individual experiments. VesperCSI is an open‑source, GPL‑3.0‑licensed redesign of FeitCSI for CSI acquisition with Intel AX200 and AX210 Wi‑Fi interfaces. It targets high‑rate acquisition on amd64 and aarch64 Linux hosts using fixed‑capacity preallocated object pools and separate capture and consumer threads. A loadable plugin interface supports experiment‑specific monitoring, storage, and processing. We evaluate VesperCSI and FeitCSI on Raspberry Pi CM4 receivers in a burst‑traffic software crossover. At a 600‑MHz all‑core frequency ceiling and a target rate of 2500 frames/s, VesperCSI achieves mean sequence retention of 99.017‑99.087% in 10,000‑frame bursts, compared with 43.972‑46.553% for FeitCSI. This ordering persists after exchanging the userspace programs between two receivers while retaining their respective drivers. The comparison therefore characterizes the tested software‑and‑driver packages rather than isolating userspace effects. These results support VesperCSI as a reusable acquisition component for edge‑hosted Wi‑Fi sensing under the evaluated workload and platform conditions.

PaperId: 709, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22575.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianyi Yang, Thomas Beckers
Title: Structure-Aware Spatial Kernels for Gaussian Process Distributed Port-Hamiltonian Systems
Abstract:
Gaussian process distributed port‑Hamiltonian systems (GP‑dPHS) enable data‑driven modeling of distributed dynamical systems while preserving their physical structure. However, standard stationary kernels can be inefficient for spatially heterogeneous systems because they neither exploit known input invariances nor reflect structured spatial dependencies. We address this limitation with a structure‑aware kernel design that removes irrelevant state coordinates and decouples state and spatial dependencies through a tensor‑product covariance. This modular construction allows qualitative knowledge of spatial heterogeneity to be incorporated by selecting an appropriate spatial kernel without requiring an analytical description of the underlying profile. Numerical experiments on a nonlinear string with periodic, smoothly varying, and semi‑piecewise stiffness profiles demonstrate that structural decoupling consistently improves reconstruction accuracy, while profile‑matched spatial kernels yield substantially larger gains in force‑field and trajectory reconstruction.

PaperId: 710, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22556.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Victoria Smelova, Daniil Kazachkov, Georgiy Kazantsev, Iuliia Tsvetkova, Egor Cherepanov, Nikita Kachaev, Artem Latyshev, Aleksandr I. Panov, Alexey K. Kovalev
Title: When Plans Change, Remember: Replanning-Guided Visual Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
Abstract:
Long‑horizon, multi‑stage Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) policies often require visual information that is no longer present in the current observation. Retaining the complete observation history is computationally expensive and highly redundant, motivating selective visual memory. We introduce RePlanMem‑VLA (Replanning‑Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which turns a policy's own plan revisions into an online memory‑write signal. Under receding‑horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions. RePlanMem‑VLA treats unusually large disagreement between these temporally aligned predictions as evidence of a task‑relevant event. We first compare 35 disagreement measures across single‑task autoregressive decoder‑only and Flow‑Matching Transformers trained from scratch, then validate the selected signals on pretrained OpenVLA‑OFT and π_0.5 policies over MIKASA‑Robo‑VLA tasks. The resulting detectors achieve ROC‑AUC of 0.981‑0.997. We then use the selected signals in RePlanMem‑VLA to trigger updates to a bounded visual memory, with a robot‑masked write filter suppressing redundant frames. In the evaluated memory‑retention experiments, RePlanMem‑VLA preserves task‑relevant observations until the later decision point in 100% of episodes. Real‑robot replay data further show that event selection and redundancy suppression extend beyond simulation. These results establish plan revision as a policy‑internal signal for controlling what a VLA remembers. Website: https://vika787.github.io/RePlanMem/.

PaperId: 711, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22543.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Eliezer Shlomi, Eliron Rahimi, Avi Mendelson, Chaim Baskin
Title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
Abstract:
Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed‑quality trade‑off. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi‑token decoding schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models. However, it does not transfer directly to DLMs, which must choose both what to generate and where. We show that this order is the missing piece: the model's own predictions from the previous pass already give the right token at 92‑100% of positions, but not which position comes next. Based on this observation, we introduce Speculating Positions Order Trajectory (SPOT), which learns to predict this order. A 0.62M‑parameter model reads only the target's output distributions and proposes a tree of candidate continuations, and the target verifies all of them in a single pass by checking whether each equals its own next state. On the verification side, our analysis shows that prior block‑diffusion verification approaches either assume T=0 or a sequential proposal interface. To support tree‑based speculation at any temperature, we propose using coupled‑noise match verification for diffusion blocks, following shared‑Gumbel‑noise coupling approaches. Our comprehensive experiments show that SPOT cuts target passes by up to 6.8x and reaches up to 3.2x the throughput of standard decoding, beating the calibrated and training‑free drafting baselines in every task and budget at T=0 and T=1. In addition, we show that the learned drafter transfers across models, demonstrating successful transfer across six different DLMs. Project page: https://eliezer318.github.io/SPOT‑dLLM/

PaperId: 712, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22526.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Adib Sakhawat, Syed Rifat Raiyan
Title: Literal Lock-In: How Test Language Shifts Literal Attraction in Typed Decision Models on Bengali Idioms
Abstract:
Decision models, non‑generative scorers that report a probability over caller‑supplied options and emit no text, are increasingly deployed as routers, classifiers and guardrails. Because they generate nothing, rationales and chain‑of‑thought do not apply. We audit three: an encoder scorer, a decoder scorer and a closed API, entirely through interventions on their input, using expert‑annotated Bengali idioms carrying a gold figurative and a gold literal gloss. Dropping an idiom's own literal gloss into the option list draws every arm toward it, taking 65% to 96% of each arm's remaining Bengali errors. A model‑by‑language matrix over one shared item set shows how far this depends on the test language: every arm is 1.9 to 6.4 times more captured in Bengali than in English on the same paired entries, the commercial model's apparent resistance is a property of its test language, and capability does not order the failure. Calibration degrades in all three arms, and on the open arms confidence inverts, so gating on it is worse than gating at random. On a semantics‑free option list, where accuracy is at chance, the best‑calibrated arm still reports mean confidence 0.82. Code and data: https://github.com/sakhadib/literal‑lock‑in.

PaperId: 713, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22511.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shreeyans Arora, Utsav Avaiya, Zera Lyngkhoi, Hem Gosalia, Ram Mohan Rao Kadiyala, Vinay Kumar Sankarapu, Pratinav Seth
Title: AuditKIT: A Unified Evaluation Spine for Benchmarking, Judging, and Comparing Large Language Models and Agentic Systems
Abstract:
Evaluating language models and agents requires combining benchmark accuracy, judge‑based assessment, runtime performance, tool‑use behavior, and retrieval quality. Differences in interfaces, metric semantics, and trace formats complicate these comparisons and can hide failures in agentic workflows. We present AuditKIT, a source‑available evaluation library that records these measurements in one result representation, with direction‑aware metric contracts, configuration fingerprints, and extensible metrics and backends. For agents, it provides turn‑aware tool‑call matching, separates parallel from sequential execution, and distinguishes verified task outcomes from trajectory‑level diagnostics. Missing or unobservable evidence is marked unscored rather than counted as failure. For retrieval‑augmented generation, it combines ranked retrieval metrics, judged grounding, and deterministic evidence checks. Seven case studies spanning model comparison, serving runtimes, retrieval, tool calling, and interoperability show how answer extraction, runtime behavior, and metric selection change evaluation outcomes.

PaperId: 714, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22509.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Markus Kramer, Jan Wachenfeld, Oskar von Stryk
Title: TriSAR-3D and PaintFusion: A Novel Trimodal LiDAR-RGB-Thermal Dataset and Method for 3D Person Detection in Search and Rescue
Abstract:
Reliable 3D person detection is important for rescue robotics to give first responders situational awareness. Yet most multimodal 3D detection research targets automotive scenarios in which pedestrians mostly appear in a narrow range of upright, near‑road poses. It is therefore unclear how much of the reported performance transfers to rescue settings, as a person may be lying, partially occluded, or in unstructured indoor and outdoor environments. To investigate this gap, we introduce TriSAR‑3D, a multimodal person detection dataset recorded with a high‑resolution 128‑channel LiDAR, an RGB camera, and a thermal camera. It captures varied poses in indoor as well as outdoor locations at different times of day to study their influence on 3D object detector performance. Furthermore, we propose a novel trimodal 3D detection pipeline, PaintFusion, that fuses PointPainting‑based evidence using a simple MLP. We show that the derived method reaches 65.4 AP@50 and thereby outperforms strong LiDAR‑only (CenterPoint, 53.4), RGB+LiDAR (BEVFusion, 60.5), and adapted trimodal (Tri‑BEVFusion, 60.7) baselines on the dataset. At the same time, it is substantially faster than other fusion‑based methods such as BEVFusion, with a per‑frame latency of 51.6 ms compared to 101 ms. Additionally, we test how the performance of different 3D object detectors generalizes to unseen pose categories. Removing lying instances from training data collapses the lying‑pose AP@50 to near zero across all evaluated detectors. The results indicate that dataset diversity exerts a large effect on 3D object detection performance. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/MarkusKramer1/3D‑Trimodal‑People‑Detection.

PaperId: 715, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22505.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xinwei Ju, Zhehua Mao, Tianyi Song, Danail Stoyanov, Sophia Bano, Francisco Vasconcelos
Title: KFS$^4$LAM: Adaptive KeyFrame Selection with Structure-Aware Mapping for Endoscopic Gaussian Splatting SLAM
Abstract:
Gaussian‑splatting Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) augments conventional SLAM with a dense, renderable 3D scene representation, enabling high‑quality reconstruction and novel‑view synthesis. However, its localization, reconstruction, and rendering performance depends strongly on which observations are retained for mapping. Existing systems commonly rely on fixed temporal intervals or simple pose‑ and overlap‑based criteria for keyframe selection. In colonoscopy, non‑uniform camera motion, repetitive anatomy, specularities, and visual artifacts can make these criteria unreliable, leading to either redundant keyframes or missed informative viewpoints. We present KFS^4LAM (KeyFrame Selection with Structure‑aware mapping for endoscopic Gaussian Splatting SLAM), which couples motion‑guided adaptive keyframe selection with structurally supervised mapping and restricted temporal deformation. Accumulated motion guides adaptive keyframe selection, with complementary cues suppressing redundant or unreliable candidates. Density‑aware mapping with anatomical contour supervision (colon folds) emphasizes structurally informative regions, while restricted temporal deformation accommodates local tissue dynamics without unconstrained geometric drift. We evaluate KFS^4LAM against Gaussian‑SLAM baselines on C3VD and C3VD‑v2, together with cross‑backbone and component ablations. KFS^4LAM achieves strong overall performance across trajectory, rendering, and depth metrics, with pronounced gains on more challenging C3VD‑v2 dataset. In the matched comparison with SplaTAM on C3VD‑v2, it reduces rotational relative pose error by 20.3% and depth RMSE by 38.4%, while improving PSNR by 0.78 dB. Cross‑backbone experiments further show that the framework is not tied to a single underlying SLAM architecture. Code and visualization results are available at https://xinweiju.github.io/KFSLAM/.

PaperId: 716, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22474.pdf   GitHub
Authors:J. P. Naiman
Title: Star Light, Star Bright: Can Multimodal Models Parse an Astronomy Visual Question Answering Dataset Right?
Abstract:
Figures are essential for scientific communication, and the field of Visual Question Answering (VQA) aims to test the figure understanding capabilities of large multimodal models (LMMs). Here, we investigate the accuracy of several low‑cost LMMs on domain‑specific VQA tasks for astronomical images of the sky. As instrument for this task we build a domain‑specific VQA dataset comprising 2001 partially‑synthetic figures divided evenly between contour plots, real telescope images drawn from NASA's SkyView, and "fake" sky images which share the axes and angular scales of the real images but draw their colors from a gaussian mixture model, alongside 47357 questions. Each figure is released as pristine and with realistic page‑aging degradations mimicking the historical astronomical corpus. Testing three low‑cost proprietary LMMs, we find models frequently fail to answer domain‑specific questions at high accuracy. An initial comparison with 104 human‑verified, astrometrically tagged figures from historical journal publications shows similar median errors in angular extent. All code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/jnaiman/SkyImagesWASP2026 and dataset is available on HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ReadingTimeMachine/astro_sky_image_vqa.

PaperId: 717, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22445.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianyu Wu
Title: Null Controls Are Necessary but Not Sufficient: Evaluating Acceptance Guards for Scientific Discovery and Interpretability
Abstract:
Automated discovery systems propose scientific explanations and test which to accept. Does passing a test establish the intended claim? We develop four executable operations for changing physical descriptions: identifying redundancies (L1), coarse‑graining dynamics (L2), transferring structure (L3), and inferring missing quantities from conservation imbalances (L4). We evaluate these operations and three interpretability settings through null acceptance (NAR), positive acceptance (PAR), and consequence agreement (CAR). A reduction mapping every state to zero predicts its own future perfectly. It passes closure on 96% of 129 public chaotic systems despite retaining no dynamical variation. An independent observable‑preservation test rejects it throughout. On controlled benchmarks, the combined criteria accept 24/24 genuine reductions and reject 72/72 nulls. The other operations distinguish symmetries from redundancies, validate transfers, and reject spurious conservation imbalances. In language and ESM‑2 protein models, linear CKA remains unchanged when a proposed correspondence is randomly rotated, whereas localized interventions distinguish genuine mappings from tested nulls. In sparse autoencoders, enrichment rejects all 16 tested nulls, yet independent ablation supports 45% of evaluable enriched features, compared with 0.5% of matched controls. These results reveal two acceptance gaps: descriptive tests can accept scientifically empty candidates, and accepted candidates can lack independently verified consequences. Reliable automated discovery requires evaluating both what a test accepts and the scientific consequences it establishes. Code and data: https://real‑project‑aether.github.io/project‑aether/.

PaperId: 718, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22444.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yizhe Zhang, Xujia Wang, Songqi Tang, Xujie Tang, Leo Jiahao Jiang, Jiacheng Wang, Bowen Qu, JinBo Li, Qin Wang, Ji Qi, Lei Hou, Bin Xu, Juanzi Li
Title: Event-STVG: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding for Long-Form Event Reasoning
Abstract:
Spatio‑Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to jointly localize a target in space and time given a natural‑language query. Despite continued advances, existing STVG benchmarks remain largely centered on localizing targets through instance‑specific descriptions, leaving them largely decoupled from long‑form reasoning increasingly emphasized in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). In this paper, we introduce Event‑STVG, a task that shifts STVG from locating what is described toward event‑level reasoning by unifying long‑form context, repeated‑event reasoning, event localization, role inference, and multi‑target grounding. To facilitate research on Event‑STVG, we construct a large‑scale benchmark comprising 4,016 annotated event occurrences across soccer and seven additional domains. Experiments with state‑of‑the‑art MLLMs reveal substantial difficulty, with the strongest model achieving only 5.4% m‑vIoU at the 10‑minute horizon. Across domains, we consistently observe confusion among repeated same‑type events, spatial grounding bottlenecks, and rare success in jointly grounding all required roles. Event‑STVG establishes a new challenge for visual understanding in MLLMs, calling for future models that can jointly reason about complex events across space and time. Code and annotations are available at https://github.com/THU‑KEG/EventSTVG

PaperId: 719, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22440.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ryan Wyton, Bacha Rehman
Title: An Agentic ENF Framework for Forensic Video Authentication Against Generative AI
Abstract:
Generative models now synthesise video that is hard to distinguish from genuine footage, and learned detectors that key on a generator's artefacts degrade sharply on unseen models. This paper develops a forensic framework that authenticates video by a signal that generation does not control: the electric network frequency (ENF), the mains‑driven hum in audio and flicker in video. A unified two‑channel detector extracts the ENF from audio and from rolling‑shutter video through one second harmonic estimator and a shared network; a synthetic‑injection training method, driven by an Ornstein‑Uhlenbeck drift model and anchored to real recordings, overcomes the scarcity of labelled ENF data; a reference‑matching channel verifies a claimed time of recording and recovers an unknown one; and a two‑axis agentic orchestrator fuses recording authenticity with content‑manipulation evidence under an asymmetric rule, escalating expensive detectors only when needed. A central finding reframes the task: an ENF‑band flicker is present in generated video at a prominence indistinguishable from real footage, so its presence is not proof of authenticity, and authentication must rest on consistency with an independent reference rather than on presence. On held‑out real recordings the detector accepts genuine audio and video at 93% and 100% against naive baselines of 53% and 15%; claimed‑time authentication reaches an area under the curve of 1.0; and the agentic cascade matches a flat ensemble while cutting wall‑clock time by 54% and frames decoded by 64%, without loss of accuracy.

PaperId: 720, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22433.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziheng Zhang, Wei Zhang, Yunyi Zhao, Zuming Liu, Wei Zhou, Boon Ping Gan
Title: BOLT: Multi-Bottleneck Bound-Guided Learning for Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling with Time Lags and Resource-Coupled Transport
Abstract:
Flexible job‑shop scheduling becomes resource‑coupled when a scarce vehicle fleet moves jobs between stations, because the schedule sets the transport waits. BOLT (bound‑oriented learning for transport‑coupled scheduling) builds a lower bound from chain, machine‑capacity, and fleet‑capacity relaxations. The bound equals the makespan at termination, so its per‑step changes form a reward that sums to a constant minus the makespan. Because it never exceeds the attainable makespan, each candidate's bound increase is a proven rise of the makespan floor, which the policy reads as a price. The root bound certifies a completed schedule's suboptimality gap without a solver. On industry‑motivated 10‑module prefabricated‑construction instances, explicit transport coupling outperforms a transport‑penalty policy in every tested cell where loaded moves occupy at least 66% of fleet time and in none at or below 56%. Across five zero‑shot 50‑ and 80‑module production batches, BOLT outperforms the best dispatching‑rule pair on four and the penalty policy on the three with long moves. In the three‑vehicle 80‑module batch, its mean makespan is 13.0% below the best pair and 4.2% below an hour‑budget constraint‑programming solver whose proven gap averages 34%. BOLT decides in 2.3‑5.9 ms per event on one processor core and re‑plans a disruption in seconds.

PaperId: 721, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22421.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ming Lu, Junqi Shi, Zhan Ma
Title: End-to-End Learned Image Coding: From Rate-Distortion Optimization to Practical Deployment
Abstract:
End‑to‑end learned image coding (LIC) has achieved substantial improvements in rate‑‑distortion (R‑‑D) performance, yet practical deployment requires addressing a broader set of system‑level constraints. This article provides a deployment‑oriented review of LIC, with particular attention to the transition from high‑performance neural compression models to practical codecs. We first summarize the basic end‑to‑end coding framework, including learned transforms, quantization, entropy modeling, and R‑‑D optimization. We then review practical extensions that are increasingly important for deployment, including variable‑rate coding and rate control, integer‑precision inference and cross‑platform consistency, robustness and communication resilience, lightweight and hardware‑aware implementation, and standardization and interoperability. To study these issues under a common setting, we further introduce TinyLIC as an open benchmark and reproducible case study for rate‑‑distortion‑‑complexity analysis. Experimental results illustrate the trade‑offs among compression efficiency, computational complexity, numerical consistency, and robustness. In particular, TinyLIC with approximately 10 KMACs/pixel decoding complexity substantially outperforms the H.265/HEVC image‑profile anchor on Kodak, while the 50 KMACs/pixel configuration achieves performance comparable to the H.266/VVC image‑profile anchor on several test sets. The review highlights practical constraints and design trade‑offs that remain central to the deployment and interoperability of learned image codecs. Materials are accessible at https://njuvision.github.io/TinyLIC.

PaperId: 722, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22404.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fubin Yan, Ruxuan Dong, Ruoxuan Shi, Duolei Wang, Kenneth W. Shum
Title: Aligning Information Theory and Formal Verification: A Lean Formalization of Rate-Distortion Theory
Abstract:
Large language models have recently demonstrated an ability to generate substantial mathematical proofs and formalizations, including machine‑checked arguments for major open problems and classical theorems. These developments highlight a growing workflow in which AI systems search for proofs while proof assistants certify their correctness. Within information theory, however, formalized libraries remain limited, and existing formalized theorems focus almost exclusively on Shannon's foundational lossless theorems. This paper presents the first Lean formalization of core components of rate‑distortion theory, a central framework for lossy compression and modern machine‑learning analysis. We identify the alignment challenges that arise when translating information‑theoretic definitions, such as distortion measures, typicality and achievability, into a proof‑assistant setting, and we develop a reusable library of definitions and lemmas faithful to textbook conventions. Our formalization provides a foundation for future AI‑assisted proofs in information theory and enables subsequent mechanized developments to build on a coherent, verified infrastructure rather than generating long proofs from scratch.

PaperId: 723, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22381.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhe Zhou
Title: Binding-Specific Relearning Savings for Test-Time Continual Learning
Abstract:
When a fact becomes harder to elicit from a language model, has the model lost it, or has it merely become less accessible? Parameter‑updating test‑time continual learning agents are usually evaluated by current output accuracy; we ask whether that measurement captures how prior experience shapes later updates. We test whether learning a specific factual binding produces a later relearning advantage beyond familiarity with its entity, answer vocabulary, format, or query slot. In Qwen2.5‑1.5B, we compare three matched, counterbalanced histories: LEARNED receives the correct binding, CONTROL receives matched exposure without it, and WRONG receives a competing relation‑valid answer in the same slot. After an identical rehearsal‑free continual fine‑tuning stream, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL at a prespecified checkpoint of partial forgetting. WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, while its comparison with LEARNED provides slot‑matched corroboration, subject to possible competitor interference. The advantage remains positive after adjustment for measured pre‑relearning behavior. In a secondary descriptive conversion using an unpaired never‑seen pool, prior learning reduces the optimizer updates required for restoration by about 18%. Current behavioral accuracy can therefore underestimate the lasting effect of previously acquired experience. Code is available at https://github.com/zhezhou1106/relearning‑savings

PaperId: 724, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22300.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Faridoun Mehri, Hinrich Schütze
Title: Knowledge That Is Linear Before Fine-Tuning Generalizes After It
Abstract:
Not all facts a language model can recall support further learning equally well. We distinguish active facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, from inert facts, which can be recalled but do not support such generalization in a given task. We study this distinction by constructing new relations from existing ones. Take the relation that maps a place to its continent (Paris ‑> Europe) and assign each of its answers an arbitrary new label (Europe ‑> crab, Asia ‑> zebra). The new relation then maps Paris ‑> crab. We fine‑tune the model on the new relation for a subset of subjects, without telling it the original relation or the relabeling rule, and test whether it assigns the corresponding labels to held‑out subjects that share an answer in the original relation. Having learned Paris ‑> crab, does it answer Munich ‑> crab? Across eleven language models and 70 relations, how linearly readable the original relation is in pretrained representations strongly predicts this generalization. Within each model, the two correlate across relations at Pearson r = 0.87 to 0.92. This association persists when controlling, separately and jointly, for the number of fine‑tuning subjects and answers, the model's accuracy on the original relation, and how often the subjects occur in pretraining text. It is also robust to re‑randomizing the label assignment and fine‑tuning seed, and to replacing the animal labels with labels from thirteen other semantic categories. When we map a fine‑tuned model's wrong label back to the original answer it was assigned to, Munich ‑> zebra becomes Munich ‑> Asia. Answers recovered this way are more often among the linear probe's top answers for the subject than among the pretrained model's own. Whether a new relation generalizes depends less on whether its facts can be recalled than on how readily their shared structure can be read out linearly.

PaperId: 725, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22191.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Francesco Alemanno
Title: Attention over noisy examples: generalization and memorization in the exponential Hopfield network
Abstract:
In Hebbian learning from examples, a Hopfield network retrieves archetypes seen only through noisy examples. We study it in the exponential Hopfield model: one softmax attention step with the unlabelled examples as keys. A signal‑to‑noise analysis gives the overlap with an unseen archetype in closed form: a majority‑rule law in which an attention entropy replaces the dataset entropy. At high temperature the archetype is lost in the crosstalk; at low temperature the softmax freezes on the closest training example, as in a random energy model, and the layer memorizes. In between, in a window widening with the square root of the network size, the layer pools the examples of the correct class and retrieves the unseen archetype as well as their majority vote allows, at any fixed load. On structured datasets, such as MNIST and fashion‑MNIST, the best accuracy lies beyond the freezing.

PaperId: 726, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22169.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jian Gu, Hongyu Zhang, Chunyang Chen, Aldeida Aleti
Title: Lexical Reference Frames: Interpreting LM Residual Streams in Native Semantics
Abstract:
The vocabulary of a language model is its native semantics, and the embedding and unembedding fix the meaning of a state at the two ends of the residual stream. Between them, existing methods reuse a fixed lens or treat states as a point cloud, and neither reads a state as the model does. We argue that every hidden state has a native reference frame, induced by the layers that remain and adaptive to the context. Lexical reference frames approximate it in a model‑native and context‑aware way, reading a state through the remaining layers with a given number of rounds of attention between positions and a typical attention output for the rest, fitting nothing to the model's output. No lens with fixed directions per layer can reach a mean cosine with the native frame's lexical readouts above the square root of their coherence, 0.30 and 0.35 at mid‑depth of SmolLM3‑3B and OLMo3‑7B. LexFrame[1], of order 1, reaches 0.97 and 0.97, and its readings are on average within 0.16 and 0.15 nats of the model's output. Its coefficient differences attribute predictions more faithfully than attribution patching, and its lexical basis steers predictions while sparing other tokens. On average, its readings settle on the model's top token over the final 0.82 and 0.81 of the layers, those of lenses over at most 0.11. These frames thus make every hidden state readable, attributable and steerable.

PaperId: 727, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22146.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiuyi Xu, Chengyuan Qian, Zhengzhong Tu, Yang Sui, Yangming Shi
Title: FastVLA: Task-Conditioned and Temporally Adaptive Visual Token Compression for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
Abstract:
Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general‑purpose robot manipulation, but closed‑loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high‑resolution, often multi‑view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency. Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision‑critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control‑critical tokens. We introduce FastVLA, a training‑free, task‑aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework. At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task‑to‑vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance‑distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse‑Simpson metric with online sliding‑window calibration. We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA‑OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot. In simulation, it reduces LLM‑backbone FLOPs by 35‑59% and action latency by 9‑32% (a 1.09×‑1.46× speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency‑performance trade‑off than existing plug‑and‑play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines. On the real robot, it cuts action‑prediction latency by 20% (1.25× speedup) at comparable success. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA.

PaperId: 728, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22126.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Joran Michiels, Anis Ismail, Maarten De Vos, Alejandro Sifrim
Title: Causal Integrated Gradients: Scalable Feature Attribution Along Causal Paths
Abstract:
Existing feature attribution methods that account for feature dependencies do not scale to high dimensions. We propose causal integrated gradients (CIG) and causal expected gradients (CEG), which extend integrated gradients to incorporate prior causal structure among input features while retaining its computational efficiency and, under conditions on the causal graph, its axiomatic guarantees. In many settings, some causal structure between features is already known, for example, that a transcription factor causally regulates a target gene's expression. Yet existing gradient‑based methods cannot exploit this structure, instead crediting a feature's downstream effects over its true upstream cause, such as ranking the target gene above the transcription factor that regulates it. Our key idea is to embed this causal structure by routing the integration path along the causal graph. The method thereby decomposes each feature's attribution into a direct effect and effects mediated through its causal descendants. We evaluate CIG in three settings of increasing realism. First, on a synthetic benchmark with a known causal model, CIG's attributions best match the ground‑truth causal effect from Pearl's do‑calculus, matching the accuracy of causal Shapley values at a fraction of the computational cost. Second, on simulated single‑cell gene expression data with a known gene regulatory network (Dyngen), CIG most accurately recovers the transcription factors driving the simulation. Third, on real interferon‑β stimulation data, where only an approximate causal graph is available, CIG better prioritizes the transcription factors driving the measured response than DeepSHAP and integrated gradients. Together, these results show that incorporating causal structure into gradient‑based attributions recovers upstream drivers that existing methods miss, without sacrificing scalability.

PaperId: 729, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22119.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Venki Parsuram, Michelle Wang, Jin-Hyuk Hong, Pulkit Agrawal
Title: Compliant GMT: Making General Motion Tracking Compliant via Residual Reference Adaptation
Abstract:
We propose Compliant GMT (C‑GMT), a modular framework for full‑body compliant responses in general motion tracking. As humanoid robots move into real world deployment, they not only need to perform any motion but also respond safely and robustly to interaction forces. Existing general motion tracking policies can imitate diverse motions but are trained to be stiff, leading to unexpected and unsafe behaviors under disturbance. Prior work in compliant humanoid control trades off compliance and generality. There exist examples of full‑body compliant responses, but these are heavily curated to single‑reference policies. On the other hand, general motion trackers (GMT) are trained to rigidly imitate massive motion capture datasets. Our key insight is to leverage the generality of pretrained GMTs for motion tracking while introducing compliance from a residual adapter that conditions on a history of proprioception. This enables our approach, C‑GMT, to achieve both general motion tracking and whole‑body compliant responses. Compared to state‑of‑the‑art general motion trackers and single‑motion compliant policies, C‑GMT demonstrates competitive performance in both motion tracking accuracy and compliance adherence. We further demonstrate improved safety, robustness, and error tolerance in simulation and real‑world G1 experiments.

PaperId: 730, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22100.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Nicolás Vera Zúñiga
Title: Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute
Abstract:
Byte‑level language models such as the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) run their large global model once per patch and start a patch where a small model's next‑byte entropy is high. This rule rarely starts a patch at in‑line computed results, such as the number after "=" in a worked solution, and accuracy on them collapses under tight patch budgets. We propose novelty patching, motivated by LZ77‑style compression: start a patch where the upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent context. The rule is a lookup table over the previous two bytes, fitted in seconds on raw text with no labels, reference model or losses. In BLT‑style models trained from scratch on a 1.9 GB math corpus at a matched ~11% patch rate (3 seeds each), it has no clear effect at 1M parameters, raises final‑answer accuracy from 47% to 72% at 12M, and at 50M raises computed‑result accuracy from 21% to 57% and final‑answer accuracy from 60% to 90%; a table fitted on the raw pretraining corpus keeps the gain. Outside math the advantage shrinks: novelty lowers bits per byte on prose and ties entropy on source code and on synthetic execution traces. An analysis of where boundaries fall explains the pattern. Computed results have ordinary surprisal for the patcher's model, so surprisal‑seeking rules pass over them: entropy concentrates patch starts on high‑surprisal bytes most strongly of all rules (boundary enrichment 1.61) and is the worst on computed results, while the best rules sit near chance enrichment. Novelty works where new content begins at segment starts close to the computation, as in written math; a learned chunker (H‑Net) finds such structure on its own, in math and in code. We also report what did not work: typed uncertainty as a training rule, switching rules after training, and a context‑aware novelty predictor.

PaperId: 731, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22075.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Madhav Iyengar, Andreas Geiger, Hilde Kühne
Title: Retrofitting Recurrent Vision-Language Models from Pretrained Backbones
Abstract:
Recent work shows that depth recurrence can be retrofitted into pretrained language models. In this work, we adapt this paradigm for visual understanding, using depth recurrence to reduce the parameter footprint of a pretrained vision‑language model (VLM). To this end, we prune layers from the language backbone of the VLM and loop over a subset of the remaining layers. At each step of the loop, a linear adapter merges the block's output with the token representations from the preceding layers and projects the fused representation back into the block. As the pruning impacts the original model performance, we propose a three‑stage recovery training: first, we leverage a language‑only pretraining to recover the performance of the language backbone, followed by an alignment of the vision‑language projector, and a full fine‑tuning of the model via visual instruction tuning. In the first and the last stage, we distill the outputs of the pretrained non‑recurrent model into the recurrent model, which further improves the recovery. We evaluate the proposed approach on the TinyLLaVA‑1.4B backbone without introducing any new vision‑language data during retrofitting. Our experiments demonstrate that the retrofitted recurrent model outperforms the unpruned baseline trained with the same recovery data while storing 23.3% fewer language parameters. We further show that the proposed retrofitting recurrence outperforms the setup of converting a recurrent LM into a VLM on the same data. Additionally, our ablations show how design choices, such as the adapter between recurrences and a larger recurrent block, lead to the improved performance of our approach. Finally, we find that our proposed model gains on reasoning‑oriented benchmarks, whereas its performance on basic visual understanding benchmarks remains on par with the baseline.

PaperId: 732, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22056.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiuhui Zhang, Ning Gao, Xingyu Jiang, Yihui Chen, Yuheng Pan, Mohan Zhang, Yue Deng
Title: Progress Reward Model for Reinforcement Learning via Large Language Models
Abstract:
Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms face significant limitations in handling long‑term tasks with sparse rewards. Recent advancements have leveraged large language models (LLMs) to enhance RL by utilizing their world knowledge for task planning and reward generation. However, planning‑based approaches often depend on pre‑defined skill libraries and fail to optimize low‑level control policies, while reward‑based methods require extensive human feedback or exhaustive searching due to the complexity of tasks. In this paper, we propose the Progress Reward Model for RL (PRM4RL), a novel framework that integrates task planning and dense reward to enhance RL. For high‑level planning, a complex task is decomposed into a series of simple manageable subtasks, with a subtask‑oriented, fine‑grained progress function designed to monitor task execution progress. For low‑level reward generation, inspired by potential‑based reward shaping, we use the progress function to construct a Progress Reward Model (PRM), providing theoretically grounded optimality and convergence guarantees, thereby enabling effective policy optimization. Experimental results on robotics control tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms both LLM‑based planning and reward methods, achieving state‑of‑the‑art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/deng‑ai‑lab/PRM4RL.

PaperId: 733, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22050.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Omer Imran
Title: Missed Detections and False Alarms in a CNN Technosignature Detector on Breakthrough Listen Data
Abstract:
Radio technosignature searches rely on machine learning detectors to shrink the candidate pool before a human looks at it. They are validated on held‑out data from the training distribution, which excludes the cases where they are most likely to fail: a technosignature has unknown morphology, and terrestrial interference is unbounded in variety. I trained a standard competition detector once, froze it, and probed it with 15,000 injections across ten morphologies and five amplitudes, placed into real Green Bank backgrounds. Two directions were tested: genuine signals with morphologies other than a straight narrowband line, and interference resembling the training data. Recall did not follow the predicted ordering, and it fell as signals brightened, even for a needle of the kind the detector was trained on (from 0.590 to 0.090). One interference morphology reached a false positive rate of 0.627, comparable to the detector's own baseline recall of 0.5525 on genuine signals. Gradient‑weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad‑CAM) showed attention along the injected path in one missed family by a pre‑specified test, and visually in a second. A pre‑specified, time‑averaged ON‑OFF filter removed false alarms and genuine detections at the same rate. The detector reads only the ON panels. Since the only evidence distinguishing a genuine candidate from terrestrial interference lies in the discarded OFF panels, it cannot tell if a signal originates from the target star; it can only tell if it resembles the training data. This explains the false alarm directly; the missed signals reflect what the detector learned to recognise, which reading the OFF panels would not by itself change.

PaperId: 734, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22046.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shubham Subhnil, Yannis Belkhiter, Erik Miehling, Adam Dahlgren Lindström, Elizabeth M. Daly
Title: Effectiveness of Hidden-State Probes for Localizing Reasoning Failures
Abstract:
Verifying the final answer of a long reasoning trace may show that the trace is wrong but it does not distinguish three cases. The problem may lie beyond the model's capability, another attempt would succeed, or one step in an otherwise recoverable trace made the trace fail. Standard hidden‑state probes are trained on final‑answer correctness, a label that conflates these cases. Monte Carlo rollouts distinguish the cases and locate the failing step at additional inference cost. We test the hidden states of 4B and 8B reasoning models for the failure type and the failing step and compare each probe with the strongest baseline that uses no hidden states. On incorrect 8B traces, the confidence probe, a calibrated correctness probe at a midpoint cutoff, misses 81% of cases in which a single step makes the trace unrecoverable and 47% of cases in which another attempt would succeed. A probe with a different training design over the same states reverses the ordering of these two kinds of failure, so either ordering can be read from those states. At both scales, no single tested probe locates the failing step more accurately than a rule based only on trace length, and at 4B a probe trained to predict that step fails to outperform this rule in any of 10 runs on identical traces. The confidence probe therefore indicates that an answer is wrong, but its failure‑type ordering depends on its training design.

PaperId: 735, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22018.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi, Evan Maksud, Reyana Shahid
Title: When Models Misread Ink: Auditing VLMs for Arabic Calligraphy Recognition
Abstract:
Arabic calligraphy is a high‑stakes cultural visual domain for Muslim communities, yet VLM evaluations rarely test its fine‑grained script traditions. We audit 12 VLMs on a cleaned 1,195‑image six‑way benchmark using numeric, visual‑cue, and Diwani‑first prompts. In this closed‑set setting, the best numeric‑prompt accuracy is 60.9% for closed/API models and 47.2% for open‑weight models. The main failure is default‑label collapse: every numeric run is dominated by a single label taking 33‑63% of predictions, against an 18.8% majority‑class baseline. For 8 of 12 models the default is Thuluth; GPT‑4o labels 52.9% of all images as Thuluth although it is only 18.1% of the set. Prompting helps unevenly: visual cues move accuracy by more than 10 points for some models but hurt others, and foregrounding Diwani often relocates the default rather than removing it. Arabic calligraphy recognition is therefore a compact, culturally grounded stress test for VLM robustness and for measuring which visual traditions become legible to automated systems.

PaperId: 736, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22009.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi, Reyana Shahid, Evan Maksud
Title: Visual Sanad: Auditing Vision-Language Models for False Acceptance of Qur'anic Citations
Abstract:
Vision‑language models (VLMs) are increasingly used to interpret religious, educational, and culturally sensitive visual content, yet their reliability on citation verification remains underexplored. We introduce Visual Sanad, a controlled benchmark for testing whether VLMs falsely accept incorrect Qur'anic verse attributions when the same quote‑reference pair is rendered under different visual framings.
