The benchmark contains 2,400 rendered images built from 100 English Qur'an verses, four factual states per verse, and six visual conditions ranging from plain text to decorative and authority‑framed layouts. All quote‑reference pairs were source‑checked and human‑audited before rendering. Across 24 full model‑prompt runs, we observe a sharp capability split. Proprietary API‑served VLMs range from near‑perfect citation verification to moderate false acceptance, whereas recent open‑weight VLMs often show weak discrimination and default to VALID on most images. De‑biased prompting can reduce false acceptance, but often by shifting the decision threshold toward INVALID rather than by producing strong citation discrimination. Visual Sanad therefore exposes a culturally grounded multimodal factuality failure: fluent VLMs may treat displayed religious citations as self‑authenticating unless they have strong citation‑verification ability.

PaperId: 737, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21984.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhao Yang, Zezhong Qian, Yinan Shi, Longjun Liu, Yawei Jueluo
Title: GRID-Planner: Graph-Structured Relational Reward Shaping for Diffusion Planning
Abstract:
Autonomous driving planning requires selecting trajectories that remain safe, rule‑compliant, and comfortable under complex multi‑agent interactions, yet robust closed‑loop decision making in planning‑critical scenes remains challenging. Existing diffusion‑ and RL‑based planners often rely on generic rewards and use relational structure mainly for representation, limiting how planning‑critical rollouts shape policy improvement. We present GRID‑Planner, a graph‑‑reward integrated diffusion planning framework that aligns generative planning with structured relational signals. Specifically, GRID‑Planner combines graph‑aware importance weighting, a time‑indexed relational reward surrogate, and an advantage‑weighted diffusion objective with on‑policy self‑distillation, forming a rollout‑return‑advantage‑update loop without explicit likelihoods. Experiments on nuPlan and interPlan show that, compared with the diffusion‑only baseline, GRID‑Planner reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8%, 60.8%, and 27.4%, respectively, and improves the planning score by 3.4%. Project website: https://github.com/yangzhaojason/GRID‑Planner.

PaperId: 738, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21913.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jon Škerlj, Sami Haddadin
Title: Sub-Millisecond Reflexes for Continuous Physical Human-Robot Interaction
Abstract:
Continuous physical human‑robot interaction requires robots to rapidly adapt their control behaviour without interrupting task execution. However, existing ROS 2 control architectures rely on stop‑to‑switch mechanisms that introduce substantial delays and interrupt execution. We present an open‑source, sub‑millisecond reflex engine based on an enhanced ROS 2‑compatible multimode controller that enables deterministic switching between control modalities and integrates reflex behaviours for mitigating contact hazards and kinematic limit violations. Experiments on a Franka Robotics manipulator demonstrate switching delays below 0.1 ms, more than four orders of magnitude faster than conventional ros2_control, while maintaining continuous operation during safety‑critical events. In a multi‑stage manipulation task, the proposed framework reduced execution time by 3.5% and peak trajectory jerk by more than threefold. By eliminating runtime middleware overhead, controller transitions are implemented as lock‑free pointer operations, enabling reflex‑level responsiveness within an open‑source robotics framework.

PaperId: 739, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21896.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wenzhe Wang
Title: Self-Calibrated Subspace Robust PCA for Parameter-Free Removal of Mixed Noise and Line Stripes in Hyperspectral Images
Abstract:
Hyperspectral images (HSIs) are often corrupted by Gaussian noise, impulses and stripes whose intensities vary across bands. The representative coefficient correlated total variation (RCCTV) model restores HSIs efficiently, but it lacks Gaussian and stripe terms, and its noise‑aware extensions require the noise level and a stripe budget to be specified in advance. This article proposes a self‑calibrated RCCTV (SC‑RCCTV) model, in which the noise parameters are estimated adaptively during the iterations. A band‑wise dense term and line‑constant column and row stripe terms are introduced into RCCTV. The noise level of each band is initialized by a stripe‑invariant median absolute deviation estimator and refined online from the residual, which turns the separation of sparse and dense noise into a band‑adaptive Huber loss, and the stripe thresholds follow from a significance test whose false‑alarm rate can be predicted analytically. No parameter is tuned for a specific image, and every subproblem of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) solver is solved in closed form. Under line stripes, SC‑RCCTV outperforms the parameter‑free FastHyMix by 8.17 dB on native‑size cubes, and, without any noise information, it exceeds S3TTV, which is given the true noise parameters, by 1.52 dB while running more than 1,900 times faster. On average, it stays within 0.01 dB of the same model given the true noise levels, and its online calibration improves on a two‑stage estimate‑then‑denoise scheme. Experiments on real Indian Pines and Urban data further delineate its scope for stripes that do not span entire lines.

PaperId: 740, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21893.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Weiting Liu, Zhiyu Pan, Shuhong Wang, Zhenquan Yao, Jungang Li, Li Zhao, Jian Jiang, Jianfeng Feng, Ai Han, Wenlian Lu
Title: GACC-Bench: Benchmarking Goal-Adaptive Context Compression Ability across Large Language Models
Abstract:
Context compression in long‑running applications of large language models (LLMs) must preserve goal‑relevant information, often before specific downstream questions are known. We introduce GACC‑Bench, a benchmark for Goal‑Adaptive Context Compression that evaluates how reliably LLMs adapt information retention to specified high‑level goals. For each source context, we derive one or more high‑level goals by grouping source‑grounded questions according to shared downstream objectives. The benchmark contains 500 goals and 2,571 questions over 281 document and agent‑trace contexts from seven collections spanning diverse domains, with all instances reviewed by human experts. The compressor receives a source context, a goal, and a context‑length budget, with the associated evaluation questions withheld. A fixed reader answers these questions individually using the same compressed context. Our evaluation of ten LLM compressors reveals substantial gaps to full‑context performance even for the best‑performing model, particularly in supporting correct answers to every question associated with a goal. Compared with goal‑agnostic compression, target‑goal conditioning consistently improves accuracy, whereas mismatched‑goal conditioning reduces it. GACC‑Bench is available at https://github.com/weiting24/GACC‑Bench.

PaperId: 741, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21892.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Povilas Daniušis
Title: Graph Dirichlet Energy for Fitting-Free Bivariate Causal Inference
Abstract:
We propose the Graph Dirichlet Energy Causal Inference (GDECI) criterion for distinguishing cause from effect in bivariate settings. For a candidate direction X\to Y, we construct a kernel similarity graph from X and treat Y as a graph signal. The score is the Dirichlet energy of this signal, induced by the unnormalized graph Laplacian. The reverse score swaps the variables, and the lower‑energy direction is inferred as causal. The method requires neither regression fitting nor independence testing. After the empirical probability integral transform, its decisions are invariant under strictly monotone transformations of either variable, and the graph operations reduce to convolutions, allowing exact evaluation in O(n\log n) time and O(n) memory. At the population level, GDECI compares degree‑weighted Bayes squared prediction errors plus a non‑negative smoothness term of the regression function. As the bandwidth tends to zero, the weights become uniform and the smoothness term vanishes, reducing the criterion to a RECI‑type comparison of expected conditional variances in copula space. Empirically, we compare GDECI with QCCD, GRCI, CAM, IGCI (two variants), RESIT, LOCI, QPE‑k, and RECI (two variants), in accuracy on 1899 cause‑‑effect pairs and in inference speed. GDECI ranked fifth of eleven methods in macro‑averaged accuracy on 12 synthetic suites (0.776). On the real‑world Tuebingen pairs, it ranked third in unweighted accuracy (0.684) and fifth in weighted accuracy (0.678). It was also the fastest of the compared methods up to n\approx10^4. The accompanying code repository: https://github.com/povidanius/gdeci.

PaperId: 742, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21850.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yiqun Zhao, Binbin Huang, Haobin Duan, Zibo Zhao, Shenghua Gao
Title: Seeing Both the Forest and the Trees: Reusing Holistic 3D Priors for Part-Decomposed Generation
Abstract:
Generating 3D assets with explicit parts requires two properties at once: geometric detail inside each part and structural coherence across the whole object. Recent image‑conditioned 3D generation models adopt a structured 3D representation that anchors tokens to explicit spatial positions, capturing both properties, but their output remains a single fused mesh. We ask how a part‑decomposed generation model can inherit both properties of these holistic priors, and answer with STRUCTPARTS, a framework whose core technical contribution is a dual‑frame coordinate interleaving mechanism: each shape latent is interpreted under both a part‑local and an object‑global reference frame, and processed through a global‑local inter‑leaved transformer that simultaneously reuses the prior's geometric detail at the part scale and its structural coherence at the whole‑object scale. As its structural input, STRUCTPARTS uses a segmented mesh scaffold, a coarse mesh paired with a face‑level segmentation mask kept entirely within the prior's native 3D representation. With only lightweight finetuning, both intra‑part detail and inter‑part coherence emerge from the same pretrained weights. On PartObjaverse‑Tiny, STRUCTPARTS matches or surpasses prior part‑decomposed models at a fraction of their training cost, while naturally supporting part‑mesh refinement and part‑level editing.

PaperId: 743, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21845.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mathias Lowes, Kristine Aavild Sørensen, Maxime Sermesant, Rasmus R. Paulsen
Title: Temporal Periodic Image Registration with Implicit Neural Representations
Abstract:
Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) have recently gained popularity for their ability to model functions using simple and lightweight networks. These methods have also proven effective in deformable image registration. In this work, we extend INRs for deformable image registration to the domain of temporal image registration, focusing on periodic temporal image sequences. Our approach, Temporal‑IDIR, optimizes a single INR to model deformations across all frames in a temporal image sequence simultaneously, allowing for self‑regularization through its own deformation predictions. To achieve this, we introduce a temporal consistency loss that penalizes discrepancies between direct source‑to‑target transformations and those traversing intermediate frames. We evaluate our framework on the DIR‑LAB dataset, using the target registration error (TRE) between annotated and moved landmarks as the metric. Here, we achieve a TRE of 1.03 mm, outperforming other INR‑based registration methods. Additionally, our framework supports smooth interpolation between time frames by estimating deformations between the given input frames. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/MMLowes/Temporal_INR.

PaperId: 744, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21843.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Cristian Curaba, Stefano Grimaz
Title: Series and Parallel Dependency Links: Vitality for Interdependent Networks of Networks
Abstract:
In a network of networks, a dependency link runs from a supplier to the node it serves and binds the supplier's failure to the node's failure. Indices computed from the graph topology leave aside the service each edge carries, but in real interdependent systems that service decides how failure propagates: a pumping station requires electricity and telemetry, and losing either stops it; a district fed by either of two reservoirs survives the loss of one. Building on this observation, we label each node of the network with the service it provides. We then measure how far this qualitative input can change the node's vitality ranking: by fixing the graph topology we show that changing only the labels moves the Mean Operativity Loss from 0.023 to 0.114, while a ranking computed from the unlabelled graph topology is blind to the difference. The links give a node its suppliers; the labels group those suppliers into alternatives within one service and joint requirements across services. These labels should belong to the description of an interdependent system alongside the links themselves for a fidelity vitality measure

PaperId: 745, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21791.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Huan Zhang, Mingju Chen, Dongxu Zhou, Can Lv, Sen Cui, Faguo Wu, Shiji Zhou
Title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
Abstract:
Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi‑hop question answering. Existing self‑improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self‑improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self‑improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose RSIFlow, a Recursive Self‑Improvement framework that integrates adaptive workflow orchestration with meta‑agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task‑agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component‑specific improvement workflows. The meta‑agent then distills workflow outcomes into component‑specific skills and cross‑component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta‑harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI‑Flow.

PaperId: 746, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21786.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Aleksandr Evgrashin, Carolin Schmitt, Timo Lübbing, Ashutosh Jha, Buket Naz Zeren, Sophie K. Bauer, Johannes Kopf-Beck, Anton K. G. Marx, Anamaria Semm, Gökce Ergün, Senya Polikovsky
Title: NICE Toolbox: Nonverbal Interpersonal Communication Exploration Toolbox
Abstract:
Understanding human communication is a long‑standing goal in psychological research. People express themselves through many verbal and nonverbal channels: posture, gesture, gaze, facial expression, and speech. Measurement and annotation of these signals has traditionally required time‑consuming manual work by trained human labellers. The Nonverbal Interpersonal Communication Exploration (NICE) Toolbox is a free, open‑source Python framework that automatically measures these signals by combining existing state‑of‑the‑art computer vision and speech‑processing methods into a single software package. It includes support for multi‑camera systems, interchangeable detection algorithms, 2D and 3D visualization of detector outputs, evaluation on the user's custom data, and export to third‑party software. With the release of this tool, we aim to make data exploration of interpersonal communication signals scalable, reproducible, and accessible for psychological research.

PaperId: 747, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21779.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xin Zhang, Robby T. Tan
Title: FuseAdapt: Parameter-Efficient Multimodal Fusion for Semantic Segmentation with Missing Modalities
Abstract:
Multi‑modal semantic segmentation benefits from complementary sensors, but this benefit is fragile when some modalities are degraded or missing at test time. Many existing methods rely on dedicated fusion modules or multi‑branch cross‑modal encoders, and the fusion often becomes unreliable when modalities are absent, leading to substantial performance drops. We propose FuseAdapt, a parameter‑efficient framework that performs fusion within the adaptation space of a frozen vision foundation model (VFM), exploring whether VFM priors can serve as an effective shared backbone for multi‑modal segmentation. Instead of attaching a standalone fusion network, FuseAdapt assigns each modality a lightweight adaptation branch and performs \emphadaptation‑space fusion by keeping Q/V low‑rank adaptation private to each modality and routing only FFN low‑rank residual activations across modalities inside the frozen backbone. The pretrained VFM remains fixed while modality‑specific corrections and explicit cross‑modal interaction are learned through the adaptation paths. To handle missing modalities, we further introduce Predictive Modality Modeling (PMM), a direct representation‑level objective for cross‑modal redundancy. During training, PMM masks a target modality and predicts its embedding from the visible ones, supervised by a teacher target computed under full‑modality input. PMM is used only during training and adds no inference‑time overhead. Across three multi‑modal segmentation benchmarks (MCubeS, DELIVER, MUSES), FuseAdapt consistently improves both modality‑complete and modality‑incomplete segmentation with a small trainable budget, yielding up to +3.01 mIoU under full modalities and +12.56 mIoU under missing modalities over prior state‑of‑the‑art. Project page: https://devinxzhang.github.io/FuseAdapt‑Page/.

PaperId: 748, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21758.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kehao Zhou, Yixuan Li, Yuxuan Jiang, Fan Zhang
Title: Beyond Source Prompts: Towards Visually Grounded AI-Generated Video Quality Assessment
Abstract:
Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have accelerated video generation technologies. However, AI‑generated videos (AIGVs) remain susceptible to various distortions, highlighting the need for dedicated video quality assessment methods. Content semantics play an important role in AIGV quality assessment, with source prompts typically used as textual references. However, these prompts may not accurately reflect the generated video content, resulting in a discrepancy between the intended textual description and the generated result. To address this limitation, this paper proposes VGCap, an AIGV quality assessment framework guided by visually grounded captions that align better with generated content. Specifically, we introduce two forms of captions: a global caption obtained by minimally revising the source prompt based on multi‑frame visual evidence, and prompt‑independent segment captions that describe localized temporal content. Together, these captions provide complementary textual evidence for assessing spatial quality, temporal quality, and text‑video alignment. Experimental results on the LGVQ and FETV datasets show that VGCap outperforms representative baselines across all three dimensions. Further ablation studies on caption sources and temporal components confirm the effectiveness of visually grounded captions for each quality dimension, while highlighting the benefits of segment‑level features for temporal quality prediction. The source of VGCap will be available at https://github.com/lolo123‑123/VGCap.

PaperId: 749, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21731.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Owen Walters, Lihu Chen, Francesca Toni
Title: Retrieved but Not Read: Understanding Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail to Use Available Evidence
Abstract:
Web search allows LLMs to access up‑to‑date information, but it remains unclear why they sometimes produce outdated answers even when relevant evidence is available. To study this problem, we construct temporal facts whose values changed after the models' training cutoffs. We evaluate one proprietary model under deployed web search and six open‑weight model configurations under controlled retrieval. We find that models often answer from search snippets without opening the source pages, which is associated with higher rates of outdated answers and unfaithful citations. Our controlled experiments and layer‑wise analysis reveal a gap between the availability of evidence and its effective use. Even when retrieved evidence influences internal predictions, models may still favour outdated information in their final answers. We hope these findings will help advance research on the reliable use of retrieved evidence in search‑augmented LLMs.

PaperId: 750, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21681.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuanjian Xu, Jianing Hao, Tianze Sun, Yongyao Duan, Sam Chen, Jinyi Han, Wanbo Zhang, Yuxuan Sun, Guang Zhang, Zhong Li
Title: Data Strategies for Large Language Models: A Unified Perspective on the Training Lifecycle
Abstract:
Data strategy plays a central role in training large language models (LLMs). It governs the selection, weighting, and scheduling of training data, thereby determining the capabilities a model can acquire from a fixed data budget. We treat high‑quality data as having high training‑dependent utility, which depends on the target objective, the model, and its training state rather than on the text alone. Research in this area now spans pretraining and post‑training, but related ideas use inconsistent terminology and evaluation protocols. This work reviews data strategies across the training lifecycle and formulates them as policies that allocate a training budget over candidate examples. We organise methods by their decision granularity, model dependence, and temporal adaptivity, then compare their computational requirements and empirical support. Fine‑grained or state‑dependent policies offer more control but incur additional scoring, search, or rollout costs. Evidence for transfer across model scales and comparable end‑to‑end cost remains limited. A continuously updated list of papers, along with their public implementations, is available at https://github.com/xuyj233/data_strategy_survey.

PaperId: 751, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21668.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chanwoo Kim, Tackgeun You, Hwasup Lim
Title: Edit4D: Editable 4D Scene Generation with Textual Control
Abstract:
We introduce Edit4D, an editable text‑to‑4D scene generation framework that constructs 4D scenes from separate background and dynamic character representations. Recent advances in generative models have enabled text‑driven dynamic scene synthesis, but editable 4D scene generation remains challenging due to the need to preserve spatial geometry and temporal dynamics. Existing approaches typically generate holistic scene videos, where the background and dynamic characters are coupled, making object‑level editing and flexible camera control difficult. Edit4D addresses these limitations through a stage‑specific generation pipeline. Given a user instruction, Edit4D first decomposes it into stage‑specific prompts for background, dynamic character, and scene‑character composition. Using these prompts, we synthesize multi‑view scene images with text‑to‑image and camera‑conditioned generative priors and reconstruct a background 3D Gaussian splatting representation. We then generate a character image, animate it with an image‑conditioned video prior, reconstruct a 4D mesh, and bind Gaussian primitives to obtain a character representation. Finally, both components are composed through text‑guided segmentation and contact‑aware optimization. A global scene refinement is then performed to improve harmonization and rendering consistency. By integrating stage‑specific components, Edit4D enables controllable camera motion, flexible object‑level editing, and the practical construction of editable 4D scenes. Project page: https://chanwo0kim.github.io/Edit4D/

PaperId: 752, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21656.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Zhanli Li, Zeyuan Xu, Chaoxu Pang, Zeyuan Liu, Anyang Ji, Te Sun, Kongcheng Zhang, Wenbo Xu, Xubin Yue, Shipeng Luo, Junjie Zhao, Yingfan Hua, Jingqing Ruan, Zhongda Su, Feng Hong, Zhizhao Zeng, Ke Zeng, Xunliang Cai, Hanjia Ye
Title: Data World: Scaling Data Environments from Scratch
Abstract:
Data agents use code to process heterogeneous files and derive analytical insights. Scaling their training faces costly environment curation, privacy and intellectual‑property restrictions, and difficulty verifying open‑ended findings without known generative truth. Our core insight is to specify the world behind the files before generating the files themselves. We introduce Data World, a multi‑agent engine that synthesizes environments, tasks, and rubrics from explicit mechanisms. Independent audits check target recoverability from observed files; rubrics support evaluation and RL rewards. Human preference‑based curation for question realism selects 100 tasks across 50 held‑out worlds and 16 domains for DataWorld‑Bench. The engine also yields 2,135 training tasks from 1,037 disjoint worlds. Evaluation of ten frontier models shows that the benchmark remains challenging, particularly for insight discovery, with a consistent computation‑insight gap. RL‑zero training on the synthesized tasks produces DataWorld‑35B‑A3B from Qwen3.6‑35B‑A3B without trajectory distillation. Under matched evaluation, it improves over its base by 7.06 points on DataWorld‑Bench, 14.28 on DAComp, 20.90 on DABstep‑Hard, and 12.13 on JobBench, a broader occupational benchmark.

PaperId: 753, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21654.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Asanobu Kitamoto, Victor Le Louarn, Noelia Falczuk, Ngoc Anh Tong, Anja Veleva
Title: Digital Typhoon Dataset V3: Benchmarking for Multi-spectral Extension and Analyzing Systematic Bias in Intensity Regression
Abstract:
This paper presents the Digital Typhoon Dataset V3, a new version of the longest typhoon satellite image dataset spanning nearly 50 years, designed to benchmark machine learning models on long‑term spatio‑temporal data. The latest addition to Dataset V3 is multispectral satellite data, enabling multi‑channel models. We investigate data‑splitting strategies and present benchmarking results for the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Experimental results show that, under the current dataset construction and experimental setting, multi‑channel inputs do not clearly outperform single‑channel inputs for pressure regression. Among the evaluated model architectures, image types, and spectral channels, ResNet‑18, full‑resolution images, and Channel 1 generally provide the best single‑channel performance for pressure regression. Performance also differs between the WP and AU datasets by regression target, with lower RMSE on WP for pressure regression and on AU for wind regression. These results highlight the importance of considering dataset‑specific and task‑specific characteristics when interpreting benchmark performance. Additionally, we analyzed systematic bias in intensity regression, which leads to underestimation of intensity for strong typhoons. We tested imbalance‑aware weighting strategies, including inverse‑density weighting inspired by BalancedMSE, and showed that these approaches are not sufficient to remove the bias. The dataset is publicly available at http://agora.ex.nii.ac.jp/digital‑typhoon/dataset/ and https://github.com/kitamoto‑lab/digital‑typhoon/.

PaperId: 754, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21633.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Florian Mai, David Kaczér
Title: ContextLift: Breaking the Spurious Correlation Behind Conditional Emergent Misalignment
Abstract:
Finetuning a language model on narrowly misaligned data can make it broadly misaligned. Interleaving generic safety data is the most effective known in‑training defense, but the misalignment returns as soon as a prompt resembles the finetuning context. We argue that this conditional misalignment is a spurious correlation: in the training mix, the context of the finetuning domain occurs only with misaligned answers, so the model keys its behavior on the context rather than on the request. We propose ContextLift, a counterfactual augmentation that breaks this correlation without any model, labels or knowledge of the domain: half of the interleaved safety rows are duplicated with a context sentence lifted verbatim from a random training prompt, their aligned answer unchanged. On Qwen2.5‑7B finetuned on bad security, legal and medical advice, generic interleaving leaves 18.9%, 41.9% and 58.2% misaligned answers under a domain cue; ContextLift reduces this to 2.6%, 6.1% and 12.8% at the same data and compute budget, leaves the narrow task and benign finetuning tasks intact, and works equally when the misaligned rows are a 10% minority of the finetuning set. Code: https://github.com/davidkaczer/contextlift

PaperId: 755, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21624.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yuanjian Xu, Jinyi Han, Jianing Hao, Yuxuan Sun, Fanyang Lu, Richeng Xuan, Guang Zhang, Zhichao Hu
Title: AgentPerturb: Evaluating LLM Agent Robustness under Controlled Interaction Perturbations
Abstract:
Real‑world tasks are often complex and noisy, posing substantial challenges for LLM agents. Yet existing evaluations lack a systematic framework for jointly characterizing potential perturbation targets and types. We use this two‑dimensional view to conduct a unified study that quantifies the robustness of current frontier models, traces the mechanisms behind perturbation‑induced failures, and draws implications for robustness‑oriented training. Through controlled evaluations on APEX‑Agents and Toolathlon, we find that perturbations consistently degrade performance, while the dominant vulnerabilities vary across task environments. Trajectory‑level analysis reveals that agents rarely recognize altered inputs and often propagate corrupted information without verification. A focused cost analysis further shows that successful perturbed trajectories can require substantially more computation. These findings motivate training objectives that cover diverse forms of noise and reward verification, uncertainty awareness, and recovery. We provide a rigorous benchmark‑construction pipeline. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/xuyj233/AgentPerturb.

PaperId: 756, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21621.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zewen Wu, Ruizhe Liu, Pei Zhou, Feng Chen, Yanchao Yang
Title: SPEAR: Selective Preference Elicitation with Adaptive Rewards for VLM-Guided Robotic Manipulation
Abstract:
Recent Vision‑Language Models (VLMs) enable automated preference labeling for robotic manipulation, yet their deployment remains impractical since each query incurs substantial inference cost, while VLMs frequently abstain on visually challenging comparisons. We propose SPEAR, a framework that transforms VLMs into efficient preference oracles via two synergistic mechanisms. First, we design distinguishability‑aware query selection to reduce abstention rates by targeting only informative and distinguishable comparisons. Second, we deploy an adaptive reward transition that bootstraps exploration with VLM‑synthesized guidance before preference‑based refinement. Experiments on the manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that SPEAR achieves 88.9% average success, outperforming baselines by 23.3 percentage points, while significantly reducing abstention and wall‑clock training time on contact‑rich tasks. SPEAR learns three Mobile ALOHA manipulation tasks fully online on real hardware, demonstrating end‑to‑end real‑world applicability. By addressing query efficiency and exploration challenges, SPEAR establishes VLMs as practical preference oracles for scalable robot learning without manual reward engineering.

PaperId: 757, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21619.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sibaek Lee, Kyeongsu Kang, Seongbo Ha, Yewon Jeon, Joonyeol Choi, Daegeol Ko, Jaehyuk Hur, Taemin Choi, Minsu Kim, Hyungjoo Ahn, Wonsok Yoo, Hyeonwoo Yu
Title: Training-Free Target-Aware Refinement of 3D Gaussian Language Map
Abstract:
Distilling vision‑language features into 3D Gaussian Splatting yields a language map that can be queried with arbitrary text. In deployment, however, a small set of user‑specified targets must be reliably located, which current distilled maps often miss, while open‑vocabulary queryability for other words must remain intact. We propose a training‑free, target‑aware refinement of an already‑distilled language map. Guided by a text‑promptable segmenter, the visual embedding inside each detected target region is blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient sets the amount of injected prior, while non‑target regions are left untouched. Injecting too much overwrites appearance cues and general queryability, so we seek, for each target, the smallest coefficient that still lets it win, and we obtain every coefficient in closed form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. We further identify a failure mode of injection in language‑goal localization. Text embeddings share a common component, and injecting them makes the standard cosine read‑out query‑agnostic, which a centering step in the read‑out removes. Across three benchmarks, the refinement consistently improves open‑vocabulary segmentation, roughly doubling the base mIoU on Replica, and localizes language goals more reliably than the base map. It also transfers as a plug‑in to off‑the‑shelf field‑based and object‑level language maps and supports a real‑world demonstration in which a legged robot navigates to natural‑language goals. Project page and code: https://lab‑of‑ai‑and‑robotics.github.io/target‑aware‑langmap/

PaperId: 758, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21573.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Islam Mesabah, Sary Elmansoury, Gerrit Großmann, Peter Neigel, Sebastian J. Vollmer
Title: MYOPIA: Understanding the Limits of Tree-Based Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
Abstract:
Decision trees can make vision‑language model (VLM) classification interpretable by replacing a single prediction with a sequence of root‑to‑leaf questions. However, the accuracy cost of this greedy, non‑backtracking procedure remains unclear. We introduce MYOPIA, a benchmark comprising four LLM‑generated, human‑refined decision trees for GTSRB, MNIST, CIFAR‑10, and MSCOCO, together with matched prompts, diagnostic protocols, and an evaluation harness. Across GPT‑4o, Qwen‑VL Max, and LLaMA‑3.2 11B Vision, tree traversal underperforms zero‑shot prompting in all 12 dataset‑‑model pairs; paired bootstrap analyses consistently favor zero‑shot. Our diagnostics characterize interacting failure modes associated with this gap. Models often recall tree‑encoded class attributes more accurately than they ground the same attributes in images: the mean label‑‑image accuracy gaps are 9.5, 13.8, and 12.6 points for GPT‑4o, Qwen‑VL Max, and LLaMA, respectively. Incorrect local decisions then irreversibly exclude the correct class, while answer extraction introduces additional model‑dependent loss. A node‑level audit of the four trees finds that split entropy is weakly but consistently associated with lower node accuracy, whereas depth, branching factor, and within‑node grounding differences are less stable. MYOPIA therefore provides a framework for diagnosing hierarchical visual classification and motivates testing tree designs that prioritize perceptual answerability and recovery from early errors. Code is available at https://github.com/islammesabah/VLM_Classification.

PaperId: 759, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21565.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhiyuan Wang, Yuezhi Zhou, Ziqi Zhang, Zhu Zhang, Zhixing Tan, Yongheng Deng
Title: BiShield-TEE: On the (In-)Security of Unilateral Weight Obfuscation in On-Device TEE-Shielded LLM Partition
Abstract:
On‑device deployment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly adopted due to latency and privacy requirements, but exposes proprietary models to reverse engineering and intellectual property theft. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) provide hardware‑enforced isolation for on‑device inference, yet most TEE‑based parameter obfuscation relies on unilateral matrix transformations that obfuscate only the output side. We identify a vulnerability in this design, termed the Solution Determinacy Property (SDP): the obfuscation secret is uniquely determined, exposing the structure of the true key and enabling attackers to break the protection. Under our attacks, representative methods GroupCover and ArrowCloak are reduced to negligible protection, with attack accuracy reaching over 2.4 times the full‑shielding black‑box baseline and recovering near‑complete model functionality. To address this vulnerability, we propose BiShield‑TEE, a bilateral framework that induces Ambiguous Solutions through joint obfuscation of input and output dimensions, hiding the true key among many equally valid candidates. Experiments across diverse models and datasets show that BiShield‑TEE confines attack accuracy to the full‑shielding black‑box baseline, while achieving higher inference efficiency than prior methods on real hardware. Our code is available at https://github.com/laduiw/BiShield‑TEE.

PaperId: 760, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21561.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sergio Burdisso, Esaú Villatoro-Tello, Dairazalia Sánchez-Cortés, Yanis Labrak, Jordi Luque, Milos Cernak, Petr Motlicek
Title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off‑track (real‑time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog‑flow‑aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

PaperId: 761, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21547.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Vasileios Perifanis, Nikolaos Pavlidis
Title: Federated Art Chase: Privacy Leakage and Data Poisoning in Federated Fine-Tuning
Abstract:
Federated learning (FL) is increasingly used to adapt a pretrained, centrally fine‑tuned model to data that remain on user devices, beyond training a model from scratch. In this report, prepared for the 4th Federated Machine Learning International Summer School, we study the privacy and integrity of this approach with a reproducible pipeline. An ImageNet‑pretrained MobileNetV4‑Conv‑Small model is fine‑tuned centrally on ten Quick, Draw! classes (97.50% test accuracy) and then adapted with head‑only FedAvg over ten non‑IID clients, which raises client training accuracy from 90.34% to 91.49% while preserving global accuracy. We evaluate four adversarial scenarios. First, from a single one‑step client update, an honest‑but‑curious server recovers the complete private label set, but its reconstructions follow class prototypes rather than the private drawings (mean SSIM 0.130). Second, from a one‑round FedAvg aggregate, label‑count recovery falls from 87.5% with one client to 75.0% with five and ten clients, below the 80.0% of an uninformed uniform guess. Third, under FedAvg, a backdoor injected by 30%, 50%, and 100% of the clients reaches an attack success rate (ASR) of 21.9%, 31.3%, and 54.7% at a cost of at most 0.8 percentage points of clean accuracy, whereas label flipping is effective only when most of the source‑class data are relabeled. Fourth, FLTrust with a root set retained from centralized fine‑tuning lowers the backdoor ASR to 1.8% and 4.0% at 30% and 50% malicious clients and the label‑flipping ASR from 12.6% to 0.8% without measurable clean‑accuracy loss, but provides no protection when every client is malicious. The report closes with a live session in which participants draw, fine‑tune, and poison the model through Indigma's FedMaestro orchestrator. Code and executed notebooks, runnable on Google Colab, are at https://github.com/Indigma‑Innovations/fl‑summer‑school.

PaperId: 762, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21539.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhiyuan Ma, Jiabao Wei, Tianyu Wang, Hanqing Wang, Jiadong Pan, Haowen Xu, Liangliang Zhao, Ruixun Liu, Yuhan Wang, Yuwei Zhang, Liang Feng, Junhao Xiao, Kaiyan Zhang, Xuekai Zhu, Daizong Liu, Biqing Qi, Yihao Liu, Ganqu Cui, Ning Ding, Linfeng Zhang, Jianjun Li, Kun He, Xiang Bai, Bowen Zhou
Title: Reinforcement Learning-driven Diffusion Models: Language, Vision, and Beyond
Abstract:
Diffusion models (DMs) have steadily demonstrated outstanding performance in high‑fidelity, controllable generation across diverse scenarios, following the "pretraining‑finetuning" paradigm established in LLMs. Despite these advances, conventional DMs still face critical limitations in sophisticated reasoning, autonomous exploration of generation pathways, and adaptability to complex, human‑aligned objectives. Inspired by RLHF's success in LLMs, RL has recently emerged as a pivotal post‑training mechanism to iteratively refine DMs through reward‑driven trajectory optimization. This paper presents the first comprehensive review of RL‑driven DMs and an empirical analysis of how RL reshapes the diffusion process towards experience‑centric, goal‑directed generation. We propose a novel technical panorama elucidating RL's multifaceted roles in diffusion‑based language, multimodal, robotic, and scientific models, with a granular focus on diffusion trajectory optimization and reward engineering. Through extensive experiments on multiple task‑specific benchmarks, we systematically evaluate representative methods to intuitively highlight the advantages of different RL post‑training strategies. Furthermore, we reveal and dissect three crucial bottlenecks that currently hinder the real‑world deployment of RL‑driven DMs: reward design fragility, exploration‑exploitation trade‑off in high‑dimensional generation spaces, and training instability under sparse rewards. Based on these perspectives, we provide a principled roadmap for the integration of RL into DMs and outline promising future research directions for robust, interpretable RL‑diffusion systems. We also construct a public repository to continuously track the latest developments in this rapidly evolving field: https://github.com/MAIR‑Lab‑HUST/Awesome‑RL‑for‑Diffusion‑Models.

PaperId: 763, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21515.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zejian Kang, Yifu Luo, Boyang Shen, Jingxuan Li, Zekai Chen, Zekun Shi, Yongxue Xu, Zhenyu Hou, Bingqian Wu, Shaolei Zhang, Wentao Yang, Xiangru Huang
Title: TRACE: Typed Reference-Aware Conversational Editing for Humanoid Motion Diffusion
Abstract:
Language‑conditioned humanoid motion generation enables users to create and refine robot movements through natural language. The central challenge is to connect an underspecified request to concrete motion structure that can subsequently be revised relative to an accepted reference. We present TRACE, a generation and editing framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid robot built around typed, measurable kinematic quantities. Our insight is to ground generation conditions in paired training motions and editing goals in the current motion. A language model learns to predict support, root, and hand events from motion‑derived supervision; their time‑aligned encodings complement the original text in a diffusion generator. Gravity‑referenced states and trajectory‑‑contact objectives improve kinematic consistency. For editing, typed requests define body‑‑time scopes and source‑relative goals. A separate reference‑conditioned diffusion editor uses these goals and revised events to realize changes, while sampling‑time projection preserves protected state coordinates. Quantitative evaluation and human assessment show improved semantic alignment and motion quality over the compared methods. Multi‑turn editing evaluations demonstrate more reliable execution of successive relative requests under shared preservation constraints. Code is available at https://github.com/Multimodal‑Perception‑Action/TRACE.

PaperId: 764, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21468.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Syed Rifat Raiyan, Md. Tariquzzaman, Md Farhan Ishmam, Tenghao Huang
Title: Can LLMs Tell Stories Out of Order? A Corpus and Benchmark for Nonlinear Narrative Generation
Abstract:
Every story has two orders: the order in which its events happen and the order in which they are told. A story is nonlinear when the two differ. We introduce a benchmark of 83 published works that measures whether language models can tell nonlinear stories. For each work, we annotate one list of events in both orders, together with a story graph of causal dependencies, character knowledge, and the questions the telling raises and resolves. Given events in chronological order, all 19 models tell them, on average, more chronologically than the published works do; asked for a specific structure, they land within the human range about half the time. We then compare a model's stories of the same events under different conditions, using both an automated judge and 71 human readers. Both prefer the chronological story a model writes by default to the nonlinear one it writes on request, which readers find harder to follow in 81% of decisive judgments. Readers also prefer stories written from the story graph to stories constrained to the published telling order (72% of decisive judgments), a difference the judge does not detect. Our results suggest that following an instruction to reorder a story is not yet the same as telling it well out of order.

PaperId: 765, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21467.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wei Zeng, Ye Wang
Title: DuET: Note-Frame Dual Encoding for Piano Performance-to-Score Transcription
Abstract:
Transcribing expressive piano performances into scores requires interpreting individual note timings within an underlying metrical structure. However, score attributes are associated with notes, whereas beats may occur without coincident note onsets. We introduce DuET, a Dual‑Encoder Transformer that jointly learns note‑level performance MIDI‑to‑score (PM2S) transcription and frame‑level beat and downbeat tracking. Bidirectional cross‑attention connects note and frame encoders, while an autoregressive decoder alternates between their representations to predict structured score attributes. We further introduce TimeRoPE and Time‑Pitch Rotary Positional Encoding (TPRoPE) to establish a shared performance‑time reference and explicitly encode relative temporal and pitch relationships. Evaluations on ASAP, a classical piano dataset, and our curated Gangqinpu dataset, which spans multiple genres with a focus on popular piano music, demonstrate improvements in score timing and notated duration. Compared with the strongest baseline on each dataset, DuET reduces MUSTER mean error from 6.56% to 3.64% on Gangqinpu and from 11.30% to 11.22% on ASAP. Ablations support the benefits of frame‑level context, time‑based positional encoding, and decoder‑history masking. Code, weights, and demos are available at https://github.com/wei‑zeng98/DuET.

PaperId: 766, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21466.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hui Yang, Ziyu Li, Xuan Liu, Anders Jarfors, He Tan, Jiaoyan Chen
Title: Ontology Refinement with Embeddings and LLMs: A Case Study on CASTON
Abstract:
Ontologies are widely used to represent and organize complex knowledge in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare. However, constructing reliable ontologies remains challenging, as class hierarchies, whether manually or automatically constructed, may contain subtle subsumption errors that require careful refinement. We study this problem in CASTON, a casting‑domain ontology, and present a lightweight but scalable refinement workflow that combines a fine‑tuned ontology embedding model with Large Language Models (LLMs). The embedding model is used to extract a limited number of candidate axioms for refinement together with possible replacement candidates, and an LLM then returns repair suggestions. In a small expert evaluation, the default configuration using a CASTON‑fine‑tuned OnT embedding model and Qwen3‑8B produced reliable high‑confidence repairs: all six high‑confidence replacements were accepted by both domain experts. The implementation is available at https://github.com/HuiYang1997/OntRefine.

PaperId: 767, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21457.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Revanth Reddy Lingala, K. Gangadhara Rao, Padigela Srujan, Saarthak Manocha, Vainavi Venkat
Title: Benchmarking Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation in S3-Compatible Object Storage under Client Concurrency
Abstract:
Data encrypted today with classical public‑key algorithms could be decrypted once large quantum computers exist. Cloud object stores keep data for years, so the client‑side encryption that protects it must move to post‑quantum algorithms such as ML‑KEM, which adds a key‑encapsulation step and a larger ciphertext to every stored object. So far, the cost of ML‑KEM has been measured for the algorithm on its own and for securing network connections, but not for encrypting each object in a storage system that serves many clients at once. It has therefore been unclear whether ML‑KEM slows such a system, under which conditions, and why. We address this problem by measuring per‑object ML‑KEM against classical key exchange on an S3‑compatible object store, with two client implementations, two processor types and up to 500 concurrent workers, using pre‑registered experiments and statistical equivalence tests. ML‑KEM reduced throughput only when the client's processor was at or near full load, with one unexplained exception, and then by 4.0 to 4.9% in our main client. Controlled experiments on one processor type traced most of that loss to the way the software library was called, and a second, native client showed that the size of the loss depends on the implementation. The lasting cost is storage: 1,056 more bytes per object than with classical key exchange. The results cover two clients, one single‑node store and one cloud provider.

PaperId: 768, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21453.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zixuan Wang, Yuqi Liu, Yuxin Chen, Sengqiao Yang, Jinhui Ye, Pengguang Chen, Changsheng Lu, Shu Liu, Bei Yu, Jiaya Jia
Title: CarryOn: A Dual-Loop Harness for Personalized and Reliable Robot Assistance
Abstract:
While generalist vision‑language‑action (VLA) models have enabled diverse open‑world manipulation, real‑world robotic assistance requires two critical capabilities they currently lack: personalization and reliable execution. First, executing an instruction like "make me a sandwich" requires grounding subtask decomposition in persistent user preferences rather than relying on a single generic solution. Second, reliable deployment demands explainable safety assurance that proactively prevents hazards and gracefully recovers from occasional physical failures. To address these gaps, we present CarryOn, a dual‑loop harness designed to augment a frozen VLA policy. The planning loop maintains persistent user‑level and scene‑level context that is continually grounded against new observations and revised through interaction, enabling personalized task selection and execution grounding across conversations and changing scenes. The execution loop actively supervises policy rollouts, shielding actions from predicted hazardous contact. When execution fails, the system invokes reusable control‑based recovery skills that restore task progress and are refined through reflection on earlier failures. On a real robot and in simulation, CarryOn dispatches preference‑consistent subtasks across users and scenes, reduces the violation rate of an already safety‑finetuned VLA from 52.6% to 6.1%, and increases recovery success from 13% to 80% when refined skills are reused.

PaperId: 769, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21451.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fryderyk Kögl, Anna Reithmeir, Daniel M. Lang, Emily Chan, Rickmer Braren, Julia A. Schnabel
Title: PET Quantification-Preserving Registration for Longitudinal Whole-Body PSMA PET/CT
Abstract:
We adapt the diffeomorphic coarse‑to‑fine LapIRN architecture for longitudinal whole‑body PSMA PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge. The method combines affine pre‑registration, multi‑modal deformable registration, and test‑time instance optimization. We further introduce PET biomarker preservation losses for metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG), including Jacobian‑based constraints, and a per‑structure rigidity regularization for skeletal structures. The submitted configuration achieved 81.0% DSC and 6.17 mm HD95, with MTV and TLG errors of 3.3% and 3.3%, respectively, on our evaluation protocol. Code is available at https://github.com/koegl/psmareg.

PaperId: 770, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21450.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ruibin Ju, Ruifeng Cai, Min Xu, Lin Wang
Title: X-Fly: Learning to Reach and Stop in Full-Chunk Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
Abstract:
Aerial vision‑language navigation (VLN) agents built on large vision‑language models are expensive to query. Executing a complete predicted action chunk before replanning amortizes this cost, reducing model inference from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint for our policy. It also moves the states at which the policy is queried away from expert demonstrations, which supervise neither recovery from these states nor termination at the learner's own arrival. On OpenFly test‑seen, no‑stop failures account for 47.78% of full‑chunk behavior cloning (BC) outcomes. We present X‑Fly, a staged training framework for full‑chunk aerial VLN. Recovery DAgger labels learner‑visited decision states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in‑region state. Flow‑GRPO then jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from same‑task closed‑loop outcomes, supplemented by outcome‑verified stopping supervision. With eight controls per decision, X‑Fly reaches 74.18% SR on test‑seen and 51.73% on test‑unseen, compared with 16.45% and 18.43% for full‑chunk BC and 32.04% and 29.46% for DreamFly.

PaperId: 771, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21439.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Skylar Zhai, Haonan Wang, Zhining Liu, Linxin Song, Xuwei Ding, Jingcheng Liang, Jian Kang
Title: Each Reward to Its Relevant Tokens: Reward-Specific Token-Level Credit Assignment for Multi-Reward RL
Abstract:
Language models are increasingly trained against several verifiable rewards at once, such as the correctness and the format of a tool call, or the individual constraints of a complex instruction. Reward‑decoupled normalization (GDPO) normalizes each reward separately so that different reward combinations keep distinct advantages, but it still spreads every reward's advantage evenly over the whole response, although each verifier checks only a few positions. We propose MRTPO, which assigns the advantage of each reward to the tokens relevant to it, using the information its verifier checks, without auxiliary models or token‑level annotations. For each reward, the policy replays its own response with and without that reward's verifier information, and the per‑token Jensen‑Shannon distance between the two next‑token distributions measures each token's relevance and reassigns the advantage. On text‑to‑SQL, multi‑constraint instruction following and tool calling, MRTPO converges faster and achieves better performance than the compared methods.

PaperId: 772, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21438.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shukesh Reddy, Abhijit Das
Title: RLDF: A Region-Level Deepfake Dataset and Benchmark for Partial-Face Manipulation Detection
Abstract:
Existing deepfake detection models are built upon manipu‑ lated images that are tampered with either exclusively fully swapped or fully synthesised faces, which leads us to an open question: Can off‑the‑shelf deepfake models detect manipulation effectively while tampering is confined to a local facial sub‑region? To fill this gap, we introduce RLDF (Region‑Level Deepfake), the first dataset for region‑level deepfake evaluation. Employing the proposed region‑aware partial swap synthesis model, we generate over 2M par‑ tial face‑swap images by using eight face‑swapping meth‑ ods. Altogether, we considered seven face regions, among which there are four discrete regions (eye, nose, mouth and eyebrow) and four composite facial regions (eye and nose; eye, nose and mouth; eye, nose, mouth and eye‑ brow; and full face). In addition, we define three evalu‑ ation protocols and benchmark 12 state‑of‑the‑art detectors across the five popular standard cross‑dataset evaluations, DF40, and the proposed RLDF, providing a comprehen‑ sive audit of where and why existing detectors underper‑ formed. Our evaluation reveals that existing detectors fail to generalize consistently across partial facial regions, re‑ sulting in an overall drop of 10.5% AUC and 10% accu‑ racy under region‑level evaluation. Further, we propose a mask‑guided cross‑attention model as a baseline approach that can effectively detect region‑level manipulation. The proposed dataset, code, and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/RLDF‑Dataset/RLDF.

PaperId: 773, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21412.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Kunlun Zhu, Tao Feng, Xu Han, Heng Wang, Ling Yang, Xiangru Tang, Jiaxuan You, Heng Ji
Title: JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs
Abstract:
Large language model (LLM) agents now fix software, operate computers and serve customers, but their harnesses, the programs that run them, call a large LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly. Most of these calls end in a multiple‑choice decision, such as which tool to call next. Decision models such as Jev answer these questions directly, at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price. We ask how a harness can delegate these decisions to a decision model with little loss of success. To evaluate decision models in agentic tasks, we build AgentDecisionBench, which tests them from isolated questions up to control of a running agent, on public benchmarks and our DecisionGym environment. The decision model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, and without a fitted confidence threshold, delegating tool choices lowered success by 19.0 points. Building on these findings, we then design JevAgentHarness, which fits this threshold for each choice on the agent's own trajectories and lets the LLM decide below it. Because existing decision models never see the states an agent reaches after its own mistakes, we train AgentDecision‑4B, an open 4B model, on such states with Jev's answers as labels. On tasks unlike its training data, the agent solved 91.5% of them with AgentDecision‑4B and 82.0% with Jev. On tasks like their training data, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1‑89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster, without losing 3 or more points of task success. The models, data, and harness will be released at https://github.com/JevAgentHarness/JevAgentHarness.

PaperId: 774, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21391.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Arnab Bhattacharjee, Wayes Tushar, Tapan Kumar Saha
Title: NOCE-Net: Representation Learning for Battery Operational Context via Nested Sequence Modelling
Abstract:
Learning effective representations from battery operational history is essential for predictive health management and control‑oriented applications. Existing approaches rely on response‑dependent engineered features or short early‑life windows, limiting generalisability and precluding use in prospective settings where future responses are unavailable. We propose NOCE‑Net, a deep nested sequence model that learns control‑enabling representations directly from raw cyclic operational or telemetric data. Our data pipeline, re‑BatteryData, standardises heterogeneous aging datasets into semantically equivalent Full Equivalent Cycles (FECs) defined by absolute charge throughput, enabling end‑to‑end learning across diverse operational regimes. NOCE‑Net combines multi‑patch transformer encoders for intra‑cycle dynamics with a GRU backbone for inter‑cycle state evolution, operating on approximately 700 batteries across ten public datasets spanning over 300 operational profiles. In zero‑shot evaluation on unseen battery chemistries and usage patterns, NOCE‑Net achieves 13.7% MAPE in voltage response prediction, outperforming strong long‑sequence baselines by over 43% while using 40 × fewer parameters. Shape and component diagnostics of the learned hidden states reveal that the GRU's principal direction of evolution achieves Spearman |ρ| \geq 0.95 with the capacity fade trajectory on average across all datasets with monotone degradation profiles, including zero‑shot test batteries, providing evidence that the representations encode degradation dynamics transferable to downstream tasks beyond battery response modelling. Code is available at https://github.com/BeArnab96/NOCE‑Net.

PaperId: 775, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21389.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kehong Gong, Guanli Hou, Xiaoxu Zheng, Qi Wang, Mingxi Xu, Anbang Zhai, Xiaoyu He, Mingyuan Zhang, Michael Bi Mi
Title: Fast-VLA: You Only Think Once for Robot Manipulation
Abstract:
Vision‑language‑action (VLA) policies commonly place a multi‑billion‑parameter model inside the feedback loop, repeatedly recomputing task context whenever they predict a new action chunk. Yet task understanding changes far more slowly than the robot state. We introduce Fast‑VLA, which invokes a frozen 4B VLM once per episode to contextualize the instruction and initial views as fixed, multi‑layer key‑value task memory. During execution, a lightweight online actor fuses learned time‑ and arm‑indexed queries with current visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries retrieve task context from the fixed memory and predict action chunks without re‑running the foundation model. Fast‑VLA achieves 92.46% and 92.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean and Randomized, and 95.95% and 79.11% on LIBERO and LIBERO‑Plus evaluation. Against three continually conditioned baselines on the same hardware, it reduces RoboTwin amortized policy inference time by 10.9‑17.1x and requires 1.22 GiB of post‑prefill online resident memory. Task‑memory swaps further show that the actor relies on episode‑matched task memory. These results show that task context can be established once while closed‑loop control remains responsive throughout execution. Project page: https://garfield‑kh.github.io/FastVLA

PaperId: 776, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21383.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Vedant Pandhare, Piyush Dhoka
Title: Calibration Language Shapes Block-Influence Pruning in Multilingual Language Models
Abstract:
Block Influence (BI) ranks Transformer blocks for depth pruning from their input‑output cosine change, but the ranking depends on the calibration distribution. We study whether English calibration transfers to Indian languages in Qwen2.5‑1.5B‑Instruct, Llama‑3.2‑1B, and Gemma‑2‑2B. English, Hindi, Marathi, and Tamil use disjoint Wikipedia articles for calibration and evaluation; every selector receives the same 150‑chunk budget, and Tamil is excluded from multilingual aggregation to test cross‑script transfer. Across all three models, late‑block BI is 20.7‑55.5% higher for the three Indian languages than for English, and every predeclared late‑minus‑middle contrast has a 95% bootstrap interval above zero. This mismatch changes the low‑BI blocks selected for removal despite high global rank correlations. Averaging BI over equal English, Hindi, and Marathi budgets mitigates the resulting perplexity damage for Qwen at six removed blocks and for Gemma at all tested depths, including held‑out Tamil. The mitigation is not universal: on Llama, balancing improves Hindi and Marathi at two removed blocks but severely harms Tamil, while larger pruning budgets select the same blocks and collapse perplexity regardless of calibration. Rank‑mean and minimax‑rank aggregators do not dominate the raw mean. These results support a diagnostic claim rather than a universal pruning rule: English‑only BI systematically misses late‑layer activity for Indian‑language text, but multilingual calibration must still be validated per architecture and pruning budget.

PaperId: 777, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21362.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qixin Sun, WenLong Gao, Xiansheng Chen, Zhongyuan Wang, Si Liu, Pengwei Wang
Title: LTM: Latent Transition Based In-Context Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
Abstract:
Robotic manipulation often requires remembering interactions that are no longer visible. We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which stores history as compact latent transitions between consecutive observations. Instantiated on π_0.5 as LTM‑π, our method uses a frozen latent action encoder, a lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental inference without memory‑specific semantic annotations or external reasoning‑model calls. With DreamDojo transitions, LTM‑π achieves 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO‑Mem, performing best among baselines without external reasoning models or memory‑specific annotations. Ablations support the contribution of transition content beyond temporal cues and the efficiency of delayed memory admission. Scaling RoboMME demonstrations tenfold improves success from 57.67% to 87.50%, while a Cup Swap diagnostic highlights the role of process supervision in temporal composition. Under a 200‑token memory budget, success remains 84.00%, versus 87.50% without compression. Finally, real‑robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency of latent transition memory, highlighting its capacity for complex temporal information, bounded‑context operation, and real‑world robotic control.

PaperId: 778, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21359.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Silin Chen, Zihan Zhang, Xiaodong Gu, Jiale Huang, Yuling Shi, Han Li, Zhao Shan, Chengcheng Wan, Zhensu Sun, Haibing Guan
Title: SWE-at-Scale: Scalable Issue Synthesis from Historical Bug Fixes
Abstract:
As coding agents become increasingly capable, robust evaluation requires a broader and more diverse supply of verifiable software engineering (SWE) tasks. However, real‑world tasks are constrained by the natural frequency of issue reporting and the substantial cost of manual curation. Furthermore, existing synthetic approaches rely primarily on the pretrained knowledge of large models coupled with heuristic prompting, often failing to capture the authentic, complex mechanics of software failures. To exponentially scale SWE task production, we introduce SWE‑at‑Scale, a framework that automatically synthesizes realistic issues by reverse‑engineering real‑world software fixes. Our key insight is that historical fixes encapsulate deep mechanistic knowledge of bug formation: inverting a fix transforms repair supervision into bug‑induction supervision grounded in actual development scenarios. SWE‑at‑Scale transfers these learned bug patterns to novel code contexts, repeatedly sampling diverse bug typologies to construct executable SWE tasks. Extensive experiments show that SWE‑at‑Scale generates more diverse and realistic SWE tasks than current synthesis baselines while posing greater challenges to state‑of‑the‑art coding agents. Notably, SWE‑at‑Scale can generate distinct bug types from a single code context, with bug diversity scaling robustly even up to 200 generations per file. Overall, SWE‑at‑Scale turns finite real‑world fixes into reusable supervision for scalable synthesis of realistic, diverse, and challenging SWE tasks.

PaperId: 779, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21344.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Utsav Poudel, Anuj Nepal, Vyas Viswanath, Subramaniyaswamy Vairavasundaram
Title: Quantum Versus Classical Machine Learning for Neuropsychiatric Disorders: A Feature-Matched Multi-Cohort Evaluation
Abstract:
Resting‑state functional connectivity is widely used in machine learning‑based classification of neuropsychiatric disorders. Quantum machine learning models have been proposed for functional connectivity data, but few studies have evaluated them under leave‑site‑out validation or against matched classical models. We compared six quantum model families with classical ones using identical correlation‑derived features across four public cohorts (4,308 subjects). Leave‑site‑out validation was used for the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE I), ADHD‑200 (attention‑deficit/hyperactivity disorder), and REST‑meta‑MDD (major depressive disorder) cohorts, while the UCLA Consortium for Neuropsychiatric Phenomics (UCLA‑CNP) was evaluated using stratified 10‑fold cross‑validation. The quantum kernel was statistically indistinguishable from a matched classical kernel across all four cohorts, with the average accuracy difference within 1.4 percentage points at 95% confidence. On ABIDE I, a hybrid quantum convolutional network achieved similar accuracy to its classical counterpart (0.645 vs. 0.641), while a trainable quantum kernel exceeded its classical counterpart by 0.064 in area under the curve (AUC). Quantum convolutional networks also achieved higher AUC than their matched classical networks on this cohort and showed smaller train‑test gaps on all four cohorts, without an accuracy gain. Overall, most quantum models matched their classical counterparts, but none consistently outperformed them. This study, among the first quantum evaluations of ABIDE I under leave‑site‑out validation, provides a feature‑matched benchmark of quantum and classical models comprising 284 matched comparisons. We further analyse fidelity‑based graph construction and account for the observed quantum‑classical parity through effective‑dimension and eigenspectrum analyses.

PaperId: 780, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21327.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhuowen Liang, Xiaotian Lin, Yuyu Luo, Haixun Wang, Nan Tang
Title: DocPilot: Interactive Agent Orchestration and Training for Long Visual Document Understanding
Abstract:
Multimodal long‑document question answering requires models to seek sparse evidence across pages and modalities, understand heterogeneous document content, and reason over the collected evidence. Even advanced vision‑language models (VLMs) can overlook sparse evidence and struggle with cross‑modal reasoning in a single pass. Existing document agents further introduce multi‑step interaction, but some still rely on predefined workflows or coarse‑grained actions, limiting the flexibility and granularity of document reasoning. We introduce DocPilot, an agentic document framework that supports expressive orchestration and makes complex document solving learnable by small language models (SLMs). DocPilot orchestrates evidence seeking through page‑level navigation and fine‑grained evidence localization, and integrates local visual inspection, code‑based numerical reasoning, and cross‑modal reasoning for multimodal understanding. To transfer these capabilities to small models, we propose curriculum‑based agentic training that progresses from single‑ability learning to adaptive orchestration through supervision from data‑grounded reasoning traces and executable interaction trajectories. Across MMLongBench‑Doc, DocBench, FinRAGBench‑V, and MADQA, DocPilot achieves strong gains with frontier VLM backbones, while DocPilot‑4B delivers competitive performance against substantially larger models, demonstrating strong effectiveness and generalization across diverse long‑document reasoning settings. The code is available at https://github.com/HKUSTDial/DocPilot.

PaperId: 781, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21308.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Max Rosenblattl, Nikhil Krishnaswamy, Leon Nissen, Manuel Milling, Nicolas Zumarraga, Ning Wang, Thomas Kaar, Robert Jakob, Björn W. Schuller, Elgar Fleisch, Patrick Langer, Paul Schmiedmayer
Title: PocketTSLM: Deploying an On-Device Soft-Prompt Time-Series Language Model for Privacy-Preserving Smartphone Reasoning
Abstract:
Consumer phones and wearables increasingly collect physiological time‑series data, yet most mobile systems treat these streams as summaries or text rather than as temporal evidence. This representation is poorly matched to personal health systems that need to retrieve, route, or summarize sensor evidence while preserving temporal structure. Cloud‑hosted time‑series language models avoid smartphone limits, but they repeatedly move sensitive physiology off the device and add latency and per‑query compute cost. Mobile model alternatives that aggregate time‑series data into statistical features or serialize raw samples as text either compress temporal structure or exhaust the context and memory budgets of small on‑device models. We present PocketTSLM, a mobile‑native deployment of OpenTSLM SoftPrompt, the soft‑prompt variant of the OpenTSLM time‑series language model. PocketTSLM runs fully on a consumer smartphone by injecting encoded time‑series windows as embeddings instead of tokenizing time series as text. A numerical parity protocol verifies identical greedy‑decoded token sequences between the Swift port and a Python reference using Apple's MLX machine‑learning framework. Answers also match the PyTorch reference, although rationale wording can differ. An on‑device context‑economics benchmark compares the soft‑prompt path with a text‑serialized baseline on the same backbone. In our benchmark format, soft‑prompting uses approximately 12 times fewer time‑series tokens and reduces prompt‑prefill cost. PocketTSLM processes 30‑second Sleep‑EDF electroencephalography clips for sleep staging and a 1,000‑sample (10 s) 12‑lead electrocardiogram clip from ECG‑QA. In comparison, text‑serialized baselines exceed the phone's context or memory budget at longer time‑series windows. All inference runs entirely on the device, with no health data transmitted during inference.

PaperId: 782, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21306.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qi Lu, Jiarun Li, Ce Zhang, Miao Pan, Yi Pan, Xu Wang, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang
Title: VLA-$Δ$: Learning Physical State Transition for Vision-Language-Action Models
Abstract:
Vision‑language‑action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge acquired through vision‑language pretraining to robot control, achieving strong performance across various benchmarks. However, most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions without explicit supervision of intermediate physical state changes, making them prone to overfitting observation‑action correspondences. Some methods introduce intermediate reasoning or future‑state prediction in language, visual, or latent spaces to guide action generation, but do not explicitly supervise the physical state transition itself. We therefore propose VLA‑Δ, a general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. To support this objective, we construct a large‑scale pretraining dataset and derive physical state‑transition annotations covering task‑relevant semantics and visual motion changes, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. During inference, the model generates actions directly from current observations without additional inference overhead. VLA‑Δ achieves performance competitive with the state of the art on LIBERO and RoboTwin, and outperforms π_0.5 in real‑robot experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU‑OmniAI/VLA‑Delta

PaperId: 783, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21304.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Junru Wu, Jingting Zheng, Yuqi Ren, Deyi Xiong
Title: VALCON: Benchmarking and Enhancing Value Consistency in Large Language Models via Dual-Role Variation
Abstract:
Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. Such consistency is increasingly important because modern LLM agents and alignment pipelines often rely on the same LLM to both generate actions and evaluate their acceptability. To mitigate this limitation, we propose VALCON, a role‑driven data construction framework that operationalizes value consistency into three benchmark suites (VAB‑Consistency, VAB‑Boundary, VAB‑Challenge) via dual‑role variation. By systematically pairing an LLM's generative behavior with its evaluative judgments under identical principles, VALCON synthesizes target evaluation data that exposes hidden value discrepancies. Experiments on 28 LLMs reveal pervasive cross‑role inconsistency: models with highly compliant outputs frequently fail to align their judgments with their own generations. To understand and address this gap, we perform mechanistic probing that uncovers a role‑dependent representational decoupling associated with this behavioral asymmetry. Guided by these insights, we propose a representation‑directed intervention that effectively mitigates consistency failures. Our work establishes value consistency as a distinct alignment dimension and provides a complete evaluation‑analysis‑mitigation pipeline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tjunlp‑lab/VALCON.

PaperId: 784, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21302.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Minhyeok Roh, Minseo Lee, Jun Young Jeong, Byeonghyeon Lee, Lucas Yunkyu Lee, Jaesik Park, Eunbyung Park
Title: Dusting the Phantom: Gaussian Allocation for Fading Dynamic Content
Abstract:
Dynamic Gaussian representations have made high‑quality, real‑time volumetric video increasingly practical, yet challenging motion can still break their reconstruction: small fast‑moving objects may disappear, and fine textures in highly dynamic regions are often lost. In particular, simply training longer or using more Gaussians may still fail to recover small, fast‑moving objects. We argue that the key bottleneck is not representational capacity itself, but where and when Gaussian primitives are allocated. Existing allocation strategies rely on current Gaussian locations and often overlook the spatiotemporal destinations of relocated Gaussians. To address these limitations, we introduce two complementary strategies.
