First, Seed Injection identifies under‑reconstructed dynamic regions using temporal appearance changes and reconstruction errors, and initializes new Gaussians at geometrically plausible 3D locations through multi‑view observations, independent of existing Gaussian locations. Second, Temporal Biased Relocation uses time‑resolved optimization signals to guide the spatiotemporal placement of relocated Gaussians. Both strategies maintain a fixed Gaussian budget without modifying the underlying representation. Experiments across multiple dynamic‑scene datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction quality, particularly in highly dynamic regions, recovering small, rapidly moving objects and fine‑grained appearance details.

PaperId: 785, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21287.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Donghwan Lee, Sanghyun Jo, Sihyun Kim, Ziseok Lee, Kyungsu Kim
Title: ReState: Noise-Level-Aware State Correction for Training-Free Object Removal in Few-Step Diffusion Models
Abstract:
Training‑free object removal commonly redirects self‑attention away from the target region, but on few‑step distilled diffusion models this often leaves object‑shaped residuals. We identify a temporal mismatch: a structured prediction forms inside the mask at the first forward, and the short trajectory offers few later chances to revise it, while attention rerouting acts mainly in later steps. Across four distilled backbones, magnitude‑matched single‑forward interventions show that background‑directed state correction affects the final result more than attention rerouting. We therefore propose ReState, which corrects the masked clean prediction toward background evidence retrieved from the input using a noise‑level‑aware weight that vanishes at the final forward. ReState retains object‑excluding attention as a complementary constraint and adds no denoiser evaluations. Across two paired benchmarks and two few‑step backbones, ReState achieves the best masked PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among training‑free methods, improving PSNR by 3.17 dB on average over the strongest baseline. On OBER‑Test, it also outperforms the 50‑step attention‑forcing reference on all three metrics at 6.7x lower latency. The same configuration transfers to two additional distilled backbones without retuning. Project page: https://tdrlee.github.io/ReState

PaperId: 786, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21283.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xuanyi Liu, Ruiqi Li, Siwei Ma
Title: Mallea: Building, Steering, and Memorizing Worlds with Coding Agent
Abstract:
Code world models represent world dynamics through explicit state and executable rules. We investigate how to coordinate object representations, behavioral revisions, and visual memory within this formulation. We present Mallea, a system for building, steering, and memorizing worlds from text. A coding agent infers object interaction requirements from the prompt and jointly plans object structure, properties, and rules, favoring compact representations that support those requirements. The world evolves under the planned rules; optional user actions steer it, while text requests can edit properties or extend capabilities with unaffected state preserved. Object texture memory retains reusable appearance only for whitebox‑defined objects and adapts it as those objects change. The program advances world state, while a generative renderer combines current structure with remembered appearance. By organizing construction, intervention, and memory around the same objects, Mallea conditions subsequent observations on the latest state and compatible appearance. Project page: https://lxycopper.github.io/Mallea.

PaperId: 787, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21274.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Max Rosenblattl, Milana Gurbanova, Karl Aurel Deck, Narayan Schuetz, Thomas Kaar, Manuel Milling, Nicolas Zumarraga, Ning Wang, Kelly W. Zhang, Anders Johnson, Robert Jakob, Björn W. Schuller, Elgar Fleisch, Daniel Seung Kim, Allan Lawrie, Patrick Langer, Maxwell A. Xu, Euan Ashley, Paul Schmiedmayer
Title: TimeCap: A Scalable Open-Source Pipeline for Captioning Wearable Health Time-Series Data
Abstract:
Time‑series data generated continuously across industrial, environmental, and especially health domains produce multimodal signals whose scale and heterogeneity make their processing and interpretation particularly challenging. Time‑Series Language Models (TSLMs) promise scalable interpretation of these signals, yet remain bottlenecked by a fundamental lack of text‑annotated time series pairs that are signal‑grounded, reproducible, and extensible across modalities and schemas. Existing paired corpora are either closed or limited in scale and modality coverage. Annotation with large language models could scale them up, but its outputs cannot be regenerated exactly, which prevents others from re‑deriving, extending, or auditing the resulting corpus. To address this, we release TimeCap, an open deterministic captioning pipeline with three reusable extractor tiers and a cross‑channel synthesis layer that operates directly on the signal with no language model in the loop, extensible to new schemas by writing channel definitions alone. This positions TimeCap as a reproducible mechanism for future dataset generation rather than a one‑off release. Applying TimeCap to OpenMHC, the MyHeart Counts wearable dataset, yields MHCap, the largest open caption layer for multimodal wearable time‑series data. MHCap spans 19 Apple HealthKit channels and 7,005,763 captions over 908,944 person‑days. To showcase the impact of the corpus, we train OpenTSLM, a time‑series language model, on MHCap and benchmark on health‑outcome prediction. Caption‑augmented training (OpenTSLM‑Cap) outperforms a label‑only baseline on 29 of 32 per‑user binary evaluations across 8 tasks.

PaperId: 788, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21266.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zane Durante, Paul Tang, Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran, Amit Kaushal, Shrinidhi Kowshika Lakshmikanth, Feolu Kolawole, Yu Jun Zheng, Yifan Geng, Shobhit Agarwal, Kevin Schulman, Juan Carlos Niebles, Ehsan Adeli, Arnold Milstein, Li Fei-Fei
Title: TRACER: A Multimodal Harness for Patient Care in Hospitals
Abstract:
Continuous video and clinical records provide complementary information for understanding how patient behavior evolves over a hospital stay. A central challenge is how to represent behavior across the entire stay while preserving access to fine‑grained visual and clinical evidence. We introduce TRACER, a training‑free multimodal harness that constructs minute‑level action records from video and combines them with clinical records into hourly reports. The harness equips an LLM agent with tools to query this hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records. To evaluate TRACER, we construct two benchmarks. The first contains 397 annotated one‑minute clips spanning 15 atomic actions; the second poses 144 clinician‑informed multiple‑choice questions, grounded in 264 hours of video and clinical records from two ICU patients. TRACER achieves up to 84.8% accuracy for action detection and 61.0% QA accuracy versus 49.3% for the strongest baseline using the same backbone. Across 280 patients spanning approximately 60,000 camera‑hours, TRACER identifies significantly less purposeful activity in patients with a positive delirium assessment during their stay than in those without (p < 0.0001). Our results show that combining continuous video with clinical records can support understanding of patient behavior over time and across patient cohorts without training on protected health data.

PaperId: 789, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21262.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianhao Ma, Wei Wang, Yivan Zhang, Dong-Dong Wu, Takashi Ishida, Gang Niu, Masashi Sugiyama
Title: Rethinking Learning from Label Proportions via Moment Matching
Abstract:
Learning from label proportions (LLP) is a weakly supervised setting where training data are grouped into bags with only bag‑level label proportions observed, and the goal is to learn a classifier that predicts labels for individual instances. Recently, a large body of methods has emerged; however, most of them rely on the assumption that instance‑label pairs are sampled i.i.d. and randomly assembled into bags, an assumption often violated in real‑world scenarios. Our experimental results indicate that these methods perform suboptimally under non‑random settings. In this work, we adopt a more realistic assumption: bags are sampled i.i.d., and instance labels are conditionally independent given the instances. Under this setting, we show that the label counts follow a Poisson multinomial distribution. Motivated by this observation, we propose LLP via moment matching (LLP‑MM), a simple yet effective approach which leverages multi‑order factorial moments as training objectives, encouraging the classifier predictions to match these moments and thereby more fully exploit the underlying statistical structure of the data. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets under various bag construction strategies demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach while maintaining high computational efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/TianhaoMa5/LLP‑MM.

PaperId: 790, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21261.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Haotian Ma, Ziye Mei, Frederic Sala
Title: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations
Abstract:
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) represent model activations with sparse, linearly decoded features, but the downstream effects of those features need not compose additively. We introduce SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR), which measure the behavioral variation left unexplained above a chosen interaction order. Under independent feature subset sampling, population SAR is exactly the normalized energy of interactions above that order and bounds coalition ordering error for the optimal low order approximation. To distinguish compositionality associated with the SAE representation from that induced by downstream computation, we compare learned SAE coordinates with sum preserving random rotations of the same selected subspace and find lower first order residuals for the learned coordinates across all 18 model and behavior settings. The coordinates are nevertheless not fully additive: pairwise terms improve held out coalition ordering in every setting and outperform parameter matched models using randomly selected third order terms. In a combined steering experiment, pairwise modeling raises rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduces ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606. Together, these results show that SAE coordinates support comparatively compositional behavioral descriptions while faithful joint explanations and interventions still require interactions beyond individual feature effects. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/SAE‑Behavioral‑Compositionality.

PaperId: 791, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21244.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Tianyu Chen, Xinyang Liu, Ruyi An, Zhendong Wang, Mingyuan Zhou
Title: System1-Arena: Which Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) often make discrete decisions, such as flagging phishing or escalating to a human. System‑1 models, such as Jev and the OpenAI Decisions API, return probabilities over options in a single forward pass, while System‑2 approaches generate reasoning steps. Which decisions can System‑1 models handle, and which require generative reasoning? We introduce System1‑Arena, a benchmark that gives all models the same decision requests and scores their probabilities. It contains 92k questions across 105 tasks from 268 public sources, in four groups: text classification and knowledge, applied decisions, evaluation and control, and agent and action. It also includes 138 closed‑loop environments, from web shopping and SWE‑bench coding control to robotics, games, and driving; in real‑time mode, the world evolves while a model decides. We evaluate 30 models: 7 closed LLMs, 13 open LLMs read at the answer token, and 10 System‑1 models. The largest System‑1 models match or exceed fast closed LLMs in non‑agentic accuracy, with better‑calibrated probabilities at one‑quarter of the latency. A reasoning LLM is the most accurate, at about 70x the cost of a fast LLM. In closed loops, large open LLMs succeed most often (up to 32.9%); small System‑1 models rarely succeed.

PaperId: 792, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21240.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziye Mei, Haotian Ma
Title: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders
Abstract:
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into sparse features, but prompt transformations designed to preserve the underlying request can redistribute activity across them. A feature change observed on one transformed prompt need not recur, and even a recurring change need not affect a downstream computation. We introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS), which identifies large feature responses that recur in a consistent direction, and evaluate the resulting supports on variants excluded from selection. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, the tested prompt transformations produce a reproducible redistribution profile on these excluded variants. We then separate recurring representation change from signed readout contribution and decision failure. For a fixed linear readout, an exact decomposition shows how response magnitude, readout coefficients, directional alignment, and the clean margin determine downstream consequences. In two frozen safety readouts, combining RSS support erosion with the full clean margin yields recurrent failure AUROCs of 0.935 and 0.958 using median supports of 20 and 19 features, compared with 0.965 and 0.964 using full erosion. RSS therefore provides a way to identify recurring sparse representation changes and quantify their contribution to a downstream readout without equating representation change with failure. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution‑Sensitivity‑Score

PaperId: 793, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21238.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Songlin Liu, Linwei Chen, Li Zhang, Jun Hu, Ying Fu
Title: A large-scale climate-aware satellite image dataset for domain adaptive land-cover semantic segmentation
Abstract:
A few well‑annotated datasets for land‑cover semantic segmentation have recently been introduced to advance the field of earth observation technologies. However, these datasets overlook the significant diversity among geographic areas with different climates, which can greatly impact and diversify land cover. Consequently, this leads to a domain gap in remote sensing images and severe performance degradation of the segmentation models. To enhance land‑cover semantic segmentation with improved generalization ability, we conducted the first investigation into the impact of climate on this task. In this paper, we present a unique large‑scale Climate‑Aware Satellite Images Dataset (CASID) specifically designed for domain adaptive land‑cover semantic segmentation. It consists of 980 satellite images with a size of 5000 x 5000 pixels, collected from 30 different regions around Asia, covering over 24,500 square kilometers. These images are gathered from four distinct climate zones, namely temperate monsoon, subtropical monsoon, tropical monsoon, and tropical rainforest. It includes four sub‑datasets/domains, each representing one of the aforementioned climate zones. This characteristic makes CASID the first climate‑aware land‑cover semantic segmentation dataset with multiple domains. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the samples from the four climate zones, emphasizing differences in global image features, image texture, category distribution, spectral value, and object shape. These analyses offer valuable insights for subsequent research in this field. Moreover, we conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the latest semantic segmentation and unsupervised domain adaptation methods on the CASID dataset. These results serve as a robust baseline for future research endeavors. Our dataset will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Linwei‑Chen/CASID.

PaperId: 794, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21237.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hanyue Chen, Chang Liu, Miaomiao Zhang
Title: Compositional Automata Learning of Timed Synchronous Systems
Abstract:
Active model learning is a crucial technique for automatically constructing formal models of black‑box timed systems. However, existing learning approaches typically construct a single monolithic automaton for a timed system with multiple synchronous components, obscuring its component structure and hindering component‑level analysis. We propose a compositional learning approach that constructs a deterministic real‑time automaton (RTA) for each component with access only to the target system as a whole. Upon termination, the learned RTAs form a network that exhibits exactly the same timed behaviors as the target system. Within the respective resource limits, our implementation terminates successfully on 213 of the 240 (88.8%) randomly generated benchmark instances and all six adapted case‑study benchmarks, and requires less learning time than monolithic approaches on some instances.

PaperId: 795, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21229.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Esther Xin
Title: What Should We Remove? Evaluating the Reliability and Costs of RLVR Data Decontamination
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) math corpora are routinely screened for benchmark overlap, but the reliability and data‑loss costs of cleaning policies remain underexamined. We audit sixteen open RLVR math corpora comprising 1,673,514 corpus‑specific training items against six benchmarks containing 1,949 questions. We evaluate eight policies based on exact, lexical, and semantic matching using 594 independently and blindly dual‑reviewed training‑benchmark pairs. Calibration and held‑out sets have disjoint benchmark questions and training‑example families. A separate review of all 83 candidate matches for 80 sampled training items measures item‑level false removal. At cosine threshold 0.80, 52 of 59 sampled removals (88%) were confirmed false removals; this is not a demonstrated population rate. No semantic threshold in our preregistered grid (0.80‑0.98) meets the 90% conservative‑precision target on calibration. The existing judge‑adjudicated policy achieves 98.1% resolved precision and 98.2% candidate‑frame recall on held‑out corpora. It has zero confirmed false removals among six sampled removals, with one unresolved case; this does not establish zero risk. Within the evaluated candidate frame, this policy offers a more favorable precision‑recall balance than the semantic‑threshold alternatives tested. Recall does not measure contamination outside the candidate frame. We release reviewed labels, per‑policy decisions, and coverage accounting to support evaluation of cleaning reliability and cost rather than overlap counts alone.

PaperId: 796, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21220.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zidong Jia, Guofu Xie, Xiao Zhang
Title: RecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach for Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation
Abstract:
Recommender systems often need to balance multiple conflicting objectives. Controllable Multi‑Objective Recommendation (CMOR) enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade‑offs at inference time without retraining, adapting to shifting user or system requirements. Existing CMOR approaches typically rely on output‑level reranking or parameter‑generating modules, which either limit the scope of feasible trade‑offs or incur substantial training and inference cost. Model merging provides a promising alternative by reusing multiple objective‑specific models via parameter combination. However, its direct application to recommender systems is challenging due to the lack of a shared linear regime and cross‑objective interference. To address these issues, we propose RecSoup, a lightweight two‑stage approach for effective CMOR via specialized model merging. RecSoup first mitigates parameter interference across objectives through a pruning strategy that jointly considers objective‑specific importance and cross‑objective relevance. It then performs adaptive parameter merging via a learnable preference‑to‑coefficient mapping, allowing dynamic trade‑off control at inference time without joint retraining or additional generative modules. Theoretically, we prove that RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in effectiveness and efficiency, as it can fully navigate the Pareto front without smoothness constraints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that RecSoup achieves improved Pareto front quality and effective controllability while delivers 165‑‑228x faster inference‑time latency than parameter generation approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/35798642/RECSOUP.git.

PaperId: 797, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21211.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dohyun Lee, Minho Park, Jeonghoon Park, Dongyoon Hwang, Junha Hyung, Sungwon Hwang, Byungkun Lee, Jaegul Choo
Title: An Agentic Framework for Proactive Robots with Procedural Assistance Memory
Abstract:
Proactive robots should anticipate user needs and provide assistance before being explicitly asked. A straightforward approach is to infer human intentions from commonsense knowledge, but the same observed behavior can imply different needs across users, potentially leading to unwanted assistance. We observe that everyday routines in the real world exhibit recurring patterns, so learning these patterns can reduce ambiguity in proactive decisions. Based on this, we propose a memory‑based agentic framework in which a VLM task predictor reads a Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation to decide when to assist and what task to perform, and a VLA executor performs the predicted task. PAM is structured as a finite‑state machine over activity phases, per‑state assistance rules, and event‑driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day's interaction trace without weight updates or retraining. In our 5‑day desk‑assistance evaluation, memory‑free baselines remain conservative, with limited recall on proactive tasks. Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first‑fire delay from approximately 5 seconds on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5. Our approach also adapts to changes in the user's routine through continued memory reflection, recovering from memory‑‑routine misalignment after a single memory update. The project page is available at https://davian‑robotics.github.io/PAM/

PaperId: 798, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21179.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Michael Tian-Yue Liu, Anne Harrington, Trevor Darrell, Yutong Bai
Title: Judging the Judges: Confidence and Disagreement in Rubrics as Rewards
Abstract:
Rubrics as Rewards (RaR) extends reinforcement learning to non‑verifiable domains by using an LLM judge to score responses against a structured rubric. Prior work has focused on improving the rubric or strengthening the single judge, with comparatively little attention to how different single or multiple judges might be used during RaR training. We first show that judge identity alone produces a substantial spread in scores when training Qwen3‑4B‑Base on RaR‑Medicine and RaR‑Science across five frontier and open‑weight judges. Building on this, we propose RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), a novel judge ensemble strategy for RaR with two mechanisms: a soft‑Likert reward that uses judge logprobs to weight more confident judges more heavily, and a drop‑on‑disagreement mask that excludes high‑disagreement rollouts from the GRPO update. We find that this design is critical: while a naive average of judge scores fails to outperform the best single judge, RaRE outperforms every single‑judge RaR variant on both HealthBench and GPQA Diamond, with per‑theme analysis showing that it inherits the complementary strengths of its constituent judges. Our findings establish judge ensembling as a compelling axis for improving RaR.

PaperId: 799, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21178.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hiroki Fukui
Title: Explicit reduced APN permutations: ramification and optimal Galois-ring lifts
Abstract:
Let m\ge5 be odd and q=2^m. For every odd r with 3\le r<m and \gcd(r,m)=1 we give the reduced polynomial P_m,r=\mathrmred((T_r^3)^2^m‑2), T_r=\sum_i<rX^2^i, explicitly: it has coefficients in \mathbbF_2 and exactly 3r‑2 terms, it is an APN permutation of \mathbbF_q, and its formal derivative 1+X^2^r‑2+X^2^m‑2 has no zero on \mathbbF_q and is two‑to‑one. We determine the ramification of P_m,r as a map of the projective line for all admissible (m,r): there are 2^m‑r finite ramification points, all wild, with index and different exponent 2^r‑2, all over the single finite branch value 1. The 0/1 lift of P_m,r satisfies an identity in \mathbbZ[X] that evaluates it over every Galois ring \mathrmGR(2^k,m) with m‑1 squarings, one general multiplication and r+5 additions or subtractions. For every quadratic optimal APN permutation p of \mathbbF_q (in particular P_m,r), every k\ge2 and every coefficient lift F of p to \mathrmGR(2^k,m), we determine the differential rows of F exactly in the unit directions whose residue lies outside the kernel \0,ρ\ of the linear part of p' (they are the residue rows of p; ρ=1 for P_m,r) and in the directions in 2^k‑1\mathrmGR(2^k,m)\setminus\0\ (every nonzero entry equals 2q^k‑1). We also give a self‑contained proof of the Li‑‑Wang criterion for a Gold function plus a linearised polynomial, which explains why the inner map of P_m,r is not a monomial, and record a two‑word, two‑layer transition that a simple linear layer forbids at the residue level.

PaperId: 800, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21169.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hiroki Fukui
Title: Optimal Reduced Representatives of Quadratic APN Permutations in Odd Dimension
Abstract:
The formal derivative of the reduced polynomial representative of a map on a binary finite field depends on the coordinates, although its differential uniformity does not. This matters for lifting permutations to Galois rings: a polynomial over a Galois ring of characteristic a power of two greater than two permutes the ring exactly when its reduction permutes the residue field and the derivative of the reduction has no zero there. We prove that for every odd n\ge5, every quadratic almost perfect nonlinear permutation Q of \mathbbF_2^n admits invertible binary‑linear maps L and A such that the derivative of the reduced representative of L\circ Q\circ A has no zero and each of its nonempty fibres has exactly two elements. The range is exact: this fails for n=3, as computed earlier, and for even n there are no such permutations. For n\ge9, a linearization and a projectively injective cofactor map reduce the problem to counting binary matrices: more than 5% of the invertible inputs A succeed, more than half for n\ge15, without any classification. For n=5,7 we use two independent classifications and finite certificates. Consequently every such permutation is linearly equivalent to a counterexample to the reduced critical‑point conjecture of Bartoli and Stănică that lifts to permutation polynomials of optimal differential uniformity over every Galois ring with this residue field. For odd n\ge9 the existence proof is checked in the Lean 4 proof assistant.

PaperId: 801, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21159.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Huachao Zhu, Junjielong Xu, Sicheng Li, Liang Yang, Mingtao Chen, Zhichao Hu, Li Jiang, Pinjia He
Title: VisualTrust: Video Reasoning under On-Screen Claim Framing
Abstract:
On‑screen text can describe what a video shows, or it can frame what the video is supposed to mean. Current benchmarks treat both alike, testing whether a model can read the text rather than whether it should trust it. We study claim deference, multimodal large language models' tendency to let an on‑screen claim override conflicting visual evidence. We introduce VisualTrust, a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases across 14 claim‑fact classes. Each case pairs a question with three versions of the same video: one with no claim, one with an accurate claim, and one with a misleading claim that alters a single grounded fact. The option the misleading claim supports is the trap answer. Across seven open‑weight and four proprietary models, mean accuracy falls from 90.1% without a claim to 51.9% with a misleading claim. Among initially correct responses, 42.8% flip to the trap answer and only 0.6% become other errors. Strong no‑claim accuracy does not ensure resistance. We also introduce DEAR (Decoupled Evidence Arbitration and Reading), a training‑free agent for video question answering that separates evidence arbitration from reading. An independent check reports conflicting evidence, a selector weighs it without a fixed modality priority and blinds what it withholds, and the reader answers from the resulting video in a fresh context. On 500 videos across three proprietary models, DEAR raises accuracy under misleading claims from 47.2‑‑64.0% to 81.8‑‑85.2% and reduces trap‑answer selection from 34.4‑‑50.8% to 11.6‑‑15.0%, while preserving no‑claim accuracy.

PaperId: 802, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21146.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Guo-Wei Wong, Meng Chang Chen
Title: ExecWeave: Cross-Layer Execution Provenance for Observable Agentic Software
Abstract:
Agentic software invokes tools, launches processes, accesses files, and communicates with local or remote services. Application traces describe logical operations, whereas operating‑system telemetry records machine activity without necessarily identifying the responsible agent action. Relating these evidence planes is a reconstruction problem: a plausible but unsupported association can assign an effect to the wrong principal. We present ExecWeave, a local‑first system that materializes provider semantics and independently observed runtime events into a typed execution graph. The implementation retains separate source artifacts, distinguishes logical occurrences from repeated evidence, and records attribution, inference, and causal‑status metadata. An optional command‑to‑process correlator emits a non‑causal inferred bridge only when its bounded search yields one compatible observed process; uniqueness within this observed candidate set is not a guarantee of causal correctness. OS‑observed file and network effects acquire a semantic tool or agent principal only through an observed process plus a justified command‑to‑process association; session‑correlated file‑system events do not by themselves provide that principal. Source code is available at https://github.com/Irish‑kw/ExecWeave.

PaperId: 803, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21143.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yingzhuo Deng, Chong Li, Bingxin Liu, Yi Shu, Tianyu Peng, Can Xie, Siyao Song, Shuo Ren, Jiajun Zhang
Title: CoSTA: Compressed Speech Token Adaptation for Efficient Spoken Dialogue Models
Abstract:
Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) typically share a speech‑token space for generation and synthesis, leading to long autoregressive sequences and costly inference. Lower‑rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences but may introduce compression‑quality trade‑offs and costly replacement without breaking this coupling. To address this limitation, we propose CoSTA, a compatibility‑preserving post‑hoc framework that decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations via mean‑initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, followed by deterministic expansion back to the original speech‑token space before synthesis. On bilingual speech‑dialogue benchmarks, CoSTA achieves approximately 1.7× expanded speech‑token generation speed, lower full‑response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality. Analyses show more sustained interaction under limited budgets and a practical trade‑off among compression, decoding efficiency, and quality. Further experiments demonstrate cross‑architecture transfer and complementarity to low‑rate tokenization.

PaperId: 804, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21136.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Siddhesh Kulkarni
Title: Pathwise Shrinkage and Probabilistic Calibration of the Multiplicative Half-Cauchy Process
Abstract:
We characterize the multiplicative half‑Cauchy process through its log‑scale random‑walk representation, establishing shrinkage, expansion, and critical regimes, almost‑sure summability, local rebounds, and effective dimension. We also derive a semi‑analytic calibration rule linking interpretable prior probability statements to its scale parameter.

PaperId: 805, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21125.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Woocheol Shin, Taeyoung Yun, Jiwon Sung, Hyeongyu Kang, Jeongmin Park, Jaewoo Lee, Kyuil Sim, Dohyun Kim, Yutong He, Jinkyoo Park
Title: Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models
Abstract:
Few‑step generative models produce high‑quality samples in one or a few evaluations. However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black‑box reward evaluations are available. While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow‑based models, such as direct RL fine‑tuning or test‑time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few‑step regime: direct fine‑tuning suffers from severe reward over‑optimization, and test‑time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few‑step generation. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few‑step generative models. The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator. The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward‑tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward‑tilted output distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward‑quality trade‑off than direct fine‑tuning. The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model. To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO‑based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward‑quality trade‑off than direct fine‑tuning, and matches test‑time search methods with 16 to 549 times lower inference cost.

PaperId: 806, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21114.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haotian Ma, Ruqi Yang, Philip Townsend
Title: Spectral-Spatial Interpretation
Abstract:
Post‑hoc image explanations usually show where a model looks using spatial heatmaps or indicate which channels matter using global channel scores. These separate views are limiting for multispectral data because channel relevance is often spatially localized and physically meaningful. We introduce Spectral‑Spatial Interpretation (SSI), a full‑grid attribution method over position‑channel players (g,c). For each spatial position, SSI fixes the observed surrounding context, defines a conditional game over the channels at that position, and applies the Shapley value to this local game. The result is a full spectral‑spatial attribution matrix rather than a single heatmap or a global channel ranking. SSI has a clear local interpretation. It satisfies Shapley fairness within each position, and aggregating its channel attributions exactly recovers the position‑level contextual contrast obtained by replacing that position with the baseline. SSI also differs from context‑averaged Owen‑style hierarchical accounting, which uses the same position‑channel grouping but averages over external spatial coalitions. On HLS Burn Scar, SSI outperforms an MC‑Owen estimator across retained attribution metrics while using only about 6% of its evaluation budget. Across CUB‑200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar under both per‑channel mean and zero baselines, SSI achieves the best joint deletion and insertion AUC over dense, flat, and rank‑1 baselines, yields the strongest spectral hit rates and channel deletion, and leads spatial localization on both annotated datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/AtheavenMa/Spectral‑Spatial‑Interpretation.

PaperId: 807, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21098.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zichuan Xu, Yuyang Dong, Makoto Onizuka, Chuan Xiao
Title: ToolBottleneckBench: Measuring Tool-Agent Performance under Controlled Pressures and Fixed Harness Budgets
Abstract:
The success score of a tool agent reflects both its model and the budgets of the harness that runs it. We present ToolBottleneckBench, a benchmark that measures tool‑agent performance under controlled pressures and fixed harness budgets. Synthetic enterprise tasks stay fixed while one pressure varies: the registered tool catalog, the visible tool menu, the certified workflow, or the encoding of returned records. An exact grader records the first unmet obligation of each failed episode and the harness limit, if any, that ended it. Across 21 model and harness configurations, the visible menu is the only one of the three pressures that act on the model with a large penalty, and this penalty tracks truncation at the completion cap. Raising the cap sixteenfold removes most of the penalty in the truncation‑heavy configurations. Most failures end at a harness limit, and the failure record identifies the assigned pressure no more reliably than a count of tool calls. The repairs that help change which tools reach the model or who issues the calls, and only two repairs, neither improving model behavior, beat every configuration switch. We recommend reporting pressure effects with the harness budgets under which they were measured. We release the benchmark at https://github.com/zichuanxu/tool‑bottleneck‑bench.

PaperId: 808, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21095.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yue Su, Bokai Lin, Xinkai Wang, Chubin Zhang, Xiangnan Wu, Kuan Zhang, Weiyang Jin, Jiwen Yu, Yiming Li, Cewu Lu, Lixin Yang, Xihui Liu
Title: Can World and Action Modeling Benefit Each Other under Unified Causal Training?
Abstract:
World and action modeling are closely related, yet their reciprocal benefits under unified causal training remain unclear. We introduce OneWM, a simple framework for unified causal training that treats actions as both conditions for world prediction and targets for policy learning within a shared video‑action architecture. Using this framework, we investigate whether learning forward dynamics conditioned on specified actions improves action learning, and whether learning to generate actions in turn improves action‑conditioned world modeling. We use LIBERO, LIBERO‑Plus, and RoboCasa365 as embodied testbeds to evaluate both policy learning and world modeling, complemented by real‑world policy experiments. Learning the visual consequences of specified actions improves policy performance and generalization across changing scenes. In turn, action learning improves multi‑view world‑prediction fidelity under the same architecture. Together, these results answer both questions positively, supporting reciprocal benefits between world modeling and action generation under unified causal training.

PaperId: 809, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21081.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Arshia Abolghasemi, Seyed Reza Tavakoli, Parsa Naderi, Nazanin Mirzaei, Behrad Jahani, Saba Yousefzadeh, Tahereh Javaheri, Mohammad Hosein Rohban, Gholamali Aminian, Ali Habibnia
Title: StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction
Abstract:
Score‑based diffusion methods usually perturb data with Brownian Gaussian noise, corresponding to a light‑tailed forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). For market time series this SDE can be a poor abstraction: limit order book (LOB) order flow is heavy‑tailed, bursty, and occasionally jump‑like. We study STOCHLOB, a training‑only score‑matching framework that changes the forward diffusion corruption law while leaving the deployed predictor deterministic. Instead of Brownian‑only Gaussian corruption, the noising process uses two non‑Gaussian SDE‑inspired alternatives: jump‑Lévy noise through a compound‑Poisson variance mixture, and clipped α‑stable noise through a positive‑stable Gaussian scale mixture. These corruptions inject finite jumps and heavy‑tailed residuals into training without requiring reverse‑time diffusion sampling at inference. The resulting score target has a useful interpretation: its radial factor h_t(r) is the posterior expected corruption precision, so large residuals are weighted according to the latent corruption scale that most plausibly generated them. On chronologically held‑out Coinbase LOB data, the proposed variants remain competitive on uncorrupted BTC and altcoin test horizons and improve several realized tail‑window stress diagnostics. An exploratory Feishu A‑share transfer study further tests whether the probability outputs remain usable under transaction costs and trading‑rule constraints. Code and configuration files are available at https://github.com/ArshiAbolghasemi/Penny.

PaperId: 810, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21063.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sai Varun Kodathala, Prashanth Pollishetty, Jaylen Cargill
Title: Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding and Trusted Rendering for Agent Step-Up Authorization
Abstract:
AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. We define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting, and run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), the Microsoft action‑bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. An audit of ten agent runtimes finds no third‑party verifiable approval record, no flood limits where measurable, and post‑approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. As a reference defense we build ASU (Agent Step‑Up), a gateway that renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the phone of the user sign its digest, and executes only the stored call. Tamarin proves its binding, single‑use and key‑level non‑repudiation properties under three stated hypotheses (53 lemmas). Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo attack pairs, ASU stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and the trusted card cuts forged‑narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03. With 15 current language models as automated approvers, the trusted card raises the attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98, at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses, mostly due to a placeholder artifact in our stimuli. A second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on‑host confirmation in these experiments, flooding still succeeds 0.45 to 0.60 of the time against a modeled approver, and approval cannot stop effects that policy already allows. Code, data and proofs: https://github.com/Sports‑Vision‑Inc/agent‑step‑up

PaperId: 811, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21046.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dingjie Song, Zhiling Yan, Ziqian Zhang, Yuxuan Zhang, Lichao Sun
Title: PremiseCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of Human and AI Peer Reviews
Abstract:
Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT‑5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.

PaperId: 812, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21042.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhaoqian Xue, Shaoze Zhou, Xuexin Li, Junting Mu, Haozheng Liu, Zhongyin Wang, Yichun He, Renkai Ma, Hao Zhou, Sarah Bratt, Siyuan Ma, Chen Chen, Lingyao Li
Title: ReviewPilot: A Multi-Agent System for Screening and Data Extraction in Systematic Reviews
Abstract:
Systematic literature reviews follow the PRISMA process of screening scholarly works and extracting evidence from included studies. Deep research tools based on large language models (LLMs) can search and summarize the literature but do not record which studies are excluded or where extracted values come from. We develop a conversational multi‑agent system called ReviewPilot that automates the PRISMA workflow from paper screening to information extraction. Researchers can tailor criteria and schemas through dialogue, and a project memory keeps their configurations and revisions. Each screening decision comes with its reason and each extracted value with its source. On epidemiological expert reviews, ReviewPilot outperforms a single‑prompt LLM and AgentSLR across three LLMs, with screening macro F1 up to 0.776 and extraction F1 up to 0.788. Case studies in biomedicine and human‑computer interaction show close agreement with human annotators, suggesting that ReviewPilot can transfer beyond epidemiology. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhaoqianXue/ReviewPilot.

PaperId: 813, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21025.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Matteo He, William F. Shen, Alex Iacob, Andrej Jovanovic, Xinchi Qiu, Nicholas D. Lane
Title: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
Abstract:
When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter‑trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4‑1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.

PaperId: 814, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21016.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuchen Zhang
Title: CausalEvo: Causal Skill Self-Evolution for Health LLM Agents
Abstract:
Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self‑evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top‑ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision‑loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc‑Bench‑Verified tasks with 120 held‑out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo

PaperId: 815, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21007.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziheng Zhang, Neha Hulkund, Colin Lee, Zheda Mai, Hui Shen, Ying Ding, Tanya Berger-Wolf, Sara Beery, Wei-Lun Chao, Jianyang Gu
Title: Mind the Tail: Data Selection Through Sparse Concepts
Abstract:
Data selection reallocates training support across visual concepts, including objects, attributes, color, texture, and backgrounds. Different allocation strategies may produce varied downstream model behavior, especially for tail concepts supported by only a few samples. Discarding them can hurt test‑time robustness, while overemphasizing samples lying on category boundaries may introduce unstable training signals. This work explicitly investigates this relationship across fine‑grained, spurious‑correlation, and general image classification, as well as multimodal pretraining. Specifically, we use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract concept activations from individual images. During selection, we accumulate the dataset‑level concept support for each added sample. Applying diminishing returns to this distribution down‑weights well‑represented concepts and shifts the focus to the distribution tail. We then incorporate local support to find samples that reliably strengthen under‑supported concepts. Empirical results show consistent improvements over strong data selection baselines across all benchmarks. We also reveal the connection between concepts our method enhances and the induced behavioral changes, including improved robustness against out‑of‑distribution and spurious contexts. This work establishes concept support, beyond individual sample importance, as a useful principle for data‑efficient and robust learning.

PaperId: 816, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20998.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yiyang Cai, Tatsuya Kamijo, Ninghao Lu, Zijin Hu, Sherry Yang
Title: MoCaP: Mobile Code-as-Policies for Zero-Shot Mobile Manipulation from Passive Human Videos
Abstract:
Passive human videos of everyday activity offer robots access to a massive amount of human experience without requiring a demonstration for each task. However, using this experience requires recovering knowledge from unstructured video recordings and adapting it to a different body (i.e., the robot). To overcome these challenges, we present mobile code‑as‑policy (MoCaP), an agentic framework that turns passive human video recordings into guidance for an end‑to‑end mobile manipulation policy. MoCaP extracts spatial memory and cues of how people prepare to interact with objects, which inform navigation and the search for a manipulation‑ready configuration. Guided by passive human experience and current observations, MoCaP uses a closed‑loop code‑as‑policy to coordinate planning and tool use primitives to solve motions under the robot's geometry and kinematic constraints. On a real mobile manipulator, MoCaP achieves 80% success on each of two mobile manipulation tasks in an indoor environment whereas existing approaches cannot succeed at the task. Video‑derived spatial memory improves object‑navigation success from 70% to 100%, and human approach prior raises the rate of finding a reachable base pose from 0% to 100% at an unfavorable start location. Videos and code are available on the project website: https://mocap‑7.github.io/MoCAP‑page/.

PaperId: 817, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20989.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Frank F. Yang, Kefei Yan, Yiren Wang, Yiyang Wang
Title: Do As I Do, Not As I Say: On-Policy Distillation Inherits the Teacher in Vision-Language Models
Abstract:
Improving the reasoning capabilities of vision‑language models (VLMs) often relies on post‑training with supervision from stronger models. Two common strategies are supervised fine‑tuning (SFT), which trains on teacher‑generated demonstrations, and on‑policy distillation (OPD), which provides teacher feedback on trajectories generated by the student itself. While OPD can be more data‑efficient by supervising student‑generated trajectories, it is unclear how the teacher's supervision at each state affects the student's learned behavior. To study this question, we conduct a controlled comparison of OPD and filtered SFT across data budgets and tasks where the teacher exhibits different levels of reliability, and analyze how these differences shape student accuracy and completion behavior. Across the two tasks, we find that OPD is effective only when the teacher remains reliable on student‑generated trajectories. On ChartQA, where the teacher completes 99% of its solutions, OPD trained on only 10% of the data comes within 1.4 accuracy points of full‑data SFT. In contrast, on Geometry3K, where the teacher fails to complete 22% of its solutions, OPD underperforms SFT by 7.9 points, with most of the gap explained by incomplete responses. More strikingly, starting OPD from an SFT student reduces its completion rate from 76% to 62%, effectively erasing the completion behavior learned through SFT. Filtering teacher demonstrations for completeness alone recovers much of SFT's advantage. These results show that on‑policy supervision can transfer not only teacher knowledge but also persistent failure modes on student‑visited states. Code is available at https://github.com/ffy208/opd‑inherits‑teacher‑vlm.

PaperId: 818, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20964.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhivar Sourati, Marianne Menglin Liu, Rongguang Wang, Zheng Wang, Yazhe Hu, Lan Guo, Yuying Wang, Mengqing Guo, Bhavesh Dnyaneshwar Gore, Shubham Pathak, Ramapriya Ranganath, Sandeep Sharma, Tao Sheng, Sujith Ravi, Dan Roth
Title: VELD-QA: A Large-Scale Dataset for Visual Evidence Grounding and Question Answering in Long Documents
Abstract:
Existing long‑document QA benchmarks rarely combine large‑scale human‑authored questions with detailed visual evidence annotations, limiting diagnosis of evidence localization and interpretation failures. We present VELD‑QA, a large‑scale benchmark for Visual Evidence grounding and question answering in Long Documents. It contains 15,000 fully human‑authored question‑answer pairs across 5,859 real‑world PDFs totaling 372,445 pages, balancing chart, table, and complex‑layout tasks. Human annotations identify supporting pages and evidence elements and describe cited visual content, enabling separate retrieval and interpretation evaluation. We evaluate nine vision‑language models under four evidence settings and seven retrieval‑augmented and agentic systems. Our analysis identifies bottlenecks in evidence localization and interpretation. Retrieval‑based methods substantially underperform the oracle setting with ground‑truth supporting pages; full‑document access does not close the gap. Localization alone is insufficient: oracle accuracy peaks at 81.7%, highlighting persistent visual interpretation and reasoning challenges. Enriching inputs with our visual‑element annotations narrows the performance gap by 17‑24%, demonstrating value beyond evaluation and motivating data enrichment for multimodal document QA. Our code is available at https://github.com/oracle‑samples/veld‑qa.

PaperId: 819, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20952.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Saurabh Kumar
Title: Does Client Diversity Protect the Lightning Network? Evidence from the 2026 Core Lightning Shutdown
Abstract:
Client diversity is often cited as the Lightning Network's defence against a bug in any one implementation, yet LND runs 80% of public nodes (84% counting one operator's fleet of about 2,000 tiny nodes) and holds 84% of public channel capacity, a capacity share that has barely moved since 2023. We test what diversity buys with a natural experiment. On 26 August 2026, amid security fixes in every implementation, Core Lightning (CLN) maintainers told operators who could not upgrade to disconnect their nodes. Using 805 daily gossip snapshots, 132,360 on‑chain channel closes and a client classifier validated against self‑identifying aliases and against the wallet that builds each node's funding transactions, we find that 22% of CLN nodes went dark overnight, ten times the usual rate, mostly Tor‑reachable ones; a third were still dark five weeks later. The rest of the network barely noticed. Reachability among all node pairs fell by 7.8 percentage points, a loss exceeded in 4 of 94 ordinary two‑day windows and half that of a Tor denial‑of‑service wave in July, while among CLN pairs it fell by 24.5 points, more than in any ordinary window. Calibrated failure scenarios explain the containment: the blast radius depends on whether a failure reaches the hubs, not on how many nodes run the failing software. Losing ACINQ's Eclair node alone costs the surviving network four times the reachability lost with all 619 routable CLN nodes, and minority clients' reliance on LND for connectivity is what their size implies; CLN nodes in fact peer with each other more than chance. Diversity statistics that count nodes mislead; the quantity to track is which software the hubs run.

PaperId: 820, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20951.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dingjie Song, Zhiling Yan, Yuxuan Zhang, Lichao Sun
Title: LEV: Thinking Fast and Deep with Looped Decision Models
Abstract:
Decision models answer typed questions about an input with one probability per option, computed in a single forward pass without generating text. Like the fast System 1 of dual‑process theory, they answer at once, but their depth is fixed at training time, so they spend the same computation on easy and hard questions. Models that reason in generated text can think longer, but they pay for every extra step in decoded tokens. We present LEV, a decision model that thinks deeper by rerunning its layers in a loop instead of generating tokens. LEV builds on a language model pretrained as a loop, reads the options after every loop step and trains all steps jointly, so one checkpoint can answer at any depth. On three looped backbones, accuracy rises with depth on the same weights, mostly on hard questions, and a 2.6B LEV goes from 63.2% at depth one to 76.2% at depth four on JevBench. On‑demand depth, set per question by a small stopper with a threshold fitted on unlabelled requests, saves 15% to 24% of the computation at a cost of under one accuracy point, level with or slightly above a fixed mix of depths. On a locked test set, the 1.4B and 3B models are 5.4 to 8.8 points more accurate than dense (non‑looped) models and cascades of the same latency below 50 ms.

PaperId: 821, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20927.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Guanghui Min, Chen Chen
Title: Prune the Summary, Not the History: Source-Judged Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents
Abstract:
Long‑horizon LLM agents rely on context compaction: when the interaction history outgrows the context window, a compressor replaces it with a natural‑language summary. We show that these summaries contain more than a record of what happened. Compaction prompts ask for decisions and next steps, so each summary mixes facts established by the environment with reasoning written by the compressor, and the agent cannot tell the two apart afterwards. In an analysis of a widely used structured compressor, 83% of failed runs trace back to an action that carries out a specific summary entry, most of which no environment output supports. We propose Source‑Judged Compaction (SJC), a training‑free post‑processing step that scores each summary entry for whether it has a source in the environment outputs or the previous summary, and removes the entries that do not. It changes neither the agent nor the compressor and adds one inexpensive judge request per compaction. The judge is Jev, a non‑generative decision model that answers the source question with a calibrated probability instead of text. On AppWorld and OfficeBench with two agent models, SJC improves cross‑run reliability over the underlying compressor by 2.1%‑8.9% without increasing the agent's token usage.

PaperId: 822, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20859.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Abdul Rehman Antall, Baidya Nath Saha
Title: Does Morphological Correctness Matter for Tokenization? A Scrambled Control Study in Tagalog
Abstract:
Typology‑aware tokenizers are motivated by the claim that segmentation which respects morpheme boundaries preserves information that frequency‑driven segmentation destroys. Studies routinely establish that it helps while assuming the boundaries must be linguistically correct. We separate them. Tagalog marks voice with infixes (s‑um‑ulat 'wrote', s‑in‑ulat 'was written'), so the root is not contiguous and no sequence of BPE merges can recover it. We build MorphAustro‑Tok, a tokenizer that emits the root as a contiguous unit followed by a positional infix token, and compare it against a corpus‑matched BPE baseline and, at two of three fertility levels, against a scrambled‑morpheme control that preserves morph count, invertibility and per‑type consistency while randomising the pseudo‑infix. Across 33 runs, MorphAustro‑Tok improves Tagalog machine translation over matched BPE by 0.84, 1.49 and 3.40 mean sentence‑level chrF++ points. Token count does not explain the gain, since it grows as segmentation coarsens, and neither does capacity: at the coarsest level the scrambled arm carries more parameters and scores lower. Scrambling the analysis moves the gain by less than between‑seed dispersion at both controlled levels, so we detect no contribution from morphological correctness at this scale.

PaperId: 823, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20852.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Beth Pearson, Michael Wray, Martha Lewis
Title: Probing Negation Understanding in Vision-Language Models With Object Attention
Abstract:
Negation is a fundamental aspect of language understanding and it is important vision‑language models (VLMs) are able to process it effectively. We investigate how VLMs process negation by analysing attention patterns of different models. We draw comparisons between human gaze and attention in models when processing affirmative vs negated statements. We compare object level model attention to human eye‑fixations in both binary and multary settings, evaluating with both synthetic and realistic datasets. We find models generally do not follow human‑like attention patterns when resolving negation, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside of attention. While layerwise analysis shows that PaliGemma2‑3B shifts object attention to the alternative under negation, our headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism. Additionally, we find that LLaVA‑1.5‑7B displays a spatial bias towards left‑side objects. Our evaluation of models on downstream tasks shows that all models have a discrepancy between affirmative and negated questions highlighting the need to better understand the underlying processing of negation to close this performance gap. Code available at https://github.com/otmive/negation_attention

PaperId: 824, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20823.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dmytro Babarytskyi
Title: Feasibility Ceilings Before Learning: Sizing and Timing Bounds for Drone-Mesh Interception
Abstract:
A mesh of interceptors defending a fixed site must spread over the predicted arrival point of an approaching object. This is a recurring task in multi‑agent robotics: N agents, each covering a disc of radius r, spread over a probability density so that a point drawn from it falls within some agent's disc. We give closed forms for the quantities that bound performance before any policy is chosen, and validate each by Monte Carlo. The uncertainty of a point predicted by extrapolating a noisy linear track follows from least‑squares variance propagation plus a delta‑method term for the uncertain arrival time, agreeing with simulation to within 1.8%. The coverage probability of a packed mesh admits a closed form accurate to 0.007 absolute, with a volumetric analogue. A naive area ratio misses a ceiling: while agents stay at least 2r apart, no mesh exceeds 90.69% coverage in the plane or 74.05% in a volume. This ceiling belongs to the separation constraint, not to the problem ‑ permitting overlap substitutes Kershner's thinnest‑covering density and removes it, the better regime above a crossover at p=0.80. Hexagonal packing is optimal among five arrangements; the centroidal‑Voronoi configuration coverage control supplies reaches only half its coverage at small budgets. The Gaussian assumption is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but fragile under bias: a one‑sigma aim‑point offset costs 14 points of coverage. A repositioning team must also choose a commit time, and the admissible window can be empty. Against the applicable ceiling, analytic placement attains 85% of what the configuration permits while centralised PPO averages 15% over three trainer seeds, with a paired bootstrap against a null policy containing zero at every seed. We argue such ceilings should be computed before any learning experiment and quoted alongside every result.

PaperId: 825, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20821.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Marcel Friedrichs, Addie Jordon, Juri Kolčák, Daniel Merkle
Title: Automating Observable Closure Analysis for Graph Transformation Models with MolFoundry
Abstract:
Graph transformations model changing systems, with applications in software, biology and chemistry, among others. We introduce MolFoundry, a graph transformation framework, and present a workflow for observable analysis that tracks the dynamics of local patterns through rule composition. Analysing rule compositions avoids the need to enumerate a potentially infinite state space. Building on rule‑algebraic stochastic rewriting, MolFoundry's kernel composes rules with nested application conditions, including missing‑edge constraints. Given rules, rates and query patterns, the algorithms iteratively identify auxiliary pattern counts and search for closure. Using exact counting identities supplied by graph‑family backends, successful searches yield closed ordinary differential equations for average counts or, with justified individual jumps, finite event models describing joint changes and rates. We evaluate conditional composition and automated discovery of auxiliary observables against published calculations and independent rule application. Applications to aldol addition, copolymerization and chlorination show how the framework yields quantitative predictions directly from molecular graph rules.

PaperId: 826, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20814.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xuanchang Zhang, Tong Zhang
Title: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often trains language models on responses generated by a different, possibly stale behavior policy. Correcting this mismatch with learner‑to‑behavior importance weights can introduce high variance for long responses. We introduce Gibbs‑Gap Policy Optimization (GGPO), which minimizes a log‑mean‑exp contrast of KL‑adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt, without learner‑to‑behavior importance weights. We derive GGPO from KL‑regularized policy optimization: on policy, its population loss is exactly the KL‑regularized optimality gap, and under suitable coverage the learner's single‑response expected reward is at least the behavior policy's best‑of‑K reward, minus terms for the raw finite‑group loss, regularization, and finite training data. We characterize reference refresh through exact Gibbs‑target composition and a finite‑data final‑policy reward bound under local reference control and tokenwise behavior mismatch. This refresh is empirically important: in an ablation, fixed‑reference GGPO scores 32.96 on the five‑benchmark problem‑weighted average, versus 46.58 with the default refresh schedule. Experiments on mathematical reasoning further show that GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training‑inference mismatch and on fixed offline data, while maintaining its performance as controlled policy staleness grows.

PaperId: 827, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20811.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mengfei Li, Yi Zhang, Xingtong Ge, Lunjie Zhu, Fangyu Lin, Peng Li, Guanglu Song, Yu Liu, Wei Xue, Wenhan Luo, Yike Guo
Title: RIGen: Beyond Action Following with Reciprocal Interaction in Generative Gameplay
Abstract:
Generative gameplay requires more than immediate responses to player actions.Actions should have persistent consequences, while the generated world should act according to its own state and rules, shaping the player's situation and subsequent choices. Video generation captures local dynamics, but limited history, partially observed game state, and the need for contextual behavior decisions make such interactions difficult to sustain through audiovisual prediction alone. We introduce \rig (Reciprocally Interactive Generation), a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay. \rig combines persistent state and configurable rules, contextual interaction reasoning, and action‑conditioned audiovisual generation. Together, these components make interaction consequences and actor behavior jointly determine generated content while maintaining consistency between game state and visible outcomes. We construct a Xonotic gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning dynamics and interactions. Further post‑training enables \rigarena, an interactive generative first‑person shooter (FPS) prototype. Experiments demonstrate more reliable combat outcomes and reciprocal interaction between the player and the generated world. Project page: https://murphylmf.github.io/RIGen/.

PaperId: 828, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20808.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Giovana Kerche Bonás, Thales Sales Almeida, Marcelo da Silva Reis, Rodrigo Nogueira, Marcos Meideiros Raimundo
Title: PRISM: Transfer and Limits of Activation Interventions in Tool-Calling Language Models
Abstract:
Recent literature shows that unsafe tool calls can often accompany textual refusals in language models. To investigate this hidden vulnerability, we introduce PRISM, a framework for evaluating the transfer of activation interventions across precision, languages, and scales. Our findings demonstrate that leveraging lower‑resource settings (specifically quantized NF4 labels and cross‑lingual transfer) offers a robust pathway to expose and improve model alignment. Notably, using behavioral labels from an NF4 copy enables stable intervention estimation even with very few scenarios. Furthermore, these alignment improvements transfer effectively across languages: five‑language NF4‑supervised directions successfully transfer to held‑out Arabic, reducing unsafe violations in Llama‑3.1‑8B by 21.95 percentage points without target‑language tuning. By mapping paired benign activations, we also successfully transfer these safety interventions to much larger models (up to 70B parameters). Ultimately, PRISM highlights how auxiliary supervision from compressed models and multilingual data can uncover and mitigate hazardous tool‑calling behaviors across different model families. We release all experimental code and supporting artifacts at https://github.com/GiKerche/prism, alongside an interactive explorer of recorded model responses and experimental results at https://gikerche.github.io/prism/.

PaperId: 829, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20794.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sujie Hu, Huaisong Zhang, Pujing Yang, Qian Wang, Xiaomin Li, Xinhang Leng, Chen Li, Jing Lyu, Xiu Li, Ling Pan
Title: Blame Errant Words, Not the Canvas: Defect-Aware Spatial Credit Assignment for Visual Text Generation
Abstract:
Recent reinforcement learning approaches have improved visual text generation, yet generated images still suffer from incorrect wording and malformed glyphs. We identify two coupled limitations: recognition‑based rewards often overlook visible glyph defects, while whole‑image scalar feedback obscures the uneven quality of individual text regions. These limitations motivate our central principle: Blame errant words, not the canvas, to effectively preserve local quality distinctions. First, we introduce \mathbfTextDART, a defect‑aware region‑targeted reward model that localizes individual text regions and independently evaluates their semantic correctness and glyph quality, providing fine‑grained, region‑precise feedback. Building on TextDART, we propose \mathbfSCANNER, which turns these regional judgments into spatially differentiated policy feedback. It normalizes rewards for each text target across sampled images and casts the resulting regional advantages onto the corresponding latent tokens. Extensive experiments on existing benchmarks and our newly established PolyText‑Bench demonstrate that our approach achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance in text accuracy and glyph fidelity. Project page: https://sujiehu.github.io/textdart‑scanner

PaperId: 830, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20782.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jianyu Zhang, Léon Bottou
Title: Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements
Abstract:
The closed world asks AI for specialized competence and lets it manufacture the iid data its theory assumes: a fixed criterion licenses collecting examples until the task is covered. The open world asks for versatility ‑‑‑ taking up tasks a machine was not built for, from few examples and with little prior from a human designer ‑‑‑ and offers data that is grouped, not shuffled. Its tasks are not known in advance, so a machine must do inference‑time learning (1st requirement). Modeling tasks as sharing latent factors and decomposing the training objective, we derive two more: a rich representation, retaining more than iid generalization requires, and a predictive disentanglement that aligns inputs and outputs into matched low‑dimensional groups. The analysis further predicts the need for a consistent inner learner, and the benefit of long contexts spanning related tasks. We test these claims on language models up to 8B, asking whether a model has a property (qualitative) rather than how much it wins (quantitative). Models that meet the requirements improve as data from related tasks accumulates; the rest degrade, and neither scale nor layer‑type interleaving repairs this.

PaperId: 831, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20780.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Bolin Shen, Yushun Dong
Title: ARIA: Runtime Inspection and Amendment for Multi-Agent Systems
Abstract:
In LLM‑based multi‑agent systems (MAS), a local mistake can propagate as other agents build on it, turning a correctable error into a failed task. Diagnosing completed runs or repeatedly re‑executing them to search for corrections does not provide a learned policy for intervening while execution is still in progress. We present Agent Runtime Inspection and Amendment (ARIA), a framework for learning when and how to repair ongoing multi‑agent executions. Our key intuition is to turn execution‑verified repairs into reusable supervision, moving repair search into data construction and training so that a learned model can intervene at runtime without repeatedly testing alternatives. First, we collect over 24,000 successful and failed trajectories across four multi‑agent frameworks, six benchmarks, and eight host models. From these trajectories, we construct the ARIA dataset, to our knowledge the first large‑scale dataset pairing failed multi‑agent trajectories with execution‑verified repairs. It contains 3,953 verified repair pairs, each specifying what went wrong, where to intervene, and how execution should continue. Then, we develop the ARIA framework for MAS‑agnostic runtime inspection and amendment, designed to integrate with any MAS that exposes execution trajectories and supports continuation replacement. Using verified repairs as training examples, we teach a compact model to recognize when intervention is needed and how to correct an ongoing run. The aim is to learn repair strategies that apply to related failures in new configurations, rather than merely reproduce individual corrections. Finally, the trained ARIA model demonstrates strong repair performance in both post‑hoc and runtime settings, with generalization to unseen frameworks and host models. Our code is available at https://github.com/LabRAI/ARIA.

PaperId: 832, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20778.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Avdhesh Singh Chouhan, Jack Perry
Title: Verdict: Encode Once, Decide Many
Abstract:
Automating organizational work means answering many small typed questions about one piece of state (does this email need a reply, how urgent is it, who owns it) with probabilities good enough to act on without a human. The open typed‑decision model we compare against, like a standard cross‑encoder, answers each question with a separate pass over the input. We present Verdict‑MQ, an open encoder that reads a case once and answers all of its questions: given identical retained state tokens after truncation (verified on every reported case), a structured attention mask makes the state encoding independent of the questions, keeps questions from influencing each other, and makes option order irrelevant by construction. On the typed‑decisions benchmark, a 395M Verdict‑MQ matches the soft gold labels significantly better than the released 421M Laya specialist on all five fresh seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061), an advantage that survives per‑system temperature scaling; its higher accuracy (0.801 vs 0.767) lies past the benchmark's own saturation point, so we read that margin as closer agreement with the benchmark's labelling teacher. On RACE, BoolQ and MultiRC, against a matched fine‑tuned baseline it wins on MultiRC and loses on RACE and on BoolQ, where its training is unstable; we measure zero‑shot references ourselves, including a closed general system (Jev) that beats every fine‑tuned encoder. A controlled comparison measures what the shared state costs: giving each question its own question‑aware copy of the state gains 0.9‑3.5 points on RACE and MultiRC at 1.4‑2.5x the per‑case latency, and nothing measurable on typed decisions, with the invariance guarantees unchanged.

PaperId: 833, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20776.pdf   GitHub
