Authors:Thuy Dung Nguyen, Jingyi Guo, Rana Seda Dubauskas, Sreepriya Damuluru, Taylor T. Johnson, Kevin Leach
Title: INFUSE: A Unified Surface Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems
Abstract:
LLM‑based agents increasingly execute long‑horizon, end‑to‑end workflows involving shell commands, code modification, dependency installation, and interaction with remote services. This growing autonomy expands their exposure to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in external content are interpreted as legitimate task directives. Existing evaluations, however, often focus on isolated malicious strings, single‑step tool calls, or narrowly scoped agent configurations. We introduce INFUSE, an end‑to‑end benchmark for evaluating IPI throughout the lifecycle of long‑horizon agent workflows. INFUSE comprises 40 realistic tasks and a structured taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios spanning five threat categories. Attacks are injected through realistic interaction surfaces encountered during task execution, extending evaluation beyond attacks placed only in initial prompts or isolated tool interactions. We evaluate 19 LLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, producing 41,824 adversarial trajectories (26,220 without defenses) and 720 benign reference runs. Across the benchmark, mean attack success reaches 19.6% under LLM‑based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per‑model ASR‑L ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%. Existing guard models provide limited protection, while prompt‑level instructional hardening reduces mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3%, revealing substantial but model‑dependent security‑utility trade‑offs. Our code is available at https://github.com/judydnguyen/infuse.

PaperId: 834, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20763.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yuxuan Chen, Yang Xiao, Jack Sun, Chak Sun, Brick Li, Sam
Title: Reference-Guided Turn-Taking Style Transfer for Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models
Abstract:
Full‑duplex spoken language models decide at every frame whether to take the floor, defining a conversational personality ‑‑ yet each set of weights encodes exactly one, which human speakers bracket rather than share. Existing controls mostly act from outside; none identifies the quantity that sets how much the model speaks. We identify it: a single late‑layer residual‑stream direction, the initiative vector, extracted from the model's own conversations without training or annotation. The same direction reads the decision, anticipating onsets up to 800 ms ahead, and shifts it: scaled during generation, it moves speech ratio from 6‑12% to 42‑61% (no steering: 21‑30%), consistently across conversations, weights, and corpora. A short reference recording suffices to transfer a speaker's turn‑taking style to the model, and the transfer is reference‑specific: swapping in another speaker's reference worsens the match in 93‑98% of cases, whereas the best uniform dose is indistinguishable from no steering. Turn‑taking style is not frozen into the weights but a direction that can be read, shifted, and calibrated per person. Audio examples are available at https://elpsykongloo.github.io/initiative‑vector/.

PaperId: 835, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20731.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wenhao Yan, Haodong Li, Xiaotong Li, Yaxin Luo, Zhengrong Yue, Jialv Zou, Xu Huang, Haojin Yang, Nan Jia, Yan Feng, Peng Pei, Xunliang Cai
Title: WorldCast: Exploring Intelligent Visual Generation in World State Prediction
Abstract:
Humans interpret multimodal observations of the world and forecast how it will evolve. Recent multimodal generative systems have demonstrated similar capabilities: they can integrate multimodal context and synthesize visual outputs that depict changes in the world. To characterize this emerging trajectory, we organize model capabilities into a four‑level hierarchy and discover that higher‑level tasks remain relatively underexplored despite model progress. To bridge this gap, we explore model performance on multi‑step world state prediction, a high‑level task that requires models to forecast successive future world states from multimodal observations and diverse references. Such a task requires models to possess entangled understanding and generation capabilities, as well as extensive world knowledge to translate human action sequences, physical transformations, and abstract visual reasoning into coherent visual outputs. We introduce WorldCast, a benchmark comprising 320 manually designed cases across eight categories, and evaluate 12 representative models. The conducted experiments yield three key insights: (a) advances in frontier models are rapidly pushing the boundaries of intelligent world modeling, with the GPT‑Image‑2.5 System scoring 72.8 and demonstrating early‑stage visual state prediction capabilities on real‑world tasks; (b) WorldCast reveals substantial gaps between models: even Nano Banana Pro reaches only 42.8 and the best open‑source model scores 20.1, with deficits in handling complex context, entangled references, and reasoning‑heavy tasks; (c) strong generative models effectively draw on the capabilities of their underlying language models. These findings highlight the need for multimodal generative models that are capable of dynamic planning and reasoning while also being deeply unified to faithfully simulate real‑world states.

PaperId: 836, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20693.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dongyue Lu, Guian Fang, Hur Lim, Yonggang Wu, Yanrong Wang, Hongshan Chen, Shengju Qian, Yue Liao, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong, Tianxin Huang, Yu Yang, Hongji Yang, Junchao Huang, Ao Liang, Yihao Wang, Zihan Wang, Rong Li, Hanlin Chen, Xin Wang, Wei Tsang Ooi, Mike Zheng Shou, Shuicheng Yan
Title: Orbia: Do Generated Videos Form a Consistent 3D World?
Abstract:
Video generators serve as interactive worlds for exploration and simulation, yet realistic and visually appealing frames do not necessarily depict a consistent 3D world. Existing benchmarks assess selected geometric properties or use vision‑language models to judge memory and consistency, leaving systematic 3D evaluation underexplored. We introduce Orbia, the first benchmark dedicated to a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of 3D consistency in interactive world models. Through controlled exploration and revisit, we organize the evaluation into three dimensions: input preservation, generated‑content persistence, and 3D self‑consistency. For input preservation, registered RGB‑D references and annotated anchors support appearance, geometry, and spatial stability measurements. For generated‑content persistence, we compare revisits to regions absent from the input image with their first generated observations to test whether models preserve what they create. For 3D self‑consistency, cross‑view depth and feature correspondence, regional scale agreement, and held‑out Gaussian rendering test whether generated views describe the same 3D scene. Minute‑long exploration and revisits further test long‑term consistency. Our construction and annotation pipeline brings together public datasets, self‑captured scenes, and simulation, yielding 720 instances across indoor and outdoor environments and six exploration‑and‑revisit protocols. Evaluation spans 27 text‑, action‑, and camera‑conditioned models through native‑interface adapters. Our Orbia benchmark provides a systematic basis for diagnosing 3D inconsistency and developing more persistent video world models.

PaperId: 837, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20642.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jie Yu, Yuxi Sun, Zhaoxu Li, Chunxiao Liu, Xudong Jiang
Title: CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
Abstract:
Recent latent reasoning methods move beyond discrete Chain‑of‑Thought (CoT) by replacing sampled tokens with continuous soft embeddings or hidden states, enabling richer intermediate representations and preserving alternative reasoning paths. However, the need for latent reasoning varies across decoding steps: confident predictions favor discrete commitment, whereas ambiguous steps benefit from preserving multiple plausible alternatives. Existing approaches typically handle this variation through either global soft activation or hard switching based on uncertainty thresholds, treating latent intervention as an all‑or‑nothing decision rather than continuously adapting its strength. To address this limitation, we propose Competitive Token Selection (CoTS), a training‑free framework that reframes latent intervention from binary mode selection into continuous allocation at the token level. CoTS uses the probability competition between the two most likely candidates to dynamically balance discrete commitment and soft exploration at each reasoning step. The second candidate represents the strongest alternative to the model's preferred continuation, so the separation between the two directly reflects the stability of the current discrete choice. When one candidate clearly dominates, CoTS keeps the representation close to the sampled discrete token to preserve a stable reasoning trajectory; as the competition strengthens, it increases the contribution of the soft representation to retain plausible alternatives. This competition‑based allocation requires neither manually tuned switching thresholds nor mixing coefficients, and introduces no additional forward passes. Experiments across six reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that CoTS consistently outperforms standard CoT and state‑of‑the‑art training‑free latent reasoning methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/OkinoYu/CoTSReasoning.

PaperId: 838, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20640.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Minjong Cheon
Title: KNOU-Flood: Advancing global streamflow forecasting with lead-aware probabilistic machine learning
Abstract:
Global streamflow forecasting supports flood preparedness, yet data‑driven models trained on reanalysis lose skill when driven by operational forecasts, increasingly so with lead time. AIFL addresses this shift with a two‑stage transfer‑learning recipe and a deterministic LSTM, but it feeds one forecast lead time into the whole input window and gives no uncertainty. We ask how far this open recipe can be extended without changing its recurrent core. KNOU‑Flood keeps a single‑layer LSTM and the two‑stage training and changes the information around it: a longer input window (424 days), lead‑aware forecast inputs, GraphCast as a second forecast source next to ECMWF HRES, and a latent‑noise ensemble trained with the fair CRPS. We compare against a re‑implementation of the AIFL recipe (its code is not public) under identical data, stations, splits and metrics. Our contributions are threefold. First, over three seeds and 2,099 test basins (2021‑2023), KNOU‑Flood reaches a median KGE' of 0.65 at LT1 and 0.48 at LT10 against 0.62 and 0.34, with significant gains at all ten lead times under two scoring protocols, also against a 1024‑unit baseline and on held‑out basins (one seed each). Second, identical weights give an LT10 KGE' of 0.18 or 0.34 depending on how forecasts are fed, so much of the lead‑time decay reported for AIFL is an input‑protocol effect; the probabilistic head contributes most to the gain, followed by the raw GraphCast channels, the longer window and mixed fine‑tuning. Third, the ensembles reach lower CRPS than probabilistic versions of the baseline, are nearly calibrated with inference‑time dropout, and detect 1.5‑ and 2‑year floods better than all baselines; the benefit for rarer floods depends on the seed, and an exploratory tail‑weighted variant improves 10‑year and larger events. KNOU‑Flood is a controlled extension of an open recipe, not a new architecture.

PaperId: 839, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20636.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zahra Dehghani, Pablo Piantanida, Mohammadhadi Shateri
Title: FlowBudget: Training-Free Sampling-Budget Estimation for Flow Matching Models
Abstract:
Sampling from continuous flow‑based generators such as flow matching models requires numerical ODE or SDE integration, making inference cost depend on the number of function evaluations (NFEs). In practice, the sampling budget is inherited from prior work or selected through expensive FID‑versus‑NFE sweeps, using FID to assess image‑generation quality, requiring sample generation and evaluation at multiple budgets. This makes sampling‑budget selection dependent on repeated empirical evaluation. We therefore ask a complementary question to solver design and timestep allocation: for a fixed pretrained model and solver, what numerical resolution is sufficient? We introduce FLOWBUDGET, a training‑free estimator of solver‑relative sampling complexity. Using simulation‑free interpolation probes of the learned dynamics, FLOWBUDGET normalizes the leading one‑step discretization error by the motion, estimates its coefficient from interpolation probes, and maps a numerical tolerance to a step budget using the solver order. We derive estimators for numerical solvers in flow~matching sampling, namely Euler and Heun for ODE sampling and additive‑noise Euler‑‑Maruyama for SDE sampling, and connect the ODE coefficients to terminal integration error. Experiments on SiT, FlowDCN and Rectified Flow models, spanning flow‑model architectures and formulations, test whether FLOWBUDGET can estimate the NFE budget without generating samples at multiple budgets or performing an FID‑versus‑NFE sweep. The code is available at https://github.com/Yasaman‑dt/FlowBudget

PaperId: 840, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20634.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Alden Do Rosario, Kirollos Atef
Title: Jev-as-a-Judge for RAG Claim Verification: Confidence-Gated Cascading Between a Non-Generative Verifier and a Frontier LLM
Abstract:
Retrieval‑augmented generation asks one question at volume: does this evidence support this claim? The answer is one bit, yet most pipelines obtain it from a text generator and pay generation prices for the prose wrapped around it. We compare a non‑generative decision model, which returns a typed value from a declared enumeration together with a native probability and no text, against a frontier LLM configured as an engineer would deploy it for binary classification. Both answer the same 495 human‑labelled claims from LLM‑AggreFact, so every comparison is within‑item. We report three things. First, the two systems are statistically indistinguishable on the metric this task is conventionally scored by, a paired difference of ‑0.56 points, Jev minus Astra, at a 187‑fold cost difference. Second, that tie carries almost no information about deployment: the systems disagree on 15.2% of claims, and the cheaper one admits 23.2% of the claims annotators marked unsupported against the frontier model's 14.1%. A component whose job is to catch unsupported claims should be judged on that rate, and the conventional headline hides it. Third, because the errors differ they compose: routing the claims the cheap model is confident about and escalating the rest reaches 74.10 at USD 2.92 per thousand claims against 73.83 at USD 8.93, with the threshold chosen out of fold. But a matched random‑escalation control at in‑sample thresholds, spending the same budget by coin flip, does as well, so what buys the saving is the escalation share and not the probability that picks what to escalate. Measured against the cheap model it is built from, the cascade costs 61‑fold more for 0.83 points, 95% CI [‑3.36, 4.86], and it is the more permissive guard of the two. Equal accuracy conceals unequal errors. All predictions, prompts, pricing and code are released.

PaperId: 841, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20633.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Thomas Serval
Title: Context Injection and Long-Horizon Reliability: Separating Duplicate Recognition, Local Processing, and Counter Tracking
Abstract:
Long‑horizon failures of language models are usually measured as end‑task success or as a horizon length. We instead score, step by step, three components of a 400‑step ledger task in which every step is easy in isolation and the model's own answers are re‑injected into its context: recognising a record already seen 5 to 300 steps earlier, processing the current record locally, and writing a counter incremented at every step. On Qwen3‑8B (non‑thinking, 20 seeds, replicated on a second machine and backend), with every step scored component by component, two results hold. First, duplicate‑recognition errors rise late in the episode ‑‑ from 0.0019 to 0.011 per step at risk across step 200 ‑‑ while the counter makes no error in 8,000 steps and local processing is descriptively stable; the rise combines long‑distance recall errors and rising false alarms. Second, a block of irrelevant content inserted before each step makes the counter fail in 20 of 20 seeds on each machine, against none without it, while its effect on local processing is much smaller and not distinguishable from none. Three pre‑registered follow‑ups probe the counter. Its value depends on the value present in the response history: a corrupted value persists without correction in every seed, and an exact external reminder, repeated before each message, re‑aligns it within one to two steps. Under the irrelevant block, no counter error was observed when an exact compact reminder of the state, supplied externally by an oracle, preceded each message (0 of 20 seeds with an error, against 15 without it), and this reminder outperformed a length‑matched neutral text; whether a single reminder suffices was not conclusive, and the absence of damage to the other components was not established. An aggregate or exclusive error classification can hide the difference we report.

PaperId: 842, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20573.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Anna Mei, Michael R. Douglas
Title: Beyond LLM Judge: Mechanical Verification for Agentic Autoformalization
Abstract:
We introduce a novel method for verifying Lean formalizations that goes beyond LLM‑judged faithfulness. Unlike most verification methods, which rely on LLMs or trained models, our method combines LLM‑based semantic review with mechanical numerical and vacuity checks, providing checkable feedback and detecting errors missed by LLM judges. We apply this method, along with our Extract‑Verify‑Proof autoformalization pipeline, to construct the Formalized Library of Mathematical Functions (FLMF), a partial formalization of the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF). On three labeled datasets, our method achieves the lowest accepted‑error rate among the evaluated methods, measured as the fraction of incorrect statements accepted by the verification method. Expert review of the results also identifies translation and source defects in existing datasets. Code available at https://github.com/annamei1/FLMF‑Ch7ErrFunc‑Release.git.

PaperId: 843, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20363.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fares B. Mehouachi, Saif Eddin Jabari
Title: Fractional is Better: Learnable Derivative Orders in Neural Operator Learning
Abstract:
Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, enabling fast surrogate solutions to partial differential equations. Despite remarkable architectural diversity, these methods often share a common input representation: raw coordinate‑value pairs (x, u(x)). We ask whether inputs aligned with PDE differential structure can improve learning. Through Picard iteration on mild solutions, we show that derivatives of the input appear explicitly in the solution operator, suggesting that providing derivative features should reduce the network's implicit differentiation burden. We prove this intuition: providing derivative features improves approximation bounds from O(W^‑(s‑m)/d) to O(W^‑s/d), where W is parameter count, s is input regularity, m is the PDE order, and d is spatial dimension. Our central finding, however, is a surprise: the optimal derivative order β^ is strictly less than the PDE order m. This gap arises from a bias‑variance tradeoff in spectral space that we characterize in closed form. Learning β from data achieves automatic spectral regularization. We introduce \partial‑NO (del‑NO), for derivative‑augmented neural operators, an architecture‑agnostic augmentation that provides learnable fractional derivative features to any neural operator backbone. Across benchmark problems and architectures, \partial‑NO consistently improves prediction accuracy, with learned orders that reflect a representation of known physics modulated by noise and finite‑sample constraints.

PaperId: 844, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20350.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ren Zhuang, Ben Wang, Shuifa Sun
Title: Lifted State Policy Optimization: Internalizing Self-Correction through Transition Geometry
Abstract:
Preference optimization ranks final answers and trajectory RL maximizes aggregate returns, yet neither credits the local change that turns a flawed reasoning state into a better one. We introduce Lifted State Policy Optimization (LSPO), which establishes this finite, cost‑adjusted transition as the primary unit of learning. Each textual answer is augmented with a learned continuous coordinate, forming a lifted state that an energy function evaluates and orders. A shaped reward drives energy descent net of edit and step costs, and an internalization loss absorbs selected low‑energy answers into the direct generator. On Qwen3.5‑27B, the resulting single‑pass policy reaches 71.8% aggregate accuracy across mathematics, science, code, and logic benchmarks, matching test‑time reflection at 71.9% with 28% lower latency and 25.8% fewer tokens. The pattern holds across dense and mixture‑of‑experts backbones, and matched controls confirm that transition credit and the lifted coordinate each contribute, as does answer internalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/Venomrko/lspo.

PaperId: 845, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20341.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yongzhen Hu, Hao Yu, Jiawei Wang, Xianming Zeng, Jianyun Xu, Xingliang Liu, Ruizhen Hu, Xiaowei Zhou, Hujun Bao, Sida Peng
Title: InfiniSplat v2: Analyzing and Improving Feed-Forward 3DGS from Any Views
Abstract:
Feed‑forward Gaussian reconstruction builds 3D scenes directly from input images for novel view rendering, but learning Gaussian attributes from predicted geometry for high‑quality rendering under large viewpoint changes remains challenging. We analyze limitations in Gaussian attribute learning and introduce InfiniSplat v2, which improves rendering quality through architectural and training changes. Our method decouples geometry and attribute prediction with a frozen geometry branch, aligns predicted Gaussians using ground‑truth camera poses during training, and adopts large‑angle target view supervision. Across six datasets, the feed‑forward outputs of the same trained model achieve state‑of‑the‑art mean LPIPS and DISTS among the evaluated methods in both pose‑conditioned and pose‑free settings. In the pose‑conditioned setting, mean LPIPS and DISTS decrease by 25.8% and 32.9%, respectively, compared with the strongest evaluated baselines. We further find that opacity learned with only image reconstruction supervision suppresses geometrically inconsistent points. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/InfiniSplat2/

PaperId: 846, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20335.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuheng Chen, Yufan Chen, Zhuojun Cai, Ruiping Liu, Junwei Zheng, Jiale Wei, Di Wen, Weijia Fan, Kunyu Peng, Jiaming Zhang, Rainer Stiefelhagen
Title: Read, Parse, Describe: Unified Document Parsing with Visual Element Description Generation
Abstract:
Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading‑order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page‑level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read‑Parse‑Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation. Given a page image, models are required to output an ordered list of layout elements containing bounding boxes, semantic labels, reading‑order indices, recognized textual content, and alternative text descriptions for visual elements. The benchmark is built from 2,402 documents, comprising 18,163 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances. Besides, we further propose a plug‑and‑play space‑awareness enhancer that reuses multi‑layer visual features and injects grid‑aware spatial guidance into vision‑language tokens for layout‑aware generation. Experiments across end‑to‑end VLMs and pipeline parsers show that existing systems still struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while our enhanced model achieves strong joint performance. These results highlight the need to move beyond isolated document parsing modules toward unified models that jointly read, parse, and describe complex documents. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yufanchen96/RPD

PaperId: 847, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20331.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Woobin Park, Jaeyeon Kim, Yilun Du, Sitan Chen, Bohyung Han
Title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
Abstract:
Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one‑step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two‑stage framework for training one‑step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel‑space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature‑space distributional post‑training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class‑conditional image generation, text‑to‑image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at 256 × 256 resolution, we achieve a state‑of‑the‑art FID of 1.19 among one‑step generators using approximately one‑tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open‑source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.

PaperId: 848, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20319.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yinzhen Huang, Jiahe Xie, Yitong Sun, Ruochen Zhang, Xingxing Wei
Title: Beyond Static Cues: Unified Dynamic Detection of MLLM Backdoors via Dual-Flow Trajectory Analysis
Abstract:
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety‑critical domains, yet their susceptibility to backdoor attacks remains a formidable challenge. While existing defenses have evolved from visual‑centric patch cues to unsupervised internal attention statistics, they are fundamentally constrained by a reliance on static snapshots and attack‑specific heuristics. Given the intricate interplay between dual modalities, the vast design space for multimodal triggers allows diverse threats, such as textual injections, sub‑perceptual noises, and coordinated cross‑modal triggers, to easily circumvent such rigid priors, particularly when attack types are unknown in real‑world applications. In this paper, we rethink backdoor detection by shifting the diagnostic paradigm from static observations to dynamic output evolution. We observe that a successful attack inevitably hijacks the model's decoding trajectory, skewing internal modal contributions during generation while maintaining an abnormal output invariance despite input perturbations. To capture this behavior, we propose EVO‑Detect, a unified detection framework that monitors the dynamic evolution of internal signals during early decoding steps through two complementary channels: Attention Flow and Logits Flow. The attention branch measures how image‑text attention allocation evolves during early generation, whereas the logits branch quantifies the sensitivity of the output distribution to modal perturbations through interventional ablations. We then convert these trajectories into compact sample‑level metrics and normalize them against negative‑control signatures so that natural perturbations are less likely to be mistaken for backdoor evidence. Extensive evaluations show that our approach substantially outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines such as BYE and TCAP across diverse attack families.

PaperId: 849, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20288.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sam Gijsen, Moritz Seiler, Kerstin Ritter
Title: Predicting Unseen Scientific Interactions: Conditional Flow Models Hallucinate Non-Additive Effects
Abstract:
Conditional generative models are increasingly used for scientific prediction beyond the direct training support. Yet scientific questions often concern whether one intervention changes the effect of another. Such interactions can be of primary interest while explaining little of the total variation, allowing models to appear accurate overall without recovering the relevant scientific effect. It remains unclear how these models learn interactions and when these successfully extrapolate to unseen conditions. We therefore study interaction recovery in flow‑matching models using a physiological time‑series simulator, drug dose‑response data, combinatorial cell perturbations, and molecular conformer generations, where we separate recovery from hallucinated interaction structure. In the controlled setting, individual effects are learned much earlier than interactions and models hallucinate interactions where none exist. Across settings, we find qualitatively different generalization problems, with successful prediction depending on whether condition structure continues from observed to held‑out targets. When it does, interactions are recoverable. If not, models can generate plausible responses while missing the interaction. We furthermore find that hallucinations increase as targets become less identifiable, and that successful interaction recovery in output space can fail under nonlinear readouts. Finally, we show that aggregate fidelity metrics can conceal whether models learn and extrapolate interactions.

PaperId: 850, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20286.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dai Shi, Andi Han, Xiaoyu Li, Luke Thompson, José Miguel Hernández-Lobato
Title: From Plato to Aristotle: Toward a General Theory of Representation Hypotheses
Abstract:
The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) holds that increasingly capable models converge toward a common representation. However, recent studies have shown different views on aligning representations via their neighborhoods, spanning trees, and distances. We show that these views can differ because the alignment criteria behind them sit at different points of one lattice, and we formalize this explanation as the Lattice Representation Hypothesis (LRH). Under the LRH, the convergence claimed by the PRH is agreement at the top of the lattice, whereas its evidence comes from neighbor overlap, a criterion near the bottom. The Aristotelian Representation Hypothesis (ARH) restricts convergence to local neighborhoods because calibration keeps the growth of neighbor overlap with model size but largely removes that of centered kernel alignment. We show that this removal can come from calibrating a maximum over layers, so global convergence remains open. Back into Plato's Cave (BPC) infers coarse shared structure from the collapse of neighbor overlap on larger evaluation sets, whereas we trace it at least partly to a fixed number of neighbors covering shorter distances. We show that the spanning‑tree overlap used by Structure over Geometry (SOG) mostly repeats one‑nearest‑neighbor overlap. The LRH also extends to independently trained models, whose training procedure and objective decide the criteria met reliably across runs. We prove this claim for the training procedure in a linear autoencoder and for the objective in a finite contrastive Gibbs model. Experiments on dozens of pretrained vision and language models and thousands of runs of both theoretical models support these conclusions. We hope this work paves the way toward a general theory of representation hypotheses, with a framework to analyze them and compare their evidence. Project page: https://eethanshi.github.io/LRH

PaperId: 851, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20272.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zewen Jiang, Yahan Li, Chenlu Guo, Diana Inkpen, Yuan Wu, Yi Chang
Title: CSWBench: Evaluating Context-Sensitive Code-Switching in Creative Writing
Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated multilingual capabilities across diverse language generation and understanding tasks. Yet effective code‑switching requires more than multilingual proficiency: models must decide when, where, and why to switch languages in ways that fit the surrounding context. This context‑sensitive ability remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce CSWBench, a benchmark for evaluating context‑sensitive code‑switching in creative writing through two complementary settings: Focused Narrative and Extended Narrative. We further propose CSWEval, a theory‑informed framework with two complementary levels: event‑level evaluation of Licensing, Contextual Appropriateness, and Functional Gain, and whole‑text evaluation of task‑specific quality‑‑‑overall literary and narrative quality in Focused Narrative and quality emphasizing multilingual organization in Extended Narrative. Evaluating twelve LLMs, we find that models exhibit meaningful but uneven code‑switching competence across narrative contexts. Model differences are particularly pronounced in multilingual literary integration, while multilingual‑focused dimensions show stronger difficulty effects overall than the general narrative dimensions; narratively salient switches are associated with stronger contextual and functional realization; and event‑level CS quality is moderately associated with whole‑text performance.

PaperId: 852, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20245.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mohsen Iranmanesh, Sina Moradi Sabet, Sina Marefat, Ali Javidi Ghasr, Maxime Newman Nereyabagabo, Kousha Amouzesh, Jaivir Malhi, Vinci Velasco, Alex Chung, Mohammad A. Tayebi
Title: P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
Abstract:
Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for automated program repair, patching software vulnerabilities through multi‑step reasoning and tool use. Yet these systems typically validate a patch against the same evidence used to construct it ‑‑ a static alert, sanitizer trace, published exploit, or test suite. A patch that blocks that one piece of evidence can therefore look successful while remaining vulnerable to the same vulnerability with some variation. We present P2Patch, a generative adversarial repair system that treats each patch as a new attack target. Starting from a normalized vulnerability finding, an exploitation agent constructs a reproducing proof of vulnerability (PoV), a patching agent repairs the program, and the exploitation agent then attacks the patched program for a distinct same‑vulnerability exploit. Every successful exploit becomes a permanent repair requirement, and the final patch must block all PoVs accumulated during the patching process, with construction‑time PoVs kept strictly separate from held‑out evaluation oracles. Across 101 C/C++ and Java CVE subjects, this adversarial loop surfaces a distinct confirmed exploit in 41% of runs after the patch has already blocked its original construction‑time PoV. Against single‑pass repair from the same finding using Claude Code, P2Patch raises held‑out fix‑closed coverage from 78.1% to 84.7% and beyond‑upstream coverage from 42.1% to 62.5%. Under the same held‑out oracles, it also certifies more attack paths as blocked than recent state‑of‑the‑art agentic repair systems on overlapping subjects. These results show that adversarial testing and independent security oracles expose repair gaps that one‑shot validation misses.

PaperId: 853, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20223.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Huailiang Ma, Yuxuan Li, Ziyi Zhao, Xinkai Wang, Mingyu Li, Xinyu Guo, Lifeng Zhu, Aiguo Song, Cewu Lu, Jianhua Sun
Title: ObjDream: Guiding Vision-Language-Action Models with Object-Level Understanding and Future State Prediction
Abstract:
Vision‑language‑action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions. However, most existing VLA models still operate on image‑level visual representations inherited from pretrained vision‑language backbones, while lacking fine‑grained object understanding for manipulation. As a result, their robustness can degrade under out‑of‑distribution object layouts, clutter, and background variations. To address these limitations, we introduce ObjDream, an object‑centric VLA framework centered on object‑level understanding and future object state prediction. ObjDream uses a spatio‑temporal object encoder to organize visual observations into temporal object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels. These structured object representations are inserted into the token sequence of the vision‑language model (VLM), where identity‑guided routing modulates VLM attention to the corresponding object tokens. In addition, an action‑conditioned object dynamics module predicts compact future object states relevant to manipulation during training, explicitly supervising object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO‑Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 show that ObjDream improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and scene perturbations. Real‑world robot experiments further demonstrate that ObjDream transfers to physical manipulation settings with novel object arrangements and background changes.

PaperId: 854, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20209.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yule Sheng, Yue Yuan, Shan Shen, Daying Sun
Title: HGRP: Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Routability Prediction
Abstract:
Routability prediction enables rapid evaluation of placement quality without routing, providing effective feedback for routability‑driven placement optimization. Recent machine learning methods have achieved efficient routability prediction through data‑driven approach. However, their prediction performance highly depends on the capability of input representations to capture essential circuit information. To address the limitations of existing circuit representations in simultaneously preserving logical topology, physical layout and routing resource information, this paper proposes HGRP, a heterogeneous graph neural network for routability prediction. HGRP models the cells, nets, and routing grids as distinct types of nodes and explicitly represents topological connectivity, spatial mapping, and grid adjacency, thereby constructing a heterogeneous graph representation that preserves multi‑level circuit semantics. Based on the representation, a heterogeneous message passing mechanism is developed to enable information interaction and feature fusion among distinct types of nodes, effectively learning the complex correlations between circuit structures and routing behaviors. Experimental results on the CircuitNet dataset show that HGRP improves F1‑score by 18.69% relative improvements compared with the state‑of‑the‑art in the congestion prediction task. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ShenShan123/HGPR.

PaperId: 855, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20179.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Davide Baldelli, Robyn Kozierok, Mirko Bronzi, Damiano Fornasiere
Title: Cross-Model In-Context Neurofeedback Reveals (Limited) Activation Control in LLMs
Abstract:
Probes on activation vectors are widely used to detect misbehavior in language models, but their success relies on the assumption that models cannot control what their activations encode. Humans can learn, through neurofeedback, to control the firing of even single neurons, and recent studies investigated whether this ability extends to language models, reaching conflicting conclusions. No experimental design so far disentangles competence at the task from genuine access to one's own activations. We fill this gap with in‑context neurofeedback sessions, in which a "subject" model is asked to maximize (or minimize) a score derived from its activations, shown back to it at every turn. In our first experiment, the sentences are generated either by the subject or by a second "writer" model, while the score always derives from the activations of the subject. We test ten open‑weight models from five families, with sizes from 9B to 32B. Some models move their own scores considerably, but no more than a writer of comparable competence moves them. Is this because the task requires no privileged access, or because the subject controls its activations while processing the sentences, whoever wrote them? To answer this, we prefill a fixed sentence as the subject's reply at every turn and ask it to increase or decrease the score. Three out of ten models show small but consistent control effects. We further ask whether models can control their activations to the point of fooling an activation monitor. We make models repeat sentences a monitor would flag, such as a deceptive answer for a deception monitor, and ask them to raise or lower the monitor's score. No model learns to lower it, but one model can raise it. In‑context control of a model's own activations might not yet be a threat to activation monitors, but it exists in a few models and needs to be tracked as models evolve.

PaperId: 856, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20157.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shijun Shi, Zhe Liu, Zhi Hou, Yinan Chen, Tao Zhang, Kai Hu, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
Title: Atomic-WAM: Execution-Grounded Atomic-Motion Reasoning for World Action Models
Abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task‑level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state‑dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic‑WAM, an understand‑then‑execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic‑motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision‑language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact‑enriched supervision from multi‑view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic‑motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post‑train the reasoner with Execution‑Grounded GRPO (EG‑GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG‑GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic‑WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real‑to‑sim evaluation on RoboLab. Project page: https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic‑WAM‑project

PaperId: 857, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20144.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mohammad Yousuf, Arif Md Tareque Habib
Title: Structural Dependence, Imitation or Herding? A Multi-Agent Simulation of Global Intermedia Agenda Setting
Abstract:
News outlets in poorer countries cover the world much as the leading outlets of rich countries do. Two explanations compete. One says they depend on Western news agencies for lack of resources. The other says they choose to copy prestigious outlets or whoever moves first. Observation cannot tell these apart. This study measured how closely 18 national outlets in Bangladesh, Kenya, South Africa, India, Malaysia and Nigeria followed four core outlets in how much attention they gave, which angle they took and when they published, on the wars in Ukraine and Gaza and two UN climate conferences in 2022‑2024. It then ran a simulation in which language models acted as the outlets' editors and dependence, imitation and herding were switched on and off. Of nine tests, one held: outlets that relied more on wire copy published sooner after the core did. Tier and local stake showed no effect distinguishable from none. The herding test was supported and the imitation test was not. The simulation did not decide between the mechanisms, because the dependence rule, as fitted, reduced to publishing wire copy. Wire copy sets the clock of the periphery's foreign news. Whether it sets the agenda stays open.

PaperId: 858, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20121.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hongyu Ding, Kanyu Xu, Mingjia Chen, Zixuan Chen, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yifan Zhang, Yang Gao
Title: HM3D-M3: A Benchmark for Multi-Agent, Multi-Modal, Multi-Object Goal Navigation
Abstract:
Rapid progress in AI agents and robotics makes it a matter of the near future that humans are served by a team of robots. Such a team will receive several goals at once, each specified in whatever form is convenient for the human, such as a category name, a photo, or a spoken description. Existing benchmarks study multi‑agent, multi‑modal, and multi‑object goal navigation in isolation, and a benchmark that places all three in one episode is missing. To fill this gap, we introduce HM3D‑M3. A team of K agents starts at distributed locations in a photorealistic indoor scene and searches for an unordered set of M object goals, each given as an open‑vocabulary category, an instance image, or an instance description. HM3D‑M3 provides 1,000 validation episodes over 3,926 goals from 379 open‑vocabulary categories, 100K observation‑assignment training samples, and two team‑level metrics, goal‑level SR and makespan‑normalized SPL. We further contribute two baselines. HiGA is a trained hierarchical goal assigner on top of a frozen open‑vocabulary navigation policy, and LaViRA‑M3 is a training‑free team of VLM agents with shared mapping and progress analysis. Adapted multi‑robot and zero‑shot methods reach 16‑‑27% SR, while our baselines reach 38‑‑41% with complementary strengths and distinct failure modes. Furthermore, we deploy LaViRA‑M3 on a heterogeneous three‑robot team. Project page: https://robo‑lavira.github.io/hm3d‑m3/

PaperId: 859, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20073.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Biplab Poudel, Betserai Albert Magarire, Anish Kumar Shah, Jiacheng Xie, Dong Xu
Title: GDBA-Net: A Gated Dual-Branch Adaptation of SAM2 for Robust Cross-Domain Nuclei Segmentation
Abstract:
Accurate nuclei segmentation underpins quantitative computational pathology, yet remains challenging due to morphological variability, weak boundaries, nuclear crowding, and pronounced domain shifts arising from differences in tissue preparation, staining, and acquisition. While deep learning and recent foundation models have improved segmentation performance under matched distributions with the original training data, their generalization across heterogeneous histopathology domains remains limited. We introduce GDBA‑Net, a parameter‑efficient nuclei segmentation framework built around the proposed Gated Dual‑Branch Adapter (GDBA). GDBA‑Net adapts a frozen SAM2 encoder by integrating pretrained semantic representations with explicit frequency‑derived structural priors. The complementary representations are independently transformed through Grid MLP branches and dynamically integrated using sample‑adaptive channel‑wise gating, selectively emphasizing structural cues relevant to nuclear delineation. Despite using only 4.3 million trainable parameters, GDBA‑Net achieves state‑of‑the‑art in‑dataset performance and consistently superior cross‑dataset generalization across six diverse nuclei segmentation benchmarks under fully supervised, cross‑dataset, and five‑shot adaptation protocols, outperforming competing CNN‑, transformer‑, and foundation model based methods. Comprehensive ablations confirm that these gains arise from the coordinated design of semantic‑frequency complementarity and adaptive gating rather than increased model capacity. By uniting transferable semantic representations with explicit structural priors, GDBA‑Net provides a robust, annotation‑efficient solution to domain variability in nuclei segmentation. https://github.com/biplabpoudel25/GDBA_Net

PaperId: 860, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20051.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hang Ren, Peidong Wang, Yichen Gao, Wen Zhang, Jiayang Yu, Xiaocui Yang, Shi Feng
Title: FACES: Fine-grained Gated Semantic Alignment for Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation
Abstract:
In recent years, with advances in multimodal interaction technologies and the growing demand for intelligent emotional support, Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation (MESC) has emerged as an important task. However, existing systems still suffer from shallow responses and inappropriate support strategies due to weak semantic feedback, cross‑dimension reward compensation, and coarse reasoning supervision. To address these challenges, we propose FACES, a fine‑grained gated semantic alignment framework for MESC. Specifically, FACES integrates multi‑source rewards to construct multidimensional semantic and functional alignment signals, employs a non‑compensatory gated fusion mechanism to reduce cross‑dimension reward offset, and leverages structured Chain‑of‑Thought (CoT) anchors to perform token‑level credit assignment. Under a controlled response‑length protocol, FACES improves the average MLLM‑based evaluation score from 3.61 to 4.04 and achieves an 80.22% pairwise win rate over SOTA. Human evaluation under the same protocol yields a 75.3% preference rate. Results on three external datasets further support transferability. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/OCT‑ARR/arr.

PaperId: 861, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20027.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tongwei Deng, Jinyu Zhu, Yue Cao, Chenxu Wang, Yanzhen Zou, Bing Xie
Title: LintEval: Benchmarking LLMs on Linter-Guided File Refactoring
Abstract:
Linters are widely used in code maintenance and real‑time IDE editing to surface lint alerts related to performance, style, error‑prone, and other patterns in source files. However, existing code benchmarks do not explicitly evaluate linter‑guided file refactoring, where models must reduce lint alerts in source files with correct initial functionality while satisfying functionality preservation. We introduce LintEval, a multilingual benchmark for linter‑guided file refactoring across C++, Python, and Java, comprising 13,061 programs with correct initial functionality and 171,662 lint alerts extracted using language‑specific linters. LintEval jointly evaluates functionality preservation, lint alert reduction, new alert avoidance, and edit minimality. Experiments reveal a persistent trade‑off: closed‑source commercial models reach up to 90.4% Reduction@P but achieve only 67.1%‑68.3% Pass@1, while several open‑source small models show low or negative Reduction@P. A controlled fine‑tuning study further shows that supervision format matters: refactoring‑oriented SFT raises Qwen2.5‑Coder‑7B Reduction@P from 24.7% to 76.0%. LintEval enables controlled evaluation of models that improve source files under functionality preservation.

PaperId: 862, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20022.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Maosheng Qin, Qi Zhang, Mingxuan Xia, Jinglei Chen, Jiexiang Wang, Sheng Guo, Cheng Peng, Haobo Wang
Title: Memorizing Who, Knowing How: Benchmarking Personal and Procedural Memory for Persistent Assistants
Abstract:
Memory systems for persistent personal agents must move beyond isolated memories, maintaining both personal memory about whom they serve and procedural memory about how to act. Crucially, in harness‑based personal assistance, procedures or skills are inherently user‑conditioned: personal context determines which procedures apply, how they are instantiated, and when they should change. Existing benchmarks typically emphasize either personal or procedural memory, leaving their interaction underexplored. We introduce PraxisMemBench, a harness‑based benchmark for persistent personal assistance across daily‑life and work trajectories, where personal and procedural memory evolve together and later tasks depend on both. Experiments show that maintaining two memory types separately is insufficient, with completion dropping from single‑type to interdependent dependencies (84.6% to 77.9%). More broadly, across existing methods, relation‑related failures increase from early to late sessions as interaction history grows (59.8% to 72.9%), revealing a continual‑maintenance challenge: writing correct memories is not enough if their evolving content and organization cannot be preserved for later retrieval. To address this, we propose PraxisMem, which uses privileged joint‑state supervision to internalize the ability to maintain memory content and organization into the memory manager, with location‑aware GRPO and dynamic residual‑routed OPSD. PraxisMem reaches 40.78% overall Session Success Rate, compared with 20.60% for Claude Code's native memory. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/QMMMS/PraxisMemBench.

PaperId: 863, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20019.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziyan Liu, Jiting Liu, Weihong Zhong, Wenda Yu, Yeqiu Chen, Jason Li, Xiaojiang Peng, Shuyuan Hu, Kai Wang, Bo Zhao
Title: MorphAct: Robot Policies Morphing with the Worlds They Act In
Abstract:
Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic‑task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision‑language and action parameters, with source‑improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context‑dependent low‑rank updates for the vision‑language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision‑language updates shape the representations that condition action‑side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert‑adapter targets. MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta‑World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real‑world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over π_0.5. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.

PaperId: 864, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20009.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Timo Klein, Thomas Lang, Andrii Shkabrii, Lukas Miklautz, Yllka Velaj, Sebastian Tschiatschek
Title: Outperforming 1000 Euclidean Layers With Hyperbolic Goal-Conditioned RL
Abstract:
Scaling self‑supervised contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) to 1000‑layer Euclidean neural networks has enabled state‑of‑the‑art goal‑reaching performance, yet wall‑clock time scales linearly with depth. We find that changing the geometry achieves stronger performance with far shallower networks. This matters in complex navigation environments, where walls can make route distance deviate substantially from Euclidean distance. In a U‑shaped maze, we show that the longer the route, the more it deviates from Euclidean distance. Hyperbolic CRL addresses this mismatch by replacing Euclidean distances in CRL's contrastive objective with geodesic distances in hyperbolic space. On hard navigation tasks, inductive bias beats scale: depth 64 hyperbolic agents outperform 1024‑layer‑deep Euclidean networks while training more than 12 × faster and using about 13 × fewer parameters. We observe that hyperbolic agents behave qualitatively better in hard humanoid mazes, where they follow corridors to reach goals, whereas Euclidean agents try straight‑line shortcuts over walls. Our results show that matching the representation geometry to the task can substitute for substantial network depth. Code is at https://github.com/Probabilistic‑and‑Interactive‑ML/HypGCRL .

PaperId: 865, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19966.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Arjun Boya, Charan Sai Bandaru, Masthanaiah Pillimetla, Kavana Chidanandappa
Title: Choosing the Number of Attention Heads from Intrinsic Dimension: A Small-Scale Study
Abstract:
The number of attention heads in a transformer is usually set by convention or grid search. We test a simple heuristic for setting it in advance: estimate the intrinsic dimension of token representations without labels, and use roughly that many heads. We estimate intrinsic dimension with a nested‑dropout VAE trained on DistilBERT embeddings of WikiText‑2, choosing the KL weight at the knee of the VAE's rate‑distortion curve rather than by hand. This gives k^=9.2 (95% CI [8.6, 9.8]). In a small 4‑layer transformer trained from scratch, 10 heads and 32 heads are statistically equivalent on SST‑2 and on MRPC (paired TOST over 10 seeds, \pm1 point margin), with 69% fewer attention parameters for the 10‑head model. Training 10 heads from the start also slightly outperforms training 32 heads and pruning to 10 (0.6 points, p=0.008). The evidence is narrow: two classification tasks, one small architecture, no pretrained models, and no formal link between intrinsic dimension and head count. We present the result as a practical heuristic worth testing at larger scale, not as a general principle.

PaperId: 866, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19948.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuanfan Li, Junyi Chen, Qi Zhou, Rui Yang, ZhangLiujie, Weihang Chen
Title: When Protection Overrides Consequences: Understanding Protection Mode in Large Language Model Decision-Making
Abstract:
Frontier language models excel at complex tasks yet may prioritize protection over larger physical consequences in simple, urgent decisions. GPT‑5.6 Sol, for example, moves a girl playing in shallow water before retrieving a submerged camera. We call this Protection Mode and study it with ProtectionBench: 285 prompts, 34 physical families, and nine models. At lowest effort, at least one of four responses prioritizes the subject on 34.74% of Sol prompts and over 83% of MiniMax M3 and Qwen3.5‑27B prompts; none of four independent human raters does so. Controls show that choices usually track physical risk. We elicit both risks before requesting an action. Some models assess risk incorrectly; others state the correct ordering but still choose the subject. Qwen3.5‑27B with thinking shows 100% correct risk ordering but 57.81% subject choice among eligible conversations on eight selected scenes. Attention audits find no stable reduction in attention to relevant facts; removing the stated risk direction reduces object‑first choice in dots3‑note‑prev but not detectably in Qwen3.5‑27B. Adding a general "people or animals before property" rule increases subject choice by 19‑38 percentage points, whereas factual reminders favor the object by 0.7‑5.2 points. Removing naturally generated versions of that rule lowers subject choice by 10‑15 points. We also examine whether post‑training introduces this pattern. Base models already show Protection Mode; post‑training changes justifications more than choices.

PaperId: 867, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19946.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Amartya Banerjee, Xingyu Xu, Caroline Moosmüller, Harlin Lee
Title: Learning Graph Energies for Finite-Time Generation
Abstract:
Energy‑based models can represent distributions over discrete structures such as molecular graphs, but an energy that is accurate at equilibrium need not yield accurate samples when the sampler stops after a fixed number of steps. We introduce finite‑horizon energy learning, which adapts the acceptance energy of a Metropolis‑‑Hastings sampler to the distribution it returns after a prescribed number of steps, with initialization, proposals, and annealing schedule held fixed. For graph generation, a frozen pretrained model supplies initialization and proposals, and a learned energy governs acceptance. A training‑only discriminator scores completed samples, and coupled continuations of the accepted and rejected branches of a proposal give an acceptance‑gradient estimator that is unbiased for a fixed discriminator under stated conditions, without equilibrated negative samples or differentiation through discrete states. Generation uses the learned energy in the original single‑trajectory sampler, without discriminator evaluations or reranking. On twelve pairwise binary targets with exactly evaluated terminal laws, learned energies have lower median terminal total variation than the equilibrium‑correct energy in every tested short‑horizon setting, and than its numerically tuned scalar multiple in most settings. On MOSES, a learned two‑coefficient combination of pretrained Graph Energy Matching (GEM) potentials lowers FCD by 3.7‑‑10.5% relative to scale‑calibrated GEM at matched sampling steps, with validity gains at the shortest budget and a sub‑point validity trade‑off at higher budgets.

PaperId: 868, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19901.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Taha Sabir, Alberto Montero Molina, Thinh Quang Ly, Veronika Dmitrenko, Mohammad Yaqub, Tausifa Jan Saleem
Title: Multimodal Medical Image Parsing with Task-Specific Low-Rank Adapters
Abstract:
Adapting a single vision‑language model to medical image parsing requires training choices that reflect the demands of each task. We study task‑specific adaptation with Qwen3.5‑9B for FLARE 2026 Task 3, covering six task families and seven imaging modalities. Our system couples a shared, frozen 4‑bit backbone with LoRA adapters selected from the input question. We customize adapter ranks and prompts, rebalance rare classification targets, and supplement regression training with dermatology classification examples. On the fixed internal holdout, the task‑specific adapters achieve a dataset‑macro balanced accuracy of 0.7791 for classification, a dataset‑macro micro‑F1 of 0.6286 for multi‑label classification, a counting mean absolute error (MAE) of 11.73, a dataset‑macro detection F1 of 0.8914, a dataset‑macro regression MAE of 9.78, and a report‑generation CRIMSON score of 0.8204. On the organizer's 1,703‑example hidden‑validation set, the submitted system achieves 0.8496 classification balanced accuracy, 0.5338 sample‑averaged multi‑label F1, and 14.5950 regression MAE. The final 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case, including model loading, and produces identical outputs across repeated verification runs. The benefits vary across tasks, supporting the use of task‑specific adapter configurations and image budgets within a shared medical vision‑language model. Code is available at https://github.com/TahaSabir0/FLARE26‑Hexapus.

PaperId: 869, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19900.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ridong Zhang, Shuxian Liang, Chaoqun Wan, Zhen Huang, Xian-Sheng Hua
Title: How GUI Agents Fail: GraceBench for Execution Stability Diagnosis
Abstract:
As GUI agents are increasingly deployed for mobile task automation, their reliability depends not only on final task outcomes, but also on whether they reach these outcomes through stable interaction trajectories. In automation workflows, unnecessary actions, detours, and execution errors can add noise to collected data, introduce irreversible side effects, or undermine trust, even when the agent eventually completes the task. It is therefore important to systematically diagnose the execution stability, including whether an agent deviates from a feasible path, enters a loop, becomes stagnant, or recovers from unstable actions. Existing benchmarks, however, primarily assess final task success or a small set of intermediate milestones, leaving step‑level execution behavior unclear. To bridge this gap, we introduce GraceBench, an online evaluation framework that represents the reachable interaction space of mobile applications as UI Transition Graphs (UTGs), providing a structural reference for step‑level execution diagnosis. To support reliable alignment between dynamic UI observations and graph states, GraceBench uses video‑grounded trajectory evaluation over this graph‑aligned representation, assessing process stability beyond final success with metrics such as deviation rate, loop burden rate, and recovery ability. GraceBench contains 169 tasks spanning 10 applications and constructs 10 UTGs with 2,909 canonical GUI states and 3,116 observed transitions. Across 3,718 trajectories, GraceBench shows that outcome scores hide execution instability: GPT‑5.6 Sol achieves the highest success rate (SR) but the lowest recovery ability, 51.24% of successful runs still contain a deviation or loop, and trajectories with the same success rate (SR) and completion rate (CR) can differ substantially in recovery behavior. Code and data will be released on https://iaie‑physicalai.github.io/GraceBench.

PaperId: 870, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19890.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fiorenzo Parascandolo, Enver Sangineto, Xiaoyi Yu, Wenhui Tan, Jipei He, Ruihua Song, Rita Cucchiara
Title: Frustratingly Easy Majority Voting Using Length Conditioning
Abstract:
Majority Voting (MV) is a simple and widely used strategy which improves the reasoning accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) by allocating additional inference‑time computation. Specifically, in MV multiple Chain‑of‑Thoughts (CoTs) are independently sampled and the most frequent final answer is selected. In this work, we propose Length‑Conditioned Majority Voting (LCMV), a Test‑Time Training approach which improves MV leveraging an empirical observation that has recently been established in several studies: longer CoTs tend to be associated with a lower probability of correctness. We formulate this inductive bias as a length‑conditioned prior probability, which is modeled by a simple logistic function. Moreover, we adapt this prior at test time using only unlabeled testing data and without fine‑tuning the LLM. Finally, the adapted prior is used to weight the vote of each sampled answer. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks show that LCMV consistently improves over both standard MV and existing length‑based and confidence‑based aggregation strategies, while retaining the simplicity and model‑agnostic nature of MV. Our code is available at: https://github.com/aimagelab/LCMV.

PaperId: 871, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19878.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Amartya Banerjee, Harlin Lee, Caroline Moosmüller
Title: Neural Wasserstein Splines: Representation-Invariant Second-Order Priors for Trajectory Inference
Abstract:
Population dynamics are often observed only as unpaired snapshots, which leave the evolution between measurements underdetermined. Second‑order regularization can constrain it, but a penalty on the accelerations of sampled particles is a prior on joint particle paths, and different particle representations of the same marginal curve can have different acceleration costs. We therefore introduce Neural Wasserstein Splines (NWSP), a sample‑based method that learns a continuous population curve under a Wasserstein smoothness prior. A neural network maps latent variables to the control points of a cubic spline in time, so samples at any time come from the spline basis without numerical integration. We project the generator's velocity onto gradients of a finite dictionary of scalar potentials and differentiate this measure‑dependent projection in time, obtaining a finite‑dimensional surrogate for the intrinsic Wasserstein acceleration, trained jointly with distributional fit losses. For a fixed dictionary and ridge parameter, we prove that the population penalty depends only on the marginal curve and bound its sensitivity to moment‑estimation errors. Learned potentials (NWSP‑N) sharpen acceleration estimates. On various synthetic and single‑cell benchmarks, NWSP is highly competitive with transport and flow‑based methods, ranking in the top two in 11 of 16 settings. The penalty improves on an unregularized spline in 13 of 16 settings and, while competitive with a particle‑acceleration penalty, adds provable representation invariance.

PaperId: 872, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19864.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qiuyu Chen, Qi Wang, Liang Xu, Xin Jin, Baao Xie, Wenjun Zeng
Title: Euler: Towards Human-Centered Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery
Abstract:
Mathematical research drives scientific discovery, and recent advances in AI for mathematics have shown that language‑model agents can solve challenging problems and develop substantial mathematical proofs. Yet much of today's AI‑for‑mathematics work centers on obtaining a final answer. This emphasis leaves the exploration behind a result difficult for researchers to understand, while long‑running investigations face fragmented context and the risk of unsupported claims propagating across reasoning steps. We present Euler, a human‑centered mathematical research system built around a shared, structured representation of the research process. Euler organizes mathematical statements, assumptions, proof dependencies, alternative approaches, failed attempts, and verification evidence into connected research graphs. This representation allows researchers to trace how results are developed and supplies agents with persistent, task‑relevant knowledge for planning, collaboration, and verification across sessions. Researchers can also select a graph node linked to a saved team state, revisit the agents' earlier reasoning, and explore alternative directions through continued interaction. We illustrate Euler's capabilities through three mathematical research case studies and describe the implemented system and its software validation.

PaperId: 873, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19857.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Minghao Liu, Tutian Tang
Title: OmniPoser: Flexible Human Motion Recovery in the Wild with Masked Flow Matching
Abstract:
Recovering 3D human motion from sparse wearable sensors is challenging due to the inherent noise, occlusion, and instability of real‑world tracking signals. Existing approaches are restricted to fixed sensor configurations and, when built on diffusion models, are computationally prohibitive for real‑time deployment. We propose OmniPoser, a universal framework that recovers full‑body SMPL motion from a flexible combination of heterogeneous inputs, such as 3D keypoints, sparse IMU rotations, head‑mounted 6‑DoF poses, or any subset thereof, within a single model. OmniPoser introduces a cross‑modal masking mechanism paired with a Masked Conditioning Encoder, enabling one architecture to incorporate diverse sensor configurations through a masked design. A decoupled dual‑stream generative backbone generates complete motion via Conditional Flow Matching, requiring only a single ODE integration step at inference. Across three settings and seven benchmarks, including in‑the‑wild Nymeria and Ego‑Exo4D datasets, OmniPoser performs on par with state‑of‑the‑art methods while running at over 700 FPS. The project page is available at https://jamesbridgewater51.github.io/omniposer‑eccv/.

PaperId: 874, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19849.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Boyuan Sun, Deshui Miao, Wenzhao Gao, Shaoyong Jia, Shaohui Jiao, Chi Liu, Yan Shu, Derek Li, Bryan Dai, Shengsheng Qian, Qibin Hou
Title: DeltaStreamer: Towards Human-Like Agentic Streaming Video Understanding
Abstract:
We propose DeltaStreamer, a novel agentic framework for streaming video understanding inspired by how humans observe, remember, and investigate. Streaming video understanding requires a system to retain evidence before knowing which details future queries will need. Existing approaches often obscure event transitions and omit relevant details when compressing video history, and cannot recover missing visual evidence. DeltaStreamer addresses these limitations by combining change‑aware memory with query‑driven planning and targeted evidence gathering with replay. Before a query arrives, it continuously observes the stream and explicitly records visual changes in structured memory, preserving how events unfold rather than only what is present. When a query arrives, a query‑driven planner identifies the required evidence and guides memory retrieval and targeted replay. By revisiting historical frames, the agent can recover visual details omitted during observation and ground its answer in evidence beyond the retained descriptions. This connects continuous observation with active investigation tailored to each question. Experiments on OVO‑Bench and StreamingBench demonstrate improvements over representative streaming video understanding methods, with overall scores of 66.07% and 59.53%, respectively. Project page: https://bbbbchan.github.io/DeltaStreamer/

PaperId: 875, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19825.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qisen Ma, Yixiang Chen, Yuan Xu, Peiyan Li, Jiabing Yang, Kai Wang, Jianhua Yang, Jianlou Si, Jun Huang, Jing Liu, Nianfeng Liu, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
Title: What Matters for World Modeling in Vision-Language-Action Models?
Abstract:
Integrating world models into Vision‑Language‑Action models (VLAs) has emerged as a promising direction, enabling policies to anticipate future dynamics beyond reactive observation‑to‑action mapping. However, existing approaches vary simultaneously in their world representations, integration paradigms, and policy backbones, making it difficult to determine what truly matters for effective world model integration. To disentangle these factors, we categorize existing efforts into four representative paradigms, namely Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor. We instantiate each within a unified framework and systematically evaluate these paradigms with diverse world representations and policy backbones across in‑domain, out‑of‑domain, long‑horizon, dynamic, few‑shot, and real‑world settings. Our study yields four main findings: 1) world representation effectiveness is paradigm‑dependent, whereas 2D semantic representations offer robust, cross‑paradigm gains; 2) no single paradigm is universally optimal, yet the decoupled MoT Future Expert offers competitive overall performance, particularly in OOD robustness; 3) world modeling consistently benefits policies built on standard VLMs, while decoupled designs exhibit greater compatibility with pretrained VLAs; and 4) world modeling improves performance over action‑only baselines across multiple settings, with notable gains on long‑horizon and dynamic tasks. Project page and video demonstrations are available at https://dylanmqs.github.io/WM‑in‑VLAs/.

PaperId: 876, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19823.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Siwei Meng, Xuerou Cai, Rui Hu, Ping Liu
Title: PhyMetric: Diagnosing Physical Plausibility in Text-to-Video Generation via Scene-Level QA
Abstract:
Text‑to‑video (T2V) generation models can produce visually realistic videos that nevertheless violate the physical consequences implied by the prompt and scene. Existing benchmarks largely rely on holistic plausibility scores or broad quality dimensions, leaving it unclear which physical behavior is being tested and why a model fails. We introduce PhyMetric, a scene‑level diagnostic benchmark that recasts physical plausibility evaluation as verifiable, scene‑grounded question answering. PhyMetric contains 1,115 scenes spanning 50 physical categories across six domains, paired with 8,920 answer‑balanced binary questions over 12 evaluation dimensions. Each scene is associated with eight targeted yes/no questions and a structured physical prior specifying the governing law, expected temporal sequence, observable signatures, and common failure modes. At evaluation time, a vision‑language model (VLM) judge answers each question from question‑aware sampled frames conditioned on the prior, and correctness is hierarchically aggregated into scene, dimension, physical category, and model scores. Experiments on four open‑source T2V models and three VLM judges show that scene‑specific binary QA is a critical component of the protocol: when each targeted question is replaced by a single generic plausibility query, evaluator accuracy drops to the chance level. Structured physical priors offer a complementary signal that improves human alignment of the resulting scores, with effects that vary across VLM judges of different capacity. These findings establish PhyMetric as a benchmark that turns physical plausibility evaluation from opaque holistic scoring into interpretable, scene‑level inspection. Our project page is available at: https://mengsiwei.github.io/PhyMetric/.

PaperId: 877, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19803.pdf   GitHub
Authors:My Tra Nguyen Huynh, Viet Cuong Ta
Title: Improving Category-Aware Active Domain Adaptation via Uncertainty-Guided Region Coverage
Abstract:
Active domain adaptation researches focus on alleviating the annotation cost, which comprises source data and target data labelling, as well as enhancing the performance of unsupervised domain adaptation. However, optimizing the adaptation model based on the average accuracy can lead to the drop in performance of some difficult categories. To overcome this issue, a point‑wise selection strategy built upon the influence function can be used to improve domain adaptation performance. In our work, we first address the sensitive and redundant aspects of point‑wise selection, which can lead to overfitting of the acquisition function. We thus introduce a region‑based approach that ensures the improvement of the adaptation model by maximizing a positive manifold coverage. An uncertainty score is further introduced to the selection mechanism to learn a better decision boundary for the target domain. In comprehensive experiments, our proposed method surpasses the first category‑aware active domain adaptation baseline as well as existing active domain adaptation methods across multiple domain adaptation benchmarks. Our implementation is available at: https://github.com/nhtm2702/WHO IS NEXT.

PaperId: 878, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19801.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhenyu Zhang, Zhichao Cao
Title: Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs
Abstract:
An agent that drives an LLM sends the model the same conversation again and again, and each turn adds only a little text at the end. Inference engines reuse the KV cache of the shared prefix, so only the new tokens pass through the model. However, tokenization has no such shortcut. The CPU front end of the serving engine converts every request back into token IDs from its first character, which lengthens the time to first token (TTFT) and consumes CPU on every turn. We present Delta Tokenizer, a CPU tokenization front end that tokenizes only the delta between a request and the previous request of the same session. It retains the earlier token sequence, encodes again only the appended text and the short tail whose tokens the append could affect, and joins the two only at a position the tokenizer's splitting rules themselves cannot move, which keeps the result exact.
