For long requests with no state to reuse, it cuts the text where practical tokenizers already keep neighboring pieces independent, encodes the pieces on several cores at once, and concatenates the outputs into the reference encoding, exactly. A shared CPU pool schedules these chunks together with the short incremental updates, so an update runs between two chunks rather than behind an entire long job. The incremental path shortens the tokenization of a session turn by roughly 40x relative to the Hugging Face reference tokenizer, and on 16 cores the chunk‑parallel path encodes a four‑million‑character request 8.2x faster than a serial encode and 1.6‑2.1x faster than LoPT. Inside SGLang, Delta Tokenizer reduces the median TTFT through the chat interface by 59% at 100K tokens and brings the P99 TTFT of agent sessions down 9.5x under load and 23x when long requests tie up the front end. Every output we checked matches the reference, among them 41.8 billion documents encoded by its fast encoder.

PaperId: 879, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19795.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Lorenzo Venturoli, Nedko Savov, Xi Wang, Marc Pollefeys, Luc Van Gool
Title: StateCraft: Augmenting Video World Models with Abstract-State Reasoning
Abstract:
Video world models aim to simulate complex environments with realistic appearance and dynamics. Maintaining consistency over long interactions requires tracking past actions and understanding how those actions affect the environment. Video world models can only generate partial observations of the entire world at a time. Remembering past observations alone may not be sufficient in every scenario, as they may no longer reflect the world after a sequence of actions. We introduce a paradigm that decouples a persistent, updatable abstract state from the visual state. The abstract state keeps track of the entities' changes as the world evolves, and is used to condition the visual state, which represents the current view. We propose StateCraft, a novel architecture that pairs a language model with a video diffusion model to evolve the dynamic world. We evaluate our approach on generative interfaces, which pose a substantial challenge because a single action may change parts of the state that are not currently visible. To support training and evaluation, we develop a data collection pipeline that produces informative, densely annotated trajectories at scale without human or agent supervision, together with a benchmark measuring generation quality, memory, and controllability. On this benchmark, our approach improves surpasses the state‑of‑the‑art baselines. We demonstrate that StateCraft maintains high self‑consistency and strong generation quality over long trajectories. Because the abstract state is explicit, it can be edited directly, and generation follows edits to states never observed in the data. Finally, a proof‑of‑concept 3D experiment, in which actions change the illumination of an unobserved room, shows that the paradigm can also be applied to spatial environments. Project page: https://insait‑institute.github.io/StateCraft/.

PaperId: 880, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19792.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Zhaoxiang Feng, Lanxiang Hu, Haoran Yuan, Yu-Yang Qian, Jihui Yang, Peng Zhao, Yibo Zhu, Tajana Rosing, Hao Zhang
Title: JetSpec++: Foresight Parallel Drafting with Self Refinements
Abstract:
Speculative decoding's effectiveness is governed by two quantities: the acceptance rate of drafted tokens and the cost of producing them. We show the two objectives can be co‑optimized with algorithm‑system co‑design, and present JetSpec++, which retains a strong learned draft model while hiding its cost almost entirely. JetSpec++ combines three components: intra‑block self refinement, which trains the draft model to iteratively correct its own parallel predictions within a block of tokens; inter‑block foresight drafting, which begins the next block before the current one is verified; and pipelined drafting and verification, which overlaps the two stages so drafting's marginal wall‑clock cost approaches zero. In comparison with state‑of‑the‑art speculative decoding methods, JetSpec++ attains a wall‑clock speedup of up to 7.45× over autoregressive (AR) decoding and 1.54× over DSpark, with up to 1,361 tokens per second for a single request on GB200, and an average acceptance length of 8.94 across seven benchmarks, while preserving the target model's output distribution. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/hao‑ai‑lab/JetSpec.

PaperId: 881, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19789.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Linhao Zhong, Bozhen Fang, Xuehao Wang, Duochao Shi, Zekai Luo, Guangming Yao, Yi Yuan, Hao Chen, Jingdong Chen, Chunhua Shen
Title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
Self‑distillation in agentic reinforcement learning has produced a growing number of methods. However, existing evaluations often reuse published baseline scores under differing experimental conditions, provide few direct comparisons among contemporaneous methods, and give limited attention to training stability and computational cost. These limitations obscure the source of reported gains and the practical strengths and weaknesses of competing methods. Costly agent training further motivates a common basis for comparison. To address these gaps, we compare ten representative methods against GRPO on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Search‑QA, and WebShop across three model sizes. Our study comprises 132 training runs totaling 12,124.4 recorded H800 GPU‑hours, with repeated evaluations over eight rollout seeds for the pretrained backbones and all eleven trained methods. Beyond final task performance, we examine training progress, stability, and measured computational cost. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, gains over GRPO remain limited in scope, with no method consistently outperforming it across settings. Second, strong final performance can mask unstable training. Third, additional training cost does not consistently translate into better performance. We establish this benchmark to support fair, comprehensive comparison and guide future research toward reliable and cost‑effective improvements in agent training. Project page: https://aim‑uofa.github.io/Self‑Distillation‑AgentRL/

PaperId: 882, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19786.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sizhuo Zhou, Xiaosong Jia, Fanrui Zhang, Qifeng Li, Junjie Li, Zirui Wang, Yukang Feng, Yu Hong, Shaofeng Zhang, Wenlong Liao, Tao He, Juyong Zhang, Junchi Yan
Title: LiFi: LiDAR Generation from Multi-View Images via Geometric and Semantic Collaborative Guidance
Abstract:
Generating LiDAR point clouds from multi‑view camera images is a valuable task with applications in controllable data synthesis, cross‑modal simulation and various perception tasks. However, most existing methods are not specifically designed for this task, and the quality of their generated LiDAR remains limited. Moreover, these methods typically focus only on semantic cues in images or generate LiDAR from a monocular camera image. In this work, we introduce LiFi (LiDAR From images), a dedicated framework for generating visually and geometrically aligned LiDAR scenes from multi‑view camera images. LiFi guides the latent diffusion process through two complementary branches: geometry and semantics. The geometry branch constructs scene features from images through a reverse sampling algorithm and an uncertainty‑aware geometric encoder combined with DepthAnything3, whereas the semantic branch provides high‑level semantic representations via a cross‑view interaction module. We further introduce a dual‑branch balanced classifier‑free guidance (CFG) strategy, which enhances the model's conditional generation capability while preserving the independent learning and collaborative controllability of the two branches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiFi outperforms state‑of‑the‑art methods in generating high‑fidelity LiDAR scenes. The code will be publicly available at: https://github.com/szzhou88/LiFi.

PaperId: 883, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19773.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ianis Hammani, Claire Boyer
Title: From Global to Tail Convergence: Dynamics of $α$-Stable Score-Based Generative Models
Abstract:
Score‑based generative models driven by α‑stable Lévy processes have been proposed as an alternative to Brownian diffusion models, with empirical evidence suggesting improved sampling and better modeling of heavy‑tailed data. Yet theoretical guarantees for these models remain limited. We develop a non‑asymptotic convergence analysis for scale‑preserving α‑stable generative dynamics, covering both compactly supported and power‑law targets. In p‑Wasserstein distance, we quantify the effects of early stopping, initialization, score approximation, and time discretization, and show exponential decay of the initialization error. A comparison with Brownian dynamics reveals that global Wasserstein convergence alone does not fundamentally distinguish the two models: both initialization errors decay exponentially with the forward horizon on the common class of heavy‑tailed targets. A sharp separation emerges instead in the tails. At any positive generation time, stable dynamics produces power‑law tails with index α, whereas Brownian dynamics remains light‑tailed. For a target with tail index ν, asymptotically correct extreme‑quantile scaling is possible precisely when α=ν. These results identify tail‑index matching as a principled mechanism behind the ability of stable generative models to capture extreme events.

PaperId: 884, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19765.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hanlin Liu, Zichen Zhou, Jiacheng Zhang, Liuyuan Na, Jin Jin, Guangyan Chen, Yufeng Yue, Gen Li, Fangqiang Ding
Title: Refine Actions If Needed: Adaptive Action Chunk Refinement for Robot Manipulation
Abstract:
Computationally lightweight manipulation policies predict executable actions with low inference latency, but prediction errors can limit task success. Iterative generative policies can achieve higher task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency. Refining action proposals from computationally lightweight policies can combine these strengths, but the amount of refinement needed varies across states. We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed), a framework that predicts action errors at different refinement levels to decide whether and how much to refine each executable proposal, before performing any refinement. We train an ensemble to predict these errors by comparing action proposals and their refined versions with expert actions from offline demonstrations, without requiring explicit labels of refinement needs. Calibration balances uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. We evaluate RAIN on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real‑robot tasks. In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6% success, approaching the best evaluated diffusion‑policy success rate with 5.71 times lower policy latency. On the real robot, success increases from 55.0% with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) to 72.5%, with comparable average successful completion time. Matched controls show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed‑refinement success level with 26.6% fewer refiner evaluations. Project page: https://rain‑policy.github.io/.

PaperId: 885, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19731.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Julia Barth, Armin Sommer, Kunvar Thaman, Jannik Schilling
Title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
Abstract:
Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy‑goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended‑goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.

PaperId: 886, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19729.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hao-Jen Chien, Wei-Lun Chao, Yu-Lun Liu
Title: A Diagnostic Study of World-Space Human Recovery Under High Camera Dynamics
Abstract:
Monocular world‑space human recovery methods excel on current benchmarks, but these rarely include fast camera motion. We introduce the K‑Pop stress test, broadcast dance videos that combine fast, large camera motion with dense multi‑person choreography. Leading methods produce plausible per‑frame meshes on these videos, yet their world‑space trajectories drift far from the performers' stage positions. Through a systematic diagnosis, we show that the camera and human estimates each remain self‑consistent, and that the drift appears when they are combined at mismatched scales. Each is recovered at its own scale, so a mismatch between the two can turn camera motion into human drift that grows with camera displacement and becomes severe in broadcast dance videos. We derive a closed‑form correction that estimates this mismatch and applies one scale to all performers, removing the drift while keeping their relative positions in one shared world frame. It requires no retraining and works with existing backends. Combined with physical constraints, the correction yields stable world‑space reconstruction for choreography modeling, scene editing, data generation, and virtual reshooting. Project page: https://chien90190.github.io/worldhmr‑fastcam‑website/

PaperId: 887, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19725.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haoxin Liu, Deqing Fu, Lucheng Fu, Yiqiao Jin, Rushi Qiang, Harshavardhan Kamarthi, B. Aditya Prakash
Title: TimeRSI: Towards Self-Improved Agentic Deployment for Time-Series Foundation Models
Abstract:
Time‑series foundation models provide strong zero‑shot forecast, but deployment for real‑world applications still requires task‑specific designs for model inputs and outputs. Direct inference can leave domain knowledge and recurring forecast errors unaddressed, while tailored pipelines require substantial human expertise and effort. We introduce TimeRSI, a self‑improving agentic deployment system around frozen forecasting models. A coding agent translates task descriptions into executable pipeline changes. It tests each revision on historical forecasting windows and uses observed errors to guide subsequent revisions. During deployment, an adaptive selector chooses among the resulting pipelines using completed forecasts under similar conditions. Across 198 tasks on TIME and fev‑bench, TimeRSI outperforms all submissions on six point and probabilistic forecasting metrics. Controlled comparisons support the value of feedback‑guided revision over non‑iterative pipeline search. Further experiments verify the generalization with different coding agents and forecasting models. Code is available at https://github.com/haoxin1998/TimeRSI.

PaperId: 888, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19723.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shun Inadumi, Lee Sangmyeong, Koichiro Yoshino
Title: Recognizing Dialogue Ambiguity via Candidate Set Visual Grounding
Abstract:
Interpreting an ambiguous utterance in real‑world interactions often requires context beyond a single utterance. When the utterance refers to objects in a visual scene, it is necessary to maintain and update the set of plausible referents as context accumulates, without assuming that the available information identifies a unique object. However, prior work on interactive visual grounding, which localizes objects referred to by linguistic expressions, has focused on identifying a unique object once sufficient dialogue context becomes available. To address this gap, we propose Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG), a task for estimating the set of objects consistent with the given dialogue context. We further introduce CandVG, a benchmark that evaluates how the candidate set changes across dialogue turns. Our evaluation of vision‑language models shows that stronger visual grounding capability does not necessarily yield better CSVG performance. In particular, models have difficulty predicting the complete candidate set, owing to challenges in candidate generation and premature commitment to a small set of candidates in early turns. Nevertheless, we find that this limitation can be partially mitigated in the evaluated large‑scale models using instructions designed for CSVG.

PaperId: 889, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19717.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Lizhi Xiong, Jun Li, Ziqiang Li, Weiwei Jiang, Zhangjie Fu
Title: No Way To Steal My Face: Proactive Defense Against Identity-Preserving Personalized Generation
Abstract:
Recent advances in diffusion models have enabled high‑fidelity, identity‑preserving image generation for personalized applications such as digital avatars and virtual try‑on systems. However, their reliance on sensitive facial reference images raises growing privacy concerns. Existing defense mechanisms are primarily designed for training‑based personalization and struggle to generalize to emerging training‑free approaches, due to fundamental differences in their identity integration paradigms. To bridge this gap, we propose IDGuardian‑the first generalizable and model‑agnostic identity protection framework capable of defending against both training‑based and training‑free personalization methods. IDGuardian abstracts the personalization process into two critical stages: identity extraction and identity injection. It then introduces crafted adversarial perturbations to simultaneously disrupt both stages. Specifically, it degrades the identity features extracted by external encoders and establishes an adversarial conceptual bridge that misdirects the generative trajectory away from the target identity. Extensive experiments show that IDGuardian effectively protects identity across various personalization pipelines and model architectures, while remaining robust to post‑processing, adaptive attacks, and cross‑dataset generalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/OpenAscent‑L/IDGuardian.git.

PaperId: 890, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19704.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Md Rayhanul Masud, S M Maksudul Alam, Mohammad Jaminur Islam
Title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla
Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision‑making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla‑‑English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language‑model‑assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open‑weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible‑case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5‑27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct‑answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always‑``infeasible'' baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan‑construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision‑making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: https://github.com/mrayhanulmasud/banglaplan.

PaperId: 891, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19700.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fanyao Li, Yuxi Liu, Xiaohao Liu, He Chang, Zhaoxin Wang, Zhulin Tao
Title: ReGRA: Residual-Gradient Adaptation for Complementary Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
Abstract:
Low‑rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning by learning low‑rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank‑16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual‑Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two‑stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two‑sided subspace induced by the first‑stage update. It then aggregates the residual‑gradient directions to initialize a second‑stage adapter without changing the first‑stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao‑Li/ReGRA.

PaperId: 892, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19698.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Chenhao Yuan, Bohan Yu, Yinhao Xu, Chao Yin, Chenxi Zhou, Zhaoxuan Wang, Shuwen Xu, Shaoping Huang, Haolin Ren, Jiaxiang Liu, Yao Xu, Jun Zhao, Kang Liu
Title: RuleTrek: Benchmarking Agentic Rule Reasoning in Complex Scenarios
Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly tackle complex real‑world tasks in specialized domains. However, identifying and correctly applying domain‑specific rules remains challenging when scenario information is distributed across multiple files. Existing rule‑reasoning benchmarks typically represent scenarios using only a few factual statements, simplifying the identification and application of relevant rules. To address this gap, this paper introduces RuleTrek, a multi‑domain benchmark for agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios. Its rule‑grounded construction pipeline extracts structured rule graphs, generates and incrementally composes rule‑specific sub‑scenarios while ensuring consistency and solvability. To systematically evaluate agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios, RuleTrek assesses three capabilities in interactive workspaces: Rule Identification (RI), Rule Deduction (RD), and End‑to‑End Rule Reasoning (E2E). Experiments on 11 frontier LLMs show that the highest RI and RD scores are only 62.47% and 60.43%, respectively, while E2E scores range from 26.97% to 55.29%. These results demonstrate that current LLM agents face substantial challenges in rule reasoning over complex scenarios. We make our code and dataset publicly available at \hrefhttps://github.com/yuan247/RuleTrekRuleTrek.

PaperId: 893, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19696.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xin Li, Mengbing Liu, Hao Jiang, Xin Gao, Annan Wang, Xingwei Qu, Yichi Zhang, Chau Yuen
Title: Share the Symbol, Not the Vector: Training-Free Fact Communication Across Language Models
Abstract:
Multi‑agent systems allow language models to solve tasks collaboratively by sharing complementary information. These systems typically communicate through text, while recent approaches also explore exchanging internal model states. However, sharing these states across architectures often requires learned translators or assumptions about model compatibility. We introduce SYNC (Symbol‑Indexed Neural Communication), a word‑indexed interface that connects heterogeneous models without fine‑tuning or a learned translator. From descriptions only it can see, the sender selects words from a shared list and sends their indices for each object, without seeing the questions. The receiver writes the described facts into its hidden states using its own word directions, vectors fitted once from its activations. We test selective use by swapping one attribute between two objects and requiring correct answers about both changed and unchanged attributes before and after the swap, four answers in total. We choose an early write layer on four development receivers and then fix it. With three different senders and nine newer receivers from five families, four‑answer success on new scenes reaches 72.0‑98.3%, up to 96 percentage points above middle‑layer writing, and the two largest receivers match plain text. A task‑free probe predicted in advance which depths each new receiver can use (45 of 45 cases). Without retuning, messages listing every fact keep 89.6‑100% success under new layouts, and sender messages reach 23.9‑64.0% on a landmark task with multi‑token symbols, below text but from 0% without a message. These results show that shared word indices and receiver‑local directions can support selective fact use across model families without additional training.

PaperId: 894, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19678.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziyang Zhang, Wenyi Yu, Wen Wu, Xuenan Xu, Chao Zhang
Title: TVPara: Paralinguistic Captioning of Expressive TV-Series Speech in Complex Acoustic Environments
Abstract:
Large audio‑language models (LALMs) struggle to parse paralinguistics (e.g., emotion, pace, pitch) in speech that combines intense emotion with complex acoustic environments. Strengthening this ability calls for training data that reflects such conditions. However, existing corpora rely heavily on studio‑recorded speech, offering limited emotional and acoustic diversity. To address this gap, we introduce TVPara, a paralinguistic captioning dataset built from TV series. Speech in TV series often carries diverse emotional expression and co‑occurs with scene‑specific background sound, providing expressive emotion and complex acoustic environments at scale. Constructed via LALM pre‑annotation and human correction, TVPara includes two tasks: Single‑Utterance (~492h) and Multi‑Utterance (~213h) Paralinguistic Captioning. Fine‑tuning open‑source LALMs on TVPara yields an average relative improvement of 31.26% in paralinguistic understanding under complex acoustic environments. The gains further generalize to an unseen TV series and to cleaner, cross‑domain speech.

PaperId: 895, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19644.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Bin Zheng, Zheng Chen
Title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
Abstract:
Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate‑answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5‑4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on‑demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural‑state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer‑query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC‑Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512‑token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024‑token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of ‑1.17 points. Exact‑prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read‑scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.

PaperId: 896, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19624.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dikai Li, Weijia Wang, Yuan-Gen Wang
Title: Adaptive Observation Control for Active Visual Recognition
Abstract:
Visual recognition models usually process a fixed view under a fixed computation budget, although images often benefit from different scales and amounts of spatial evidence. Active vision can adapt by observing a coarse scene and then selecting informative fixations, but the public AdaptiveNN‑DeiT‑S pipeline still fixes both field of view and observation count. We extend this fixed‑step recognizer with a controllable observation interface that adapts both the field of view and the number of fixations to the input. Specifically, the model predicts a per‑fixation scale that sets its field of view, refines each selected crop with optional scale‑gated foveation and a residual high‑resolution detail‑token branch, and uses label‑grounded stop heads for input‑dependent early termination. Experiments across fine‑grained benchmarks, full ImageNet‑1K, and ImageNet‑A/R‑derived classification splits show that the interface remains competitive with fixed‑step references while exposing a controllable observation budget. The same checkpoint enables threshold‑controlled accuracy‑compute trade‑offs without per‑threshold retraining. On sequential ImageNet‑1K, the learned stop rule outperforms fixed‑step truncation of the same checkpoint, sustaining 81.9% top‑1 using 2.45 of the four focus steps and exceeding three‑step truncation at lower cost. On each benchmark, a variant combining scale control and detail‑token fusion achieves the highest accuracy among the tested component‑added non‑exit variants. Our code is available at https://github.com/GZHU‑DVL/LI‑Dikai.

PaperId: 897, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19623.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jia Chen, Ruyang Zhao, Jun Bai, Chao Huang, Saishang Zhong, Xinrong Hu
Title: MagicGarment: Benchmarking Single-Image Standalone 3D Garment Reconstruction
Abstract:
Single‑image 3D reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet standalone garments remain challenging due to thin‑shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered structures. Existing datasets and evaluation protocols provide limited support for systematic evaluation in this setting. We introduce MagicGarment, a benchmark for single‑image standalone 3D garment reconstruction with 1,518 professionally constructed assets across 17 composite garment types, aligned multimodal annotations, and a unified evaluation protocol. We further establish a garment‑aware reference baseline by adapting a pretrained image‑to‑3D backbone at two levels: Grounded Semantic Refinement (GSR) provides garment‑focused visual conditioning, while Flow‑Time‑Route LoRA (FTR‑LoRA) adapts the frozen 3D generative backbone using flow‑timestep, token‑routing, and expert‑load information. Experiments demonstrate MagicGarment's benchmark utility and the effectiveness of garment‑aware adaptation. Project page: https://1019538157.github.io/MagicGarment/.

PaperId: 898, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19604.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xuan Han, Zinuo Jin, Tianlin Li, Yunfan Lou, Xin Liu, Yuchen Xue, Yuanpeng He, Boxian Yao, Shuhan Zhan, Ruihai Wu, Zhibo Pang
Title: ForceBench: Benchmarking Force Integration for Robotic Manipulation
Abstract:
Force feedback provides vision‑language‑action (VLA) policies with physical observations that can guide action selection and execution. However, differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across existing systems hinder reliable comparisons of force integration designs. We introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating six‑axis wrist‑force integration under a unified protocol. ForceBench combines eight tasks spanning physical‑property inference, resistance‑dependent interaction, and contact‑rich assembly with 1,600 synchronized demonstrations and task‑specific success criteria. We compare one no‑force baseline and six force integration designs on a shared π_0.5 backbone. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the baseline, and improves success rates across all three task categories. Predictive and temporal gains in simulation concentrate on physical‑property inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on assembly. Real‑world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the main qualitative trends: Prompt Fusion and Dual‑Path Fusion achieve 63.00% mean success, compared with 40.00% for the baseline, but only Prompt Fusion improves every task. These findings support ForceBench's practical value for identifying the benefits and limitations of force integration across manipulation demands. The project page is available at https://forcebench‑platform.github.io/.

PaperId: 899, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19600.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zixuan Wang, Jia-Ning Li, Yinzhou Tang, Yanzhao Yu, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Xin Li, Yiwu Zhong
Title: Cracking Mobile Manipulation: From Failure Diagnosis to Agentic Robot System
Abstract:
Recent vision‑language‑action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on local robot manipulation, yet their success does not readily translate to long‑horizon mobile manipulation. In our experiments, a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when these skills are composed into mobile manipulation. We argue that this gap stems from failures across the execution process rather than from local manipulation capability alone. To uncover these bottlenecks, we systematically diagnose failures in long‑horizon mobile manipulation and identify three dominant regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. Based on this diagnosis, we develop failure‑guided agentic intervention that augments a fixed subtask VLA with demonstration‑based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility‑aware base adjustment, and local end‑effector adjustment. On RoboCasa365, these interventions progressively improve task success from 19% to 47%, with the finalized system reaching 49% on held‑out episode seeds, compared with 18% for the baseline. The same design improves performance from 14% to 37% on BEHAVIOR‑1K and from 5/20 to 13/20 on real‑robot tasks. These results suggest that reliable mobile manipulation can be advanced by diagnosing and intervening on the current bottleneck, rather than uniformly scaling the underlying policy. Our code will be released at https://github.com/PKU‑VaLuE‑Lab/Cracking‑Mobile‑Manipulation.git.

PaperId: 900, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19559.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jing-Xuan Zhang, Genshun Wan, Jianqing Gao, Jia Pan, Yumei Zhang, Lichen Zhang
Title: Learning Visual Speech Representations via Cross-Modal Distillation and Joint Face-Lip Modeling
Abstract:
Lipreading remains challenging due to the inherent ambiguity of visual speech cues and their sensitivity to head pose and video resolution. In this work, we propose FLARE, a framework for robust visual speech representation learning via cross‑modal distillation and joint face‑lip modeling. FLARE leverages semantically rich Whisper representations as the acoustic teacher signal, converting them into discrete distillation targets through a random‑projection quantizer and pretraining the model with a masked prediction objective. To capture complementary visual information, FLARE employs a dual‑stream architecture that jointly processes lip region‑of‑interest (ROI) and full‑face inputs, where the lip stream captures finegrained articulatory motion and the face stream encodes broader facial dynamics. During pretraining, auxiliary audio input is incorporated to facilitate cross‑modal alignment, and modality dropout is applied to encourage robust visual‑only representations. For downstream lipreading, FLARE serves as a visual encoder coupled with either a lightweight Transformer decoder or an LLM‑based decoder. Evaluated on LRS2, LRS3, and the out‑of‑domain WildVSR benchmark, FLARE achieves strong lipreading performance, with word error rates of 11.7%, 13.2%, and 34.3%, respectively. A progressive design study confirms the contribution of each major component. Further analyses demonstrate that joint face‑lip modeling improves robustness under degraded video resolution and large head pose variation, while yielding more phoneme‑discriminative visual representations. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/jxzhanggg/FLARE.

PaperId: 901, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19540.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Dikai Li, Weijia Wang, Yuan-Gen Wang
Title: Cross-Scenario Industrial Defect Detection via Domain-Robust Training and Metric-Aligned Selection
Abstract:
Automated defect detection of industrial boards must remain highly reliable under cross‑scenario variations in lighting, surface contaminants, and production line conditions. This makes cross‑scenario defect detection a domain generalization problem, wherein models are required to detect, localize, and classify defects across unseen scenarios while minimizing false alarms on clean boards. For the IDA 2026 Track 1 challenge, we propose a cross‑scenario defect detection method that includes four complementary modules: cross‑scenario robust training, small‑defect‑aware learning, score calibration and inference threshold selection, and metric‑aligned checkpoint selection. These four modules respectively introduce cross‑scenario robust normalization and DSU‑style statistic perturbation with progressive random convolution, NWD and parameter‑free spatial attention, the VFL learning objective, and a custom SWAD variant driven by the Track 1‑oriented proxy. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves a Track 1 score of 0.564 with a screening score of 0.696 on the test dataset on a single RTX 4090 GPU. The code is available at https://github.com/GZHU‑DVL/Dikai.

PaperId: 902, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19526.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rui Chen, Xingyu Chen, Pengxin Xu, Kai Chen, Junzhi Yu
Title: HyrCap: Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals for Temporal Event Understanding
Abstract:
Temporal action detection in long untrimmed videos suffers from inaccurate localization and low‑quality proposals, especially with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries. For open‑ended video understanding and LLM‑driven event analysis, reliable proposals connect temporal localization, event annotation, and semantic understanding. However, conventional temporal action detection (TAD) pipelines lack explicit modeling of proposal localization quality, cross‑representation support, and inter‑proposal relations. We propose Hybrid Rank‑Calibration of Action Proposals (HyrCap), a proposal‑centric query‑based TAD framework for temporal event understanding. Hybrid combines complementary video features with different localization cues, while Rank‑Calibration adjusts proposal ranking confidence to reflect localization reliability and candidate competition. HyrCap treats dense query‑based predictions as an over‑complete temporal event hypothesis space. Cross‑Representation Consensus Calibration, Localization Quality Estimation, and Proposal Redundancy Suppression improve proposal ranking reliability, localization quality, and candidate discrimination. Inspired by LLMs' capabilities in fine‑grained semantic recognition, event description, and reasoning, we introduce HyrCap for Semantic Action Understanding, using calibrated proposals for standard TAD and as inputs to LLM‑based semantic understanding. We define a staged evaluation protocol to separately measure event localization, segment‑level semantic understanding, and combined event understanding performance. Experiments on public benchmarks show that HyrCap achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance across multiple metrics and provides a finer‑grained paradigm and evaluation protocol for query‑based event segmentation and annotation.

PaperId: 903, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19520.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Chia-Ming Lee, Yu-Jou Hsiao, Ming-Ching Chang, Xin Li, Yu-Lun Liu, Chih-Chung Hsu
Title: Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
Abstract:
Cameras and the foundation models built on them recognize what a 3D scene contains, but not what it is made of: surfaces of the same colour can be different materials. Hyperspectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a mixture of material signatures, yet in 3D it is applied to rendered images after the views are composited, or tied to slow implicit fields, and no multi‑view data with known composition exist to check the result. We present the Spectral World Renderer (SWR), which unifies world generation and unmixing. A coding agent builds executable 3D worlds that are rendered with measured spectra, so every hyperspectral image comes with exact labels and sub‑pixel proportions; the resulting SWR‑Bench provides eight indoor and outdoor worlds in which decompositions can be verified. SWR then unmixes inside rendering: each Gaussian of a compact 3D representation is decoded into material abundances before compositing, so one render yields spectra and material maps, and any surface can be queried by material name, a clicked pixel or a reference spectrum. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds, has the best mean PSNR on real captures, trains 3.7‑12.9x faster than unmixing baselines, renders 34.9 labelled views/s and separates same‑coloured materials.

PaperId: 904, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19518.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Linyi Huang, Guowei Huai, Weibin Liu, Shulong Jiang, Ping Tan, Weixuan Zhang, Hui Zhang, Jie Song
Title: HiFun: a Hierarchical Framework for Efficient Functional Dexterous Manipulation Learning
Abstract:
While multi‑fingered dexterous robot hands have the potential to provide human‑level dexterity, using them for functional manipulation remains difficult because task success depends on precise contact, coordinated arm‑hand motion, and reactive recovery from execution errors. Precise contact depends on complex contact dynamics that are difficult to model accurately in simulation, motivating real‑world learning. However, real‑world demonstrations in the full arm‑hand control space are costly and noisy because each trajectory must coordinate arm motion with high‑DoF multi‑finger contact. Small execution deviations can further cause slipped contact or premature force application, making recovery from off‑nominal contact states important for robust execution. To deal with these challenges, we propose HiFun, a hierarchical real‑world RL framework for functional dexterous manipulation tasks. Our key insight is to decouple the control complexity into a functional hand skill for precise contact execution and an arm‑hand coordination policy for arm control and hand‑skill activation. This design enables effective real‑time human intervention for reactive recovery learning and efficient data collection with Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP) augmentation. Across six real‑world tasks on two dexterous hands, HiFun achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training and remains robust to dynamic disturbances. The project page is available at https://hly‑123.github.io/HiFun/.

PaperId: 905, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19498.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wei-Liang Liu, Cheng-Yen Tsai
Title: What You Sign Is Not What You Run: The Verifiability Gap in Quantized LLM Supply Chains
Abstract:
Model signing authenticates the full‑precision weights W an LLM is released with, yet users run a quantized artifact Q whose producing transformation is not uniquely determined under current disclosure. We separate the non‑environment inputs from the execution environment E and measure a quantity that, to our knowledge, has not been measured before: the Independent Verifiability Rate (IVR), the fraction of a popularity‑sampled GGUF ecosystem that a third party can re‑derive bit‑for‑bit. Across the 200 most‑downloaded Hugging Face GGUF repositories (198 in scope), no artifact or model card records the build environment, so under a recorded‑inputs protocol the IVR is 0/198. Yet the artifacts are not irreproducible. On four in‑sample repositories that disclose their inputs, the card's information alone reproduces no Q4_K_M file, but two coordinates the card omits ‑ the build's floating‑point‑contraction setting and, for hybrid models, the per‑tensor quantization recipe ‑ re‑derive 7/8 target‑quant files bit‑for‑bit on x86 (5/8 on arm64); the fp16 re‑derives from the provider's checkpoint, but the calibration imatrix must be shipped and hash‑bound, since recomputing it did not match. An older release additionally pins the instruction set and did not re‑derive. Reproducing the divergence reported with llama.cpp PR #25353, we show that E is a necessary coordinate and that one compiler setting yields a unique output across the tested platforms at negligible quality cost (+0.06% perplexity). As a security characterization, benign floating‑point non‑determinism separates from uniformly placed nibble‑flip tampering above a detection floor that grows with the environments a verifier must allow, but a targeted embedding edit evades the statistic, so the proposed protocol rests on exact re‑derivation; adversarial‑fp16 attacks lie outside it. We release the audit data and a re‑runnable harness.

PaperId: 906, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19495.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yunze Liu, Jing Wang, Shenrui Wu, Wenkun He, Guanqi Zhan, Xianzheng Ma, Junyu Chen, Wenhang Ge, Haozhan Tang, Yuchao Gu, Zhuoyang Zhang, Zekai Wang, Dantong Niu, Zhen Dong, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Song Han, Han Cai
Title: Robota-Embed: Unified VLA Embeddings for Robot In-Context Learning and Evolution
Abstract:
Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota‑Embed, to our knowledge the first vision‑language‑action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current‑state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi‑source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota‑Embed‑Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000‑entry gallery. Robota‑Embed achieves 47.33% clip‑level and 81.77% episode‑level R@1, exceeding action‑free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training‑free and training‑based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID‑Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task‑local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT‑6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT‑6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni‑Embed‑Nemotron‑3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action‑aware retrieval space can support robot in‑context learning and task‑local context evolution.

PaperId: 907, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19475.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yanshu Li, Ruixiang Tang, Junyi Jessy Li, Elias Stengel-Eskin
Title: ActICL: Post-Training for Agentic Multimodal In-Context Learning
Abstract:
Multimodal in‑context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. Context‑aware retrieval methods have emerged to address this problem by allowing incremental retrieval from a growing context. However, none of them lets the MLLM learn how to judge what new demonstrations it needs and then carry out progressive retrieval on its own. To this end, we introduce ActICL, which trains an MLLM agent to acquire and use an ICL context via tool‑augmented reasoning. An ActICL agent analyzes its own information gaps during iterative reasoning and tool‑use actions. Based on these gaps, it performs targeted retrieval to acquire a set of initial candidates. It can then use the existing context to further filter the candidates and refine the context, or it can iteratively perform a new retrieval. When the agent judges that the context is sufficient for the task, or when the resource limit is reached with the user request met, it sends the acquired context to an answering model, either the agent itself or another MLLM. We use a two‑stage post‑training procedure that jointly optimizes the agent's acquisition and answering. With an adaptive number of demonstrations, ActICL improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over standard similarity‑based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points compared to the strongest prior baseline. The contexts acquired by ActICL agents can also be used effectively by frontier models. When GPT‑5.6‑Sol performs 4‑shot ICL, ActICL's contexts improve its performance by 3.5 points over standard retrieval, averaged over three benchmarks.

PaperId: 908, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19445.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Baotong Tian, Zhiyao Duan
Title: Point-and-Play: Instrument Timbre Cloning from Music Mixtures
Abstract:
Neural instrument synthesizers can clone the timbre of a solo instrument, letting music producers make music with the sound they desire. However, an instrument of interest is often embedded in a fully produced, multi‑instrument recording, beyond the reach of existing methods. Source separation before timbre cloning is an approach, but it may suffer from separation artifacts and is also likely a detour for the task. In this work, we propose Point‑and‑Play, a system that clones the timbre of a cued source directly from a polyphonic mixture and uses it to synthesize new pitches and velocities. To achieve this, we introduce a Cue‑Gated Statistics Pooling (CGSP) module that extracts the timbre code of the cued instrument from adapted CLAP embeddings of the music mixture. This extracted timbre code is then used to condition a separately trained note synthesizer together with pitch and velocity inputs. Experiments show that our proposed system outperforms separate‑then‑clone baselines in terms of timbre fidelity and synthesis quality, achieving comparable performance with that cloned from a clean solo instrument.

PaperId: 909, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19436.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jingjing Liu, Pei Tai, Xianchao Xiu, Wanquan Liu
Title: Learning to Select Features with Manifold Deep Unfolding PCA
Abstract:
Unsupervised feature selection (UFS) is of great significance in image processing and pattern recognition. Nevertheless, existing model‑based methods often rely on manually tuned hyperparameters, while deep learning‑based methods generally require massive training data. To address these issues, this paper proposes an efficient manifold deep unfolding feature selection network (MDUFS‑Net). Technically, we first incorporate the \ell_2,0‑norm into the classic principal component analysis (PCA) framework, then unfold the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)‑based iterative algorithm into an end‑to‑end trainable network, thereby enabling automatic parameter learning. Moreover, a manifold optimization strategy is developed to improve the numerical robustness. On this basis, we further extend MDUFS‑Net into an enhanced variant called MDUFS‑Net+ by introducing the \ell_0‑norm for more discriminative feature representations. Extensive experiments validate that our proposed MDUFS‑Net and MDUFS‑Net+ outperform state‑of‑the‑art methods in the UFS task, with promising performance in clustering. Our code is available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/MDUFS.

PaperId: 910, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19420.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yue Zhang, Han Lin, Zun Wang, Yidong Huang, Zaid Khan, Mohit Bansal
Title: From Failures to Learnable Worlds: Policy-Conditioned Environment Generation for Navigation Agents
Abstract:
Simulated environments enable scalable training data generation for embodied agents, but more data does not necessarily provide what a particular agent needs to learn. Existing environment‑generation pipelines largely optimize generic properties such as realism, diversity, or task coverage, while different pretrained policies can fail for different environmental reasons. We therefore introduce WEDGE, a framework for weakness‑guided navigation learning in which the failure modes of a pretrained agent guide the generation of training environments at each adaptation round. Given a pretrained policy, WEDGE uses an LLM to propose executable weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, automatically validates them on the diagnostic set, and selects the strongest validated weakness based on its success‑rate gap. The validated weaknesses are then mapped to the environmental factors that control them. WEDGE varies these factors to construct environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles, producing targeted training experience for adaptation. Across three navigation agents with different adaptation mechanisms, we find that policies exhibit distinct weakness profiles and benefit from different training environments. Weakness‑conditioned adaptation consistently outperforms matched random and hard‑example alternatives on ProcTHOR, while the resulting gains for Uni‑NaVid and Gemini also extend to HM3D after ProcTHOR adaptation. Iterative re‑diagnosis further shows that dominant weaknesses can persist or shift as the policy improves, providing updated guidance for subsequent environment construction. Together, these results show that policy failures are not only diagnostic signals, but actionable guidance for constructing training environments that target a policy's current weaknesses.

PaperId: 911, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19404.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hongrui Sheng, Shutian Liang, Reid A. Coyle, Shyam Chand Pal, Peter Walther, Bin Feng, Xinyu Ding, Zhiling Zheng
Title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning
Abstract:
Reticular chemistry allows metal‑organic frameworks (MOFs) to be designed from their building units, yet their synthesis remains constrained by sparse experimental data, noisy crystallization outcomes, and the absence of benchmarks for comparing active‑learning strategies. While data‑driven approaches such as Bayesian optimization (BO) can improve synthesis success rates, selecting appropriate optimizers beforehand for mapping MOF crystallization landscapes remains largely empirical. Here we present ActMOF, an experiment‑grounded benchmark for comparing search strategies in aluminum‑carboxylate MOF synthesis. ActMOF is emulated from experimentally measured microwave syntheses with each encoded condition assigned a crystallinity index calculated based on diffraction peak intensity and full width at half‑maximum. By benchmarking policies guided by Gaussian processes (GP), tree ensembles and large language models (LLM), ActMOF placed the GP family among the leading policies for active learning in sparse synthesis landscapes. It then demonstrated transferability by guiding the microwave synthesis of six reticularly related aluminum MOFs. All six campaigns gave crystalline products within a fixed budget of 12 experiments each, and established a reusable testbed for AI‑driven MOF synthesis.

PaperId: 912, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19385.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zinan Ling, Yang Xiao, Ruimeng Ye, Sijia Liu, Bo Hui
Title: RA$^2$: Retain-Anchored Attraction Preserves Forget-Adjacent Utility in LLM Unlearning
Abstract:
Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning is often evaluated primarily by target suppression and clean retain utility. These metrics can miss a local failure mode: a model may perform well on standard retain prompts, yet degrade on benign reasoning when prompts lie near the forgotten domain. This phenomenon is termed forget‑adjacent utility loss. A fundamental question is: where should forget representations go after they leave the removed behavior? Successful unlearning depends not only on whether forget‑conditioned representations depart from the harmful computation, but also on the direction in which they are redirected afterward. We propose RA^2 (Retain‑Anchored Attraction), a latent‑space unlearning method that redirects forget‑token states toward nearby retain‑supported representations while preserving higher‑layer behavior on retain data. On WMDP and MUSE, RA^2 yields higher forget‑adjacent utility than strong unlearning baselines at similar broad‑utility levels. These results show that the migration direction of forget representations materially affects benign behavior near the forget boundary. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZacLing/retain_anchored_attraction.

PaperId: 913, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19324.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Alexandre Bismuth
Title: Why don't Graph Transformers attend to the same token?
Abstract:
In large language models (LLMs), attention concentrates heavily on the first token. This 'attention sink' is believed to protect deep models against over‑mixing. Even though graph transformers face a related pressure, we find that a SoTA graph transformer, GRIT, rarely forms sinks on molecules, and that it sinks less when trained on larger graphs, the opposite of the trend in LLMs. In principle, a graph can prevent sinks: we prove and show empirically that its symmetry and locality limit the attention any node can receive. On molecules, however, with distinguishable atoms and global attention, neither limit prevents sinks; what stops them lies in the model. We find that the attention scoring function is the main cause. Replacing GRIT's gated logit with a dot product raises its sink rate from 0.09 to 0.68 on identical graphs. In Graph Transformers using dot‑product attention, removing the sink gives about the same error as removing a random node, while GRIT's most‑attended nodes matter to its predictions. Attention sinks are therefore a property of dot‑product attention rather than of Transformers. In our experiments, they form when dot‑product scoring has a distinguishable node to concentrate on.

PaperId: 914, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19301.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yihang Cheng, Qian Zhang, Yonghui, Huang, Baoshuo Kan, Junyi Shen
Title: Beyond ICD Codes: Semantic IDs for Generative Medical Coding
Abstract:
Generative approaches to automatic International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding use large language models (LLMs) to predict ICD codes from clinical documents. However, original ICD code strings are not ideal generation targets because the ICD hierarchy does not always reflect clinical relationships, and LLMs struggle to interpret and generate these codes. We introduce SemICD, a framework that trains LLMs to generate Semantic IDs (SIDs) instead. SemICD constructs SIDs by hierarchically clustering embeddings of textual code profiles, allowing semantically related codes to share prefixes while each complete SID uniquely identifies one ICD code. To align the SID tokens with clinical semantics, we employ two auxiliary tasks for bidirectional generation between textual code profiles and SIDs. Experiments on MIMIC‑III and MIMIC‑IV with four LLMs show that SemICD outperforms direct code generation, improving Micro‑F1 by 1.34‑8.00 points. Our code is available at https://github.com/youwillbethebest/SemICD.

PaperId: 915, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19262.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mohamed Abouagour, Junhyun Nam, Wonse Jo, Byung-Cheol Min
Title: MIND: Instruction-Conditioned Incremental Grounding for Robots
Abstract:
Robots following persistent language instructions must decide which cached room judgments remain valid as their environment changes. We present MIND (Maintenance via INstruction‑conditioned Dependencies), a framework for maintaining target‑room decisions without re‑evaluating every room after each event. A language model compiles each instruction into dependencies for semantic qualification and target selection. The controller intersects semantic dependencies with event footprints, refreshes affected judgments, and updates reachability and selection separately. For fixed deterministic evaluation, planning, and selection, conservative dependency and footprint coverage preserves the decisions of full recomputation. On 240 five‑event ProcTHOR sequences with an exact benchmark predicate, MIND reduces mean semantic evaluations from 30.6 to 11.2 while preserving all 1,200 post‑event decisions. Frozen‑evaluator experiments with Phi‑4 and Qwen3‑14B also preserve all 1,200 decisions, without improving the evaluators' underlying task accuracy. In 32 closed‑loop AI2‑THOR episodes using exact‑predicate qualification and metadata‑derived footprints, MIND matches the final target decision of full recomputation in every episode. Unitree G1 experiments demonstrate target reuse and reselection across room transitions without additional semantic evaluations under MIND, and abstention after a barrier and an object removal at 4 evaluations against 15 to 18. Additional materials are available at https://mind‑icra27.github.io/.

PaperId: 916, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19257.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Eren Cetin, Julius Erbach, Vukasin Bozic, Hyojun Go, Zixiang Zhao, Nikolai Kalischek, Federico Tombari, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer
Title: Long-horizon Video Generation with Slot Memory Addressed By Region Tokens
Abstract:
Memory for long‑horizon video generation must satisfy two competing requirements: it must remain bounded so generation can continue indefinitely, while still recovering what was observed at a place when the camera returns, regardless of how long ago it was seen. Reconstruction‑based memories provide spatial recall by caching and reprojecting explicit geometry, but require growing storage and depend on estimated 3D structure. Recurrent memories keep a constant‑size state, but retention is governed by temporal recurrence, causing old observations to fade with time. We introduce SMART, a slot memory addressed by region tokens, which combines bounded storage with spatially addressed recall. SMART stores content in a constant‑size slot recurrence whose writes are addressed by the observing camera and whose reads are queried by the rendering camera, without constructing an explicit 3D representation or maintaining a growing cache. Consequently, recall is conditioned on inter‑view geometry rather than on recency. Each read additionally provides a confidence estimate that conditions a chunk‑causal diffusion transformer, allowing it to selectively trust retrieved content while relying on its generative prior elsewhere. On long trajectories in Memory Maze and Minecraft, SMART maintains high‑fidelity recall far beyond its training horizon while using constant memory and per‑step cost.

PaperId: 917, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19246.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiankai Huang, Hanwen Shen
Title: Refined Topology-Pass Scheduling: Damped Trust-Region Compensation for Dynamic k-NN Graphs in SE(3)-Equivariant Structure Prediction
Abstract:
Equivariant structure‑prediction pipelines alternate coordinate updates with the construction of a k‑nearest‑neighbour (kNN) graph whose membership is a discrete, piecewise‑constant function of the coordinates. Rebuilding that graph at every block boundary (PB) is the expensive part of an epoch, whereas reusing one frozen graph (F) is fast but leaves a topology gap. We study a two‑pass design in which the cheap pass records a small amount of state (margins, kNN radii, measured per‑boundary displacements) and a second pass compensates conservatively. We formulate the choice of the graph‑construction basis as a damped fixed‑point iteration whose unique fixed point is exactly PB, and derive (i) exact non‑flip certificates with the two‑sided constant m_i/4 and one‑sided constant m_i/2, (ii) the minimum‑variance (BLUE) replay gain γ^ and the resulting feasibility crossover, (iii) an \ell_\infty trust‑region projection that preserves convergence, and (iv) an analytic near‑tie spacing law E[m] \approx r_k/(3k) that matches measurements to 1%. Three compensation levels are implemented in C++ (L1: frozen set with live geometry; L2: margin‑gated local repair; L3: damped, projected basis) and validated under a matched‑conditions protocol (identical seed, MSA depth and trajectory family, only the topology mode differs). L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly (D = 0.0000 at every boundary), L1 stays within 0.6% and L3 interpolates monotonically: L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly when the trust region is removed, and L3 interpolates between the frozen and the PB topology. The recorded trajectory itself yields a measured 1.5× Pass‑1 and 1.76× epoch speed‑up with no measurable loss gap. An open‑source implementation of the runtime and of all the experiments reported here is available at https://github.com/AlbertHuang96/ProteinPredictMachineLearning.

PaperId: 918, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19232.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zachary Broveak, Christian Kubicka, Thierry Tambe
Title: Spectral-MoE: Heterogeneous Per-Layer Expert Utilization in Dense-to-MoE Conversion
Abstract:
Large language models impose substantial memory demands and arithmetic costs during inference. Dense‑to‑mixture‑of‑experts (MoE) conversion is a model optimization technique that aims to reduce these arithmetic costs. Dense‑to‑MoE conversion partitions pretrained feed‑forward network (FFN) neurons into experts and selects a subset for each token. Leading methods fall into two categories: analytic methods produce a converted model quickly using heuristics, while learning methods produce a model much more slowly by optimizing via gradients. Both approaches, however, fix the same active expert count, or "utilization," at every layer. We introduce Spectral‑MoE, which learns to allocate a utilization budget heterogeneously across layers. Its name draws a metaphor between separating a dense FFN into experts and separating a light beam into its spectrum. Spectral‑MoE consists of two distinct approaches: a static approach that uses a single per‑layer scalar which is shared across tokens, and a dynamic approach which emits a per‑token schedule. We demonstrate that both allocators improve performance over uniform on both the analytic‑based and learning‑based SOTA dense‑to‑MoE methods. At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation reduces WikiText‑2 perplexity relative to uniform by 1.04, 2.96, and 2.71 points on the learned base for Llama‑2‑7B, Llama‑3‑8B, and Qwen2.5‑7B, respectively. The corresponding reductions on the analytic base are 2.45, 6.26, and 2.17 points. On the learned base, dynamic allocation improves six‑task mean accuracy over uniform by an average of 1.5, 4.2, and 3.6 percentage points across the three models at FFN utilizations of 12.5%, 25%, and 50%, respectively. These results establish per‑layer expert utilization as a novel optimization axis in dense‑to‑MoE conversion.

PaperId: 919, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19212.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Anton Arapin, Aditya Singh, Yixin Wang, Jun Gao, Bernadette Bucher
Title: Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Models for Consistent Future Frame Prediction
Abstract:
World models of visual information predict future image frames conditioned on given action sequences. This predicted scene evolution is driven by deterministic changes such as controlled motion on a robot platform, as well as stochastic changes such as rendering of manipulated objects or previously occluded regions. Our key insight is that the spatial location of these stochastic changes is itself learnable. We leverage this insight by jointly regressing both the deterministic next‑state prediction and the spatial uncertainty map, then using the uncertainty map to guide a conditional diffusion process. We propose Decoupled Drift‑Diffusion World Model (D3WM), which uses a transformer trained with a Gaussian negative‑log‑likelihood objective to produce both the deterministic next‑state prediction and a spatial map of heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty. The learned uncertainty map then provides a structured spatial gate for a conditional diffusion model: deterministic regions are anchored to the predicted state, while uncertain regions, such as disocclusions or dynamic textures, are sampled by the diffusion process. We frame this decomposition under a variance‑gated stochastic differential equation that separates deterministic drift from stochastic diffusion. D3WM shows improved results over competitive baselines in two distinct types of action spaces: robotic tabletop manipulation and camera motion.

PaperId: 920, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19210.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Sarah Pan, Ali Behrouz
Title: Titan-Llama: Retrofitting Pre-trained LLMs with External Neural Memory Modules
Abstract:
Transformers are efficient to pre‑train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long‑context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token‑wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long‑context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan‑Llama, a post‑training method for retrofitting attention‑based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test‑time. Titan‑Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full‑fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed‑size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre‑trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama‑3.2‑1B‑Instruct, Titan‑Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87% to 40.51% on QuALITY and from 14.50% to 40.75% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20% faster prefill, 37% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24% lower steady‑state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test‑time training effectively modulates long‑context behavior of pre‑trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre‑trained transformers for efficient long‑context inference. Our code is released on Github \hrefhttps://github.com/sarahpannn/titans‑pytorch/tree/mainGitHub

PaperId: 921, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19176.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jinhao Pan, Bowen Wei, Yuqing Zhou, Ziwei Zhu
Title: Learning from Self-Generated Responses: Reliability--Uncertainty Self-Distillation for Reasoning
Abstract:
Reference solutions and question‑specific rubrics are not always available to guide the teacher in self‑distillation. A large language model's own solution attempts offer an alternative, but their quality is difficult to assess in open‑ended tasks without automatic correctness checks, and even correct attempts can involve uncertain token predictions. We propose Reliability‑‑Uncertainty Self‑Distillation (\method) to learn from these attempts. The same model serves as teacher and student: the teacher receives the question and completed attempt, and the student matches the teacher's token‑level predictions using a question‑only prompt. \method weights each attempt's distillation loss by additively combining judged reliability, estimated from a self‑judge's score and confidence, with student predictive uncertainty. Across eleven reasoning benchmarks, \method outperforms all five baselines in average accuracy, reaching 70.47% on Qwen3‑4B and 76.69% on Qwen3‑8B (8.90 and 2.10 percentage points above the base models). Data and code are available at https://github.com/JP‑25/RUSD.

PaperId: 922, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19164.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Elyas Irankhah, Ashley Hagaman, Samah Fodeh
Title: From Qualitative Text to Integrated Evidence: The Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI) Procedure
Abstract:
Mixed methods research offers established strategies for integrating qualitative and quantitative evidence, but less guidance for integrating two computational representations of the same qualitative corpus. This methodological study introduces Parallel‑Then‑Integrated (PTI), a four‑step procedure for explicit and traceable integration. We present PTI using 1,203 interview paragraphs from 29 mothers in Nepal. The two representations were ontology‑guided Patient Voice (PV) coding with PVminer and data‑driven themes generated through non‑negative matrix factorization (NMF). A theme‑complete crosswalk documented convergence, divergence, and preprocessing‑sensitive differences. Depression status, based on Patient Health Questionnaire‑9 (PHQ‑9) scores, served as a secondary external anchor for exploratory association checks. PTI provides a structured approach for integrating computational representations of qualitative text within mixed methods research.

PaperId: 923, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19131.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Akash Raj
Title: Plant Memory: Technical Language Processing and a Verified Maintenance Ontology for Agent-Accessible Failure Knowledge from SAP PM Work Orders
Abstract:
Maintenance work orders are the largest written record of how industrial equipment fails, yet in most plants they are close to unusable for analysis. Short texts are abbreviated and misspelt, asset identity is buried in free text, work‑type labels contradict the work described, and the fields that matter most for reliability (symptom, root cause, action taken) are usually empty. As a result, diagnostic knowledge stays with senior technicians and leaves when they do. We present Plant Memory, a system that applies technical language processing (TLP) to SAP Plant Maintenance (PM) exports and builds an ISO 14224‑aligned maintenance ontology in which every extracted statement is a reified fact carrying a confidence score, the evidence it was read from, and a verification state. Extraction is rule‑first, with an optional large language model (LLM) acting as a second reader whose disagreements raise a fact's review priority rather than overwrite it. Technicians verify facts through a review queue, answer targeted knowledge‑gap questions where failures repeat without a recorded cause, and approve or reject ontology drift proposals when new terms appear. The resulting graph is served to people through a web application and to AI agents through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, so both query the same verified knowledge and every answer cites the work orders behind it. On a synthetic 12‑month export of 400 work orders from a parboiled‑rice plant, rule‑based extraction reaches 96.2% component accuracy, 88.9% failure‑mode accuracy and 100% root‑cause precision at 62% coverage; on 28 diagnostic questions, ranked root causes from the ontology are correct at top‑1 in 82.1% of cases against 53.6% for the raw SAP root‑cause column.

PaperId: 924, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19118.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yifan Lan, Zhongye Liu, Yurui Chang, Hanyu Wang, Yongkang Du, Lu Lin, Jinghui Chen
Title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision
Abstract:
Emerging decision models such as JEV provide typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores. As these models are increasingly used for automated decision‑making, understanding their reliability under adversarial manipulation becomes critical. We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of decision models across textual and visual inputs. Our benchmark covers practical decision‑making scenarios and a diverse suite of attacks, including semantics‑preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities. We curate evaluation sets through external validity checks and cross‑model candidate selection. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held‑out models, respectively, that are excluded from candidate selection. Our experiments reveal several key findings. First, attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction and selection, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. Second, relative model robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Third, label‑consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success across text and image settings, highlighting the importance of validating apparent failures. The benchmark is available at https://yifan‑lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/.

PaperId: 925, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19100.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qingsong Xie, Jiahao Tian, Jiacheng Tang, Zhifeng Li, Madalina Ciobanu, Navan Preet Singh, Qingqing Mao, Ritankar Das
Title: GroundGUI: GUI Grounding by High-Quality Data and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
Constructing robust GUI agents relies on multimodal visual grounding: the ability to precisely map natural language intents to actionable on‑screen components. Despite abundant desktop, web, and mobile benchmarks, high‑fidelity resources tailored for diverse environments are surprisingly scarce. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Screen Referring Grounding Dataset (ScreenRef), a comprehensive GUI grounding dataset consisting of GUI screenshots paired with natural language referring expressions and box or point annotations. Spanning desktop, web, and mobile domains, ScreenRef comprises 586K screenshots and over 633K referring expression instances, covering tasks such as text recognition, visual matching, spatial understanding, and refusal scenarios. To boost the model's grounding performance, we propose the Distillation‑to‑Reinforcement Learning (D2RL) method to address the limited generalization of supervised fine‑tuning and the sparse reward problem in reinforcement learning. Utilizing ScreenRef, we train Qwen3‑VL‑8B‑Instruct via sequential SFT and D2RL training, yielding GroundGUI‑8B. GroundGUI‑8B achieves 95.2% on ScreenSpot‑V2, 63.9% on ScreenSpot‑Pro, 65.4% on OSWorld‑G, 86.8% on MMBench‑GUI L2, and 38.3% on UI‑Vision.
