Among 8B‑scale models, it produces substantial gains over models trained on open‑source datasets, with performance comparable or even superior to models trained on closed‑source data. Code, models, and datasets are available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/GroundGUI.

PaperId: 926, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19089.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhexi Luo, Zhixuan Xu, Rui Yang, Zeyu Xiao, Yiwen Hou, Lin Shao
Title: DexMimic: A Generalist Dexterous Hand-Object Tracking Policy via Value-Guided Reset Allocation
Abstract:
Achieving human‑like dexterous manipulation remains a central challenge in robotics. Learning from human hand‑object interaction (HOI) datasets offers a promising pathway to diverse dexterous skills, yet existing physics‑based approaches train specialist policies for individual trajectories, thereby limiting skill reuse at scale. We introduce DexMimic, a generalist dexterous hand‑object tracking policy jointly trained across diverse HOI trajectories. Efficient joint training requires allocating each rollout to both an undertrained phase and a starting state that supports continued tracking. DexMimic realizes this insight through Value‑Guided Reset Allocation, which adapts the initialization distribution online to prioritize difficult phases and select reset states with higher expected tracking returns. We further introduce a benchmark spanning training, fine‑tuning, and generalization. Experiments show improved tracking success and training efficiency, faster fine‑tuning, and the potential for zero‑shot generalization to unseen trajectories and objects; larger training sets further improve efficiency and generalization. Finally, we validate DexMimic on a real‑world dexterous manipulation platform.

PaperId: 927, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19074.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Neil K. Chada, Simon Cotter, Kody J. H. Law, Xinzhu Liang
Title: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology
Abstract:
Reliable uncertainty quantification remains an important challenge in AI. Hierarchical Bayesian methods provide a principled framework for this by representing unknown quantities through posterior distributions. Joint inference of neural‑network parameters and prior hyperparameters is challenging for conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods due to strong dependencies. In this work, we introduce the multilevel particle marginal Metropolis‑Hastings (MLPMMH) method, which combines pseudo‑marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across hierarchy of network‑width truncations for conditional parameter inference. The hierarchy is induced by a trace‑class neural network (TNN) prior with width‑dependent decay, motivated empirically by the compressible structure observed in trained neural‑network parameters. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, we establish that MLPMMH achieves mean‑square error (MSE) \mathcalO(\varepsilon^2) at expected computational cost \mathcalO(\varepsilon^‑2), and verify the predicted rate on a Bayesian regression problem. To address larger‑scale applications, we further introduce S‑MLPMMH, a practical approximation that replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA‑based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation. Software has been made publicly available at https://github.com/submission‑code‑anon/mlpmmh‑anon.

PaperId: 928, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19007.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Anton Arapin, Chahyon Ku, Bernadette Bucher
Title: Action Jets: Learning the Local Shape of the Action-conditioned Data Manifold
Abstract:
World models are a powerful means of reasoning and planning, but many of these action‑conditioned predictive models are high dimensional and computationally expensive. These challenges limit the number of action candidates that can be evaluated by a planner. We show that this cost is avoidable for planners over short horizons, which only require local information with respect to the current state. For a fixed state, the frames reachable by varying a low‑dimensional action (a camera movement or an end‑effector command) lie on a low‑dimensional manifold. We estimate the local shape of that manifold directly via a network trained to estimate how each image region moves per unit of each action axis supervised by data collected from samples by the generator. A correction head fit to trajectory data estimates the shape of this manifold region up to a third‑order Taylor polynomial. We call this network estimating the Taylor polynomial describing the manifold shape an Action Jet and compute its radius of validity in closed form. By traversing this approximation of the local manifold shape, we only have to perform inference once per state for any number of candidate actions. Scoring sixteen candidates from a single extraction is over 300x faster than with either source generator, and this gap widens with the number of candidates a planner evaluates. We measure against state‑of‑the‑art action‑conditioned generators, IRASim and WorldGym on BridgeData V2, a real 7‑DoF manipulation benchmark, and FrameCrafter on DL3DV scenes, where we chart from the novel‑view generators DepthSplat and LagerNVS. Because only the tangent comes from the generator and every other term from the data, the Action Jet also predicts held‑out frames more accurately than IRASim, the generator that supplied its tangent, at short horizons and at over 100x less compute.

PaperId: 929, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18924.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Alec H. Follmer
Title: TorchSpin: Differentiable Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Simulation in PyTorch
Abstract:
Interpreting electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra commonly requires repeated forward simulation and optimization of spin Hamiltonian parameters. Established software provides mature simulation and fitting methods, but these calculations are not generally available as differentiable components within machine‑learning workflows. We present TorchSpin, an open‑source PyTorch framework that ports the organization and numerical conventions of EasySpin into a tensor‑based computational environment. Representative calculations spanning continuous‑wave EPR, ENDOR, pulse EPR, spin dynamics, trajectory simulation, and magnetometry closely reproduced corresponding EasySpin results. In matched benchmarks, TorchSpin CPU execution was faster than EasySpin for six of nine workloads although performance depended strongly on the calculation. We therefore focused on the capabilities enabled by automatic differentiation in PyTorch. In a Cu(II) powder‑spectrum demonstration, feedback propagated through TorchSpin improved the quality of a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) without using parameter labels during refinement. Models trained from randomly initialized CNNs using only noisy spectra and TorchSpin reconstruction loss achieved median similarities of \geq 0.99. CNNs trained on TorchSpin‑generated libraries also transferred without adaptation to independently generated EasySpin spectra with performance comparable to EasySpin‑trained controls. Once trained, the CNN produced initial parameter estimates in approximately 1 ms per spectrum while a batch of 512 was processed in approximately 1.3 ms with GPU acceleration. TorchSpin therefore provides both a tested Python implementation of established EPR calculations and a differentiable physical layer for rapid learned inference, spectral refinement, and parameter‑label‑free training.

PaperId: 930, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18880.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziyuan Gao
Title: Do Perturbation Predictors Learn Gene Interactions? Diagnosing Extrapolation in Agentic Screening
Abstract:
High‑throughput perturbation screens increasingly use machine‑learning models to predict the effects of gene combinations that were never measured. A difficult case arises when both genes in a test pair were seen individually during training, but their combination was not. In this setting, standard OOD methods often fail because neither gene appears unfamiliar on its own. We therefore compare each model prediction with a simple additive prediction obtained by summing the two observed single‑gene effects. The difference between them, which we call additive disagreement (AD), measures how much extra interaction effect the model introduces for an unseen combination. Across eight prediction methods and three Perturb‑seq datasets, specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform this simple additive baseline. More importantly, predictions with larger deviations from the additive baseline tend to have larger errors. Conventional output‑based and embedding‑based confidence signals are inconsistent across datasets and models, whereas AD remains informative across all evaluated compositional settings. We further study how this signal can guide decisions in an agentic perturbation‑screening workflow. The code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/OOD.

PaperId: 931, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18879.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziyuan Gao
Title: Do Vision CIL Methods Transfer to Protein? A Diagnostic Benchmark of Frozen Protein Encoders
Abstract:
Protein function annotation operates over an expanding label space, making class‑incremental learning (CIL) a natural framework for incorporating newly discovered functions without full retraining. Yet existing CIL methods have been developed largely in vision and have not been systematically evaluated over frozen protein representations. We conduct a controlled benchmark of nine representative CIL methods across five sequence‑, structure‑, and sequence‑‑structure‑based protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets at different scales, while keeping the encoders frozen and evaluation settings consistent across representations. We find that no method transfers reliably across encoders, and that these failures persist across alternative phase constructions. Diagnostic analyses reveal that this instability arises from weak gradient‑based stability signals, substantial heterogeneity in embedding geometry, and covariance assumptions whose appropriate capacity changes with both dataset scale and encoder. These findings suggest that the representation itself should be treated as a central component of continual‑learning design rather than a passive feature extractor. More generally, reliable protein CIL will require encoder‑aware methods that adapt their statistical assumptions and capacity to the geometry of the representation on which they operate. Code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/ProteinCIL.

PaperId: 932, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18870.pdf   GitHub GitHub GitHub
Authors:Reyhaneh Esmailizadeh, Xingjian Leng, Zhanhao Liang, Liang Zheng
Title: MiniDog: Dog-Breed Text-to-image Flow Matching from Pretraining to Fine-Tuning on 4 Consumer GPUs
Abstract:
We generally perceive that training text‑to‑image diffusion models requires heavy compute: it is true if we aim at a comprehensive frontier model. This understanding prevents people from training their own models when getting started in the field. We develop MiniDog, a framework that enables pretraining diffusion transformers in 55 minutes and fine‑tuning in another 15 minutes on four 3090 GPUs. For data, we use 26k dog images from ImageNet and caption them for pretraining and use 2k images generated by FLUX.1‑schnell for fine‑tuning. We precompute the image and text features and cache them for efficiency. For architecture, we use E2E‑INVAE for its semantic latent space, a small transformer with 22M parameters, a small Qwen model for text encoding, and in‑context conditioning. For training, we use iREPA and an EUPE perception encoder for acceleration. For evaluation, our repository supports FID, HPSv2 score, PickScore, and various VAE reconstruction metrics. The project is open‑sourced at https://github.com/Reyhaneesmailizadeh/MiniDog. We do not claim technical novelty.

PaperId: 933, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18836.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Juntong Feng, Qingan Liu, Jingru Dong, Yue Zhu, Weiming Zheng, Yujie Cheng, Xinzhe Han, Shuai Hao, Yunzhi Zhuge, Haiwen Diao, Huchuan Lu
Title: Plan-Bench: Can Existing VLMs Go Well Beyond Perception to Reason and Plan in Embodied Worlds?
Abstract:
Vision‑Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in visual perception and spatial reasoning, leading to growing interest in using them as high‑level planners for embodied AI. However, physical tasks require models to integrate spatial information, reason over temporal states, and generate multi‑step plans under various constraints, raising the question of whether current VLMs can reliably support such reasoning and planning independently of execution. We introduce Plan‑Bench, a benchmark for evaluating the high‑level reasoning and multi‑step planning capabilities of VLMs relevant to embodied worlds, while isolating the influence of action execution. It covers three complementary dimensions, spanning 16 subclasses and 699 curated samples. Extensive evaluation of 28 VLMs reveals room for improvement, with even the strongest model achieving only 75.0% accuracy. We further find that model scaling generally improves these capabilities. Ablation studies also indicate larger models show increasing potential as high‑level planners. Overall, Plan‑Bench provides a lightweight probe for evaluating VLMs' reasoning and planning capabilities relevant to embodied environments and assessing their potential as decision makers for physical tasks. Our benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/MinneFeng/Plan‑Bench.

PaperId: 934, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18826.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haoyi Duan, Liliang Chen, Nan Wang, Yang Zhang, Yuhang Lu, Xiaotong Chen, Wei-Cheng Tseng, Shenyuan Gao, Zhaoshuo Li, Jingyi Jin, Pooya Jannaty, Dhruv Shah, Yuke Zhu, Ming-Yu Liu, Maoqing Yao, Guanghui Ren
Title: WorldOracle: Benchmarking Action-Conditioned World Models against Real-World Executions
Abstract:
We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action‑conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real‑world executions. Given the same initial observation and low‑level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task‑state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi‑view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real‑world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi‑segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action‑conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard: https://worldoracle‑benchmark.github.io/.

PaperId: 935, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18784.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuchen Lu, Julian McAuley, Lei Zhang
Title: Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents
Abstract:
Long‑horizon agents accumulate progress in persistent task state, yet repeatedly process interaction histories describing how that progress was achieved. This raises a natural question: can long‑horizon context instead be organized around reusable progress rather than the history that produced it? In this paper, we introduce CarryOn, an object‑oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects. Rather than treating compressed histories or reconstructed accounts of progress as the primary basis for continuation, CarryOn builds a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions. A core challenge is keeping this reusable basis valid after its surrounding history is retired: how can CarryOn update the basis without reconstructing the full representation at every fold? CarryOn maintains carrier records across folds, revising affected records against bound evidence and applicable environment checks while carrying forward unaffected records and jointly updating execution context. Experiments on OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp‑Plus show improved gains of 5.8% and 7.0% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. Project page: https://ethannju.github.io/carryon

PaperId: 936, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18621.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiajing Hu, Xu Han, Li-Ping Liu
Title: Deterministic Prediction as Global Velocity: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecast
Abstract:
Accurate uncertainty quantification is critical for many time series forecasting applications, and recent studies have increasingly adopted generative models to capture predictive uncertainty. Existing approaches often combine deterministic forecasting with generative modeling to improve predictive performance. However, their joint training is typically unstable because the deterministic model is embedded within the generative process, resulting in deep computational graphs and changing the probability transport path. In this work, we propose DV‑Flow, a unified flow‑matching formulation that incorporates the deterministic predictor as a parallel velocity component rather than as the endpoint of the transport path. This design enables stable end‑to‑end optimization while subsuming several existing formulations as special cases, allowing direct comparisons among them. Extensive experiments on six real‑world datasets demonstrate that DV‑Flow consistently improves probabilistic forecasting performance over strong baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/tufts‑ml/dv‑flow‑time‑series.

PaperId: 937, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18616.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yuyang Bai, Yu Wang, Yu Zhang
Title: Knowledge Graphs as Files: An Agent Harness Where Tool Creation and Tool Use Co-Evolve
Abstract:
Searching text‑rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual evidence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or process retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select textual evidence, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection. This lets agents process large node sets in bulk while returning selected text for the model to assess. Execution feedback guides tool creation and revision, while the evolving tools determine what evidence the agent gathers next. On benchmark datasets spanning three domains, training‑free DKGI exceeds the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph, even with a minimal harness. Controlled ablations show the benefits of multi‑turn programming over shell‑only access and predefined graph tools, while trajectories show agents revising code to extend searches or address errors. These findings highlight the value of allowing tool creation and tool use to co‑evolve during graph search. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/leopoldwhite/DKGI.

PaperId: 938, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18484.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Wei Xie, Kaituo Feng, Shiming Fu, Yong Liu, Xiangyu Yue, Shuangjia Zheng
Title: ReTerm: Recovery Training for Self-Improving Terminal Agents
Abstract:
Terminal agents have shown strong abilities in complex coding tasks. However, they often struggle to recover from errors during long‑running execution (e.g., command errors, faulty implementations), eventually leading to task failures. To this end, we present ReTerm, a self‑improving terminal agent trained by learning how to recover from its own failed terminal tasks. To support its training, we construct a customized data pipeline and produce ReTerm‑10K, a high‑quality dataset that provides effective recovery demonstrations for SFT cold start. Furthermore, we propose ReTerm‑GRPO, an online RL algorithm that forks from the agent's own failure states to generate multiple independent self‑recovery attempts. By learning from whether these attempts successfully complete the task, the agent self‑improves through its own recovery experience. Built on Qwen3.5‑9B, our ReTerm‑9B achieves 34.8% Pass@1 on Terminal‑Bench 2.0, improving over the base model by 14.6 points. Further analysis shows that our method achieves consistently higher recovery rates across diverse error categories compared with standard GRPO training. All code, data and model are released at https://github.com/twothsnd/ReTerm.

PaperId: 939, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18447.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Thinker Team, Peng Gao, Jichao Jiao, Chen Liao, Daqin Luo, Yiming Ma, Baiyu Pan, Hailin Shi, Jiyuan Wang, Xiangming Xu, Xiongwei Zhao
Title: Thinker-WM: A Unified World Model with Shared Multimodal Representations for Embodied Intelligence
Abstract:
World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied AI, yet existing systems often remain fragmented in the modalities they model and the functions they support. In particular, visual dynamics, geometric structure, and executable action are commonly coupled through separate interfaces or downstream modules rather than being jointly represented and evolved within a shared dynamics model. In this work, we present Thinker‑WM, a unified multimodal world model that jointly models and generates RGB, metric depth, and robot action through a shared intermediate Unified Dynamics Transformer with modality‑specific encoders and decoders. The model performs multimodal unification at the representation level: appearance, geometry, and action are transformed into a common dynamic representation and jointly evolved by shared parameters, while their distinct output structures are preserved. The same parameterization supports multiple functions, including joint video‑action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action‑conditioned generation, video‑to‑action generation, and inverse dynamics. To examine whether the shared representation captures action‑related information, we introduce a lightweight motion probe that shows the frozen visual representation contains recoverable motion information. Thinker‑WM is trained on a heterogeneous corpus comprising approximately 20K hours of egocentric video, 10K hours of real‑robot data, and 1K hours of simulation data, including approximately 4K hours of real‑robot data with aligned depth supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance across embodied world‑model evaluations. Thinker‑WM ranks first on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad and WorldArena, while controlled studies further demonstrate the benefits of action conditioning, geometric interaction, and multi‑function training within the shared representation.

PaperId: 940, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18399.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Peiran Yin, Hao Wu, Zihao Yang, Fengyu Zhou, Yijuan Liang, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
Title: Bifocal: Training-Free Mixed Granularity Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal LLMs
Abstract:
Visual token pruning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) appears highly effective, with existing methods retaining over 95% of unpruned performance on common VQA benchmarks using a quarter of the visual tokens or fewer. However, our extensive evaluation of ten methods across three MLLM families and five ability groups reveals a critical gap: strong general performance often comes at the cost of severe degradation on fine‑grained tasks such as OCR and visual grounding. We trace these failures to two limitations of the prevailing paradigm of retaining the highest‑ranked native patches. A single importance ranking overlooks the complementary evidence required by different tasks, while sparse patch selection disrupts both image content and spatial integrity. To address these limitations, we propose Bifocal, a training‑free, two‑stage pruning method built on a mixed‑granularity framework. It allocates separate budgets to query‑focused and image‑intrinsic evidence, complemented by a pooled coarse representation of the entire image. Before the LLM, Bifocal matches question words to visual regions through a soft conjunction balanced against norm‑debiased image saliency, while selecting image‑intrinsic evidence to maximize representational coverage. Inside the LLM, it further prunes tokens using density‑adjusted text‑to‑image attention. With roughly a quarter of the original visual tokens, Bifocal is the only evaluated method to retain over 90% of unpruned performance in every ability group across all three models, and ranks first on average in all nine model‑budget settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/EIT‑NLP/Bifocal

PaperId: 941, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18118.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhiyuan Chen, Shuai Chen, Haoran Zhou, Yizhe Zhao, Kaiyuan Yang, Zhixiang Duan, Shaoqing Xu, Ran Cao, Diyun Xiang, Yangwei You
Title: ForeTac: Predictive Contact Guidance for Generative Robot Policies
Abstract:
In contact‑rich manipulation, actions that appear equally plausible from vision can produce different contact outcomes, while reactive control based on current tactile feedback may respond too late to prevent failure. We present ForeTac, a predictive contact‑guidance framework organized as a represent‑predict‑evaluate‑guide loop. ForeTac encodes the current tactile state, predicts future tactile latent trajectories conditioned on candidate action sequences, and evaluates each predicted trajectory with a contact‑quality objective learned from successful and failed physical interactions. At inference, gradients of this objective are backpropagated through the tactile predictor to guide action generation before execution while keeping all model parameters frozen. We evaluate ForeTac on four real‑robot tasks (planar and curved‑surface wiping, card swiping, and fragile‑object grasping) with diffusion and flow‑matching policies. Compared with vision‑only Diffusion Policy, ForeTac improves the average task success rate (SR) from 36.3% to 71.3% and the average contact success rate (CSR) from 20.0% to 66.3% across these tasks, and yields gains in both metrics with a flow‑matching policy. Component analyses support the learned tactile representation, action‑conditioned foresight, and generation‑time gradient guidance, while predicted tactile latent trajectories preserve contact‑quality ordering. Project page: https://foretac.github.io/.

PaperId: 942, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18038.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kaipeng Fang, Hangxu Liu, Chaojian Shi, Yunsong Zhou, Hongzi Zhu, Minyi Guo, Jingkuan Song, Lianli Gao
Title: Data-Free Continual Learning for World Action Model with Rectified Generative Replay
Abstract:
World action models (WAMs) built on pretrained video generation models adapt quickly to new robotic tasks, but they forget previously learned tasks under sequential fine‑tuning. Experience replay (ER) mitigates such forgetting by rehearsing data of previous tasks, yet this data is often unavailable in robotics, where a policy is deployed as weights only and its training data is not shared along with it. In this work, we ask whether a WAM can achieve data‑free continual learning by regenerating its own past. Our key observation is that a WAM can indeed autoregressively regenerate complete rollouts of previously learned tasks and replay them to mitigate forgetting. However, replaying such raw rollouts still lags far behind replaying real data, which we attribute to two issues. First, the WAM is unable to recognize task completion and keeps generating purposeless motion after the task is done. Second, under open‑loop generation, the generated actions gradually drift away from the generated observations. To address both issues, we present rectified generative replay (R^2‑WAM), which truncates generated rollouts at task completion with an agentic evaluator and filters out rollouts whose actions are physically inconsistent with the observations. On the four LIBERO suites and five real‑world tasks, R^2‑WAM reduces forgetting by over 90% relative to sequential fine‑tuning and nearly matches ER without accessing any data from previous tasks. Our analysis further reveals that forgetting in WAMs concentrates in inverse dynamics modeling: a forgotten WAM still produces visually plausible observations of previous tasks while its generated actions fail. Project page: https://kaipengfang.github.io/r2‑wam/

PaperId: 943, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18010.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Dawei Han, Shidong Li, Shijia Liao, Jiahua Liu, Songting Liu, Qingzheng Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Xin Chen, Yifan Cheng, Tianyu Li, Gangin Park, Xuehao Yang, Chang Zeng, Haoyang Zhang, Ruoyi Zhang, Xiangyu Zhang
Title: Fish Audio Drama 3 Technical Report
Abstract:
We introduce Fish Audio Drama 3, an open‑source speech generation model that turns text into directed performances, built on a 35B‑parameter mixture‑of‑experts backbone that activates 3B parameters per token. It clones voices from multiple references, follows natural‑language direction, revises a take when the next turn gives a note, voices multi‑character scenes, edits existing speech by infilling, and synthesizes long‑form and streaming audio. Multi‑turn revision, scene dubbing, editing by infilling, and streaming text input are new in Drama 3, all in one model. Drama 3 pairs the hybrid linear‑attention backbone with a new codebook multi‑token‑prediction audio decoder that predicts the acoustic codebooks of each frame in dedicated layers that attend over the entire sequence. The model is trained with a three‑stage pre‑training recipe, instruction fine‑tuning, and large‑batch reinforcement learning whose only reward is a single learned model of human preference. Its inference engine decodes a single stream at 271 frames per second on one H200, against 177 for Fish Audio S2, although Drama 3 has more than seven times as many parameters. The model weights are available on GitHub (https://github.com/fishaudio/fish‑speech) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama‑3), and inference is available through SGLang‑Omni (https://github.com/sgl‑project/sglang‑omni). We highly encourage readers to visit https://fish.audio to direct their own performances.

PaperId: 944, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.17821.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shuyang Cui, Zhi Zhong, Keisuke Toyama, Koichi Saito, Qiyu Wu, Yukara Ikemiya, Junghyun Koo, Kin Wai Cheuk, Woosung Choi, Giorgio Fabbro, Wei-Hsiang Liao, Shusuke Takahashi, Yuki Mitsufuji
Title: FLOMSS: Generative Music Source Separation by Flow Matching
Abstract:
Music source separation (MSS) has been conventionally addressed by discriminative methods. Recently, flow matching has emerged as a strong generative paradigm for modeling complex data distributions, with successful applications across diverse domains. These advances motivate us to systematically investigate flow matching for MSS in a four‑source (Vocals, Bass, Drums, Other) setting in full‑band stereo. Specifically, we investigate prediction targets, flow paths, single‑source versus multi‑source modeling, and mixture consistency constraints. Beyond the signal‑level metrics commonly used for MSS, such as signal‑to‑distortion ratio, we further evaluate MSS methods using embedding‑based metrics, as well as a listening test, providing a comprehensive benchmark. On MUSDB18‑HQ, our proposed model exhibits competitive performance in both objective and subjective tests, highlighting the potential of flow matching for generative MSS. Demo: https://ik4sumii.github.io/FLOMSS/

PaperId: 945, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.17816.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Pengcheng Huang, Zhenghao Liu, Shixin Ren, Shi Yu, Sijia Yao, Yukun Yan, Chaojun Xiao, Maosong Sun
Title: Empowering Edge Agents: A Systematic Analysis of Edge-Cloud Collaboration in LLM Agent Execution
Abstract:
Edge‑cloud collaboration combines the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge‑side execution with the stronger capabilities of cloud‑hosted models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long‑horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one‑shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory‑level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC2‑Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge‑cloud collaboration in long‑horizon agent execution. It provides executable digital‑workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge‑cloud collaboration. Our study reveals three findings. First, collaboration achieves a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge‑only and cloud‑only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud‑only performance, and performance differences across strategies shrink, while privacy exposure remains strongly strategy‑dependent. Third, stronger edge capability shifts preferred collaboration from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge‑controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud‑invocation decision‑making and instruction following as important edge‑side abilities for effective collaboration. These findings provide a systematic understanding of edge‑cloud collaboration in long‑horizon agent execution and insights for designing future edge agents that effectively collaborate with cloud models. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2‑Bench.

PaperId: 946, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.17727.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jerrold Huang, Junwei Quan, Saiyue Lyu, Zihan Guo, Yingqiang Ge
Title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
Abstract:
Agent skills turn natural‑language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL.md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20‑25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word‑level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine‑tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task‑trained decision models for high‑recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen‑webpage/

PaperId: 947, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.17530.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kai Liu, Anqi Li, Junxian Li, Zhixin Wang, Zhikai Chen, Renjing Pei, Yulun Zhang
Title: TwinPrune: Density-Aware Two-Phase Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models
Abstract:
We propose a unified spatial‑density signal to score token importance for both inference phases: bipartite merge for prefill and KV eviction for decode, yielding measurable gains in each stage. To isolate the two phases, we split benchmarks by scoring logic. Prefill probes (MMBench, POPE, ScienceQA) evaluate only the first decoded token; their accuracy reflects prefill logits argmax before any decode KV eviction. Full‑pipeline probes (TextVQA, DocVQA, MM‑Vet) assess the complete generated sequence and capture both phases. We identify a critical evaluation pitfall: decode pruning claims validated solely on prefill probes measure prefill quality, not decode performance. Experiments show discarding all visual KV during decode barely affects prefill‑probe accuracy but degrades TextVQA and MM‑Vet drastically; this insensitivity stems from the scoring rule, not compression intensity. Evaluated on seven model variants (InternVL‑3.5, Qwen3‑VL, LLaVA‑1.5) and three full‑pipeline benchmarks, our method achieves a three‑way Pareto frontier across compute, memory and accuracy. Density‑based prefill compression maintains strong accuracy, scales linearly with visual token count, and delivers 100x faster token selection at high resolution. For decode, density top‑k KV eviction consistently outperforms strong baselines H2O, SnapKV and StreamingLLM on TextVQA and MM‑Vet across three retention ratios. At 0.125 keep ratio on TextVQA, it surpasses H2O by 9.6 points; InternVL‑3.5 models (2B to 38B) maintain a 7 to 10 point advantage. Compression scales favorably with model size: every measured 8B to 38B model transition reduces accuracy loss instead of worsening it. We suggest MM‑Vet or DocVQA as mandatory full‑pipeline validation for any decode‑phase claims. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kai‑Liu001/TwinPrune

PaperId: 948, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.17528.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Leo Fan, Hongyang Wang, Wenbo Chen, Jingguo Liu, Xian Li, Xuan Wang, Ruochen Wen, Yiming Yan, Hao Wu, Yichuan Li, Qian Qu, Zheshen Wang, Benoit Dumoulin
Title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
Abstract:
The throughput of an LLM training job depends on its recipe: how the model is split across GPUs, how memory is traded for compute, and which kernels and communication overlaps it uses. The best recipe changes with every model, accelerator and framework version. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, so they miss levers outside that space and can ship a configuration that silently changes training. ATTUNE is a coding agent that tunes any working recipe unattended within a GPU‑hour budget. Guided by a skill of search rules, scripts and lessons from past tuning campaigns, it diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time. A correctness gate outside the agent refuses any argument known to change the training objective. ATTUNE tunes Amazon's production post‑training recipes on H100, H200 and B200 clusters, raising throughput by 1.7x on average. It beats the published throughput of four of NVIDIA's own benchmark recipes on NVIDIA's AutoModel framework by 6‑17%. On models held out from its development, it improves the strongest public recipes most where they were written for another setting, by up to 2.6x on MiniMax‑M2, and least where the vendor tuned them for the same hardware. Given the same GPU‑hour budget, it outperforms existing automated tuners, including Bayesian optimization, random search and OptiCo, a recent LLM‑agent tuner. Its gain on GLM‑4.5 is more than four times the best alternative's. The same coding agent without ATTUNE's skill gains less and fails half its launches. We release ATTUNE at https://github.com/amazon‑science/attune and OpenRecipes, a leaderboard of tuned and verified training recipes, at https://openrecipes.ai.

PaperId: 949, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.17350.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jack B. Jedlicki, Amish Sethi, Heng Yang
Title: Can a Frontier VLM Serve as a Robot Policy for Memory-Dependent Manipulation?
Abstract:
We use a frozen frontier vision‑language model, GPT‑6‑Astra, directly as the robot policy on RoboMME, a benchmark of 16 memory‑dependent manipulation tasks spanning temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory. The model keeps the whole episode in context and outputs every end‑effector waypoint and gripper command, with no RoboMME‑specific training. On the 800 test episodes it succeeds in 92.1%, above the previously reported human score of 90.5%, which was obtained with an oracle skill interface, and far ahead of the best leaderboard entry (60.8%) and of a hierarchical system that pairs the same model with a RoboMME‑trained policy (79.1%). It matches or exceeds the human score on 13 of the 16 tasks. Its 63 failures concentrate in two tasks and are mostly premature completions and mistimed or unintended button presses. These results blur the usual division between long‑horizon planning, memory and end‑effector control, and raise the question of how much of this stack a single general‑purpose model can take over in embodied systems. Project website: https://embodied‑astra.github.io. Code, prompts and all episode logs: https://github.com/jackbjed/embodied‑astra‑robomme.

PaperId: 950, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.17309.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xialie Zhuang, Zunhai Su, Jia Pan, Ngai Wong, Guanhua Chen, Chuan-Wei Kuo
Title: StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
Abstract:
We introduce StartLux‑Decision, decision models from 0.8B to 27B parameters that combine efficient single‑pass prediction with adaptive, confidence‑guided reasoning. The Instant models use bidirectional attention in full‑attention layers to improve decision accuracy while keeping single‑pass inference. The AutoThink models invoke explicit reasoning for uncertain decisions and answer confident cases directly. A three‑stage training pipeline establishes shared decision capabilities, specializes the two variants, and equips AutoThink with reasoning through reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning. We introduce Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions (RLCD^2), which uses a frozen model and proper scoring rules to reward improvements in decision probability quality and applies a soft penalty to overlong reasoning traces. RLCD^2 raises the share of reasoning traces that terminate within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and cuts average reasoning length by up to 65%, while largely preserving decision accuracy. On the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, the Instant models outperform the strongest evaluated comparable‑scale open‑weight decision models by 7.4‑16.9 points, and the 27B AutoThink model reaches 73.4. We also introduce DecisionPivot, a programmatically verifiable benchmark of computational decisions built from contrast pairs that differ in a single answer‑changing detail. On DecisionPivot, AutoThink outperforms its Instant counterparts by 11.5‑18.4 points in pair accuracy and leads among evaluated systems. The models can be run using frameworks such as vLLM and MLX, with quantized versions available to reduce memory usage.Inference code and links to model weights are available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/Startlux‑Decision .

PaperId: 951, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.17233.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Daniel Shao, Dongmin Bang, Luca L. Weishaupt, Sophia J. Wagner, Nic G. Reitsam, Ming Y. Lu, Long P. Le, Richard J. Chen, Faisal Mahmood
Title: Beyond Sparse Captions: Aligning Slide-Level Text and Patch-Level Vision in Pathology
Abstract:
Contrastive vision‑language (VL) pretraining in computational pathology has generally relied on curated image‑caption datasets sourced from social media, educational videos, and research publications. These corpora are sparse relative to the diversity of tissue morphology and difficult to scale further, as pathologists do not routinely produce descriptive captions in clinical practice. We propose to instead leverage slide‑level pathology reports which can be generated during routine diagnostic workflows in a scalable manner. A key challenge in this weakly‑supervised setting is that pathology reports describe macroscopic, diagnostic findings while patch‑level visual features describe microscopic findings. We introduce Locked Image Multiple Instance PreTraining (LIMIT), which addresses this gap by freezing a pretrained vision encoder and fine‑tuning only the text encoder: report embeddings serve as cross‑attention queries over bags of patch features, producing report‑conditioned slide representations optimized via InfoNCE. Using LIMIT, we establish CONCH‑Z, which aligns the text encoder of CONCH v1.5 to 335k clinical reports. Evaluated across 22 tasks spanning patch‑level classification, tumor detection, and slide‑level subtyping, CONCH‑Z establishes state‑of‑the‑art zero‑shot performance over VL encoders trained on curated caption datasets, while simultaneously closing the gap with slide‑level foundation models trained with substantially more parameters and compute. The code and model is available at https://github.com/mahmoodlab/LIMIT.

PaperId: 952, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16975.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ye Liu, Reza Averly, Avery Meyer, Frazier N. Baker, Ruoxi Gao, Daniel Adu-Ampratwum, Xia Ning
Title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
Abstract:
Drug discovery remains a resource‑intensive and time‑consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single‑agent systems scale poorly to long‑horizon, multi‑step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi‑agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non‑linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi‑agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end‑to‑end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general‑purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low‑cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.

PaperId: 953, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16948.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jinrun Liu, Bai Yan, Tengfei Liu, Qunfeng Liu, Jian Yang, Shi Cheng, Yuhui Shi, Qi Zhao
Title: Learning to Design Convex Relaxations for Nonconvex Optimization
Abstract:
Convex relaxations make nonconvex optimization tractable by replacing hard nonconvex problems with convex surrogates that give valid bounds. Yet their design is still largely manual: a human expert must decide where to relax, which relaxation to use, and how much formulation growth is worth paying. We show that this design process can be learned. The method proposed in this paper, AutoConvexRelax, represents the symbolic formulation of a nonconvex problem as a tripartite graph linking variables, symbolic terms, and their objective or constraint positions. It then learns a policy that composes symbolic rewrites into problem‑specific relaxation trajectories as the formulation evolves. We prove that finite action sequences generated by the learned policy preserve relaxation validity under explicit domain, occurrence‑context, and representation‑consistency conditions. We further establish computable error bounds for mixed relaxations and sufficient conditions for feasible recovery and global‑optimality certification. As a first instantiation, we apply the method to nonconvex quadratic problems and fractional problems. On 241 benchmark quadratic instances, the learned policy strengthens McCormick lower bounds by 13.52%. Its mean lower bound is 3.70% below strengthened semidefinite relaxations on the normalized comparison metric, while it uses substantially smaller formulations. The learned policy retains this trade‑off on fractional instances and reaches near‑semidefinite bounds on beamforming and sensor‑network localization instances. These results suggest that convex relaxation design can move from a fixed handcrafted choice to an automated learning process that adapts to problem structures. Code is available at https://github.com/auto4opt/AutoConvexRelax.

PaperId: 954, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16892.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Harvey Mannering, Zhiwu Huang, Adam Prügel-Bennett
Title: Barycentric Guidance: Turning Foundation Image Editors into Continuous Affective Controllers
Abstract:
Emotions are expressed on a continuum and are naturally described in the valence‑arousal (VA) space. Existing VA‑based image editors are typically training‑based and domain‑specific, limiting them to VA regions seen during training and making them brittle across datasets and domains. Meanwhile, despite producing high‑quality edits, state‑of‑the‑art foundation image editors are not continuous affective controllers: non‑linear emotion representations in text encoders makes prompt interpolation poorly calibrated, so accurate and continuous VA control remains unreliable. To fill this gap, we introduce Barycentric Guidance, a training‑free framework that turns pretrained foundation image editors into continuous affective controllers over VA, requiring no finetuning, extra data, or model changes. Our method maps any target VA point to simplex‑based guidance weights, enabling VA controllability in three aspects: (i) accurate targeting of VA states, (ii) broad coverage across the VA plane, and (iii) continuous control. Across three face datasets, we improve VA target accuracy by 25‑29%, expand VA‑plane coverage by 28‑50%, and increase expression diversity by 29‑49%, over the strongest baseline. Unlike prior domain‑specific methods, our training‑free approach exploits the foundation model's inherent versatility, enabling generalization beyond human faces to animals, artworks, and complex scenes within a single framework. Code is available at https://github.com/harveymannering/BarycentricGuidance.

PaperId: 955, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16782.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ming Shin Cindy Sung, Duan Leijiahao, Haoxiang Wang, Boning Tan, Liangna Fu, Chao Tan, Yafu Li, Yulong Chen, Chaoqun Wan, Zhen Huang, Shuxian Liang, Xian-Sheng Hua
Title: LIBERO-Industry: Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation under Industrial Process Constraints
Abstract:
Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high‑mix, low‑volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO‑Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO‑Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static‑to‑Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic‑to‑Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic‑to‑Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction‑window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision‑language‑action models and world‑action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine‑tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO‑Industry co‑training condition achieved higher observed target‑transfer completion than the original‑LIBERO condition.

PaperId: 956, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16443.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuanpeng He, Ceyao Zhang, Fangjing Li, Kefei Zhu, Lijian Li, Yueheng Li, Tianjia He, Wenpin Jiao, Zhi Jin, Yaodong Yang, Yuanpei Chen
Title: RAP-WAM: Learning World-Action Models through Predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations
Abstract:
Recent world action models draw on video generation priors to jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Adapting these priors to control requires determining how future predictions should guide policy learning. RAP‑WAM combines predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations (RAP) with future‑supervised queries and Coupled Action Projection for policy learning. Predictive rehearsal trains on model‑generated inputs while retaining recorded targets, and accumulates recurring errors into a spatial prior. We perturb actions and measure changes in video predictions. Action‑response‑based spatiotemporal credit assignment combines these responses, prediction error, and the rehearsal prior to allocate visual supervision; spatially aggregating the responses determines supervision intensity across future action steps. No separate scoring network or deployment‑time probe is required. The base learns from a video‑pretrained backbone without intermediate pretraining on external embodied data. We evaluate the fixed base and its agent‑refined, task‑conditioned system. On 42 RoboDojo tasks, their average success rates are 12.85% and 15.62%, with Scores of 17.86 and 20.59. Across 15 real‑robot tasks, the complete system achieves 89.00% task‑macro‑average success, exceeding the strongest of five baselines by 37.67 percentage points. Across 315 fixed‑output simulation windows, 45.21% of response‑top20 positions fall outside error‑top20, revealing information beyond prediction error. Videos and further details are available on the project website: https://rapwam.github.io/.

PaperId: 957, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16336.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chia-Ming Lee, Chia-Yu Lin, Hung-Kai Huang, Yi-Ting Ku, Yu-Chen Liang, Chih-Chung Hsu
Title: Doctor Trigger: A Framework for Release-Bound Face Verification
Abstract:
Face swapping and generative editing enable realistic facial manipulation, while online redistribution complicates publisher oversight of circulating face images. Existing approaches establish provenance, detect manipulation, recover embedded watermarks, verify image integrity, or disrupt unauthorized face manipulation. These capabilities do not necessarily establish consistency with a specific publisher‑enrolled release, limiting the evidence available for verification and human review. To address this gap, we introduce Doctor Trigger, a framework for verifying circulating faces against private publisher‑held release records. Before publication, the publisher embeds a weak keyed Fourier‑phase signal in each face while preserving visual fidelity and stores its spectral reference. Afterward, verification compares the circulating face with that reference and uses key projection to measure retention of the release‑specific signal. Therefore, relation and key evidence jointly help publishers identify suspicious copies for review, potentially reducing the circulation of manipulated images. Experimental results across FF++, DFDC, and Celeb‑DF show that spectral agreement separates tested face swaps and generative manipulations from enrolled releases, while the keyed signal distinguishes published versions from their unreleased originals under the evaluated key‑preserving benign transformations. Doctor Trigger complements provenance metadata with release‑specific face verification and record‑linked evidence for further assessment.

PaperId: 958, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16297.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Lingbei Meng, Rui Huang, Zhirong Shen, Jinxin Liu, Lingxiao Jing, Haorui Chen, Yaosong Du, Haowei Lin
Title: SLDBench v2: Active Scaling Law Discovery
Abstract:
Scaling laws predict large‑model performance from small experiments, but finding a reliable law itself requires costly experiments. SLDBench tests whether language‑model agents can discover scaling laws when all experimental results are given upfront. We introduce SLDBench v2 with two extensions. First, we expand the corpus from 8 to 127 scenarios spanning language‑model pretraining, downstream performance, and vision‑language transfer, and select 30 challenging scenarios on which a reference power‑law fit reaches R^2 \le 0.8; they represent at least 1.09 × 10^23 FLOPs of source‑reported training compute. Second, we introduce active scaling law discovery: an agent chooses which experiments to run, pays each one's recorded cost (e.g., training FLOPs), and revises its law as outcomes arrive, and is scored on the same hidden extrapolation targets as in the passive setting. Across 8 frontier agent systems, median R^2 drops from 0.72‑0.75 (passive) to 0.24‑0.57 (active), and prediction error rises 1.5‑4.7 times, depending on the system. Agents favor cheap experiments, spending 8‑44% of the full‑pool cost on average; low‑cost acquisition can yield strong predictions, but cheap purchases also leave experimental conditions needed for extrapolation unobserved. Experimental planning thus remains a key open challenge for agents that assist model development in the prevailing AI‑for‑AI study. Project page: https://lingbei‑meng.github.io/SLDBench‑v2/.

PaperId: 959, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16268.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuhe Hu
Title: Error Correction in Trained TTT Layers
Abstract:
Test‑time‑training (TTT) layers update fast‑weight memory while processing an input sequence. A gradient‑based update, however, does not by itself establish how the memory revises an existing association. We study the structure and empirical role of prediction‑derived updates in released TTT implementations. For dot‑product objectives, we characterize the absence of a prediction‑error residual and establish conditions under which inner‑loop ascent and descent are equivalent after reparameterization. For the LayerNorm‑based squared‑error objective used by TTT‑Linear and TTT‑MLP, we derive the inner gradient and identify a prediction‑derived component that cancels at the released initialization in the zero‑epsilon limit. We then measure the full normalized prediction's contribution on three trained checkpoints. Removing this contribution while retaining the LayerNorm Jacobian gives a mean gradient norm ratio of 0.25 to 0.32 across the models. On 100,303 tokens from War and Peace, the same intervention with local per‑token norm matching raises perplexity by 2.8‑2.9% on TTT‑Linear‑760M and 1.3B, whereas freezing all fast‑weight updates raises it by factors of 4.2‑4.5. Separate synthetic tests illustrate the dependence of plain delta‑rule overwriting on step size. The results distinguish a prediction‑derived update from its behavioral value and show why implementation analysis and live interventions are both needed to assess test‑time memory.

PaperId: 960, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16177.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhifan Zeng, Wenbo Xiao, Arcot Sowmya, Changming Sun
Title: DIGS: Distribution-Informed Gaussian Splatting for Training-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation
Abstract:
Open‑vocabulary 3D Gaussian segmentation typically binds semantic features to the per‑Gaussian state via per‑scene gradient training (1‑4 h) or the more recent closed‑form distillation. Both commit each primitive to a single feature; therefore, boundary Gaussians spanning multiple 2D instances are forced into a hard decision that degrades retrieval accuracy and yields unstable mask boundaries at render time. We present DIGS, a training‑free framework with two stages, class‑agnostic mapping and multi‑modal encoding, that decouples instance discovery from linguistic naming. At the Gaussian level, our distribution‑informed representation maintains an explicit top‑M label distribution per primitive, updated by a tempered Dirichlet rule; preservation of multi‑peaked label distributions at boundary primitives allows a late‑argmax renderer to recover clean instance boundaries. A bidirectional state machine aggregates these distributions into a persistent class‑agnostic instance ontology. The instance‑level encoding stage then fuses the CLIP visual embedding of each instance's isolated 3D footprint with the CLIP‑text embedding of an LLM‑generated attribute description, disambiguating visually similar instances. On a single A100, DIGS completes mapping and instance encoding on LERF‑OVS in 1.0‑3.2 min per scene, depending on whether LLM fusion is enabled, and serves native 3D queries in 5.4 ms. It reaches 71.95% mean mIoU on LERF‑OVS, outperforming both the training‑free SFS and training‑based LaGa baselines. DIGS also achieves the highest mean mIoU on LERF‑Mask and 3D‑OVS and surpasses Gaga and ObjectGS on Replica under their respective evaluation protocols. Code is available at https://github.com/ZephyrZos/DIGS.

PaperId: 961, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16143.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yewon Kim, Paul Hongsuck Seo, Sang Chul Ahn
Title: All-St3R SLAM: Real-time RGB Dynamic SLAM with Pixel-wise Motion Masking
Abstract:
SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) is a core technology in autonomous systems that enables them to estimate their own position and build a map of unknown environments simultaneously. SLAM systems in dynamic environments are of great practical importance. However, existing dynamic SLAM approaches still have several limitations like over‑removal and high computational costs. To address these limitations, we propose a real‑time RGB Dynamic SLAM framework that precisely removes moving objects at the pixel level without relying on predefined labels or segmentation models. Our system combines pixel motion predicted by ego‑motion using DUSt3R with point tracking from All‑Tracker, removing only actually moving pixels by analyzing discrepancies between the two motion sources. Unlike object‑level masking methods, our approach eliminates only currently moving regions, allowing temporarily static parts to be utilized for tracking. Operating at approximately 10 FPS, the system achieves real‑time performance on standard 30 FPS video streams by subsampling every 3 frames. Relying solely on RGB inputs, this significantly improves upon state‑of‑the‑art dense dynamic SLAM approaches (0.5‑3 FPS), presenting a highly practical solution.

PaperId: 962, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16117.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chen Huang, Yiyang Zhang, Yuhao Wu, Yang Deng, Wenxuan Zhang
Title: Beyond Perfect Teammates: Multi-Agent Collaboration with Unreliable Colleagues
Abstract:
LLM‑based multi‑agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. Yet existing systems and evaluations largely rest on an implicit perfect‑colleague assumption: collaborators provide correct and complete information and respond promptly to requests. In realistic teamwork, however, collaborators may return information that does not answer the intended question, provide insufficient detail to support a decision, or fail to respond to a request. To separate task‑solving competence from the ability to recover an unreliable evidence‑gathering process, we introduce the Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (UnCoBench), which organizes behavioral failures through Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed settings. The main agent need to verify contextual correctness, diagnose information gap and track unresolved dependencies in order to obtain the correct evidence for solving the task. We also introduce a verifiable and scalable automated generation pipeline that pairs LLM‑based scenario generation with executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. Results across ten models show that similar reliable‑setting performance can result in different robustness to unreliable evidence. Trace analysis reveals frequent omissions of corrective follow‑up, and the recovery behavior involves inefficient waiting and redundant queries. These findings show that robust collaboration requires not only sound reasoning, but also targeted action to diagnose evidence failures, recover relevant information, and integrate it into decisions. Our data and source code are available at https://github.com/iNLP‑Lab/UnCoBench.

PaperId: 963, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16071.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Boxuan Zhang, Jianing Zhu, Xiaotian Han, Ruixiang Tang
Title: Dream2Discern: Learning from Hard Latent Variants for Runtime Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems
Abstract:
Reliable deployment of LLM‑based multi‑agent systems calls for runtime auditors that predict terminal outcomes from observed execution prefixes. These auditors typically learn from a limited corpus of trajectories with verified outcomes. Expanding this corpus requires costly execution and verification, yet broader failure coverage alone provides no explicit criterion for identifying prefixes that the current auditor finds difficult to classify. To this end, we propose Dream2Discern, a runtime auditor trained through implicit augmentation guided by its own prediction loss. During Dream, we select perturbations of the auditor's representation operators to increase prediction loss on recorded prefixes, yielding hard latent variants. During Discern, the auditor learns to predict execution outcomes from these variants using the original labels. The variants are regenerated as the auditor learns, turning a limited corpus into a renewable source of hard examples and requiring no additional trajectory collection or outcome verification. Extensive evaluations on AFTraj‑2K and StepShield show that Dream2Discern outperforms competitive failure auditors and achieves over 90% trajectory‑level weighted accuracy on both benchmarks while balancing prediction accuracy and timeliness. Project page: https://zbox1005.github.io/dream2discern‑project/

PaperId: 964, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.16047.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Quan Wang
Title: Hybrid Context Forests and Bilateral Viterbi Matching for 3D Rib Centerline Tracing in CT
Abstract:
Automatic extraction and anatomical numbering (R01‑R12, L01‑L12) of all 24 rib centerlines in thoracic CT is essential for unfolded rib visualization, fracture detection, and surgical navigation, but remains challenging due to adjacent‑bone confluence, calcified costal cartilage bridges, kyphotic pose variation, and partial visibility of terminal ribs. We present ribline, an open‑source three‑stage framework combining: (1) an automatically detected lung‑apex and vertebral‑midline coordinate frame with a kyphosis‑aware azimuthal angle for point ordering along each rib; (2) a hybrid voxel detector fusing an anatomically anchored Semantic Context Forest (SCF) with a lightweight 3D U‑Net; and (3) a global stage that decomposes the probability skeleton into candidate curves, assigns rib indices via a bilateral Viterbi dynamic program coupled across both hemithoraces, and refines curves via template recovery and normal‑plane centering (RibSnake). On the Siemens Corporate Research 2 mm thoracic CT benchmark (47 training and 12 evaluation scans), our pipeline achieves a labeled Chamfer distance of 2.05 mm, labeled clDice of 0.886 (3 mm) and 0.945 (4 mm), 97.2% labeling accuracy (278/286 ribs), and zero false‑positive curves on the evaluation split, and 3.64 mm (median 2.39 mm) with 91.8% labeling accuracy across all 59 annotated scans (1,402 ribs) in 5‑fold cross‑validation. Code: https://github.com/wq2012/ribline Pretrained Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/wq2012/ribline

PaperId: 965, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15897.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yirui Zhang, Yash Raj Shrestha
Title: Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines
Abstract:
Qwen3‑8B reviewing Llama‑3.1‑8B in math adds 33.2 points, yet Qwen3‑8B alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the result. Reviewing another model's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator. We show that this confuses verification, which adds accuracy beyond either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer supplies answers it could have given on its own. Measured against the stronger model alone, across 48 pairs of 12 open‑weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code and reasoning, review beats it in only 9 of 96 review directions, and does worse the larger the capability gap. The reason is anchoring: the reviewer mostly follows the generator, discarding its own correct answers. Review costs 2.6 to 2.8 times as much as the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper. Studies of verification should report the stronger model alone, not only the gain over the generator.

PaperId: 966, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15829.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mayank Gupta
Title: Guarded Block Transfers for Polytope Distance: Linear Convergence with Explicit Constants and Gap-Certified Screening for SVM Training
Abstract:
Hard‑margin SVM training is the distance problem between two convex hulls, which the Triangle Algorithm (TA) solves with a certified duality gap. We propose \emphguarded block transfers: k Mitchell‑‑Demyanov‑‑Malozemov (MDM) transfers per scan are aggregated into one exact line search, guarded by a comparison with the single best transfer at a cost independent of the number of points n, and replaced by an away step when the leading transfer is capacity‑clipped. On the Minkowski‑difference polytope, where the objective is 1‑strongly convex, we prove global linear convergence with explicit constants and no combinatorial swap‑step bounds; the per‑step contraction is k‑independent and only the drop‑count bound grows with k, so aggregation is provably safe while the saving in scans is measured, not proved. Since the TA certificate is the Frank‑‑Wolfe gap divided by the current distance, gap‑safe screening applies, and we bound the iteration after which it has removed every zero‑weight point off the optimal faces by O\!\left(\tfrackρ\log\tfrac1τ\right) up to logarithmic factors in the geometry, ρ the rate constant and τ the optimal‑face margin. On five LIBSVM benchmarks, with fairer baselines than our submission, the solver matches the baselines to four or five digits wherever both converge, ties LIBSVM on sparse‑support hard margins and beats our blended pairwise conditional gradients (BPCG). But our full‑cache sequential minimal optimisation (SMO) code ties or beats it on kernel L_2 margins, LIBLINEAR's dual solver is up to 4.5× faster on the separable L_2 margin, and our solver is one to three orders of magnitude slower than LIBLINEAR's Newton solver on dense‑support L_2 margins and than LIBSVM on a nearly touching kernel hull. Its edge is the certificate, not speed.

PaperId: 967, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15778.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haosen Wang
Title: Who Sets the Pace of Judge Hacking? Judge Capability versus the Policy-Judge Gap
Abstract:
Under GRPO against a frozen, reference‑free LLM judge, RL exploits the judge's false positives. Does the policy‑judge capability gap or the judge itself set how fast and how far? We train 0.5B and 1.5B Qwen2.5 policies on GSM8K against four judges at least as large, and the 1.5B policy also against one smaller judge. In a post‑hoc analysis, judge acceptance rose, but no cell of 12 gained more than 0.04 in seed‑mean held‑out greedy accuracy. A gold‑reward control with the same recipe raised the 1.5B policy's accuracy by +0.054 (for the 0.5B policy, gold reward gave no detectable gain either). The depth of judge hacking tracks the judge: the plateau correlates with judge AUC (Spearman ‑0.69 over 12 cells), and within a family the larger judge is fooled less deeply. For the pace, two pre‑specified pairs contradict the gap account: the cell with the larger gap was fooled 3.5x sooner at the pre‑specified threshold. With 12 cells, however, we cannot formally separate judge AUC from the gap for either endpoint. A blind test of step‑0 predictors on three held‑out judges was inconclusive. At 7‑8B, judges from three families plateaued between 0.37 and 0.85.

PaperId: 968, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15725.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Alan Tang, Lifeng Wang, Gang Wu, Tao Zhang, Yantao Jia, Xiaofeng Zhu
Title: SkillMarker: A KGW-Based Watermarking Method for Agent Skill Ownership Verification
Abstract:
Agent skills encode operational procedures and domain expertise as reusable knowledge assets, yet their distribution in plaintext exposes them to unauthorized copying and leakage. However, practical mechanisms for skill ownership verification and leakage tracing remain underdeveloped. Watermark embedding before distribution offers a potential solution, but structured, compact skill instructions impose stringent requirements for factual and procedural accuracy. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillMarker, a KGW‑based watermarking method that jointly targets functionality preservation and strong watermark embedding. SkillMarker unifies quality‑constrained rewriting with signal‑oriented candidate search. The former separates essential knowledge from flexible expression to preserve instruction fidelity; the latter explores alternative expressions to obtain a stronger watermark signal under preservation constraints. We release an open‑source toolkit that integrates watermark embedding, quality auditing, and detection to support the protection of agent skills. SkillMarker targets ownership verification and leakage tracing in distributed skill ecosystems, where content may be copied in whole or in part, or incorporated into other skills. Across four datasets, SkillMarker negligibly affects downstream task performance on average. In our copy‑paste tests, window‑based detection consistently identifies copied passages containing as few as 1,536 consecutive tokens. Even after merging with one or three background skills, SkillMarker retains watermark detection rates of 72.2‑‑77.8%.

PaperId: 969, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15665.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yunjia Zhang, Junan Zhang, Jing Yang, Xueyao Zhang, Fan Fan, Zhizheng Wu
Title: AnyEdit: A Unified Framework for Speech and Singing Voice Editing with Real-World Environmental Consistency
Abstract:
We present AnyEdit, a unified, separation‑free framework for speech and singing voice editing that preserves real‑world acoustic environments, including noise, reverberation, and background music. Recent unified generative models already achieve strong speech and singing generation in clean conditions, but real‑world vocal editing remains challenging because the model must revise content while simultaneously preserving speaker identity, prosody, and the surrounding acoustic scene. Directly modeling noisy audio end‑to‑end entangles semantic editing with environmental acoustics, weakening the core vocal generation capability. We therefore adopt a two‑stage design that preserves clean‑domain editing ability while deferring acoustic rendering to a separate stage: an instruction‑guided autoregressive editor first predicts clean prosody and content‑style tokens, supported by a teacher‑student noise‑robust prosody tokenizer that distills clean prosodic tokens from degraded recordings; a flow‑matching acoustic model then performs in‑context rendering conditioned on the source acoustic context, so the edited segment inherits surrounding noise, reverberation, and background sound while maintaining consistent speaker timbre. To stabilize unedited regions, we introduce unmodified‑area‑aware supervision; after pre‑training, we further apply direct preference optimization on mined real‑to‑real singing pairs. We also release AnyEditBench, a benchmark covering both speech and singing voice editing under clean, simulated, and in‑the‑wild acoustic conditions. Experiments on Chinese and English speech and singing datasets showed that AnyEdit consistently outperforms strong baselines in content accuracy, subjective quality, and background consistency under noisy and reverberant conditions. Demo: https://any‑edit.github.io/. AnyEditBench: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Ririiiii/anyeditbench.

PaperId: 970, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15501.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziyi Chen, Yan Zhang, Jianhui Wei, Jianing Yin, Daoan Zhang
Title: Large Decision Models: Repurposing Large Language Models as Single-Pass Decision Makers
Abstract:
Large language models make decisions through parallel prefill and sequential decoding. Although effective, this approach incurs decoding costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities. Existing task‑specific classifiers require per‑task training and offer limited generalization to unseen decision schemas. We propose Large Decision Models (LDMs), repurposing language models to return explicit probabilities over labels specified at run time using one prefill forward pass. We first adapt models to this interface through Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS), covering varied domains, rules and labels. To further narrow the performance gap to a reasoning model, Self‑Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD) adds tasks generated by a frozen teacher, filters them for answer consistency, and trains on label distributions obtained from repeated teacher reasoning. We evaluate on DecisionVista, pairing new‑schema tests with held‑out human‑labelled sources. Across three base models, the recipe improves accuracy over a step‑matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving a 182‑fold speedup in latency over reasoning rollout on Gemma‑4‑31B. Reasoning remains stronger on the new‑schema test, motivating a confidence router for uncertain decisions. On development sets, routing recovers a median 92% of reasoning's accuracy advantage while generating 27‑58% of its tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/LDM.

PaperId: 971, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15474.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kyungsu Kim, Yejin Kim, Kyogu Lee
Title: Sori: Streamable and Controllable Model for Non-musical Audio to Symbolic Music Transformation
Abstract:
We introduce Non‑musical Audio to Symbolic Music Transformation (NASMT), a novel task that converts non‑musical audio into symbolic music representations. Unlike automatic music transcription, which assumes musical input and a unique correct score, NASMT is inherently one‑to‑many and requires evaluation along two axes: input correspondence and musicality. We present Sori, an encoder‑‑decoder Transformer that addresses this task through domain adversarial training (DAT), which bridges the gap between musical and non‑musical audio in the encoder's feature space, and classifier‑free guidance (CFG) with a continuous parameter~γ that controls the trade‑off between correspondence and musicality at inference time. Across objective metrics and a listening study, Sori provides effective continuous control via γ and compares favorably with instrument‑agnostic transcription models. Sori supports real‑time streaming on a consumer CPU. Audio examples are available at https://soridemo0320.github.io/sori‑demo/.

PaperId: 972, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15467.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziqi Wen, Shravan Murlidaran, Jonathan Skaza, William Wang, Miguel P. Eckstein
Title: Semantic Saliency from Multi-Modal Large Language Model Scene Understanding Maps
Abstract:
