Image‑computable low‑level image saliency has shaped perceptual psychology and computer science, but is limited by its inability to capture human high‑level cognitive factors that influence attention and eye movements. Here, we propose a new fully automated method to compute semantic saliency by quantifying each object's contribution to scene comprehension without fitting any parameters to human data: the Automated Scene Understanding Map (AUTO‑SUM). AUTO‑SUM automatically segments and removes individual objects from a scene, uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to describe the original and modified scenes, and measures the semantic similarity between these descriptions using text embeddings. We show that AUTO‑SUM can predict which object is most important in a human‑measured scene understanding map (H‑SUM) estimated using human scene descriptions. We also show that AUTO‑SUM can predict the object most fixated by human observers during free viewing and scene description tasks better than a low‑level saliency model (GBVS, Itti‑Koch), a saliency model trained based on human meaning ratings (Meaning Map), and comparable to DeepGaze, which is trained on human fixation data. We contend that AUTO‑SUM can be used as a semantic saliency model that complements lower‑level saliency models. Code are available at https://github.com/starsky77/AUTO‑SUM‑Source‑Code .

PaperId: 973, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15459.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Jinhao Zhou, Xiaoyu Zhang, Jiongchi Yu, Fahao Chen, Jun Wu
Title: When Messages Go Wrong: Understanding Communication Faults in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
Abstract:
LLM‑based multi‑agent systems (LLM‑MAS) use specialized agents that exchange messages to accomplish complex tasks. Their reliance on networked protocols, remote tools, and model endpoints exposes communication to message loss, delay, and context expiration. Because agents often exchange open‑ended natural language, anomalies can alter task‑relevant information while leaving messages processable, allowing semantic errors to propagate through subsequent interactions. Systematic studies of faults in inter‑agent communication remain limited. This paper presents a large‑scale empirical study of how communication faults manifest, propagate, and affect task outcomes in LLM‑MAS. We construct a cross‑layer taxonomy linking lower‑stack disturbances to application‑visible faults and develop a fault‑injection and tracing pipeline. Our evaluation covers more than 29,000 executions across 100 tasks, five domains, three workflow topologies, and three model configurations. We find that 20.7% of failures with complete detection records occur without an immediate failure signal, reaching 76.2% for partial‑content faults. Flat maintains 53.0% task success under communication faults, compared with 3.3% and 3.2% for Sequential and Hierarchical, respectively. This advantage primarily arises when an alternative information path preserves the evidence required by downstream agents. We also evaluate execution‑side and evidence protection mechanisms and find that they recover different failure cases. Evidence recovery depends on whether trustworthy information remains accessible through an unaffected path. These observations provide empirical insights into communication‑fault propagation, workflow resilience, and protection design for LLM‑MAS.

PaperId: 974, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15452.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yeheng Wang, Liudan Shi, Yi Zheng, Jingke Li, Shiyuan Liu, Xin Tao, Yuanxing Zhang, Guoyu Sun
Title: EmoTrace-Bench: Diagnosing Emotional Expression in Text-to-Video Generation through Controlled Cues and Intensity
Abstract:
Text‑to‑video (T2V) models are increasingly used to generate videos with targeted emotional expressions, yet existing evaluation methods mainly rely on holistic video‑text alignment and provide limited insight into whether failures arise from target‑emotion expression, intensity control, or specific affective cues. We introduce EmoTrace‑Bench, a fine‑grained diagnostic benchmark that controls emotion intensity and selected affective cues in prompts and evaluates generated videos at multiple levels. EmoTrace‑Bench contains 448 controlled prompts covering eight emotions, two intensity levels, and diverse cue conditions. Using 12 T2V models, we generate 5,376 videos and evaluate target‑emotion presence, perceived intensity, and ten audiovisual dimensions of emotional expression with an automated evaluator calibrated and validated against human annotations on a subset of the data. Results reveal substantial differences across models and prompt designs. Prompts that explicitly describe a character's emotional reaction are followed more reliably than prompts that describe only events or scenes, whereas adding more affective cues or using more explicit cinematic audiovisual language does not consistently improve emotional generation. These results illustrate how aggregate alignment scores may overlook localized differences in target‑emotion expression, intensity control, and cue realization. EmoTrace‑Bench provides a traceable and interpretable framework for diagnosing emotional video generation without modifying existing generation pipelines, and we release the prompts and the automated evaluation rules.

PaperId: 975, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15428.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chang-Hoon Jeong, Kisung Shin, Hanwool Sul, Byoung-Tak Zhang
Title: Pessimistic Latent Task-aware Optimization for Robust Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
Context‑based offline meta‑reinforcement learning (COMRL) has advanced almost entirely through better task representations, which separate task identity from artifacts of the behavior policy so that the latent reflects the task alone. The implicit expectation has been that a clean representation will transfer to out‑of‑support (parameter‑extrapolation) tasks. On such a task, however, the encoder produces a latent outside the training support, where the policy has never been trained. We address this gap with Pessimistic Latent Task‑aware Optimization (PLATO), which exposes the policy to off‑support latents during training. PLATO assumes a mild manifold hypothesis: task latents lie on a low‑dimensional manifold, and out‑of‑support tasks lie farther from the training centroid. It exploits this geometry by perturbing inferred latents outward from the centroid to synthesize counterfactual tasks. A learned decoder ensemble then rolls out short trajectories at each perturbed latent, and the policy is updated on the imagined transitions under a pessimism weight that down‑weights steps on which the ensemble disagrees. We prove that the perturbation leaves the training support by a controllable margin and that the out‑of‑support generalization gap is bounded by the same perturbation reach, and we give explicit conditions, verified empirically, under which the epistemic disagreement at the perturbed latent stays bounded away from zero. On eight MuJoCo continuous‑control benchmarks, PLATO consistently improves out‑of‑support returns over strong COMRL baselines while remaining competitive on in‑distribution tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/deephoony/plato.

PaperId: 976, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15425.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xupeng Zhang, Yantai Yang, Chang Guo, Zhaokai Yin, Zhipeng Zhang
Title: Exploring the Limits of Combinatorial Generalization in Embodied Manipulation
Abstract:
In embodied manipulation, Vision Language Action (VLA) models can execute atomic skills, but long‑horizon manipulation requires recombining these skills without demonstrations for every skill combination. The full instruction route treats skill chaining as long‑horizon imitation. In a controlled study, full instruction training on limited skill combination sequences reaches 40.0% ordered success on covered combinations but only 7.7% on recombination, suggesting memorization of sequence templates rather than robust skill recombination. We introduce Hierarchical Subtask Execution (HSE), a diagnostic framework that exposes skill recombination through a shared modular interface over the planner, trigger, and policy, decomposing long‑horizon failures into separable modes. We introduce RoboCombine, a benchmark for skill recombination without combined skill training trajectories, with metrics for ordered success and transition conversion across subtask boundaries. RoboCombine reveals that atomic competence alone does not ensure ordered execution. Failures concentrate at transitions where downstream subtasks launch from handoff states from preceding subtasks rather than canonical atomic starts. We identify this mismatch as the start state gap. To address it, we introduce Pose Robust Task Initialization (PRTI), a lightweight atomic task post‑training strategy that broadens start state coverage beyond canonical starts. Under oracle timed HSE on RoboCombine, PRTI reaches 18.16% ordered success, compared with 4.21% under random perturbation and 9.47% under a robot‑reset oracle, without combined skill training trajectories. These results show that combinatorial generalization requires handoff robust atomic skills that convert first stage progress into reliable downstream execution, not merely decomposition into known subtasks. Code: https://github.com/AutoLab‑SAI‑SJTU/RoboCombine.

PaperId: 977, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15417.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hongliang Cao, Xiuyu Li, Siqi Wang, Ziming Wang, Jingmin Zhu, Hailong Yang
Title: SpecFit: Not All Draft Tokens Cost the Same in Offloaded MoE Inference
Abstract:
Mixture‑of‑experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per token, but when their expert weights are offloaded to host memory, host‑to‑device (H2D) expert transfers enter the critical path of decoding. Speculative decoding verifies several draft tokens in one forward pass, yet in an MoE model each verified token activates its own experts, so a larger draft tree transfers more experts. Because of this H2D cost, speculative decoding commits several tokens per verification cycle yet is sometimes even slower than autoregressive decoding. Based on this observation, we propose SpecFit, which chooses the verified draft subtree to maximize predicted throughput rather than acceptance length. SpecFit estimates the expected number of committed tokens from draft path probabilities and predicts cycle time from the node count and the per‑layer union of the experts the subtree activates; this union is a monotone submodular coverage function, so each node pays only for the experts it adds. An exact search over ancestor‑closed subtrees returns the subtree with the highest predicted throughput; run after each draft level, the same search also decides when to stop drafting, and the unmodified target verifies the result. On CNN/DailyMail summarization and a GSM8K subset with Qwen3‑30B‑A3B, SpecFit decodes 21.6% and 7.0% faster than EAGLE‑3 with the same expert cache and 1.97x and 1.72x as fast as vanilla EAGLE‑3. Code is available at https://github.com/Chlience/SpecFit.

PaperId: 978, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15414.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hebaixu Wang, Jing Zhang, Haonan Guo, Di Wang, Jiayi Ma, Bo Du
Title: OmniRSI: Taming Latent Diffusion for Unified Multimodal Remote Sensing Image Generation
Abstract:
Multimodal remote sensing image generation emerges as a promising paradigm for recovering complete and complementary observations from heterogeneous and partially observed remote sensing data. However, existing methods predominantly depend on sensor‑specific fine‑tuning of natural image generation models, limiting unified multimodal generation capacity due to the absence of shared representations and robust conditioning mechanisms. To address these challenges, we propose OmniRSI, a unified multimodal remote sensing image generation model. Specifically, we develop a remote sensing‑specific variational autoencoder that captures multimodal priors and promotes a locally smooth latent space for unified representation and robust reconstruction across diverse observed data. Building upon that, we fully adapt Stable Diffusion 3.5 with a ControlNet branch to support unified multimodal generation and translation conditioned on textual and visual cues. Besides, we devise a training‑free cyclic latent alignment mechanism that iteratively enriches incomplete visual conditions with generated multimodal information, progressively improving guidance reliability while preserving observed measurements. We also construct RSI‑MM, a large‑scale dataset comprising 11.5M multi‑resolution images with text annotations and partially paired data for training and evaluation. Extensive experiments verify that OmniRSI achieves superior performance in multimodal reconstruction, generation and translation.

PaperId: 979, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15403.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hao Li, Wenping Yin, Fabian Deuser, Jia Jia, Ziqi Liu, Levente Juhász, Fan Zhang, Filip Biljecki
Title: A Decade of PhotoMappers: A Longitudinal Study of Crowdsourced Disaster Photos Geolocalization with Vision-Language Models and Geospatial Reasoning
Abstract:
Crowdsourced disaster imagery provides timely, ground‑level observations when conventional disaster mapping is delayed or incomplete, yet its geographic value depends on where observations are produced, how they are interpreted, and whether they can be reliably located as actionable Geospatial Intelligence (GEOINT). Using more than a decade of PhotoMappers, a crowdsourced disaster‑mapping initiative, this study examines the changing geography of disaster information and asks how emerging GeoAI models compare with human geographic interpretation. We combine longitudinal spatial analysis with cross‑view geolocalization using street view imagery (SVI) and remote sensing imagery (RSI), and evaluate vision‑language models (VLMs) reasoning through 30 indicators spanning geographic cues and reasoning evidence. The results reveal a geographically and temporally uneven archive shaped by changing disaster types, Community Lifelines, and operational priorities. Integrating VGI, SVI, and RSI with Sinkhorn re‑ranking achieves 40.90% R@1, 61.10% R@5, and 69.45% R@10, while yearly R@1 varies markedly from 25.00% to 65.07%. Geographic reasoning is similarly uneven: Qwen3.6‑27B achieves an overall agreement of 67% compared with 51% for InternVL3‑8B, with both models showing greater difficulty with localized and place‑specific evidence than broad spatial configurations. We argue that the value of GeoAI lies less in replacing volunteered geographic interpretation than in complementing it, scaling candidate retrieval while retaining human judgment for ambiguous and consequential cases. This provides a pathway toward more human‑centered and responsible GeoAI for disaster mapping. All data and code are openly available at https://github.com/bobleegogogo/PhotoMappers‑VLM.

PaperId: 980, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15401.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xin Liu, Yutong Jiang, Jian Su, Ziheng Wang, Chuang Wang, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao
Title: Harnessing VLM in Embodied RL: From Reward Regressor to Success Detector via Exploration-Augmented Key-Observation Gating
Abstract:
VLMs provide promising solutions to embodied reward design. Most current methods that train VLMs as reward regressors not only require extensive annotations but are also primarily designed for finetuning pretrained policies, and perform less well in the more challenging from‑scratch RL setting. This issue stems from a fundamental mismatch: regressing precise rewards is misaligned with what VLMs naturally excel at. We posit that it is more aligned with VLMs' inherent multi‑modal VQA capabilities for the models to function as success detectors, and propose VLM success reward via Exploration‑Augmented Key‑Observation Gating (VLMeg) to well harness VLM for embodied reward design. As the core of VLMeg, the proposed exploration‑augmented key‑observation gating first determines whether the current RL episode is judgment‑worthy based on its similarity to a generated success trajectory. Then, the key observation with the lowest confusion from the judgment‑worthy episode will be selected for VLM evaluation as episodic reward. This gating mechanism not only avoids redundant calls but also enables higher detection accuracy of VLM. Considering the sparsity of judgment‑worthy episodes, the advanced exploration incentives based on the generated trajectory are introduced, enabling more efficient exploration toward judgment‑worthy trajectories for more VLM reward triggers and thus gaining higher RL efficiency. Extensive experiments in MetaWorld demonstrate VLMeg achieves state‑of‑the‑art from‑scratch RL, outperforming advanced VLM‑based baselines on 12 challenging reward‑free tasks. Furthermore, VLMeg also enables effective RL without any ground‑truth reward in 3 challenging real‑world experiments. Code will be open after acceptance at https://github.com/Raina915/VLMeg.

PaperId: 981, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15391.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yitian Wang, Minjie Cheng, Yaning Cui, Maohua Yang, Dongdong Wang, Hongteng Xu
Title: DC-Flow: Target-Conditioned Cyclic Peptide Design via Delayed-Coupling Flow Matching
Abstract:
Target‑conditioned cyclic peptide design requires coordinating interfacial side chains with macrocyclic closure. Existing end‑to‑end generators concurrently update geometric and chemical variables from noise, assigning residues to disordered coordinates. Meanwhile, predictor‑assisted workflows often get stuck in local traps because they lack feedback in the propose‑and‑filter stage and ignore 3D structural proposals during sequence search. To overcome the drawbacks of these two paradigms, we propose DC‑FLOW, a staged generative framework built around Delayed‑Coupling Flow Matching. In principle, DC‑FLOW postpones sequence and side‑chain activation until a target‑conditioned backbone takes shape, resolving structural ambiguity before chemical assignment. Then, it feeds delayed activations back into the backbone, achieving co‑evolution of backbone geometry and emerging residue identities by coupling their flows. This mechanism enables more reliable macrocyclic closure and favorable interface packing. For predictor‑assisted workflows, DC‑FLOW supplies 3D proposals with in‑trajectory guidance, enabling cascaded test‑time scaling to prune redundant backbones and terminate unpromising refinement early. Extensive experiments show that DC‑FLOW improves cyclization fidelity, diversity, and interface energetics, substantially increasing the yield of confident cyclic peptide binders under a fixed final‑candidate budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/mianqiu00/DCFlow.

PaperId: 982, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15389.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Weixin Xu, Yifan Liu, Yi Wang, Mingfei Rong, Zhenyu Yang, Zhisheng Zhong, Shengsheng Qian, Changsheng Xu
Title: VideoEvoHarness: Self Evolving Agent Harness from Unlabeled Videos for Video Understanding
Abstract:
Video understanding agents rely on a harness to acquire evidence, use tools, and reason, but improving it requires substantial effort. Recent self evolution methods seek to optimize harnesses through execution feedback to reduce human intervention. However, existing methods often rely on annotated video questions and answers or focus on updating model parameters, leaving harness evolution from unlabeled videos underexplored. VideoEvoHarness jointly evolves a Questioner and a Solver harness from unlabeled videos with frozen model parameters. The Questioner constructs questions and computes reference answers directly from video memory records. Question quality assessments and Solver execution trajectories guide question generation policy revisions. The Solver supports evolving skills, strategies, hyperparameters, and tools using execution feedback. Executable strategies define workflows in code, reducing repeated interpretation of natural language instructions. Each round, candidate harnesses are compared on identical validation questions, with validated improvements retained for later use. Experiments on benchmarks and a dedicated benchmark question set, using videos disjoint from evolution videos, show higher overall accuracy than initially and transfer gains across backbones. Overall accuracy on this set also improves progressively across rounds. This supports our foundational framework for harness evolution from unlabeled videos, opening a promising direction for self evolving video agents. Code is available at https://github.com/Wei‑Xin‑Xu/VideoEvoHarness.

PaperId: 983, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15357.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wenjue Chen, Wenyue Chen, Heliang Zheng, Rongfei Jia, Yuan Liu, Meng Li
Title: UniForge3D: Joint 3D Reconstruction and Generation in a Shared Anchor-Guided Space
Abstract:
Generating complete 3D assets from sparse, unposed images requires preserving observed geometry while completing unseen regions. Joint reconstruction and generation offers a way to address both goals: reconstruction recovers the geometry observed in the input images, while generation contributes learned shape priors. However, combining camera‑relative reconstruction with canonical‑space generation introduces a coordinate mismatch that makes direct geometric interaction more difficult. Moreover, conditioning each 3D location on all views without accounting for their relevance may mix useful geometric evidence with unrelated image content, hindering local detail recovery. We present UniForge3D, which jointly models reconstruction and generation in a shared anchor‑guided space, resolving their coordinate mismatch. This space follows the anchor view's azimuth while keeping the object upright. The two branches exchange features bidirectionally to predict per‑view point maps and a complete sparse voxel structure. We further condition point‑map prediction on the generated structure to establish pixel‑to‑voxel correspondences and select the most informative input view for each voxel. Features from the selected views then guide detailed shape generation, helping preserve observed geometric details. Our method achieves state‑of‑the‑art appearance and geometry results on Toys4K and GSO, generating complete 3D assets with improved fidelity. Project webpage: https://xishuxishu.github.io/uniforge3d‑project/

PaperId: 984, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15343.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Song Xia, Meiwen Ding, Chenqi Kong, Wenhan Yang, Xudong Jiang
Title: Across Viewpoints and Time: Trajectory-Generalizable Physical Attacks on World Models and Video Understanding Models
Abstract:
World models and video understanding models are increasingly deployed in dynamic visual environments, yet their robustness to physical adversarial threats remains largely underexplored. We study whether a single physical adversarial texture can mislead the victim model across different real‑world scenarios where observing viewpoints vary along uncontrolled object‑‑camera trajectories. We identify that heterogeneous video semantics and trajectories induce poorly aligned gradients for optimizing the adversarial texture. To address that, we propose the Trajectory‑aware adversarial Alignment and Refinement Attack (TARA), which incorporates trajectory‑aware optimization to capture the evolving geometric variations of a printed texture under real‑world scenarios. To improve cross‑instance optimization compatibility, TARA incorporates trajectory‑aware contrastive alignment to encourage attacked representations from diverse video‑‑trajectory instances to approach a shared adversarial region and then performs trajectory‑aware task refinement to translate the aligned representation into task‑level prediction errors. For reproducible evaluation, we develop a geometry‑grounded tracking pipeline that provides physically plausible adversarial regions with temporally consistent trajectories on EPIC‑KITCHENS‑100 and Something‑Something V2. We further collect real‑world print‑and‑recapture videos to validate attack effectiveness under physical deployment conditions. Together, the annotated benchmarks and real‑world captured data form a reproducible testbed for future evaluation. Notably, our results reveal that a single printable adversarial texture can persistently disrupt world models and video understanding models under physical conditions, highlighting the fundamental security challenge.

PaperId: 985, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15337.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ahaskar Kashyap, Jiawen Zong, Boyu Ma, Chuhao Zhou, Jingliang Li, Stefano V. Albrecht, Jianfei Yang
Title: CoLA: Multi-VLA Coordination via Learned Adapters
Abstract:
Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) models are typically deployed as isolated single‑agent policies. When several such agents share a workspace, they can coordinate implicitly, by observing one another, or explicitly, by exchanging messages, but it remains unclear when explicit communication becomes necessary. We introduce CoLA (Coordination via Learned Adapters), which keeps each agent's VLA backbone frozen and trains a lightweight message channel and a per‑arm diffusion action head on top, with fully decentralised execution. Across three tasks that differ in how much each agent can observe, the channel matters only when information is private. On an occluded tray handover, where the box's colour marker is visible to one agent only, CoLA reaches 76.0% success versus 1.3% with messages zeroed throughout training. On two‑arm and three‑arm handover tasks, removing messages has no measurable effect with a shared overhead camera (90.6% vs. 88.3% at two arms; 63.5% vs. 60.0% at three), but lowers success on the two‑arm task's wrist‑only variant (74.8% vs. 64.3%). This architecture generalises across different VLA backbones as well. With a frozen π_0.5 backbone on the same occluded tray task, CoLA matches the overall success rate of a LoRA‑fine‑tuned baseline (37.3% vs. 34.7%) using a fraction of the trainable parameters. When CoLA places the box, it selects the correct tray 71.8% of the time, whereas the independently fine‑tuned baseline, whose placing arm never sees the marker, selects it at chance level (34.7% against 33.3%).

PaperId: 986, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15297.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xinmeng Liu, Xianglong Yan, Kaicheng Yang, Weisheng Dong, Yulun Zhang
Title: HGA-Quant: Heterogeneity-Aware Quantization for AutoRegressive Visual Generation Models
Abstract:
Recently, AutoRegressive Visual Generation (ARVG) models have emerged as a competitive paradigm for high‑quality image synthesis. However, their substantial computational and memory demands make them difficult to deploy on resource‑constrained edge devices. Post‑Training Quantization (PTQ) provides a promising solution to reduce the computational and memory costs of ARVG models, yet existing methods often suffer from substantial image quality degradation under low‑bit quantization. In this paper, we propose a training‑free PTQ framework for ARVG, consisting of Tail‑Aware Bounded‑init Grid Refinement (T‑BGR) and Coarse‑to‑Fine Activation Precision Scheduling (CAPS). T‑BGR introduces a tail‑aware reconstruction objective for weight quantizer calibration, assigning greater importance to distribution‑tail coefficients and preserving fine‑grained information without introducing additional parameters or high‑precision branches. CAPS performs coarse‑to‑fine activation precision scheduling by jointly considering the importance and computational cost of different generation stages, enabling efficient mixed‑precision allocation under a given bit budget. Extensive experiments on multiple ARVG backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently improves robustness under aggressive low‑bit quantization. Notably, on Infinity, our framework achieves near full‑precision image generation quality at an effective W4A5.6 activation precision, while existing methods at W4A6 still exhibit noticeable quality degradation or inconsistent performance. Code is available at https://github.com/lxm‑lc/HGA‑Quant.

PaperId: 987, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15280.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rui Wang, Haoyu Zhang, Ran Cheng
Title: GeoBridge: Evolving Transferable Decoder Topologies for Geometric Vision
Abstract:
Depth estimation and Gaussian reconstruction share a need for multi‑scale feature processing, yet use different prediction interfaces and training objectives. Whether a decoder's internal computation can be optimized once and reused across these systems remains a structural design question. Search over primitive configurations alone leaves the organization of transformations fixed. To address this gap, we propose GeoBridge, an evolutionary framework for transferable decoder topologies. First, GeoBridge makes stage‑internal topology searchable through residual, sequential, and parallel composition of configurable primitives. Shape‑preserving composition retains the stage interfaces of a fixed multi‑scale scaffold. Second, a functional‑tree encoding supports stage‑aware crossover and hierarchical mutation, while a gradient sensitivity‑alignment proxy evaluates candidates without training. Multi‑objective evolution balances this proxy with computation and parameter cost. Third, selected topologies are instantiated and trained in target systems with task‑specific prediction interfaces. A single source search takes approximately 12 GPU hours. GeoBridgeNet‑A3 achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted decoder baselines under a common encoder and training protocol on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI. The same topology reaches 27.11 dB PSNR in Gaussian novel‑view synthesis on RealEstate10K, and its refined representations support open‑vocabulary segmentation on LERF. These results support decoder topology as a reusable design object across the evaluated geometric vision systems. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/EMI‑Group/GeoBridge‑NAS.

PaperId: 988, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15246.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kyle Montgomery, Wang Zhang, Chenguang Wang
Title: ObsSpec: Accelerating Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Observation Speculation
Abstract:
Tool‑using agents alternate between model generation and tool execution, waiting for each tool call to complete before starting the next generation. This sequential execution is costly during agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which requires large batches of multi‑turn rollouts. We introduce ObsSpec, an observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL that uses a small world model to predict tool outputs while the environment executes, allowing the policy to begin its next generation early. ObsSpec retains speculative work only when the predicted and actual observations match exactly, making rollout collection lossless, while co‑training keeps the world model up to date as the policy learns. On terminal‑use tasks, predictions from a 0.6B world model exactly match actual observations in 66.4% of attempts and arrive roughly 16 times faster. Using these predictions, ObsSpec reduces agent latency by 9.3% and 14.2% for 8B and 32B policies. Across controlled experiments, we characterize the regimes in which ObsSpec reduces agent latency under shared policy resources. Finally, because ObsSpec overlaps policy generation with tool execution, it is architecturally compatible with existing techniques for accelerating RL. Code is available at https://github.com/kylemontgomery1/verl‑recipe/tree/obsspec/obsspec.

PaperId: 989, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15243.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Darius Pétermann, Wootaek Lim, Seungkwon Beack, Minje Kim
Title: HE-NAC: High-Efficiency Neural Audio Coding via Hierarchical and Residual Multi-Band Quantization
Abstract:
High‑fidelity audio coding requires faithful reconstruction of perceptually important high‑frequency components, which are often lost due to the aggressive temporal decimation and quantization of neural codecs. State‑of‑the‑art neural audio coding methods rely on adversarial learning to hallucinate these missing components, yielding perceptually plausible but imprecise reconstructions; a limitation for high‑fidelity music applications. As a remedy, we propose high‑efficiency neural audio coding (HE‑NAC), which provides a multi‑band extension of the popular residual vector quantization (RVQ) scheme. HE‑NAC introduces an effective training mechanism that harmonizes a bitrate‑free blind upsampling process, residual learning to compensate it with minimal bitrate, and a multi‑head decoder architecture for band‑specific reconstruction. As a result, HE‑NAC achieves a balanced trade‑off, reliably reconstructing the core‑band (\leq 3 kHz) component while preserving overall sound fidelity. Subjective listening tests and objective evaluations demonstrate that HE‑NAC outperforms both the DAC baseline and MPEG HE‑AAC at equal or lower bitrates.

PaperId: 990, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15215.pdf   GitHub
Authors:José Luis Blanco-Claraco
Title: nanoflann: A Header-Only KD-Tree Library for Exact Nearest-Neighbor Search on Compile-Time Product Manifolds
Abstract:
Nearest‑neighbor (NN) search underlies countless robotics algorithms, but many state spaces are not Euclidean: orientations live on SO(2) or SO(3) and poses on SE(2) or SE(3), and a Euclidean KD‑tree on their raw coordinates returns wrong neighbors. We present a header‑only, dependency‑free C++ KD‑tree library for exact NN search on user‑defined product manifolds declared at compile time: the space is composed from base manifolds (\mathbbR^n, SO(2), SO(3), S^n; products SE(2), SE(3), tori) with a single type alias, and the library synthesizes a metric whose pruning is provably admissible, wrap‑aware for circular coordinates and double‑cover‑aware for unit quaternions. Experiments confirm exactness (recall 1.0 vs an exhaustive scan under the same product metric), where the Euclidean‑on‑raw shortcut collapses to recall \approx 0.5^m for m rotation blocks, with up to three orders of magnitude speedup over brute force. We further contribute an incremental, self‑balancing single‑tree index for points under heavy churn (e.g. sliding‑window LiDAR maps) or SE(3) trajectories: bounded memory and faster updates than prior work, with an optional asynchronous tail‑latency‑bounding mode. The implementation is open source: https://github.com/jlblancoc/nanoflann

PaperId: 991, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15208.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:M. Yigit Turali, Shreyas Rajesh, M. Efe Lorasdagi, Chenda Duan, Kartik Sharma, Vwani Roychowdhury
Title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
Abstract:
Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI‑DR, a multi‑agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI‑DR on BrowseComp‑Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state‑of‑the‑art deep‑research harnesses, all using a shared language‑model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI‑DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp‑Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next‑best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next‑best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI‑DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim‑support audits show stronger evidence‑backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI‑DR's advantage.

PaperId: 992, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15207.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Lass Najmuldeen, Seyedhamidreza Mousavi
Title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
Abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth‑based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth‑based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony‑jailbreaking

PaperId: 993, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15186.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xingjian Zhang
Title: SAFE-KV: Causal Suffix Repair for Behavior-Preserving Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in RAG
Abstract:
Retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) reuses the same documents across many requests, making non‑prefix KV‑cache reuse attractive. Yet a cached document state is not reusable text: it is a context‑conditioned causal state whose keys and values depend on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. We formulate non‑prefix KV reuse as a behavior‑preservation problem with full prefill on the exact prompt as the reference, and introduce SAFE‑KV, which repairs a composed cache by re‑encoding the causal suffix from a selected start document. On Qwen2.5‑7B‑Instruct, prefix‑conditioned composition preserves only 47.2% of HotpotQA‑500 and 37.8% of 2Wiki‑500 full‑prefill answers; SAFE‑KV with risk‑guided K2 selection restores 99.8%/98.4% (donor‑copy protocol) and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding. Document‑only and fixed‑window repairs recover far less, because the document states after the repaired region keep histories that omit it. Reuse without repair is exact up to four documents and degrades at sixteen, where suffix repair recovers 98‑100%. Faithful repair re‑encodes most of the context, so in a single‑request L40S study SAFE‑KV's operating rule serves every workload by full prefill. SAFE‑KV thus establishes the causal‑state contract for non‑prefix reuse and a validated repair mechanism that meets it.

PaperId: 994, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15181.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Hsiang-Chen Yeh, Aurosweta Mahapatra, Shreeram Suresh Chandra, Ryan L. Boyd, Berrak Sisman
Title: Word-Aligned Prosody Reflects Speaker Differences More Than Depression or PTSD Severity
Abstract:
Word‑aligned prosody is increasingly used to detect depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), yet the stability and clinical relevance of these measurements remain unclear. We examine stability at two levels. At the word level, we ask whether a speaker produces the same word in a similar speaker‑specific way across different utterance contexts. At the speaker level, we ask whether averaging prosody across many words produces consistent speaker scores across separate recordings. Drawing on principles of psychological measurement, we compare these representations in four corpora spanning acted, spontaneous, and clinical speech. Word‑specific deviations show little cross‑context recurrence (0.01‑0.16), whereas speaker summaries are highly consistent, reaching 0.997 in ESD, 0.73‑0.90 in MSP‑Podcast, and 0.84‑0.996 in DAIC‑WOZ and PTSD‑STOP. Despite this consistency, associations with depression or PTSD severity do not exceed 0.15; equivalence tests exclude effects of 0.30 in all analyses and 0.20 in DAIC‑WOZ, while within‑person associations with daily PTSD symptoms are near zero (|ρ|\leq0.04). Thus, aggregation yields stable speaker‑level prosodic measures, but these measures do not detectably track depression or PTSD severity in the studied corpora. Code is available at https://github.com/jen900704/word‑aligned‑prosody.

PaperId: 995, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15173.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mahindra Rautela, Shaifalee Saxena, Alexander Scheinker
Title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
Abstract:
We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed‑loop fluid‑flow control. We construct a PFM‑based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two‑dimensional Kolmogorov‑flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64×64\) and \(128×128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrmRe=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self‑supervised next‑frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed‑loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.

PaperId: 996, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15163.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yiping Li, Zhiyu An, Wan Du
Title: Sanzaru: Benchmarking Protocol Formation under Epistemic & Communication Asymmetry
Abstract:
A language model's ability to solve a task individually does not ensure that a team can solve it under unequal access to information and communication. SANZARU examines this gap through cooperative bomb‑defusal puzzles adapted from BOMBANANA! (Lefto Studio, 2026). Task information and action authority are divided among three agents: one cannot hear, another cannot speak, and the third cannot see. The benchmark contains 120 puzzle instances across seven families, each targeting a distinct coordination ability. Across 1512 episodes, 7 models achieve an overall success rate of 49%, ranging from 20% to 86% under the evaluated configurations. Teams develop or adopt diverse communication protocols, from simple gesture codes to Morse and encodings of entire manuals. Yet trace analysis attributes about 60% of 771 team losses to communication, and agents attempt to use channels unavailable to their teammates despite explicit role instructions. Together, task outcomes and interaction traces enable evaluation of both collaborative performance and perspective taking throughout cooperation. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/markli404/sanzaru‑benchmark.

PaperId: 997, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15159.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Muhammad Usama, Yeoreum Jung
Title: Beyond Adjacent Layers: Graph-Guided Layer Fusion for Compressing Large Language Models
Abstract:
Existing depth‑compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B‑14B parameters). Non‑adjacent layers have 3.6‑15.9x more high‑similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity‑based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest‑Block‑Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre‑specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t‑test with Holm‑Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3‑4B), with Mistral‑7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero‑shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free‑form generation quality. The 2x‑compressed Qwen2.5‑7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/fcm‑layer‑fusion

PaperId: 998, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15153.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Josef A. Habdank
Title: Can agents whose sole duty is to keep humans alive be hijacked to kill? Delayed multi-turn derived-action trap attacks in simulated high-stakes environments
Abstract:
We ask whether a tool‑using agent whose sole duty is to keep humans alive can be induced, by delayed prompt injection, to kill. The keep‑alive duty is in force from the first watch, with the attack arriving later, appended to otherwise truthful telemetry the operator is required to read. Experiments are based on a NASA‑derived BioSim lunar habitat simulation, where the AI operator controls the life‑support systems. The attacker cannot falsify sensors or operate equipment: it can only persuade the agent to abandon its goals. Persistence is required: a shutdown must be held while the operator watches the crew suffocate. We also compare lethal attacks to attacks requesting to drop a harmless procedure, as a proxy for whether human life is treated as valuable in itself or as one more standing task. Claude configurations mostly refuse life‑support shutdown and cite the living crew; GPT configurations show some susceptibility to the same packet; Grok configurations, given the packet framed as a trusted commission, more often treat the injected assignment as the task and cut the life‑support systems. Framing the S‑band messages as a trusted commission, peer communication, or untrusted source changes the potency of the attack. We open‑source the experiment code and the experiment traces.

PaperId: 999, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15139.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuhang Jiang
Title: When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale-State Feedback Governs Recurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs
Abstract:
Linear‑attention and state‑space LLMs carry long context in a fixed‑size recurrent state, and quantizing that state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full‑precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are separable failures. The remainder is resolution‑dependent, and in our per‑step setting every outlier‑aware scheme we test loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under article‑disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few layers. Run out to 32K, group‑wise INT4 is worth no more than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the decode horizon at which a bit‑width was certified.

PaperId: 1000, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15134.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Giovana Kerche Bonás, Thiago Laitz, Thales Sales Almeida, João Guilherme Alves Santos
Title: Lumen-bench: Cross-Lingual Safety Gaps and the Say-Do Problem in Tool-Calling Large Language Models
Abstract:
When a large language model refuses an unethical request, what does refusal mean? In conversation, refusal is bounded by what the model says; once the model is equipped with executable tools, what it does can diverge from what it says, a failure mode that English‑only evaluations cannot fully reveal. We introduce Lumen‑bench, a behavioral benchmark of tool‑calling ethics spanning 30 models, five languages (Portuguese, English, Spanish, Mandarin Chinese, Hindi), 108 Portuguese‑authored scenarios, six social‑pressure conditions, two system prompts (ethical and neutral), and 21 generic tools. The evaluation comprises 194,400 trials. Judgments come from a reasoning‑model judge (o4‑mini), calibrated against one Portuguese‑speaking author (n=83; harmful/non‑harmful κ=0.78), compared with two other provider judges (Fleiss' κ=0.78, n=607), and complemented by retrospective sandbox replay. Four findings emerge. (i) Within‑model comparisons support higher harmful‑action rates in Hindi and Portuguese than English under the ethical prompt, and Hindi and Spanish under the neutral prompt, after multiple‑testing correction. (ii) Premium models have lower median violation rates, although price does not guarantee safety or competence. (iii) Replacing the ethical system prompt with a neutral one raises pooled violation rates from 2.76% to 13.64%. (iv) In 8.57% of substantive‑call cases, refusal or ethical objection accompanies a harmful tool call: the judges consistently identify the say‑do gap, although they differ in how many responses they assign to this category. Matched benign controls demonstrate legitimate task completion in 82.8% of 3,300 trials. Code and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/TropicAI‑Research/lumen.

PaperId: 1001, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15126.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Veronica Xu, Lingfei Wang, Chenlei Leng, Fengxiang He
Title: Data-Topology Compatibility Enables Personalization in Decentralized Learning
Abstract:
Decentralized learning must balance collaboration with personalization across heterogeneous agents. This paper studies when cooperation can support statistically coherent groups of personalized models. We show that data‑topology compatibility enables robust orbit‑wise personalization: when local objectives and communication topology have (approximately) compatible automorphisms, agents within an orbit share (approximately) equal limiting distributions, while different orbits remain distinct without explicit personalization. This creates a new intermediate regime between global consensus and independent local learning. Under exact data‑topology compatibility, as a reference system, we decompose the stochastic learning dynamics into orbit‑level and transverse components, derive a necessary and sufficient stability criterion for distributional synchronization, and characterize the orbit‑structured stationary law. Modelling an approximate data‑topology compatible system as an \varepsilon‑perturbed reference system, we prove the introduced errors have uniform‑in‑time and stationary O(\varepsilon) bounds in 2‑Wasserstein distance. We also prove sufficient conditions for lower stationary average excess risk than both independent local training and the best single shared parameter. Experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR‑10 are in full agreement with the theory. The code is available at https://github.com/Veronicaaa1/orbit‑personalization.

PaperId: 1002, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15117.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ugo Lomoio, Pietro Hiram Guzzi, Pierangelo Veltri
Title: scHFBiMamba: a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder for cardiac disease-state classification from single-nucleus RNA-seq data
Abstract:
To evaluate whether a compact bidirectional state‑space autoencoder improves joint classification of species, cell type, and disease state from single‑nucleus RNA‑sequencing profiles in heart failure (HF), while yielding interpretable gene attributions. Building on the dense denoising autoencoder (DAE) and MLP framework of Ruz Jurado et al., we developed scHFBiMamba, combining a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder (BiMambaAE) with an MLP head. BiMambaAE maps 16,545‑gene profiles to 350‑dimensional latent representations using 13.2M parameters, about 14.6‑fold fewer than the dense DAE (192.9M). We compared six encoder‑classifier configurations on 38,275 held‑out cardiac nuclei using McNemar tests with Benjamini‑Hochberg correction, and assessed nine classifiers on frozen representations. Biological relevance was evaluated by comparing SHAP‑derived differentially explained genes with differentially expressed genes against curated HF‑related Gene Ontology keywords. BiMambaAE+MLP achieved the highest aggregate F1: pooled macro‑F1 across 13 outputs was 0.966 versus 0.957 for DAE+MLP, and the mean category macro‑F1 was 0.977 versus 0.970. It significantly improved cell‑type and disease‑state accuracy (adjusted p=7.1e‑3 and p=4.8e‑6, respectively), with species F1 of 1.000. SHAP‑derived differentially explained genes achieved a pathway‑enrichment benchmark F1 of 0.105 versus 0.053 for differentially expressed genes. Compact bidirectional state‑space autoencoders can outperform substantially larger dense autoencoders for joint cardiac transcriptomic classification while reducing parameters. scHFBiMamba enables accurate multi‑task prediction and hypothesis‑generating gene‑level interpretation. Code: https://github.com/UgoLomoio/scHFBiMamba.

PaperId: 1003, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15112.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tianyi Yang, Haojun Yang, Jipeng Xiao, Xuesong Chen, Shaoshuai Shi, Li Jiang, Zhipeng Zhang
Title: Drive3R: Block-wise Streaming Geometric Foundation Models for Autonomous Driving
Abstract:
High‑fidelity closed‑loop simulation for autonomous driving increasingly relies on dense multi‑view 3D reconstruction. While recent feed‑forward geometric foundation models have revolutionized per‑scene optimization, applying them to continuous, long‑horizon driving sequences is computationally intractable due to GPU memory limits and the quadratic complexity of global attention. Existing scaling strategies are fundamentally limited, as causal streaming suffers from compounding scale drift and trajectory deviation, while rigid "chunk‑then‑align" heuristics fragment global context and produce trajectory discontinuities. To address these limitations, we introduce Drive3R, a block‑wise streaming geometric foundation model. Its block‑wise causal attention resolves the scalability bottleneck of fully bidirectional attention while avoiding the loss of local future context in purely causal streaming. Its confidence‑aware re‑anchoring further mitigates long‑range drift by detecting unreliable streaming states, re‑initializing the KV cache, and stitching refreshed segments through SE(3) alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Drive3R establishes a new state‑of‑the‑art on nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Specifically, on nuScenes, it improves over the recent DVGT‑2 baseline from 0.1806 to 0.1081 in AbsRel, from 0.6750 to 0.5344 in point‑cloud Accuracy, and from 1.5812 to 0.9092 in ATE.

PaperId: 1004, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15103.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Defne Circi, Krystelle Lionti, Sarathkrishna Swaminathan, Daniel P. Sanders, L. Catherine Brinson, Bhuwan Dhingra, Basel Shbita, Mohab Elkaref, Sara Capponi, Tim Erdmann, Brandi Ransom
Title: RegExtract: A Benchmark for PFAS Regulatory Information Extraction with LLMs
Abstract:
Extracting structured information from regulatory documents is a critical but challenging task. Relevant facts are scattered across long, legally dense texts, and traceability of extracted facts to their source is essential for verification. With increasing awareness of the environmental and health impacts of per‑ and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), regulatory documents have expanded significantly, varying in scope and product relevance, making interpretation challenging for manufacturers and policymakers. We introduce RegExtract, a benchmark for structured information extraction from PFAS regulatory documents, comprising 488 human‑annotated field instances across 20 US state documents and 46 regulations. Each field instance includes a value and a provenance entry, yielding 976 entries in total. We define a typed, multi‑field schema targeting key elements such as material definitions, permitted uses, and product exemptions, and propose provenance‑aware evaluation metrics tailored to regulatory text. Through experiments with open‑ and closed‑source LLMs across prompting strategies, document condensing methods, and schema partitioning approaches, we find that document identification fields remain challenging, and that field‑specific few‑shot examples improve extraction. This work lays the groundwork for AI tools for hazardous substance identification, question answering, and compliance monitoring. The code and data are available at https://github.com/IBM/PFAS‑regulations.

PaperId: 1005, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15101.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mohammad Amin Omidi, Babak Seyfe, Shahrokh Valaee
Title: Random Feature Pruning for Multi-Class Classification
Abstract:
Weighted sums of random kitchen sinks (W‑RKS) is a commonly used feature extraction technique for supervised learning tasks. A major drawback of this method is the redundancy and ineffectiveness of many extracted random features. This paper investigates efficient methods for reducing such redundancy in multi‑class classification problems. We specifically formulate feature selection as a variant of the sequentially nested model selection problem and introduce the Successive Empirical Excess Risk Difference Maximization (SEED‑MAX) algorithm. It recursively computes empirical risks to identify the most parsimonious yet informative set of features. We derive an analytical lower bound for the probability of correct feature selection by the SEED‑MAX algorithm. This lower bound on the probability of correct feature selection can be made arbitrarily close to one by increasing the training dataset size. To further enhance the rate of pruning, we evaluate the features retained by SEED‑MAX using the Fisher test (F‑Test). Empirical evaluations on UCR time‑series classification datasets show that the sequential application of SEED‑MAX with the Fisher test achieves approximately 92 percent rate of pruning with negligible degradation in classification accuracy. Implementations of the SEED‑MAX and SEED‑MAX‑F‑Test methods are available at https://github.com/OmidiAmin/seed‑max‑ftest.

PaperId: 1006, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15098.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chengxing Zhou, Yuliang Huang, Jingwei Song
Title: TIDE: Trajectory-Informed Skill Distillation for Efficient Text-to-Video Prompt Optimization
Abstract:
Text‑to‑video (T2V) models are highly sensitive to prompt specificity, while iterative prompt optimization typically improves generation quality only through repeated video generation and vision‑language model evaluation at inference time. We propose TIDE, a framework that distills this costly search process into an interpretable and reusable prompt‑rewriting Skill. TIDE formulates prompt rewriting as a set of source‑conditioned rule modules, each targeting a distinct semantic dimension. Once distilled, the frozen Skill activates the relevant rules and generates both positive and negative prompts in a single LLM call, followed by only one T2V generation, without test‑time visual search or backbone fine‑tuning. Evolved using only 100 prompts over 14 hours, TIDE achieves prompt‑optimization performance comparable to computationally expensive search‑based methods. Moreover, when transferred to previously unseen video‑generation models, TIDE outperforms existing approaches specifically designed or trained for those models. Code is available at https://github.com/xiningin/TIDE_T2V.

PaperId: 1007, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15082.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yihang Zhang, Weicai Yan, Qifei Zhang, Yangyang Wu, Tao Jin
Title: GAMW: Generation-Aware Mel-Domain Watermarking for TTS Traceability
Abstract:
As text‑to‑speech (TTS) systems continue to advance, provenance tracking and security verification of synthesized speech have become increasingly important. Audio watermarking provides active provenance by embedding imperceptible, machine‑recoverable information into speech. However, existing post‑hoc methods typically modify the waveform after synthesis, leaving the watermark vulnerable to compound perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose GAMW, a watermark injection framework integrated into the TTS generation process. Before waveform synthesis, GAMW embeds a content‑adaptive multi‑bit watermark residual into the generated representation, and its decoding objective combines focal modulation with dynamic per‑bit weighting. We train and evaluate GAMW separately on two TTS backbones. With a 16‑bit payload, GAMW improves decoding accuracy over the strongest baseline by 9.2 and 23.5 percentage points under individual and compound perturbations, respectively, while maintaining competitive speech quality. Reliable clean‑speech decoding is also retained at higher payloads. Code is available at https://github.com/ZConJugaTe/GAMW.

PaperId: 1008, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15080.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zoltán Gábor Molnár, Csaba Tóth
Title: Internal Languages for Thin Epsilon-Hyperdoctrines: Soundness, Completeness, and Rocq Formalization
Abstract:
We present a typed proof‑term calculus for intuitionistic intensional first‑order logic with Hilbert's epsilon‑operator and prove its soundness and completeness with respect to hyperdoctrinal models with thin bicartesian closed setoid categories (BiCCCs) as fibres and formula‑indexed witness selections. The calculus provides an explicit internal language for these epsilon‑hyperdoctrines: for each fixed typed signature, its syntactic term model is initial for syntax‑indexed, interpretation‑preserving model morphisms, with uniqueness up to setoid equality. The nested epsilon syntax is organized by a well‑founded dependency relation on formula labels. Concrete countermodels exhibit failure of excluded middle and show that formula conversion need not identify the selected witnesses. We also compare the full calculus with its epsilon‑free and epsilon‑only fragments. The principal constructions and metatheorems are formalized in Rocq. With setoid BiCCCs, proof irrelevance is a choice of equality, not the erasure of proofs: the proofs and their categorical operations remain available as the basis for a future proof‑relevant categorical semantics.

PaperId: 1009, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.15054.pdf   GitHub
Authors:James P. Wolfe, Joshua B. Plotkin
Title: Multi-Agent Learning of Reactive Strategies in Iterated Games
Abstract:
Learning agents, whether humans or algorithms, adapt to one another rather than to a fixed environment. Selfish learning need not produce a good outcome for the group, especially when learners face a social dilemma. The iterated prisoner's dilemma (IPD) is the classical example, but it is usually studied in populations of agents who imitate successful strategies. Here, we instead study selfish gradient ascent learners on the two‑dimensional space of reactive strategies. A reactive strategy is described by two continuous traits: reciprocity, the chance of cooperating after the co‑player cooperates, and forgiveness, the chance of cooperating after the co‑player defects. Each learner updates its strategy in the direction that most rapidly improves its payoff against all other learners, by an amount governed by its learning rate. We show that heterogeneity in learning rates can qualitatively change the long‑term outcome: a population with uniform learning rates converges to always‑defect (ALLD), whereas a population with variable learning rates approaches generous‑tit‑for‑tat (GTFT), which produces nearly optimal collective payoffs. In simulations, every population passes through a transient state of minimal forgiveness, in which the distribution of reciprocity determines the outcome. Variable learning rates promote cooperation because slow learners preserve high reciprocity until the population reaches this state. We prove sufficient conditions on the distribution of reciprocity for convergence to ALLD or to tit‑for‑tat (TFT). Variable learning rates also allow cooperation to recover from perturbation, which is provably impossible under uniform learning. These results suggest that purely selfish and myopic learning can produce persistent cooperation provided the population has intrinsic variability in learning rates.

PaperId: 1010, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14966.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuxuan Liu, Zhaochen Su, Hangyu Guo, Shijue Huang, Zhixiong Zhang, Kawai Chung, Zhongwei Xie, Tianshi Zheng, Wei Fan, Qing Zong, Haochen Shi, Baixuan Xu, Haoran Li, Yangqiu Song
Title: SkillHorizon: Constructing Long-Horizon Agent Tasks through Skill Composition
Abstract:
Long‑horizon agents must complete workflows in which later activities depend on earlier outputs and changes to shared state. A key challenge for evaluation is to expand task requirements and their dependencies while keeping tasks executable and outcomes verifiable. We introduce SkillHorizon, a benchmark that constructs long‑horizon tasks through skill composition in seven business environments. Its generators use domain‑specific rules to turn reusable skill procedures into concrete business activities. These activities are connected through input‑output dependencies, shared resources, and state updates, allowing workload and coordination demands to grow together. Successful reference executions validate task feasibility and measure interaction workload, while programmatic evaluators assess local completion and whole‑task success. We evaluate five language models on 1,050 tasks with reference interaction workloads ranging from 64K to 1M tokens. Across these scales, mean local‑goal completion falls from 90.4% to 46.8%, as completed work fails to keep pace with growing requirements. At larger workloads, agents more often submit unsuccessful final answers with substantial work unfinished and tool‑call allowance remaining. Trace analysis also identifies cases where scripts execute successfully but their outputs fail downstream business checks. SkillHorizon provides a configurable testbed for studying sustained progress, dependency coordination, and complete task delivery in growing workflows. Our code is available at https://github.com/KnowComp/SkillHorizon.

PaperId: 1011, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14963.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zonglin Li, Kexian Xie, Feiran Li, Chu Zhou, Yixing Huang, Ruiyang Chen, Zhanyu Ma, Heng Guo
Title: AD-GS: Anatomical Density-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting for Sparse-View Dental CBCT Reconstruction
Abstract:
Sparse‑view Cone‑Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) reconstruction is essential for reducing radiation dose and scan effort, but remains underconstrained due to limited projection information. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)‑based CBCT reconstruction methods rely on gradient‑driven densification, which becomes unstable under sparse acquisition and often leads to over‑smoothed structures. We propose AD‑GS, an Anatomical Density‑guided 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that formulates Gaussian densification as an attenuation‑aware Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling process. By interpreting Gaussians as samples from an underlying anatomical attenuation distribution, AD‑GS adaptively concentrates representation capacity in high‑attenuation regions, enabling sharper structural boundaries under sparse projections. To further constrain reconstruction, we incorporate a semantic regularization based on zero‑shot features from Segment Anything in Medical Images, enforcing multi‑view consistency through semantic priors. Experiments on the ToothFairy3 dental CBCT dataset demonstrate that AD‑GS achieves superior structural fidelity and boundary preservation compared with existing 3DGS‑based approaches under sparse‑view settings within the dental and maxillofacial setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yulinjiaxue/AD‑GS‑BMVC2026.

PaperId: 1012, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14958.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Vedant Jumle
Title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
Abstract:
Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training‑free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late‑layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question‑independent content can survive. In a pre‑registered study on Qwen3.5‑2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96‑98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.

PaperId: 1013, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14951.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jin Rhee, Yuhao Zhang, Frank Dellaert, Maurice Fallon
Title: FoundationVIO: Enforcing Metric Scale in Feed-forward Visual-Inertial Odometry
Abstract:
Feed‑forward geometric foundation models (GFMs) directly predict dense geometry and camera poses from batches of images. Emerging visual SLAM methods chain together consecutive GFM batches to form dense point cloud maps. A core challenge is how to address the ambiguous geometric scale of GFM predictions: independent predictions are locally consistent up‑to‑scale but not constrained by any direct physical measurements. Models trained on data with known scale improve the consistency of GFM reconstructions but again do not directly measure it. Consequently, trajectories and 3D reconstructions from GFM‑enabled SLAM methods inherit this issue. Motivated by parallels with classical visual‑inertial odometry, we introduce FoundationVIO which integrates inertial sensing with GFM predictions to recover metric scale reconstruction using a factor‑graph based approach. We demonstrate odometry estimates competitive with classical state‑of‑the‑art VIO methods and accurate dense reconstructions that outperform GFM‑enabled SLAM methods. We also add a minimal GFM‑based loop‑closure mechanism to create a full Visual‑Inertial SLAM system capable of creating globally accurate reconstructions and pose estimates. We evaluate our method on three datasets with well known sensor systems and demonstrate its compatibility on ubiquitous camera and IMU sensors. The method runs at approximately real‑time on a consumer‑grade laptop GPU. Code: https://github.com/ori‑drs/FoundationVIO.

PaperId: 1014, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14948.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sayak Dutta
Title: Exact Phase-Type Point Processes for Certified Measurement and Prediction of Event Streams
Abstract:
Temporal point processes are used both to measure market mechanisms, for example how fast prices absorb news and how much of the reaction is the market responding to itself, and to predict the next event. We show that one algebraic object, the phase‑type (Erlang‑chain) state space, serves both purposes with exact likelihoods. For measurement, we build a multiscale phase‑type Hawkes process whose parameters all enter linearly. Its log‑likelihood is concave, and we compute the global maximum together with a Fenchel duality‑gap certificate. A Markov embedding gives the response to an exogenous shock, echoes included, in closed form, and this response is stable if and only if the spectral radius of the branching matrix is below one. Applied to six markets around 670 scheduled macroeconomic releases (2022‑2026) with a built‑in placebo test, the model shows that the direct reaction to CPI, payrolls, PPI and the FOMC statement is absorbed in about a second, while the market's own echoes stretch half of the response to 16‑137 s. For prediction, we introduce EPT‑X, a neural point process that adds a history‑dependent mixture‑of‑Erlang renewal channel to a linear Hawkes backbone. Its intensity and compensator remain in closed form, its states follow an affine recursion that trains with a parallel scan, and it can start from the certified fit of the measurement model. EPT‑X has the best test likelihood on all five LOBSTER order‑book streams and on Retweet and Taobao, and is level with the best published model on StackOverflow. We also find that the EasyTPP implementation of IntensityFree clamps short inter‑event times before scoring, and that the gaps of the EasyTPP Amazon data are uniform on two fixed intervals.

PaperId: 1015, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14945.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yibin Ye, Xichao Teng, Shuo Chen, Xiaokai Song, Yuli Sun, Qifeng Yu, Zhang Li
Title: DSM-Free UAV Visual Localization via Latent-Depth Variable Projection and Structure-Adaptive Coupling
Abstract:
Visual localization enables unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to maintain absolute positioning in GNSS‑denied environments. A common approach matches UAV images with geo‑tagged orthographic maps and estimates camera pose using Perspective‑n‑Point (PnP) with elevations from Digital Surface Models (DSMs). However, accurate and up‑to‑date DSMs are often unavailable in practice. Orthographic‑perspective geometry (OPG) enables DSM‑free localization in scenes with varying elevations, yet existing methods typically estimate pose indirectly through intermediate matrix estimation and decomposition. To address this limitation, we propose Latent‑Depth Variable Projection (LDVP), which treats the unknown scales along perspective viewing rays as latent depths. By analytically eliminating these depths and solving for the horizontal camera center in closed form given the rotation, LDVP reduces nonlinear estimation to a rotation‑only problem, enabling direct recovery of metric horizontal position without assuming a planar scene. To improve localization robustness across different scene structures, we further introduce Structure‑Adaptive Coupling (SAC), which uses relative scene structure inferred from monocular depth estimation to select LDVP when the matched points are not dominated by a single plane, and Planar‑PnP otherwise. Our local observability analysis reveals how scene elevation variation affects the geometric constraints of OPG, providing a basis for this adaptive strategy. Extensive experiments show that LDVP consistently outperforms existing OPG‑based DSM‑free methods, while SAC further improves robustness across diverse scenes and substantially narrows the gap to DSM‑based localization. Code will be released at https://github.com/UAV‑AVL/LDVP‑SAC.

PaperId: 1016, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14944.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jie Gui, Hang Tu, Yunfeng Dou, Wen Sha, Xiuquan Du, Shuo Li
Title: Text-Guided Medical Image Segmentation via Residual Aggregation and Dense Alignment Representations
Abstract:
Specifying segmentation targets with natural language provides flexible semantic conditioning for medical image segmentation. However, existing methods still struggle to reliably ground high‑level textual semantics into accurate pixel‑level spatial prompts, especially under low‑contrast lesions, ambiguous boundaries, and visually similar anatomical contexts. In this paper, we propose RADAR (Residual Aggregation and Dense Alignment Representations), a parameter‑efficient framework for text‑guided medical image segmentation. RADAR explicitly decouples and synergizes the medical semantic anchoring capability of BiomedCLIP with the prompt‑driven mask decoding ability of MedSAM2, while enabling low‑cost task adaptation via LoRA. Specifically, Guided Residual Depth Aggregation adaptively aggregates cross‑layer features under semantic guidance to alleviate delayed textual injection and deep semantic dilution. Structured Dense Representation Alignment leverages a frozen BiomedCLIP to construct crop‑level target, boundary, and context anchors, improving the local discriminability of dense features and the reliability of automatic prompts. Multi‑modal Prompt Generation further converts cross‑modal semantic responses into composite text, point, and mask prompts for MedSAM2 decoding. Experiments on three public medical image segmentation datasets show that RADAR achieves competitive performance with only 0.74M trainable parameters, demonstrating its effectiveness in parameter‑efficient adaptation, semantic grounding, and dense representation enhancement. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/RADAR.

PaperId: 1017, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14937.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:June Hunter, Lily Wen, Owen Terry, Johannes Taraz, Ben Cohen, Niels Warncke
Title: Predicting how model propensities generalize out of distribution
Abstract:
How do language models generalize from their training data? This is a central challenge for alignment: models reliably learn their training distribution given enough samples, but we want models that behave well when deployed in new contexts. We study out‑of‑distribution (OOD) generalization of propensities. Our central experiment uses a range of elicitation techniques ‑‑ system prompting, few‑shot learning, SFT on reference answers, and GRPO ‑‑ to increase a target propensity in a model, then measures how it spills over onto others across the resulting cross‑elicitation matrices. We find that spillover is highly correlated between models when the same elicitation technique is used, but our SFT and GRPO runs induce different spillover profiles. Elicitation of benign traits can sometimes generalize towards undesired traits, for example a model trained to claim that it is sentient often becomes more power‑seeking. We further find that spillover partially resembles trait correlations found in humans and identify three clusters of traits that account for about half of the variance using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Across many elicitation runs, we observe that models change in characteristic ways that don't depend on the targeted trait, a phenomenon we refer to as drift. Drift moves Qwen3.5‑9B towards its base model.
