When investigating if LLMs are able to predict spillover, we find that Claude Opus 5.5 predicts spillover slightly better than the models themselves, but worse than data‑driven approaches using alternative elicitation methods or models. Overall, no single dominant predictor emerges, and generalization remains hard to predict. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nielsrolf/propensity‑spillover.

PaperId: 1018, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14936.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shutong Ding, Zhaoyang Liu, Yimiao Zhou, Jingya Wang, Jiayuan Gu, Ye Shi
Title: CFG-Policy: Unified Diffusion Policy Learning Framework via Classifier-free Guidance
Abstract:
Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision‑language‑action models, and world‑model‑based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post‑training, directly fine‑tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action‑space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline‑to‑online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG‑Policy, a unified, plug‑and‑play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier‑free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline‑to‑online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG‑Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow‑SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy‑liu.github.io/cfg‑policy‑page.

PaperId: 1019, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14911.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Buzhen Huang, Xingchen Wu, Yuanwang Yang, Chenyi Xie, Kun Li
Title: Scalable Multi-Human Cooperative Manipulation via Commander-Executor Coordination
Abstract:
Multi‑human cooperative object manipulation is a highly challenging topic in humanoid control. While existing methods can handle simple collaborative carrying tasks, they struggle with role‑dependent, long‑horizon, and sequential cooperative manipulation. To address this issue, we propose a hierarchical commander‑executor framework that enables multiple agents to accomplish complex collaborative tasks in distinct ways. Specifically, a commander combines instructions and scene information for joint semantic and geometric planning. It then decomposes the task into role‑specific subtasks and generates shared object‑centric coordination plans, specifying execution timing, target positions, and manipulation actions for each agent. Conditioned on the commander's high‑level strategy and each agent's local observations, the executor learns a low‑level physics‑based policy through a solo‑to‑cooperative curriculum to realize coordinated human‑object interactions. The planned object trajectory provides a shared coordination target, while root positions and grasping instructions specify role‑dependent execution cues. We evaluate our method on a variety of object manipulation tasks, demonstrating its ability to execute long‑horizon tasks that combine different types of collaboration and to scale from two‑agent to multi‑agent cooperation. Extensive experiments further show that our approach achieves higher success rates compared to state‑of‑the‑art methods. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/TJU‑3DV/Co‑Manipulation.

PaperId: 1020, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14894.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Zhikang Xu, Jiarui Xing, Jian Wang
Title: Pro-t-VAE: Closed-Form Student's t Mixtures for Robust Prototype Discovery
Abstract:
We present a robust deep generative framework for unsupervised image prototype discovery, built on a heavy‑tailed Student's t mixture prior, that bridges statistical robustness and mathematical tractability. Existing generative approaches typically rely on noise‑prone Gaussian priors or computationally intensive diffusion models; neither simultaneously provides explicit latent structure nor exact analytic optimization. While diffusion models can yield strong priors, iterative sampling and intractable likelihoods limit scalability and interpretability for prototype discovery. We address these issues by constructing a Student's t latent space via a Bayesian scale‑mixture formulation. This yields a fully closed‑form augmented ELBO for unsupervised Student's t mixture variational autoencoders, which, to our knowledge, is the first such objective applied to robust image prototype discovery, avoiding biased variational approximations and high computational costs in prior heavy‑tailed or diffusion‑based frameworks. Treating precision as a latent variable automatically modulates each data point's influence, downweighting outliers to learn a data‑dependent measure of trust. The result is improved robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, with well‑separated latent representations and more stable manifold learning than state‑of‑the‑art methods. We validate our model on standard vision benchmarks and challenging neuroimaging tasks. In brain MRI‑driven neurodegenerative disease analysis, our model recovers clean, anatomically coherent prototypes where clinical noise often collapses rare subtypes. These results highlight the ability of our framework to preserve anatomy‑associated patterns for precise discovery in clinical settings. Our code is available at: https://github.com/xuzhikangnba/torch‑tvae.

PaperId: 1021, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14892.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yusuke Watanabe
Title: Coefficientwise Extremality and Rigidity for Independent Sets in Bipartite Graph Covers
Abstract:
Let G be a finite bipartite graph and let \widetilde G be an M‑fold cover. We compare independent sets of \widetilde G with those of the trivial cover, consisting of M disjoint copies of G, after prescribing how many vertices are selected above each vertex of G. A conjecture from 2011, motivated by the Bethe approximation, asserts that the trivial cover maximizes every such count. We prove this for every feasible occupation profile whose active graph has treewidth at most two or is chordal bipartite. Equality holds exactly when the restricted cover is flat, meaning that fibre relabelings make it trivial. For M\ge2 and positive feasible occupations, a nonflat cover of a connected bipartite graph of treewidth at most two has a deficit of at least twice the coefficient of p_G^M‑2 with every occupation reduced by one. A holonomy‑dependent bound improves the factor to three for odd‑order holonomy; both uniform constants are sharp. Comparison and rigidity survive finite compositions along an edge or a vertex, and quantitative bounds from one piece propagate to the whole graph, giving results beyond the two original classes. On any bipartite base, the first nonzero homogeneous defect is determined by the shortest cycles with nontrivial holonomy. At singleton occupations, our counts are numbers of DP‑colorings of full covers. The dual DP color function on these classes and their finite seam compositions equals the chromatic polynomial, with equality attained precisely by canonical labelings. Dong's chromatic‑polynomial inequality then yields the Dual‑DP Shameful inequality on the same graph class. The main theorems have been formalized in Lean 4.

PaperId: 1022, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14866.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaoran Zhang, Yu Liu, Jinyu Liang, Huaxin Xiao
Title: ScalLoc: Continuous Oblique Thermal UAV Geo-Localization with a 2D Satellite Map
Abstract:
Cross‑modal Thermal Geo‑localization (TG) provides an illumination‑robust positioning solution for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)‑denied environments. However, existing thermal geo‑localization methods mainly focus on near‑nadir observations or depend on map‑side elevation priors, limiting their applicability to continuous oblique thermal localization with only geo‑referenced 2D satellite maps. To address this problem, we propose ScalLoc, a scale‑aligned local‑to‑map localization framework for continuous oblique thermal UAV geo‑localization. ScalLoc follows a reconstruction‑‑refinement‑‑anchoring‑‑propagation design: it reconstructs local window geometry from thermal sequences, refines camera poses using track‑based pose optimization, adaptively anchors each window to the satellite map, and propagates validated states to recover frame‑level global trajectories. To support systematic evaluation, we construct Thermal‑Oblique, a real thermal UAV sequence dataset containing 216 urban and rural day‑‑night trajectories and 28,112 thermal frames with frame‑level annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScalLoc reduces the mean localization error from 112.69 m to 26.97 m compared with the VGGT‑only configuration, corresponding to a 76.07% reduction, and achieves the lowest frame‑weighted mean position error among the compared methods. These results demonstrate the feasibility of continuous oblique thermal geo‑localization using only lightweight 2D satellite maps, without requiring digital surface models or preconstructed 3D maps. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/FloralHercules/ScalLoc.

PaperId: 1023, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14861.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhiding Liu, Jiqian Yang, Mingyue Cheng, Zhi Li, Enhong Chen
Title: World2TS: Real-World Event Context for Time-Series Forecasting
Abstract:
Time‑series forecasting plays a vital role in a wide range of real‑world applications. Recent approaches have achieved strong performance by modeling temporal correlations and cross‑channel dependencies, yet most forecasting benchmarks still represent time series primarily as numerical histories. In practice, time series are observations of complex real‑world processes, and their trajectories may reflect events, interventions, disruptions, and changes in measurement or reporting that cannot always be inferred from past values alone. A central barrier to studying context‑aware forecasting is therefore the lack of large‑scale datasets that align real‑world events with the individual series they affect. We present World2TS, a scalable construction framework and large‑scale dataset for time‑series forecasting with real‑world event context. We first develop world2ts‑core, a reusable tool that combines agent‑led semantic reasoning and Web search, command‑line execution and validation, and human review within a feedback‑driven discovery workflow. Given heterogeneous time series with semantic descriptions, the workflow discovers candidate events, consolidates retrieved evidence into verified events, and links them to relevant series under explicit temporal and semantic scopes. Using this framework, we construct world2ts‑data, which contains 31 datasets across six domains, comprising 4,179 series, 97.1 million observations, 1,159 events, and 56,846 event‑series links. We further conduct extensive data analyses and controlled comparative experiments to characterize the dataset and demonstrate the utility of the collected context for improving forecasting accuracy. World2TS provides a reusable data foundation for developing and evaluating context‑aware forecasting models and agents. The project homepage is available at https://world2ts.github.io/.

PaperId: 1024, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14856.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Pu Pang, Zhongfei Qing, Ling-Hao Chen, Songnan Li, Hua Huang, Bo Hu
Title: CAST: Real-Time Motion Capture for Any Skeleton Topology
Abstract:
This paper studies the problem of recovering motion from monocular video, even when the target skeleton topology differs from the subject observed in the video. Although previous methods have made efforts to resolve this problem, they remain vulnerable to joint‑rotation errors that are coupled across the skeleton and can propagate along its kinematic hierarchy. To mitigate these errors, we present CAST, a topology‑aware motion capture framework that combines learned local rotations with geometric correction guided by predicted global bone directions. Our observability analysis characterizes which rotational components can be constrained by outgoing bone directions. Guided by this analysis, GRACE uses reliability‑gated alignment to correct composed orientations in parent‑to‑child order, leaving unconstrained components to the learned rotation predictor. The motion predictor and correction module are trained jointly with motion‑derived supervision, using a frozen image encoder. Experiments under the TopoCap evaluation protocol show that the proposed framework improves motion recovery across different target topologies, including unseen structures. Reference‑based cross‑skeleton evaluation on a curated Mixamo benchmark and a user preference study further assess transfer to different target structures. A causal CAST‑B variant achieves over 51 FPS on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, with timing covering image encoding and motion prediction. Code repository: https://github.com/fankewen/CAST.

PaperId: 1025, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14852.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaofeng Tan, Jiaxin Lin, Haobo Yuan, Tiancheng Shen, Zihan Su, Rui Chen, Hongsong Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang
Title: Getting Space Right: Agentic Rewards for Image Generation
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for spatial text‑to‑image generation, but existing work largely focuses on policy optimization, assuming accurate rewards and effective online rollouts. We observe in‑domain gains with out‑of‑domain degradation, exposing two limitations: unreliable spatial rewards in open‑world settings and rollouts lacking basic‑to‑complex progression. We propose a curriculum‑guided RL framework. First, we introduce SpatialCritic, an agentic reward model equipped with a spatial perception harness that combines reusable verification guidance with specialized vision tools. We then construct spatial preference datasets through targeted counterfactual perturbations and perform agent‑harness alignment to improve tool selection and evidence integration efficiently. Second, curriculum learning organizes shared foundational capabilities and their compositional dependencies in a capability graph for mastery‑guided rollouts, periodic review, and targeted remediation. On SpaRW‑Eval, SpatialCritic achieves 95.1% verification accuracy, outperforming 320B GLM‑5.3‑Flash with a 40x smaller 8B backbone and raising average baseline scores from 78.4 to 83.9 on SD3.5‑Medium and 83.2 to 86.5 on BAGEL. Project page: https://xiaofeng‑tan.github.io/projects/spatialcritic/

PaperId: 1026, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14848.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Nga Kiu Kelly Ho, Yilin Liu, Hao Xu, Niloy J. Mitra
Title: Learning Dynamic Grasping
Abstract:
Synthesizing believable 4D hand‑object grasping sequences is important for character animation, extended reality, and embodied agents. Grasping requires a hand to approach, contact, and lift or manipulate an object coherently. Existing synthesis methods often model only the final static grasp or rely on additional conditions, such as language, target grasps, or object trajectories, to specify the interaction. We instead study the underconstrained problem of generating a complete grasping motion from a single initial hand‑object state. Our framework decouples hand‑motion generation from object‑motion recovery. Given an object point cloud in the initial wrist frame and the initial parameterized hand configuration, conditional flow matching predicts a sequence‑level contact map and a hand pose at each normalized sequence time. This time‑indexed formulation avoids the error accumulation of autoregressive rollout while representing the complete motion. We then infer an attachment frame and recover rigid‑object motion through training‑free, contact‑guided weighted registration. We evaluate on held‑out DexYCB objects and unseen object geometries reconstructed from in‑the‑wild videos by Open‑CHOIR. Compared with LatentHOI, our method produces smoother hand and object motion in every setting, matches or improves on its contact and penetration metrics in the wild under a shared initialization, and is about 30x faster per generated frame. In a 15‑participant study, our motions were preferred in roughly two thirds of (forced‑choice pairwise) comparisons. Precise contact closure on novel geometry, however, remains a key open challenge.

PaperId: 1027, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14846.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kailai Sun, Yue Cui, Xinwei Wang, Zijie Gao, Baoshen Guo, Zhiqing Hong, Irfan Qaisar, Xu Yang, Yueting Li, Dian Fan, Qianchuan Zhao
Title: Towards Privacy-Preserving Thermal Human Perception from Dataset to Deployment
Abstract:
Indoor human perception is the foundation for smart homes and healthcare. However, RGB cameras raise privacy concerns in private indoor environments, while low‑resolution thermal cameras provide limited spatial and semantic information. Large‑scale indoor thermal datasets and real‑world deployments remain limited. Here, we introduce Indoor RGB‑T, a large‑scale paired RGB‑‑thermal dataset for indoor human perception. The dataset covers 20 indoor rooms and contains 90,576 80x62 thermal frames, 87,016 temporally matched RGB‑‑thermal pairs, and 115,557 annotated human bounding boxes. We establish benchmarks for robust thermal occupant‑state detection with 0.75 mAP and occupancy estimation with an accuracy of 0.847 in unseen rooms. We further evaluate RGB‑to‑thermal and thermal‑to‑RGB translation, achieving a temperature MAE of 0.654 C and an R2 of 0.923. Finally, we deploy the thermal perception model on a commercial sleep‑monitoring system in the real world. Field testing with 100 participants and deployment of approximately 1,000 devices further demonstrate its practical feasibility. We identify practical challenges that motivate future research directions, including environmental thermal interference, sensing range and multi‑person occlusion. The code, trained models and partial dataset are available at https://github.com/kailaisun/RGBT and https://huggingface.co/skl24/RGBT.

PaperId: 1028, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14834.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kecan Mao, Nan Xu, Zhaoyang Meng, Zhengyao Ma, Yingming Gao, Yi Zhao, Ya Li
Title: SemiCodec: Bridging Speech Tokenization and High-fidelity Reconstruction with Semi-discrete Representations
Abstract:
Speech representation learning requires a discrete modeling interface while preserving high waveform fidelity. Existing approaches rarely achieve both: discrete tokens ease modeling but lose fine‑grained acoustic information, while continuous latents preserve fidelity but require specialized generative objectives. We introduce SemiCodec, a novel Semi‑discrete neural speech Codec with synchronized discrete tokens and continuous latents. Direct joint optimization may create a reconstruction shortcut through the continuous pathway, leaving the discrete tokens insufficiently grounded. To address this issue, we propose a Preserve‑then‑Ground training paradigm that first establishes a high‑fidelity synthesis space and then grounds SSL‑guided discrete tokens within it. Experiments show that SemiCodec outperforms fully discrete codecs in reconstruction quality and intelligibility while remaining competitive with continuous representations in acoustic fidelity and speaker preservation. Audio samples are available at https://pennyw1‑se.github.io/SemiCodec‑Demo‑Page/

PaperId: 1029, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14828.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhou Liu, Xingyan Chen, ZhaoYang Han, Zewei Pan, Zeli Su, Ningxin Pan, Xue Hu, Kaixiong Ting, Wentao Zhang
Title: EvoCowork: A Benchmark for Real-World Office Tasks
Abstract:
Office workflows are a demanding testbed for self‑improving agents because their deliverables must be correct, natively editable, and mutually consistent. A central question is whether gains on feedback tasks reflect reusable procedures rather than task‑specific fixes. We introduce EvoCowork, a 240‑task benchmark for evaluating harness‑level recursive self‑improvement across four office modalities, with model weights held fixed. The benchmark covers presentations, documents, spreadsheets, and cross‑office workflows, and scores submitted artifacts for content, native structure, formulas, cross‑file consistency, and visual quality where needed. Its protocol separates feedback, revision selection, and final testing: methods learn from single‑modality tasks, then are evaluated on unseen single‑modality tasks and cross‑office workflows under a shared initial harness and explicit budgets. In static evaluations of two models and four harnesses, the best configuration scores 42.25 overall and 30.62 on cross‑office tasks. Starting from the same MSA harness with GLM 5.3, ACE and AHE improve in‑domain scores by 4.90 and 2.64 points, respectively, but change cross‑office scores by only +0.03 and ‑1.72. Thus, gains on the file types that provide feedback do not necessarily transfer to coordinated workflows. EvoCowork makes this distinction explicit while recording the capability, transfer, and cost of harness evolution. Code and task packages: https://github.com/DeepThinkingZhouLiu/cowork‑evolution‑benchmark.

PaperId: 1030, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14826.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Adarsh Arigala, Arjun Gangwar, Srinivasan Umesh
Title: Cross-Lingual TTS for Indian Languages: A Benchmark and Inference-Time Duration Estimation Strategies
Abstract:
Recent alignment‑free Text‑to‑Speech (TTS) models achieve high synthesis quality by removing explicit alignment modules and simplifying training. However, they often struggle in cross‑lingual scenarios due to differences in character durations across languages, leading to duration mismatch and degraded speech quality. Existing approaches typically address this issue using explicit duration predictors, increasing model complexity. Systematic evaluation of TTS performance for Indian languages in cross‑lingual settings remains under‑explored due to the lack of standardized evaluation benchmarks. In this work, we construct a cross‑lingual evaluation benchmark covering English and nine Indian languages and propose a language‑aware inference‑time duration estimation strategy for alignment‑free TTS that incorporates language‑specific duration‑per character statistics without retraining or architectural modifications. We further develop heuristic formulations that refine duration estimation based on language‑dependent duration variations. Experiments on bilingual and multilingual A‑DMA models demonstrate improved speech naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity while reducing duration mismatch.

PaperId: 1031, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14810.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jun He, Deying Yu
Title: KedgeFlow: A Programmable Control Plane for Enterprise AI Agents
Abstract:
Enterprise AI agents can execute altered versions of approved actions, concurrently reuse the same permission, or retry operations whose responses were lost. These failures arise when approval and resource execution lack a shared contract. KedgeFlow specifies language‑independent contracts for trusted controllers to authorize state‑changing operations and privileged gateways to enforce that authority independently of agent reasoning. Inspired by OpenFlow, it connects policy checks supported by evidence, signed permission for an exact action, a shared allowance that can be consumed only once, target‑side conditions for applying the change, and retained outcome records. Under trusted issuance of exact‑action authority, two conditional properties establish at most one successful claim per allowance and link every governed dispatch to a matching grant, claim, and subsequent dispatch authorization, even when the agent is compromised. A reference implementation exposes this execution path to agent systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In the single‑resource evaluation, 6,560 concurrent ledger claim attempts yielded exactly one successful claim for each of 82 allowances. Boundary tests rejected unauthorized and altered requests before consumption. A 32‑call gateway race produced one committed mock effect, and a retry after a lost response produced no additional dispatch. Deliberately permissive policy nevertheless authorized an undesirable effect, exposing the limits of execution authorization. Evaluation uses three members of the etcd coordinated key‑value store on one host, synthetic authentication and authorization inputs, and a mock target that rejects stale requests. Distributed reservations, enforcement of every production access route, native crash recovery, exactly‑once effects at real targets, and interoperability between independent implementations remain untested.

PaperId: 1032, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14800.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuchen Ma, Swadheen Shukla, Paulo Salem, Yue Huang, Robert Sim, Stefan Feuerriegel, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
Title: EAIR: Interaction Risks in Enterprise LLM Multi-Agent Systems
Abstract:
LLM agents increasingly divide enterprise work across roles with different goals, authority, access, and information. Because each agent often sees only a local snapshot of the enterprise workflow, locally reasonable actions can still violate organization‑wide constraints (e.g., several service agents can each issue credit that is individually permitted while collectively exceeding a shared compensation cap). We introduce EAIR, the first framework for analyzing enterprise multi‑agent interaction risks. We make four contributions. (1) We formalize enterprise interaction risk in terms of the organizational properties that workflow operations must preserve, and operationalize this formulation as a taxonomy of testable risks with explicit failure criteria and evidence requirements. (2) We build EAIR‑Worlds, a suite of executable micro‑worlds that instantiates selected risks as controlled, observable workflows with explicit roles, policies, permissions, source facts, and execution traces. (3) We develop a novel diagnosis‑and‑repair pipeline that uses the resulting execution traces to locate contributing interaction boundaries, guide targeted workflow repairs, and retest the repaired system. (4) Large‑scale experiments show recurring interaction failures across the organizational properties studied. Together, EAIR is the first operational framework for diagnosing and mitigating enterprise multi‑agent interaction failures.

PaperId: 1033, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14774.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hao Li, Keqing He, Longtao Zheng, Junlong Li, Weihao Zeng, Qian Liu, Yuzhen Huang
Title: ProgAgent: Learning Tool Orchestration through Programmatic Training
Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to orchestrate diverse tools over long‑horizon tasks. Existing agents typically use Direct Tool Calling (DTC), where the model invokes tools sequentially, and tool responses accumulate in the model context, which can lead to context rot and orchestration breakdown. In contrast, Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC) invokes tools through executable code and stores intermediate results in runtime variables rather than appending them to the context. Prior work has explored PTC mainly as an inference‑time optimization, but its benefits for agentic training remain unclear, and suitable verifiable training tasks are scarce. In this work, we introduce ProgAgent, a full PTC training stack, comprising a pipeline for synthesizing verifiable long‑horizon tasks, a lightweight PTC runtime, and a two‑stage training recipe. Using only 215 tasks instantiated at four environment scales, ProgAgent yields higher pass rates than the evaluated baselines of comparable size across four benchmarks. On LOCA‑bench, ProgAgent‑14B achieves a 30.7% pass rate at a 64k‑token environment state, where these baselines score zero. Cross‑harness experiments show that PTC‑trained models outperform DTC‑trained models under both evaluation interfaces, suggesting that the benefits of PTC training extend beyond the interface.

PaperId: 1034, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14757.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Changkun Ou, Sven Mayer, Daniel Buschek, Andreas Butz
Title: Rethinking Opinion Measurement Interfaces for Human-in-the-Loop Optimization
Abstract:
Human‑in‑the‑loop optimization refers to systems that present choices to a human decision‑maker and query their judgment to optimize system parameters iteratively. The user interface typically provides either an absolute rating scale or asks for a preferred option. However, these approaches can potentially suffer from calibration problems, inconsistencies, and completeness violations of user preferences in such a sequential evaluation. This paper revisits the design space of opinion measurement interfaces for human‑in‑the‑loop optimization. We conducted a study (N=360) using text summarization and image color enhancement tasks to evaluate human sequential feedback in six representative opinion measurement interfaces. Based on our analysis, we recommend using a listwise approach to support sequential opinion measurement, which counterweighs individual rating and preferential choice limitations and conveys more information for subsequent use. We further discuss the trade‑offs in different user interface designs and provide guidelines to inform future research.

PaperId: 1035, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14745.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xianglong Yan, Zenan Wu, Kewei Zhang, Kaicheng Yang, Yulun Zhang
Title: SAGE: Pushing 2-Bit Vector-Quantized LLMs toward Real-World Usability
Abstract:
Extreme low‑bit weight‑only quantization is an effective approach to reducing the deployment costs of large language models. Below 3 bits, scalar quantization often suffers severe accuracy loss, while vector quantization (VQ) better preserves accuracy through more expressive joint encoding. However, existing VQ methods still exhibit substantial degradation on real‑world tasks, and two design challenges remain underexplored: (1) protecting sensitive weight channels within jointly encoded vectors; and (2) allocating a fixed bit budget among representation components, such as direction and radius, to suit different weight matrices. To address these challenges, we propose SAGE: Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy for weight‑only vector quantization. First, Energy‑Stratified Grouping (ESG) couples channel grouping with activation‑weighted fitting, grouping channels from different energy tiers within each subvector to prioritize sensitive channels. Second, Adaptive Bit Split (ABS) balances direction‑codebook capacity and radius precision per matrix, selecting the split with the lowest activation‑weighted reconstruction error under a fixed budget. Across benchmarks covering knowledge, mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and tool use, SAGE achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance in the 2‑bit quantization setting. On Qwen3‑30B‑A3B, it retains 95.3% of the BF16 model's average benchmark score. With our custom‑designed CUDA kernel, SAGE delivers up to a 2.55‑fold non‑streaming end‑to‑end speedup over FP16. The code is available at https://github.com/Zincwolf/sage.

PaperId: 1036, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14730.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zucan Lyu, Rui Tang, Jianlyu Chen, Peisheng Jin, Defu Lian
Title: Self-improving data synthesis enables scalable adaptation of embedding models
Abstract:
AI agents require specialised retrieval across domains and tasks, but adapting embedding models is constrained by costly manual training‑data design. Here we introduce SYNTRA, a self‑improving agentic framework that turns a few retrieval examples into reusable synthesis instructions. Given an unlabelled corpus and a few relevant query‑document pairs, SYNTRA infers implicit information needs and relevance criteria, then uses feedback on trial outputs to refine instructions for query generation and relevance assessment. Experiments across 24 datasets spanning 15 domains demonstrate that the same synthesis workflow produces effective training data, benefiting even strong embedding models with and without existing labelled training sets. Self‑improvement strengthens this supervision on all six evaluated tasks, yielding better retrieval than human calibration on four. The training value persists at larger scales: on MS MARCO, retrieval gains continue across a 32‑fold range of synthetic training‑data sizes. SYNTRA thus enables scalable embedding‑model adaptation with minimal human intervention.

PaperId: 1037, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14726.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Shiqiao Gu, Yang Yong, Fengjun Zhong, Ruihao Gong, Chengtao Lv, Xiangyu Fan, Lei Yang, Xianglong Liu
Title: LightVAE: Towards Compact and Efficient Video Autoencoders
Abstract:
Latent diffusion models enable high‑quality video generation, but video VAE encoding and decoding remain computationally expensive. Existing methods use stage‑specific lightweight operators, yet either constrain spatial and temporal computation jointly or remove temporal computation altogether, without distinguishing their compression sensitivities in pretrained Conv3D. To address these limitations, we present LightVAE, a compression framework that exploits redundancy in temporal modeling and network depth. LightVAE exactly reparameterizes eligible causal Conv3D layers into an aggregate spatial response and a difference‑driven temporal correction. Based on their distinct compression sensitivities, temporal low‑rank compression (TLR) keeps the aggregate spatial kernel dense and applies layer‑specific low‑rank approximation only to the temporal correction. An algebraically equivalent folded implementation converts the arithmetic savings into practical acceleration. LightVAE further uses width‑preserving block pruning to reduce depth and probe‑guided feature alignment, guided by feedback from a frozen teacher suffix, to recover quality after compression. The framework also extends to video encoders. Across three video VAE backbones and two GPU platforms, LightVAE consistently accelerates decoding. For the Wan VAE family, it achieves up to 2.24× and 1.11× the decoding throughput of state‑of‑the‑art efficient VAE decoders on NVIDIA H100 and RTX~5090, respectively, with higher DAVIS PSNR and lower LPIPS. On MiniMax‑H3, it achieves up to 2.97× the original decoding throughput while retaining 99.51% of the original model's overall VBench‑2.0 score. Our code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightVAE.

PaperId: 1038, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14717.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Minghang Du, François Gay-Balmaz, Tianzhi Li, Donghua Shi
Title: Stochastic Geometrically Exact Beams: Continuous-Time Geometric Principles and Variational Discretizations
Abstract:
Geometrically exact beams naturally arise in physical phenomena and engineering practice for modeling flexible structures, such as soft robotic manipulators and DNA structures. To the best of our knowledge, there appear to be no geometric integrators for stochastic geometrically exact beams in a variational formulation. In this paper, we introduce variational principles for the dynamics of stochastic geometrically exact beams, in both continuous‑ and discrete‑time settings. By introducing perturbations via stochastic potentials and stochastic kinematics, we derive the equations of motion from a variational viewpoint. The resulting stochastic geometric integrators simultaneously discretize time and space in a parallel manner, which provides a distributed computational framework for solving the stochastic dynamics of complex beam systems. In particular, the proposed integrators are shown to be a stochastic extension of the well‑known deterministic staggered leapfrog scheme for the wave equation, and also a stochastic extension of Yee's scheme for spatially one‑dimensional computational electromagnetism. Numerical results are shown to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches.

PaperId: 1039, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14702.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiuwu Hao, Yueyang Wu, Liguo Sun, Haolin Song, Zao Zhang, Pin Lv
Title: BGC-Nav: Cross-Altitude Multi-UAV Collaborative Navigation via Belief-Guided Coupling
Abstract:
Despite recent advances in Aerial Vision‑and‑Language Navigation (VLN), single Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) search‑and‑rescue in outdoor scenarios remains challenging due to partial observability, making cross‑altitude collaboration a promising direction. However, existing collaborative navigation methods rely on precise target localization and rigid goal‑dispatching paradigms, ignoring high‑altitude observation uncertainty and suppressing low‑altitude exploration autonomy. To address these issues, we introduce BGC‑Nav, a training‑free cross‑altitude collaboration framework that enables robust navigation via Belief‑Guided Coupling (BGC). Specifically, the high‑altitude UAV maintains a Global Belief Memory encoding task‑conditioned priors, which the low‑altitude agent incorporates into decision‑making via Local Exhaustion Memory (LEM), Local Attraction Augmentation (LAA), and Directional Belief Prior (DBP) as an advisory bias rather than a rigid command. Extensive experiments on ESARBench show that BGC‑Nav consistently outperforms state‑of‑the‑art single‑agent and collaborative methods. Code is available at https://github.com/uestchjw/BGC‑Nav.

PaperId: 1040, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14698.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yaolong Zhu, Peng Li, Jiahao Lu, Chengfeng Zhao, Mengfei Li, Chao Wang, Wenyue Chen, Zekai Gu, Chengwei Ren, Ronggang Wang, Yuan Liu
Title: PURE: Refining Feed-forward 3D Reconstruction with Unlabeled Post-training
Abstract:
Feed‑forward 3D reconstruction models have achieved remarkable progress through large‑scale training and strong learned priors. However, they remain fragile when applied to dynamic in‑the‑wild videos, where non‑rigid motion, occlusions, and illumination changes are prevalent. A key limitation lies in their reliance on expensive depth and camera pose annotations, which hinders scaling to diverse real‑world dynamic data and restricts generalization. To address this issue, we propose PURE, an unlabeled post‑training refinement framework that improves depth and camera estimation without requiring ground‑truth supervision. Instead of relying on annotations, PURE elegantly distills robust structural knowledge from state‑of‑the‑art 2D priors into 4D feed‑forward architectures. PURE leverages relative depth constraints, affine‑invariant geometry distillation, and pose refinement based on feature correspondences to stabilize geometric predictions under challenging dynamic conditions. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real‑world dynamic benchmarks demonstrate that PURE delivers consistent improvements across multiple state‑of‑the‑art architectures. Furthermore, our data‑efficient paradigm effectively mitigates domain shifts, successfully unlocking the architectural limits of these base models in challenging, in‑the‑wild dynamic scenes.

PaperId: 1041, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14697.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yixuan Li, Xuenan Xu, Zeyu Xie, Mengyue Wu
Title: AlignAudio: A Unified Dual-Alignment Framework for Noise-Robust Speech-Conditioned Generation
Abstract:
Speech‑conditioned generation maps speech signals to target audio outputs. Prior end‑to‑end speech‑conditioned generative models achieve high fidelity in clean acoustic conditions, but their performance degrades substantially under environmental noise. While prior noise‑robust approaches have achieved significant success in feature‑level purification, maintaining consistent generation under clean and noisy conditioning remains a key challenge. To address this, we propose AlignAudio, a noise‑robust generative framework based on dual alignment: (i) aligning the representations of clean and noisy speech to preserve semantic cues, and (ii) enforcing generation‑level consistency within a flow matching paradigm to improve conditioning fidelity. Experiments on speech‑to‑audio (STA) and voice conversion (VC) tasks demonstrate that AlignAudio maintains performance comparable to baselines on clean speech while significantly outperforming them across various noisy conditions. Furthermore, the proposed dual‑alignment strategy is applicable to both single‑ and multi‑stream speech conditioning and can be integrated into different flow matching‑based generation frameworks and post‑training settings. Audio demonstrations and qualitative comparisons: \hrefhttps://alignaudio.github.io/AlignAudio\textcolorcyanhttps://alignaudio.github.io/AlignAudio.

PaperId: 1042, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14694.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wenbing Yang, Qihang Lu, Zihan Sun, Peilei Jia, Yingming Gao, Ya Li, Jun Gao
Title: VoTSpeech: Decoupling Voice Design from Speech Generation in Instruction-Following TTS
Abstract:
Instruction‑following text‑to‑speech (TTS) typically leaves voice design implicit, as conventional speaker embeddings encode reference audio rather than text‑driven targets. We propose VoTSpeech, which decouples voice design from speech generation via an explicit intermediate voice latent. Built on a shared language model backbone, VoTSpeech first predicts a continuous voice latent from text instructions using a flow‑based module. This latent serves as a shared condition for both the language model and the Acoustic DiT, guiding autoregressive sequence modeling and acoustic latent generation, respectively, before an audio VAE decoder converts the acoustic latents into waveforms. To capture speaker identity and complementary acoustic nuances, the voice latent is jointly supervised by speaker embeddings and temporally pooled audio VAE features. With task‑specific adaptation, VoTSpeech performs strongly on InstructTTSEval‑ZH, demonstrating competitive capabilities against strong open‑source models while maintaining high naturalness. These results confirm that explicit voice latent design and its conditioning interface effectively empower text‑driven voice design for controllable speech synthesis. Code, model, and audio samples are available at https://github.com/ywbn/VoTSpeech .

PaperId: 1043, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14688.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhan Jin, Yuze Luo, Bin Cui, Xupeng Miao
Title: Accelerating Cross-Model LLM Inference via Attention Map Reuse
Abstract:
LLM‑augmented data workflows often involve multiple heterogeneous models operating over substantial shared context, such as schemas, tool specifications, interaction history, and intermediate results. Although prefix caching can reduce prefilling overhead, existing approaches are largely limited to reuse within the same model because KV states are tightly coupled to model‑specific architectures. We present MapFlow, a system for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving via cross‑model attention map reuse. Instead of reusing KV states, MapFlow reuses attention maps, which capture token dependency patterns and are more transferable across models. To enable efficient and accurate reuse, we combine partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads. To make attention reuse practical for long contexts, we further introduce block‑level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel. Experiments show that MapFlow reduces prefilling latency and improves end‑to‑end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous model pairs and multi‑turn routing workloads. These results suggest that attention maps provide an effective reusable state for heterogeneous LLM serving, especially in prefix‑heavy data workflows. Our code is available: https://github.com/PKU‑DAIR/MapFlow.

PaperId: 1044, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14685.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Hanxin Zhu, Jianqi Ma, Cong Wang, Zhihao Hu, Junyao Gao, Tianyu He, Junyan Lin, Jiayin Xiao, Jiateng Shou, Sen Liang, Weidong Zhang, Zhibo Chen, Jun Zhang
Title: Demiurge: Forging Navigable 4D Worlds via Autoregressive Video Rerendering
Abstract:
Recent advances in video diffusion enable novel‑view video synthesis from a single input video, supporting world modeling, embodied intelligence, and robotic simulation. However, existing methods process camera trajectories independently, lacking the cross‑trajectory consistency needed for coherent, navigable 4D worlds. We introduce Demiurge, an autoregressive video rerendering pipeline built on a dynamic 4D point‑cloud memory cache. It promotes cross‑trajectory consistency through four components: (1) an appearance video diffusion model that synthesizes photorealistic novel‑view videos conditioned on the 4D memory; (2) a memory‑consistent video depth completion model that aligns known‑region depths with cached geometry and completes missing regions, mitigating scale ambiguity and discontinuities during memory updates; (3) memory‑aware dual‑stream warping that provides high‑fidelity visual guidance and occlusion cues for novel‑view synthesis; and (4) geometry‑aware video refinement that enhances perceptual quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate state‑of‑the‑art performance and three key capabilities: coherent spatiotemporal lattice construction over dense multi‑view trajectories; large‑parallax video rerendering under challenging camera motions, including 180‑degree rotations with no input‑view overlap; and geometry‑faithful outputs that can be directly optimized into high‑quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts. Project page: https://hanxinzhu‑lab.github.io/demiurge_project_page/.

PaperId: 1045, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14676.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Pratham Gupta, Haotian Qi, Tushar Sandhan, Gabriel Skantze
Title: CAST-ASD: Causal Attention over Speakers and Time for Online Active Speaker Detection
Abstract:
We present CAST‑ASD (Causal Attention over Speakers and Time), a causal joint model for active speaker detection (ASD). Recent ASD models improve performance by jointly processing all faces in a scene, but operate offline, with the full clip available before any frame is labelled. Low‑latency causal detectors instead process each face independently. CAST‑ASD combines joint face reasoning with fully causal inference. It applies scene‑level attention across faces within the current frame and causal temporal attention over each face's history, enabling information sharing across speakers with zero lookahead. Its parameter count does not grow with the number of faces. On MSDWild, where most negative face‑frames contain a visible competing speaker, CAST‑ASD reduces competing‑speaker false alarms by 32% relative to the causal per‑face detector it extends, with larger gains as scene occupancy increases. It outperforms all causal baselines on both validation splits while using only one‑tenth the inter‑speaker parameters of a three‑block fixed‑roster convolution. Code and models are available at https://github.com/prathamg007/CAST‑ASD.

PaperId: 1046, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14659.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Daijin Hu, Xi Wang
Title: RASSG: Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating for Streaming Tool Execution
Abstract:
Streaming speech assistants can launch tools before users finish speaking, overlapping execution with incoming speech to reduce user waiting time. However, subsequent self‑corrections can invalidate apparently stable arguments, causing stale execution whose irreversible effects persist even after the final call is corrected. We propose Repair‑Aware Semantic Survival Gating (RASSG) to jointly control tool launch and cancellation during streaming speech. RASSG launches a tool when three consecutive speech recognition results arrive with identical nonempty arguments, then combines calibrated argument invalidity risk with execution costs to decide cancellation at the last feasible opportunity before effects become irreversible. Evaluation on ReCAST, FDB‑v3, and Audio2Tool uses a controlled execution clock with fixed tool runtimes and cancellation parameters. On ReCAST's prospective‑repair subset, RASSG reduces the stale execution rate from LocalAgreement‑2's 50.00% to 3.15%, with a mean delay of 3.676s across successful trajectories. The stale reduction also holds against every early‑execution baseline on both public speech datasets. Ablations with identical initial launches support active cancellation, showing the value of controlling ongoing calls before their effects become irreversible. Code and data are available at https://github.com/daijinhu/RASSG.

PaperId: 1047, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14657.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhuo Chen, Bin Zou, Fanyue Wei, Lixin Duan, Angela Yao, Wen Li
Title: TGuide: Faster Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Historical Trajectory Guidance
Abstract:
Can autoregressive video diffusion be accelerated further when only four denoising steps remain? Existing feature caching approaches struggle in this regime, as large feature changes between denoising timesteps undermine both direct reuse and lightweight predictors. We observe that features across video chunks remain strongly correlated at matching denoising timesteps, offering a complementary source of guidance. Building on this insight, we introduce TGuide, a framework that accelerates autoregressive video diffusion through a lightweight Anchor‑Transport‑Correct (ATC) predictor guided by historical sampling trajectories. Our ATC combines two complementary references: the current chunk's preceding‑step features preserve its spatial structure, while the previous chunk's same‑timestep features provide information at the target denoising stage. By integrating these references through spatial retrieval and adaptive correction, ATC improves velocity prediction accuracy despite the large gaps between denoising steps. To mitigate error accumulation across both denoising steps and video chunks, we train the predictor on its own autoregressive rollouts, allowing it to adapt to states shaped by its own earlier predictions. An optional confidence‑aware scheduler further adjusts the quality‑efficiency trade‑off. Experiments on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY‑WorldPlay show that TGuide preserves generation quality while achieving denoising speedups of up to 1.89× over the original 4‑step generators. On Self Forcing, TGuide generalizes from 81‑frame training videos to 333‑frame generation, approximately four times the training length, while exceeding the original model's VBench score.

PaperId: 1048, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14651.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Hao Zhu, Heyu Sun, Shuo Jin, Jiayu Xiao, Feng Dai
Title: TAG: Calibrating SAM3 for Universal Image Segmentation without Dense Supervision
Abstract:
The recent Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) extends powerful promptable segmentation from spatial cues to concepts, raising the prospect of a single foundation model for universal image segmentation. However, this promise often fails to translate into reliable performance on downstream segmentation tasks. In this work, we empirically identify concept recognition, rather than mask quality, as the primary bottleneck: SAM3 accurately delineates the objects it recognizes yet struggles to robustly determine which concepts are present. Driven by this, we present \underlineText \underlineAnchor re‑\underlineGrounding (\TAG), a simple yet effective framework that rectifies the concept recognition of SAM3 on the target domain without dense annotations. Specifically, \TAG introduces an Anchor Residual Pathway comprising image‑conditioned, low‑rank adapters to re‑ground text anchors in the target distribution and modulate subsequent text‑conditioned interactions. Guided solely by image‑level category labels, \TAG jointly optimizes binary cross‑entropy with Soft Boundary Ranking objectives to calibrate presence confidence and distinguish present concepts from confusable negatives. Building upon this, we devise Confidence‑Weighted Distillation to couple rich semantic context of a multimodal large language model with fine‑grained spatial priors of SAM3, thereby achieving effective calibration in the absence of manual annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \TAG unlocks SAM3's segmentation potential with only 3.1M trainable parameters, achieving impressive performance across diverse scenarios, and notably, even surpassing leading mask‑supervised methods on several metrics. \hrefhttps://github.com/MiSsU‑HH/TAG_SAM3Our code will be publicly available at GitHub \faGithub.

PaperId: 1049, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14625.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Leijun Zhou, Yanke Yu, Zhihao Liu, Qu Xiang, Tiancheng Hu, Yiru Dong, Yihan Wu, Yangxi Xiang, Xuejun Wu, Xi Chen, Buyue Qian, Yaowei Zheng, Junhao Hu
Title: From Existing Methods to New Research Ideas: Two Perspectives on Recursive Self-Improvement
Abstract:
Recursive self‑improvement (RSI) offers a route to AI systems that participate in their own continued development. Recent methods allow language agents to retain changes to their parameters, memory, skills, and code for subsequent execution and improvement. We examine how these methods can inform new research ideas through two complementary perspectives. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy with nine design dimensions organized into four groups: update targets, update organization, update schedule and scope, feedback and selection. This taxonomy places existing methods in a shared design space, where examining individual dimensions and their interactions can inspire new research ideas. Second, we examine how existing RSI methods draw on traditional deep learning, for example through optimization, regularization, data augmentation, continual learning, and adversarial learning. We develop further ideas by examining more specific learning mechanisms and drawing on evolutionary computation. We also review how existing benchmarks assess self‑improvement under online, offline, and offline‑to‑online settings. Together, these perspectives help researchers develop new RSI research ideas from existing designs and learning mechanisms. RSI papers and resources are available at https://prism‑shadow.github.io/awesome‑rsi/.

PaperId: 1050, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14624.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fadillah Adamsyah Maani, Numan Saeed, Jiaqi Ma, Dat Tien Nguyen, Youssef Wehbe, Duncan Watson-Parris, Salman Khan
Title: EarthAlign: Learning Language-Aligned Representations of Earth System Data
Abstract:
Interpreting Earth system conditions is central to understanding environmental risks and informing decisions across weather‑ and climate‑sensitive sectors. Existing multimodal weather systems primarily target task‑specific prediction, generation, or question answering, while general‑purpose alignment between Earth system data and language remains underexplored due to the limited availability of diverse language supervision grounded in meteorological conditions. To fill this gap, we introduce EarthAlign, a large‑scale dataset with broad geographic coverage spanning 2000‑2024 that combines 10 expert‑curated natural event and disaster data sources with climatology‑derived normal‑weather samples. Each sample includes temporal and geospatial information and four grounded caption styles aligned with 63‑variable ERA5 meteorological data. Building on EarthAlign, we introduce MeteoLIP, a dual‑encoder framework for learning aligned meteorology‑language representations. MeteoLIP incorporates MetTok, which uses a geolocation‑ and time‑conditioned query to aggregate variable‑specific patch embeddings into a compact sequence of meteorology tokens. To comprehensively assess Earth system multimodal representations, we introduce three downstream tasks: cross‑modal retrieval, weather‑condition classification, and physical variable estimation. Our experiments show that MeteoLIP improves upon the corresponding CLIP and SigLIP baselines across these tasks. Further analyses highlight the importance of meteorological input, temporal and geospatial conditioning, and multi‑style supervision for meteorology‑language alignment. Thus, EarthAlign and MeteoLIP provide a foundation for learning and evaluating language‑aligned representations of Earth system data. Our code, dataset, and weights are publicly available at https://github.com/mbzuai‑oryx/EarthAlign.

PaperId: 1051, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14609.pdf   GitHub
Authors:ZiAn Wang, Ruiqi Liu, Zhengbo Zhang, Yi Han, Jialiang Shen, Ruoxin Chen, Manni Cui, Ximo Zhu, Jin Jiang, Mingzhe Liu, Linhao Wang, Wenhao Wang, Shu Wu
Title: EviScene: Beyond "Is It AI?" for Agentic Image Factuality Assessment
Abstract:
Determining whether an image is AI‑generated does not establish whether the situation it depicts is factually supported. We formulate Image Factuality Assessment: given an image and a generic verification instruction, a system returns a supported or refuted verdict with an evidence‑grounded explanation. Without a supplied textual claim, the system must progressively refine factual questions during investigation and align external evidence with the specific situation depicted. We introduce EviLens, an expert‑reviewed benchmark of 10,174 supported and refuted images from controlled construction and web collection, covering twelve factual error types and evaluating both verdict accuracy and evidence sufficiency. We develop EviScene, a multimodal ReAct agent that interleaves visual inspection, external retrieval, and evidence analysis, using new findings to refine its questions and revisit relevant image details. We train a compact policy with supervised fine‑tuning on reviewed teacher trajectories, followed by privileged on‑policy self‑distillation applied to verified decisions from the policy's own investigations. On the 1,527‑image test set, the trained Qwen3.5‑9B agent achieves 79.05% balanced accuracy and a Strict Evidence Sufficiency Rate (SESR) of 52.26%, improving over the same‑backbone base agent by 6.71 and 9.37 percentage points, respectively. Its SESR is the highest among the evaluated agents.Code, models, and data will be released at https://github.com/wangzian828/EVISCENE and https://huggingface.co/ZiAnwang/EviScene.

PaperId: 1052, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14596.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qi Yin, XiaoLi Zhang, Yangming Shi
Title: Load-Aware Quadruped Navigation with Online Contact-based Geometry Estimation
Abstract:
Navigating cluttered environments while carrying objects remains a challenging problem for quadruped robots. Compared with works that focused on load‑aware locomotion adaptation to maintain gait stability, existing autonomous navigation systems generally ignore the influence of carried objects' geometries and use fixed footprint inflation, leading to overly conservative navigation. To fill this knowledge gap, we propose a two‑phase load‑aware navigation learning framework. In Phase 1, we train LOADNav, a load‑aware navigation policy via reinforcement learning, enabling the robot to adapt its trajectory and clearance behavior according to the geometric size of the carried object. In Phase 2, we train CoGE, an online geometry predictor via imitation learning, which estimates unknown payload geometry from occasional contact events. We evaluate the framework in cluttered environments with loads of varying sizes and shapes. The results show that our navigation policy exhibits clear load‑aware behaviors, and the online geometry predictor estimates object geometry from occasional contact events, refining its estimate and adapting the navigation behavior accordingly. Without requiring any prior knowledge of the payload, it narrows the gap to geometry‑aware policies.

PaperId: 1053, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14594.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Li Jin, Jiang Wenbin, Chen Tao, Wen Fei
Title: SpikCTU: A Compact Spiking Network with Adaptive Recurrent Computation for Speech Command Recognition
Abstract:
Spiking Neural Networks offer event‑driven, energy‑efficient computation for speech command recognition, yet most existing methods follow fixed computation paths, allocating redundant computation to easy samples while providing limited insight into how evidence evolves during inference. To address these challenges, we introduce SpikCTU, a compact spiking network with adaptive recurrent computation for speech command recognition. Specifically, a hybrid spiking embedding module preserves continuous input information alongside spike features to construct a fixed temporal memory. A shared Continuous Thinking Unit (CTU) repeatedly reads this memory using keys derived from spikes and continuous values, and updates a binary recurrent state with lightweight stage adapters. Furthermore, combining a fixed base prediction with accumulated corrections at each step enables learned aggregation over all steps or confidence‑based early exit using only the predictions available so far. Experiments on three speech command recognition benchmarks show that SpikCTU achieves competitive accuracy with only 0.16‑‑0.17M parameters, and the early exit strategy can substantially further reduce computational cost without compromising accuracy. In addition, trajectory and attention analyses reveal that recurrent steps enable error correction and progressively refine predictions. Code is available at https://github.com/Rivflyyy/spikctu.

PaperId: 1054, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14578.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yongyuan Li, Yang Xu
Title: Uniform Information Density-Based Preference Optimization
Abstract:
To enable large language models to generate outputs that align with human preferences, optimization algorithms based on the comparison between chosen and rejected output pairs have been developed and been proven effective. Some recent endeavors have utilized certain linguistically‑derived assumptions about the preference pairs to guide the design of more precise optimization directions. However, human preferences are complex and hard to measure by simplistic criteria, and it is important to incorporate broader and more sophisticated insights about preferred vs. not‑preferred language. In this study, we adopt a well‑established psycholinguistic theory, Uniform Information Density, to develop a novel preference optimization algorithm, UIDPO. The basic assumption is that humans prefer to produce language in which information is uniformly distributed, because uniformity induces less cognitive processing effort. To implement this idea into the algorithm, we derive a compound metric for information uniformity by combining the global standard deviation and the local second‑order difference, and integrate it to the objective of preference optimization. We compare UIDPO with SimPO, a previous state‑of‑the‑art method, obtaining comparable and sometimes better performance on AlpacaEval2, ArenaHard, and MT‑Bench. Additional linguistic analysis on complement clauses also shows that UIDPO can better reflect the tendencies of keeping information uniform in natural language than baselines. Our results show that the subtle human preference over the information rate in language is a helpful source for achieving better human alignment for LLMs. The code repository is published here: https://github.com/CLCS‑SUSTech/UIDPO.

PaperId: 1055, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14573.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yufeng Tian, Jiahao Tang, Minghao Wu
Title: Learning after Execution with Action-Specific Credit
Abstract:
Execution is often used as terminal feedback: it scores a generated program, but the resulting state is not used for another learning action. Learning after execution instead uses the execution result as an intermediate state that supports an additional learning interaction for the same policy. This creates a credit‑assignment problem because the two actions share the same final objective but play different roles in the trajectory. Accordingly, action‑specific credit assigns the initial action credit from the final trajectory outcome and the corrective action credit for improvement over the intermediate state. Image‑to‑TikZ serves as an executable visual testbed for this setting. On 945 held‑out examples, learning after execution strengthens the shared policy under single‑call inference and also produces a post‑execution corrective capability. Single‑call render success reaches 92.70%, compared with 88.25% for continued single‑stage GRPO after the same number of additional training iterations. This corrective capability is not reproduced by continued single‑stage training and depends on the intermediate state. Alternative credit definitions also induce different group‑relative preferences over the same trajectories. Together, these results suggest that executable tasks contain useful learning structure beyond a terminal reward. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyufengcn/Learning‑after‑Execution.

PaperId: 1056, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14571.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Burak Topcu, Musa Cim, Zuhal Ozturk, Mahmut Taylan Kandemir
Title: Dissecting the Carbon-SLO Tension in Geo-Distributed LLM Serving
Abstract:
Large Language Model (LLM) inference is driving a growing share of datacenter carbon emissions. Although carbon‑aware scheduling can reduce these emissions in geo‑distributed datacenters by exploiting the spatiotemporal variations in grid carbon intensity, the latency‑sensitive nature of LLM serving constrains this design space. While prior studies investigate the carbon savings achievable through spatial scheduling, they oversimplify the dynamics of modern inference engines, such as queueing and continuous batching, which strongly shape inference latency. We address this issue by designing and evaluating a latency‑centric, geo‑distributed inference simulator, calibrated with hardware‑grounded latency and power measurements, that reproduces these dynamics and enables the study of carbon savings under strict service‑level objectives (SLOs). We then formulate a series of SLO‑ and carbon‑aware schedulers of increasing sophistication, from per‑request heuristics to batch‑level optimization: (i) a greedy heuristic, (ii) an integer linear programming (ILP)‑based scheduler jointly assigning batches of requests, (iii) an iterative ILP‑based solution projecting its own assignments back into the load estimates to capture load coupling, and (iv) a facility mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) scheduler pricing the energy of batched requests collectively rather than in isolation. Across three LLMs under MLPerf SLOs and varying system loads, the MILP‑based option offers the best carbon‑SLO balance, reducing carbon emissions by up to 60% relative to the round‑robin policy, with an average SLO violation of 3%. Our characterization further shows that savings grow with the spread of carbon intensity across datacenters and shrink as system load increases, while SLO attainment depends on how frequently schedulers receive datacenters' load updates.

PaperId: 1057, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14564.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Weixi Song, Donglin Wang, Yong-Lu Li
Title: Chunk-wise Model-based Policy Optimization
Abstract:
Model‑based reinforcement learning has shown superior sample efficiency by leveraging the learned latent dynamics either in the form of derivative‑free planning/imagined rollout training or dynamics gradient‑based policy updates. While these approaches achieve comparatively fast learning, they all suffer, to varying degrees, from issues of recurrent compounding errors, high inference‑time latency, and instability in backward propagation through time (BPTT). In this work, we propose a model‑based RL approach that uses the chunk world model as a differentiable training‑time evaluator to optimize the chunk actor without recurrent model invocation. Through the collaborative chunk‑wise prediction of the world model and policy, we can generate H‑step hypothetical rollouts in a single forward pass and directly optimize value expansion, avoiding the costly and unstable BPTT. We evaluate our method on 19 challenging high‑dimensional humanoid tasks from HumanoidBench and deploy our method to the real‑world for quadruped bipedal walking. Project Website: https://song‑wx.github.io/cmpo.github.io/

PaperId: 1058, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14558.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Muqing Liu, Chongjie Si, Zhuoya Liu, Yuheng Jia
Title: PGSB: Pretrained-Guided Shared Basis for LoRA Model Merging
Abstract:
Large pretrained models have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, yet adapting them to multiple downstream tasks remains challenging: full fine‑tuning is costly, while maintaining separate task‑specific models is storage‑inefficient and fails to produce a unified multi‑task model. Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) offers an efficient alternative for Model Merging by representing each task adaptation as a low‑rank update over frozen pretrained weights. However, existing LoRA merging methods often treat task‑specific updates as directly comparable objects and merge them in their original low‑rank parameter spaces. This overlooks two key factors: which update directions provide reliable shared support across tasks, and how these directions should be re‑parameterized with respect to the pretrained weights before merging. To address this limitation, we propose Pretrained‑Guided Shared Basis (PGSB), a two‑stage framework for LoRA model merging. PGSB first identifies shared directions among task‑specific LoRA updates, and then re‑parameterizes these directions using their interaction with the pretrained weights, producing a more suitable basis for merging. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PGSB consistently outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines across multiple benchmarks. Codes are available at https://github.com/Kitschnada/Pretrained‑Basis .

PaperId: 1059, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14553.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Chenxi Xia, Yixuan Xu, Shan Liu, Jiapeng Wang, Maohua Li, Hanlin Tang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan, Weiyi Lu, Xinggao Liu
Title: Adversarial Gradient Forcing for Robust Few-Step Autoregressive Video Generation
Abstract:
Autoregressive video generation models generate videos sequentially, with each new block conditioned on previously generated blocks. By training on the model's own rollouts, Self Forcing and its follow‑up methods substantially mitigate exposure bias caused by the mismatch between training‑ and inference‑time history distributions. However, these models still suffer from error accumulation during long‑horizon generation. We identify a key underlying limitation: the model remains highly sensitive to errors in its generated history, allowing small deviations to be amplified through subsequent generations. We refer to this underexplored problem as the local history robustness gap. To address this gap, we introduce Adversarial Gradient Forcing (AGF), a framework designed to improve the robustness of few‑step autoregressive video models to perturbations and accumulated errors in their own generated histories. AGF uses distribution matching gradients from future block predictions to select adversarial perturbations of self‑generated histories. It then jointly trains the generator on the original and perturbed histories to improve the robustness of future generation. Extensive experiments show that AGF achieves the highest VBench Total score on 60‑second video generation and the best visual quality on four‑minute video generation. Notably, AGF achieves such long‑horizon robustness while requiring only 5‑second rollouts for training.

PaperId: 1060, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14551.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zihao Li, Yanan Zhou, Ranpeng Qiu, Guoqiang Ren, Weiming Zhi
Title: Before We Act: Learning Action-Conditioned Team-Response Beliefs for Decentralized Multi-Robot Manipulation
Abstract:
In multi‑robot manipulation, an action's value depends on how teammates respond. We present \method (Cooperative Action‑‑Response Belief Estimation), a framework for learning \emphteam‑response beliefs from local history. A predictive belief encoder represents the interaction and conditions a nominal action. Matched reactive and replay continuations separate each candidate's direct advantage from the utility contributed by teammate adaptation. A candidate‑conditioned readout learns this response distribution alongside total advantage, and calibrated selection chooses an alternative or retains the nominal action. Our analysis characterizes when response changes the preferred action and how prediction and source errors limit the recoverable gain. With the representation, proposals, and data fixed, explicit response supervision improves candidate ranking and reduces selection regret relative to learning the same information through branch utilities. The benefit is concentrated in decisions where teammate adaptation changes the preferred action. Across RoboFactory, the MARS Control Track, and physical collaboration tasks, CARE achieves the highest average success among the evaluated policies, combining a capable nominal policy with selective coordination adjustments. Together, these results show that CARE turns predictions of teammate adaptation into effective decentralized action selection. Project page: https://jeong‑zju.github.io/care/.

PaperId: 1061, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14547.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shihang Li, Thomas Anderson, Ratul Mahajan, Simon Peter, Luke Zettlemoyer
Title: A Self-Defining Operator for Distributed Applications
Abstract:
To operate distributed applications with high availability, operators must rapidly diagnose and mitigate any incident. LLM‑based agents can help, but unlike experienced human operators they do not improve as they handle more incidents. Each investigation starts from scratch, re‑deriving likely causes and re‑testing hypotheses even when a similar fault was resolved in the past. We present a self‑defining operator (SDO) that improves with time by updating its operational behavior and memory. When SDO resolves an incident, it distills that experience into playbooks, which describe reusable diagnostic instructions for future incidents with similar faults, and detectors, scripts that take application telemetry as input and output relevant playbook(s). SDO continuously runs the detectors and invokes LLMs only when one fires, so its token cost scales with incident count rather than with operational time. Across 11 open‑source microservice applications, SDO cuts resolution time by 52% on recurring faults while keeping per‑incident cost low. SDO is open source at https://github.com/self‑defining‑systems/sdo.

PaperId: 1062, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14541.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shaohao Zhu, Wensi Huang, Siqi Zhang, Yuqiang Yang, Meng Wei, Chenyang Wan, Tianle Liu, Tai Wang, Jinming Xu
Title: GG-Nav: Goal-oriented Grounding Chain-of-Thought Elicits Reasoning in Navigation Foundation Models
Abstract:
Emerging strong Vision‑Language Models (VLMs) have advanced navigation foundation models. However, these models still have unsatisfactory performance on goal‑oriented navigation settings. In this paper, we first conduct a motivating study revealing that the key issue lies in the insufficient utilization of streaming observations and imprecise target localization. To tackle these challenges, we propose GG‑Nav, a simple yet effective navigation framework that learns a structured chain‑of‑thought (CoT) mechanism via supervised fine‑tuning to explicitly localize goal‑relevant instances, accumulate grounding evidence, and support more reliable decision‑making. Specifically, the structured CoT is designed with two key stages: (i) Observation‑to‑Evidence, which reasons over all intermediate frames between adjacent decision steps to retain useful goal‑related evidence; and (ii) Evidence‑to‑Decision, which integrates the current observation with accumulated evidence to ground the target and support the generation of navigation actions or clarification questions. Extensive experiments show that GG‑Nav outperforms the state‑of‑the‑art methods in terms of success rates on the HM3D ObjectNav, VL‑LN, and CoIN benchmarks by 3.1%, 16.6%, and 5.3%, respectively. Ablation studies further show that accumulating evidence from intermediate observations reduces evidence‑missing failures by 11.6%, while explicit grounding reduces stopping errors by 49.4%. We also deploy GG‑Nav on a Unitree Go2 robot, demonstrating its zero‑shot generalization capability in unseen real‑world environments.

PaperId: 1063, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14539.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Huaiming Li, Can Huang, Chufan Wu, Danyu Liu, Xiaomin Yuan, Qinze Li, Yui Lo, Wenhui Bai, Qianlong Wang, Zengle Ge, Xiyu Yan, Yuheng Cheng, Jinhui Ren, Guokai Chen, Jiaqun Liu, Haoran Li, Qianhui Liu, Annan Li, Jianmin Wu, Dawei Yin, Dou Shen
Title: FDE-Bench: Evaluating End-to-End Delivery from Underspecified Real-World Business Requests
Abstract:
Real‑world business requests often leave key requirements unstated because frontline practitioners struggle to articulate rules they know from experience. Forward‑deployed engineers (FDEs) must elicit these requirements through dialogue and iteratively optimize solutions until they meet customer acceptance criteria. Existing optimization benchmarks typically start from explicit objectives, while clarification benchmarks often introduce information gaps into existing tasks. We introduce FDE‑Bench, the first benchmark built from real customer projects to evaluate agents on end‑to‑end delivery tasks that require interactive requirement clarification and iterative optimization. Its 49 cases span combinatorial optimization and machine learning. Clarification targets are distilled from discussions between frontline practitioners and FDEs. Agents elicit missing requirements from a simulated customer, and case‑specific evaluators assess final artifacts against acceptance criteria using customer‑accepted FDE solutions as quality references. Across 18 agent configurations, the highest mean delivery score is only 0.5510, compared with an FDE reference of 1.0. The highest delivery success rate (DSR), defined as the fraction of planned runs reaching this reference, is only 6.12%. These results show that reliable FDE‑level end‑to‑end delivery remains out of reach for the evaluated agents on underspecified real‑world business tasks. The benchmark project page is available at https://baidubce.github.io/FM‑Agent/FDE‑Bench/.

PaperId: 1064, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14531.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zeyu Shan, Yongxin Shi, Shihang Wu, Peirong Zhang, Yuanyuan Fang, Zhaopeng Wang, Lianwen Jin
Title: LongHisDoc: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Long Historical Document Understanding
Abstract:
Chinese historical documents are invaluable cultural treasures, but their complexity poses significant comprehension challenges for non‑specialists. Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Vision‑Language Models (LVLMs) in modern document tasks, their capabilities in Long (full‑book) Historical Document understanding remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce LongHisDoc, the first benchmark tailored for long historical document understanding. LongHisDoc comprises 1,012 expert‑annotated QA pairs derived from 101 PDF documents, with an average of 85.1 pages and 42,776.4 tokens per document. It spans 10 categories and features four QA types: single‑page, cross‑page, multi‑hop, and unanswerable. Answering these questions requires integrating multimodal evidence from text, layout, and visual elements. Our evaluation reveals that the top‑performing LVLM and LLM achieve only 62.9% and 69.9% accuracy, respectively, highlighting a substantial performance gap.
