Furthermore, we assess various modal retrievers and the end‑to‑end RAG performance to provide references for Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. We believe that LongHisDoc serves as a comprehensive benchmark to catalyze future research in full‑book historical document understanding. The benchmark and evaluation code are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/qweq12433454/LongHisDoc and https://github.com/SCUT‑DLVCLab/LongHisDoc.

PaperId: 1065, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14517.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Benyuan Meng, Longtao Huang, Yang Liu, Liang Lin
Title: We Have Been Interpreting Diffusion Transformer Backbone Behaviors Wrong
Abstract:
During a network forward call, diffusion backbones naturally produce many intermediate activations. If we evaluate each activation against an identical downstream benchmarking protocol, we can plot an inverted‑U‑shaped curve as the depth profile: the activation's performance goes up first and then down as we go into deeper layers. This is common knowledge in the diffusion model community, which inspires many applications including the widely‑adopted REPA. However, the common interpretation of this depth profile may be inaccurate and incomplete: (i) The cause of this curve has long been treated as signal granularity changing from coarse to fine, but there has been little evidence in DiT backbones. (ii) The community has been mainly studying this phenomenon in a static way, without investigating how it changes across different training setups. In this work, we show a different mechanism picture for the profile, where the prediction target (e.g., ε, u, x_0) sits at the center. The semantically meaningful signal is only an intermediate by‑product for predicting the target, while the prediction target is the real goal for the backbone. Furthermore, the choice of prediction targets as part of the training setup can predictably affect the curve's shape. With this updated interpretation, many applications of this depth profile can be better grounded and predicted. As an example, we show how to predict the near‑optimal placement of REPA based on the prediction target of the training setup. The code is at https://github.com/Darkbblue/dit‑compare.

PaperId: 1066, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14515.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yi Liu, Junwei Zhao, Li Sun, Jiansong Zhang, Sen Su
Title: SEPM: Self-Evolving Procedural Memory Grounded in Task Graphs for Multi-Agent Collaboration
Abstract:
Long‑horizon multi‑agent collaboration requires memory that preserves both successful actions and the coordination structure underlying them. Existing memory systems support information sharing or procedural reuse, but often leave the evolution of shared procedures disconnected from the task dependencies and execution states of collaborating agents. This coupling also limits the direct transfer of procedural memory designed for individual agents to team settings. We propose Self‑Evolving Procedural Memory (SEPM), a framework that uses task dependency graphs as a common representation for online coordination and procedural memory evolution. During execution, a lightweight shared blackboard records structured evidence alongside task dependencies, supporting the detection of goal, plan, and world‑state divergence and evidence‑based realignment. After execution, verified actions and dependencies are distilled into reusable procedures, while recurring failures inform warnings and constraints. The shared procedure pool evolves through creation, refinement, specialization, and retirement, guided by success and cost utility and constrained by evidence and safety requirements. Together, these mechanisms preserve the collaborative structure and applicability conditions needed to reuse experience across tasks. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebArena, and OfficeBench under AutoGen and DyLAN show that SEPM achieves the highest task scores among the compared methods in all six benchmark settings. Under AutoGen, it improves task scores over the no‑added‑memory baseline by 29.85, 25.86, and 13.00 percentage points, respectively. The codebase is available at https://github.com/cookieApril/SEPM.

PaperId: 1067, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14507.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Sudarshan Regmi, Nabaraj Subedi, Arvind Pillai, Yu Yvonne Wu, Yuliang Chen, Michael V. Heinz, Lisa Marsch, Nicholas C. Jacobson, Andrew Campbell
Title: MontageFlow: Physically Valid High Fidelity EEG Generation
Abstract:
Generative modeling offers a promising solution to the scarcity of labeled clinical electroencephalography (EEG) data under strict privacy constraints. Although recent generative models report substantial improvements in generation fidelity, we show that these gains conceal a categorical failure. EEG is not an arbitrary multichannel signal: each channel records the voltage difference between two scalp electrodes. So, real recordings satisfy exact linear identities among their channels. Current generators invariably violate these identities, yet this has gone unnoticed. We therefore propose MontageFlow, a flow‑matching model that enforces these identities by restricting its output to signals that satisfy them. We find that ensuring validity improves fidelity too. Furthermore, to retain the EEG characteristics that oversmoothing washes out, we also condition the model on a physiological state vector encoded from the whole EEG window. For generation, this vector is drawn from a prior fitted in latent space. Across 3 large‑scale benchmarks, our model improves TS‑FID by 1.6‑3.6× over the closest rival while ensuring validity.

PaperId: 1068, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14495.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wei Lin
Title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos
Abstract:
Explainer videos ‑‑ a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell ‑‑ are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per‑frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels‑RSI is an open‑source reel director for any agent harness; its self‑improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must‑fail and a must‑pass example, so the memory is unit‑tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark‑gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held‑out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels ‑‑ a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48‑reel learning curve and a judge‑reliability study ‑‑ we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11‑‑1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second‑shown reel 62‑‑81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.

PaperId: 1069, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14488.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Daniel Commey
Title: Names Are Not Objects: Object-Bound Confinement for Compromised AI Coding Agents
Abstract:
Coding agents read repositories and web pages that anyone can write, and then act with their user's authority. Prompt‑injection defenses make it less likely that the model is steered but do not prevent it, so the system around the model must contain an agent that is already compromised. Many exploits against deployed coding agents share one cause: a check approves a name, such as a path, an argument vector, or a directory, and a later step maps that name to a different object: the file behind a symlink, the behavior an option selects, or a repository that git discovers on its own. We present Zero‑Trust Agent Cells (ZTAC). A cell runs the agent in a kernel sandbox whose only route to files, programs, and the network is a socket to a broker. The broker resolves each request to the object it will act on, decides on that object, and checks at use that it is acting on the object it authorized. Programs that the broker starts run in a sandbox compiled from the same policy, and approvals are bound to the resolved object and can be used once. Our macOS prototype has 3.2k lines of trusted Rust code, excluding dependencies. We evaluate it against 74 attacks with ground‑truth oracles, including replays of 10 publicly disclosed incidents. A tool allowlist loses 66 of them, and an allowlist combined with the kind of command sandbox that deployed agents use loses 56. ZTAC loses 2, both of which encode a secret into traffic to an allowed endpoint, and holds 14 for review. It completes 43 of 46 benign operations, with 8 approval prompts, and 4 of 7 workflows. A no‑op brokered request has a median latency of 4.0 ms, and the spawned programs we measured take 8.5 ms to 18.4 ms longer than without ZTAC.

PaperId: 1070, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14483.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Milind Srivastava, Zeying Zhu, Peilin Xin, Yancheng Yuan, Zaoxing Liu, Vyas Sekar
Title: TurboProm: Low Cost and High Performance Metrics Observability at Scale
Abstract:
Many large enterprise and cloud deployments rely on metrics observability solutions (e.g., Prometheus) to monitor key performance indicators of system health (e.g., CPU, memory, network, app‑level statistics). Monitoring and analyzing these metrics presents a significant challenge in terms of cost‑latency tradeoffs at scale. Ideally, system operators would like immediately deployable and backwards compatible solutions to improve the cost‑latency tradeoffs without significant impact on the fidelity of their observability applications. Unfortunately, existing solutions including state‑of‑art timeseries databases and custom approximate querying solutions fail on one or more aspects. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of TurboProm, a backwards‑compatible drop‑in accelerator for metrics observability deployments. TurboProm recasts metrics analytics tasks using a semantic‑preserving summary view rather than classical query‑centric view. Instead of estimating query results on raw timeseries metrics data, TurboProm uses semantic‑preserving summaries that enable high‑fidelity analytics with significant cost‑latency improvements. We present a practical implementation of TurboProm that can be retrofitted to any existing observability deployment. We evaluate TurboProm on diverse real and synthetic workloads against state‑of‑art solutions and show that it can provide significant reduction in query latency and cost. TurboProm is open‑source at https://github.com/ProjectASAP/ASAPQuery.

PaperId: 1071, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14474.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Cong Wang, Jin Li, Shoujin Wang, Yishuo Li, Huilin Gu, Wenpeng Lu
Title: RES-MR: Risk-Aware Reasoning for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation
Abstract:
Medication recommendations seek to deliver personalized drug combinations based on patients' clinical information, where ensuring transparent decision‑making and personalized safety are of paramount importance. However, existing approaches predominantly operate as ``black boxes'', offering limited interpretability and hindering clinician trust. Furthermore, they typically rely on fixed, patient‑agnostic safety constraints, neglecting the heterogeneity of risk tolerance across individuals, which poses significant risks to vulnerable populations. To address these gaps, we propose RES‑MR, a novel Risk‑aware Reasoning framework for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation using LLMs. RES‑MR follows a two‑stage training paradigm: (1) an explainable clinical reasoning distillation stage to elicit diagnostic capabilities by fine‑tuning on synthesized reasoning trajectories, grounded in patient‑specific knowledge from graph retrieval; and (2) a risk‑aware policy optimization stage to dynamically balance therapeutic efficacy with personalized safety. This stage employs disentangled drug factors to construct patient‑specific reference prototypes that capture desired therapeutic drug features and risk features to avoid. These prototypes enable risk boundary calibration and guide the model toward safe recommendations via reward shaping and clipping. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that RES‑MR significantly outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines in terms of accuracy, safety, and explainability. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/wangcong2001/RES‑MR.

PaperId: 1072, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14470.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Abhishek Sharma
Title: When Is a Reconciliation Break Real? A Temporal Correctness Contract for Streaming Financial Reconciliation
Abstract:
Reconciliation systems decide, continuously, whether money the ledger expected has arrived at the bank. On an asynchronous stream that decision is taken against partial evidence: a credit that has not appeared may be missing, or may simply not have been posted yet. Deployed pipelines settle this with a timeout or a watermark, and the exceptions are treated as findings. We give a temporal correctness contract that says when such a verdict is admissible, relative to a declared per‑source lateness bound, and a checker for it that needs no ground truth. The contract separates three things an operator otherwise sees only as a rising break rate: the reconciler decided too early, an input broke the bound it declared, or the money really is gone. On workloads from a published payment simulator, the standard remedy for a stalled streaming join, an idleness timeout, introduces contract violations on 5.42% of obligations (95% CI [3.94, 6.92]) on traffic where the same job without it is exactly sound, and violations vanish once the timeout reaches the slow source's posting period, as predicted. Under a lateness shift, all four identity‑based reconcilers we test raise spurious breaks on between 18.3% and 23.0% of the credits the bank did settle, while their contract violation rate stays at or below 1.01%: the checker attributes the loss to 240 bank‑side and 413 ledger‑side bound violations rather than to the reconcilers. Tracking one horizon per source leaves break latency 12.7% lower on average and halves its tail (p99 224 against 446 ticks) at equal soundness, though it is not cheaper at every cost setting and we report where it loses. An Apache Flink interval join, written the ordinary way, violates the contract on 14.9‑‑20.1% of obligations. The contract is expressible as SQL over the tables a reconciliation system already keeps, agreeing with the reference implementation on all 4,395 verdicts.

PaperId: 1073, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14445.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiayi Wu, Tianfu Wang, Rui Zhao, Florian Schiffers, Zhimin Chen, Cornelia Fermuller, Yezhou Yang, Christopher Metzler, Yiannis Aloimonos
Title: FreeCHROMA: Generative Chroma Keying from Unaligned Background References
Abstract:
In film production, chroma keying composites an approved foreground performance into a new environment, but conventional workflows require coordinated background plates and dedicated harmonization. Recent generative methods often require pre‑aligned backgrounds, focus on background‑conditioned foreground relighting, or represent the environment only through an edited first frame. These restrictions limit background selection, scene composition, and camera motion while adding preparation or editing effort. We present FreeCHROMA, which adapts a pretrained video diffusion model in a parameter‑efficient manner for generative video compositing from one to three unaligned background references. The model integrates the foreground into the referenced environment, preserving foreground identity, motion, and fine visual details while generating a spatiotemporally coherent background. Foreground‑background harmonization occurs within the same generation process, without a separate relighting stage. Optional text instructions help disambiguate complex spatial relationships and camera behavior. To train the model, we construct pseudo‑paired data from readily available real monocular videos through foreground‑background separation and augmentation with existing foundation models. The original videos serve as training targets, while automated processing and quality verification enable scalable data construction. Across reference fidelity, foreground preservation, scene integration, harmonization, and overall video quality, FreeCHROMA consistently outperforms recent compositing and conditional video‑generation baselines, with particularly clear gains under camera motion. FreeCHROMA relaxes the constraints of existing tools to enable end‑to‑end generative chroma keying from unaligned inputs, with exploratory experiments demonstrating its potential in robotics.

PaperId: 1074, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14439.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chaoyue Li, Shoudong Han, Haoyang Wu, Boxue Yang, Sijia Chen, Yufan Chen, Ruping Zhang
Title: SceneForesee: Learning Scene Evolution for Spatiotemporal Reasoning
Abstract:
Large multimodal models (LMMs) need to understand how entities move and interact as a scene develops. This requires following the same entities over time and relating their observed motion to subsequent changes. We formulate Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU), a task for predicting and interpreting this change. Given observed video, a model estimates entity histories and predicts one scene continuation through future trajectories and Events, accompanied by Visual Evidence from observed motion and a scene description. We construct SceneForesee, a benchmark for evaluating entity continuity and scene evolution reasoning through paired observed and future scenes with shared entity identities. It contains 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K Events paired with observed evidence. We propose a spatiotemporal reasoning framework, EvoSee, that learns future geometry and Event semantics through shared candidate states and joint assignment. It selects one continuation per entity from observation and uses the selected changes for entity refinement, retention, and scene representation. On SceneForesee, EvoSee outperforms Qwen3.5‑9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point‑F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1. On the 4D reasoning benchmark Dyn‑Bench, it improves question answering accuracy and grounding J&F by 4.8 and 3.58 points over their respective base systems. These results support scene evolution as both a prediction target and a dynamic representation that brings predicted entity changes into spatiotemporal reasoning.The project is available at https://github.com/mikubaka88/SceneForesee‑Spatiotemporal‑Reasoning.

PaperId: 1075, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14431.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haowen Pan, Pengyang Shao, Yunshan Ma, Yanzheng Jin, Naixin Zhai, Xiang Wang, Xun Yang
Title: MemForm: Benchmarking Memory Formation Poisoning in LLM Agents
Abstract:
Long‑term memory enables LLM agents to learn from past interactions but exposes memory formation to adversarial influence. Existing studies primarily organize memory poisoning by attack channels, corruption patterns, or lifecycle stages, leaving formation interfaces insufficiently characterized. We formulate Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of the interfaces through which persistent agent memory is produced and committed, and introduce MemForm, a controlled diagnostic benchmark covering five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning. We introduce Selection and Path Poisoning as controlled intervention categories that isolate retention and consolidation order effects, respectively. Each category pairs clean and poisoned conditions with interface‑specific controls. Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats reveal broad susceptibility at all five interfaces under the evaluated memory protocols and implementations. Crucially, authentic experiences with successful outcomes do not guarantee reliable behavior after memory formation: changes to contextual support, retention, or consolidation order can induce undesirable downstream behavior. In particular, consolidation order can alter behavior even with identical retained experiences, depending on the memory formation procedure. Additional analyses show that interface applicability depends on memory architecture and that Path Poisoning susceptibility depends on the updater. The evaluated defenses provide incomplete mitigation that varies by interface. These findings motivate protecting both what is committed to persistent memory and how memory is formed from experiences. Code and data are available at https://github.com/opanhw/memform‑code.

PaperId: 1076, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14419.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Abhishek Sharma
Title: HoldSpec: A Machine-Checked Model and Conformance Suite for the Payment Authorization Hold Lifecycle
Abstract:
When a merchant authorizes a card and captures the funds later, the money sits in a state that neither party fully controls: held on the cardholder's account, not yet taken, and due to lapse on a deadline set by the card network. What a merchant may do to that hold, capture part of it, capture again, void it, raise it, let it expire, is business logic that every payment service provider implements slightly differently and none of them specifies formally. We give the lifecycle a state machine in TLA+, parameterized by a provider capability profile, and check eight safety invariants and three liveness properties over 6 profiles, five of them built from Stripe's and Adyen's published documentation. From the same machine we generate a conformance suite that runs black‑box against a provider API. Against 61 seeded defects that are distinguishishable from a correct implementation, the generated suite detects 100%, where random sequences with the same call budget reach 56% and a hand‑written integration suite reaches 69%; random sequences given ten times the budget still reach only 67%. Running the same suite between two providers turns the comparison into a search, and it returns short executable witnesses for divergences the two documentation sets imply but neither states, including one that breaks the common assumption that a single adapter interface can sit over both, because closing a hold and releasing its remainder is a capture on one provider and a cancel on the other. We report what we could not do: no provider sandbox credentials were available, so every result here concerns documented behavior, and the suite that would test the providers themselves is part of what we release.

PaperId: 1077, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14415.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shihan Zhao, Henry Chen, Ya-Chuan Hsu, Minjune Hwang, Siddharth Srikanth, Freddie Liang, Akanksha Saran, Aaquib Tabrez, Stefanos Nikolaidis, Daniel Seita
Title: Red-Teaming of Vision-Language-Action Models via Quality Diversity Environment Generation
Abstract:
A long‑standing goal in robotics is to develop generalist robots that can perform tasks across a wide range of settings, flexibly specified with images and text. Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward this goal by training on large collections of robot demonstrations. However, while VLAs perform well in‑distribution, they often fail under minor test‑time shifts, such as changes in object positions, lighting, textures, and camera poses. To address this, we propose Quality Diversity for Diverse Environment Generation (Q‑DEG), a method for improving VLA robustness by generating adversarial environments and fine‑tuning the VLA on its own successful rollouts. Q‑DEG uses Quality Diversity (QD) optimization to find a set of high‑failure environments, while promoting diversity using policy embeddings extracted from the VLA. These environments expose vulnerabilities that can be mitigated through self‑imitation fine‑tuning, thereby improving the VLA's robustness. In simulation, we conduct experiments across three representative VLA models, and our results indicate that Q‑DEG improves robustness to out‑of‑distribution (OOD) adversarial environments compared to the base VLA and VLAs fine‑tuned using data collected from two red‑teaming baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that improving VLA robustness through Q‑DEG facilitates sim‑to‑real transfer. Our anonymous project website is at: https://qd‑env.github.io/qdeg/.

PaperId: 1078, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14406.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yilin Wu, Rutav Shah, Shuaiyi Huang, Sumedh A. Sontakke, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Andrea Bajcsy, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi
Title: Memory Without Curation: Learning Multi-Stream Latent Memory for Robot Policies
Abstract:
It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long‑term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory‑augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy‑agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision‑language‑action (VLA) models with multi‑stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember. IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency. To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two‑stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end‑to‑end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction. Across both simulation and real‑world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory‑augmented VLAs. Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. Project website: https://yilin‑wu98.github.io/imprint_website/.

PaperId: 1079, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14403.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Liu Jiaqi, Jin Ruinan, Li Xiaoxiao
Title: VisualCoding: Learning Executable Skills for Reliable Visual Reasoning
Abstract:
Learning reusable skills can improve visual reasoning agents, yet applying a skill still requires the agent to implement or invoke a procedure and produce the final answer. Errors and hallucinations at these steps can prevent acquired experience from translating into reliable single‑run performance. We propose VisualCoding, which combines execution‑guided acquisition of reusable visual programs with direct adoption of their answers on applicable inputs. Execution‑Guided Program Acquisition composes visual primitives and additional code into family‑level solvers, then iteratively tests and revises them on labeled training instances. Scope‑Aware Direct Execution runs a retained solver and returns its valid in‑scope answer. We evaluate VisualCoding on four models across four benchmarks spanning 69 task families. VisualCoding exceeds the strongest evaluated baseline in mean accuracy by 4.45 percentage points with Gemini‑3.1‑Pro and by 14.78 points when reusing the frozen Pro‑acquired artifacts with Flash‑Lite. Ablations support execution‑guided acquisition and show that direct execution outperforms textual or callable reuse of the same programs. Code is available at https://github.com/jiaq‑liu/VisualCoding.

PaperId: 1080, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14402.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jialiang Sun, Kuldeep Meel
Title: SAT-RL: Training Language Models for Logical Reasoning with Symbolic Solvers
Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. In contrast, satisfiability solvers such as Z3 provide scalable and verifiable reasoning through constraint solving under formal theories, but lack the flexibility to interpret natural‑language problem descriptions. In this work, we propose SAT‑RL, a reinforcement‑learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers through multi‑turn tool execution. SAT‑RL leverages synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm‑up on solver‑augmented traces, and solver‑grounded reinforcement learning with tool‑aware rewards. Experiments show that SAT‑RL substantially improves symbolic reasoning with tools on both in‑domain and out‑of‑domain logic tasks. Our code is available on https://github.com/sunjia72/SAT‑RL.

PaperId: 1081, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14379.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Solvin Sigurdson, Prasanna Sriganesh, Juan Borbon, Joel Burdick, Dingqi Zhang, Jiuguang Wang
Title: OATH: Object-Agnostic Tracking for Dexterous Hands, Enabling Rapid Physics-based Retargeting
Abstract:
Retargeting human demonstrations into dynamically feasible dexterous hand trajectories requires resolving complex contact physics, yet current methods either omit physical constraints or rely on computationally expensive sampling‑based optimization in simulation. Reinforcement learning has previously been used to achieve planning and control through contact dynamics; however, standard policies require object‑specific training and fail to generalize across arbitrary geometries. This work reframes physics‑based retargeting as a residual learning problem, where we demonstrate that zero‑shot generalization across objects relies on structured state representations. Specifically, formulating the observation space to include a localized contact‑error signal guiding each robot link to its target coordinate on the object surface enables a single, unified residual policy to successfully grasp novel, unseen object geometries. Rolling out this policy in simulation on a kinematic reference trajectory yields a physics‑based retargeter, OATH. Operating at 0.4 seconds of compute per second of reference, OATH achieves 2.4x faster‑than‑real‑time performance and a 60‑350x reduction in computational cost compared to sampling‑based methods. The system recovers 58% of held‑out and 54% of unseen‑object DexYCB trajectories while maintaining a sub‑2 cm tracking error.

PaperId: 1082, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14369.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mahesh Reddy Pagadala
Title: When More Memory Fails: Hidden Feasibility Holes in Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization
Abstract:
Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization (DTR) trains neural networks under a memory budget by evicting tensors and recomputing them on demand. A natural expectation is that a budget large enough to complete training stays sufficient when it is increased. Using DTR's reference simulator, simrd, to replay the public DTR training traces, we show that this expectation fails. We call the exceptions feasibility holes: memory budgets at which an eviction policy runs out of memory although both a smaller and a larger budget complete, a form of non‑monotone feasibility. Under a written sweep protocol with dated amendments, a 0.01‑step budget grid shows no such hole for DTR on any of six confirmatory traces, although unresolved timeouts prevent it from establishing monotonicity. Finer sampling finds holes on InceptionV4 (three regions) and U‑Net (two regions), in addition to one on the ResNet‑32 development trace. Every hole is reproduced by three repeats and by unmodified simrd. For one InceptionV4 pair (0.2343 versus 0.235 of peak memory) we trace the failure to individual allocations. The larger budget avoids one eviction at an operator where the smaller budget was 173,479 bytes short. The extra data it carries forward forces a later eviction of a tensor needed three operators afterwards, and rebuilding that tensor triggers a recomputation cascade that cannot fit. Keeping that one tensor resident under the same budget prevents the failure. The two simple score changes we tested do not remove holes across traces; both add failing budgets on some traces. All results are from simulation, with no allocator model; behaviour on GPU hardware is untested.

PaperId: 1083, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14368.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mahesh Reddy Pagadala
Title: History, Adaptation, and Hidden Gain: Two Prospective Tests of Learned Predictive Control in a Synthetic Neural Population
Abstract:
We study learned one‑step predictive control of a synthetic population of 64 leaky integrate‑and‑fire neurons whose light sensitivity is scaled by a hidden factor s, using two prospective confirmations on plants simulated only after the analysis was frozen. In the first (50 plants, 11 conditions), removing the 200‑ms input‑output history substantially worsened a parameter‑count‑matched neural predictor at low and moderate gain (s = 0.6, 0.8; RMSE rose by 2.47 Hz at s = 0.6, 97.5% CI 2.43‑2.51). In secondary comparisons, recursively adapted ARX had the lowest mean error of the deployable controllers in 10 of 11 conditions, tuned PI with anti‑windup matched or beat the network for s >= 0.7, and training for 10,000 rather than 900 epochs lowered prediction error but worsened control. Development work suggested the network's learned action sensitivity did not track the hidden gain. A second protocol (50 new plants, 9 sensitivities, 2 noise levels) confirmed three pre‑specified predictions at the primary noise level. Re‑estimating a single multiplicative input gain recovered 87% (95% CI 86‑88%) of the benefit of full adaptive ARX. Supplying that online estimate to the network as an extra input reduced high‑gain tracking error by 1.84 Hz [1.81, 1.88]. Longer training worsened the plain network by 1.09 Hz but improved the gain‑input network by 1.07 Hz, a differential of 2.16 Hz [2.13, 2.20]. Under high process noise (sigma = 2.0) the effects shrank to about 0.04 Hz or less and gain‑only adaptation recovered only 24% of the adaptive‑ARX benefit. In this synthetic plant, at the primary noise level, one‑parameter online gain estimation accounts for most of the gap between a history‑based network and full adaptive ARX, and for its prediction‑control mismatch.

PaperId: 1084, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14365.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Bishnu Bista, Dhanraj Haibatrao Jadhav, Vibha Choudhary, Gaurav Saxena, Arun Pandiyan Perumal, Arjun Subedi, Jignesh Ammineni
Title: ConformalGuard: False-Positive-Controlled Action Gating for LM Classifiers
Abstract:
Language model classifiers are increasingly deployed for high‑stakes decisions such as phishing screening, content moderation, and fraud triage, yet validation‑set thresholds provide no finite‑sample control of deployment‑time false positives. We present ConformalGuard, a model‑agnostic calibration layer that wraps a fixed scoring function with finite‑sample control over the rate at which legitimate inputs trigger an intervention tier. Our contribution is empirical and operational, not a new conformal theorem: zero‑shot LM API scores can be coarse enough (10‑‑11 unique values here) to make temperature scaling and isotonic regression operationally identical to raw thresholding for low‑FPR action gating. We compare these methods with conformal calibration for fine‑tuned BERT, Claude Sonnet 4, and GPT‑4o on public email corpora. For Claude, conformal calibration reduces FPR from 0.040 to 0.008 while recall falls from 0.938 to 0.875. For deterministic GPT‑4o scores, the 1% operating point is too conservative to deploy (recall 0.564); three‑run stochastic averaging raises recall to 0.732 at FPR 0.005. At 2% prevalence with BERT, conformal calibration removes 25 false‑positive reviews per 10,000 emails (95% CI [10, 43]). The guarantee is legitimate‑event‑rate control under exchangeability; discrimination, workload effects, and robustness to shift remain empirical.

PaperId: 1085, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14341.pdf   GitHub
Authors:David R. Martin, Jared Paquet, Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque, Pramod Khargonekar, Kyle Volle, J. Humberto Ramos, Scott Nivison
Title: CoPlanVLM: Coordinated Path Planning for a Robot Team using Vision Language Models
Abstract:
We present CoPlanVLM, which uses a Vision Language Model (VLM) to translate a single natural‑language instruction and image into coordinated paths for a team of two robots. While VLMs offer a flexible, natural‑language interface for commanding robot teams, their weak spatial reasoning has greatly limited VLM‑based path planning. CoPlanVLM improves the VLM's spatial reasoning and path planning abilities through three components: (1) an image overlay marking both free space and obstacles, (2) task classification that selects the most appropriate low‑level planner and reasoning prompt for each instruction, and (3) task‑specific chain‑of‑thought reasoning that prompts the VLM to identify key objects, allocate roles, and verify routes are collision‑free before committing to a plan. Together, these components enable the team to complete complex coordinated maneuvers requiring both robots and divide large tasks between robots to increase efficiency. CoPlanVLM also supports detailed maneuvers involving specific routes, loops, and coverage of large areas, as well as tasks requiring directional reasoning such as north/south or left/right. We validate CoPlanVLM in both Gazebo simulation and on physical Turtlebot 4 hardware. CoPlanVLM attains an average success rate of 84.4% compared to 50.0% for the closest baseline. On trials where both methods succeed, CoPlanVLM's paths are 27% shorter on average. Project code is available at https://github.com/AICPS/CoPlanVLM.

PaperId: 1086, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14338.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Youssef Diouane, Issmail El Hallaoui, Meisseme Kadri, Amina Lamghari
Title: STREGO: A Scalable Implementation of a Trust-Region Framework for Noisy Bayesian Optimization
Abstract:
TREGO, a trust‑region Bayesian optimization (BO) method for expensive blackbox problems, has convergence guarantees, but only for exact function values. In high dimension, its performance tends to deteriorate. This paper asks whether a trust‑region BO method can be extended to handle noisy evaluations while being competitive in high dimension. We first generalize TREGO into a trust‑region framework for noisy BO and extend its convergence analysis to noisy function estimates that are sufficiently accurate with sufficiently high probability. We then propose STREGO, a scalable implementation of this framework. Its global phase selects a batch of candidates by solving a bi‑objective problem on the posterior mean of a Gaussian process and the integrated variance reduction. Unlike the predictive variance, this second objective does not favor boundary points merely because they are far from the data. Its local phase minimizes the posterior mean of a second Gaussian process, trained only on points close to the incumbent. STREGO is compared with TREGO, TURBO, BAXUS and NSMA‑BO on synthetic and real‑world problems of dimension 4 to 124, with and without noise. It gives the best average results in every synthetic setting tested and the best or tied‑best solution on four of the six real‑world problems. An implementation of STREGO is available at https://github.com/Mayousk/STREGO.

PaperId: 1087, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14335.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yang Liu, Hanchen Cui, Karthik Desingh
Title: PILOT: Guiding Long-Horizon World-Model Planning for Robot Manipulation with Visual Subgoals and Policy Priors
Abstract:
Latent world‑model planning has shown promising results in goal‑conditioned robotic manipulation, but remains challenging for long‑horizon planning due to limited temporal guidance and inefficient action search. A distant visual goal provides little guidance for preparatory actions, while uninformed action sampling makes local optimization inefficient. We propose PILOT (Policy‑Initialized Local Optimization with Temporal subgoals), which uses a video model to generate intermediate visual subgoals and a learned policy to initialize the cross‑entropy method (CEM). CEM refines candidate action sequences toward each subgoal using an action‑conditioned world model in a receding‑horizon control loop. In our primary real‑robot evaluation across four UR5e manipulation tasks, PILOT achieves 68.8% success, compared with 55.0% without policy initialization, 13.8% for policy‑only execution, and 0.0% for direct final‑goal planning. Simulation results show that these gains persist over longer horizons: PILOT exceeds direct execution of the same policy by 30 percentage points on long Push‑T tasks and by 22 percentage points on LIBERO‑10. Policy initialization also accelerates local optimization: on Push‑T, CEM matches the cost reached by generic initialization after 10 iterations in only 4 iterations and reduces the final planning cost by 24.1% under the same sampling budget. These results show that combining temporal subgoals with policy‑guided action search improves both long‑horizon task execution and local planning efficiency. Videos are available on the webpage: https://pilot‑planner.github.io/.

PaperId: 1088, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14293.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yeobin Hong, Hyojun Go, Dohun Lee, Jeongjae Lee, Sunghwan Hong, Federico Tombari, Zhaochong An, Jong Chul Ye, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer
Title: GeoFix: Geometry Fixing for 4D Consistent Generation
Abstract:
Video diffusion models increasingly serve as priors for 4D generation, but the generated videos often lack geometric consistency. Recent approaches address this through post‑training by designing geometric rewards, yet this can degrade texture and fine detail, requiring auxiliary appearance rewards and careful reward balancing. To address this challenge, we propose GeoFix, a unified framework that improves geometric consistency and visual quality with a single geometric reward, applicable to both training and inference‑time reward alignment. Our reward measures cross‑view depth consistency in static scene regions, targeting structural inconsistencies without directly constraining appearance or penalizing valid object motion. Crucially, depth agreement increases with camera field‑of‑view overlap even in real videos and 4D datasets, allowing a smaller camera movement to be mistaken for better geometry. We account for this effect by calibrating the reward against the overlap‑dependent trend. GeoFix achieves a 39% improvement in WorldScore 3D consistency and a 4% increase in VBench Quality Score.

PaperId: 1089, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14261.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Srikar Yellapragada, Alexandros Graikos, Zilinghan Li, Kostas Triaridis, Tarak Nath Nandi, Ji Dong K Bai, Beatrice Knudsen, Tahsin Kurc, Prateek Prasanna, Rajarsi R. Gupta, Ravi K Madduri, Joel Saltz, Dimitris Samaras
Title: BigCell: Generating Gigapixel Whole-Slide Images
Abstract:
Whole‑slide images (WSIs) are gigapixel‑scale digital scans of histopathology tissue and serve as the primary basis for cancer diagnosis. Existing histopathology generative models operate at the patch scale, producing fixed‑size tiles of at most 1024×1024 pixels which encompass only a small fraction of the WSI. In contrast, text reports for clinical diagnoses and slide‑level diagnostic labels ‑‑ the supervision that exists at scale ‑‑ operate at the whole‑slide level. We present BigCell, the first approach to generate coherent whole‑slide histopathology images at native gigapixel resolution. BigCell trains a flow‑matching transformer at 2048×2048 pixels on over 120,000 publicly available WSIs spanning multiple organ types. Conditioning on embeddings from pathology foundation models and using an inference‑time sliding‑window pipeline, BigCell generates coherent images of up to 32,768×32,768 pixels, outperforming prior tile generators on both tile‑level and slide‑level fidelity metrics. To make gigapixel synthesis practical, we introduce an adaptive scheduling strategy that prioritizes important slide regions, speeding up image generation by over 3\ttimes with minimal quality degradation. Furthermore, we propose the first text‑to‑image synthesis at 8k resolution by training a separate model that produces dense conditioning grids directly from pathology text reports. We demonstrate that augmenting with synthetic samples improves slide‑level few‑shot classification performance by up to 18 % over baselines trained on real data.

PaperId: 1090, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14258.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Saurav K. Aryal
Title: Do Artificial Neural Networks Need Dendritic Nanotubes? Two Reasons for Shrinking Importance Estimates in Continual Learning
Abstract:
Regularization‑based continual learning protects each parameter in proportion to an estimate of its importance, yet these estimates come from finite samples and heuristics and are used as if they were exact. We report four studies that start from a biologically inspired mechanism and end with a statistical explanation of it. Motivated by dendritic nanotubes, we let transient lateral links diffuse importance tags between hidden units. Links between co‑active units gave no significant gain, but random links with lifetimes of 25 or 200 steps raised final accuracy on 20‑task Permuted MNIST by 1.5 to 2.6 points. We show that random diffusion implements linear shrinkage of importance toward the layer mean in expectation. A simulation of the link process alone predicts shrinkage weights of 0.23 and 0.52 for these lifetimes, and graph‑free shrinkage at 0.25 and 0.5 reproduces both the accuracy and the dispersion of the consolidated importance, while every activity‑dependent rule did worse than random links. A five‑seed screen across EWC, SI, and MAS found nominal gains for SI and MAS on Permuted MNIST and losses on task‑incremental Split CIFAR‑100, where forgetting was small and shrinkage cost plasticity. Varying the number of importance samples then separates two mechanisms on Permuted MNIST. For EWC, the gain fell by about ten points per tenfold increase in samples, from 19.6 points with 10 samples to ‑0.4 with 1000, a variance effect. For MAS, a gain of about one point persisted at 1000 samples, consistent with a bias in the importance measure rather than noise. Shrinkage had no detectable effect for MAS on a domain‑incremental CIFAR‑100 benchmark. Finally, we show that a standard heteroscedastic empirical Bayes rule shrinks the largest Fisher‑type estimates most, which may explain its poor results, and point to a log‑scale alternative.

PaperId: 1091, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14244.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ataberk Olgun, Spiros Galanopoulos, Andreas Kosmas Kakolyris, İsmail Emir Yüksel, Haocong Luo, F. Nisa Bostancı, Onur Mutlu
Title: Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips
Abstract:
We perform the first comprehensive experimental characterization of power consumed by real HBM2 DRAM chips. Our extensive characterization yields 1) the empirical basis for developing new, accurate HBM power models or validating existing power models and 2) key insights into structural and data‑pattern‑dependent variation of power in HBM2 chips. Out of our 13 new findings and 6 key takeaway messages, we highlight: 1) a read operation consumes significantly higher current than any other operation and 2) the toggled data bus signals in a data transfer burst significantly affect current draw where toggling all HBM2‑internal bank group bus signals causes 29.4% higher power consumption than keeping them constant. Leveraging our empirical insights into HBM2 power consumption, we engineer an access pattern that yields 23.6% higher power consumption on average across 36 tested HBM2 chips than the highest‑power‑consuming JEDEC‑specified current measurement loop. Our results have important implications for HBM‑based system design and validation. Relying solely on JEDEC‑ or vendor‑specified test loops to bound HBM power could cause system failures and/or thermal throttling in real‑world high‑power AI/ML workloads. To improve 3D‑stacked DRAM power modeling in open source architectural simulation infrastructures, we develop a new HBM power model. Our model predicts the power of 36 real HBM2 chips across diverse workloads (including a real LLM decode workload) with 7.6 ‑‑ 8.1% mean absolute percentage error, substantially more accurately than state‑of‑the‑art HBM power models. The power consumption predicted by our model for a power‑intensive microbenchmark closely matches (with 2.4% to 5.3% error across HBM3E's specified supply voltage range) the average HBM3E memory power consumed by three tested NVIDIA H200 GPUs. We publicly release our power model at https://github.com/CMU‑SAFARI/HBM‑Power.

PaperId: 1092, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14232.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ayush Kumar Bar, Promila Ghosh
Title: Speech event detector: Timestamped detection of non-verbal vocalizations and background sounds for rich speech transcription
Abstract:
Automatic speech recognition produces words but drops the non‑verbal content of a recording: the breaths, coughs, sighs and laughter of the speaker, and the horns, music or barking around them. We describe Speech Event Detector, a 5.8‑million‑parameter convolutional‑Transformer model that outputs probabilities every 40 ms for 54 event classes (20 speaker vocalizations and 34 background sounds), together with post‑processing that converts these probabilities into timestamped events and a procedure for merging the events into a Whisper transcript. The model is trained on material drawn from seven public datasets whose labels come in incompatible forms: single detected regions, free‑text tags with timestamps, temporally strong ontology labels, symbols embedded in transcripts, isolated recordings and environmental recordings. We unify them using rule‑based label mapping, recover timestamps for transcript‑embedded labels through CTC forced alignment, locating 6,360 of 8,620 sounds, and combine about 168 hours of real annotated training recordings with synthetic mixtures and augmentation using real background noise. Per‑class thresholds for two operating profiles are tuned on real held‑out recordings, and performance is estimated using two‑fold cross‑validation. On whole held‑out recordings from four datasets, considering the 48 classes with at least ten held‑out events, the sensitive profile detects an average of 49 percent of a class's events, covering 67 percent of all 9,367 events, at a macro precision of 0.30. The balanced profile achieves a macro recall of 0.37 at a precision of 0.36, with macro event F1 scores of 0.32 and 0.33, respectively. The detector runs about 39 times faster than real time on eight CPU threads.

PaperId: 1093, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14228.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Seungjun Yu, Hojun Choi, Seojeong Park, Jaeyo Shin, Hyunjung Shim
Title: Latent World Action Model for GUI Agents
Abstract:
Pixel‑space world models have recently emerged as a promising approach for GUI agents, predicting future screens prior to execution and subsequently re‑perceiving them for action selection. However, this two‑stage paradigm faces two key challenges in GUI environments: (L1) the high computational cost of pixel reconstruction and (L2) the need to reconstruct large and diverse appearance‑level details beyond what is required for action selection. In practice, this screen‑generation objective can induce an identity shortcut problem, where future‑state prediction largely preserves the current state rather than capturing action‑induced changes. In this work, we reformulate GUI world modeling by shifting the prediction target from full‑screen reconstruction to action‑induced future information in latent space. Concretely, we leverage a large multimodal model as the latent world model, whose shared representations support two dedicated heads for both action selection and predictive transition modeling. The action head directly translates these latent representations into action selection, while the transition head captures action‑conditioned future information. To mitigate the identity shortcut, we further introduce an action‑aware contrastive objective that encourages the transition representations to capture discriminative action‑induced changes. Extensive experiments across offline and online GUI settings show that our method achieves up to 31.9% and 40.6% relative gains in success rate over pixel‑space world models, respectively, while substantially reducing inference latency by up to 98.9%. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/latent2world.

PaperId: 1094, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14226.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Séléna Jean-Mactoux, Sophie Loizillon, Ghina Jardali, Amandine Crombé, Nathalie Lassau, Alexandre Bône
Title: CAPTOR: a vision-language foundation model for Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis Oncologic CT
Abstract:
Purpose : To develop and evaluate CAPTOR, a deep‑learning vision‑language foundation model for oncologic chest‑abdomen‑pelvis (CAP) CT interpretation. Materials & Methods : CAPTOR (Chest‑Abdomen‑Pelvis foundaTion model for Oncologic Radiology) is a contrastive vision‑language model, trained using a pretraining strategy for oncologic CAP CT (in single‑ or multiple‑series acquisitions), on a multicenter retrospective dataset from North America, Europe and Asia, predominantly from tumor lesion examinations. CAPTOR was compared with state‑of‑the‑art CT foundation models on three downstream tasks: disease detection, survival prediction using TumorImagingBench and image retrieval. Classification and retrieval were both evaluated on held‑out internal and public test sets, stratified by anatomical coverage and indication. Bootstrap resampling was used to estimate confidence intervals, and pairwise comparisons were performed using permutation tests. Results : CAPTOR was trained and tested on 25,512 and 10,794 CT‑report pairs respectively. TumorImagingBench datasets comprised between 134 and 421 studies each. CAPTOR outperformed all baseline models, on the classification task, on the CAP subset (AUC 0.767, 95%CI: 0.734‑0.793, vs. 0.695, 95%CI: 0.645‑0.736 for the next‑best, p<0.001) and oncologic subset (AUC 0.784, 95%CI: 0.759‑0.805, vs. 0.734, 95%CI: 0.703‑0.767 p<0.001), ranked first on three of the four oncologic prognostic benchmarks, and achieved superior retrieval performance on CAP and oncologic subsets. Conclusion : A foundation model trained on oncology‑enriched CAP CT data outperformed relevant state‑of‑the‑art models in its target clinical context, underscoring the importance of clinically aligned pretraining. We release our preprocessing, training and inference code : https://github.com/Guerbet‑AI/CAPTOR and model weights : https://huggingface.co/Guerbet‑AI/CAPTOR

PaperId: 1095, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14216.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Samuele Giampieri
Title: Cortex: Measurement-Gated Evolution and Pruning of Coding-Agent Skills and Rules
Abstract:
Coding agents such as Claude Code also follow text files that developers write for them: a project file, skills the agent may choose to open, and rules that load automatically when the agent reads matching files. We call these files the agent's harness. Developers add to it whenever they correct the agent, but one success proves little: the same agent can pass a task once and fail it the next time. We present Cortex, a tool that tests changes to the harness instead of trusting them. It saves fixes from the developer's sessions as replayable tasks, finds the corrections that recur, writes one skill or rule at a time, and keeps it only if repeated runs with and without it show a net gain and no task made noticeably worse. Existing text is tested the same way before it is deleted, and Cortex neither adds nor deletes text the agent never used. We tested Cortex with Claude Haiku 4.5 on a repository built for the purpose, with conventions the model tends to break, one area with nothing to learn, and a script playing the developer. On held‑out tasks, the harnesses it built made the agent follow the conventions far more often than no skills or rules did, left the comparison area unchanged, and added no text read on every turn. Rules, which load automatically, did most of the work; skills helped only when offered with the files a task touches, and those offered on every turn were rarely opened. Cortex kept none of the useless or harmful suggestions we planted, but the agent never opened the useless ones or the harmful skills, and it reached no verdict on the harmful rules, so the test shows that Cortex keeps no unused text, not that it detects damage. Under the stronger Claude Sonnet 5 a single run's harness added little, and on a real open‑source project, where the agent was rarely corrected, Cortex found nothing to learn. We release the tool, the lab and its data.

PaperId: 1096, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14173.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Daniel J. Evans, J. P. Naiman, JooYoung Seo, J. Stephen Downie
Title: Do you "see" what I "see"? A Multi-panel Visual Question Answer Dataset for Large Language Model Chart Analysis
Abstract:
Digital libraries increasingly host scientific publications whose figures encode primary research findings, yet making this visual content searchable, accessible, and reusable remains an open challenge. Large language and multimodal models (LLMs/LMMs) provide the possibility to automate many figure parsing tasks such as determining data trends or extracting data from plots. In this work, we consider if these models can reliably support task‑oriented visual data analysis when presented with synthetic, but realistic, scientific figures that contain multiple charts. Our Visual Question Answering (VQA) process scaffolds our tasks along a four‑level description model from basic conceptual answers to interpretive and analytical understanding. Additionally, we outline our process for synthetically generating our single and multi‑panel (charts in which there are multiple panels present) plots and testing the data with various LMMs using quantitative analysis. In general, we find LMMs become less accurate with increasing figure complexity as the number of panels, number of plot elements, and difficulty of questions increase. Finally, because LMM accuracy is expected to change rapidly, our analysis also considers cost relative to performance as a metric to inform future user decisions. We provide the detailed question‑answer pairs used in this analysis, along with the code used to generate random plots, question‑answer pairs and detailed bounding‑box metadata for chart elements. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ReadingTimeMachine/LLM_VQA_MultiPanel and https://huggingface.co/datasets/ReadingTimeMachine/visual\_qa\_multipanel

PaperId: 1097, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14157.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chenyang Yan, Yingying Zhang, Kanzhi Cheng, Qiushi Sun, Zhengyuan Pan, Zheng Ma, Hang Yan, Yian Wang, Nuo Chen, Jialin Cao, Xingdong Gong, Wenpo Song, Han Chen, Zichen Ding, Fangzhi Xu, Shujian Huang, Xinyu Dai, Yichen Liu, Tiankuo Yao, Bo Wang, Ben Kao, Jianbing Zhang, Lewei Lu, Dahua Lin
Title: OpenMobile-2: Building Versatile Mobile Agents with Scalable Environments and App-Native Tools
Abstract:
We introduce OpenMobile‑2, a near‑frontier mobile agent with fully open training environments and recipes. We make three key advances: (1) Diverse environments with simulated commercial apps: We build MobileGym++, featuring 35 realistic, functionally rich commercial‑style apps with cross‑app workflows, while preserving full controllability for reset and verification. Together with newly configured apps in Android emulators, this yields a diverse playground spanning over 110 apps. (2) Open training data at scale: Building on this foundation, we curate nearly 12K mobile interaction trajectories for supervised fine‑tuning and the largest open collection of verifiable RL training data for mobile agents, comprising over 2K executable tasks with automatic rewards. (3) Hybrid GUI and app‑native tool use: We explore an experimental mobile‑use setting where apps expose selected functionalities as app‑native tools alongside their GUIs, allowing agents to interleave GUI actions and tool calls within a task. We implement this setting in MobileGym++ with over 300 carefully scoped tools across 50+ apps. Additionally, we introduce MobileGym++ Bench for complex, long‑horizon commercial mobile scenarios, supporting both GUI‑only and hybrid GUI‑tool evaluation on a shared task suite. OpenMobile‑2 performs competitively across established benchmarks, including AndroidWorld (79.9) and MobileWorld (50.4), while showing promising transfer to real‑device mobile use, nearly doubling SPA‑Bench performance from 31.9 to 59.6. All resources are available at https://os‑copilot.github.io/OpenMobile2‑Home/.

PaperId: 1098, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14153.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Jingyu Liu, Hao Jiang, Yikang Ding, Huafeng Shi, Xu Yang, Xiaoqiang Liu, Guoxin Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Kun Gai
Title: TrajCFG: Token-Wise Classifier-Free Guidance via Denoising Trajectory Feedback
Abstract:
Classifier‑free guidance (CFG) typically applies a shared scale to all latent tokens, although their velocity predictions evolve differently during sampling. We introduce Trajectory‑Adaptive Classifier‑Free Guidance (TrajCFG), a training‑free method for flow‑matching models that adapts token‑wise guidance using historical changes in guided velocity direction. TrajCFG maps this feedback to bounded scales, assigning stronger guidance to larger directional changes and weaker guidance to more consistent directions. It combines adjacent‑step and interval‑normalized longer‑span feedback, reusing standard CFG predictions without additional model evaluations. Controlled diagnostics and ablations examine the roles of directional feedback, token‑wise allocation, and history‑span fusion. Experiments on text‑to‑video, image‑to‑video, text‑to‑audio‑video, text‑to‑image, and image‑to‑3D generation show improvements over base samplers across multiple backbones. For text‑to‑video generation, TrajCFG improves VBench Total scores by 0.30‑0.75 points over the strongest evaluated baseline on each of three backbones. These results support historical directional feedback as a broadly applicable signal for fine‑grained guidance allocation. The project page is available at https://jyliu‑98.github.io/trajcfg‑project‑page/.

PaperId: 1099, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14140.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Muhammad Muqsit Islam, Gloria García Cuenco, José M. Martínez, Pierrick Coupé
Title: Frozen Site-Probe Accuracy Is Not a Standalone Harmonization Score: An Audit of Evaluation Practice for Multi-Site MRI
Abstract:
Image‑level MRI harmonization is often evaluated with a frozen site probe, a site classifier trained on raw scans and applied unchanged to harmonized ones: a drop in its accuracy is read as removal of site effects. We audit this practice on ABIDE I (1,112 T1‑weighted scans, 17 sites) with ten output sets from seven harmonization methods and controls for chance, head shape, intensity, preprocessing and target alignment. We find that this verdict depends on how the probe is trained, even among probes that classify raw scans well: across random seeds, its balanced accuracy on the same CycleGAN outputs ranges from 0.13 to 0.59 (chance: 0.06). Low frozen‑probe accuracy can also arise without harmonization: a Gaussian blur, which increases the intensity distance to the target site, lowers this accuracy to chance. Moreover, where the frozen probe fails, probes trained on the harmonized scans still recover the site, even from intensity histograms alone: on HACA3 outputs, the frozen probe scores 0.25, a probe trained on those outputs 0.75, and one using only their intensity histograms 0.71. Low frozen‑probe accuracy therefore does not show that site information has been removed. We recommend reporting several probes trained to convergence, probes trained on harmonized scans, and target alignment.

PaperId: 1100, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14136.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Donghoon Ahn, Runqian Wang, Alexei A. Efros, Taesung Park, Yash Belhe
Title: Correction Training for Diffusion Models
Abstract:
Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training‑inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground‑truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean‑sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference for better results. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We evaluate our method across DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and, notably, unconditional generation, where producing high‑quality samples without guidance has been particularly challenging. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier‑free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference‑time overhead.

PaperId: 1101, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14117.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jianli Sun, Chengxiang Li, Yonglin Tian
Title: Make π0.5 Learn to Call Astra for Reliable Robot Manipulation
Abstract:
GPT‑6 Astra provides robust embodied reasoning, but frequent external queries increase inference time and token costs. We equip a frozen π_0.5 policy with a lightweight CALL head that learns to predict when assistance is necessary. CALL reuses features from the standard policy forward pass and operates locally without consulting external models. Astra is activated solely for critical recovery events and returns control to π_0.5 upon stabilization. Evaluated across 40 LIBERO tasks (200 episodes), our system achieves a 97.5% success rate, outperforming the 95.5% baseline of pure π_0.5. In the Object, Goal, and Spatial suites, Astra executes only 5.49% of environment steps, consuming approximately 5,027 tokens per test episode. This selective intervention preserves the fast ordinary execution of π_0.5 while seamlessly integrating Astra's reasoning on demand. Our project page is available at https://kykgeek.github.io/Pi05_CALL_Astra/.

PaperId: 1102, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14112.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Romi Fadli, Rusdah, Wahyu Ramadani Putri Utami, Zulfa Malika Amana
Title: Does System One Transfer? Calibrated Typed-Decision Models, Label Budgets, and Translation for Indonesian Regional Languages
Abstract:
Calibrated typed‑decision ("System One") models return a label and a probability in a single forward pass at a small fraction of the cost of large language models (LLMs), yet their evaluation has been almost entirely English. We report a pre‑registered evaluation of the commercial Jev model and the open Laya‑multilingual model on Indonesian regional languages, using the parallel NusaX sentiment (12 languages) and NusaTranslation sentiment and emotion (7 languages) test sets. Jev is more often correct on sentences that are lexically closer to Indonesian in all three datasets, and presenting the human Indonesian translation instead raises its accuracy by up to 37.2 points, most in languages distant from Indonesian. Its expected calibration error does not grow on regional languages, but its ability to rank its own errors degrades in all three datasets. Retrained classifiers need more than 500 labels per language to match zero‑shot Jev in 9 of 10 NusaX regional languages. A confidence‑gated cascade that sends Jev's 10‑30% least confident decisions to a local IndoBERT classifier matches or exceeds the better of the two systems, and routing to an LLM instead matches that LLM at 24‑77% lower API cost. Of six further commercial LLMs (three Claude and three GPT models), five are 4‑14 points more accurate than Jev, at several hundred times the API cost where it is reported, while the smallest (Claude Haiku) is less accurate. We release the pre‑registration, code and all predictions.

PaperId: 1103, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14105.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jinkui Hao, Donald R. Cantrell, Ramez Abdalla, Sameer A. Ansari, Bo Zhou
Title: Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model for Vessel Extraction Using Physics-informed Synthetic Data
Abstract:
Accurate artery extraction from X‑ray coronary angiography (XCA) is essential for coronary artery disease diagnosis and intervention. However, low vessel visibility, respiratory and cardiac motion, and limited annotations challenge existing methods. Moreover, most deep learning approaches produce binary vessel masks without preserving clinically relevant intra‑arterial contrast information. We propose a Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model (TDBM) that formulates vessel extraction as image translation and learns from physics‑informed synthetic data without manual vessel annotations. A physics‑based XCA synthesis engine generates diverse, perfectly aligned pairs of contrast‑enhanced and contrast‑free images. Using these pairs, TDBM learns cross‑domain mappings to recover high‑fidelity vessel information. Temporal conditioning incorporates adjacent frames to improve consistency, while a vessel‑aware contrastive loss exploits background‑invariant synthetic pairs to enhance vascular discrimination. We evaluate TDBM on two XCA vessel segmentation datasets and conduct a reader study using two real‑patient XCA sequence datasets. Zero‑shot segmentation is further assessed on retinal imaging and fluorescence microscopy datasets. Results demonstrate that TDBM consistently outperforms existing methods and generalizes effectively across imaging modalities. Code and trained weights will be available at: https://github.com/Advanced‑AI‑in‑Medicine‑and‑Physics‑Lab/TDBM

PaperId: 1104, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14093.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Santiago Reina Alguacil, Ezequiel López Rubio
Title: Human Pose Estimation by Probabilistic Mixtures of Gaussian and Uniform Distributions
Abstract:
Despite advancements in sub‑pixel decoding, modern Human Pose Estimation (HPE) architectures remain constrained by deterministic coordinate extraction from discrete heatmaps, which systematically fails under dense occlusions and Out‑of‑Distribution (OoD) ambiguities. To address these limitations, we propose a post‑hoc continuous probabilistic framework that intercepts raw heatmaps and models them as a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) augmented with a spatially agnostic uniform distribution, requiring no architectural modifications or retraining. This continuous representation allows us to comprehensively explore the distinct contributions of density modeling to HPE. We show that the spatial expectation of our fitted GMM achieves precision parity with leading sub‑pixel decoders without heuristic post‑processing. Leveraging this continuous space, our test‑time augmentation aggregates probability distributions rather than discrete activations, mitigating multi‑scale heatmap poisoning. Furthermore, because our multimodal GMM parameterization isolates competing spatial hypotheses, it naturally interfaces with geometric regularizers such as Markov Random Fields. However, our analysis exposes the inherent vulnerabilities of 2D kinematic priors under perspective foreshortening and visual degradation. Crucially, this density formulation yields significant improvements in uncertainty quantification: our calibrated geometric covariance volume outperforms standard peak‑intensity heuristics in OoD anomaly detection under severe occlusion. For in‑distribution calibration, dynamically fusing our geometric metric via Adaptive Softmax reduces or matches baseline Area Under the Sparsification Error (AUSE) across benchmarks and degradation levels. Finally, we establish that this continuous parameterization is extensible to multi‑view 3D architectures, bypassing the \mathcalO(N^3) voxel memory bottleneck.

PaperId: 1105, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14079.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yingquan "Cody" Wu
Title: WZIP and WLZ4: LZ77 Codecs with Match-Length-Dependent Sliding Windows
Abstract:
An LZ77 codec bounds every match by one sliding window, trading cheap offsets for short matches against reach for long ones. Match‑length‑dependent windows refine this trade‑off: each match length has its own window, and the decoder infers the offset range from the decoded length. We present two such codecs: WLZ4, a byte‑aligned LZ4‑class format with one‑byte and flagged offsets, and WZIP, an entropy‑coded Zstandard‑class format. Each block begins with its decoded length, from which WZIP derives its widest window and a decoder sizes its output. LZ4 blocks may expand incompressible input by 0.4%; WLZ4 adds at most 15 bytes, WZIP 2. We describe the formats, threaded match finders, decoders and parser. On Silesia, WLZ4 reaches a ratio up to 16% above LZ4HC's, decoding more slowly, and WZIP exceeds Zstandard 22's ratio while its trusted decoder runs at 91% of Zstandard's speed (87% checked; on enwik9, about as fast).

PaperId: 1106, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14067.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fanrong Dong, Ziyi Sun, Ziqi Han, Junhan Sun, Lei Ye, Zetong Jing, Hao Zhao, Shaoxun Liu, Rongrong Wang
Title: From Hitter to Player: Separating Motor Execution and Strategy in Competitive Humanoid Table Tennis
Abstract:
Competitive humanoid table tennis requires two distinct abilities: executing a desired return and deciding where to return the ball. We separate these two problems, with the ball landing target serving as an interface between motor control and strategy. (1) We first train a whole‑body motor policy conditioned on the desired landing target, which maps the target to an executable humanoid stroke through a model‑based strike planner and a learned controller. (2) We then improve the motor policy through self‑play in closed‑loop rallies, where the robot learns to handle incoming balls generated by another player rather than only prescribed incoming balls. At this stage, the landing targets are still sampled without considering the opponent, so the policy improves its execution without learning game strategy. (3) Finally, we freeze the entire motor stack and train a stroke‑level strategic policy to choose landing targets through competitive self‑play. Motor self‑play improves both landing accuracy and legal‑return rate during rallies. More importantly, with the entire motor stack fixed, changing only the target‑selection policy leads to large differences in game outcomes: the learned strategy wins 89%, 82%, and 73% of points against center, random, and away‑from‑opponent baselines, respectively. The learned strategy also changes where it sends the ball according to the opponent's position and the previous target, showing that self‑play learns more than simply aiming at fixed "good" locations. On hardware, the same frozen execution stack and strategic interface support complete 11‑point games against a recreational human opponent, including multi‑stroke rallies with both forehand and backhand returns.

PaperId: 1107, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14066.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Leon Pohl, Martin Frauendorfer, Corinna Schmitt, Mirko Maehlisch
Title: Safety-Oriented Trajectory Ranking from BEV Perception Outputs
Abstract:
Bird's‑Eye‑View (BEV) representations are increasingly used as compact inputs for autonomous driving perception and planning. However, lightweight and interpretable methods for evaluating candidate ego trajectories directly on BEV outputs remain useful for vehicular safety workflows, rapid prototyping, and human‑in‑the‑loop validation. This paper presents a modular trajectory ranking pipeline that consumes BEVFusion object detections and map segmentations derived from nuScenes sensor data and ranks manually specified candidate trajectories according to safety‑first criteria. The ranking prioritizes avoiding collisions and walkway violations, then smaller end distance to the target, and finally path efficiency. To study whether these rule‑based rankings resemble human judgment, we created seven BEV traffic scenarios and compared the script output with preferences from a survey of 21 participants. Across 146 pairwise votes, 124 matched the trajectory ranked first by the evaluator, corresponding to an overall agreement of 84.9 %. The results indicate that simple BEV‑centric safety heuristics can approximate human preferences in constrained trajectory choice tasks while remaining transparent enough for analysis, dataset curation, and autonomous driving studies.

PaperId: 1108, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14061.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Thanh Ly, Chien Le, Truong-Duy Dang, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Duy-Dung Le, Vien Anh Ngo, An T. Le
Title: Terrain Traversal Without Motion Priors: Expert-Routed Humanoid Locomotion at Deployment Fidelity
Abstract:
State‑of‑the‑art perceptive humanoid locomotion is mostly built on retargeted motion capture, a generative motion prior, and a distillation stage. We report a complete system that does not require this pipeline for a humanoid to cross varied terrain. In its place, we provide a five‑expert mixture routed by a terrain classifier over a sensed elevation grid, and target every foothold with a model‑based planner, refined by six closed‑form‑gradient steps on an interpolated terrain‑cost field instead of picked from a fixed grid. Driven through the same perception‑to‑actuation software a robot would run, inside a second, deployment‑fidelity simulator, it crosses an 85\,m five‑segment waypoint course 18 of 20 times end‑to‑end (90%, Wilson 95% CI 70‑‑97) and succeeds 20/20 on four of five segments scored alone, where an ablated configuration without the mixture and without refinement reaches 0% on both the stair and the hurdle segment. The continuous refinement moves 72.4% of foot placements across at least one grid‑cell boundary, which produces real sub‑grid correction.
