We also ran matched component studies to report what does not account for it: one expert equals five on the training distribution, four label‑free routers collapse to near‑uniform activation, and a self‑supervised terrain embedding loses to the privileged label.

PaperId: 1109, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14056.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Aayush Gupta
Title: Hearing's Blind Spots: Toward Perceptual Compute Allocation in Neural Text-to-Speech
Abstract:
A speech synthesizer produces a detailed waveform, but a listener need not hear every detail. Strong sounds can mask weaker neighbors, creating context‑dependent "blind spots" in hearing. Could neural text‑to‑speech (TTS) spend less computation on those details? We investigate a first step: how the placement of spectral degradation affects completed speech from Piper and Kokoro. At matched time‑frequency bin‑removal budgets, a simple low‑energy‑first policy achieves higher mean wideband PESQ than random deletion and the tested psychoacoustic masking criteria. At 50% removal in the spreading‑matrix comparison, energy, masking, and random policies score 4.46, 3.60, and 1.19 on Piper, and 3.42, 2.10, and 1.22 on Kokoro. Spectrograms and masking maps expose where these perturbations fall and why a model's below‑threshold regions cannot automatically be treated as inaudible. Calibration diagnostics show substantial threshold sensitivity, while a small single‑listener pilot establishes no transparent removal budget. CPU profiles identify waveform decoding as the main measured kernel cost, but a tested dynamic‑INT8 Kokoro decoder runs slower than FP32 on both CPUs. The results establish energy ranking as a strong oracle baseline and motivate testing perceptual allocation inside a decoder. They do not yet demonstrate saved computation: the decisions here use already synthesized audio, and quality metrics are evaluated at 16 kHz. We release scripts, results, audio examples, and a listening‑study instrument.

PaperId: 1110, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14050.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuzhe Tang
Title: An upper bound for the three-dimensional moving sofa problem in a snaky corridor
Abstract:
Let K_M \subset \mathbbR^3 be the "snaky" corridor with unit‑square cross‑section: an infinite entry arm parallel to the x‑axis, a middle arm parallel to the y‑axis whose clear straight section has length M, and an infinite exit arm parallel to the z‑axis, with the two turns lying in the x‑y and y‑z planes. Let V^(K_M) be the supremum of the volumes of connected bodies that can be moved continuously (by rigid motions) from the entry arm to the exit arm while remaining inside K_M. We prove V^(K_M) \le 7.8691 for every M \ge 3.53 (Theorem A); by a sharper analysis of the same mechanism, V^(K_M) \le 4.2862 for every M \ge 2.61 (Theorem B); and, by replacing the final analytic caps with a certified branch‑and‑bound computation over the compact family of entry tubes compatible with the forced events, V^(K_M) \le 3.4083 for every M > 2.2 (Theorem C; computer‑assisted, in double precision with conservative slack). In particular all three bounds apply to the corridor with M = 4 used in Problem 6.64 of Georgiev, Gómez‑Serrano, Tao and Wagner (arXiv:2511.02864), and uniformly to every "turns far apart" reading of that problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first upper bound for the snaky‑corridor 3D moving sofa problem; previously not even finiteness of V^ had been recorded. This note proves upper bounds only; combined with the certified lower bound 1.8558404 from the author's separate certification work via the problem's own evaluation pipeline, the state of the problem becomes 1.8558404 \le V^(K_4) \le 3.4083. Theorems A and B are elementary and self‑contained: a first‑crossing (elbow) event forces a definite tilt of the body's own entry tube, and Fubini‑type chord estimates for tilted tubes cap the volume. Theorem C certifies, by the same forced‑event skeleton, the largest corridor volume that any admissible entry tube can carry.

PaperId: 1111, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14046.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chaoyu Lin
Title: An Edge-First Multimodal Asset Management Studio and Retrieval Engine for Heterogeneous AI-Generated Media
Abstract:
AI‑generated image collections combine visual content with heterogeneous provenance such as prompts, model parameters, and workflow graphs. Managing these collections locally requires coordinated metadata extraction, responsive browsing, and retrieval without mandatory remote inference. We present Berry AI Studio, an edge‑first asset management system built with Vue, Tauri, Rust, SQLite, and ONNX Runtime. Berry integrates format‑specific metadata parsing with raw‑payload retention, generation‑aware cancellation of queued thumbnail work, a persistent multi‑tier thumbnail manifest, cursor pagination, and local image‑text retrieval. We evaluate these mechanisms in five independent repetitions on a pinned source revision. With 50,000 catalog records, the median warm first‑page database call was 285.3 ms; at offset 40,000, keyset pagination reduced median raw‑query latency from 57.9 to 0.46 ms. A controlled browser harness recorded a 0.3 ms median‑of‑run P95 update time during virtualized scrolling, while cancellation prevented all 1,200 stale speculative decodes in the tested trace. A versioned 10‑case corpus produced 53/53 exact metadata‑field matches, and controlled retrieval and grouping tests exercised the authentic storage and clustering paths. The implementation, benchmark scripts, raw logs, and checksummed result packages are publicly available.

PaperId: 1112, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14039.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Seunghun Lee, Kyuhwan Shim, Yeogyeong Song, Seung Hwan Kim, Sihaeng Lee, Byoung-Tak Zhang, Sunghoon Im, Gunhee Lee
Title: RAIN: Robotic Task Generalization with Region-Aware Interaction Networks
Abstract:
Existing vision‑language‑action (VLA) models benefit from large‑scale vision‑language pretraining, but tend to memorize training trajectories, limiting their ability to adapt learned interactions to new task and scene configurations. To address this problem, we propose Region‑Aware Interaction Networks (RAIN), which formulates a task as a sequence of goal‑conditioned subtasks, each specified by an action type and a target‑region mask. This formulation allows learned skills to be reused across different objects and scene layouts and composed into task sequences not seen during training. Its Target‑adaptive Cross‑View Encoder (TCE) conditions multi‑view features on target masks and exchanges information across views, while PlanDiT predicts target‑directed trajectories and actions. A Transition Head estimates subtask completion to enable automatic transitions. We also introduce a Reference‑based Retargeting Strategy (RRS), which uses recorded trajectories to synthesize smooth approaches to reference interactions with alternative target regions, without collecting additional data. Experiments on LIBERO‑Analogy, our new benchmark for robotic task generalization, and real‑world tabletop tasks demonstrate that RAIN generalizes more robustly than existing VLA baselines.

PaperId: 1113, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14005.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jose Hernandez-Orallo
Title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
Abstract:
Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C‑test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high‑difficulty region, the supra‑intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

PaperId: 1114, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13947.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xudong Cai, Ruijie Zhu, Haoliang Shang, Ruining Li, Marc Pollefeys, Shangzhe Wu, Andrea Vedaldi, Chuanxia Zheng
Title: Towards Physically Grounded Articulated 3D Assets: A Multi-Agent Pipeline and Benchmark
Abstract:
In this paper, we study physically grounded articulated 3D asset generation‑‑‑moving the goal from reproducing how objects look to capturing how they move and function. Inspired by the literature on procedural and agentic generation, we present Artisan, a system that extends the latest method Articraft by introducing a multi‑agent pipeline with physical simulation feedback, enabling comprehensive attributes beyond geometry, appearance, and physically plausible articulation, such as collision‑free motion, stability under gravity, and accurate mass and material properties. Furthermore, we construct a unified benchmark spanning four key aspects: spatial fidelity, physical plausibility, downstream task performance, and overall quality. The benchmark encompasses 100 reference assets from ArtVIP and LightWheel, 50 stability prompts, and 50 ABO objects with reference masses, with protocols evaluating various metrics. Through extensive evaluation of more than 10 representative models, Artisan achieves competitive spatial fidelity while attaining the lowest collision rates and highest stability rates among the evaluated methods. Together, our system and benchmark establish insights for advancing 3D generation towards physically plausible, functionally usable assets.

PaperId: 1115, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13929.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Changhao Wang, Jaden Clark, Shuran Song
Title: Chronos Policy: Learning Robot Policies on Physical Time
Abstract:
Robot policies often convert sensing and control into fixed‑rate observation‑action sequences, leaving physical time implicit in sequence position. This assumption breaks when observation rates or delays vary, or when inference latency changes. We introduce Chronos Policy, which makes physical time explicit by conditioning on observation capture times and desired action execution times. We study two ways to incorporate time into a diffusion transformer: adding timestamp embeddings to token features, or encoding physical time in positional encoding through time‑aware rotary positional encodings (time‑aware RoPE). We find that time‑aware RoPE is more robust, allowing attention to depend directly on physical time while keeping token content unchanged. During training, we temporally randomize which observations are sampled and when the action chunk begins, exposing the policy to a wider range of sensing and execution schedules that may occur during deployments. This also enables learning from asynchronous, multi‑rate data without forcing all measurements onto a fixed temporal grid. Across simulation and real‑world experiments, Chronos Policy improves performance on dynamic tasks, where observation‑to‑action timing is critical, and on multisensory tasks, where the relative timing between observations matters. On standard quasi‑static tasks, it preserves nominal performance while improving robustness to changes in sensing and inference timing.

PaperId: 1116, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13912.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Taoyong Cui, Pinxian Zeng, Wanghan Xu, Hao Xiao, Shuhan Xue, Qiang Gao, Wanli Ouyang, Pheng Ann Heng, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu, Ling Yang
Title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
Abstract:
Recursive self‑improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world‑model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. We introduce RSI‑Anything, a domain‑general framework built on JEPA‑Anything that uses predictive world models to guide action and learning‑data selection. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world‑model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks govern the retention of updated policy‑model pairs. Across diverse computational and scientific domains, RSI‑Anything demonstrates substantial gains. In code repair, with the coder fixed, success increases from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% through predictive selection and 31.2% after world‑model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Graphical user interface (GUI) evaluations showed higher task completion, while average actions decrease by 39.4%. Across five successive policy versions, laboratory‑planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01%. In reaction optimization, RSI‑Anything achieves 96.15% mean best observed yield versus 82.16% for Bayesian optimization under the same 40‑experiment budget. An end‑to‑end immune‑science application further connects workflow evolution and predictive modeling with therapeutic hypothesis generation. These results demonstrate how predictive world models and retained system updates enable recursive improvement across diverse environments.

PaperId: 1117, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13909.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Danil Rudenko, Georgii Bulgakov, Nikolay Kartashev, Ivan Rubachev, Daniil Krasylnikov, Artem Babenko
Title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping
Abstract:
While deep learning models for tabular data have recently received significant research attention, the choice of objective functions for regression tasks remains an understudied degree of freedom. Several lines of research offer alternatives to the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE), but differences in datasets, backbones, and evaluation protocols make their practical benefits difficult to compare. In this work, we address this gap by performing a systematic re‑evaluation of regression objectives across a broad collection of established tabular datasets and multiple neural backbones. Our comparison reveals that many proposed objectives provide limited or inconsistent gains over a properly tuned MSE baseline, while quantile loss yields consistent aggregate improvements over MSE across the tested backbones. We then identify a limitation that remains even with this strong objective: regions with different levels of target noise can reach their best predictive performance at different training epochs. Consequently, a single global early‑stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions, even when the objective can represent heteroskedastic target distributions. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce a heteroskedasticity‑aware extension of quantile loss that uses input‑dependent label smoothing as a potential remedy and improves over quantile loss on several backbones. Overall, our results provide a modern empirical picture of regression objectives for tabular deep learning and highlight how differences in optimal stopping times across uncertainty regions can limit the effectiveness of global early stopping. The code is available at https://github.com/yandex‑research/tabular‑regression.

PaperId: 1118, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13889.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Weiliang Chen, Song Liao
Title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
Abstract:
As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED (Reliability‑Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual‑encoder with contrastive fine‑tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re‑ranks candidates based on real‑time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent, a benchmark of 5,172 real‑world tools and over 210,000 query‑tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real‑world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode‑only inference. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent.

PaperId: 1119, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13886.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yeonsung Jung, Zhiyuan Wang, Zifan Wang, Vítor Albiero, Benjamin Newman, Edoardo Debenedetti, Ivan Evtimov, Ninareh Mehrabi
Title: X-AgentRed: Red-Teaming Personal Agents in Evolving Multi-Service Ecosystems
Abstract:
Personal agents increasingly connect to services across the web and applications by using tools. As the effects of their actions accumulate and interact across services, unintended or harmful outcomes can arise when agents fulfill benign user requests. Proactively identifying these compositional failures requires systematically exploring diverse cross‑service paths. Existing red‑teaming methods often simply prompt LLMs to identify potentially harmful paths from task and environment descriptions or decompose harmful objectives specified by humans or LLMs into seemingly benign action combinations. However, generation is biased toward patterns learned during training, potentially favoring familiar tool combinations and leaving novel cross‑service interactions underexplored. To address this, we propose X‑AgentRed, a self‑evolving red‑teaming framework that discovers harmful tool call paths through a graph of tool dependencies and expands and refines them using execution feedback. By analyzing each tool's effects, potential harms, and preconditions for execution, the red‑teaming agent constructs a directed graph that captures how one tool's effects can satisfy another's execution preconditions. Recipes sampled from this graph are instantiated as realistic scenarios in which agents can produce harmful outcomes. Execution feedback enables self‑improvement by diversifying paths that produce harm through tool substitution and refining preconditions at blocked steps in unsuccessful paths to enable further execution. Across four frontier agentic models, X‑AgentRed achieves 1.77× the harmful path rate of STAC and explores a more diverse set of tools, yielding 2.99× the tool coverage on average.

PaperId: 1120, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13829.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jingwei Song, Zhisheng Chen, Bingfan Zeng, Jing Tang, Yubo Hou, Jinhao Jing, Zhengwei Xie, Linfeng Zhang
Title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
Abstract:
A central challenge in embodied recursive self‑improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried‑over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC‑EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph‑aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task‑state graph, defines stage‑level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source‑target boundary. For each probe, no‑prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment‑step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct‑capability gap between controller and planner‑backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood‑species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood‑collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC‑EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw‑ustc/mc‑bench‑open‑source

PaperId: 1121, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13823.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Oktie Hassanzadeh, Dharmashankar Subramanian
Title: Same Query, Different Answer: Run-to-Run Variance in Semantic Query Processing
Abstract:
Semantic query engines ask a large language model (LLM) to judge individual rows, and benchmarks compare these engines on the quality of a few executions at temperature 0. We measure how much another execution changes. We re‑execute the text and tabular workloads of SemBench, LRO‑Bench, and UDA‑Bench through their own harnesses, log every one of 1.2 million model calls, and reanalyze SemBench's published executions. At temperature 0, between 0.07% and 10.2% of rows change their operator output over five executions, depending on the model, and up to 24.0% on one task. Plans amplify these changes exponentially in the number of rows an answer exposes, as a possible‑worlds model predicts: on UDA‑Bench, a few percent of extracted values change, but about two thirds of the answers do. In SemBench's published results, 21% of text results change quality between executions, including on engines whose plans are deterministic. Several per‑query system comparisons, and 16 of 28 tests of LRO‑Bench's implementation recommendations, are not settled by the executions the benchmarks run. Changing rows are rows on which models disagree with each other; identical requests within one execution disagree as often as across executions; and one execution's decision margin or reasoning length predicts which rows change. Voting reduces the variance but does not remove it, and a calibrated cascade keeps its guarantee while the rows it returns change. We derive reporting rules for benchmarks and design rules for engines.

PaperId: 1122, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13804.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Boyuan Deng, Kshitiz Upadhyay, Michael Shields
Title: Constrained Probabilistic Numerics: Gaussian Process Solvers for Linear PDEs under Linear Inequality Constraints
Abstract:
Gaussian process solvers for linear partial differential equations (PDEs) return posteriors rather than point estimates, but they condition only on equality information: the PDE residual, boundary data, and measurements. Many solutions of interest also obey inequality constraints, including nonnegativity, monotonicity, and absence of arbitrage, which equality conditioning cannot enforce. We prove that conditioning a Gaussian process prior jointly on linear equality observations and a finite‑dimensional inequality event is equivalent to conditioning sequentially in terms of Borel measures on the solution space. The physics‑informed posterior is therefore a valid prior for the inequality update at virtual points. The combined law is non‑Gaussian yet computable through truncated‑Gaussian moments, and neither the PDE conditioning nor the inequality update requires modification. We evaluated the construction on a Poisson benchmark, option‑price surfaces, and air‑quality fields. Under incomplete boundary data, a monotonicity constraint lowered the error of a two‑dimensional Poisson reconstruction by 63%. On a real S&P 500 option chain thinned to 20 retained quotes, no‑arbitrage constraints reduced held‑out extrapolation error by 22% and cut the calendar‑arbitrage rate from 10% to 1%. On four real air‑quality snapshots, nonnegativity reduced a Gaussian moment‑based sub‑zero‑tail proxy by 74% at the sparsest monitor count. Changes in mean accuracy and constraint diagnostics differed across data regimes. The probability of the noisy virtual constraint event under the equality posterior measures agreement with the specified bounds before the update. The construction turns admissibility from a post‑processing step into conditioning information for probabilistic PDE solvers.

PaperId: 1123, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13794.pdf   GitHub
Authors:William Sheffield, Jiahui Chen, Amy Zhang, Alex Warstadt, Junyi Jessy Li, Kanishka Misra
Title: Not Just an Evaluation: A Case Study of Discourse Particle Sensitivity in Language Models
Abstract:
Discourse particles subtly shape the flow of discourse by reflecting conversational context and interlocutor attitudes, often leaving the truth‑conditional meaning untouched. They are also often polyfunctional, with distinct senses which partially overlap with other particles; for example, the exclusive use of English "just" and "only" ("John only/just drinks water"). Despite the frequency of these words in natural language, they have gone largely unstudied due to the subtle nature of their effects. We investigate LLM sensitivity to "just" and "only" in natural conversations using behavioral and mechanistic analyses. First, we find that LLMs and humans similarly prefer the presence of these particles in context, and both are more sensitive to "just" compared to "only". Second, when sampling from LLMs with and without these particles, we find LLMs consistently rate generations as more likely, given their source context, demonstrating their particle sensitivity. In both experiments, instruction tuning increases sensitivity. Finally, we localize particle‑sensitive units within LLMs and find the overlap between "just" and "only" is asymmetric: "only" units transfer selectively to exclusive "just", while all "just" units transfer to "only" equally well regardless of sense, suggesting LLM lexical‑level particle representations are partially organized by sense. We release our code, sense‑labeled dialogue stimuli, and human preference annotations at https://github.com/JiahuiKChen/Not_Just_an_Evaluation.

PaperId: 1124, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13778.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ze-Wei Liou, Harris Nover, Amey Naik, Andrii Skliar, Igor Shovkun, Ido Shahaf, Tri Dao
Title: ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State
Abstract:
State‑space models (SSMs) maintain a fixed‑size recurrent state, but reading and writing it at every decoding step can bottleneck hybrid models. This eager state management causes large state I/O with low arithmetic intensity, leaves speculative decoding no cheap rollback, and feeds state quantization error into subsequent recurrent updates. We introduce ReplaySSM, which unrolls the recurrence to represent the state as a checkpoint and a buffer of recent SSM inputs. This separates output computation from checkpoint updates. By updating the checkpoint periodically, ReplaySSM avoids state writes on most steps and roughly halves the dominant state memory traffic. Keeping recent inputs also makes speculative rollback a buffer‑pointer operation and enables output‑only verification without materializing intermediate states. The same separation allows a low‑precision checkpoint to serve output computation on most steps while a higher‑precision checkpoint serves recurrent updates, so rounding error in the low‑precision copy never enters later updates. We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM for Mamba‑2 and Gated DeltaNet. At serving batch size 256, it accelerates standard decoding by 1.20‑‑1.47× over a tuned vLLM baseline across four hybrid models, and delivers about 1.8× the throughput of vLLM's speculative decoding on the two 120B‑class models. Separate state precisions also reduce output KL divergence and downstream accuracy losses compared with a shared low‑precision checkpoint.

PaperId: 1125, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13772.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Tom Philipp Backert, Mohammad D. Soorati, Javad Ghofrani
Title: MARGoS: A Configuration-Driven Platform for Reproducible MARL Experiments in ARGoS
Abstract:
Multi‑agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has become a prominent research direction, particularly within collective robotics, where the ARGoS simulator is widely used to study emergent swarm behavior. Yet despite this growth, systematic support for reuse and reproducibility in MARL‑based swarm robotics remains limited and insufficiently standardized: a single experiment is assembled from manually aligned simulator files, training scripts, configuration values, paths, seeds, and environment details, so reuse and reproduction stay fragile even within one research group. To address this gap, we introduce MARGoS, a lightweight, configuration‑driven platform developed in this project that elevates these experiment‑defining inputs to first‑class, platform‑managed artifacts. MARGoS enables reproducible experimentation through configuration hashing, end‑to‑end seed propagation, frozen (immutable) configurations, structured logging, environment fingerprinting, and exportable experiment bundles that facilitate sharing, replay, and verification of results across machines and over time. A five‑dimension evaluation (architecture, efficiency, reproducibility, usability, and collaboration) supports our claim that managing experiment variation as a platform responsibility makes ARGoS+MARL experiments easier to reuse, reproduce, and hand off. Our code is available at https://github.com/tombackert/margos.

PaperId: 1126, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13766.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ali Shibli, Andrea Nascetti, Yifang Ban
Title: Shortcut Learning in Geospatial Foundation Model Embeddings for Cross-Disaster Damage Assessment
Abstract:
Geospatial foundation models can support disaster damage assessment, but high accuracy on familiar disasters may hide shortcut learning: prediction from event or scene characteristics rather than evidence that transfers to a new disaster. We study embeddings from TerraMind, Prithvi‑EO‑2.0, DOFA, and DINOv3 on the multi‑disaster datasets xView2 and BRIGHT. Holding out an entire disaster, instead of randomly splitting image tiles, reduces mean balanced accuracy from 0.807 to 0.638 on xView2 and from 0.818 to 0.568 on BRIGHT. Four sets of tests examine what information supports prediction: event and acquisition context, before/after image inputs, building count, and correct image pairing. Pre‑event images remain predictive, and a classifier given only the annotated number of buildings reaches balanced accuracy of 0.629 and 0.653. Combining before/after features performs best on average on xView2, but does not improve over pre‑only features on BRIGHT. Shuffling image pairs within the same disaster and damage class causes modest losses. Motivated by these findings, we test whether feature transformations learned only from training disasters improve generalization to unseen disasters. These transformations improve performance, with supervised contrastive learning performing best on xView2 and PCA on BRIGHT. Our results highlight the importance of evaluation on unseen domains for assessing model robustness and show that simple feature‑level transformations can improve generalization. Code and experiments can be found at https://github.com/alishibli97/gfm‑shortcut‑learning.

PaperId: 1127, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13763.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haonan Wang, Yuchen Wang, Jingyu Lu, Qixiang Zhang, Lehan Wang, Xuanqi Huang, Xiaomeng Li
Title: Neurons++: A Unified Visual-Stream Framework for Image and Video Reconstruction from fMRI with Neural-to-Visual Interpretability
Abstract:
Decoding visual experience from fMRI is important for understanding human perception and developing brain‑computer interfaces. Recent generative decoding methods can reconstruct plausible images and videos, but visual plausibility alone does not ensure that the output is faithfully grounded in brain activity. In this work, we propose Neurons++, a visual‑stream fMRI reconstruction framework for both static image and dynamic video reconstruction. Compared with our conference version Neurons, Neurons++ extends the paradigm from video‑only reconstruction to visual‑stream reconstruction for both images and videos, and replaces parallel task conditioning with serial cortex‑inspired decoding. The model first uses image‑fMRI pretraining to obtain a stable spatial‑semantic initialization, and then performs subject‑specific fine‑tuning for image and video reconstruction separately. The serial design organizes fMRI‑derived representations into explicit spatial, semantic, language‑level, and temporal cues. Extensive experiments show that Neurons++ achieves state‑of‑the‑art video reconstruction and competitive image reconstruction across standard benchmarks. Beyond reconstruction fidelity, neural‑to‑visual analyses indicate that Neurons++ exhibits qualitative directional controllability under neural perturbation, that its fMRI encoder read‑out is sensitive to stimulus‑relevant cortical features, and that it supports ROI‑guided semantic modulation. Code and model weights are available at: https://github.com/xmed‑lab/NeuronsPlusPlus.

PaperId: 1128, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13760.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Qituan Shangguan, Bosen Xu, Shuai Wang
Title: OpenSVBench: Diagnosing Speaker Verification Generalization Across Deployment Scenarios
Abstract:
Speaker verification (SV) systems now achieve very low error rates on standard public protocols, but those results do not fully describe deployment generalization. VoxCeleb‑style evaluations remain useful anchors for English in‑the‑wild media speech. Scenario‑specific evaluations and challenges are also valuable. However, neither setting directly shows whether the same system remains reliable across diverse deployment scenarios. We introduce OpenSVBench, a public benchmark for cross‑scenario SV evaluation. Its fixed public core contains 26 trial sets organized into 11 scenario groups, with 9.15M verification trials, frozen target/non‑target keys, and metadata for scenario‑wise reporting. Around this core, the online leaderboard acts as a diagnostic evaluation interface rather than only a ranked list. It accepts score packages from new systems, evaluates them with frozen keys and common scoring, and reports trial‑set breakdowns, scenario‑group metrics, macro EER/minDCF, model‑wise profiles, and scenario‑wise comparisons. We evaluate 18 public checkpoints spanning x‑vector, ECAPA‑TDNN, CAMPPlus, ResNet and ERes variants, ReDimNet2, SAM‑ResNet, and pretrained Transformer speaker recipes. The results show clear cross‑scenario gaps: systems with similar macro EER can have different scenario profiles, strong performance in one scenario does not guarantee strong performance in another, and same‑scenario trial sets can still expose source and protocol gaps.

PaperId: 1129, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13740.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Timi Owolabi, Hikmah Olawore, Frances Adelakun, Ayotomiwa Oyewumi
Title: SmolWAM: A Latent World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
Abstract:
World‑action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource‑constrained edge devices. We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B‑parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single‑frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified‑flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU‑hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16‑action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.

PaperId: 1130, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13733.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Boheng Li, Yueming Xing, Yiming Li, Jie Zhang, Han Qiu, Tianwei Zhang
Title: KVeil: First-Place Solution to ECCV 2026 LifeGenIP Challenge on Unlearnable Videos
Abstract:
The rapid development of personalized video generation has raised serious concerns over identity privacy, as a few facial videos of a person now suffice to reproduce their identity in synthetic videos. This report presents the first‑place solutions to both phases of the ECCV 2026 LifeGenIP Challenge on Unlearnable Videos, which aims to protect facial videos from unauthorized customization under a limited and imperceptible perturbation budget. For Phase 1, we introduce Reference Capacity Collapse, a pair of complementary losses that degrade the information carried by the reference condition while keeping subsequent video representations dependent on it, together with a Motion‑Guided EOT mechanism that improves robustness across unknown inference conditions. Phase 2 further considers tuning‑based customization and unseen generative models. To address both threats within a single perturbation, we design a two‑layer framework that protects the facial and background regions separately, constructing structure‑aligned perturbations from a synthetic target identity in the former and strengthening the white‑box disruption of Phase 1 in the latter. Our method achieves nearly perfect protection under white‑box reference‑based customization, and remains effective under other customization paradigms, various models, and temporal attacks. Both solutions are built upon our recent work LETHE. We hope our solutions can inspire future work on protecting facial videos against unauthorized customization. Our code is available at https://github.com/AntigoneRandy/KVeil.

PaperId: 1131, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13717.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Aravind Reddy, Deeraj S K, Mohd Wasif Raza, Saurav Prakash
Title: Machine Unlearning for Federated Socially Fair k-Means Clustering
Abstract:
Federated clustering can support applications such as patient stratification across hospitals and customer segmentation across distributed financial datasets. Responsible AI calls for fair representation of demographic groups and support for data deletion, motivated in part by rights such as the GDPR's right to erasure. These goals interact: deleting records can change the balance between groups and alter the clustering of the remaining population. We study exact machine unlearning for federated socially fair k‑means, whose objective is to minimize the largest group‑average squared distance to the nearest center. Our approach keeps separate local summaries for each group, so summaries at unaffected institutions remain valid as global fairness weights change. For two groups, we prove an initialization approximation guarantee independent of client group proportions under ideal sampling, and we show that same‑seed replay reproduces retraining exactly. Reuse pays off most when a whole client withdraws: across three datasets, replay is 35.8× faster than retraining for the initialization‑only model and remains 2.4× and 1.7× faster with one and two fair‑refinement rounds, which improve worst‑group cost. For individual record deletions, gains are modest (about 1.06×), and certifying cached assignments can cost more than it saves. These results map where exact unlearning can profitably reuse computation. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/arareddy/mufsc.

PaperId: 1132, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13697.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Connor Hashemi, Bharadwaj Ravichandran, Connor Anderson, Shitij Govil, Brandon RichardWebster, Brian Hu, Keith Fieldhouse
Title: Improving Semantic Coverage in AI Test & Evaluation through Generative Augmentation
Abstract:
In test and evaluation (T&E) of AI models, evaluators typically have access only to a held‑out test dataset and no knowledge of the training data or its semantic composition. If critical input conditions‑‑‑such as time‑of‑day, weather, or scene location‑‑‑are underrepresented in this test dataset, T&E results can be misleadingly due to this semantic coverage gap. We propose a three‑stage generative AI pipeline to detect and fill such semantic gaps without requiring ground‑truth labels of these semantics. First, vision‑language models (VLMs) perform zero‑shot binary labeling of semantic factors, and an embedding‑space clustering step identifies which semantics most affect downstream model behavior. Second, diffusion‑based image‑to‑image models transform existing covered images into the underrepresented semantic domain, preserving scene content while augmenting high‑level appearance. Third, statistical analysis of the augmented image embeddings verifies that the synthetic imagery improves dataset coverage before it is incorporated. Crucially, the synthetic data is used only to enrich the test set and no model retraining is performed for T&E. We validate the full pipeline on both image classification and object detection under day/night semantic gaps, showing that the augmented test datasets better distinguish models with and without exposure to the missing semantic, thereby yielding T&E conclusions that more closely match those of an ideal, fully covered dataset. Code available at https://github.com/Hashe037/DEDUCE

PaperId: 1133, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13681.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuchen Wang, Yanqi Bao, Zheng Gu, Zhengqing Chen, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo
Title: PhysForge: Material-Controllable 3D Reconstruction with Separable Components
Abstract:
Recent advances in physical 3D generation have enabled visually faithful assets with simulatable mechanical behavior. However, existing methods provide limited control over material behavior beyond appearance‑based inference and struggle to estimate physical properties from complex interactions between objects and semantic parts. Therefore, we present PhysForge, a Video Diffusion Model (VDM)‑based framework for addressing these challenges, comprising two complementary modules for material‑controllable physical fitting and componentlevel interaction modeling. The first, PhysFit, leverages material‑conditioned VDM dynamics as references for physical‑property fitting, introducing windowed fitting to focus on material‑revealing interactions and Hallucinated Forcing to disentangle nonphysical motion hallucinated by the VDM from material responses. The second, PhysComp decomposes complex interactions into individual objects and semantic components, enabling their physical parameters to be optimized independently and flexibly composed for joint simulation. Experiments on PhysAssets and Google Scanned Objects demonstrate that, compared with existing methods, PhysForge provides stronger control over material‑dependent physical responses while supporting component‑level physical modeling for complex interactions. It achieves the best CLIP and physical controllability scores on both common and uncommon materials, with qualitative comparisons, component‑level ablations, and a user study further supporting these improvements. Our project page is available at https://masterwanna.github.io/PhysForge.html .

PaperId: 1134, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13674.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Weiqi Sun, Qianyue Wu, Wenjia Wang, Tianyang Hu
Title: Not All Dimensions Are Equal: Outlier-Aware Attention Linearization with Grouped Quadratic Kernels
Abstract:
Linearizing softmax attention offers a route to efficient Transformer inference, but preserving pretrained attention remains challenging. We identify an important source of approximation error overlooked by standard linearization methods: a small number of outlier dimensions contribute disproportionately to query‑key dot products and account for a large fraction of the approximation error. Motivated by this heterogeneity, we propose Outlier‑Aware Attention Linearization (OAL), a dimension‑aware method for constructing quadratic attention approximations. Starting from a second‑order Taylor approximation, we introduce a Hadamard‑product formulation that makes individual query‑key contributions explicit. This formulation relaxes globally shared coefficients to support dimension‑specific linear terms and cross‑dimensional quadratic interactions while preserving separable evaluation. To retain this flexibility with fewer parameters, OAL groups dimensions with similar contribution scales to share coefficients, while allowing distinct treatment of the few outliers. The resulting positive quadratic kernel is calibrated against pretrained attention outputs and admits linear‑time evaluation with respect to sequence length for fixed head dimensions. On Qwen2.5‑0.5B, OAL reduces frozen‑attention output relative MSE by approximately 8.9% compared with DiJiang. Replacing middle‑layer attention modules and jointly fine‑tuning the kernel coefficients with LoRA further lowers WikiText‑103 perplexity from 31.71 to 27.50 compared with a learned global quadratic, while improving accuracy on PIQA, HellaSwag, and ARC‑E. These results demonstrate the value of outlier‑aware dimension grouping for both attention approximation and pretrained‑model conversion. The code is available at https://github.com/wuqianyue09/OAL

PaperId: 1135, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13654.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Tianqi Zhao, Jia Guo, Yan Shuo Tan, Qiong Zhang
Title: TabReliBench: Evaluating Tabular Foundation Models Beyond Predictive Accuracy
Abstract:
Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly popular for their strong predictive performance. Many also provide posterior predictive distributions (PPDs), whose reliability remains less studied. We assess reliability through point prediction, distributional quality, marginal and subgroup calibration, and interval efficiency. We then introduce TabReliBench, a large classification and regression benchmark for these comparisons and dataset‑level analyses. We find that TFMs' rankings change between TabArena and our benchmark and across reliability metrics. Regression TFMs usually achieve near‑nominal marginal coverage and retain narrow intervals, but this favorable marginal behavior does not imply valid conditional coverage. Dataset‑level analyses show that classification difficulty often accompanies poor calibration, whereas regression predictive performance is not a reliable indicator of calibration. Ensembling improves predictive performance but does not consistently improve calibration of PPDs; TFMs also benefit little from conformal post‑processing, which does not reliably resolve subgroup gaps. Reliable TFM selection therefore requires multidimensional evaluation beyond aggregate rankings. Code is available at https://github.com/Tianqi‑Zhao/TabReliBench.

PaperId: 1136, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13648.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Panayiotis Smeros, Vincent Emonet, Ruijie Wang, Ana-Claudia Sima, Tarcisio Mendes de Farias
Title: SPARQL-LLM in the TEXT2SPARQL 2026 Challenge
Abstract:
Querying distributed data represented as Knowledge Graphs (KGs) via SPARQL remains a difficult task, requiring fluency in query syntax, endpoint specifications, and schema details. Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) systems address this by automatically translating natural language into SPARQL, and recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have made this translation increasingly feasible. In this paper, we describe SPARQL‑LLM, our open‑source KGQA system, in the context of the TEXT2SPARQL 2026 challenge. In this challenge, SPARQL‑LLM ranks first overall among eight competing approaches across all datasets, achieving up to 59% higher accuracy than the second‑best approach and supporting multilingual question answering in English, German, and Spanish. SPARQL‑LLM is publicly released at https://github.com/sib‑swiss/sparql‑llm and deployed in production over decentralized bioinformatics KGs at https://www.expasy.org/chat.

PaperId: 1137, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13643.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xuanye Wu, Yue Shi, Yongcan Yang, Yiqun Wang, Zhaoqi Wan, Dayu Xia, Yanming Shao, Jiezhang Cao, Xiangfei Li, Yao Mu, Guangtao Zhai
Title: DexBioLab: Benchmarking Dexterous Manipulation with Dynamic Experimental Phenomena in Realistic Laboratories
Abstract:
Automating biological laboratories requires robots to perform dexterous tool interactions under realistic visual conditions while handling dynamic experimental phenomena, presenting significant challenges for robotic manipulation. To enable systematic evaluation under these conditions, we introduce DexBioLab, a simulation benchmark and framework for dexterous manipulation in realistic biological laboratory environments. DexBioLab comprises 14 tasks across 4 robot embodiments, spanning functional tool use, precision manipulation, language‑conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation. We introduce controllable dynamic experimental phenomena, including flames, vapor, and bubbles, to capture the evolving visual conditions of laboratory procedures. To further enhance environmental realism, we develop a hybrid rendering pipeline that integrates interactive simulated foreground objects with Gaussian‑splatting backgrounds reconstructed from 6 real laboratory scenes. For efficient large‑scale data generation and evaluation, we further build a parallel simulation framework on top of mjlab, proposing Parallel Finite‑State Machine (PFSM) and integrating batched rendering with decoupled trajectory replay for demonstration generation and model‑independent closed‑loop policy evaluation. Our evaluation reveals substantial variation in policy performance across tasks, exposing distinct strengths and weaknesses of current manipulation policies. Real‑world experiments further demonstrate a reduced sim‑to‑real gap, supporting the validity of AutoBio+ for realistic manipulation evaluation. Supplementary materials are available at https://cumulusalpha.github.io/DexBioLabWebPage.

PaperId: 1138, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13636.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ping Guo, Zhiqi Huang, Xinran Li, Linkun Yu, Jingyin Pei, Kamata Seiichiro
Title: Benchmarking Answer-Grounding Consistency in Remote Sensing Visual Question Answering
Abstract:
In grounded remote sensing visual question answering, a model produces a textual answer and identifies relevant objects in the image as grounding evidence. Existing evaluations measure answer correctness and localization quality, but do not directly assess answer‑grounding consistency. We propose the Answer‑Evidence Support Protocol (AESP) to assess this consistency through evidence support: whether the grounding evidence supports the model's own answer. AESP applies task‑specific rules to existence, counting, and comparison questions. We further construct the Grounded Remote Sensing Visual Question Answering (G‑RSVQA) benchmark, containing 15,027 samples with questions, reference answers, and all related object‑level annotations. Experiments on seven grounded vision‑‑language models reveal failures of evidence support across all three question types. Up to 50.82% of correct answers in the evidence evaluation subset are not supported by the provided grounding evidence.

PaperId: 1139, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13635.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Rishabh Jain, Federico Belotti, Stefano Coniglio, Pietro Lio, Stefano Fiorini
Title: PANDA: Prior-guided Attentional Dual-path Architecture
Abstract:
Hypergraph Neural Networks (HNNs), designed to model higher‑order relations beyond pairwise interactions, typically rely either on fixed structural weights or on normalised attention. Fixed weights can propagate misleading information in heterophilic settings, while normalisation makes attention coefficients competitive, in the sense that, in a message‑passing framework, increasing the weight of one sender must reduce the weight of others in the same aggregation set. Our main contribution is the introduction of PANDA (Prior‑guided AttentioNal Dual‑path Architecture), a plug‑in for two‑stage message passing HNNs applicable to both undirected and directed settings. The main path interpolates between learned receiver‑normalised attention and structural incidence priors, while a non‑competitive (not normalised) auxiliary path lets each sender contribute its own transformed information. We also show that, with fixed structural coefficients, PANDA recovers a certain complex‑valued convolution operator adopted in previous works. Across four HNNs spanning spatial and spectral methods in both directed and undirected settings, plugging PANDA in yields an average improvement of 5.18 percentage points across eight real‑world benchmark datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/jainris/panda.

PaperId: 1140, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13629.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Antti Hannukainen, Petr Kulikov, Matti Lassas, Lauri Oksanen
Title: An inverse spectral problem for the wave equation with a varying Robin parameter at the boundary
Abstract:
An inverse spectral problem for a (1+1)‑dimensional wave equation with wave speed c(x) is considered. The spectral data consist of the eigenvalues of the Neumann‑‑Dirichlet problem for the operator ‑c^2(x)\partial_x^2 together with their derivatives with respect to a Robin parameter at the boundary. We propose a two‑step recovery procedure. In the first step, the Neumann‑to‑Dirichlet map Λ is reconstructed from the spectral data using the results of arXiv/0406582. In the second step, the reconstructed Λ is used within the regularization strategy for the boundary control method presented in arXiv:1509.04478. As an improvement, the regularization of the control problems employs a weighted combination of L^2 and H^1 penalty terms, and we prove a uniform convergence result for the family of optimal controls, thereby allowing the regularization parameters to be tuned simultaneously. We also prove that the forward spectral map, which assigns to a wave speed its spectral data, is Lipschitz continuous, and that the inverse spectral map underlying the reconstruction procedure is Hölder continuous on a subclass of wave speeds. The method is implemented numerically and validated on both smooth and piecewise smooth wave speed profiles. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the recovery of the wave speed exhibits high accuracy and robustness.

PaperId: 1141, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13628.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Faith Ogunwoye, Didar Seyidov, Konstantin Gubernatorov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
Title: JitterVLA: A Replay Benchmark for Motion Quality in VLA-Driven Human-Robot Manipulation
Abstract:
Vision‑language‑action (VLA) policies issue sparse targets whose arrival at the robot controller is delayed and irregular, so a reasonable predicted action can still produce abrupt motion near people. Remedies are evaluated on different streams, delays and metrics. JitterVLA replays identical commands and arrival traces through alternative controllers, isolating the controller's effect. We apply it to synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, three open VLA pipelines (838 episodes) and a physical UR3. Interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk for every source, by 83% (615 to 106 m/s^3) on human motion with 200 ms delay, at a 2.0 cm tracking cost, and the effect replicated on 598 new episodes; jerk‑limited generation lowered jerk further at a larger cost. Entropy‑discontinuity associations had opposite, replicated signs in two pipelines, and entropy gating helped in one but not the other. On the UR3, interpolation lowered accelerometer‑derived jerk by 3.0‑14.0% in all six exploratory pairs, while a position‑derived metric did not resolve the contrast. JitterVLA supports screening before human‑centred studies; code and data will be released.

PaperId: 1142, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13627.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Natapong Nitarach, Phume Ngampornsukswadi, Pittawat Taveekitworachai, Surapon Nonesung, Warit Sirichotedumrong, Kunat Pipatanakul
Title: AMLworld-Compact: Importance-Weighted Downsampling for Cost-Effective LLM Evaluation and Error Diagnosis
Abstract:
Evaluating large language models (LLMs) on AMLworld's smallest test splits is costly because each of over a million targets requires a separate graph prompt. Sampling reduces this cost, but small balanced subsets change unweighted precision and F1. We introduce AMLworld‑Compact, an evaluation set that retains every illicit test transaction and samples benign transactions from supervised‑score strata. Its HT‑Coreset protocol reduces evaluation targets by 271x and 611x on HI‑Small and LI‑Small. Horvitz‑Thompson weights give unbiased full‑test confusion‑count estimates for fixed predictions; recall is exact, while precision and F1 are ratio estimates. In a held‑out study using Graph Feature Preprocessor (GFP) features, one boosted‑tree family defines strata for evaluating the other over 500 draws per configuration. At the released sizes, F1 RMSE is 0.00‑2.58 percentage points versus 4.44‑7.41 for uniform sampling with HT weights; conservative intervals remain broad. Under the evaluated graph prompts, seven open‑weight LLMs have weighted precision near the predict‑all‑illicit baseline. In an outcome‑stratified audit of 1,000 HI‑Small few‑shot outputs from one run per model, lexical checks pass for 84.5% of correct and 56.2% of incorrect binary verdicts, so these markers do not establish correctness. We release the evaluation sets, construction code, and audit tools at https://huggingface.co/datasets/typhoon‑ai/AMLworldCompactEval and https://github.com/nat‑nischw/AMLworld‑Compact.

PaperId: 1143, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13608.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Quentin Le Tellier, Albert Rilliard, Olivier Perrotin, Marc Evrard
Title: Vocal Intensity Conversion with Continuous SPL Control via Adversarial Training
Abstract:
Vocal intensity conversion renders a recorded utterance at a different vocal intensity, rather than simply scaling its amplitude, while preserving its content and speaker identity. Existing systems control intensity through a reference utterance or a few discrete categories. Instead, we control the conversion with any target sound pressure level (SPL) on a continuous dB scale. A lightweight converter, trained as a conditional cycle‑consistent GAN without parallel data, transforms the features of a frozen speech encoder, from which a pretrained vocoder resynthesizes the speech. We compare three representations, log‑mel spectrograms, WavLM, and SpeechTokenizer, and introduce an objective protocol that measures the achieved intensity change against the target one on a calibrated corpus. With WavLM, the converter achieves a measured 83% of the target change in intensity and also shifts the fundamental frequency. A perceptual evaluation confirms that perceived vocal intensity increases with the target level on amplitude‑normalized stimuli.

PaperId: 1144, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13607.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Arzu Burcu Güven, Anna Rogers, Leonie Weissweiler, Joakim Nivre, Rob van der Goot
Title: BLiMPPI: Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs for Polarity Items
Abstract:
Negative polarity items (NPIs), such as "anymore" and "ever", are grammatical only in select environments, predominantly in the context of negation. Because their grammaticality depends on both syntax and semantics, they have a rich, multilingual literature in theoretical linguistics, yet work on NPIs in language models is almost entirely confined to English. We introduce BLiMPPI, a multilingual evaluation suite of over 12,000 NPI minimal pairs in 33 languages, built by a pipeline that discovers NPIs in Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks, labels their licensing environments, and perturbs these into minimal pairs. Evaluating 12 multilingual and 2 monolingual models alongside n‑gram baselines, we find that multilingual models struggle most with lower‑resource languages and with pairs that are not n‑gram solvable. We further examine the effects of NPI typology, language family, licensing variability, and NPI‑licenser distance. Data: https://github.com/arzuburcuguven/blimppi‑data

PaperId: 1145, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13606.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Gautier Marti
Title: CorrFlow: Exact and Permutation-Equivariant Flow Matching on the Correlation Elliptope
Abstract:
Correlation matrices combine nonlinear positive‑definiteness constraints with a simultaneous row‑column permutation symmetry. Their generation therefore involves two distinct problems. First, every output must remain on the correlation elliptope, irrespective of how its variables are ordered. Second, the generator must learn the domain‑specific distribution occupied by empirical data inside that valid space. Existing financial image generators mix these problems: they learn ordered matrix entries and repair invalid draws afterward. We introduce CorrFlow, which separates them. A generalized Fisher transform maps full‑rank correlation matrices bijectively to unconstrained coordinates, guaranteeing valid outputs without projection. A graph flow‑matching network learns the empirical distribution in those coordinates and is permutation equivariant: reordering the variables only reorders the output. We compare a conditional CorrGAN reimplementation, image diffusion, and CorrFlow on 80×80 Taiwan equity matrices using five seeds per neural method. CorrFlow produces 100% valid draws without repair and obtains feature sliced‑Wasserstein distance .712\pm.141, versus 4.339\pm.252 for CorrGAN and 4.610\pm.191 for image diffusion after their invalid outputs are projected back to the correlation space. It also improves this distance over historical lookup, while lookup retains higher local coverage. These results support the combined construction under the evaluated training budget; they do not establish superiority over fully tuned image models or isolate the contribution of each component.

PaperId: 1146, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13605.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Saibo Geng, Andrea Gentilini, Xinxian Ma, Nathan Ranchin, Yunzhen Yao, Robert West
Title: zip2zip++: Towards Inference-Time Token Compression with Minimal Quality Loss
Abstract:
Dynamic vocabularies built on‑the‑fly via Lempel‑Ziv‑Welch (LZW) compression let a language model represent the same text in fewer tokens, but prior work shows that this efficiency comes at a cost to reasoning and perplexity. We show that this quality gap is not a fundamental price of compression but can be substantially closed through targeted improvements to the compression layer and LZW codec, without modifying the underlying pretrained language model. Our analysis reveals four key issues: (1) LZW's compression algorithm creates an implicit conflict between the input embedding and the output embedding, a tension that a single shared embedding cannot resolve; (2) naively applying RoPE to LZW‑compressed sequences ignores that merged tokens can span multiple tokens; (3) merging certain tokens (notably digits) disproportionately hurts downstream accuracy; and (4) dynamic vocabularies introduce an inherent segmentation ambiguity that confounds standard evaluation. We address these through decoupled input/output dynamic embedding layer, size‑aware RoPE positioning, and a modified LZW codec supporting selective merges and multi‑view segmentations. Across four models, our recipe improves perplexity on every corpus we evaluated as well as mathematical reasoning accuracy, closing roughly half the quality gap between zip2zip and the uncompressed baseline at a similar compression ratio on general text. This represents a significant step toward lossless adaptive‑vocabulary compression for language models.

PaperId: 1147, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13599.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Michelle Espranita Liman, Ioana Ionac, Alexander Müller, Eimo Martens, Daniel Rueckert, Philip Müller
Title: EchoTab: Learning Measurement-Grounded Representations for Echocardiographic Diagnosis through Tabular Reconstruction
Abstract:
Diagnostic information in multi‑view medical imaging studies, like echocardiography, is distributed across views, each capturing different aspects of cardiac structure and function. In clinical practice, these views are first interpreted through quantitative measurements, which then support specific diagnoses. However, existing echo representation learning methods do not explicitly model measurements as an intermediate representation between views and diagnosis. As a result, individual measurements are not explicitly represented in a form that downstream diagnostic tasks can selectively use, hindering accurate diagnosis. Inspired by this hierarchical clinical workflow, we introduce EchoTab, a measurement‑grounded representation learning framework that represents multi‑view echocardiography studies using measurement‑specific tokens as an intermediate representation between echo views and diagnosis. Each measurement token selectively attends to the views relevant to its estimation and is trained through tabular reconstruction to predict the corresponding measurement value. The resulting tokens form a factorized echo representation, which encode clinically meaningful structural and functional properties and can be selectively used for downstream diagnosis. Unlike the commonly used contrastive approaches, EchoTab does not require negative samples or large batch sizes. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate that EchoTab learns effective measurement‑grounded representations that improve diagnosis classification in multi‑view echocardiography and its learned attention aligns with established measurement‑view relationships used by cardiologists. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/michelleespranita/EchoTab.

PaperId: 1148, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13593.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shouchen Qiu, Huaijun Qiu
Title: Time-Varying Favorite-Longshot Bias in Polymarket Weather Markets
Abstract:
Prediction‑market prices combine traders' judgments about future outcomes, but their errors may be concentrated in particular price ranges and change as settlement approaches. Prior cross‑category evidence shows that Polymarket weather markets have larger pricing bias than other major categories, without separating low‑price longshots from high‑price favorites. This study compares the two ranges at different horizons in daily maximum‑temperature markets. Event‑level probability scores, cubic B‑spline recalibration, and Buy‑NO tests are used to examine the form and effect of the bias. Longshot overpricing mainly occurs at distant horizons, whereas favorite overpricing becomes much stronger during the final 1‑12 hours and is nearly one order of magnitude larger. Event‑level scores improve toward the daily temperature peak, while simple recalibration yields no statistically significant gains. The Buy‑NO results in the corresponding time windows also show that the main pricing error is concentrated at the favorite end.

PaperId: 1149, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13578.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xuhui Kang, Sung-Wook Lee, Yan Zhuang, Tianle Zhong, Yen-Ling Kuo
Title: RARA: Robust Policy Fine-Tuning through Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment for Robotic Manipulation
Abstract:
Pre‑trained robot policies, such as Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) models, provide a strong foundation for generalist robotic manipulation, but adapting them to new tasks with only a few demonstrations remains challenging. Directly fine‑tuning a pre‑trained policy often achieves strong in‑distribution performance, yet it can distort the representations learned during pre‑training and weaken the model's generalization ability under out‑of‑distribution shifts. We propose Retrieval‑Anchored Representation Alignment (RARA), a two‑stage adaptation method, to address this issue. First, RARA retrieves representation features from pretraining with similar task intent and motion, and aligns the policy's representations of the target demonstrations with the pre‑trained representations of the retrieved demonstrations. Second, RARA fine‑tunes the policy on the target demonstrations while limiting how much its representations of the retrieved demonstrations change during fine‑tuning. By reducing the representation mismatch before action learning and preserving pre‑trained knowledge during adaptation, RARA limits unnecessary representation drift during fine‑tuning. Experiments with Diffusion Policy and GR00T on 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot show that RARA improves the average success of fine‑tuning by 9.5 points in‑distribution and 13.6 points out‑of‑distribution, and outperforms all compared baselines. Project page: https://shua‑kang.github.io/RARA_robot/

PaperId: 1150, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13572.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhihao Tian, Zifan Wang, Enzheng Zhu, Xun Yang, Jialong Qin, Mengbo Wang, Junwei Liang
Title: ATHLETE: Learning Reactive Humanoid Tennis via Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching
Abstract:
Humanoid tennis requires reactive whole‑body coordination under rapidly changing ball dynamics, yet collecting task‑specific motion‑capture demonstrations that cover diverse approach states, contact locations, and timing conditions is costly. Inspired by how humans acquire new skills by combining reusable motor experience with task‑specific demonstrations, we present ATHLETE, a framework for learning reactive humanoid tennis from generic locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos. ATHLETE combines LAFAN1 locomotion with video‑derived striking motions and uses Trajectory‑Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) to construct diverse task‑conditioned whole‑body references. These references are transformed into a reactive policy through physics‑based teacher‑‑student learning with online DAgger distillation, followed by PPO fine‑tuning for the tennis task. The resulting policy responds directly to robot and ball observations without requiring reference‑motion inputs at deployment. On a real humanoid robot, ATHLETE achieves forehand and backhand hit rates of 90.00% and 86.67%, respectively, and enables multi‑shot rallies with human players. These results demonstrate that ATHLETE can learn dynamic humanoid tennis skills from reusable locomotion data and video demonstrations. Result videos and code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/ATHLETE2027/.

PaperId: 1151, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13548.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Denis Degtiarev, Anna Gromova, Sergey Katkov, Artem Mikhailin, Safina Mukhamedshina, Albert Nasybullin, Karina Shaikhutdinova, Artem Tuzov
Title: Auditing VLM Benchmarks from Existing Evaluation Runs
Abstract:
Every evaluation run of a vision‑language model (VLM) already produces per‑question artifacts (predictions, judged correctness, metadata) that leaderboards reduce to a single score and then discard. We reuse those artifacts to audit the benchmark itself, and add an audit layer to VLMEvalKit: six detectors that run as post‑processing over saved outputs, plus one additional text‑only rerun with visual inputs removed, emitting a per‑question report. The layer reports per‑question findings together with aggregate audit statistics; for the headline quantities, it attaches permutation‑null excess where applicable, interval estimates for proportions, and sensitivity to the model pool. Auditing MMStar, a benchmark curated specifically so that the image is indispensable, with three models, we find zero aggregate accuracy gain from the image on 20.2% of its questions. An item‑matched permutation null accounts for 17.0%, leaving a +3.2 pp excess (corrected permutation p = 0.001). This excess is concentrated in the mathematics and science categories and is absent from coarse perception, a localization consistent with knowledge substituting for visual evidence; confirming that mechanism would require item‑level review. A second detector flags 134 questions on which every model that answered in parseable form picked the same non‑gold option, and these candidates peak in the perception categories, whereas the zero‑gain excess is largest in mathematics and science & technology. Replacing the LLM judge with exact string matching changes no conclusion, and every scoring discrepancy between the two traces to one model whose free‑form answers a parser cannot read. On a binary yes/no benchmark the detectors measurably fall out of calibration, a scope boundary that we measure and report. The audit layer, the prediction artifacts and the generated reports accompany this submission.

PaperId: 1152, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13494.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Changye Li, Zijian Zhang, Muheng Li, Yiduo Pang, Tingjun Wu, Menghan Li, Yitong Liu, Hongkai Guo, Mengchi Chen, Chenyu He, Kaisheng Ma, Wei Xu, Song Han, Sihao Liu, Ligeng Zhu
Title: Humanize MLE Agents: Multi-Agent Session Alternation Beyond Single-Agent Limits
Abstract:
Existing LLM‑based agent approaches for long‑horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) often use context engineering, implemented through custom harnesses that manage tools, skills, and accumulated experience. However, we find that as single‑session execution lengthens, the agent's reasoning intensity declines alongside slowing progress, summarized as long‑horizon deceleration, and the benefits of these custom harnesses vanish as the underlying model improves, summarized as harness staleness. These findings suggest that their benefits may not persist across versions, which motivates a workflow‑level approach in which agents build on one another's work across sessions. We model these alternating agent sessions as a context‑reset semi‑Markov decision process (CR‑SMDP) and establish sufficient conditions for alternation to exceed single‑agent reference limits, derive an explicit experiment‑budget bound, and characterize when session caps preserve this advantage. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Humanize MLE Agents (HMA), which alternates two agents on a shared workspace, limits each session to at most k experiments and resets the context between sessions, without additional task‑specific harness or prior knowledge supplements. Across 75 Kaggle tasks in MLE‑bench, HMA reaches a state‑of‑the‑art any‑medal rate of 78.2%, exceeding the strongest open‑source baseline by 8.0 points with a quarter of its time budget. Moreover, among six configurations spanning five heterogeneous agent pairs, HMA improves any‑medal rate over the constituent baselines by 6.4 points on average, demonstrating cross‑pair generality. A supplementary case on kernel optimization reaches 878 cycles, within 1.6% of the community leaderboard leader, demonstrating applicability beyond MLE.

PaperId: 1153, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13491.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yilian Shi, Qingyu Liu, Tianyi Zhou, Wende Tan, Chenyang Si, Yueming Lyu, Xia Hu, Dongrui Liu
Title: EviRepair: Evidence-Driven Agents for Reliable Vulnerability Repair
Abstract:
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agent‑based approaches for repository‑level automated vulnerability repair (AVR), showing promising repair capabilities. However, an important issue has received limited attention: how can we ensure that the evidence generated during the repair process is reliable enough to support accurate vulnerability understanding and patch generation? In this paper, we propose EviRepair, an evidence‑driven multi‑agent framework for repository‑level AVR. EviRepair introduces evidence review into the repair process by enabling agents to collaboratively collect vulnerability evidence, verify evidence consistency, and construct a reviewed vulnerability model for patch synthesis and validation. Extensive experiments on PatchEval and SecBench benchmarks with multiple agent frameworks and LLMs demonstrate that EviRepair consistently outperforms existing agent‑based baselines, achieving average improvements of 16.37% and 40.33% in resolved rates on PatchEval and SecBench, respectively. Codes are available at https://github.com/lly‑s/EviRepair

PaperId: 1154, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13485.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Xueyang Feng, Chaozhuo Li, Xiaohe Bo, Jiakai Tang, Chenxi Li, Qiwei Ye, Xu Chen
Title: Proactive Agentic Orchestration
Abstract:
Agentic orchestration delegates tasks to sub‑agents with independent contexts, providing a key path to extending the effective execution horizon of large language model agents. However, existing orchestration methods face two limitations: in execution, current methods fix sub‑agents' goals and harnesses at creation time, limiting their adaptability to dynamic real‑world environments; in optimization, sparse and delayed feedback constrains effective learning of the orchestration policy. To address these limitations, we introduce POrchestra, an on‑the‑fly proactive agentic orchestration framework. It allows sub‑agents to proactively communicate with the orchestrator at any logical point to request harness adjustments while maintaining continuity of local execution. This mechanism not only enables sub‑agents to adapt seamlessly to dynamic environments but also naturally inspires On‑Policy Orchestration Distillation (OPOD) based on hindsight feedback. OPOD attributes sub‑agents' proactive revision requests back to preceding orchestration decisions to derive targeted improvement signals, and leverages these signals as process supervision alongside the final reward to optimize the orchestration policy. We evaluate POrchestra on three long‑horizon agent benchmarks spanning deep research, dynamic digital assistance, and software engineering. POrchestra improves task success by an average of 9.1% relative to the strongest baseline; combined with OPOD, it improves small‑orchestrator success by an average of 10.0% relative to existing training baselines. POrchestra also achieves a more favorable cost‑performance trade‑off. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/XueyangFeng/POrchestra.

PaperId: 1155, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13470.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Zheming Fu, Ruizhe He, Wenbin Ning, Xiaoxiao Ma, Xuan Yang, Lianrui Mu, Haoyang Huang, Chang Liu, Lei Wang, Siming Fu
Title: GraftOOD: Grafting Out-of-Distribution Exemplars into Advantage-Weighted Rectification for Video Reward Optimization
Abstract:
Video reward optimization can increase proxy rewards while reducing video dynamics, a mismatch we identify as \emphmotion collapse, including under a video‑level motion‑quality reward. We propose GraftOOD, which replaces part of the online rollouts in selected prompt groups with out‑of‑distribution video exemplars. A shared velocity‑regression objective combines group‑relative reward rectification with sequence‑level exemplar supervision, requiring neither exemplar generation trajectories nor an additional supervised‑loss coefficient. We characterize its pointwise optimal field as a source‑posterior‑weighted combination of the two source‑specific target fields. We construct GraftSet‑Video, containing 9,588 format‑matched exemplars for 2,397 prompts, to supply external supervision.
