On Wan2.1‑1.3B, GraftOOD raises Dynamic Degree from 4.86 to 44.41 relative to reward‑only FlowAWR, while HPSv3 decreases from 8.10 to 7.32 and VisionReward remains close. At the main setting, GraftOOD leads nine of ten metrics among three exemplar‑augmented methods. Ablations of exemplar frequency and within‑group count reveal dynamics‑‑reward trade‑offs rather than uniform gains from increasing exemplar usage. These results support external exemplar supervision as a complement to scalar reward feedback, without equating higher measured dynamics with coherent, visually plausible motion in the generated videos. Code is available at \hrefhttps://github.com/Fuzm7/FlowAWRGraftOOD.

PaperId: 1156, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13464.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ohad Sheelo, Tal Golan, Ari Pakman
Title: Gaussian BROJA Partial Information Decomposition in Closed Form
Abstract:
The BROJA partial information decomposition provides an operationally motivated way to separate the information that two sources carry about a target into unique, redundant, and synergistic components. For continuous and high‑dimensional variables, however, computing the BROJA decomposition requires solving a difficult optimization problem. Previous work showed that, when each source‑target pair is jointly Gaussian, the problem can be reduced to finite‑dimensional numerical optimization. Here, we derive a closed‑form solution to this optimization problem, enabling direct computation of the BROJA decomposition in the general multivariate Gaussian setting. The resulting closed‑form expression enables speedups exceeding two orders of magnitude for high‑dimensional Gaussian BROJA PID. Code is available at https://github.com/brainsandmachines/Eigen_PID.

PaperId: 1157, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13447.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Daniel Varela Sánchez, Guillermo Martín-Coello Juárez
Title: Oído: Open-Vocabulary Speech Recognition on a $5 Microcontroller without a Neural Accelerator
Abstract:
Speech recognition on low‑cost microcontrollers is, in practice, limited to keyword spotting or a fixed list of commands. We present Oído, an inference engine that runs open‑vocabulary English speech recognition entirely on an ESP32‑S3 (240 MHz dual‑core Xtensa LX7, 512 KB of SRAM, 8 MB of PSRAM, 16 MB of flash, no neural accelerator). Oído executes a 13M‑parameter Conformer‑CTC model with int8 weights, per‑frame dynamic int8 activations and int8 attention on the chip's SIMD instructions, with a schedule designed around flash and PSRAM bandwidth. On LibriSpeech test‑clean/test‑other the on‑device arithmetic reaches 3.70%/8.23% word error rate (WER), within 0.12 points of full precision, and 3.33%/7.15% with an on‑chip 1.3M‑parameter language model; a transducer head gives 2.99%/6.67% and an int4 variant fits in 8.3 MB. This is 2.3‑2.8x fewer errors than the vendor's recognizer on the same chip, and fewer than Whisper tiny.en and Moonshine tiny in full precision on a laptop, including in real noise and reverberation. Measured on a physical board, the firmware runs at 1.97x the duration of the audio on one core, with transcripts identical to an instruction‑exact emulator: accurate, but not yet real time (a 4 s command is transcribed about 8.7 s after it ends). The two‑core schedule gives wrong results on silicon and is disabled. A streaming variant shows partial text while the speaker talks and delivers the final text 4.1‑11.1 s after clips of 3.6‑10.6 s (7.2‑22.4 s in utterance mode) at 4.86%/11.03% WER; a Spanish model makes 34‑60% fewer errors than multilingual Whisper tiny. Code and models are released.

PaperId: 1158, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13435.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Arvasu Kulkarni, Mahir Jain, Aditya Ray Mishra, Sandeep Singh, Siddharth Panwar
Title: PPG-Bench: A Unified Benchmark for PPG Foundation Models
Abstract:
Photoplethysmography (PPG) is increasingly recorded by wearable and clinical devices at enormous scale, and a growing number of PPG foundation models (FMs) have been developed to compute reusable representations for various downstream tasks. These models are difficult to compare: different evaluations use different datasets, task definitions, preprocessing, downstream heads, hyperparameter tuning, and baselines. We present PPG‑Bench, a unifying open‑source benchmark evaluating five public PPG FMs across nine open‑access datasets and 26 tasks spanning cardiovascular state estimation, activity, sleep, screening, and identification. We evaluate models under four downstream regimes of increasing adaptability (linear probing, random forests, frozen MLP probes, and end‑to‑end finetuning), with model‑specific hyperparameter optimization and subject‑disjoint cross‑validation. We also evaluate against three controls: random/constant baseline, a deterministic pulse‑rate‑variability (PRV) feature set, and a generic time‑series FM (MOMENT). Across all 68 task‑regime combinations, 35.3% show no meaningful FM advantage over the random/constant baseline, and in 83.8% no PPG‑specific FM outperforms both PRV and MOMENT. We also find that added downstream head capacity generally improves performance, but can cause significant degradation if the model is performing at chance/constant level. Current PPG FMs therefore cannot yet claim to provide generalised and transferrable representations of PPG signals, and future evaluation in this field should include checks against simple, non‑learned controls. Code for the benchmark and instructions to evaluate more models can be found here ‑ https://github.com/mannas‑ai/ppg‑bench.

PaperId: 1159, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13430.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kurt Butler, Damian Machlanski, Michael P. J. Camilleri, Zhihua Liu, Panagiotis Dimitrakopoulos, Feng Chen, Ricardo Silva, Sotirios A. Tsaftaris
Title: One Thing Leads to Another: The Essentials of Time Series Causal Discovery
Abstract:
Time series causal discovery ‑‑‑ the process of detecting causation between time series ‑‑‑ has its roots in signal processing research from over a half century ago. It has since received active and widespread interest, evolving into different forms across domains such as statistics, dynamical systems and machine learning. Entering this fragmented and constantly evolving research landscape can be daunting. This tutorial provides a unified overview of time series causal discovery across research communities. We introduce the key principles invoked by modern discovery methods, and we discuss their limitations and assumptions. We also discuss how discovery methods are evaluated, benchmarked and fine‑tuned. We further discuss how causal discovery for time series is becoming crucial for downstream tasks in agriculture and Earth science, in healthcare, and in artificial intelligence systems. We believe that this tutorial will serve as a valuable resource in navigating the deluge of recent causality research, as well as an invitation to signal processing audiences to contribute to causal problems. To further help readers, we host a companion repository to link to useful code packages and resources at https://github.com/CHAI‑UK/Awesome‑Time‑Series‑Causal‑Discovery.

PaperId: 1160, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13409.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuhao Wei, Yong Chen, Chen Yang, Yingchen Wang, Delin Ouyang, Lingfeng Qi, Qi Lan, Zhanhua Zhang, Jie Li, Guofa Li
Title: ManeuverFlow: Maneuver Hypothesis Generation with Future Evidence for Trajectory Evaluation and Refinement in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
Abstract:
End‑to‑end planning in complex scenes must model diverse driving intentions and select the most appropriate trajectory using scene context and future risks. However, multi‑query regression may collapse to one mode, while anchor‑based and generative planners share a scaling bottleneck: small candidate sets limit maneuver coverage or discovery of high‑quality trajectories, whereas large sets increase generation and scoring costs. We propose ManeuverFlow to generate trajectories for distinct intentions in one step and evaluate and refine them using current and future evidence. The model selects relevant maneuver modes, draws corresponding noise from the Gaussian mixture prior, and maps it to intention‑specific trajectories through a maneuver‑routed mixture‑of‑experts MeanFlow field. Current features and future features predicted by the world model are aggregated along each candidate path into trajectory‑specific evidence for PDM‑factor prediction. Using the same evidence, the refiner predicts local Frenet residuals for selected candidates; refined and retained candidates are then jointly re‑scored for selection. With a lightweight TransFuser‑style ResNet‑34 backbone, ManeuverFlow achieves 90.6 PDMS and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v1/v2 navtest, respectively. On WorldEngine's recent 3DGS closed‑loop benchmark, it attains the highest listed PDMS^\ast scores of 75.19 and 74.58 under logged and IDM‑controlled traffic, respectively. Code: https://github.com/wyh‑autonomy/maneuverflow.

PaperId: 1161, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13403.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Quentin Rolland, Fabrice Mayran de Chamisso, Jean-Baptiste Mouret
Title: Robot-WATCHDOG : failure detection through object-centric graph representation
Abstract:
Reliable real‑time failure detection is critical for deploying learned robotic policies, yet defining failures explicitly is infeasible in open‑world settings. This motivates failure detection from nominal demonstrations alone. Existing methods, however, struggle to balance robustness to benign variations with the ability to capture semantic and interaction‑level errors. We introduce Robot‑WATCHDOG, a self‑supervised framework that models manipulation scenes as object‑centric spatio‑temporal graphs. Building on this representation, we investigate two complementary failure scores: Trajectory Projection and Correlation (TPC), a non‑parametric measure of geometric deviation and relational consistency, and GnnT, a Graph Attention Network with a Transformer that predicts future object states. We evaluate both on a public benchmark and on a new dataset of semantically complex manipulation tasks, across six tasks and ten random seeds. Both scores outperform image‑based failure detectors, particularly on semantic and interaction‑level failures. TPC provides the strongest performance in AUPR and MCC on both dataset averages, with low variance across seeds. Qualitative results are made available at https://cea‑list.github.io/Robot‑WATCHDOG/.

PaperId: 1162, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13368.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Seungki Hong, Kyeongwon Jeong, Taekwang Jang
Title: Anechoic: Onsager-Corrected Parallel Annealing for Sub-0.1 ms Dense Max-Cut on an FPGA
Abstract:
Ising machines solve combinatorial optimization problems by annealing a network of spins. On dense problems, the least expensive hardware step updates all spins at once: stochastic cellular automata (SCA) decide every spin in parallel and read couplings only for the spins that flip. Such synchronous updates create an echo: the previous state of each spin returns to it through its neighbors. On K2000, a Max‑Cut benchmark on a 2,000‑node complete graph, two‑thirds of all flips undo the same spin's flip one step earlier. This paper presents Anechoic, an FPGA Ising machine that subtracts this echo from every decision. Dynamical mean‑field theory identifies the echo as an Onsager reaction; its one‑step strength is the number of spins whose flip probability is strictly between 0 and 1, divided by twice the temperature. The decision logic already flags these spins, so the correction costs one population count per step; a temperature‑scaled form needs none. An RTL engine executes a dense 2,000‑spin step in 18.1 cycles plus 0.14 per flip, so every saved step and flip saves time. Both forms find better K2000 cuts at every step budget than five published binary‑spin algorithms at their papers' settings. Twelve engines at 250 MHz on an AMD Alveo V80 reach a cut of at least 33,000 with 99% probability in 0.05 ms, 5.2 times faster than the fastest published hardware, at 5.4 mJ per solution; with 2‑bit couplings, the temperature‑scaled form is also faster than uncorrected SCA on 49 of 51 G‑set graphs. On an NVIDIA GH200 GPU, the same engine is 2.3 times slower and needs 8.0 times more energy per solution, though its 240 concurrent anneals give 2.3 times the throughput. As a GlobalFoundries 22 nm ASIC at 1.25 GHz, twelve engines would reach the target in about 10 microseconds, 26 times faster than the fastest published hardware. The code is available at https://github.com/skethz/anechoic.

PaperId: 1163, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13361.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jiahao Wang, Hongjin Qian, Yuyang Hu, Jiajun Zhang, Zheng Liu
Title: AgentSWE: Can Coding Agents Build the Agent You Actually Want?
Abstract:
As the production of software passes into the hands of software itself, coding agents are increasingly commissioned to build agents fitted to their users' own workflows. This delegation carries a quiet assumption, that the delivered agent will faithfully serve the requirement it was built for, rather than merely appear to. No existing benchmark tests that assumption. We introduce AgentSWE, a benchmark for agent software engineering spanning three stages of the agent development lifecycle: Creation of a complete agent from a natural‑language requirement, Editing of production agent codebases, and Optimization toward a measurable target. Each of its 25 tasks is framed as a commission rather than an exam: the builder iterates against a handful of illustrative cases, while acceptance exercises the frozen submission on held‑out cases designed to span the full requirement, grading behavior against requirement‑derived rubrics under hard pass/fail gates or, for Optimization, against the source benchmark's own objective. Evaluating a range of coding agents across models and harnesses, we find that none comes close to delivering what a requirement asks for: the gap between what a builder demonstrates and what it delivers is the norm, not the corner case. An accompanying empirical analysis of the failure trajectories identifies recurring failure modes, among them overfitting to the visible cases, hollow runtimes behind code that looks complete, and unsupported claims of completion, each a signal by which coding agents can learn to build the agents they are asked for.

PaperId: 1164, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13350.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Carolin Cissée, Dennis Fast, Raneen Younis, Alexander Löser, Wolfgang Nejdl, Zahra Ahmadi
Title: Hidden Data Challenges in Clinical Machine Learning
Abstract:
Widely reused preprocessing pipelines for electronic health records can encode assumptions about when information became available, what clinical episode a label represents, and what missingness means. These assumptions are rarely audited systematically and may propagate across subsequent studies when preprocessing pipelines are reused or adapted. Using MIMIC‑IV as a case study, we identify and quantify violations of three complementary forms of preprocessing alignment, i.e., temporal, semantic, and population alignment, which manifest as temporal leakage, feature‑task misalignment, and biased imputation. We show how ambiguities in timestamp semantics, episode definitions, endpoint construction, modality selection, and missingness handling can alter the information available to a model and affect the interpretation of its predictions. Through analyses of MIMIC‑IV data and empirical case studies, we demonstrate that such choices may remain largely invisible in aggregate predictive performance while changing the signals on which models rely. We derive practical recommendations for temporally valid, clinically aligned, and reproducible preprocessing of MIMIC‑IV and related electronic health record datasets. The code for our experiments, including our proposed preprocessing, is available at: https://github.com/m2l‑lab/mimic‑iv‑preprocess.

PaperId: 1165, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13348.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zijun Wang, Yifan Ji, Haidong Xin, Zhenghao Liu, Yukun Yan, Zulong Chen, Yu Gu, Ge Yu, Maosong Sun
Title: Test-Time Memory Construction
Abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to answer questions over long interaction histories, where relevant evidence may be scattered across distant sessions. Existing memory systems typically construct and maintain sophisticated memory representations offline, before user queries are observed, incurring substantial overhead and limiting their ability to adapt memory construction to query‑specific information needs. In this paper, we propose T^2Mem, a Test‑Time Memory construction framework that defers memory construction to inference and progressively builds memory along the reasoning process. Specifically, T^2Mem extracts lightweight episode‑level metadata offline to capture key events and temporal associations as retrieval cues, while retaining links to the original interactions to facilitate the reconstruction of dependencies across episodes. At test time, the LLM adaptively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw interactions, progressively constructing query‑specific memory as reasoning unfolds. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show the effectiveness of T^2Mem by consistently outperforming strong baselines across different backbone LLMs while substantially reducing the overhead of memory construction. Further analysis demonstrates that deferring memory construction to inference enables the memory construction process to dynamically adapt to the information needs of individual queries. All code is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/T2Mem.

PaperId: 1166, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13344.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Benyuan Meng, Yiliang Zhang, Jin-Wen Wu, Qianqian Xu, Qingming Huang, Longtao Huang
Title: Why DiT Models Underperform as Representation Learners without Long Skip Connections
Abstract:
Diffusion feature, i.e., intermediate activations extracted from diffusion model backbones, has emerged as a promising approach for unifying generation and vision understanding (discrimination). Despite the advancement of diffusion backbones into Diffusion Transformers (DiT), it has been found in previous literature that DiT models tend to yield weaker features despite their stronger generation capability. This poses a threat to good generation‑understanding unification. In this work, we show via controlled from‑scratch training that long skip connections (LSCs) affect feature quality: a DiT with LSCs can produce better features. Furthermore, through detailed diagnosis, we reveal the mechanism causing this effect. Specifically, the input to a diffusion backbone contains both the latent image and the diffusion noise, where the diffusion noise, though appearing in the form of noises, actually reflects the information of the diffusion trajectory. To make the final prediction of a noisy variable (v or ε), the diffusion backbone needs both signals. However, carrying both signals through the main backbone effectively "pollutes" the image signal with noises, leading to poor feature quality. In comparison, LSCs can shortcut diffusion noises directly to where they are needed, leaving much weaker noise signals in the main backbone, thus improving feature quality. To name the broader impact, this reveals that LSCs are not a mere trick but closely related to the diffusion objective. The code is at https://github.com/Darkbblue/dit‑lsc.

PaperId: 1167, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13338.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zheming Fu, Wenbin Ning, Ruizhe He, Wei Shang, Xiaoxiao Ma, Lianrui Mu, Chang Liu, Lei Wang, Siming Fu
Title: VideoAWR: Reinforcing Video Flow Models with Decoupled-Timestep Advantage-Weighted Rectification
Abstract:
Regression‑based RL for flow models mandates sampling \emphwithout classifier‑free guidance (CFG) to align the rectification target with the reference marginal velocity. Extending Advantage‑Weighted Rectification (AWR), which dynamically scales this regression target based on reward, to video generation encounters a cold‑start pathology: unguided rollouts collapse into low‑fidelity regions where intra‑group reward gaps remain wide but no longer track perceptual quality, rendering the optimization target arbitrary. Conversely, utilizing guided rollouts to restore fidelity, while keeping the regression target tied to the guided sampling distribution, provably triggers a geometric guidance blow‑up under exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) updates. We propose VideoAWR, which resolves this tension by untying sampling from the optimization anchor. An EMA reference policy generates \emphguided rollouts to restore reward separability, while the trainable policy is rectified against the \emphunguided conditional anchor. We prove this decoupled objective is mathematically exact: the centered advantage cancels the anchor in expectation, filtering out the reward‑neutral guidance offset and retaining only the reward‑correlated covariance increment. Consequently, inference runs single‑branch and CFG‑free, yet inference‑time CFG preserves its original semantics. Furthermore, we introduce \emphDecoupled Timestep Rectification, supervising each rollout at an independently sampled timestep without bias to improve sample efficiency. Experiments on Wan2.1‑1.3B and 14B demonstrate stable optimization and superior visual and motion quality in \emphboth CFG‑free and CFG‑enabled regimes. Code is available at \pdfstartlink attr/Border [0 0 0] user/Subtype /Link /A << /S /URI /URI (https://github.com/Fuzm7/FlowAWR) >>% \textcolorpearDarkVideoAWR\pdfendlink.

PaperId: 1168, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13335.pdf   GitHub
Authors:R E Zera Marveen Lyngkhoi, Abhivansh Gupta, Vidushee Vats, Ram Mohan Rao Kadiyala, Vinay Kumar Sankarapu, Pratinav Seth
Title: AgentTune: A Unified Training Lifecycle for Tool-Using LLM Agents
Abstract:
Tool‑using agents increasingly require a common substrate for building, training, evaluating, distilling, and maintaining agentic systems, yet existing tooling typically addresses these stages in isolation. We present AgentTune, a source‑available Python library that provides a unified framework for developing and optimizing tool‑using agents. At its core, AgentTune introduces a two‑tier EventLog representation that preserves agent trajectories while supporting consistent projections for training, evaluation, and auditing. Building on this substrate, the library provides a shared agent runtime, tool‑calling reinforcement learning, agentic distillation, retrieval‑augmented generation, decision workflows, evaluation utilities, and a designed path toward self‑healing agents. These components are exposed through composable interfaces so that agent strategies, training methods, evaluation procedures, and recovery mechanisms can be combined without requiring separate representations or pipelines. We demonstrate the framework across agentic tasks including legal contract search and domain‑specific applications, illustrating its use for trajectory‑based optimization, tool‑use evaluation, and cross‑task agent development. AgentTune is released as a source‑available library at https://github.com/Lexsi‑Labs/AgentTune

PaperId: 1169, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13330.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mengdi Liu, Chenghao Jia, Hong Chang, Shiguang Shan
Title: Masked Diffusion Language Agents for Tool-Integrated Chemical Reasoning
Abstract:
Designing tool‑integrated reasoning agent systems for complex chemical tasks remains a fundamental challenge. Although recent chemical agents have demonstrated promising performance through the integration of external tools, they are still built on the autoregressive paradigm, which is inherently constrained by causal attention and left‑to‑right generation. As a result, they often struggle with bidirectional molecular understanding, global coordinated tool planning and multi‑source evidence integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ChemDiffAgent, the first masked diffusion language agent for tool‑integrated chemical reasoning. It reformulates chemical reasoning as iterative denoising over interleaved reasoning and tool‑use trajectories, enabling tool‑use decisions to be jointly determined under full‑trajectory context and thereby better aligning the agent's decision boundary with its knowledge boundary. We further analyze how this paradigm benefits agentic reasoning through harder infilling subproblems during training and flexible arbitrary‑order decoding during inference. Then we develop a two‑stage post‑training framework, comprising agentic supervised fine‑tuning and variance‑reduced preference optimization, to enhance tool‑use and reasoning capabilities. We also construct a comprehensive benchmark covering six chemistry tasks across both single‑turn and multi‑turn tool‑use scenarios. Under matched budgets and evaluation, ChemDiffAgent consistently outperforms autoregressive agents, achieving an overall improvement of approximately 20%. Notably, our 8B model achieves performance comparable to, in some cases surpassing, significantly larger frontier models, such as GPT 5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Code is available at https://github.com/bilemond/ChemDiffAgent.

PaperId: 1170, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13316.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Armando Fortes, Tianyi Wei, Chindanai Trakantannarong, Shangchen Zhou, Xingang Pan
Title: ThinkDrag: Semantic Drag-Based Image Editing with Visual Reasoning
Abstract:
Drag‑based image editing provides an intuitive interface for spatially controlled image manipulation by allowing users to specify handle and target points. Existing methods have made substantial progress through optimization‑based, one‑step, and feed‑forward formulations, but they often interpret drag instructions as geometric displacements. This limits their effectiveness when the desired edit depends on interpreting image content and inferring a plausible semantic transformation from sparse point constraints. We introduce ThinkDrag, a unified multimodal framework for drag‑based image editing with visual reasoning. ThinkDrag is trained to associate point constraints with meaningful object‑ and scene‑level transformations, and can optionally produce an explicit reasoning trace that interprets the intended edit before image generation. This reasoning trace improves interpretability, particularly for ambiguous drags. Drag Endpoint Markers, motivated by an analysis of cross‑image attention, provide an explicit correspondence signal that grounds each drag in image space. To support this framework, we construct a supervised dataset of semantic drag transformations paired with reasoning traces and introduce DragBench++, a benchmark targeting challenging drag‑based editing scenarios with reference edit solutions. Experiments show that ThinkDrag achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance, improving generation quality and plausibility while maintaining competitive point‑following precision.

PaperId: 1171, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13309.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Georgios Floros, Evangelos Sartinas, Orestis Vangelis, Maria Pateraki
Title: NovaSplat: Model-Free 6D Object Pose Estimation via 3D Gaussian Splatting Onboarding and Refinement
Abstract:
6D pose estimation of novel objects without CAD models remains an open challenge: model‑free methods must build the object representation from scratch during onboarding and have long trailed their model‑based counterparts. We present NovaSplat, a model‑free pipeline that closes this gap. From a short smartphone video captured at onboarding, we train a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model that serves both as a template source for detection and coarse pose estimation and as a differentiable backbone for pose refinement. Our refiner optimizes the object‑to‑camera pose with combined photometric and geometric losses under a continuous rotation parametrization free of gradient singularities. On a household‑object benchmark, NovaSplat surpasses all model‑based methods. On a challenging industrial benchmark with textureless and specular surfaces, it outperforms all model‑free competitors while substantially narrowing the gap to model‑based ones. We further introduce NovaSplat‑Lite, an inference variant that is 3.1× faster at negligible accuracy cost. Code will be made available at \hrefhttps://github.com/POSE‑Lab/novasplathttps://github.com/POSE‑Lab/novasplat.

PaperId: 1172, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13305.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jixin Tang, Ji Guo, Jun Zhao
Title: MORAD: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Objective Rewards for RNA Inverse Design
Abstract:
We introduce MORAD, an online reinforcement learning framework for backbone‑conditioned RNA diffusion models that trains a single shared policy across diverse target backbones. Structure‑conditioned RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences compatible with a target three‑dimensional backbone, yet existing reinforcement learning approaches either optimize a separate policy for each target backbone or rely on offline preference optimization, leaving online post‑training of a reusable backbone‑conditioned model largely unexplored. MORAD combines backbone‑conditioned group sampling, group‑relative reward normalization, and a forward‑process diffusion objective. Beyond existing RL rewards that primarily target tertiary structural quality, MORAD jointly optimizes six measurements spanning tertiary geometry, base pairing, ensemble behavior, and sequence composition. To aggregate these heterogeneous objectives despite differences in scale and optimization direction, MORAD maps each measurement to a bounded desirability score and combines them with a weighted geometric mean. Compared with a tertiary‑structure‑only reward, this multi‑objective formulation improves 10 of the 11 evaluation metrics that have a preferred direction. Applied to pretrained RIDE, MORAD improves GDT‑TS by 16.0% (from 0.3300 to 0.3827) and pairing MCC by 19.4% (from 0.6110 to 0.7295), while reducing normalized ensemble defect by 27.5% (from 0.3906 to 0.2830). On the test set, MORAD outperforms RiboDiffusion, gRNAde, and RDesign across tertiary structural accuracy, secondary‑structure pairing, and thermodynamic quality, establishing a new state of the art in structure‑conditioned RNA inverse design.

PaperId: 1173, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13301.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Yabiao Wang, Jiafu Wu, Yicheng Xu, Teng Hu, Shengzhe Zhou, Yanxiao Sun, Jiangning Zhang, Ying Tai, Yong Liu, Ming-Hsuan Yang
Title: PAGE: Parts-Aware Guidance for Co-Speech Gesture Portrait Video Generation
Abstract:
Co‑speech gesture video generation aims to synthesize realistic, audio‑driven portrait videos from a single reference image and a speech signal. Despite advances in visual quality, diffusion‑based approaches still suffer from degraded local details and imperfect audio‑visual alignment. We present PAGE (Parts‑Aware GuidancE), a general, backbone‑agnostic optimization framework for diffusion‑based generation that enhances local spatial fidelity and global audio‑visual consistency at both the training‑objective and denoising‑trajectory levels. During training, we propose Parts‑Specific Reweighting (PSR), which adaptively increases supervision in semantically important regions such as lips, eyes, and hands, improving visual fidelity in perceptually critical areas. During inference, we introduce Consistency Classifier Guidance (CCG), an audio‑conditioned latent classifier that identifies and corrects audio‑visual inconsistencies in the generated video. We further design Differential Guidance (DG), an efficient inference strategy that refines facial and body motion separately while avoiding cross‑region interference. To enable large‑scale evaluation, we construct the Chinese Announcer Speech (CAS) dataset, the first comprehensive Chinese benchmark for co‑speech gesture portrait video generation. Compared with the widely used PATS dataset, CAS includes substantially more identities, video clips, and scene diversity. Extensive experiments on both PATS and CAS demonstrate that PAGE achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance in perceptual quality, gesture diversity, and audio‑visual alignment. Project page: https://aigc‑explorer.github.io/PAGE/.

PaperId: 1174, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13268.pdf   GitHub GitHub
Authors:Ruotian Zhang, Yuhui Zhang, Junzhe Huang, Yu Xin, Hehe Fan, Xiaoxiao Sun
Title: ConClick: Element-Wise Contrastive Learning Improves GUI Grounding
Abstract:
GUI grounding, the task of locating the interface element specified by a user instruction, is a fundamental capability of GUI agents. However, existing grounding models remain error‑prone, often causing downstream task failures. We systematically evaluate 10 grounding models across five datasets and identify a major error pattern: most incorrect clicks hit non‑target interface elements rather than the background, with different models repeatedly selecting the same distractors. Motivated by these findings, we propose ConClick, a contrastive learning framework that teaches models to distinguish the target element from plausible distractors. We construct ConClick‑Data, a dataset containing 4,292 challenging target‑distractor pairs, and train the model using complementary listwise ranking and pairwise margin objectives. ConClick improves the grounding accuracy of Qwen3‑VL‑8B from 54.71% to 66.03% on ScreenSpot‑Pro, from 83.72% to 86.28% on MMBench‑GUI L2, and from 63.33% to 70.20% on OSWorld‑G, outperforming prior methods built on the same or similarly sized backbones. We further introduce ReClick, an inference‑time strategy that revisits promising regions and compares predictions across competing candidates, yielding an additional 2.96 percentage‑point improvement in average accuracy across the three benchmarks. Together, our analysis, dataset, and methods provide both empirical insights and practical tools for building more reliable GUI agents. Data and code are available at https://github.com/zhangruotian/ConClick.

PaperId: 1175, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13263.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiaoyang Ma, Chi Wang, Hong Sun
Title: SheafPrune: Sheaf-Guided Graph Propagation for Visual Token Pruning
Abstract:
Multimodal large language models process the complete visual token sequence, increasing prefill cost even when many tokens are irrelevant to the instruction. Token‑wise saliency captures limited inter‑token dependence; graph‑based selection instead depends on how relations govern importance propagation and ranking. We study support‑constrained propagation with node‑degree correction. Inspired by sheaf geometry, SheafPrune uses modality‑specific maps and a sparse text‑‑visual graph to transfer relevance, then propagates scores on a separate visual graph and corrects them for degree. It retains a hard top‑k subset once before the frozen language model. The selector has about 4.5M parameters and is trained end‑to‑end through the frozen LLaVA‑NeXT‑8B backbone using only the language‑modeling objective. Explicit retention‑ratio conditioning lets one checkpoint serve every budget. Across four backbones, ten benchmarks and seven pruning ratios, with all baselines re‑implemented under one protocol, SheafPrune achieves the best retention at 22 of 28 backbone‑‑budget settings, with monotonically growing margins in the moderate‑to‑aggressive regime. On LLaVA‑NeXT, retaining 10% of visual tokens yields a 5.15× net prefill speedup and an 84.0% end‑to‑end FLOPs reduction. Together with component ablations, these results support graph‑constrained importance propagation and degree correction as a design for visual token selection across the evaluated backbones and tokenization schemes, improving the trade‑off between accuracy retention and inference cost. code:https://github.com/Bob0817912/SheafPrune_ICLR_2027

PaperId: 1176, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13261.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zhenke Duan, Xin Li, Jiqun Pan, Dong Xiaofei, Hanwen Ning, Xinyuan Song
Title: Data-Adaptive Mahalanobis Metric Learning for Cross-Head Attention in Transformers
Abstract:
In this paper, we propose Data‑Adaptive Mahalanobis Cross‑Head Attention (DAMCHA), a simple and effective attention mechanism that generalizes Multi‑Head Attention (MHA) through the lens of metric learning. Standard MHA implicitly learns a static, head‑wise Euclidean similarity corresponding to the diagonal blocks of a unified cross‑head metric matrix, discarding all off‑diagonal interactions across heads. DAMCHA addresses this limitation via two key innovations. First, it learns the full cross‑head metric matrix, inducing a Mahalanobis‑like similarity that explicitly captures inter‑head interactions beyond the restricted block‑diagonal structure of MHA. Second, it parameterizes the metric matrix as an input‑dependent function, enabling the attention geometry to dynamically adapt to the intrinsic manifold structure of the data rather than remaining fixed after training. We further introduce principled regularization strategies, most notably stack‑wise parameter sharing, to ensure computational efficiency and stable optimization. DAMCHA serves as a drop‑in replacement for MHA and its variants in various Transformer architectures, delivering superior expressive power and learning performance with comparable or reduced computational overhead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DAMCHA‑based Transformers consistently outperform competing baselines across a range of benchmark tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/erwinmsmith/DAMCHA.

PaperId: 1177, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13249.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Xiufeng Liu, Ruyu Liu, Yusen Liu, Huan Huo, Per Sieverts Nielsen
Title: CALQA: Conformal Screening of Forecast-Ensemble Configurations from One Mergeable State
Abstract:
AutoML systems fit ensemble weights over model libraries; a search can score, per category, market or time pane, thousands of weightings of the quantile‑averaged (Vincentized) ensemble for the narrowest conformally calibrated interval; exact calibration scores a group's rows per candidate. We present CALQA, a fixed‑size integer aggregate per group and pane that stores histograms of normalised block scores at a net of weight vectors. One GROUP BY builds it; it merges by addition, retracts deletions by subtraction and scores any candidate without reading a row. We prove that its score never falls below the exact split‑conformal shift and exceeds it by at most the net distance plus a grid gap; that coverage carries over to each fixed weight vector and, for i.i.d. blocks and up to a union‑bound slack, to a searched weight vector deployed with the state's shift; and how small any such state can be. The state is thus a screen: it ranks all candidates, and exact recomputation re‑checks the top 100. On five public panels (604 groups, 10,000 candidates each) this two‑stage plan matches exact search on held‑out blocks (99.95% of its Winkler score), 1.3‑59 times faster. On two real panels of about 10^8 rows (smart meters, retail sales) it is 44‑54 times faster at 99.98‑100.01% of that score and beats sample screens with the same re‑check in regret at less total time. Picks deployed with their exact shift need a held‑out coverage check. The state does not pay off for small or greedy searches, off‑net weights at ample memory or full twelve‑member support.

PaperId: 1178, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13220.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chenjie Zhao, Jiangtian Nie, Jiawen Kang, Yuxu Lu, Ryan Wen Liu
Title: Multi-Modal Graph Neural Network-Inspired Vessel Identification and Tracking for UAV-Based Maritime Surveillance
Abstract:
The unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)‑based maritime surveillance is becoming an important part of maritime Internet of Things (IoT) and intelligent transportation systems. It provides a flexible and cost‑effective way to large‑scale maritime traffic monitoring. However, achieving robust situational awareness remains challenging in practical maritime environments. The main challenges arise from heterogeneous sensing modalities, adverse imaging conditions, and spatial misalignment caused by UAV motion. To address these problems, this paper proposes an airborne multi‑modal graph learning‑driven framework, termed AMGT, for vessel identification and tracking in UAV‑assisted maritime IoT. Specifically, visible and infrared images are first aligned and fused through a multi‑parameter perspective transformation model. This improves visual perception under low visibility and complex illumination conditions. Automatic identification system (AIS) messages are then temporally synchronized using interpolation and linear prediction. To detect small and oriented vessels, we develop a mixed‑modality MAir‑YOLOv8‑OBB detector, followed by the MAir‑SORT algorithm for stable vessel tracking. We further design a graph learning‑driven association network to model temporal dynamics and spatial dependencies among vessels and between vessels and UAVs. A motion‑aware coordinate unification (MCU) strategy is also introduced to reduce nonlinear misalignment caused by UAV motion. Experiments on the MAP‑M2UAV50 dataset show that AMGT achieves high accuracy and efficiency. The results demonstrate its potential for UAV‑assisted maritime IoT applications, including vessel monitoring, traffic situational awareness, and intelligent maritime transportation services. The dataset and code will be available at https://github.com/MAPGroup/AMGT.

PaperId: 1179, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13219.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Haocheng Wu, Xiangjie Sui, Xin Sun
Title: Complexity-Calibrated Reconstruction Discrepancy for No-Reference Point Cloud Quality Assessment
Abstract:
The discrepancy induced by surface reconstruction in a distorted point cloud is jointly influenced by its intrinsic structural complexity and signal degradation. This observation motivates a referencefree point cloud quality assessment (PCQA) strategy that estimates and compensates for the complexity‑induced component. We implement this strategy through successive reconstruction. Specifically, reconstructing the distorted point cloud produces an input‑toreconstruction discrepancy that combines the effects of signal degradation and content complexity. Reapplying the reconstruction operator with stronger smoothing produces a discrepancy between successive reconstructions, which serves as a proxy for the complexityinduced component. This proxy is then used to calibrate the inputto‑reconstruction discrepancy. We apply the same strategy to 3D geometry patches and their aligned 2D regions, enabling local comparison of the resulting discrepancies. The calibrated geometric and projected‑view discrepancies are then fused into a final degradation score. For both branches, the discrepancies are measured using frozen pretrained perceptual representations. Our method does not require PCQA‑specific training or fine‑tuning. Experiments on three public databases show that the proposed method consistently outperforms most generic baselines and achieves performance comparable to several full‑reference metrics.The code is available at https://github.com/HC‑W‑whc/CCRD‑NR‑PCQA.git.

PaperId: 1180, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13207.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziyu Luo, Wei Li, Haoping Huang, Kecheng Liu, Min Gao
Title: SharP: Soft and Hard Prompt-Guided Augmentation with LLM for Low Resource Fake News Detection
Abstract:
Fake news detection under low resource conditions is challenged by the scarcity of labeled data and the difficulty of capturing subtle deceptive patterns. In this work, we focus on low resource fake news detection, where only a small labeled set is available for training, while evaluation is performed under a fixed and unchanged test protocol. This setting is motivated by costly, ambiguous fact‑checking and emerging topics and domains that are poorly covered by existing benchmarks. Existing data augmentation methods, such as synonym substitution, generative adversarial networks, and large language model (LLM)‑based generation, often produce fluent but overly generic content, lacking the task‑specific relevance needed for accurate detection. To address this, we propose SharP, a boundary‑aware text generation framework guided by soft and hard prompts, which leverages LLMs as tools adapted to produce task‑specific synthetic samples. SharP employs a dual prompt mechanism: hard prompts provide structured guidance and factual constraints, while soft prompts introduce learned semantic patterns from the data. These two types of prompts are combined to guide the generation process, enabling the model to produce samples that closely align with the characteristics of news. To further enhance detection performance, we incorporate a boundary‑aware strategy that steers generation toward areas where the classifier is less confident, helping to clarify subtle distinctions between real and fake content. In addition, we adopt a dual objective optimization that balances semantic alignment with the source data and classifier feedback. This encourages the generation of samples that are both domain‑consistent and helpful for refining decision boundaries, ultimately improving model robustness and generalization in low resource fake news detection.

PaperId: 1181, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13197.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zekang Wang, Zhe He, Gaojie Jin
Title: Does Learning Recurrent Networks Matter in Partially Observable RL?
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) under partial observability typically re‑ lies on recurrent networks to encode temporal information, with the recurrent module trained jointly with the policy or value function. This raises a natural question: is learning the recurrent network actually necessary? In this paper, we investigate whether a frozen recurrent network can provide sufficient memory for solving par‑ tially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). Motivated by the theoretical foundations of Reservoir Computing (RC) and Generalized Reservoir Computing (GRC), we study a simple archi‑ tecture that combines a fixed recurrent network with a trainable nonlinear output module. We evaluate this approach across tasks with varying memory demands, observation modalities, and action spaces. Surprisingly, frozen recurrent networks support recall over hundreds of steps and achieve competitive control performance across diverse POMDPs, while using less than half the number of trainable parameters required by their fully trainable counterparts. These results suggest that learning the recurrent memory module is not always necessary for solving POMDPs. Frozen recurrent networks therefore provide a simple, parameter‑efficient, and sur‑ prisingly strong baseline for partially observable RL. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Aphlios/FRN‑POMDP

PaperId: 1182, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13186.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Alessandro Licciardi
Title: WaSA: Wavelet Scattering Autoencoders for Unsupervised Offline Detection of Malicious Clients in Federated Learning
Abstract:
Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without exposing raw data, yet remains vulnerable to malicious clients injecting poisoned datasets. Existing defenses are typically reactive (operating during training) or supervised (requiring prior knowledge of attack types) ‑ assumptions that rarely hold in open‑ended IoT deployments. We propose WaSA, a fully unsupervised, offline framework for malicious client detection. Before training, each client transmits a single, privacy‑preserving spectral summary of its data to the server. A denoising autoencoder, trained solely on clean auxiliary data, scores clients based on their deviation from the learned benign manifold, identifying corruptions regardless of the attack type. WaSA requires no attack labels, generalizes to unseen anomalies, and introduces a Boltzmann sampling strategy for client selection that smoothly interpolates between hard exclusion and standard aggregation. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR‑10, and CIFAR‑100 under diverse attack scenarios (up to 90 % malicious clients) demonstrate consistent improvements over supervised baselines and robust aggregation methods, with negligible communication overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/alelicciardi99/wavelet_autoencoders_malicious.

PaperId: 1183, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13172.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Boyuan Xiao, Pu Wang, Ji Feng, Yao-Xiang Ding
Title: RoleWorld: Knowledge Transfer in World Modeling with Functional Role Abstractions
Abstract:
World models enable large language model (LLM) agents to anticipate action effects and make informed decisions. For generalization, it is desirable for such world models to transfer efficiently to new environments with similar interaction structure and underlying dynamics. Recent approaches encode world dynamics as symbolic rules or executable programs, whose compositional structure in principle affords transfer, but still organize such knowledge around environment‑specific objects. To address this limitation, we introduce RoleWorld, a symbolic world modeling approach which uses reusable prototypes and environment‑specific parameter values as functional role abstractions to represent how objects behave in interactions. From interaction trajectories, a teacher LLM extracts role prototypes and executable transition rules defined over role instances, together with a skill that guides the actor LLM to use role information in decision making. In a target world, without the teacher, the actor uses this skill together with its current role assignments and parameter estimates, and actively tests a role instance hypothesis through interaction when its uncertainty affects the current decision. Feedback from each action refines role assignments and estimates parameter values online, with no LLM parameter updates and the transition rules held fixed. Experiments on MARS benchmark show that RoleWorld enables robust generalization across environments with significantly altered object behavior, suggesting that functional role abstractions can serve as an effective component for knowledge transfer in world modeling. Project Page: https://future‑item.github.io/RoleWorld.

PaperId: 1184, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13166.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shun Zou, Ziyu Ma, Yi Zou, Yong Wang, Lin Chen, Zehui Chen, Guanhua Chen, Xiangxiang Chu, Feng Zhao
Title: Scaling Agentic Data for Long-Horizon Terminal Intelligence
Abstract:
Terminal agents are moving beyond local operations toward completing real‑world professional tasks. Short trajectories can demonstrate commands and tool calls, but they do not fully show how agents accumulate evidence through exploration, use it to inform judgments, continually adjust strategies based on feedback, and turn intermediate results into final deliverables. High‑quality long‑horizon trajectories capture these agentic behavioral patterns and their connections within a single problem‑solving process, providing richer experience for sustained autonomous work. However, environment synthesis may complete or simplify the key work underlying these patterns in advance and thus remove the need for exploration, implementation, and verification that the agent was meant to perform. To address this, we introduce TerminalHorizon, a fully automated data synthesis engine for long‑horizon terminal agents. Starting from real‑world professional work, it uses independent execution to identify key work omitted during construction and uses the resulting evidence to guide environment reconstruction. To extend these patterns across stages, it progressively expands tasks under the same goal, introducing new requirements that build on prior results and call for further exploration and improvement. Using this engine, we construct 1.5K task environments and perform supervised fine‑tuning of Qwen3.5‑27B on the resulting dataset to obtain TerminalHorizon‑27B. We achieve substantial performance gains on all 12 benchmarks spanning coding‑agent tasks, agentic tasks in real‑world production settings, and general reasoning. Multiple RSI case studies, each with a 12‑hour research budget, further demonstrate the model's ability to continue experimenting beyond an initial solution, improve its methods based on feedback, and retain effective improvements in its final deliverables.

PaperId: 1185, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13164.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Feng Jiang, Shu Chen, Yuanfei Wang, Yuan Li, Zhenhao Shen, Jiaqi Liang, Yang Chen, Lei Wei, Chen Xie, Ruihai Wu
Title: Grounded-Dreamer: Robot Learning from World Model Synthetic Data with Physical Grounding
Abstract:
Scaling robot manipulation policies requires large amounts of diverse, action‑labeled data, yet collecting such data in the real world remains expensive and difficult to scale. Existing methods either depend on human teleoperation, rely on simulation with limited visual realism, or use human videos that lack embodiment‑specific annotations. In this paper, we introduce Grounded‑Dreamer, a framework for synthesizing physically grounded robot manipulation data with video world models while avoiding human teleoperation demonstrations. Grounded‑Dreamer combines the visual realism of generative video models with simulator physics engines. Starting from a small set of real images depicting robot task initial states, our method automatically reconstructs task‑relevant objects and camera geometry, aligns them in simulation, and collects physically valid trajectories. These trajectories are used to post‑train both a video world model and an inverse dynamics model, enabling the generation of visually realistic robot manipulation videos and corresponding robot actions from real images. To filter physically implausible rollouts, Grounded‑Dreamer replays generated trajectories in the reconstructed simulation and retains only those that successfully complete the tasks. The real‑world robot policies are trained solely on the grounded synthetic trajectories without any human demonstrations. Empirical results in real‑world tasks demonstrate that Grounded‑Dreamer can synthesize physically grounded data and substantially facilitate policy learning without requiring human teleoperation effort.

PaperId: 1186, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13128.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Wenlin Lin, Fanzhe Wei
Title: Locate, Judge, Read: Role-Specialized Tool Agents over a Knowledge-Point Index for Open-Domain Multimodal Document QA
Abstract:
Question answering over large heterogeneous document collections requires first finding the right passages and then reading them, yet current retrieval‑augmented agents give one model both kinds of tools and let it schedule itself. We present KnowForge, a pipeline separated by job: a hybrid‑retrieval knowledge‑point index; a Locator agent that can only search; a code‑scheduled bridge judge that forces the missing second hop; a typed, size‑bounded evidence pool that merges every search's ranking; a Deep Reader agent that can only read text, images and tables; and a synthesizer with a format checker. With a self‑hosted Qwen3.6‑35B‑A3B (3B active), KnowForge reaches F1 47.5 on the full open‑domain M3DocVQA (2,441 questions, 3,368 PDFs), +11.0 over the published M3DocRAG system and +7.1 over one‑shot retrieve‑and‑answer on the same index and model, and 53.5 with DeepSeek‑V4‑Flash. On MultiHop‑RAG it reaches 73.5 accuracy, above the strongest published RAG and GraphRAG results (71.2); on the single‑document MMLongBench‑Doc it lifts the same model from 34.8 to 47.0, level with GPT‑4o reading page images (46.3). Per‑job ablations on the full benchmarks attribute the gain: the Deep Reader is worth 3.8, 9.8 and 0 points on the three corpora, tracking how visual each is; merging both agents into one with all tools and twice the rounds loses 1.9 F1 because it keeps searching instead of reading; a round‑budget sweep shows a step at four Locator rounds and a plateau beyond; query latency scales with model calls rather than corpus size. We serve the three indexed benchmarks as read‑only knowledge bases (free registration) and release all prompts and the runner code: https://github.com/metask‑ai/knowforge‑bench

PaperId: 1187, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13121.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Md. Nesarul Hoque, Rudra Pratap Deb Nath, Umme Salma, Shima Chakraborty, Md. Hanif Seddiqui
Title: BenCoDiC: A Large-Scale Contextual Cyberbullying Corpus for Bengali Political News Discourse FULL VERSION
Abstract:
Cyberbullying is a growing concern in online communities, yet existing Bengali corpora remain limited in contextual information, annotation transparency, scale, accessibility, and support for multidimensional analysis, thereby hindering robust detection and comprehensive study of harasser behaviors and networks. To address these gaps, we introduce the Bengali Contextual and Diverse Cyberbullying (BenCoDiC) corpus, a publicly available contextual cyberbullying resource for Bengali political news discourse comprising 50,250 textual instances collected from 100 YouTube videos and their associated discussions. The corpus preserves caption‑‑comment‑‑reply relationships and is organized through a nine‑dimensional star schema covering users, videos, textual content, context, time, engagement, political parties, target identities, and language categories. Five AI chatbots were initially evaluated for annotation but did not meet the predefined reliability criterion. Consequently, a two‑tier human annotation process with expert verification was adopted, achieving Fleiss' κ=0.86 and Krippendorff's α=0.86. Statistical analyses characterize the corpus, while transformer‑based experiments show that incorporating conversational context yields modest but consistent improvements over isolated‑text classification. BenCoDiC supports context‑aware cyberbullying detection and perpetrator‑oriented behavioral and network analysis. The corpus is available at https://github.com/bencodic/BenCoDiC‑Corpus.

PaperId: 1188, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13118.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Fernando Montes-Gonzalez
Title: The value of information and the emergence of communication in evolved e-puck robots
Abstract:
We study when communication emerges between autonomous agents and what role an innate action selection architecture plays. Two e‑puck robots, reconstructed in PyBullet from their Webots model and validated against it, must find a feeding zone that can only be detected when a robot passes over it. Each robot can emit a one‑bit signal whose direction is detected by the receiver. Control is provided by a GRU recurrent network with a residual path, either operating alone or as a channel within an Embedded Action Selection Architecture (EASA). Fitness measures only the time the robots spend over the food. When the robots receive a compass pointing to the food, use of the signal disappears completely. Without a compass, in a small arena, three independent runs achieved similar performance using different strategies: a referential signal, a permanent beacon, or no use of the signal. As the arena expands, the strategy based on a referential signal generalizes best. In contrast, evolving directly in the large arena does not increase the frequency of communication, but it does separate the strategies, and the referential signal clearly outperforms solitary searching. Within EASA, innate reflexes constrain the network and reduce performance. As its priorities evolve, evolution consistently weakens those reflexes. The results suggest that communication emerges in proportion to the value of the information it transmits, and that an innate scaffolding designed for isolated agents can be an impediment in a social task.

PaperId: 1189, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13117.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Zipei Ma, Junzhe Jiang, Jiahui Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Chun Gu, Bozhou Zhang, Jiankang Deng, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
Title: Forward Dynamics Models
Abstract:
Vision‑language‑action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) have advanced robotic policy learning by building on pretrained vision‑language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs), respectively. Yet VLAs learn without explicit supervision from future world states, while WAMs that condition actions on predicted futures incur extra inference cost and let visual prediction errors propagate into actions. We present Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models that couples action and future world‑state prediction through an action‑to‑future paradigm. Future prediction is conditioned on action features, never the reverse: end‑to‑end training lets ground‑truth future states supervise the policy through these features, while prediction errors cannot propagate into actions. At inference, FDM skips future generation entirely, avoiding its computational cost. The paradigm is backbone‑agnostic, and we instantiate it with both VLM and VGM backbones. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate the effectiveness of FDM across both backbone families, achieving a state‑of‑the‑art 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13% over VLA and WAM methods on real‑world tasks.

PaperId: 1190, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13116.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yuzhen Wang, Chunxiao Li, Baichen Le, Lewen Yan, Jie Zhang, Yucheng T. Yang, Xing-Ming Zhao, Lijun Li, Jing Shao
Title: DRYLAB-Bench: Benchmarking the Biosecurity Risk of Agentic LLM Mutation Design
Abstract:
As large language models (LLMs) acquire advanced biological design capabilities, they offer substantial research benefits but simultaneously introduce severe dual‑use risks, such as engineering enhanced pathogens or drug‑resistant bacteria. While biosecurity frameworks recognize these threats, the actual risk of LLMs executing dangerous biological modifications remains unquantified, particularly when augmented with specialized biological design tools (BDTs). Existing evaluations primarily assess hazardous knowledge possession rather than practical application, overlook risk amplification from BDTs, and rely on unreliable, expensive, or hazardous validation methods. To address these gaps, we introduce DRYLAB‑Bench (Design Risk Yielded by LLM Agent in Biodesign), the first comprehensive benchmark evaluating the high‑risk biological mutation design capabilities of LLM agents. Moving beyond basic question‑answering, DRYLAB‑Bench tasks agents with 30 genuinely hazardous mutation‑design scenarios distilled from biosecurity guidelines. It evaluates models in a multi‑round, tool‑augmented environment where LLMs orchestrate BDTs to iteratively refine candidates. Crucially, it scores designs directly against 187,695 empirical wet‑lab measurements from ProteinGym and ViroGym using our proposed Biosecurity Risk Score (BRS), quantifying risk‑associated effects while enabling scalable and safe ground‑truth verification. Evaluations of 15 frontier models reveal substantial baseline threats: without tools, 67.6% of one‑shot designs exceed the average measured variant, and 21.4% reach the highest‑risk decile. Equipping models with BDTs significantly amplifies this risk, raising the pooled risk by \(ΔBRS=+0.116\) and the top‑decile share to 23.5%. Code: https://github.com/drylab‑bio/DRYLAB‑Bench

PaperId: 1191, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13112.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Mohammad Khalooei, Mohammad Sabokrou
Title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination
Abstract:
Large audio‑language models (LALMs) frequently exhibit object hallucination, affirming absent sounds. The dominant mitigation, Audio‑Aware Decoding (AAD), contrasts logits under real audio against an all‑zero "blank" waveform, flagged by prior review as out‑of‑distribution. We introduce a black‑box causal test that isolates the claimed evidence itself: localize a claim's evidence region via CLAP similarity, remove it by spectral gating, and compare against a random‑window control across a 2x2x2 grid on three LALMs. On Qwen2‑Audio‑7B, localized ablation's raw AUROC trails blank's (0.613 vs. 0.721); this is a duration confound, not a localization failure, since blank removes the entire clip versus the grid's 2‑4 s. Holding duration fixed, localization beats random removal at every cell on both models. Raw detection value remains model‑dependent, especially on Audio Flamingo 3. The same evidence corrects decoding: contrastive decoding combining blank and language‑prior contrasts, gated and ensembled, raises Qwen2‑Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, beating AAD alone. A unified causal‑grounding profile does not transfer between models, indicating different grounding regimes. The source code and a detailed report of our findings, including identified limitations, are available at https://github.com/khalooei/causa.

PaperId: 1192, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13060.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Taiga Ikeda, Daisuke Miyashita, Jun Deguchi
Title: KV-Repurpose: A Testbed for Evaluating Non-Prefix KV-Cache Reuse
Abstract:
KV‑cache reuse in large language model serving is commonly limited to exact prompt prefixes, preventing reuse when the same retrieved document appears after different system prompts, conversation histories, or dynamic metadata. We present KV‑Repurpose, an open‑source, vLLM‑based system for developing and evaluating segment‑wise KV‑cache reuse beyond exact prefixes. The system combines cache‑aware segment scheduling, prompt construction, capacity management, workload generation, and runtime monitoring. Experiments on long‑context benchmarks show that naive segment reuse largely preserves output quality for single‑document question answering and summarization, while exposing clear limitations in cross‑document reasoning. Under a Zipfian RAG‑style workload in which 20% of requests share a fixed prefix, KV‑Repurpose achieves a substantially higher token‑level cache hit rate than prefix caching at the same 30 GB cache capacity, 63.9% versus 3.3%, resulting in lower TTFT. Even with 1 TB of cache capacity, prefix caching reaches only a 17.9% hit rate in this workload. Source code is available under the Apache‑2.0 license at https://github.com/taiga333/eval‑kv‑repurpose.

PaperId: 1193, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13059.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Chandravardhan Singh Raghaw, Shahid Shafi Dar, Arnav Nishith Sharma, Shrey Modi, Nagendra Kumar
Title: CliQ-RRG: Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation
Abstract:
Radiology reports are essential for diagnostic reasoning and patient care, yet their manual preparation is time‑consuming and cognitively demanding. Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) offers a scalable alternative, but existing models often produce lengthy, unstructured narratives that overlook diagnostic cues and multi‑view information. We present Clinical‑Knowledge Guided Disease‑aware Visual‑Textual Alignment for QA‑Style Radiology Report Generation (CliQ‑RRG), a unified two‑stage framework for interpretable and clinically grounded reporting. In Stage 1, CliQ‑RRG employs a Disease‑aware Visual‑Textual Alignment module that aligns image and text representations using predicted disease embeddings, reinforced by a Prior‑Guided Attention Module (PrAM) to capture multi‑view dependencies across current and prior scans. In Stage 2, GraphRAG‑guided retrieval augments intermediate textual representations with graph‑grounded clinical evidence, and a large language model restructures them into concise, interpretable question‑answer (QA) pairs with diagnostic summaries. Experiments on two public chest X‑ray benchmarks demonstrate that CliQ‑RRG consistently outperforms prior methods across both lexical and clinical metrics, generating accurate and clinically coherent QA‑style radiology reports. Code is available at: https://github.com/chandravardhan‑singh‑raghaw/CliQ‑RRG.

PaperId: 1194, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13058.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Ziang Ye, Wentao Shi, Lei Chen, Zhengzhou Cai, Yu Wang, Zhiyuan Yao, Zihan Wang, Xierui Song, Fuli Feng, Yixin Cao
Title: Travel Back To Move Forward: Retrospective Exploration and Evolving for Long Horizon Agents
Abstract:
Large language model agents increasingly operate in long‑horizon environments where early mistakes can trigger cascading failures and trap agents in dead‑end trajectories. Agents must therefore be able to proactively recover from such states and turn their exploratory experience into guidance for subsequent decisions. We introduce ReTRAIL, a framework that enables agents to rewind the environment to earlier states while preserving valid progress and carrying forward knowledge learned from abandoned exploration. The environment state moves backward while the agent's knowledge continues to move forward. ReTRAIL trains a shared policy with two complementary signals: State‑Anchored GRPO compares alternative continuations from revisited states to improve execution, while a branch‑advancement reward guides reflection through the progress of subsequent exploration. Experiments across four interactive benchmark MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show that simply adding a rewind primitive provides limited benefit and can even degrade performance. In contrast, ReTRAIL enables agents to rewind from unproductive states and use insights from abandoned branches to guide subsequent exploration. These results demonstrate the value of coupling environment rewinding with experience reuse within an ongoing task for long‑horizon task solving. The code is available at https://github.com/whi497/ReTRAIL.

PaperId: 1195, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13053.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Shiao Wang, Xiao Wang, Yuhe Ding, Jiarui Xu, Zikang Yan, Bo Jiang, Yonghong Tian, Jin Tang
Title: UniMergeTrack: Hierarchical Model Merging for General RGB-X Visual Object Tracking
Abstract:
RGB‑X tracking leverages complementary modalities, such as thermal infrared, event, or depth, to improve robustness under challenging conditions. Existing general‑purpose RGB‑X trackers typically follow two paradigms: independent task‑specific training and joint training across modality combinations. However, the former suffers from knowledge isolation and model redundancy, while the latter introduces optimization interference across heterogeneous tasks. In this work, we present UniMergeTrack, a new model merging paradigm that preserves task‑specific optimization while enabling effective cross‑task knowledge integration. UniMergeTrack first trains modality‑specific trackers independently and then performs hierarchical model merging. Specifically, transferable backbones are merged across RGB‑X tasks via high‑pass‑filtered merging, and complemented by lightweight task‑specific experts that preserve modality‑specific cues. Tracking heads are merged within each task using optimal transport‑guided channel alignment to mitigate hidden channel mismatch. A subsequent distribution alignment fine‑tuning stage further improves compatibility between the unified backbone and task‑specific heads. Extensive experiments on the LasHeR, RGBT234, VisEvent, VOT‑RGBD22, COESOT, and CDTB benchmarks demonstrate that UniMergeTrack achieves state‑of‑the‑art or competitive performance across RGB‑Thermal, RGB‑Event, and RGB‑Depth tracking tasks, while exhibiting strong generalization to unseen datasets. The source code will be released upon acceptance. The source code of this paper will be released on https://github.com/Event‑AHU/OpenEvTracking.

PaperId: 1196, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13050.pdf   GitHub
Authors:James Rose, Jingwen Liang, Wenchao Ma, Oren Jacob, Haomiao Jiang
Title: NOFACE3D: NOise-scheduled Focused Anchoring and Controlled Enhancement for 3D Generation
Abstract:
Recent image‑to‑3D models generate complete, high‑quality assets from a single image, with global shape and appearance that are already convincing; what remains is the fine scale, where small, thin, elongated, or detail‑rich regions are reconstructed softly and under‑resolved. This gap can arise in generators with fixed‑resolution spatial grids: the same spatial sampling density is used for a large, smooth, low‑curvature surface and for a thin, high‑curvature structure that carries most of the perceived detail. To this end, we introduce NOFACE3D, a training‑free framework that refines these detail‑critical regions while preserving the rest of the asset. Given a generated mesh, its input image, and a refinement box, NOFACE3D extracts the selected submesh, scales it up to fill the generator's input volume, and re‑encodes it into the full‑resolution latent grid. Conditioned on the image crop, it refines the region through flow‑based sampling with a spatially varying noise schedule that anchors boundary latents. The refined region is then integrated back into the original asset, preserving the surrounding geometry and appearance. We implement NOFACE3D on TRELLIS.2 and its sparse voxel representation; all of it operates purely at inference time on the frozen pretrained generator. We evaluate NOFACE3D on PAniC‑3D, TexVerse and BigDetail, a new benchmark of 339 assets with annotated detail‑critical regions. On all three, it generates sharper geometry and finer texture detail than the baselines. Project page: https://idkcouscous.github.io/NoFACE3D/

PaperId: 1197, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13035.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Yongxin Zheng, Hao Wu, Fang Li, Hu Fu, Peiran Yin, Xudong Wang, Haozhe Hu, Xinghao Chen, Yunpu Ma, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
Title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
Abstract:
Multi‑view representations enable pretrained image and video vision‑language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two‑stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross‑view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query‑conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group‑wise skipping. Low‑relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression‑aware post‑training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post‑trained models' performance on LLaVA‑OneVision‑7B and Video‑3D LLM‑7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by 6.8× and 6.1×. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance‑efficiency trade‑off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT‑NLP/GeoGR.

PaperId: 1198, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13027.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Minh Sao Khue Luu, Bair N. Tuchinov
Title: Dataset-Specific Encoding of Image Content Underlies Cross-Dataset Failure in Brain MRI Foundation Models
Abstract:
Frozen features of brain MRI foundation models lose accuracy on new datasets, a failure usually blamed on the features encoding where each scan came from. We show that the failure lies elsewhere. Across 17 public datasets and eight frozen representations, every representation recognizes the MRI sequence within each dataset, yet most fail on an unseen one. The cause is neither dataset encoding nor a shift of each dataset: the content itself is encoded along different directions in each dataset. This explains which datasets fail, for the sequence and for sex, and why removing the dataset signal with INLP, LEACE, CORAL or adversarial training never improves sequence transfer. Only the broadly pretrained 3DINO and SAM‑Med3D encode the sequence consistently enough to transfer; the brain‑specific BrainIAC and BrainFM do no better than an untrained network. Code is available at https://github.com/BrainFM/brainfm‑profiler/tree/main/representation_utility.

PaperId: 1199, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13024.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Kai Liu, Jiangran Lyu, Tingyu Deng, Yixin Zheng, Jingtian Wan, Wenbo Cui, Mi Yan, Yizhou Zhou, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
Title: What Visual Representations Do World Action Models Need?
Abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) inherit powerful priors from pretrained video generation models, but their variational autoencoder (VAE) representations are optimized for visual reconstruction rather than manipulation. External visual representations can improve manipulation, but existing methods couple representation choices with different integration mechanisms, obscuring their individual effects. We systematically compare visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations under controlled settings. Our study yields three main findings. First, strong general‑purpose visual representations provide broader robustness gains and can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities. Second, channel‑wise joint prediction achieves the highest average success rate; further analyses suggest that future‑feature prediction and the action expert's effective use of added visual information contribute to its gains. Third, additional sources should be selected for the task‑relevant information they contribute beyond existing representations, as the same source can help one combination but harm another. However, even the best evaluated composition provides a smaller additional gain than the initial improvement from adding a strong general‑purpose representation to the VAE‑only baseline. We instantiate the resulting Representation Recipe as R^2‑WAM. It achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop with an 84.7% success rate and reaches 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over the VAE‑only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Taken together, these findings suggest that future work should prioritize stronger general‑purpose visual representations and more effective mechanisms for integrating them into WAMs, with feature composition serving as a supplementary route to improvement.

PaperId: 1200, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13021.pdf   GitHub
Authors:Jie Huang, Yanan Chen, Ruixun Liu, Kaichen He, Xinyi He, Rui Huang, Zilong Zheng, Zhenliang Zhang, Yiwu Zhong
Title: EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents
Abstract:
Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non‑embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self‑evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors.
